en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Great Division of the Dīgha Nikāya.
1. Commentary on the Mahāpadāna Sutta:
Discourse Concerning Former Abodes 1.
"Thus have I heard... at Kareri’s Hut" refers to the Mahāpadāna Sutta. Herein, this is the commentary on the words not previously explained.
"By the Kareri hut": *Karerī* is the name of the *varuṇa* tree;

a pavilion made of *karerī* wood stands at the door of that hut, and for that reason it is called the "Kareri Hut," just as it is called the "Kosamba Hut" because of its standing at the door of a *kosamba* tree.
It is said that within the Jeta Grove there were the Kareri Hut, the Kosamba Hut, the Perfume Chamber (*gandhakuṭī*), and the Salaḷāgāra.
There were four great dwellings, each completed through the relinquishment of one hundred thousand pieces of gold.
Among them, the Salaḷāgāra was built by King Pasenadi, while the remaining three were built by Anāthapiṇḍika.
Thus, the Blessed One was dwelling in the Kareri hut—which was like a celestial mansion and constructed upon pillars by the householder Anāthapiṇḍika.

"After the meal" (*pacchābhatta*) means that for those who practice eating at a single sitting (*ekāsanika*) or those who practice taking food only after others have finished (*khalupacchābhattika*), it is "after the meal" even if they have eaten early in the morning or during the middle of the day.
However, in this context, "after the meal" is intended to mean after the regular midday meal.

"Of those who have returned from alms-round" (*piṇḍapātapaṭikkantānaṃ*) means of those who have returned from the alms-round; the meaning is: of those who have risen after completing the business of eating.
"In the Kareri-maṇḍala-māḷa" refers to the sitting hall built not far from that very Kareri pavilion.

It is said that this Kareri pavilion was situated between the Perfumed Chamber (gandhakuṭī) and the hall; therefore, the Perfumed Chamber, the Kareri hut, and the hall were all called "the Kareri-maṇḍala-māḷa. "Connected with former dwellings" means: "one birth... [and so forth].
"Even two births"—thus it is said, having been set forth in connection with "past lives," which is defined as the continuity of the aggregates (khandhas) in former existences.
"Dhammī" means connected with the Dhamma. "Udapādi" means:
"Oh, how wonderful is the knowledge of past lives of the One Possessed of Ten Powers! Who indeed can recollect past lives?"
"Who do not recollect? The followers of other sects (titthiyā) do not recollect; but disciples, paccekabuddhas, and buddhas do recollect.
Which followers of other sects recollect? Those who maintain that action is supreme recollect only forty eons, and no further than that.
Disciples recollect one hundred thousand eons. The two chief disciples recollect an incalculable [eons] and...
And for one hundred thousand eons. Paccekabuddhas [remember] two incalculable eons and one hundred thousand eons.
But for Buddhas there is no such limit; they recollect as much as they desire.
The followers of other sects recollect according to the sequence of the aggregates (*khandha*), and they are unable to do so without that sequence. [They recollect] in sequence...
Even while recollecting, they do not perceive the occurrence of the aggregates once they have reached the state of non-percipient existence;
they are like blind men fallen into a net or like the lame who have fallen into a well. Remaining there, they adopt the view: "Only this much exists; beyond this, there is nothing.
Thus, the recollection of past lives among the sectarians is like the groping with the tip of a staff by those who are blind.

It is like this: just as blind people can walk only when holding onto the end of a staff, but sit down right there if they do not, even so the sectarians (tīrthikas) are able to recollect only by means of the sequence of the aggregates (khandha), but they are unable to do so once that sequence is abandoned.

The disciples (sāvakas) likewise recollect only by means of the sequence of the aggregates; having reached the state of non-perception (asañña-bhava), they do not [recollect] the arising of the aggregates.
They see [this]. Even so, there is no time when the aggregates of those beings wandering in the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) do not exist.
However, in the non-percipient realm (asaññabhava), they proceed for five hundred eons;
having passed that much time, they remember what follows by standing upon the method given by the Buddhas, just like the Venerable Sobhita. But as for the two Chief Disciples...
Paccekabuddhas observe and recollect their own deaths and rebirths. Buddhas have no need for such functions of death and rebirth;
whatever place they wish to see, they see it immediately.
Furthermore, when non-Buddhist ascetics recollect their past lives, they recollect only what they themselves have seen, done, or heard. Likewise...
The disciples and the paccekabuddhas [recollect their past lives]. The Buddhas, however, recollect everything they have seen, done, or heard, whether by themselves or through others.
The knowledge of past lives of the sectarians is like the light of a glowworm; that of the disciples is like the light of a lamp;
that of the chief disciples is like the light of the morning star; that of the paccekabuddhas is like the light of the moon; and that of the Buddhas—

It is like the radiance of the autumn sun’s orb. For him, there is no such thing as "this many hundreds of births, thousands of births, or hundreds of thousands of births," nor "this many hundreds of eons, thousands of eons, or hundreds of thousands of eons.

When he recollects anything at all, there is neither stumbling nor resistance; it is entirely bound up with his advertence (*āvajjana*), and bound up with the arising of the mind that attends to it according to his wish.
It proceeds without obstruction, like an arrow shot with great force through a weak leaf-cup, or like Indra’s thunderbolt hurled against the peak of Mount Sineru.
"Oh, how great is the Blessed One’s knowledge of past lives!"—thus the discussion arose concerning the Blessed One alone;
the meaning is that it was born and proceeded. To show all of that in brief, [the text says]: "Itipi..."
"Past lives, indeed past lives"—this much only is stated in the text. Regarding that, "itipi" means "thus also.
As for the passage beginning "He heard... [omitted] ...then the Blessed One arrived," whatever needs to be said there has already been stated in the commentary on the Brahmajāla Sutta.
For this is the only difference: there he heard by means of the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), whereas here he heard by means of the divine ear (*dibbasota*).
In that place, discussion concerning praise and dispraise was unfinished; here, however, it was a discussion concerning past lives. Therefore the Blessed One thought:
"These monks are extolling my virtue by taking my knowledge of past lives as their theme, yet they do not know the full accomplishment of my knowledge of past lives.
Come now, I shall explain and show them its accomplishment. Having thought this, he arrived—though he was already there by nature—[and sat down].

Having sat upon the excellent Buddha-throne—which had been set aside specifically for the Buddhas to sit upon for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma, and which had been cleared by the monks at that very moment and offered to him—he sat down. Then, at the conclusion of his inquiry, "Monks, where are you from?
and their reply, "From here, venerable sir," and so forth, he desired to deliver a discourse on the Dhamma connected with their past lives. Would you wish to hear it?
He said, "Would you like to hear? (*noti iccheyyātha*). Therein, "would you like to hear" (*iccheyyātha nu*) means "would you wish to hear?

Then, with joyful minds, those monks, making a request, said to him, "Venerable Sir, [please speak] this," and so forth. Therein, "of this" (*etassa*) refers to the delivery of this discourse on the Dhamma.
Then the Blessed One, having accepted their request and desiring to speak, said: "In that case, monks, listen."

Having directed them toward the act of listening and proper attention (*sādhukamanasikāra*), and desiring to proclaim the recollection of past lives (*chinnavaṭumakānusmaraṇa*) which is not shared by others, he said, "From this time forth, monks," and so on. In that context, *yasmiṃ vipassī* means "in which eon [there was] Vipassī.
For this word *yaṃ*—just as in the passage, "Whatever, venerable sir, I heard in the presence of the Tāvatiṃsa gods..."—is used here.
In such passages as "It has been received; I announce it to the Blessed One," it appears in the nominative case (*paccattavacana*).
In such passages as "That which we asked, you have explained to us; we ask another thing, pray tell us that," it appears in the accusative case (*upayogavacana*).

In such passages as "This is impossible, monks, it is out of the question, that in a single world-system... it appears in the instrumental case (*karaṇavacana*). But here, however, it has the sense of the locative case (*bhumm-attha*).
It should be understood. Therefore it was said: "In which aeon. "Arose" means he appeared making the ten-thousandfold world-system resound.
Regarding the phrase "in a fortunate aeon" (*bhaddakappe*): because it is adorned by the arising of five Buddhas, it is a beautiful aeon;

and because it is a substantial aeon (*sārakappe*), the Blessed One spoke thus in praise of this aeon. It is said that from the time our Blessed One made his initial resolve (*abhinīhāra*), in this [aeon]...
Within a single *kappa*, it is said that there are no five Buddhas who arise simultaneously.
Prior to our Blessed One’s resolution (*abhinīhāra*), however, four Buddhas—Taṇhaṅkara, Medhaṅkara, Saraṇaṅkara, and Dīpaṅkara—arose in one *kappa*.
Following them, for one incalculable period (*asaṅkhyeyya*), there was indeed a void of Buddhas.
At the conclusion of that incalculable aeon, however, only one Buddha named Koṇḍañña appeared in a single aeon.

Even after that, there was again an incalculable period devoid of Buddhas. At the conclusion of that incalculable aeon, four Buddhas—Maṅgala, Sumana, Revata, and Sobhita—appeared in a single aeon. Even after that, there was again an incalculable period devoid of Buddhas.

...there was [no Buddha]. At the conclusion of an incalculable aeon (*asaṅkhyeyyakappa*), however, after another hundred thousand aeons beyond that incalculable period, three Buddhas—Anomadassī, Paduma, and Nārada—appeared in a single aeon.
Beyond even that, there was again an incalculable period entirely devoid of Buddhas. At the conclusion of that incalculable aeon, however, after another hundred thousand aeons beyond that...
The Blessed One Padumuttara alone appeared in one eon.
Subsequent to him, thirty thousand eons ago, two Buddhas—Sumedha and Sujāta—appeared together in one eon.
Further back than that, eighteen thousand eons ago, three Buddhas—Piyadassī, Atthadassī, and Dhammadassī—appeared together in one eon.
They have arisen. Furthermore, ninety-four *kappas* ago, only one Buddha named Siddhattha arose in a single *kappa*.
Ninety-two *kappas* ago, two Buddhas—Tissa and Phussa—arose in a single *kappa*.
Ninety-one *kappas* ago, the Blessed One Vipassī arose. Thirty-one *kappas* ago, two Buddhas—Sikhī and Vessabhū—arose.
"In this auspicious aeon, four Buddhas have appeared— Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, Kassapa, and Gotama, our Perfectly Enlightened One— and Metteyya will appear.
Thus the Blessed One spoke in this way while praising this aeon, saying that because it is adorned by the arising of five Buddhas, it is a "beautiful aeon" and a "substantial aeon."
But is this evident only to the Buddhas—namely, that "in this kappa so many Buddhas have arisen or will arise"—or is it evident to others as well?
It is evident to others too. To whom? To the Brahmās of the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa).
For at the time when the formation of a kappa occurs, for one incalculable aeon, [the world] stands as a single plain.
In this world-system, for the sake of the stability of the world, the rain-god begins to pour down rain.

At the very beginning, it is like a fall of snow during the intermediate season (*antaraṭṭhaka*). Then, streams of water appear in succession, measuring only a sesame seed, a grain of chaff, a grain of rice, a mung bean, a black gram, a jujube fruit, an emblic myrobalan, a yam, a gourd, and so on, gradually increasing to the size of a *usabha*, two *usabhas*, half a *gāvuta*, a *gāvuta*, two *gāvutas*, half a *yojana*, a *yojana*, two *yojanas*, and so forth...

Having become a mere hundred *yojanas*, a thousand *yojanas*, or a hundred thousand *yojanas* in extent, they remain filling the interior of a hundred thousand million world-systems as far as the Brahma-world that does not perish. Then that water gradually dries up;
as the water dries, the celestial realms re-establish themselves in their natural divine locations, and this is the manner of their re-establishment.
This has already been stated in the *Visuddhimagga* in the discourse on past lives (*pubbenivāsakathā*).
However, when the water has reached the place where the human world is situated, that water remains still due to the force of the wind, as if the opening of a water-pot were closed;
and upon the surface of the water, the earth solidifies like a lotus leaf floating on water. This is the Great Bodhi-couch.
When the world is dissolving, it dissolves last; when it is forming, it forms first. Therein, as a precursor sign, a single lotus stalk arises.
If a Buddha is to be born in that kappa, a flower appears upon it; if not, it does not appear. And when it does appear, if only one Buddha is to be born, [it remains as such].
One [Buddha] arises. If two, three, four, or five Buddhas are to be born, then five arise;
and these indeed appear joined together by a single stalk within one and the same calyx.
The Suddhāvāsa Brahmas come to the site of the Great Bodhi throne, saying, "Come, friends, let us behold the omen. [This is] for the Buddhas.
In an unevolving eon (*anibbattanakappa*), there are no flowers. Seeing a grove without flowers, they become despondent, thinking:
"Alas, the world will surely fall into darkness! Deceased beings will fill the states of misery (*apāya*); the six celestial worlds and the nine Brahma-worlds will become empty.
But when it is the time of flowering, seeing the blossoms, they think: "Among the omniscient Bodhisattvas..."
“We shall witness the miracles such as the shaking of the ten thousandfold world-system occurring when [Buddhas] descend into the mother’s womb,

emerge from it, awaken to enlightenment, set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, perform the Twin Miracle, descend from the heaven of the Thirty-three, relinquish the life-faculty, and attain final Nibbāna;
and we shall see how the four woeful states will diminish and the six celestial worlds and nine Brahma-worlds will increase.”
Thinking, “We shall fulfill [our aspirations],” they departed for their respective Brahma-worlds, joyful and uttering this inspired exclamation (*udāna*).
In this Auspicious Aeon (*bhaddakappa*), five lotuses appeared.
By the power of those signs, four Buddhas have arisen, and a fifth will arise. When the Suddhāvāsa Brahmas saw those lotuses, they understood this matter:
They knew it. Therefore it was said: "It becomes manifest to others as well.
[End of] the commentary on the delimitation of the lifespan (5–7).
Thus the Blessed One, by way of the delimitation of the eon (*kappa*) through the method beginning with "From this point, monks," [recalled] his former births.
Having thus shown [the previous point], he now spoke the passage beginning with "Vipassī, bhikkhus," in order to show those Buddhas by way of the limits of their lifespan and so forth.
In that context, both "limited" (*paritta*) and "light" (*lahuka*) are synonyms for what is small;
for whatever is small is both limited and light.

"Or a little more" means that for a little more than a hundred years—without reaching another hundred years—one lives for twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or sixty years. However, one so long-lived is extremely rare;
one must go here and there to see such a person, thinking, "It is said that so-and-so lives for such a long time. In this regard, Visākhā...

The female lay follower lived for one hundred and twenty years; likewise did the Brahmin Pokkharasāti, the Brahmin Brahmāyu, the Brahmin Sela, the Brahmin Bāvari, the Elder Ānanda, and the Elder Mahākassapa.
However, the Elder Anuruddha lived for one hundred and fifty years, and the Elder Bākula lived for one hundred and sixty years.
This one has the longest lifespan; even he does not live for two hundred years.

However, all Bodhisattvas beginning with Vipassī took rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) in the mother’s womb by means of a spontaneous (asaṅkhārika) consciousness associated with knowledge, accompanied by joy, and preceded by loving-kindness (mettā).
For a rebirth-linking taken by such a consciousness, [the lifespan is] incalculable (asaṅkhyeyya).
Regarding "lifespan": all Buddhas possess an incalculable lifespan (*asaṅkhyeyya-āyuka*). Why did they not remain for an [indefinite] incalculable period?
Because of the failure of the climate and food. For, depending on the climate and food, lifespan both decreases and increases.
In that regard, when kings become unrighteous, then the viceroy, the commander-in-chief, the guild-leader, and the entire city [become likewise].
The entire kingdom became indeed unrighteous; then their guardian deities [were affected], the earth-dwelling deities who were friends of those deities,
the sky-dwelling deities who were friends of those deities, the heat-bearing cloud deities who were friends of the sky-dwelling deities,
the rain-bearing cloud deities who were friends of those, and the cold-bearing cloud deities who were friends of those.
Their friends are the Vassavalāhaka deities; their friends are the Cātumahārājika deities;
their friends are the Tāvatiṃsa deities; their friends are the Yāma deities, and so forth.

Thus, up to the peak of existence (bhavagga), all the assemblies of devas and brahmās—except for the noble disciples (ariyasāvaka)—are indeed unrighteous (adhammika). Because of their unrighteousness, it is uneven.
The moon and sun do not revolve; the wind does not blow along its proper course. When the wind blows contrary to its course, it agitates the celestial mansions situated in space.
When the celestial mansions are agitated, the minds of the deities do not incline toward play.
When the minds of the deities do not incline toward play, the seasonal weather—distinguished by cold and heat—does not occur at its proper time. In that [state]...
When there is no clear comprehension, the rain does not fall properly: sometimes it rains, sometimes it does not; it rains in some places, but not in others.

Even when it does rain, it falls and ceases in such a way that it does not benefit the crops at the proper times for sowing, sprouting, stalk-forming, flowering, or harvesting milk; thus it rains and then vanishes. Therefore...
The grains ripen unevenly; they are devoid of fragrance, color, flavor, and other such qualities.
Even when rice grains are placed in a single vessel, in one spot the cooked rice is underdone, in another it is overcooked, and in another it is perfectly cooked.
When consumed, that food is digested in the stomach in three ways. Because of this, beings become afflicted with many ailments and short-lived.
Thus, first of all, life-span declines by way of the seasons and food.
But when kings are righteous, then the viceroy-queens also become righteous;
and in the same manner as before, everyone down to the Brahmā-world becomes righteous. Because they are righteous, the moon and sun move in their proper courses.
Just as the wind blows along its proper course, and by blowing along its proper course it does not shake the celestial mansions situated in the sky—
because they are unshaken, the minds of the deities incline toward sport— so too, the seasons occur in their proper time, and the rain falls correctly.
Starting from the time of sowing, it rains at the right time, providing assistance to the crops at the right time.
It vanishes; because of that, the crops become evenly ripened, fragrant, golden-hued, delicious, and full of nutritive essence (*ojā*).
The food prepared from them, even when consumed, undergoes proper digestion; because of that, sentient beings become free from disease and long-lived.
Thus, life-span increases by way of the season and food.
In that regard, the Blessed One Vipassī was born at a time when the lifespan was eighty thousand years, and Sikhi at a time when it was seventy thousand years;
this is presented as if there were a gradual decline, yet it was not actually a continuous decline. It should be understood that [the lifespan] declined after having increased again and again.
How so? First, in this very eon, the Blessed One Kakusandha appeared at a time when the lifespan was forty thousand years.
He was reborn, and having divided his lifespan into five parts, he attained final *parinibbāna* while still remaining in the fifth part after four had passed.

That lifespan, having decreased until it reached the time of ten-year lifespans, increased again until it became incalculable (*asaṅkhyeya*), and then, decreasing from there, remained at thirty thousand years;
at that time, the Blessed One Koṇāgamana was reborn. In that [lifespan] as well...

In the same way, after he had attained final Nibbāna, that lifespan reached the period of ten years, increased again until it became incalculable, and then decreased until it remained at twenty thousand years;
at that time, the Blessed One Kassapa was born.
After he too had likewise attained final Nibbāna, that lifespan reached the period of ten years, and increasing again, became incalculable.
After the lifespan had decreased for a period of one hundred years, our Sammasambuddha was born.
Thus, it should be understood that [the Buddhas] appear after the lifespan has repeatedly decreased and increased again and again.
In this regard, it should be understood that whatever the measure of the lifespan among humans may be when Buddhas are born, for them too, that very same measure of lifespan applies.
The commentary on the section on the delimitation of life is concluded.
Regarding the commentary on the section on the delimitation of enlightenment (8):
"At the foot of the Pāṭali tree" means beneath a Pāṭali tree. Now, as for that Pāṭali...
On that day, its trunk rose up to fifty cubits, and with its branches also at fifty cubits, it reached a height of one hundred cubits.
On that very day, the pāṭali tree was covered from its base upward with flowers as if bound together by a central calyx, and it emitted a divine fragrance.
Not only did this tree blossom then, but throughout the ten thousand world-systems, [the same occurred].

All the *pāṭali* trees were in bloom. Not only the *pāṭali* trees, but in the ten-thousandfold world-system, *khandha-padumas* blossomed upon the trunks of all trees, *sākha-padumas* upon the branches, *latā-padumas* upon the creepers, and *ākāsa-padumas* in the sky;
even breaking through the surface of the earth, great *mahā-padumas* arose. The great ocean, too, [was filled] with five-colored...
It was covered with lotuses— blue, red, and white— and the entire ten-thousandfold world system became filled with rows of banners,
strewn here and there with loose flower garlands and clusters of blossoms, radiant with various colored flowers, resembling the Nandana Grove,
the Citralatā Grove, the Missaka Grove, and the Phārusaka Grove. At the eastern rim of the world-system...
With their banners raised, they struck the western rim of the Cakkavāḷa. With their banners raised, they struck the southern, western, and northern rims of the Cakkavāḷa.
Thus, the Cakkavāḷas became mutually endowed with splendor and excellence.
"Abhisambuddho" (fully awakened) refers to one who has penetrated the entire splendor of the majesty of the Buddha’s qualities.
He has fully awakened to the four truths.

In such passages as, "Bhikkhus, the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was fully awakened at the foot of a white lotus tree," the commentary on the words should be understood according to this same method.
Here, however, *puṇḍarīka* refers to the white mango tree (*setambara*). Of that [tree] also...
It was of that very same size. On that day, it too was well-covered with celestial flowers and scents.
It was not covered only by flowers, but also by fruits. On one side were young fruits; on another, medium-sized fruits;
on another, fruits that were not yet fully ripe; and on another, perfectly ripe fruits infused with divine essence.

They hung down like delicious fruits. Just as that [tree] was, so too were all the flowering trees in the ten thousandfold world-systems adorned with flowers, and the fruit-bearing trees with fruits. "Sāla" refers to the *sāla* tree;
its dimensions are the same as those [previously mentioned], and its splendor of blossoms is to be understood in the same way.
The same principle applies to the Sirīsa tree as well. On the Udumbara tree there were no flowers;

however, the splendor of its fruit was exactly as described for the Amba tree, and likewise for the Nigrodha and the Assattha. Thus, while the *pallaṅka* (seat) for all Buddhas is one and the same, the trees are different.
At the foot of whichever tree [a Buddha attains] enlightenment—known as the knowledge of the four paths—
The Buddhas penetrate [this], and that penetration is called "enlightenment" (*bodhi*). This is what is known as the "delimitation of enlightenment.
9. Regarding the commentary on the section on the pair of disciples:
in the section on the pair of disciples, "Khaṇḍa-Tissa" refers to Khaṇḍa and Tissa. Among them, Khaṇḍa was the son of the same father.

The younger brother was Tissa, the son of the family priest. Khaṇḍa had reached the pinnacle of the perfection of wisdom (paññā-pāramī), while Tissa had reached the pinnacle of the perfection of concentration (samādhi-pāramī).
They were "the foremost" because, with the exception of the Blessed One Vipassī, they were peerless in their qualities among the rest.
They were called "the auspicious pair" (bhaddayuga) precisely because of their preeminence. "Abhibhū and Sambhava" refers to Abhibhū and Sambhava.
Among them, Abhibhū had reached the pinnacle of the perfection of wisdom. Together with the Blessed One Sikhi, he went from the Aruṇavati world-system to the Brahma-world.
There, displaying various miracles to the assembly of Brahmas and teaching the Dhamma, he enveloped the ten-thousandfold world-system in darkness.
When the beings there were struck with a sense of spiritual urgency, wondering, "What is this?", he emitted a radiance.
Having pervaded [the assembly] and resolved, "May all see my form and hear my voice," he announced his voice while reciting the two verses beginning with "Exert yourselves!
Sambhava had reached the pinnacle of the perfection of concentration (samādhipāramī).
As for Soṇuttara, this refers to Soṇa and Uttara; among them, Soṇa had attained the perfection of wisdom (paññāpāramī), and Uttara had attained the perfection of concentration.

Vidhura and Sañjīva attained their respective perfections. Among them, Vidhura had reached the perfection of wisdom (*paññā-pāramī*), while Sañjīva had reached the perfection of concentration (*samādhi-pāramī*).
Being frequently absorbed in meditative attainment, he would dwell in night-stations, day-stations, caves, huts, pavilions, and so forth, meditating through the power of his attainments.
One day, while dwelling in the forest, he entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*); then, the forest workers and others—

Having observed that he was dead, they cremated him. He, however, arose from his meditative attainment exactly at the predetermined time, shook out his robes, and entered the village for alms. From that time on, people recognized him as "Saṅjīva" (the Revived One). Regarding the phrase *bhiyyosuttaraṃ*:
it means both "more" (*bhiyyo*) and "superior" (*uttara*). Among these, he was superior by way of wisdom (*paññā*), and he was foremost by way of concentration (*samādhi*).

"Tissabhāradvāja" refers to Tissa and Bhāradvāja. Among them, Tissa had attained the perfection of wisdom (paññā-pāramī), while Bhāradvāja had attained the perfection of concentration (samādhi-pāramī).

"Sāriputta-Moggallāna" refers to Sāriputta and Moggallāna. Among them, Sāriputta was foremost in the domain of wisdom, and Moggallāna was foremost in the domain of concentration. This is known as the definition of the pair of chief disciples.
Commentary on the Chapter on the Assemblies of Disciples (Sāvakasannipātapariccheda) 10.
In the chapter on the assemblies of disciples, the first assembly of the Blessed One Vipassī consisted of four factors:
all were [ordained] by the "Come, monk" formula; all had bowls and robes produced through supernormal power; and all arrived without even being invited. Thus...
And it was indeed on the fifteenth day, the Uposatha day. Then the Teacher, having taken up a fan and sitting down, recited the Uposatha formula.
The same procedure occurred on the second and third days as well. And so it was at all the assemblies of the other Buddhas.
However, because this assembly of our Blessed One took place immediately after his first enlightenment, and this Sutta was delivered at a later time—
It was said; therefore, without specifying "now," it was stated, "Bhikkhus, there has been one assembly of my disciples.

In that context, "one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikkhus" refers to the thousand former jaṭilas and the two hundred and fifty followers of the two chief disciples—thus making one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikkhus. Therein, of the two chief disciples...
Having related the background story starting from the initial resolve (*abhinīhāra*), their renunciation (*pabbajjā*) should be illustrated.
Among those who had gone forth, Mahāmoggallāna attained *arahantship* on the seventh day.
On the fifteenth day, the General of the Dhamma (*Dhammasenāpati*), while in the midst of Vulture Peak Mountain, in the Sūkarakhatā cave-cavern, [attained it] for his nephew, the wanderer Dīghanakha.

While the *Dhammayāga Sutta*—the discourse on the comprehension of feelings—was being taught, he sent forth his knowledge, awakening to the teaching as it was being delivered, and attained the knowledge of the perfections of a disciple (*sāvakapāramiñāṇa*).
The Blessed One, knowing that the Elder had attained Arahantship, rose up into the air and descended right there at Veḷuvana.
The Elder, reflecting, "Where has the Blessed One gone?", perceived him at Veḷuvana.
Knowing that he was established [in the Dhamma], the Blessed One himself ascended into the air and alighted right there in the Veḷuvana grove.
Then the Blessed One recited the Pātimokkha. Referring to that assembly, the Blessed One said, "There are twelve hundred and fifty bhikkhus.
This is what is known as the delimitation of the assembly of disciples.
Commentary on the Section on Attendants (Upaṭṭhākaparicchedavaṇṇanā): 11.
Regarding the section on attendants, the name Ānanda is mentioned with reference to his status as a permanent attendant.
For during the Blessed One’s first awakening, the attendants were not permanently assigned; at one time, for instance, Nāgasamāla took charge of the bowl and robes.
At times he wandered with Nāgita, at times with Upavāna, at times with Sunakkhatta, at times with the novice Cunda, at times with Sāgata, and at times with Meghiya.
On one occasion, while traveling along a highway together with the Elder Nāgasamāla, the Blessed One reached a fork in the road.
Stepping off the path, the Elder said, "Blessed One, I shall go by this way."
He said. Then the Blessed One said to him, "Come, bhikkhu, let us go by this path.

He replied, "Very well, Blessed One, you take my bowl and robe; I shall go by this path," and he began to set his bowl and robe on the ground. Then the Blessed One said to him, "Bring them, bhikkhu," and [took] the bowl and robe.
Having taken them, he departed. As that other monk was traveling by a different path, thieves robbed him of his bowl and robes and split open his head.
Thinking, "The Blessed One is now my refuge, and no other," he went into the presence of the Blessed One while blood was still flowing.
When the Blessed One asked, "Monk, what is this?", he reported the incident to him.
Then the Blessed One said to him, “Do not worry, bhikkhu; it was precisely for this reason that we stopped you,” and thus he comforted him.
On another occasion, however, the Blessed One went with the elder Meghiya from the Eastern Bamboo Deer Park to the village of Jantu.
There too, Meghiya, having walked for alms in the village of Jantugāma, saw a beautiful mango grove on the riverbank.
He said, "Blessed One, take your bowl and robe; I shall practice the duty of a recluse in that mango grove.
Although he was refused three times by the Blessed One, he went anyway. Overcome and obsessed by unwholesome thoughts, he returned.
He reported that occurrence to him. The Blessed One, having said, "It was precisely for this reason that we forbade it," eventually arrived at Sāvatthī.
There, seated upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared in the courtyard of the Fragrant Chamber and surrounded by the community of monks, he addressed the monks: "Monks, I am now old."
“When it was said, ‘Let some bhikkhus go by this path,’ some went by another; some deposited my bowl and robes;
and you should know that one bhikkhu is my regular attendant. A sense of spiritual urgency arose in the bhikkhus.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and said: “I, Bhante, [will follow] you alone...”
“Desiring [to attain Buddhahood], I fulfilled the perfections for more than a hundred thousand aeons plus an incalculable age.
Is it not fitting that one of great wisdom like me should be an attendant? I shall serve him,” he said. The Blessed One replied to him: “Enough, Sāriputta!
The direction in which you dwell is never empty for me; your instruction is like the instruction of the Buddhas.”
“I have no need for her to attend upon me,” he refused.
By this same means, beginning with Mahāmoggallāna, all eighty great disciples rose [to offer their services], but the Blessed One refused them all.
However, the Elder Ānanda remained seated in silence. Then the bhikkhus said to him: “Friend Ānanda,…”
“The Saṅgha of bhikkhus requests an attendant; you too should request one. He replied, “Friend, what is it like to have an attendant obtained by requesting?
Does the Teacher not see me? If he approves, he will say, ‘Let Ānanda be my attendant.
Then the Blessed One said, “Bhikkhus, Ānanda need not be urged by another; knowing for himself, [he will act].”
"He will attend upon me," he said. Then the monks said, "Arise, friend Ānanda, arise, friend Ānanda;
request the position of attendant for the One of Ten Powers. The Elder arose and requested eight boons: four refusals and four entreaties.
There are four kinds of rejections: having said, "Venerable sir, if the Blessed One will not give me the fine robe he has obtained himself,
will not give me almsfood, will not allow me to dwell in the same fragrant chamber,
and will not go after accepting an invitation, then I shall attend upon the Blessed One"— what then is there in this?
When it was said, "Ānanda, do you see the danger [in this]? he replied: "Venerable sir, if I were to receive these things, there would be those who would say:
'Ānanda enjoys the fine robes obtained by the One of Ten Powers;
he enjoys the almsfood; he dwells in a single fragrant hut; he goes to a single invitation; while receiving such gain...'"
“Who would feel burdened by attending upon a Tathāgata who is attended upon in such a way? Thus he requested these four refusals.
These are called the four requests: “Venerable sir, if the Blessed One will go to the invitation accepted by me;
and if I, from across kingdoms or across districts, should bring a company to see the Blessed One, [I request that] at the very moment they arrive, the Blessed One...”
“I shall be able to see [the Blessed One]; whenever doubt arises in me, at that very moment I shall be able to approach the Blessed One;
and whatever Dhamma the Blessed One teaches to me in his absence, he will come and tell it to me—thus I shall attend upon the Blessed One.
Having said this, [the Blessed One asked]: “But what benefit do you see here, Ānanda?”
When this was said, [the Blessed One replied]: “In this case, Bhante, faithful sons of good family, not obtaining an opportunity to see the Blessed One, say to me:
‘Bhante Ānanda, tomorrow may you accept almsfood at our house together with the Blessed One.
If, Bhante, the Blessed One does not go there, how could he show his assembly and resolve their doubt at the very moment they desire it?”
I shall find no opportunity for diversion; people will say, ‘Why does Ānanda attend upon the One of Ten Powers, yet the Blessed One does not grant him even this much favor?
And when they are in the absence of the Blessed One, they will ask me, ‘Friend Ānanda, where was this verse taught? Where was this sutta taught? Where was this Jātaka taught? If I—
“I will not fulfill that request; there will be those who say: ‘Friend, you do not even know this much;
why have you wandered for so long a time, never leaving the Blessed One, like a shadow?
Therefore, I wish to speak again on the Dhamma that was taught in his absence. He made these four requests, and the Blessed One granted them as well.
Having thus taken these eight boons, he became his constant attendant (*nibaddhupaṭṭhāka*).

It was for the sake of that very position that he attained the fruit of the perfections (*pāramī*) fulfilled over a hundred thousand aeons. With reference to this state of being a constant attendant, the Blessed One said:
"Monks, at present Ānanda the monk is my attendant, my chief attendant. This is what is called the section on the attendants.
12. The section on *pīti* (rapture) is already clear in its meaning.
As for the phrase "he entered the monastery": why did he enter the monastery? It is said that after the Blessed One had spoken thus much, he thought:
"I have not yet fully explained the lineage of the seven Buddhas up to its very summit; today, by me—"
"But when he has entered the monastery, these bhikkhus will speak at even greater length concerning the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa*).
Then, having come and spoken the lineage of the Buddhas (*buddhavaṃsa*) without interruption, I shall bring it to its conclusion and present it.
Having thus granted the bhikkhus an opportunity for their discourse, he rose from his seat and entered the monastery.
Regarding this discourse (tanti) which the Blessed One delivered, nine sections are found therein:

the section on the limit of the eon (kappa), the section on the limit of birth (jāti), the section on the limit of clan (gotta), the section on the limit of lifespan (āyu), the section on the limit of enlightenment (bodhi), the section on the limit of the pair of disciples (sāvakayuga), the section on the limit of the assembly of disciples (sāvakasannipāta), the section on the limit of the attendant (upaṭṭhāka), and the section on the limit of the father (piti).
A section on "many" (sambahula) has not been included; however, having brought it in, it should be explained.
Commentary on the Section on Many [Disciples]:
For all Bodhisattvas, this indeed is the lineage and this the tradition—that when a son has been born who conforms to their own family line, they must go forth and renounce the world.
Why is that? Because from the time of entering the mother’s womb, for all Omniscient Bodhisattvas...
From that point on, there were many miracles of the kind previously described;

therein, if neither his birthplace, nor his father, nor his mother, nor his wife, nor his son were known—if neither his birthplace, nor his father, nor his wife, nor his son were known—one would think, "He is surely a god, or Sakka, or Māra, or Brahmā; for among the gods..."
If people were to think, "Such a miracle is not wonderful," they would neither deign to listen nor believe;
consequently, there would be no realization (abhisamaya). In the absence of realization, the arising of a Buddha would be purposeless, and the Teaching (sāsana) would fail to lead to liberation.
Therefore, for all Bodhisattvas—[thinking], "In one son who conforms to our family lineage..."

"Once born, one must go forth and renounce the world"—this is the lineage, this is the tradition. Therefore, by way of sons and so forth, the section on many individuals should be introduced and explained.
This is the commentary on the section on many individuals.
In that regard:
Samavattakkhandha, Atula, Suppabuddha, and Uttara;
Satthavāha, Vijitasena, and Rāhula is the seventh.
These, first of all, are to be understood as the seven sons of the seven Bodhisattvas in their respective order.
In that regard, when Rāhula Bhadda was born, they brought a leaf and placed it in the Great Man’s hand.
Immediately, a son’s affection arose within him, shaking his entire body. He thought: “First, in one case...”
"When a son is born, such affection for a son arises; it is said that I shall have more than a thousand sons.
When each one of them is born, this bond of affection will increase in this way until it becomes difficult to break. Rāhu is born; a bond is born," he said.
On that very day, he renounced his kingdom and went forth. This same principle applies to the birth of all his sons.
This is the section on the sons: Sutanā, Sabbakāmā, Sucittā, and then Rociṇī;
Rucaggatī, Sunandā, and Bimbā is the seventh.
These were the mothers of those seven sons. However, when Prince Rāhula was born, Bimbādevī became known as Rāhulamātā (the Mother of Rāhula). This concludes the section on wives.
As for the two Bodhisattvas, Vipassī and Kakusandha, they went forth on the Great Renunciation after mounting a chariot drawn by well-trained horses.
The two, Sikhī and Koṇāgamana, went forth having mounted the backs of excellent state elephants.
Vessabhū set out after seating himself in a golden palanquin.
Kassapa, while seated on the upper floor of the palace, attained the fourth jhāna based on mindfulness of breathing; then, emerging from that jhāna and making it his foundation, he resolved:
"Let the palace rise up and descend upon the seat of enlightenment. The palace traveled through the air and descended at the seat of enlightenment.
The Great Being also descended from there, stood upon the ground, and thought: "May the palace remain exactly where it was.

It remained in its original place. The Great Being, having applied himself to striving for seven days, sat upon the Bodhi throne and realized omniscience. But as for our Bodhisatta, [he removed] the thorn...
"He set out having mounted his excellent horse. This is the delimitation of the vehicle.
However, for the Blessed One Vipassī, the monastery was established over an area measuring one *yojana*;
for Sikhī, three *gāvutas*; for Vessabhū, half a *yojana*; for Kakusandha, one *gāvuta*; for Koṇāgamana, half a *gāvuta*; and for Kassapa...
At twenty usabhas—by our Blessed One’s own standard, that is sixteen karīsas, and by the royal standard, eight karīsas—the monastery was established.
This is the measurement of the monastery.
However, for the Blessed One Vipassī, there were golden bricks one ratana in length, one vitthi in width, and eight aṅgulas in height.
Having had small pieces fashioned and covered them with gold, they purchased the site for the monastery. For Sikhī, having covered it with golden staffs and plows, they purchased it.
For Vessabhū, having had golden elephant feet fashioned and covered them with small pieces [of gold], they purchased it.
For Kakusandha, in the same manner as described, having covered it with golden bricks, they purchased it. For Koṇāgamana, in the same manner as described...
They purchased it by covering it with golden tortoises. For Kassapa [Buddha], they purchased it by covering it with golden bricks alone.
For our Blessed One, they purchased it by covering a small portion with coins bearing the royal insignia. This is the extent of the wealth spent in acquiring the site for the monastery.
Therein, after purchasing the site in that manner for the Blessed Vipassi and building a monastery, Punabbasumitta was the attendant who provided service.
[The names of the attendants] were as follows: for Sikhī, his name was Sirivaḍḍhana; for Vessabhū, his name was Sotthiya; for Kakusandha, his name was Accuta;
for Koṇāgamana, his name was Ugga; for Kassapa, his name was Sumana; and for our Blessed One, his name was Sudatta.
All of these were great householders and wealthy merchants. This is the section concerning the attendants.
There are four other places that are called "unforsaken" (*avijahita*). For all Buddhas, the seat of enlightenment (*bodhipallaṅka*) is unforsaken;
it remains in one and the same place. The turning of the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakkappavattana*) at Isipatana in the Deer Park is likewise unforsaken.
At the time of the descent from heaven (*devorohana*), the first footprint-mark at the gate of the city of Saṅkassa is unforsaken. And [the same applies to] Jetavana.
The four legs of the bed in the Fragrant Chamber remain fixed in their place.
Whether the monastery is small or large, the monastery itself does not move, but the city does. When the city is to the east, then the monastery is to the west;
when the city is to the south, then the monastery is to the north. When...
When the city was to the west, the monastery was to the east; when the city was to the north, the monastery was to the south.
But now, the city is to the north and the monastery is to the south.
Furthermore, there are differences among all Buddhas regarding their lifespan, their physical stature, their lineage, their exertion, and their rays of light.
There are five kinds of diversity. Diversity of lifespan means that some are long-lived while others are short-lived;
for instance, the life-span of Dīpaṅkara was one hundred thousand years, whereas the life-span of our Blessed One was one hundred years.
Diversity of stature means that some are tall while others are short; for instance, Dīpaṅkara was eighty cubits tall, Sumana was ninety cubits tall, and our Blessed One was eighteen cubits tall.
"Difference of family" means that some are reborn in a khattiya family, while others are reborn in a brahmin family.
"Difference of exertion" means that for some, the exertion lasts only for a short time, as was the case with the Blessed One Kassapa;
for others, it is long-lasting, as is the case with our Blessed One.
Regarding the difference in radiance: the bodily radiance of the Blessed One Maṅgala extended throughout the measure of a ten-thousandfold world system;
that of our Blessed One extends only a fathom on all sides. In this regard, the difference in radiance is dependent upon one’s aspiration;
whoever desires it to extend to whatever degree, for him the bodily effulgence pervades to that extent. However, that of Maṅgala was always thus.
His aspiration was: "May it pervade a ten-thousandfold world system. However, there is no difference whatsoever among those who have realized the qualities [of enlightenment].
Furthermore, they pointed out the simultaneous birth and the astrological configuration of our very own Blessed One:
it is said that Rāhulamātā, the Elder Ānanda, Channa, Kaṇṭaka, and the treasure-pot were born together with the Omniscient Bodhisatta.
Mahābodhi and Kāḷudāyī—these seven were born together. The Great Man descended into his mother’s womb under the constellation Uttarāsāḷha;
he went forth on the Great Renunciation, set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, and performed the Twin Miracle.
He was born under the constellation Visākha, attained full enlightenment under it, and passed away into Parinibbāna under it. His [death] occurred under the constellation Māgha.

The assembly of disciples gathered, the relinquishing of the life-force occurred, and the descent from the deva realm under the constellation Assayuja—having brought these points forward, it should be explained.
This is what is called the section on the many [disciples]. 13.
Now, regarding the passage beginning with "Then those bhikkhus," those bhikkhus [said]: "Friend, as for what is called 'past lives'..."
“This is the way: namely, ascending from death to rebirth-linking.
But this—sending knowledge backward from rebirth-linking to reach the point of death—is exceedingly difficult.
It is as if the Blessed One were showing a footprint in the sky! Having become filled with great wonder, they said, “It is marvelous, friend! and so forth.
Having spoken thus, and wishing to show another reason as well, they said: "In that the Tathāgata... and so forth.
Therein, *yatra hi nāma* is a particle used in the sense of wonder; the meaning is, "he who is indeed called the Tathāgata. Regarding *chinnapapañce*:
here, *papañca* refers to these three defilements—craving (*taṇhā*), conceit (*māna*), and views (*diṭṭhi*). Regarding *chinnavaṭume*: here, *vaṭuma* means...
The cycle of wholesome and unwholesome kamma is what is meant [by "the cycle"]. "In whom the cycle has been exhausted" (*pariyādinnavaṭṭe*) is a synonym for that same thing;

the meaning is "in whom the entire cycle of kamma has been exhausted. "One who has transcended all suffering" (*sabbadukkhavītivatte*) means one who has transcended all suffering comprised within the cycle of result (*vipākavaṭṭa*).
"He will recollect" (*anussarissati*)—this is a future tense expression used by way of the particle *yattha*, but the sense here should be understood as referring to the past. The Blessed One...
For when he has recollected the Buddha, he will not now [need to] recollect him again. "Of such virtue" means:

by virtue of the path, virtue of the fruit, and mundane and supramundane virtue, they are "of such virtue. "Of such Dhamma": here, the factors (dhammas) belonging to the side of concentration are intended;
by way of the concentration of the path, the concentration of the fruit, and mundane and supramundane concentration, the meaning is "of such concentration. "Of such wisdom" means:
Such wisdom is by way of the wisdom of the path and so forth. As for the phrase "dwelling thus" (*evaṃvihārī*):
if it is asked, "Since the states belonging to the side of concentration were already included below, why is 'dwelling' mentioned again—does one take what has already been taken?"—the answer is:

this is not merely a repetition of what was already taken. For this is stated for the purpose of illustrating the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). Therefore, those Blessed Ones dwell thus in the attainment of cessation.
"‘They were’ (ahesuṃ): this is how the meaning should be understood here.

‘Thus liberated’ (evaṃvimuttā): herein, liberation is fivefold—liberation by suppression, liberation by substitution of opposites, liberation by eradication, liberation by tranquillization, and liberation by escape.
Among these, the eight attainments [are liberation] by those [defilements] which have been suppressed..."
Because they are liberated from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and so forth, they receive the designation "liberation by suppression" (*vikkhambhana-vimutti*).

The seven contemplations, beginning with the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*), receive the designation "liberation by substitution of opposites" (*tadaṅga-vimutti*) because they are liberated from the perceptions of permanence and so forth, which have been relinquished by way of their respective opposing factors.
The four noble paths (*ariyamagga*) [are liberated] from the defilements that have been completely eradicated by them...

Because they are liberated, they are reckoned as "liberation by eradication. The four fruits of asceticism are reckoned as "liberation by subsiding" because they arise when the defilements have subsided through the power of the paths.
Nibbāna is reckoned as "liberation by escape" because it has escaped from, departed from, and stands far removed from all defilements.
He goes. Thus, by way of these five kinds of liberation, the meaning of the phrase "thus liberated" should be understood here.
14. "Emerging from seclusion": emerging from a state of solitude. 16.
Regarding the sequence of the passage, "From this, monks": for this sutta belongs to the Tathāgata alone, monks...
This [teaching] is bound by these two phrases: "the element of phenomena (dhammadhātu) has been well-penetrated" and "deities also announced this matter to the Tathāgata.
Therein, the phrase regarding the announcement by the deities will be examined when it shows the clamor of the divine visit at the conclusion of the sutta.
However, this teaching was commenced by way of the connection with the phrase concerning the element of phenomena. Therein—
The eleven phrases beginning with “a khattiya by birth” are to be understood in the same manner as explained in the Nidāna-khaṇḍa.
Regarding the passage beginning “Then, monks, the Bodhisatta Vipassī,” the word “Vipassī” is his name; and that—
It was obtained through his skill in discerning various meanings. "Bodhisatta" means a wise being, a being who awakens;
or, one whose mind is intent upon, attached to, and fixed on the four paths reckoned as "bodhi," is a bodhisatta. Regarding the phrase "mindful and clearly comprehending":

here, "mindful" (*sato*) is simply mindfulness (*sati*), and "clearly comprehending" (*sampajāno*) is knowledge (*ñāṇa*). Having established mindfulness well and having delimited [the object] with knowledge...
The meaning is that he entered his mother’s womb. By the word "entered" (*okkami*), his state of having entered is shown in the text, but not the sequence of the entry itself.
However, since that sequence has been recorded in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it should be understood as follows:
For all Bodhisattvas, having fulfilled the thirty perfections (*pāramī*) and having made the five great renunciations (*mahāpariccāga*),...
Having reached the pinnacle of the conduct for the benefit of relatives, the conduct for the benefit of the world, and the conduct of a Buddha,
and having stood in his third existence as one like Vessantara, he gave the seven great gifts, caused the earth to quake seven times, and after passing away,
was reborn in the Tusita heaven during the second mental moment. The Bodhisatta Vipassī likewise did so and was reborn in the City of Tusita.
Having been reborn there, he remained for seventy-five million years plus six million.
However, Bodhisattas who are reborn in other long-lived celestial worlds do not remain for the full duration of their lifespan. Why?

Because it is difficult to fulfill the perfections (pāramīs) in those places. Having performed the act of intentional relinquishment of life (adhimuttikālakiriya), they are reborn specifically in the human realm.

But while fulfilling the perfections, because they were fulfilled in their entirety—just as he is now able to reach omniscience in a single lifetime—the Bodhisatta Vipassī remained there for the full span of his life.
However, the devas knew: "By the calculation of human time, his passing away will occur in seven days."

Five portents appear: the garlands wither, the garments become soiled, sweat breaks out from the armpits, a disfigurement comes over the body, and the deity does not remain steady on his divine throne.
In this context, "garlands" refers to the garlands worn on the day of conception; it is said that these did not wither for seventy-five million and six hundred thousand years.
Then they close. The same principle applies to their garments as well. For this duration of time, there is neither cold nor heat for the devas;
at that time, sweat is released from their bodies only in the form of tiny droplets.
And during this period, no discoloration—such as mottling or graying—is perceived upon their bodies; a divine maiden appears as if she were only sixteen years old.
They appear like young sons of the gods twenty years of age; however, at the time of death, their physical form becomes one that is exhausted.
Furthermore, during all that time in the deva-world, they experience no such thing as weariness;
yet at the time of death, they sigh, stretch out, and find no delight in their own seats.

Furthermore, just as in the world these portents—such as the falling of meteors, earthquakes, lunar eclipses, and so forth—are perceived only by those of great merit, such as kings, royal ministers, and the like, and not by everyone;
likewise, they are perceived only by deities of great power, and not by all.
And just as among humans, only astrologers and the like know these portents, and not everyone; so too...

Even those [beings] do not all know this; only the wise know it. In that regard, those sons of the gods who have been reborn there by means of weak wholesome karma fear when they arise among them, thinking: "Now who knows where we shall be reborn?
But those of great merit [think]: "The gift was given by us, the virtue was guarded, and the meditation was cultivated."
They do not fear [thinking], "Having come here, we shall experience prosperity in the higher deva-worlds.
The Bodhisatta Vipassī, too, having seen those preliminary signs, does not fear [thinking], "Now, in my very next existence, I shall become a Buddha.
Then, when those signs had appeared, the deities of ten thousand world-systems assembled and said: "O Noble One,..."
“While you were fulfilling the ten perfections, you did not do so aspiring for the status of Sakka, nor the status of Māra, nor the status of Brahmā, nor the status of a wheel-turning monarch;
rather, you fulfilled them aspiring for Buddhahood for the sake of delivering the world.
Now, dear sir, is the time for your Buddhahood; now, dear sir, is the occasion for your Buddhahood,” they entreated.

Then the Great Being, without yet giving his promise to those deities, performed what is known as the Five Great Observations by way of observing the time, the continent, the country, the lineage, and the limit of the lifespan.
Therein, he first observed the time, thinking, "Is it the right time, or is it not the right time?
In this regard, a period when the lifespan has increased beyond one hundred thousand years is not the right time. Why is that?
For at that time, birth, aging, and death are not perceived among beings, and there is no teaching of the Dhamma by the Buddhas that is not released from the three characteristics.

When they speak to them [of beings] as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self," those beings do not even think to listen or believe, wondering, "What is it they are saying? Consequently, there is no realization (abhisamaya); and in its absence, there is no leading to liberation.
The Dispensation exists. Therefore, that is not the right time. Even a period when the lifespan is less than a hundred years is not the right time.

Why? Because at that time, sentient beings have intensified defilements; and advice given to those with intensified defilements does not remain in its proper place, but quickly vanishes like a line drawn with a stick upon water.
Therefore, that too is not the right time. From a lifespan of one hundred thousand years onwards—
Below, the period of a hundred years and upwards is called "the time"; at that time, human beings had a lifespan of eighty thousand years.
Then the Great Being, perceiving that "the time for rebirth has come," looked toward the continent.
Surveying the four continents together with their surroundings, he saw that "Buddhas are not born in the three continents; they are born only in Jambudīpa. Thus he discerned the continent.
Then, looking about for the region, he thought: "Jambudīpa is indeed great, measuring ten thousand *yojanas*;
in which place, then, do Buddhas take birth? He beheld the Middle Country (*majjhima-deso*).
As for the Middle Country, it is described in the Vinaya in this manner: "In the eastern direction is the market town named Gajaṅgala," and so forth. It is three hundred *yojanas* in length.
"It is two and a half [yojanas] in width and nine hundred yojanas in circumference.

For it is in this region that Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, Chief Disciples, the eighty Great Disciples, Wheel-turning Monarchs, and other highly influential kshatriyas, brahmins, householders, and great landowners arise.
And here is the city named Bandhumatī; I must be reborn there"—thus he reached his conclusion.

Then, surveying the family, he thought: "Buddhas are born into families esteemed by the world. At present, the Kṣatriya clan is esteemed by the world; I shall be born there, and King Bandhumā will be my father.
Thus he surveyed the family. Then, surveying the mother, he thought: "The mother of a Buddha is not one who is lustful, addicted to liquor, or a gambler;
she has fulfilled the perfections for a hundred thousand aeons and has maintained the five precepts unbroken from birth onwards. And this Queen Bandhumatī—"
"Such will this mother of mine be," he thought; then, reflecting, "How long will her lifespan be?
he saw that it would be ten months plus seven days.
Having thus performed these five great observations, he said to the deities, "The time has come for me, friends, to become a Buddha."

Making a summary and giving his promise—“Go, you,” he said—he dismissed those deities and, surrounded by the Tusita deities, entered the Nandana Grove in the Tusita city. For the Nandana Grove exists in all the celestial worlds.
There, the deities move about, reminding him of the sphere of wholesome kamma performed in the past, saying: “When you pass away from here, you will go to a happy destination.”
Thus, surrounded by deities who were reminding him of his wholesome deeds, he passed away while wandering about that very place.

Having thus passed away, he knows, "I am passing away," yet he does not know the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*). Even after having taken rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), he knows it, yet he does not know the rebirth-linking consciousness itself.
However, he knows, "In this place I have taken rebirth-linking. Thus...
He knows. However, some elders say: "It is necessary to obtain the method of adverting; he will know it only during the second and third mental moments.
But the Elder Tipiṭaka Mahāsīva said: "The rebirth-linking of Great Beings is not like the rebirth-linking of others;
rather, their mindfulness and clear comprehension reach the ultimate limit. And because of that very [fact]..."
"It is not possible for that mind to know that [past] mind; therefore, it does not know the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*). Even at the moment of death, it knows, 'I am passing away.
It does not know the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*).

It knows, 'Rebirth has been taken by me in such-and-such a place,' and at that time, the ten-thousandfold world-system trembles. Thus, being mindful and clearly comprehending, he descends into the mother’s womb.

However, among the nineteen rebirth-linking consciousnesses, he took rebirth-linking with a great resultant consciousness similar to the wholesome consciousness of the preliminary stage of loving-kindness that was accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, and unprompted. But the Elder Mahāsīva said it was "accompanied by equanimity.
And just as our Blessed One did, so too did he [attain parinibbāna] on the full moon of Āsāḷhī under the constellation Uttarāsāḷha.
She took rebirth.

At that time, it is said, from the seventh day prior to the full moon, the Bodhisatta’s mother—having abstained from drinking intoxicants and being endowed with the splendor of garlands, perfumes, and other finery—enjoyed the festival of the constellations;
then, on the morning of the seventh day, she rose and [washed] with scented water.
Having bathed, adorned herself with every ornament, and eaten excellent food, she undertook the observances of the Uposatha.
Entering the bedchamber and lying down upon her magnificent couch, as she was falling asleep, she saw this dream:
"The four Great Kings, it is said, lifted her up along with her very bed, led her to Lake Anotatta, and having bathed her, [dressed her] in celestial garments..."
Having dressed her, anointed her with celestial perfumes, and adorned her with celestial flowers,
they laid her down with her head toward the east inside a golden palace situated within a silver mountain not far from there.
Then the Bodhisatta, having become a noble white elephant, wandered upon a certain golden mountain nearby, and descending from there—
“Having ascended the Silver Mountain and entered a golden palace, he circumambulated his mother, split her right side, and appeared as if he had entered her womb.
Then, having woken up, the queen reported that dream to the king. When the night had turned to dawn, the king [gathered] about sixty-four...
Having summoned the brahmins as his chief guests, he prepared a ground smeared with green grass and adorned with auspicious honors such as parched grain;
there, having arranged costly seats and filled golden and silver bowls with excellent milk-rice mixed with ghee, honey, and sugar for the brahmins seated upon them,
he presented it to them using those very golden and silver bowls as covers.
And he satisfied them with other gifts, such as unwashed cloth and tawny cows.
Then, having satisfied them in every way they desired, he related that dream to them and asked, "What will come of it? The brahmins said, "Do not worry, Great King;
a child has been conceived in the womb of your queen, and it is a male child, not a female one."
“A son shall be born to you. If he dwells at home, he will become a universal monarch (cakkavatti) king;
if he goes forth from the home into homelessness, he will become a Buddha in the world who has removed the veil [of ignorance].
This, first of all, is the sequence of the commentary on the phrase “he descended into his mother’s womb.”
"This is the natural law here" means that this is the natural law regarding the descent into the mother's womb; it is said to be the inherent nature (*sabhāva*), the fixed order (*niyāma*).
And this fixed order is fivefold: the fixed order of karma, the fixed order of season, the fixed order of seed, the fixed order of consciousness, and the fixed order of phenomena.
Among these, the giving of a desirable result by wholesome [karma] and the giving of an undesirable result by unwholesome [karma]—this is the fixed order of karma.
To illustrate this, the grounds for the verse beginning with “Not in the sky” should be told.
Furthermore, it is said that once a certain woman, having quarreled with her husband, placed her neck in a noose of rope, desiring to die by hanging herself.
A certain man, while sharpening his axe, saw this act of the woman and, wishing to cut the rope, said: “Do not fear!”
"Do not be afraid," he said, encouraging him as he ran toward him. The rope stood there having become a venomous snake. Terrified, he fled;
the other died right then and there. Such instances should be cited here as examples.
In various regions and at various times, there were cases where trees simultaneously bore flowers and fruits, and so forth.
The blowing and non-blowing of the wind, the intensity and mildness of the heat,
the raining and non-raining of the deity, the blossoming of lotuses by day and their wilting at night— such as these are the laws of season (*utuniyāma*).

Furthermore, that from a rice seed only a rice fruit arises, that from something sweet only a sweet-tasting fruit arises, and that from something bitter only a bitter-tasting fruit arises— this is the law of seed (*bījaniyāma*).
"Preceding consciousnesses and mental factors are a condition for succeeding consciousnesses and mental factors by way of decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya).
Thus, this production of receiving-consciousness and so forth immediately after eye-consciousness and so forth is what is called "mental determination" (cittaniyāma).

Furthermore, that occurrence of the shaking of the ten-thousandfold world system and so forth during the Bodhisattvas' descent into their mother's womb and other such events is called "the fixed order of things" (*dhammaniyāma*).
Among these, it is this fixed order of things that is intended here. Therefore, in order to show that very point, he said:
"This, monks, is the natural law," and so forth.
18. Regarding the phrase "enters the womb": here, "has entered the womb" is the intended meaning. For it is when he has already entered that this occurs, not while he is in the process of entering.
"Immeasurable" (*appamāṇa*) means having the measure of growth; "vast" (*vipula*) is its meaning. "Exalted" (*uḷāra*) is a synonym for that very same thing.
In such expressions as "they eat various exalted hard foods," "exalted" refers to what is sweet.
It has been said: "Indeed, Master Vacchāyana praises the ascetic Gotama with a lofty praise," and so forth;
in such cases, "lofty" (*ulāra*) is said to mean "excellent. But here, however, it is intended in the sense of "vast. Regarding the phrase "the divine power of the gods":
here, this is the power of the gods such that the radiance of their worn clothing pervades twelve *yojanas*, and likewise that of their bodies.
"Likewise [the distance] of an ornament, likewise of a celestial mansion (vimāna)"—the meaning is "having surpassed that.
Regarding the "inter-worlds" (lokantarika): between every three world-systems (cakkavāḷa), there is one inter-world;
it is like the space in the middle of three cart-wheels or three leaves placed so that they touch one another. And that is the hell of the inter-world (lokantarika-niraya).
In measurement, it is eight thousand yojanas. "Agha" means always open. "Uncovered" means that there is no foundation even below.
"Darkness" means consisting of gloom. "Blinding darkness" means possessed of a darkness that causes blindness by obstructing the arising of eye-consciousness;
for it is said that eye-consciousness does not arise there. "So powerful" refers to the moon and the sun.
It is said that they appear simultaneously in the three continents; thus they possess such great supernormal power (*mahiddhika*).
Having dispelled the darkness for nine hundred thousand yojanas in each direction, they provide light; thus they possess such great majesty (*mahānubhāva*).
"They do not suffice with their radiance" means they are unable to reach [all places] with their own effulgence. It is said that they [shine] through the middle of the Cakkavāḷa mountain range.
They roam about, even beyond the Cakkavāḷa mountains and the Lokantarika hells. Therefore, their light does not reach there.
"And those beings who are there" refers to those beings who have been reborn in that great Lokantarika hell. But what kind of karma must one perform to be reborn there?
[It is] grave and cruel [karma committed against] one's mother and father, or toward righteous recluses and brahmins.

Furthermore, they arise due to past offenses and other acts of violence committed day after day, such as the killing of living beings—just like the Abhaya thieves and the Nāga thieves in the island of Tambapaṇṇi.
Their bodies are three gavutas in height, and their claws are long like those of bats.
Like bats clinging to trees, they cling to the Cakkavāḷa mountains with their claws.
When they are crawling about and come within arm’s reach of one another,
then, thinking “we have found food,” they become intent upon that spot and, turning over and over, fall into the water that sustains the world;
even when struck by the wind, they break off like *madhuka* fruits and fall into the water, and as soon as they have fallen, they dissolve like a lump of dough in extremely caustic water.
"Indeed, sirs, there are other beings as well," they think;
"just as we experience this great suffering, so too have other beings been reborn here for the sake of experiencing this same suffering"—thus they see on that day.
Yet this radiance does not remain even for the duration of a single bowl of rice-gruel; it lasts only for the snap of a finger, like a flash of lightning.
Having emerged, it vanishes even as they are saying, "What is this?
"It quakes" means it trembles on all sides. The other two terms are synonyms for the first word. Again, the passage beginning with "And immeasurable" is stated for the purpose of a conclusion. 19.
Regarding the phrase "four sons of gods approach him for protection from the four quarters": here, "four" refers to the four...
This was stated by way of the [four] Great Kings. However, if one counts four in each of the ten thousand world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), there are forty thousand.
Among them, in this world-system, the Great Kings approached with swords in hand for the purpose of guarding the Bodhisatta and entered the inner chamber (*sirigabbha*);
the others, starting from the entrance of the chamber, [guarded against] the obstructing hosts of *paṃsupisācaka* and other *yakkhas*.
Having made them retreat, they established a protection as far as the edge of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).

But for what purpose was this protection? Was it not because at the moment of rebirth-linking, from the time of the embryo (*kalala*) onwards, even if hundreds of thousands of millions of Māras were to lift up hundreds of thousands of millions of Sinerus in order to create an obstacle for the Bodhisatta or the Bodhisatta’s mother?
They might come, but they would all vanish along the way. And this was said by the Blessed One regarding the occasion of the shedding of blood:
"It is impossible, monks, it is out of the question, that anyone could deprive a Tathāgata of life by means of an external assault.
Monks, Tathāgatas attain final Nibbāna without such an assault. Go, monks, to your respective dwellings."
“Monks, Tathāgatas are not to be protected. Even so, there was no danger to their lives due to that assault by another;

however, there were non-human beings who were deformed, hideous, and of terrifying appearance—beasts and birds—whose forms or sounds, upon being seen or heard, might have caused fear or terror to arise in the Bodhisatta’s mother. It was for the purpose of warding them off [that she was protected].
They took up their guard. Moreover, moved by the majesty of the Bodhisatta’s merit and impelled by their own sense of reverence, they acted thus.
But when those four Great Kings stood within the inner chamber, did they show themselves to the Bodhisatta’s mother or not?
They did not show themselves at times when she was engaged in bodily activities such as bathing, adorning herself, or eating; however, [they appeared] in the bedchamber...
However, they appear when she has entered and is reclining upon her excellent bed.
Although the sight of non-human beings is indeed fearful for ordinary people, the Bodhisatta’s mother, through the power of the merit of both herself and her son, does not fear them;
rather, her mind arises toward them as if toward the usual guardians of the inner palace.

20. “By nature virtuous” means she was endowed with virtue by her very essence. It is said that before the Buddha appeared, people would receive the precepts after paying homage to ascetics and wanderers and sitting in the *ukkuṭika* posture.

The mother of the Bodhisatta likewise received the precepts from the seer Kāḷadevila. However, once the Bodhisatta had entered her womb, it was no longer fitting for her to sit at the feet of another.
It is not possible [to know this] by name alone; even for one who has sat on the same seat and undertaken the precepts, it is merely a matter of mental advertence (*āvajjana*).
Therefore, it is said that he himself took up the precepts.
21. "Among men" means among certain people, beginning with the Bodhisatta’s father, [he conceived] a mind intent upon a male.
[Sexual desire] does not arise. However, even skilled artisans are unable to create the form of the Bodhisatta’s mother through painting or other such means.
One cannot say that upon seeing her, no lust arises in a man;
yet, if he approaches her with a lustful mind, his feet do not move, as if bound by a divine chain. Therefore, it was said: "unassailable," and so forth.

22. Regarding the phrase “of the five strands of sensual pleasure” (*pañcannaṃ kāmaguṇānaṃ*): previously, by the expression “connected with the strands of sensual pleasure,” the rejection of the physical basis (*vatthu*) was made from the perspective of human intention;
here, however, the acquisition of the object (*ārammaṇa*) is shown.

At that time, it is said, having heard that such a son had been conceived in the womb of the queen, kings from all directions [offered] by way of costly ornaments, musical instruments, and so forth—the objects for the five doors which serve as the physical bases.
They sent gifts as tokens of respect. Because of the great merit accumulated by both the Bodhisatta and the Bodhisatta’s mother, there was no limit to the measure of their gain and honor. 23.
"With bodies untiring" means that, unlike other women who become exhausted by the weight of the fetus and suffer from swollen hands and feet and so forth—
They reach [the womb], and thus she experienced no fatigue whatsoever. "Tirokucchigataṃ" means having entered within the womb.

"Passati" (she sees) means that she sees [the child] precisely when it has passed through the stages of the *kalala* and so forth, and has attained the state of having fully developed limbs and minor parts with unimpaired faculties.
For what purpose does she see? Solely for the sake of dwelling in comfort. For just as a mother lying down together with her son...
Or while sitting—thinking, “I shall lift up and steady his hand or foot as it hangs down”—she looks at her son for the sake of his comfort;

even so did the Bodhisatta’s mother look [at him]. Furthermore, that suffering which arises for a mother during the times of standing, walking, turning over, and sitting, and during the swallowing of food that is hot, cold, salty, sour, bitter, or pungent, [did not arise for her].
Thinking, "Is there indeed such a thing for my son? she looked for the sake of his comfortable dwelling and saw the Bodhisatta sitting cross-legged.

For whereas other beings within the womb occupy the receptacle for digested food (pakvāsaya), push up against the receptacle for undigested food (āmāsaya), place the abdominal membrane behind them, and sit hunched against the spinal column with their two fists—
When it rains, [ordinary beings] sit like monkeys in tree hollows, having placed their jaws on the ground; the Bodhisatta does not do so.

Rather, the Bodhisatta sits facing east, having crossed his legs in the full lotus posture (*pallaṅka*) upon the Dharma-seat, with his backbone turned toward the back, like a preacher of the Dharma. Furthermore, his past deeds purify the site; once purified—
In that body, the mark of fine skin is produced.

Then, because it is unable to conceal the foul skin, it appears as if standing outside for one who looks [within]. To clarify this matter by means of a simile, the Blessed One said, "Just as if," and so forth.
However, the Bodhisatta, having entered the interior of the womb, does not see his mother; for within the womb—
Eye-consciousness arises.
