24. "He passes away" means not by reason of his having been born, but solely through the exhaustion of his lifespan. For a place inhabited by a Bodhisatta becomes like a shrine-chamber;
it is unfit for others to use, and it is not possible to remove the mother of a Bodhisatta [from there].
Because another woman was to be appointed to the position of chief queen, the life-span of the Bodhisatta’s mother was exactly that much;
therefore, she passed away at that time. At what stage of life, however, did she pass away? At middle age.

For in early youth, beings have a powerful desire and attachment for their own physical existence (*attabhāva*); thus, a woman who has conceived a child at that time [would otherwise continue to live].
If she is unable to protect herself, the pregnancy becomes fraught with many ailments.
However, when two-thirds of middle age have passed and one enters the third stage, the physical basis (vatthu) becomes clear; children born when the physical basis is clear are free from disease.
Therefore, the Bodhisatta’s mother, having experienced prosperity during her early years, [enters] the third stage of middle age.
It is the natural law (*dhammatā*) that one dies after having brought forth the bodily parts.
Regarding the phrase "nine or ten," it should be understood that by way of the alternative sense of the word "or" (*vā*), this includes seven or eight, eleven or twelve, and so forth.
Among these, one born after seven months survives and is capable of enduring cold and heat.
But it does not happen that one born eight months lives; the rest live. 27.
"The gods receive [the child] first" means that the Suddhāvāsa Brahmas, whose taints are exhausted, receive it.
How do they receive it? Some say, "By assuming the disguise of a midwife. Having rejected that, however, this was said: "At that time..."
The Bodhisatta’s mother, having dressed herself in a cloth embroidered with gold and wearing a fine linen garment (*dukūla-paṭa*) resembling a fish’s eye down to her feet, stood there.
Then her easy delivery occurred, like water flowing out from a water-jar.
Then those [beings], approaching in their natural Brahmā attire, first [covered her] with a golden net.
They received it. From their hands, the Four Great Kings received it upon a cushion of antelope skin;
thereafter, humans received it upon a cushion of fine linen. Therefore it is said: "The gods receive first, afterwards humans. 28.

"Four sons of the gods" refers to the Four Great Kings. "Having received" means having received it upon a cushion of antelope skin. "Of great influence" means one of great power, great fame, and endowed with the [auspicious] marks.
29. "He emerges unhindered" means that he does not emerge like other beings who, clinging to the birth canal, emerge broken and shattered;
rather, he emerges without clinging. "By water" (*udakena*) means by means of water.
"By no impurity" means that unlike other beings who, driven by the winds of karma, enter the birth canal with feet upwards and head downwards, [and are] a hundred cubits long...
Like those falling into the precipice of hell, or like elephants being dragged out through a palm-tree opening, they experience great suffering and emerge smeared with various impurities;
but the Bodhisatta does not do so. For the winds born of karma are unable to turn the Bodhisatta head-downwards and feet-upwards;
rather, he descends like a preacher of the Dhamma stepping down from his Dhamma-seat.
Like a man descending from a ladder, he emerges with his two hands and two feet outstretched, remaining unstained by any of the impurities produced within the mother’s womb.
"Streams of water" refers to currents of water; among them, the cold ones fall into golden basins, and the warm ones into silver basins.
And this was said to show that the water for drinking and bathing on the surface of the earth is unmixed with any impurity and is not shared by others, as well as the water for play; however,
there is no limit to the water brought in golden and silver jars by others, nor to the water found in lotus ponds such as Haṃsavattaka and the like.
31. "Sampatijāto" means one who has been born for a moment. However, in the Pāḷi, he is depicted as if having just emerged from his mother’s womb;
it should not be viewed in that way. For as soon as he had emerged, first the Brahmās received him with a golden net;
from their hands, the Four Great Kings [received him] with an antelope-skin rug; and from their hands, human beings [received him] with a *dukūla* cotton swaddling cloth.
Having escaped from the hands of men, he stood firm upon the earth. "While a white parasol was being held over him" means while a divine white silk parasol was being held over him.
And here, the five royal insignia, such as the sword and so forth, which accompany the parasol, are also implicitly included.
However, in the canonical text (pāḷi), only the parasol is mentioned, just as when a king goes out, the king himself is the primary subject.

Among those, only the sunshade was visible, but not the bearer of the sunshade. Likewise, only the sword, the palm-leaf fan, the peacock-feather fan, the *vāḷa*-fan, and the *uṇhīsa* were visible, but not their bearers.
It is said that all of them were held by deities whose forms remained invisible. And this has been stated:
“With its many branches and thousand-fold circle...”
The deities held a parasol in the sky;
golden-handled yak-tail fans fell [all around],
yet no holders of the fans or the parasol were seen.
The phrase "all directions" refers to a surveying of all quarters as if he were standing upon the seven-step stride;
however, it should not be viewed in that way. For when the Great Being was released from the hands of men and stood upon the earth, he looked toward the eastern direction.
There, thousands of world-systems became a single open space. Therein, gods and humans...
Worshipping him with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, they said: "Great Being, there is no one here even equal to you; how much less anyone superior?

Having thus surveyed the ten directions—the four cardinal points, the four intermediate points, below, and above—and seeing no one equal to himself, he proceeded facing northward in seven strides with the thought: "This is the northern direction."
In this way, the meaning here is to be understood. "Pre-eminent" (*āsabhi*) means supreme. "Foremost" (*agga*) means the very first among all in terms of qualities.

The other two phrases are synonyms for this very term. By the two phrases, "This is the last birth; now there is no further becoming," he prophesied the attainment of Arahantship to be reached within this present existence.
And herein, standing on the earth with even feet is the omen of obtaining the four bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*);
facing northward is the omen of proceeding while overwhelming and surpassing the great multitude;
taking seven steps is the omen of obtaining the seven jewels of the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*); and the holding of the divine white parasol is—
The acquisition of the excellent parasol of liberation is a precursor to being liberated by the five kinds of liberation;
the acquisition of the five insignia of royalty is a precursor to being liberated by the five liberations; the surveying of all directions is a precursor to the acquisition of unobstructed knowledge;
and the utterance of the voice of a bull is a precursor to the irreversible turning of the Wheel of Dhamma.
“It is my last birth”—this lion’s roar should be understood as the precursor to the final *parinibbāna* in the element of *nibbāna* without residue (*anupādisesa*).
These sections have been handed down in the Canon; however, the section concerning the multitude [of deities] has not yet appeared, and it should be cited and explained here.
For on the day the Great Being was born, the ten-thousandfold world system (*dasasahassilokadhātu*) shook. The deities in the ten-thousandfold world system...
They assembled from within a single world-system (*cakkavāḷa*). First the gods received [the teaching], and afterwards humans.
Lutes bound with strings and drums bound with leather resounded by themselves without being played by anyone.
The shackles and fetters of humans were broken into pieces. All diseases were stilled; they vanished like the tarnish on copper washed away by acid.
Those born blind saw forms; those born deaf heard sounds; cripples became endowed with speed;
mindfulness was established even in those who were mentally dull and mute from birth; ships sailing to foreign lands reached safe harbors;
jewels situated in the sky and on the earth shone with their own radiance; and enemies regained hearts of loving-kindness.
The fires in the Avīci hell were extinguished. Light arose in the world-intervals. Water no longer flowed in the rivers.
The water in the great ocean became sweet. The wind did not blow. Birds dwelling in the sky, on mountains, and in trees descended to the earth.
The moon shone intensely. The sun was neither hot nor cold; it was stainless and possessed of perfect seasons. The deities...
Standing at the doors of their respective celestial mansions (*vimāna*), they engaged in great festivities with clapping, shouting, and the tossing of garments.
A great rain-cloud poured down over the four continents. Neither hunger nor thirst afflicted the great multitude.
The gates and door-panels opened of their own accord. Trees bearing flowers and fruits produced blossoms and fruit. Thus it was throughout the ten-thousandfold world-system (*dasasahassilokadhātu*).
There was a single row of banners.
There too, the shaking of the ten-thousandfold world system was a premonitory sign of the attainment of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
At the time of the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, the deities gathered from a single world-system, having assembled all at once, [listened to] the Dhamma.
The acceptance [of offerings] from deities is a premonitory sign of attaining the four fine-material-sphere jhānas.
Subsequently, the acceptance [of offerings] from humans is a premonitory sign of attaining the four immaterial-sphere jhānas.
The spontaneous sounding of stringed lutes bound with cords is a premonitory sign of attaining the successive meditative dwellings (*anupubbavihāra*).
It is a foretoken. The sounding of leather-bound drums is a foretoken for the proclamation by means of the great Dhamma-drum.
The cutting of fetters and the like is a foretoken for the eradication of the conceit "I am.
The cessation of disease among the populace is a foretoken for the attainment of the Four Noble Truths. The sight of forms by those born blind is a foretoken for the attainment of the divine eye.
It is a precursor. For the deaf, the hearing of sounds is a precursor to the attainment of the divine ear-element (*dibba-sota-dhātu*).
For those who are cripples, the possession of speed is a precursor to the attainment of the four bases of psychic power (*catur-iddhipāda*).

For the dull-witted, the establishment of mindfulness is a precursor to the attainment of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catusatipaṭṭhāna*). For ships setting out upon foreign lands, the reaching of a good port is a precursor.

It is a precursor to the attainment of the four analytical knowledges (*catu-paṭisambhidā*). It is a precursor to that which shall show the world the radiance of the Dhamma—the fact that the jewels shine with their own inherent brilliance.
The acquisition of a mind of loving-kindness toward enemies is a precursor to the acquisition of the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*). In the Avīci hell...

The extinguishing of the fire is a precursor to the extinguishing of the eleven fires. The light in the intermediate space between worlds, having dispelled the darkness of ignorance, is a precursor to the vision of the light of knowledge.
The sweetness of the great ocean is a precursor to the state of being of a single flavor with the taste of Nibbāna.
The non-blowing of the wind is a precursor to the shattering of the sixty-two types of views.
The birds’ descent to the earth, having heard the exhortation of the great multitude, was a premonitory sign for going for refuge with one’s life.

The moon’s excessive radiance was a premonitory sign for being beloved by many people. The sun’s avoidance of heat and cold and its state of seasonal comfort was a premonitory sign for attaining physical and mental happiness.
[The gods] standing at the doors of their celestial mansions [and engaging in] clapping and so forth...
The sporting was the precursor to attaining the state of Buddhahood; the utterance of the *udāna* was the precursor to that *udāna*.

The raining of the great cloud over the four continents was the precursor to the raining of the great cloud of Dhamma. The absence of oppression by hunger was the precursor to obtaining the nectar of mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*).
The absence of oppression by thirst was the precursor to being blissful through the bliss of liberation.
The spontaneous opening of the city gates is a premonitory sign of the opening of the door of the Eightfold Path.
The taking of flowers and fruits by the trees is a premonitory sign of their blossoming with the flowers of liberation and being laden with the burden of the fruits of recluseship.
The entire ten-thousandfold world system being adorned with a single garland of flags is a premonitory sign of its being adorned with the garland of the noble ones' flags.
This should be understood as a "foretoken. This is called the section on many [questions].
Here they ask a question: "When the Great Man, having stood upon the earth, walked facing north on foot, and uttered the lion's roar, did he go by way of the earth or through the air? Was he seen..."
"Did he go while visible, or did he go invisibly? Did he go naked, or was he dressed in fine attire?
Did he go as a youth, or as an old man? And later on, was he still the same, or had he become a young child again?
This question, which arose in the Lower Iron Palace, was indeed answered by the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷābhaya. It is said that the Elder...
In this regard, after stating many various views based on the doctrines of destiny (*niyati*), past deeds (*pubbekata*), chance (*issara*), and creation (*nimmāna*), he finally explained it thus:
"The Great Man went by way of the earth, yet to the great multitude it was as if he were going through the sky.
He went while being visible, yet to the great multitude it was as if he were invisible. He went as a naked ascetic (*acelaka*); yet to the great multitude..."
However, he appeared as if fully adorned and prepared for a festival. Although he had departed while still young, to the great multitude he seemed about sixteen years of age;
later, however, he became like a mere child and was no longer such as he had been. And the assembly was delighted, thinking:
"The Elder has answered the question as if he were the Buddha himself. The section on the intermediate space between worlds is to be understood according to the method already stated.
Furthermore, it should be understood that these universal qualities (sabbadhammatā), explained here from the beginning, belong to all Bodhisattvas. [End of] 32.
The Description of the Marks of a Great Man (Dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇavaṇṇanā). 33.
"He saw" means he saw her brought forth and laid upon a cotton-wool mattress. "Of the Great Man" refers to him by way of birth, clan, family lineage, and so forth.
Of a great man. "Two destinations" means two ends, two accomplishments.
For this word *gati*—in the passage, "Sāriputta, there are these five destinations"—it refers to the destination to be traveled to by beings, distinguished as hell and so forth.
[In contrast,] in the passage, "Monks, I do not know the coming of these virtuous monks of beautiful character... it refers to...
In the phrase "or destination," it refers to intention (*ajjhāsaya*). In the phrase "Nirvana is the destination of the Arahant," it refers to a refuge (*paṭissaraṇa*).
In the phrase "Moreover, Brahmā, I know your destination and I know your splendor; the Brahmā Baka is so powerful," it occurs in the sense of accomplishment (*nipphatti*).
It should be understood that here too, it occurs in the sense of accomplishment. *Añaññā* means...
There is no other destiny or accomplishment [than this].
"Dhammika" means one who is endowed with the ten wholesome qualities (*dasakusaladhamma*) and is free from going on wrong paths. "Dhammarāja" is a synonym for the preceding term itself;
or, he is a "Dhamma-king" because his sovereignty was obtained through the Dhamma. "Cāturanta" refers to the eastern ocean and so forth.
He is the lord of the four-cornered earth by virtue of the four oceans. "Victorious" (*vijitāvī*) means one who has won battles.
"One who has attained the stability of his realm" (*janapadatthāvariyappatto*) means that the country has reached a state of firmness and steadiness.
For when a fierce king oppresses the world with taxes, punishments, and the like, people abandon the central provinces and flee to mountains, seashores, and similar places.

Relying on [the border], they establish their dwellings in the frontier regions. When King Atimudu is reigned, people oppressed by thieves and the plundering of their wealth through violence abandon the frontiers and establish their dwellings in the heart of the country;
thus, under such a king, the country does not attain stability. But while this prince exercises sovereignty, his country [remains] upon the surface of solid rock.
Showing that [the city] will become as firm as if it were surrounded by an iron rampart, they said: "He has attained the stability of the realm.
Regarding the phrase "endowed with the seven treasures," here a "treasure" (ratana) is so called in the sense of producing delight (rati). Furthermore:
"Wondrous, of great value, incomparable, and rare to behold;..."
"Because it is enjoyed by an incomparable being, it is therefore called a 'jewel' (ratana).
From the moment the Wheel-Jewel (cakkaratana) is produced, there is no other place for the gods;
all of them perform worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, as well as acts such as salutation toward it alone. Thus, in the sense of being honored, it is a jewel. Regarding the Wheel-Jewel...
And because there is no price for it such that one could say "it is worth this much wealth," it is a *ratana* in the sense of being of great value.
Furthermore, because the Wheel-Treasure (*cakkaratana*) is unlike any other treasures existing in the world, it is a *ratana* in the sense of being incomparable.
Moreover, since Universal Monarchs (*cakkavattin*) arise in the very same eon in which Buddhas arise, and Buddhas appear only once in a great while...
They arise; therefore, it is a treasure in the sense that its sight is difficult to obtain.
Furthermore, it is a treasure in the sense that it is enjoyed only by a sublime being who is peerless in terms of birth, beauty, lineage, sovereignty, and so forth, and not by anyone else.
Just as with the Wheel-Treasure, so it is with the remaining ones. By means of these seven treasures, [he is endowed] through their state of being an entourage...
"He is endowed with all enjoyments and requisites" means he is possessed of the seven treasures (*sattaratanasamannāgata*).

Now, in order to show their specific nature, the passage beginning "In this regard, these are... is stated. Regarding the terms "wheel-treasure" (*cakkaratana*) and so forth, this is the summary of the intended meaning:
[the glory and majesty] of the four great continents, which are surrounded by two thousand islands...
The Wheel-Treasure appears, capable of being taken up and used;
likewise, before the meal itself, the Elephant-Treasure appears, capable of traveling through the earth bounded by the ocean while moving through the air, as does the Horse-Treasure;
and [the Jewel-Treasure] appears, capable of dispelling the darkness extending for a league even in fourfold darkness and providing the sight of light.

The jewel-treasure; the woman-treasure, who acts agreeably and is free from the six kinds of defects; the householder-treasure, who is capable of discovering treasures located beneath the earth within a distance of one league;
and the counselor-treasure, known as the eldest son, who is born from the womb of the chief queen and is capable of governing the entire kingdom—all these appear.
"More than a thousand" (*parosahassaṃ*) means exceeding one thousand. "Brave" (*sūrā*) means fearless. "Heroic in limb" (*vīraṅgarūpā*): "heroic limb" (*vīraṅga*) is a term for energy (*vīriya*);
those whose form (*rūpa*) consists of such heroic limbs are "heroic in limb. They were born of energy, possessed the nature of energy, were made of energy, and were untiring;
it is said that even when fighting for a whole day, they did not grow weary. "As far as the ocean's edge" (*sāgarapariyantaṃ*).
Having made the Cakkavāḷa mountain its boundary, it extends as far as the surrounding ocean.

"Without punishment" means that those who seize even a hundred or a thousand beings for their offenses rule by means of a monetary fine; those who instruct through cutting and splitting rule by means of the sword.
But he, having abandoned both kinds of punishment, dwells without punishment. "Without the sword" means...
Those who harm others with weapons such as single-edged blades are said to rule by means of the sword. But he,
without causing even a drop of blood to flow from anyone— not even from a tiny gnat— by means of Dhamma alone,
was welcomed by rival kings with the words, "Come, Great King," and [ruled] over the earth of the aforementioned kind.
"Having completely conquered, he dwells" means that having overcome [them], he dwells as a master.
Having thus explained the first accomplishment, the words "But if... and so forth are spoken in order to explain the second.
Therein, the covering—the veil consisting of the defilements known as lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, views, and craving—is opened up and destroyed.
“Vivaṭacchada” means that which covers what is uncovered; there is also a reading “vivaṭṭacchadā,” which has the same meaning.
Having thus explained the second stage of development, the passage beginning “For this prince, O King,” was spoken in order to show the characteristics that serve as their signs.
In that context, “suppatiṭṭhitapādo” (one with well-placed feet) refers to how, unlike others, his foot [rests] upon the ground...
When they set it down, either the soles, the heels, or the toes touch the ground first, or else there is a gap in the middle;
when they lift it up, one part—such as the forepart—rises first. It is not like that for him.
Rather, his entire sole touches the ground all at once, just like the surface of a golden sandal.
He rises from the ground with a single stride; therefore, he has well-placed feet.
Regarding the "wheels": there are two wheels on the two soles of the feet, and their spokes, rims, and hubs have already been described in the text.
However, by the phrase "complete in all aspects," this distinction is to be understood: it is said that of those wheels, [the details] of the soles of the feet...
The hub is visible; the circular rim demarcating the hub is visible; the band encircling the face of the hub is visible;
the opening of the axle-hole is visible; the spokes are visible; the circular lines on the spokes are visible; and the jeweled rim is visible.
This much, for now, is exactly as it appears in the text. However, the section concerning the "many" has not been included; it should be understood as follows:
— the spear, the śrīvatsa, the *nandi*, the *sovattika* flower, the ear-ornament, the *vaḍḍhamānaka* vessel, the pair of fish, the auspicious throne,
the hook, the palace, the archway, the white parasol, the sword, the palm-leaf fan, the peacock-feather fan,
the yak-tail whisk, the turban, the jewel, the bowl, the jasmine garland, the blue lotus, the red lotus, the white lotus, and the *paduma*.
The white lotus, the full water-jar, the full bowl, the ocean, the world-system, the Himalayas, Sineru, the moon and sun, the constellations,
the four great continents, the two thousand minor islands, and even including the assembly of a universal monarch—
all these are merely the retinue of the mark of the wheel.
"Long heels" means having long heels; the sense is that they are complete.
For while the forefeet of others are long such that the shank rests upon the top of the heel, as if the heel had been cut away and set there, it is not so for the Great Man.
For the Great Man, two of the four parts constitute the forefoot, and the third...
The foot rests upon the shank; in the fourth part, the heel is like a ball of red wool-cloth, as if placed there after being rounded with a file.
Regarding "long fingers": whereas for others some fingers are long and some are short, it is not so for the Great Man.
For the Great Man, however, the fingers and toes are long like those of a monkey, thick at the base and tapering gradually.
At the tips they are slender; having been rubbed with resinous oil, they become like rolled haritāla sticks. Therefore it is said: “long-fingered.
Regarding “soft and delicate hands and feet”: they are as soft as a layer of cotton that has been soaked in clarified butter and beaten a hundred times.
And just as they are now for one who has only just been born, so too at the time of old age they will remain soft and delicate.
"Soft and tender hands and feet" means that his hands and feet are soft and tender. "Webbed hands and feet" does not mean having fingers connected by skin.

For one such as Phaṇahatthaka, being impaired by a personal defect, did not obtain admission to the religious life; however, for a Great Man, the four fingers of each hand—and indeed all five—[are webbed].
The toes are of equal length; because they are of equal length, the mark of a barley grain stands between them, piercing one another.
Furthermore, his hands and feet are like latticed windows constructed by a skilled carpenter.
Therefore it is said: "He has webbed hands and feet."
Because the ankles are positioned above [the insteps], his feet are "turned upward" (ussaṅkha); thus he is "one with turned-up feet" (ussaṅkhapāda).
For in others, the ankles are on the back of the foot; therefore, their feet are bound as if by a bolt, they cannot be turned freely, and when they walk, even the soles of their feet are not visible.
But in the Great Man, having ascended, the ankles are above.
They stand firm; therefore, from the navel upwards, his upper body remains as motionless as a golden statue placed on a ship, while only the lower part moves.
His feet turn with ease, and the soles of his feet are visible to those standing and watching from the front, the back, or both sides, not only from behind as is the case with elephants.
"Eṇijaṅgha" means one whose shanks resemble those of the eṇi deer; his shanks are full due to the accumulation of flesh, not being masses of flesh bound together on one side.
The meaning is that he is endowed with well-rounded shanks, encircled by flesh that is evenly distributed all around, resembling the bellies of rice or barley ears.
"Anonamanto" means "not bending"; by this, his state of being neither hunchbacked nor dwarfed is indicated.
For the rest of humanity is either hunchbacked or dwarfed; the upper body of hunchbacks is incomplete, while the lower body of dwarfs is incomplete.
Because their bodies are incomplete, they are unable to rub their knees without bending over. But the Great Man—
Because both his bodies are fully developed, he is able [to conceal].

"With the male organ concealed in a sheath" (*kosohitavatthaguyha*): because his male organ (*vatthaguyha*) is placed within and concealed by a sheath (*kosa*) resembling the pericarp of a golden lotus, like that of a bull or an elephant, he is "one whose male organ is concealed in a sheath. "The male organ" (*vatthaguyha*) refers to that which is covered by the cloth.
The "private parts" (*aṅgajāta*) are said to be that which is to be concealed.
"Golden-colored" means resembling a solid golden image that has been rubbed with natural vermilion, polished with a leopard’s fang, and treated with red chalk;
this is the meaning. By this, his body's density, glossiness, and smoothness are demonstrated.
It is said that "the skin is like gold" for the purpose of showing the color of the complexion; or rather, this is a synonym for the preceding term.
"Dust and dirt" means either dust or grime. "Is not smeared" means it does not adhere; it rolls off like a drop of water from a lotus leaf.
However, the washing of hands and so forth is for the purpose of observing the proper time and for the sake of the fruit of merit for the donors.
And the Buddhas do this, and they certainly do it even by way of observing the proper conduct (*vatta*). For it has been said:
"A bhikkhu entering a dwelling should enter after having washed his feet.

"With hair standing on end" (*uddhaggaloma*): he is one whose body hairs stand erect at the conclusion of a smile, as if looking up toward the beauty of his face; thus he is "one with hair standing on end."
"Brahmujugatto" means straight-limbed like Brahmā; his body will be straight and tall.
For most beings bend at three places—the shoulders, the waist, and the knees.
Those who bend at the waist bend backward, while those who bend at the other two places bend forward. Furthermore, some tall-bodied individuals are crooked on one side, while others...
Lifting up their faces, they move about as if counting the constellations;
some, with little flesh and blood, become like spikes, while others lean forward and go along trembling.
But this one, having risen straight up, will be of great length, like a golden archway erected in a city of the gods—thus they declare. And just as this is so...

Thus, it should be understood that whichever mark of a Great Man (mahāpurisalakkhaṇa) was entirely incomplete at birth, that very mark was spoken of with reference to its being developed in such a way in the future.
"Seven protuberances" refers to these seven places: the two backs of the hands, the two backs of the feet, the two shoulders, and the crown of the head.
"He has flesh well-filled in seven places" means that he is *sattussada*.

In other people, however, a network of veins is visible on the backs of the hands and feet, and the ends of the bones are visible on the shoulders and the back of the neck; such persons appear like ghosts.
But the Great Man (*mahāpurisa*) is not so; rather, because his flesh is well-filled in seven places, the networks of veins are hidden in him.
With a torso that resembles a well-fashioned golden pillar turned on a lathe by the backs of hands and other tools, it appears like a stone statue and like a figure in painting.
"Sīhapubbaddhakāyo" means one whose body is like the forepart of a lion; for it is only the front part of the lion's body [that is meant].

[In others] the front part of the body is complete, while the back part is incomplete; but for the Great Man who is like a lion, the entire body is complete, just like the forepart of a lion’s body. Furthermore, it is not ill-formed or distorted through being bent or protruding here and there as in a lion’s [body];
rather, it is long where length is appropriate, and long, short, thick, thin, broad, or rounded where those respective qualities are appropriate.
He becomes exactly like that. For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Monks, when the ripening of karma that is pleasing presents itself, those limbs which shine when long become long; those limbs which shine when short become short."
“Those limbs by which he shines when they are thick become thick;
those limbs by which he shines when they are thin become thin; those limbs by which he shines when they are broad become broad;
those limbs by which he shines when they are rounded become rounded.”

Thus, the physical form of the Great Man, fashioned by a mind of merit through various thoughts and adorned with the ten perfections, cannot be matched even in appearance by anyone in the world, whether they be masters of all crafts or possessors of all supernatural powers.
*Citantaraṃso*: "antaraṃsa" refers to the space between the two shoulders; he whose such space is "cita," meaning full, is called *citantaraṃso*.
For in others, that place is sunken, [the space] between the two shoulder-blades.

They appear as distinct [features]. However, in the case of a Great Man, from the waist upwards, a layer of flesh rises up to the shoulders and remains covering the back like an elevated golden plank.
"Symmetrical like a banyan tree" means being symmetrical like a banyan tree; just as [a banyan tree] is fifty cubits or a hundred cubits in circumference...
Or, just as a banyan tree with its trunk and branches is of one and the same measure both in length and in breadth, so too his body and his fathom-length are of one and the same measure.
The meaning is that, unlike the bodies of others which may be long or wide, his is not of uneven measure.
For this very reason it was said: "As far as his body extends," and so forth. In that context, *yāvatako assa* means "as far as his [body] is."
"Evenly rounded trunk" means a trunk that is perfectly rounded.

Unlike some cranes, herons, and boars, whose necks are long, crooked, or broad, and upon whom a network of veins becomes visible when they speak and from whom only a weak sound issues, it is not so with the Great Man.
Rather, the Great Man’s [trunk] is like a well-polished golden tube.
It is a trunk; at the time of speaking, the network of veins is not visible, and his voice is as great as the thundering of a cloud.

Regarding the term *rasaggasaggī*: here, they are called *rasaggasā* because they swallow (*gasanti*) or carry away (*haranti*) the taste (*rasa*). This is a designation for the taste-carrying channels (*rasaharaṇī*); he who has these as his "peaks" (*aggā*) is a *rasaggasaggī*.
It is said that a Great Man has seventeen thousand taste-carrying channels directed upwards.
[These robes] were fastened around his neck. Even a morsel of food the size of a sesame seed, when placed on the tip of the tongue, suffuses the entire body.
For that very reason, while he was exerting himself in the Great Struggle, his body was sustained even by a single grain of rice or by a mere spoonful of pea-soup.
But because others lack such [power], the nutritive essence does not pervade their entire bodies. Therefore...
They are subject to many afflictions.

"Having a jaw like that of a lion" means *sīhahanu*. In that regard, while only the lower jaw of a lion is full and not the upper one, for the Great Man, both are as full as the lower jaw of a lion, like the full moon on the twelfth day.
They are like the moon of a lunar fortnight. Then the physiognomists, looking as far as the jaw, observed:
"In these jaws, forty teeth—twenty below and twenty above—will be established, even and without gaps," and they said:
"Sire, this prince has forty teeth," and so forth. In this regard, the meaning is as follows: for even though others may have complete teeth...
Ordinarily there are thirty-two teeth; however, this one will have forty.
Furthermore, while the teeth of others are uneven—some being high and some low—his will be even, like a conch shell cut smooth by an iron file.
While the teeth of other crocodiles are sparse when they are eating fish and meat, [his will be otherwise].

[Ordinary people] fill the gaps between their teeth. However, his teeth will be without gaps, like a row of diamonds set upon a golden plate, appearing as if demarcated by a fine brush. Furthermore, the teeth of others become decayed;
consequently, some of their fangs turn black or discolored. But he has perfectly white fangs, surpassing even the starlight of medicinal herbs.
Having transcended [all other lights], his teeth will be endowed with a radiance that shines forth.

"Possessing a large tongue" means having a broad tongue. While the tongues of others may be thick, thin, short, stiff, or uneven, the tongue of a Great Man is soft, long, broad, and perfect in color. For he—this...

To dispel the doubts of those who have come seeking to examine his marks, he rolls that tongue—because of its softness—like a stiff needle and touches both nostril apertures; because of its length, it touches both ear apertures;
and because of its breadth, it covers even the entire forehead up to the hairline. Such is the quality of its softness, length, and breadth.
By explaining [this], he dispels their doubt. Thus, with reference to the tongue endowed with these three characteristics, it is said:
"possessing a large tongue. Regarding "Brahma-voiced": others may have voices that are broken, cracked, or like the cawing of a crow;
however, this one will be endowed with a voice resembling the voice of Mahābrahmā, for Mahābrahmā’s voice is not obstructed by bile or phlegm.
The sound becomes pure. Even an action performed by a Great Man purifies its basis.
Because the basis is purified, the sound arising from the navel onwards arises endowed with all eight qualities.
One who speaks like a *karavīka* bird is called "one whose speech is like a *karavīka*"; the meaning is that his sweet voice is like the song of a rutting *karavīka*.
"Abhinīlanetta" (one with deep blue eyes) does not mean that his entire eye is blue;

rather, in the places where blue is appropriate, his eyes are endowed with an extremely pure blue color resembling the *umā* flower; in the places where yellow is appropriate, they have a yellow color resembling the *kaṇikāra* flower;

in the places where red is appropriate, they have a red color resembling the *bandhujīvaka* flower; and in the places where white is appropriate, they resemble the star of the healing herb (*osadhitāraka*).
They are endowed with white color, and in the places appropriate for black, they possess a black color resembling the *addāriṭṭhaka* fruit.
In the golden celestial mansion (*suvaṇṇavimāna*), they appear like an open jeweled lion-lattice.
Regarding the term "cow-eyelashes" (*gopakhuma*): here, "eyelashes" (*pakhuma*) refers to the entire eye-organ; that [organ] is like the eyelash of a black calf.
It possesses thick eyelashes; it is clear like that of a young red calf;
the meaning is that the organ of the eye is like that of a newborn young red calf of that very moment. For the eye-organs of others are incomplete;

they are endowed with eyes that protrude and are deep, resembling those of elephants, mice, and so forth. But the eye of the Great Man is like a gem-sphere that has been washed and polished and set in place.
The eyes are as if covered with very soft, smooth, dark blue, and fine eyelashes.
*Uṇṇā* refers to the hair of the ūrṇā. "Between the eyebrows" means it grows precisely on the bridge of the nose between the two eyebrows;
having risen up, it grows in the middle of the forehead. "White" means pure, with a color like that of the medicinal herb *osadhi* or a star. "Soft" means...

Having been immersed in the cream of clarified butter, it resembles a layer of cotton that has been beaten a hundred times. "Resembling tula-cotton" means it is equal to the tula-wool of the *simbali* tree;
this is the simile for its whiteness. When grasped by the tip and pulled, it reaches the length of half an arm;
when released, it curls back to the right, stands upright, and remains fixed. In the middle of the golden slab—

It shines with a most enchanting splendor, like a silver bubble set aside, like a stream of milk flowing from a golden vessel, and like the morning star in a portion of the sky illuminated by the light of dawn.
The term "with a protuberant head" (*uṇhīsasīsa*) is used with reference to two purposes: the fullness of the forehead and the fullness of the head.
It has been said. For from the right ear-apex of the Great Man, a fold of flesh rose up, covering and filling the entire forehead, and having gone there, it settled upon the left ear-apex;
this shone like the turban-band of a king. Indeed, it is said that upon seeing this mark of the Great Man, kings fashioned their turbans.
This, first, is one meaning. Other people, however, have heads that are incomplete;

some have heads like monkeys', some like fruits, some like bones, some like elephants', some like gourds, and some like mountain slopes. But the head of the Great Man is perfectly complete, as if turned on a lathe with a turning tool, resembling a water bubble.
In this regard, according to the first method, he is "uṇhīsa-sīsa" because his head is like one wrapped in a turban (*uṇhīsa*).
According to the second method, he is "uṇhīsa-sīsa" because his head is perfectly rounded in every respect, like a turban. This concludes the commentary on the name Vipassī.
37. Regarding the phrase "with all desires": this was stated as if it were something done afterwards after having had the marks examined, but it should not be viewed in that way.
Rather, it should be understood that he first satisfied those fortune-tellers and only afterwards had the examination of the marks performed.
The detailed account of this has already been given in the *Gabbhokkantika* (The Descent into the Womb). "They suckle" means they give milk to drink.
It is said that he appointed sixty nurses endowed with faultless and sweet milk;
likewise, for the other various tasks, he appointed sixty-six who were skilled in each of them.
He appointed sixty men as messengers to these women, and sixty ministers to observe whether each task had been performed or not. Thus, there were four groups of sixty.
There were sixty attendants for the women and sixty for the men; thus, there were sixty attendants in total. "The white umbrella" refers to a divine white umbrella.
However, the family-inheritance umbrella remains in the inner chamber itself. In phrases such as "may cold not [overcome] him," the meaning should be understood as "may it not prevail over him.
"Svāssudaṃ" means "he was indeed that. "From lap to lap" means from the lap of one person to the lap of another.
"Arm to arm" means one person's arm [is placed] against another's arm; "shoulder to shoulder" means one person's shoulder-blade against another's shoulder-blade.
"Is carried around" means it is led, which has the sense of being brought along.
38. "Melodious-voiced" means one whose voice is not harsh. "Harmonious-voiced" means one whose voice is clever and skillful. "Sweet-voiced" means one whose voice is pleasant.

"Pleasant-voiced" means a voice that produces affection. Regarding the sweetness of the voice of the *karavīka* birds, it is said that when these *karavīka* birds strike a ripe mango fruit with their beaks and drink the juice as it flows out, they clap their wings and warble;
at that time, even the four-footed animals begin to frolic as if intoxicated. Even those four-footed creatures intent on foraging—
Having cast aside the grass in their mouths, wild beasts listen to that sound;
pursuing small deer, they stand still without even setting down their raised feet; and the deer being pursued abandon the fear of death and stand still;
even birds soaring in the sky remain with their wings spread, listening to that sound; and in the water...
Even fish, clearing their ear-drums, remain there listening to that sound. Such is the sweet voice of the karavīka bird.
Queen Asandhimittā, the consort of King Dhammāsoka, asked the Saṅgha: "Venerable sirs, is there anyone whose voice is equal to the voice of a Buddha?
"There is, the voice of the karavīka bird. "Where, venerable sirs, is that bird? "In the Himalayas."
She said to the king, "Your Majesty, I wish to see the karavīka bird.
The king released the golden cage, saying, "Let the karavīka come and sit within this cage. The cage went and stood before a certain karavīka.
He thought, "The cage has come by the king's command; it is not possible not to go," and so he entered there.
He sat down. Pañjara came and stood before the king. They were unable to make the karavīka birds utter their song.
Then the king asked, "My good man, why do these not make a sound? [The man replied,] "Because they have not seen their kinsmen, Your Majesty.
Then the king had him surrounded by mirrors. Seeing his own reflection and thinking, "My kinsmen have come," he—
Striking the palm with his claw and blowing his jeweled horn as if playing it, he let out a cry.
All the people in the city frolicked as if intoxicated. Asandhimittā thought:
"If even this animal’s voice is so sweet, what must the voice of the Blessed One have been like when he attained the glory of omniscient knowledge?"
Having generated rapture and not relinquishing that rapture, he established himself in the fruit of stream-entry together with seven hundred followers.

Thus, it is said that the sound of the karavīka bird is sweet; however, it should be understood that the voice of Prince Vipassī was even sweeter than that, by a hundredfold and a thousandfold degree.

39. "Born of the ripening of kamma" means it is not produced by meditation (*bhāvanāmaya*). Rather, by way of the ripening of kamma, the fleshly eye (*maṃsacakkhu*) of the deities became exactly like the divine eye;
by means of this, having made a sign, one is able to pick out and give back even a single sesame seed placed in a cartload of sesame, saying, "This is that one.
40. Regarding "Vipassī," this is the etymological meaning: it is pure because of the absence of darkness produced by intermittent closing [of the eyes].

He sees, and he sees with open eyes, thus he is Vipassī; in the second sense, he sees having discerned repeatedly, thus he is Vipassī—the meaning being that he sees having investigated again and again.
Furthermore, "he goes toward the goal" (*atthe āyati*) means he knows and sees the goal, or he leads and sets it in motion—this is the meaning. One day, it is said...
As the king sat in the place of judgment instructing on legal matters, they brought the Great Man, adorned and prepared, and placed him in the king’s hands.
While the king was holding him in his lap and fondling him, the ministers made the master masterless.
The Bodhisatta let out a cry of distress. The king said, “What is this? Investigate!”

While they were thus holding onto it, not seeing anything else, they thought, "This must have been done because of the difficulty of determining the owner's wealth," and so they made the owner once again the actual owner.
Then, testing him further by thinking, "Does the prince act this way only after he has recognized [the object]?
they made the owner once more a non-owner. Again, the Bodhisatta let out the same sound. Then the King—
“‘The Great Man knows’—from that time forth he became diligent. It is with reference to this that it was said:
‘Having discerned and discerned, the prince proceeds toward his goal.
Regarding the terms *vassika* and so forth: that which is pleasant to dwell in during the rainy season is called *vassika*. The same applies to the others.”
The same method applies here. This, however, is the etymological explanation: *vassāvāsa* means the rains; one who is worthy of the rains is *vassika*.
The same method applies to the other terms as well.
In that regard, a *vassika* mansion is neither too high nor too low, and its doors and windows are neither too numerous nor too sparse.
In this case, even floor coverings, rugs, and various kinds of food—both hard and soft—are permitted as long as they are mixed [with other items].
During the winter, the pillars and walls are low, the doors and windows are thin with fine lattices, and wall-protrusions are constructed for the purpose of admitting warmth.
Furthermore, the floor coverings, rugs, undergarments, and upper robes used here—
Warm and powerful materials such as woolen blankets and the like are appropriate. Food and drink should be rich, pungent, and provided with plenty of water.
In summer houses, the pillars and walls are high, while the doors and windows are numerous and spacious;
floor coverings and the like made of fine linen (dukūla) are appropriate. The food and drink should be filled with sweet flavors.
And here, having placed nine water-vessels near the Vātapāna [Hall], they fill them with water and cover them with blue lotuses and other flowers.
In various places they construct water-channels from which streams of water gush forth like rain falling from the heavens.
"Nippurisehi" means devoid of men. And here, it is not only the musical instruments that are devoid of men; all the locations as well are devoid of men.
There were no men at all; even the doorkeepers were women, and even those who performed services such as bathing were women.
It is said that the king, thinking, "When my son experiences such abundance of sovereignty and happiness, the sight of a man might give rise to suspicions regarding other men;
let this not happen to him," appointed only women for all duties.
The commentary on the first recitation section is finished.
43. Commentary on the Old Man:
In the second recitation section, "crooked like a rafter" (*gopānasivaṅka*) means crooked like a rafter. "Bent" (*bhogga*) refers to the shoulders and the waist.
"Bent like a bow" means curved at three places: the knees, the waist, and the neck. "Staff-dependent" means having the staff as one's destination, having the staff as one's refuge.
"Afflicted" means afflicted by old age. "Past youth" means having transcended youth, standing in the final stage of life.
"Having seen" means when the chariot, though surrounded by a military force measuring half a *yojana* and well-guarded, [proceeded].
The chariot was in front and the army behind; in such a place, by their own power, the Suddhāvāsa Brahmas whose taints were exhausted manifested that man right before the chariot.

Having seen that man, it is said that the Suddhāvāsas thought, "The Great Man is stuck in the five strands of sensual pleasure like an elephant in the mud; we shall arouse mindfulness in him," and so they showed him. And thus he was shown.
Both the Bodhisatta and the charioteer saw him. For the Brahmās had shown him there for the sake of the Bodhisatta’s heedfulness and for the sake of the conversation and dialogue with the charioteer.
"What is this? he asked; "This is an old man"—what was meant by this?—"I have never seen such a person before, sir," he replied.

“Then indeed”: “If I too must have such hair and such a body, then indeed, dear charioteer, enough of going to the pleasure grove today”—with a heart agitated by distress, he spoke thus in accordance with his agitation:
“We were going thinking, ‘Today we shall see the pleasure grove,’ but enough of that pleasure grove. “He went to the inner palace” means [he went] to the womenfolk.
Having dismissed [the assembly], he sat alone in the inner chamber. "Yatra hi nāma" means: "May that birth, in the presence of which aging is perceived, be woe unto it!
May it be despised! This birth is loathsome! Thus, as if pierced in the heart by the first arrow, he sat down, digging up the very root of birth.
45. "Having summoned the charioteer" means that from the time the fortune-tellers spoke, the king wandered about with his ears strained for news;
hearing that "the prince, while going to the park, has turned back on the way," he summoned the charioteer.
Regarding the words "May it not be so," etc., [he thought]: "Let him rule the kingdom; let him not go forth; let the word of the brahmins not come true."
The meaning is that he thought thus.
47. Regarding the description of the man afflicted by disease:
"He saw" means he saw what was shown by the Suddhāvāsa deities in the manner previously described. "Afflicted" means [afflicted] by that which breaks up the postures (*iriyāpatha*).
"Afflicted" means afflicted by contrary suffering. "Pained" means pained by the suffering of disease. "Seriously ill" means extremely sick. "Mired" means submerged.
Regarding the words "old age will be manifest, disease will be manifest":
here too, that birth in which these two are manifest is to be condemned; thus, one digs up the root of birth, thinking, "Non-birth is security."
He sat down, as if pierced by a second arrow.
50. *Vilāta* means a palanquin (*sivika*).
*Peta* means one who has departed from here. *Kālaṅkata* means one for whom time has been made; that is, by him, however much [time]...
The meaning is: having completed and brought to an end all that ought to be lived throughout one’s lifespan, he has died.

Brahmās showed this to him as well, in the same manner as before. Regarding the phrase “yatra hi nāma” (for when): here too, since this [fact] is perceived when there is birth, that birth is to be condemned;
thus, as if pierced by a third arrow, he sat down digging up the root of birth, thinking, “Non-birth is security.”
The Description of Going Forth (Pabbajitavaṇṇanā) 52.
“Bhaṇḍu” means one with a shaven head. The Brahmās showed this to him as well in the same manner as before.

Regarding the phrases beginning with “Excellent is the practice of the Dhamma,” they thought, “O King, this state of practicing the Dhamma is excellent,” and thus [they spoke] regarding each word, saying, “He has gone forth.”
The construction [of the sentence] should be understood. All of these are indeed synonyms for the ten courses of wholesome action (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*).

At the end, however, "non-violence" (*avihiṃsā*) is the preliminary stage of compassion (*karuṇā*); "sympathy" (*anukampā*) is the preliminary stage of loving-kindness (*mettā*). The particle *tenahi* is used in the sense of exhortation.
For, having seen him who has gone forth, his mind became inclined toward the going-forth (*pabbajjā*). Then, wishing to converse with him—
Having made the offering, he spoke the words beginning with "Therefore indeed" (*tena hi*) while dispatching the charioteer.
[This concludes] the commentary on the Bodhisatta’s renunciation. 54.
Then, O monks—[referring to the passage] beginning with "For one who has gone forth, the practice of the Dhamma is good," and much else besides—
Having heard a discourse on the Dhamma concerning the disadvantages of living in a household crowded with wife and children while being guarded by a great multitude of people,
and concerning the advantages of seclusion for one who has gone forth and dwells at ease in the forest like a deer,
Prince Vipassī desired to go forth. Then, monks, Prince Vipassī addressed his charioteer.
Having seen these four sights, one is called "one who has gone forth"—this is indeed the lineage, the tradition, and the succession of all Bodhisattvas.
Other Bodhisattvas, like this Prince Vipassī, see them only after a long, long time.
But our Bodhisattva, having seen all four on a single day, went forth in the Great Renunciation.
Having gone forth on the bank of the Anomā River, he reached Rājagaha. There, when King Bimbisāra asked him, "For what purpose, wise one, have you gone forth? he replied:
"Having seen one aged, one suffering, and one diseased..."
Having seen death and the exhaustion of the lifespan,
and having seen one who has gone forth clad in saffron robes,
therefore, O King, I have gone forth.
Commentary on the Great Multitude’s Going Forth (Mahājanakāya-anupabbajjā-vaṇṇanā): 55.
“Having heard them” means that after hearing those eighty-four thousand beings, this thought occurred [to him]. “Oraka” means inferior, deficient, or lowly.
“Anupabbajiṃsu” means they went forth following [him]. But why is it not stated here in the same way as it is later regarding Khaṇḍa and Tissa?
Regarding "not going forth": it was said, "having departed from the royal capital of Bandhumatī," yet why is it not stated thus [in this context]?
Because they heard [the news] after having departed. Indeed, all these were the retinue of Prince Vipassī's attendants;
having come to pay their respects early in the morning and not seeing the prince, they went for their breakfast, and having returned after eating their meal—
Having asked, "Where is the prince? and heard that he had gone to the park grounds, they thought, "We shall see him right there.

As they were departing, they saw the charioteer returning; hearing his words, "The prince has gone forth," they immediately removed all their ornaments at the very spot where they had heard the news, and had yellow saffron-colored robes brought from a shop.
Having shaved off their hair and beard, they went forth. Thus, because it was heard that he had gone out from the city and stayed outside the city, it is not stated here:
"having departed from the royal capital of Bandhumatī. Regarding the phrase "he wandered on a journey":

having constructed great pavilions wherever he went, and having received invitations for the following day from people who came and requested alms, he wandered on his journey for four months, accepting only such alms as were thus solicited.
"Surrounded by a crowd" means he was encircled by this group. But when did this thought arise in the Bodhisatta?
It was on the fourteenth day, [thinking] "Tomorrow will be the full moon of Visākha. At that time, it is said, he thought:
"Just as these people used to follow me about when I was a householder, they do so now as well; what is the use of this crowd? Thus, regarding attachment to social circles...
Feeling weary, he thought, "I shall go this very day. But then he reconsidered: "Today is not the right time;
if I go now, everyone will find out. I shall go tomorrow.
On that day, the villagers of a village similar to Uruvelā invited him for the following morning's meal. They [invited] those eighty-four thousand renunciants as well.

And they prepared milk-rice for the Great Man alone. Then, on the following day, the Great Man, having performed his meal duties in that very village together with those who had gone forth, went back to his dwelling place.
There, those who had gone forth performed their services for the Great Man and each went to their own night-quarters and day-quarters.
They entered. The Bodhisatta also, having entered the leaf-hut, sat down.
[He thought: "At this time when midday stands, while the birds are sitting still, the great forest seems to be whispering; that fear appears to me."

At such a time—a time of fear for all beings, a time when they were longing for peace—he thought, "This is the moment," and having departed, he closed the door of his leaf-hut and set out toward the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Even on other occasions, while wandering in that place, he had seen the seat of enlightenment, yet his mind had never previously inclined toward sitting there. That—
On that day, however, his knowledge had reached full maturity; therefore, seeing the Bodhimanda adorned, his mind arose with the intention to ascend it.

Approaching from the southern direction and circumambulating it clockwise, he prepared a cross-legged seat fourteen cubits high on the eastern side. Resolving upon the fourfold energy, he thought: "Until I have become a Buddha..."
Having made the promise, "I will not eat; I shall not rise from this place," he sat down.
This was said with reference to his seclusion: "Alone, withdrawn from the crowd, he dwelt.
"They came by another way"—it is said that they, having come in the evening to attend upon the Bodhisatta, surrounded the leaf-hut.
Having sat down and said, “It has become too late; let us investigate,” they opened the leaf-hut. Not seeing him, they did not pursue him, asking, “Where has he gone?
Instead, they said, “I believe this Great Man is weary of living in a group and wishes to dwell alone;
we shall see him only when he has become a Buddha,” and set out on a journey toward the interior of Jambudīpa.
The Commentary on the Bodhisatta’s Abiding: 57.
“Having gone to dwell” means having gone to dwell for one night at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). “Having gone into seclusion” means having gone to a private place.
“Being in retreat” means being hidden through a state of solitude. “Affliction” means suffering. “Passes away and reappears.”
Furthermore, this dyad is stated with reference to successive death and rebirth-linking. Regarding the phrase "of aging-and-death":
since he went forth after seeing only those who were aged and afflicted by disease, aging-and-death alone appeared to him.
Therefore he said, "of aging-and-death. Thus, for one who has become obsessed, taking aging-and-death as the root—
As if descending from the peak of existence—then, monks, this occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:

"Yoniso-manasikāra" means skillful attention, appropriate attention, and fundamental attention. For when one attends to impermanence and so forth precisely as impermanent and so forth, that is indeed called "yoniso-manasikāra.
And he [reflected]: "In the presence of what do birth and the rest come to be? In the absence of what..."
Because it proceeds by way of the contemplation of rise and fall (*udayabbayānupassanā*), it is one of those [contemplations].
Therefore, from this reasoned attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) of his, through this attention as a means (*upāyamanasikāra*), there was a convergence of wisdom (*paññā*).
When that wisdom of the Bodhisatta exists, aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) come to be; thus, there was a meeting with that cause of aging and death. But what is that?
Birth. Therefore he said: “When there is birth, aging-and-death comes to be.
The meaning here is that the Bodhisatta’s meeting with that wisdom which discerns the cause of aging-and-death took place. All the other phrases are to be understood by this same method.
As for the statement, “When there is name-and-form, consciousness exists,” it refers here to both “when there are volitional formations, consciousness exists” and “when there is ignorance...”
One might say that "formations" (*saṅkhārā*) should be mentioned, yet neither of these two has been included. Why?
Because ignorance and formations constitute past existence; insight (*vipassanā*) does not cohere with them. For the Great Man (the Bodhisatta) was intent upon the present.
But is it not the case that it would be impossible for him to become a Buddha if ignorance and formations were not seen?
"It is not possible [to know] the truth; however, this has been seen by you through the lens of existence, clinging, and craving.
At this point, a detailed exposition on dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) should be told. That, moreover, has already been explained in the *Visuddhimagga*.
58. "It turns back" means it returns. But which consciousness here turns back? Even the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi-viññāṇa*).

There is also insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*). In this context, rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi-viññāṇa*) turns back from its condition, while insight-knowledge turns back from its object.
Neither of these two transcends name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); neither goes beyond name-and-form.
Up to this point—in the phrases "might be born" and so forth—consciousness exists as a condition for name-and-form, and name-and-form exists as a condition for consciousness.
When both [conditions] exist as mutual conditions (*aññamaññapaccaya*), by this much alone one would be born...
pe ...or would be reborn. Beyond this, what else could be born... pe ...or could be reborn? Is it not the case that precisely this is born...
pe ...and is reborn? Having thus shown the five terms together with the successive fallings away (*cuti*) and linkings-on (*paṭisandhi*), again—
Concluding the meaning thus stated by saying, "That is to say: with name-and-form as condition, consciousness;

with consciousness as condition, name-and-form," he then spoke the passage beginning with "with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases," etc., in order to show—in accordance with the method of positive conditions—that even in the future, birth, aging, and death have their root in name-and-form through the condition of consciousness. Therein, of the whole...
"The origin of the mass of suffering" means the arising of the entire heap of suffering, which is divided into birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
Thus, the Great Man saw the arising of the entire suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
"The origin, the origin," he said; "the arising, the arising," he said. "In things unheard of before" means in things not previously heard.

Regarding the phrase "the eye arose" (*cakkhuṃ udapādi*) and so forth among those things never heard before: it is a designation for the wisdom that sees the arising [of the truths]. It is called "eye" (*cakkhu*) in the sense of seeing;
"knowledge" (*ñāṇa*) in the sense of making known; "wisdom" (*paññā*) in the sense of understanding;

"true knowledge" (*vijjā*) in the sense of having arisen by piercing through and breaking out from [ignorance]; and "light" (*āloka*) in the sense of illumination. As it is said: "The eye arose in the sense of seeing."
"Knowledge arose" means in the sense of knowing. "Wisdom arose" means in the sense of understanding.

"True insight arose" means in the sense of penetration. "Light arose" means in the sense of radiance. The phenomenon of the eye has the meaning of seeing as its purpose. The phenomenon of knowledge has the meaning of knowing as its purpose.
The phenomenon of wisdom has the meaning of understanding as its purpose. The phenomenon of true insight has the meaning of penetration as its purpose. The phenomenon of light...
"The meaning is the sense of illumination. What is expressed by these words? Only the mere recognition of conditions—namely, "when this exists, that comes to be"—is expressed.
Alternatively, it is the nascent insight (*vipassanā*) that has entered the path that is expressed.
61. "This has been attained by me": "this" refers to the path; "path" refers to the path of insight (*vipassanā*); "for awakening" means...
It is for the purpose of awakening to the Four Noble Truths, or indeed for the purpose of awakening to Nibbāna. Furthermore, it "awakens," thus it is *bodhi*;

this is a name for the Noble Path, and so it is also said to be "for the sake of that. For the Noble Path has its root in insight (*vipassanā*) and the path [of practice]. Now, pointing out that path as the means of deliverance, he said: "That is to say, the cessation of name-and-form," and so forth. And herein, by the phrases beginning with "the cessation of consciousness," etc.,...
By means of these individual terms, only *nibbāna* itself is described. Thus, the Great Man saw the non-arising and cessation of the entire suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
“Cessation, cessation indeed”: this means non-arising, non-origination. The terms beginning with “the eye” have already had their meaning explained.
Here, however, by all these terms, there is merely the recognition of cessation in the sense that: “When this is not, that does not come to be.”
It has been said; or rather, it is said that there is powerful insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanā*).
"At another time" means after having thus understood both the condition and the cessation of the condition, at a subsequent stage.

"In the aggregates of clinging" (*upādānakkhandhesu*) means in the aggregates which have become the conditions for clinging. "Contemplating rise and fall" (*udayabbayānupassī*) means [contemplating] that very same...
"First, dwelling while contemplating both arising and passing away"—he dwelt carrying the insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā*) which has reached its culmination.

Why was this said? For all Bodhisattvas who have fulfilled the perfections (*pāramī*), on the very day their son is born in their final existence, go forth from the great renunciation, leave the household life, and apply themselves to the supreme effort (*padhāna*).
Having ascended the Bodhi throne and shattered the army of Māra, they recollect their past lives during the first watch of the night;

they purify the divine eye during the second watch; and during the third watch, having comprehended the principle of conditionality and emerged from the fourth jhāna based on mindfulness of breathing, they focus upon the five aggregates and, by way of their arising and passing away, perceive the fifty characteristics.
Having developed insight up to the knowledge of the lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa), they penetrate all the qualities of a Buddha by means of the Noble Path.
This Great Being, having fulfilled the perfections and performed all the aforementioned stages in due order, arose from the fourth jhāna on mindfulness of breathing in the last watch of the night;
he then focused upon the five aggregates and practiced the aforementioned insight into their arising and passing away.
It begins. To demonstrate that, this was said.

Therein, "this is form" (*iti rūpaṃ*) means: taking as the starting point both the essential nature of being afflicted (*ruppana-sabhāva*) and the classification into primary elements (*bhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāya*), the complete discernment of all form by way of its characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), function (*rasa*), manifestation (*paccupaṭṭhāna*), and proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*). This is expressed as: "This is form; this much is form; beyond this there is no further form. Thus, the entirety of form is encompassed.
It is said. Thus, by the phrase "the arising of form," the demonstration of the arising of form as thus comprehended is stated.
In this context, "thus" (iti) means "in this way, there is arising. Its detailed explanation is: "With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of form;
with the arising of craving, there is the arising of form; with the arising of kamma, there is the arising of form; with the arising of nutriment..."

Regarding the phrase "the arising of form," it should be understood as follows: even while seeing the characteristic of production (*nibbatti-lakkhaṇa*), one sees the arising of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-kkhandha*).

As for its passing away (*atthaṅgama*), the detailed explanation is: "With the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of form... [and so on]... even while seeing the characteristic of change (*vipariṇāma-lakkhaṇa*), one sees the cessation of the aggregate of form. Thus it should be understood.
In the passages beginning with "This is feeling" and so forth, [the meaning is]: "This is feeling; this much is feeling; beyond this there is no further feeling.
This is perception; these are mental formations; this is consciousness; this much is consciousness; beyond this there is no further consciousness.

Thus, taking as their starting point the respective natures of experiencing, perceiving, volitionally constructing, and cognizing—namely, the divisions of pleasantness and so forth, visible forms and so forth, contact and so forth, and eye-consciousness and so forth—one should understand them by way of their characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*), functions (*rasa*), manifestations (*paccupaṭṭhāna*), and proximate causes (*padaṭṭhāna*).
The complete discernment of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness has been stated.

Furthermore, by means of the phrases "the origin of feeling," and so forth, the demonstration of the origin of those very feelings, perceptions, mental formations, and consciousness thus discerned is stated.
Therein too, "iti" means "thus there is an origin. The detailed explanation of these is: "With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of feeling."
It should be understood in the same manner as described for form (rūpa). However, this is the distinction:

regarding the three aggregates, instead of saying "from the arising of nutriment" (āhāra-samudayā), one should say "from the arising of contact" (phassa-samudayā). Regarding the consciousness aggregate, one should say "from the arising of name-and-form" (nāma-rūpa-samudayā); the phrase concerning their "passing away" (atthaṅgama) should also be applied according to those same [aggregates].
This is the summary here; the detailed analysis, however, is found in the *Udayabbaya-vinicchaya*.
The fulfillment in all its aspects has been explained in the *Visuddhimagga*. Regarding the phrase "he dwells contemplating the rise and fall in the five aggregates of clinging":

for that Bodhisatta Vipassi, as he dwelt contemplating the rise and fall in these five aggregates of clinging—form and so forth—by way of the fifty-six characteristics, his insight-knowledge increased in due succession.
By the cessation through non-arising, while the defilements known as the taints (*āsava*) are ceasing, the mind is liberated without clinging—that is, without grasping.
This is called "being liberated" at the moment of the path (*maggakkhaṇa*), and "liberated" at the moment of the fruit (*phalakkhaṇa*);
or rather, it is both "already liberated" and "being liberated" at the moment of the path, and simply "liberated" at the moment of the fruit.
And at this point, the Great Man, completely liberated from all bonds, with the continuum of his mind fully blossomed like a lotus touched by the rays of the sun,
[attained] the four knowledges of the paths, the four knowledges of the fruits, the four analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*), the knowledge that delimits the four modes of birth,
the knowledge that delimits the five destinies, the six uncommon knowledges, and the entirety...
And having placed the qualities of a Buddha within his grasp, with his purpose fulfilled, while sitting right there on the seat of enlightenment, he [declared]:
“Through many births in saṃsāra I have wandered without relief,
seeking the builder of the house, for birth again and again is suffering.”
“House-builder, you have been seen; you shall build no house again.
All your rafters are broken, the ridge-pole is demolished;
the mind has reached the unconditioned and attained the destruction of craving.”
"Just as the course of a blazing fire struck by an iron hammer,
which has been gradually extinguished, cannot be known;
so too, for those who are rightly liberated and have crossed over the flood of the bonds of sensual desire, [their destination cannot be known]."
"There is no way to describe the unshakable happiness of those who have attained it.
Reflecting thus, he shone like the sun in autumn and like the full moon.
The commentary on the second recitation section is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on Brahmā’s Entreaty (Brahmayācanakathāvaṇṇanā) 64.
Regarding the third section of the recitation: "What if I were to teach the Dhamma?"—that is, "If I were to teach the Dhamma.
But when did this thought arise? It arose during the eighth week after he had become a Buddha. For it is said that he was a Buddha [at that time].
Having made the offering, he sat upon the Bodhi throne for seven days; for seven days he stood gazing at the Bodhi throne; for seven days he walked upon the Jewel Walk;
for seven days he sat within the Jewel Chamber contemplating the Dhamma; for seven days he sat beneath the Goatherd’s Banyan tree;
for seven days he sat beneath the Mucalinda tree; for seven days he sat beneath the Rājāyatana tree. Then, rising from there, on the eighth day...

Returning again after seven days, as soon as he had sat down at the Ajapāla banyan tree, this thought and the one immediately following it—which are the habitual and customary reflections of all Buddhas—arose in him.
In this context, "attained" means "penetrated. "Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. "Profound" is a term used to exclude the state of being shallow.

"Difficult to see" (*duddasa*) means that because of its profundity it is difficult to see; it cannot be seen with ease. Because it is difficult to see, it is "difficult to awaken to" (*duranubodha*);
it must be understood with difficulty; it cannot be understood with ease. "Peaceful" (*santa*) means extinguished (*nibbuta*). "Sublime" (*paṇīta*) means unsurpassable.
These two [terms] are stated specifically with reference to the supramundane (*lokuttara*). "Beyond the sphere of reasoning" (*atakkāvacara*) means by means of logic...
It is not something to be traversed or plunged into; it is to be traversed by knowledge alone. "Subtle" means delicate.

"To be experienced by the wise" means it is to be understood by the wise who have entered upon the right practice. "Delighting in attachment": beings cling to the five strands of sensual pleasure, therefore they are called "attachments.
The eight hundred modes of craving's movement are attachments, therefore they are called "attachments."

They are so called. They delight in those attachments (*ālaya*), thus they are "delighting in attachments" (*ālayarāmā*). They take pleasure in attachments, thus they are "pleased with attachments" (*ālayaratā*).
They are thoroughly gladdened by attachments, thus they are "excessively delighted by attachments" (*ālayasammuditā*).

For just as a king who has entered a well-prepared park, endowed with trees laden with flowers and fruit, delights in each of its excellences, becoming joyful, glad, and elated, and does not grow weary;
Just as he does not wish to go out in the evening, so too these beings delight in these abodes of sensual attachment and abodes of craving;

they dwell rejoicing and without weariness within the cycle of saṃsāra. Therefore, the Blessed One, showing both kinds of attachment to be like a pleasure garden, said: "Delighting in attachment," and so forth.

*Yadidam* is a particle; its meaning should be understood as follows: with reference to the "place," it is "that which is here" (*yadidam*); with reference to dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), it is "this which is" (*yo ayam*).
Regarding the phrase *idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppādo*: the conditions for these [factors] are "conditions-appertaining-to-this" (*idappaccayā*);
the state of being such conditions is "conditionality-appertaining-to-this" (*idappaccayatā*); and that conditionality is itself dependent origination.

And this is "conditionality by way of specific conditionality" (*idappaccayatā-paṭiccasamuppāda*). This is a designation for ignorance and the other conditions, such as volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*).
The entire passage beginning with "the stilling of all formations" refers to Nibbāna itself.
Because, by resorting to it, all the fluctuations of formations are stilled and completely pacified, it is therefore called "the stilling of all formations. And because, by resorting to it...
All acquisitions are relinquished, all cravings are exhausted, all defilements and passions fade away, and all suffering ceases;
therefore, it is called "the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the exhaustion of craving, dispassion, cessation.
Furthermore, this craving weaves together existence after existence, or it binds and entangles karma along with its fruit.
Because it is "crossed over" (*vāna*), it is called *vāna*; that which has emerged from this *vāna* is *nibbāna*.
"That would be weariness for me" means that the teaching given to those who do not understand would be weariness for me; the sense is that it would be an affliction for me.
What is meant is that there would be both bodily weariness and bodily affliction; however, in the case of the Buddhas, neither of these two exists in the mind.
65. *Apissū* is a particle used in the sense of extension (*anubrūhana*). It indicates: "Not only did this [thought] occur, but these verses also occurred to me.
Regarding *Vipassiṃ* and so forth, the meaning is: "Of the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. *Anacchariyā* means "not wonderful" (*anu-acchariyā*).
