*Paṭibhaṃsuṃ* means they became the objects of knowledge known as intuition (*paṭibhāna*), and they reached the state of being fit for thorough reflection.
"By hardship" means by suffering, not by a painful practice. For the four paths of the Buddhas are indeed practices that are easy.

However, at the time of fulfilling the perfections, while he was still possessed of lust, hatred, and delusion, he would cut off the heads of supplicants who came to him—heads adorned and prepared—and draw out the blood from their throats, and pluck out his well-anointed eyes.

This was said with reference to the path leading to rebirth for one who gives such things as "a son who is the lamp of his family lineage" or "a wife who conducts herself agreeably," and who likewise undergoes cutting, splitting, and other such ordeals in future existences similar to those of the Teacher of Forbearance (Khantivādi).
Here, *ha* in *halanti* is a mere particle; the meaning is *alaṃ* (enough). *Pakāsituṃ* means to teach. Thus, with difficulty...
"It is sufficient to teach the Dhamma that has been realized; what is the point of teaching it?"—this is what is meant.
"By those overcome by lust and hatred" means by those touched by lust and hatred, or followed by lust and hatred.

"Going against the stream" refers to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths, which proceeds against the stream of notions such as permanence and so forth, namely: impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity.
"Intoxicated by passion" means they are stained by the passion for sense-pleasures (*kāmarāga*), the passion for existence (*bhavarāga*), and the passion for views (*diṭṭhirāga*).

"They will not see" means they will not perceive [things] according to their true nature—that they are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul. While they do not see this, who would be able to make them grasp it?
"Enveloped by a mass of darkness" means they are overwhelmed by a heap of ignorance (*avijjā*).

“With indifference” means by way of a state of being free from zeal; the meaning is: with no desire to teach. But why did his mind incline in this way? Was it not said of him: “Freed, I shall set others free; crossed over, I shall help others cross”? And: “What need have I for a disguise?
Having realized the Dhamma here, and having attained omniscience, I shall safely carry across the world together with its devas.”
"Having made the aspiration and fulfilled the perfections, he attained omniscience. This is true;
however, it was through the power of his retrospective reflection (*paccavekkhaṇā*) that his mind thus inclined.

For when he had attained omniscience and was reflecting upon the density of the defilements (*kilesa*) in sentient beings and the profundity of the Dhamma, the density of the defilements in sentient beings and the profundity of the Dhamma appeared to him in every aspect.

They became visible. Then, as he reflected—“These beings are like gourds filled with sour gruel, like bowls filled with buttermilk, like rags soaked in fat and oil, like hands smeared with collyrium; they are full of defilements, exceedingly defiled, dyed by lust, corrupted by hatred, and deluded by ignorance.
What indeed will they penetrate?”—his mind inclined in this way through the power of reflecting upon the thicket of defilements.
“And this Dhamma is profound like the mass of water that supports the earth;
it is difficult to see, like a mustard seed placed on a mountain and covered over; it is difficult to penetrate, like joining the tip of a hair split a hundredfold to another hair-tip.
For was it not by striving to penetrate this Dhamma that I realized: ‘There is no such thing as giving what has not been given’?”
There was no such thing as unguarded virtue, nor was there any pericarp of a pāramī that remained unfilled.
Even as I was dispersing the host of Māra as if it were effortless, the earth did not tremble; even as I was recollecting my past lives during the first watch of the night, it did not tremble;
and even as I was purifying the divine eye during the middle watch, it did not tremble.

Furthermore, it should be understood that his mind was inclined in this way through the power of reflecting on the profundity of the Dhamma, thinking: "While I was penetrating dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) during the last watch of the night, even as I did so, the ten-thousandfold world system trembled.
Thus, even by one such as myself with keen knowledge, this Dhamma was penetrated only with great difficulty; how then will the ordinary people of the world penetrate it?"
Moreover, when requested by Brahmā, his mind inclined toward the desire to teach. For the Blessed One knew:
"When my mind inclines toward indolence, Mahābrahmā will request me to teach the Dhamma;
and these beings hold Brahmā in high esteem, thinking: 'The Teacher was indeed unwilling to teach the Dhamma, but then Mahābrahmā requested him.'"
“...he would cause them to desire to listen, thinking: ‘Truly, sirs, the Dhamma is peaceful; truly, sirs, the Dhamma is sublime.
It should be understood that for this reason as well, his mind inclined toward inaction rather than to teaching the Dhamma.
66. Regarding the phrase “of a certain one”: although it is said “a certain one,” he was nevertheless the eldest Great Brahmā in this world-system.
"He is to be known thus. "Alas, sirs, the world is perishing!
he indeed uttered this sound in such a way that the Brahmās of the ten-thousandfold world-system, upon hearing it, all assembled together.
"In which world indeed" means in whichever world. "Appeared before them" means he appeared together with those ten thousand Brahmās. "Of a nature with little dust in their eyes" means...
In their eye consisting of wisdom (*paññāmaya*), there is but little and slight dust of lust, hatred, and delusion; thus, by nature they are "of little dust" (*apparajakkhajātiko*).

"Because of not hearing" means due to not having heard [the Dhamma]. "They will become" refers to those who, in previous Buddhas, performed meritorious deeds through the ten bases of wholesome action (*dasapuññakiriyavatthu*) and have reached maturity—like lotuses at the touch of the sun's rays—and who desire only the teaching of the Dhamma.

At the conclusion of each four-line stanza, he shows that it is not just one or two, but many hundreds of thousands who will become knowers of the Dhamma and thus worthy of entering the plane of the Noble Ones.
(69) "Entreaty" means a request made three times in this manner. "With the Buddha-eye" means with the knowledge of the degrees of the faculties of others (*indriya-paropariyatta-ñāṇa*).

And by the knowledge of dispositions and underlying tendencies (*āsaya-anusaya-ñāṇa*). For these two knowledges have the name "Buddha-eye" (*buddhacakkhu*); for the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*), the name "Universal Eye" (*samantacakkhu*);
and for the three knowledges of the path, the name "Dhamma-eye" (*dhammacakkhu*). Regarding the passage beginning with "with little dust in their eyes" (*apparajakkha*):

those who, according to the method already stated, have little dust such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth in their eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*), are "those with little dust in their eyes. Those for whom that [dust] is great—
Those who have great defilements are those with great passion (*mahārajakkha*). Those whose faculties such as faith (*saddhā*) and so forth are sharp are those with sharp faculties (*tikkhindriya*).
Those whose [faculties] are dull are those with dull faculties (*mudindriya*). Those whose very modes (*ākāra*)—faith and so forth—are beautiful are those of good disposition (*svākāra*).
Those who perceive the reason when it is stated, and who can be easily instructed, are those easy to admonish (*suviññāpaya*). Those who [fear] both the next world and blame...
Those who see [evil] as fearful are called "those who see the fear of blame and the next world.
Here is the canonical text regarding this: "A person endowed with faith has little dust on their eyes; a person devoid of faith has much dust on their eyes...

one who has aroused energy... [and so on]... one who is lazy... one whose mindfulness is established... one whose mindfulness is confused... one who is concentrated... one who is unconcentrated... one who possesses wisdom..."
A person of weak wisdom has great defilement. Likewise, a person of faith has keen faculties...
[and so on] ...a person of wisdom sees the fear of blame and the next world, whereas a person of weak wisdom does not see the fear of blame and the next world.

"World" refers to the world of aggregates, the world of elements, the world of sense-bases, the world of fortunate existence, the world of unfortunate existence, and the world of the origin of fortunate existence.
The world as the source of misfortune. One world: all beings subsist by nutriment. Two worlds: name and form. Three worlds:
the three feelings. Four worlds: the four nutriments. Five worlds: the five aggregates of clinging.
Six worlds: the six internal sense bases. Seven worlds: the seven stations of consciousness. Eight...
Worlds: there are eight worldly conditions (*lokadhammā*). Nine worlds: the nine abodes of beings (*sattāvāsā*).
Ten worlds: the ten bases (*āyatanāni*). Twelve worlds: the twelve bases. Eighteen worlds: the eighteen elements (*dhātuyo*). "Faults" (*vajja*):
all defilements (*kilesā*) are faults; all misconduct (*duccarita*) is a fault; all volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhārā*) are faults; all kamma leading to existence (*bhavagāmikamma*) is a fault.
"Thus, in this world and in this [realm of] the dead, an intense perception of danger is established, just as toward an executioner with a raised sword.
In these fifty ways, he knows, sees, understands, and penetrates these five faculties;
this is the Tathāgata’s knowledge regarding the degrees of others' faculties."
"Uppaliniyaṃ" means in a grove of blue lotuses (*utpala*). The same method applies to the others as well.
"Antonimuggaposīni" refers to those other lotuses that nourish themselves while submerged within [the water]. "Udakaṃ accuggamma ṭhitāni" means standing having emerged above the water.
Among these, those that stand having emerged above [the water] are awaiting contact with the rays of the sun.
Those that stand [in the water] today are those that flower today. Those that stand level with the water will flower tomorrow.
Those that have risen above the water and are nourished within the water will flower on the third day. Furthermore, there are other lotuses and water-lilies that do not rise above the water;
these will not flower at all, but will become food for fish and turtles. These are the ones mentioned in the text.
They have not yet been illustrated. However, having been brought forward, they are now illustrated.

For just as there are those four kinds of flowers, so too are there four types of persons: one who understands through a brief summary (*ugghaṭitaññū*), one who understands through detailed exposition (*vipañcitaññū*), one who is led to understanding (*neyyo*), and one for whom the words are the limit (*padaparamo*).
Among these, the person for whom the realization of the Dhamma occurs at the very moment it is uttered is called a person who understands through a brief summary.

The person for whom the realization of the Dhamma occurs when the meaning of what was spoken in brief is analyzed in detail is called a person who gains knowledge through detailed exposition (*vipañcitaññū*). The person for whom the realization of the Dhamma occurs gradually by means of recitation, interrogation, wise attention,
and by associating with, following, and attending upon spiritual friends is called...

A person is one who needs guidance. That person who, despite hearing much, speaking much, grasping much, retaining much, and reciting much, does not achieve the penetration of the Dhamma in that very lifetime—this is called a person for whom words are the limit.
In this regard, the Blessed One, surveying the ten-thousandfold world system which was like a lotus grove and so forth, [saw those] "blooming today"—

He saw that some were like flowers that bloom on the very day they are plucked (those who understand through a condensed teaching), some like flowers that bloom the next day (those who understand through an expanded teaching), some like flowers that bloom on the third day (those who must be guided), and some like food for fish and turtles (those for whom the words are the limit). And as he observed them, he saw in every way:
"So many have little dust in their eyes; so many have much dust in their eyes; and among those, so many are those who understand through a condensed teaching."
He saw this. In that regard, for three types of persons, the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma achieves its purpose within this very lifetime;
for those who take the words as the limit, it serves to establish a latent predisposition for the future.
Then the Blessed One, having understood that his teaching of the Dhamma would bring benefit to these four types of persons, [aroused] the desire to teach.
Having produced [these insights], he again divided all beings within the three realms of existence into two classes, according to their capacity and incapacity.
Referring to them, it was said: "Those beings who are possessed of an obstruction of karma, possessed of an obstruction of kamma-result, and possessed of an obstruction of defilements;
those who lack faith, lack desire [for the good], and lack wisdom, being incapable of entering the fixed course [of salvation]..."
“...incapable of entering into the rightness of wholesome states; these are those beings who are incapable. Which beings are capable?

Those beings who are not hindered by kamma-obstruction... [and so on] ...these are those beings who are capable. Therein, having set aside all incapable persons and having discerned only the capable persons with wisdom, he says: “So many...”
He divided [beings] into six categories: "so many are those of lustful temperament, and so many are those of irascible, deluded, speculative, faithful, or intellectual temperaments.
Having done this, he thought, "I shall teach the Dhamma. Knowing this, Brahmā was filled with joy and addressed the Blessed One in verses.
It is with reference to this that it was said: "Then, monks, that Great Brahmā... and so forth.
70. *Tattha ajjhabhāsīti* means he spoke over [them], having taken them as his object and directed his speech toward them.
*Sele yathā pabbatamuddhaniṭṭhito* means just as one standing on the summit of a solid rock mountain;
for one standing there, there is no need for actions such as raising the neck or stretching out the limbs in order to see. *Tathūpamaṃ* [means] "similar to that."
It is its counterpart, like a rocky mountain. This, however, is the summary of the meaning here:

just as a man with sight standing upon the summit of a rocky mountain would see the people all around him, so too, O wise one, the Blessed One—the All-Seeing One through his beautiful wisdom and omniscient knowledge—having ascended the palace made of Dhamma and made of wisdom, himself free from sorrow, [beholds] those plunged in sorrow.
Regard the people overcome by birth and aging; contemplate them and examine them.

This is the intended meaning here: just as if, at the foot of a mountain, people were to clear a large field on all sides, build huts there among the field boundaries, and kindle a fire at night. And [there would be] darkness endowed with four factors.
Suppose, then, that a man with keen vision were standing on the summit of that mountain and looking down at the ground;
for him, neither the fields, nor the boundaries of the furrows, nor the huts, nor the people sleeping therein would be visible, but in the huts only the flickering of fire would be seen.
In the same way, for one who has ascended the palace of the Dhamma and is surveying the multitude of beings—
Regarding the Tathāgata: those beings who have not performed wholesome deeds do not come within the range of his Buddha-eye even when sitting in the same dwelling on his right knee;

they are like arrows shot in the night. However, those individuals who are ready for training and have performed wholesome deeds come within his range even though they stand far away, just as fire [reveals things] or as the Himālaya mountain does. And this has been said:
“The virtuous shine from afar, like the Himalaya mountain;
the wicked are not seen here, like arrows shot in the night.
By saying “Arise,” he speaks, requesting the Blessed One to set out on his wandering for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma. Regarding the words “O Hero,” and so forth:

The Blessed One is a hero (*vīra*) by virtue of his possession of energy; he is one who has conquered the battle because he has triumphed over the Māras of the sons of gods, death, and the defilements;
he is a caravan leader (*satthavāha*) because he is capable of acting as a guide for those to be trained in order to lead them across the various realms of birth and so forth;
and he should be understood as "debtless" (*aṇaṇo*) due to the absence of the deer of sensual desire.
71. "Opened" (*apāruta*) means disclosed. "The gate to the Deathless" (*amatassa dvāra*) refers to the Noble Path; for that is the gateway to Nibbāna, which is designated as the Deathless.
He shows that it has been opened and set forth by me. "Let them release their faith" (*pamuñcantu saddhaṃ*):
let everyone release—that is, relinquish—their own faith. Regarding the last two lines, this is the meaning: for although my [teaching] is well-mastered and flows perfectly within me...
"Perceiving the fatigue of body and speech, I did not speak this sublime and supreme Dhamma;
but now, let all people offer the vessel of faith, and I shall fulfill their aspirations.
*Commentary on the Pair of Chief Disciples*
73. "At the foot of the Bodhi tree" means that he had disappeared at the Goatherd’s Banyan tree, which was not far from the Bodhi tree.
"In the Khema Deer Park": at that time, Isipatana was a pleasure garden named Khema;
however, because it had been given as a sanctuary where deer lived without fear, it was called Migadāya (Deer Park). It is with reference to this that it is said: "In the Khema Deer Park."
Just as the Blessed One Vipassī did, so too other Buddhas, when going for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma for the first time, travel through the air and descend right there.
But our Blessed One, seeing that Upaka the Ājīvaka possessed the necessary potential (*upanissaya*), thought:
"Upaka has set out on this road; having seen me and conversed with me, he will depart. Then again—"
Knowing that he would become weary of the world and, having come [to him], would realize arhatship, [the Elder] traveled the eighteen-yojana road on foot.
Having seen the park-keeper, he looked at him again and again; then, saying, "Our venerable master has arrived, Bhante," he addressed the keeper who had approached him.

75–6. "Gradual discourse" means he spoke in successive order: first the discourse on giving (*dānakathā*), followed by virtue (*sīla*) after giving, heaven (*sagga*) after virtue, and the Path (*magga*) after heaven.
In this context, "discourse on giving" means:

this so-called giving is the source of happiness, the root of prosperity, the foundation of wealth, and for one who has fallen into adversity, it is a refuge, a shelter, a resort, and a final destination.
In this world and the world beyond, there is no refuge, support, foundation, object, shelter, cave, destination, or final resort equal to giving.
For in the sense of being a refuge, it is like a lion-throne made of jewels; in the sense of being a foundation, it is like the great earth;
in the sense of being an object, it is like a supporting rope. Indeed, in the sense of crossing over suffering, it is a boat; in the sense of providing consolation, it is—
He is a hero in battle; he is a well-constructed city in the sense of providing protection from fear; he is a lotus in the sense of being unstained by the impurities of stinginess and the like;
he is a fire in the sense of consuming those [impurities]; he is a venomous serpent in the sense of being difficult to approach;

he is a lion in the sense of being fearless; he is an elephant in the sense of possessing great strength; he is a white bull in the sense of being esteemed as auspicious; and he is [a guide] in the sense of leading one to the land of safety.

The royal horse Valāhaka. For giving indeed bestows in this world the attainment of Sakka, the attainment of Māra, the attainment of Brahmā, the attainment of a wheel-turning monarch, the knowledge of the perfections of a disciple, the knowledge of the enlightenment of a paccekabuddha, and the knowledge of supreme enlightenment—such was the discourse connected with the qualities of giving.
However, because one who gives a gift is able to undertake moral discipline (*sīla*), he therefore spoke next on the discourse of moral discipline.
Regarding the "discourse on virtue": this virtue is indeed a support, a foundation, an object of focus, a refuge, a shelter, a destination, and the ultimate resort.
For there is no support, foundation, object of focus, refuge, shelter, destination, or ultimate resort for the attainments of this world and the world beyond equal to virtue;
there is no ornament equal to virtue; there is no flower equal to the flower of virtue.
"There is no fragrance equal to the fragrance of virtue;

for even the world with its devas never tires of beholding one adorned with the ornament of virtue, bedecked with the flower of virtue, and anointed with the perfume of virtue"—such was the discourse connected with the qualities of virtue.
Furthermore, in order to show that this heaven is obtained by relying upon this very virtue, he spoke next on the topic of heaven.
"Talk on heaven" means: "This so-called heaven is desirable, lovely, and pleasing; here there is constant play and constant attainment of prosperity.
The gods of the Realm of the Four Great Kings obtain divine pleasure and divine prosperity for nine million years;
the Tāvatiṃsa gods [obtain it] for thirty-six million years," and so forth—connected with such qualities of heaven.
How so? For the mouths of the Buddhas are never exhausted when speaking of the excellence of heaven (*saggasampatti*). And this has been said:
"In many ways, monks, I might speak a discourse on heaven," and so forth.
Having thus enticed him with a discourse on heaven, he then decorated the elephant once more, as if cutting off its trunk.
In order to show that "this heaven too is impermanent and unstable;

no desire or lust should be placed herein," he spoke of the danger (*ādīnava*), the degradation (*okāra*), and the defilement (*saṃkilesa*) of sensual pleasures by way of such passages as: "Sensual pleasures provide little gratification, much suffering, and much despair;
the danger herein is greater. In this context, *ādīnava* means fault. *Okāra* means lowliness or baseness. *Saṃkilesa* means—
By these [defilements], there is the defiling of beings within saṃsāra. As it is said: "Alas, beings are indeed defiled!
Having thus shown the danger in sensual pleasures (kāma), he proclaimed the benefit in renunciation (nekkhamma); the meaning is that he proclaimed the virtue of going forth (pabbajjā).
The rest is according to the method already stated in the commentary on the Ambaṭṭha Sutta, and its meaning is clear.

77. Regarding the phrase "They obtained": how did they obtain it? By means of the "Come, monk" formula (*ehibhikkhu*). It is said that the Blessed One, while surveying the supporting conditions for their supernaturally produced bowls and robes, saw that they had given robes and other gifts in many previous births; thus he spoke the words beginning with "Come, monks.
At that very moment, they became shaven-headed, clad in saffron robes, with the eight requisites of a monk already fastened to their bodies, appearing like elders of a hundred years' standing.
They sat down as if paying homage to the Blessed One.
Regarding the phrases "He instructed," and so forth: he instructed them regarding the welfare of this world; he instructed them regarding the welfare of the other world.
While instructing them regarding the welfare of this world, he showed it to be impermanent, he showed it to be suffering, he showed it to be non-self, and he showed the aggregates.
He showed the elements; he showed the sense bases; he showed dependent origination. While showing the arising of the aggregate of form, he showed five characteristics;
likewise for the aggregates of feeling and so forth. Likewise, while showing their passing away, he showed fifty characteristics by way of both arising and passing away.
And while showing the state of the world beyond, he showed hell.
He showed [him] the animal realm, the sphere of hungry ghosts, the host of asuras, the fruition of the three wholesome [karmas],
and the prosperity of the six celestial worlds and the nine Brahma worlds.

"He incited" means he caused him to take up wholesome qualities such as the fourfold pure morality, the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas), the discourse on the bases of meritorious deeds (kathāvatthu), and so forth.
"Samuttejesī" means he thoroughly incited and uplifted them.
Having made it as if he had attained the welfare of this world and the welfare of the next world by repeatedly instilling fear, he spoke.

For when the Blessed Buddha speaks, repeatedly instilling fear regarding the welfare of this world—such as the thirty-two types of judicial torture and the twenty-five great fears—one is seized by the arm and bound with tight fetters.
Bound and beaten with a hundred blows at the crossroads, he becomes deeply moved as if being led out through the southern gate,
as if his head were placed upon the executioner’s block, as if impaled on a stake, and as if being trampled by a rutting elephant.
And when they speak of the welfare of the next world, he feels as if reborn in the hells and such realms, and yet as if experiencing the splendors of the deva-worlds.
“Sampahaṃsesi” means he exhorted him by way of the qualities already attained; the meaning is that he spoke, making it a matter of great benefit.
Regarding “the danger in formations”: previously, for the sake of attaining the first path, he spoke of the danger in sensual pleasures;
but here, for the sake of attaining the higher paths, he said: “Bhikkhus, formations are impermanent, unstable, and unreliable.”

“Bhikkhus, to this extent it is indeed enough to become disenchanted with all conditioned phenomena, enough to become dispassionate toward them, enough to be liberated from them”—in such a manner he explained the danger, the wretchedness, and the exhaustion resulting from those conditioned phenomena.
And just as there [was an explanation] regarding renunciation in that context, so here: “Bhikkhus, this so-called Nibbāna is peaceful, sublime, a refuge...”
By means of the method beginning with “a refuge,” he proclaimed the benefits of Nibbāna.
78. Regarding the description of the great multitude going forth:
“The great multitude” refers to the body of attendants belonging to those very two princes.
80. "We go for refuge to the Blessed One and to the Dhamma"—because the Saṅgha was not yet complete, they went for refuge by means of the two-fold formula alone. 81.

"They obtained [the going forth]"—they obtained it precisely through the state of being a *ehibhikkhu* (come, monk), according to the method previously described. This same principle applies to the subsequent section on those who went forth.
Commentary on the Permission for the Wanderings.
85. "The reflection arose": when did it arise? It arose after seven years, seven months, and seven days had passed since his full enlightenment.
It is said that the Blessed One remained there performing services for his father. The king also thought:
"My eldest son has gone forth and become a Buddha; my second son has also gone forth..."
“The chief disciple has been born; the son of the family priest is the second chief disciple;
and these remaining bhikkhus, even during their time as householders, used to wander about surrounded by my sons alone. All of them are now my responsibility;
I myself shall attend to them with the four requisites, and I will give no opportunity to others. Thus he spoke from the gateway of the monastery.
Having had a fence of acacia wood constructed on both sides from the starting point as far as the gate of the royal palace,
having had it thatched with palm leaves and covered with cloths, and having had it roofed over above, he had a canopy made of various flower garlands—
variegated with golden stars and reaching down to the height of a palmyra trunk— and having had the ground below strewn with variegated rugs.
Having placed garland-vines and full water-jars at both ends inside,
and having set fragrances within the flowers and flowers within the fragrances for the sake of perfuming the entire path, he announced the time to the Blessed One.
Surrounded by the community of monks, the Blessed One went to the royal palace through the inner gate itself, performed the meal ceremony, and returned to the monastery.
He returned. No one else was even able to see him, much less give him alms, offer worship, or hear the Dhamma.
The city-dwellers thought: "Today it has been seven years and seven months since the Teacher appeared in the world, yet we cannot even see him, let alone give him alms, offer worship..."
[He was unable] to do so, nor could he hear the Dhamma. The king, thinking "The Buddha is mine alone; the Dhamma is mine alone;

the Saṅgha is mine alone," cherished them as his own and personally attended upon [the Teacher]. And when the Teacher appears, he does so for the welfare and benefit of the world together with its devas.
For it is not only the king’s hell that is hot; for others, it is like a grove of blue lotuses.
"Therefore, we shall speak to the king. If he gives us our Teacher, that is well.

If he does not give him, even if we have to fight with the king, we shall take the Saṅgha and perform meritorious deeds such as giving. However, it is not possible for us to do this with ordinary citizens alone;
let us also take one of the leading men."
They approached the general and, having informed him of the matter, said:
"Sir, do you side with us, or rather with the king? He replied: "I side with you; however, the first day must be given to me.
They agreed. He then approached the king and said: "Sire, the citizens..."
“He is angry,” he said. “For what reason, father? “It is said that you yourselves are attending upon the Teacher;
we do not receive [his favor]. “If they still receive it even now, they will not be angry; but if they do not receive it, O King, these gods will wish to fight with you.
“I shall fight, father; I will not give the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus [to them]. “O King, your own slaves are fighting with you!”
They asked, "Whom will you take with you when you go to war? [The general replied,] "Are you not the commander-in-chief?
[The king said,] "I am not capable without the citizens, Your Majesty.
Then the king, realizing, "The citizens are powerful, and the commander-in-chief is on their side," said, "Let them give my Saṅgha of monks another seven years and seven months as well."
He said, "The citizens did not agree. The king reduced [the time] to six years, five, four, three, two, and one year.
Even as he was reducing it in this way, they still did not agree. He then requested seven days.
The citizens thought, "It is no longer right to act so harshly toward the king," and they granted their consent.

The king, having released for seven days the prepared alms-offering that had been set aside for more than seven years and seven months, gave the gift for six days while some people were not even looking on;
then, on the seventh day, he summoned the citizens and asked, "Dear ones, are you able to give such a gift? They replied, "Indeed..."
Saying, "It has arisen for the King because of us alone," they replied, "We shall be able to do it.
The King, wiping away his tears with the back of his hand, paid homage to the Blessed One and said, "Venerable Sir, I thought:
'I will serve six million eight hundred thousand bhikkhus for as long as I live with the four requisites, not allowing anyone else the opportunity. But the city-dwellers..."
"Now I am not permitted [to give], for the citizens will become angry, thinking, 'We do not get to give alms.
Therefore, from tomorrow onwards, may the Blessed One show favor to them.
Then, on the second day, the general prepared a great almsgiving and said: "Today, as no one else has given even a single bhikkhu..."
“He will not give it; guard him thus,” he said, and stationed men all around him. On that day, the merchant’s wife, weeping, said to her daughter:
“If, my child, your father were alive, I would feed the One of Ten Powers first today.
She replied to her: “Mother, do not worry; I shall act in such a way that the Saṅgha of monks, headed by the Buddha, [shall be fed].”

"He will be the first to enjoy our almsfood. Then, having filled a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] with rice porridge without water, having prepared it with ghee, honey, sugar, and other ingredients, and having covered it with another bowl, she surrounded it with jasmine flower-bunches, making it look like a cluster of flowers; then, at the time when the Blessed One was entering the village—
Having herself raised [the palanquin], she departed from the city surrounded by a retinue of female slaves.

Along the way, the attendants of the general said, "Mother, do not go further than this. Those who possess great merit are indeed pleasant in speech, and it is not possible to refuse the words of those who speak again and again.
She asked, "O younger uncle, O elder uncle, O uncles, for what reason..."
“You did not allow us to go,” she said. The general replied, “We have been instructed, ‘Do not give any hard or soft food to anyone else,’ mother.
She asked, “But do you see any hard or soft food in my hand? He replied, “I see a flower garland.
She asked, “Does your general not even allow you to perform a flower-garland offering? He replied, “He does.”
“‘Mother! she cried. ‘In that case, go away, go away! she said, approaching the Blessed One and saying, ‘Let the Blessed One accept this bouquet of flowers.
The Blessed One looked at one of Senapati’s attendants and had him take the bouquet.
She paid homage to the Blessed One and said: ‘Blessed One, if there is rebirth for me in existence after existence, may my life be free from agitation.’”
“Let it not be so; may I be dear wherever I am reborn, like this jasmine garland, and may my name indeed be ‘Sumanā,’” she made this aspiration.
Then the Teacher said to her, “May you be happy. Having paid homage and circumambulated him, she departed.
The Blessed One went to the general’s house and sat down on the prepared seat. The general approached, taking rice-gruel.
The Teacher covered the bowl. "Venerable sir, the community of monks is seated," he said. "We have received a single alms-offering on the way.
Having removed the garland, he saw the alms-food. The junior attendant said, "Master, a woman deceived me by telling me it was a garland.
The rice porridge was sufficient for all the monks, beginning with the Blessed One.
The general also gave his own gifts. After the Teacher had finished his meal and pronounced a blessing, he departed.
The general asked, "Who was that woman who gave the alms-food? "It was the merchant’s daughter, sir. "That woman is truly wise," he thought.
"For a man living in the house of such a woman as this, the attainment of heaven is not difficult to obtain. Having thus reflected, he brought her [to him].
He established him in the position of the eldest.
On the following day the citizens gave alms; on the next day the king did so; thus they began to give alms alternately.
The king, having stationed secret agents, gave even more than the alms given by the citizens, and the citizens likewise did the same.
Having prepared food even more abundant than that given by the king, the female dancers in the royal palace said to the young novices:
"Take it, dear ones! This was not made with hands that had wiped the limbs and clothes of householders or washed the spittle and mucus of small children;
it was made pure and exquisite. On the following day, the citizens also, as they were giving alms, said: "Take it!"
"Father, it was not made with rice, milk, curd, ghee, and so forth, gathered from cities, villages, market towns, and the like;
nor was it made by having the legs, heads, backs, and so on of others broken off and brought back. It was made only from natural ghee, milk, and such.
Thus, when seven years, seven months, and seven days had passed, then for the Blessed One...
This thought arose. Therefore it was said: "It arose after seven years, seven months, and seven days had passed since his full enlightenment.
87. "A certain Great Brahmā" refers to the very Brahmā who requested the teaching of the Dhamma.

89. “Eighty-four thousand monasteries” means eighty-four thousand *vihāras*. All of them were great monasteries capable of accommodating twelve thousand monks, similar to the Mahāvihāra, Abhayagiri, Cetiyapabbata, and Cittalapabbata Mahāvihāras.
90. “Patience is the supreme austerity”: patience in the sense of endurance is indeed the supreme austerity.
“Forbearance” (*titikkhā*) is a synonym for patience. The meaning is that patience known as forbearance is the highest austerity. Nibbāna...
Furthermore, the Buddhas declare that Nibbāna is supreme in every respect.
For one who harms others—that is, one who, being devoid of patience through endurance, harms, oppresses, or injures another—is not truly a renunciant (*pabbajita*).
The fourth line, moreover, is a synonym for that same point; for "one who is not a renunciant" means one who is not a recluse (*samaṇa*).
"Is" (*hoti*) is a synonym [for "becomes"]. "One who harms others" (*parūpaghātī*) has as its synonym "one who oppresses another.
Alternatively, "one who harms others" means one who harms virtue (*sīla*). For virtue is called "the supreme" (*para*) in the sense of being the highest.
And that ascetic who, while oppressing any being whatsoever, becomes a harmer of others—that destroyer of his own virtue—is not truly called a "renunciant" (*pabbajita*).

This is the meaning. Alternatively, one who harms others due to a lack of patience characterized by forbearance—even if he intentionally deprives another of life, down to a mere gadfly or mosquito—is not truly a renunciant.
Why is that? Because he has not renounced his defilements. For this is the defining characteristic of a renunciant:
“Having renounced the defilement within himself, therefore he is called a ‘renunciant’ (pabbajita).”
Furthermore, one who neither injures nor kills, but rather harms others with sticks and the like, is not a recluse (*śramaṇa*) while harming another.
Why? Because he has not stilled violence. For it is said: "Because he has stilled evils, he is called a recluse. This, indeed, is the defining characteristic of a recluse.

In the second verse, "of all evil" (*sabbapāpassa*) means of all that is unwholesome (*akusala*). "Non-doing" (*akaraṇam*) means non-arising. "Of the wholesome" (*kusalassa*) refers to the wholesome states belonging to the four planes.
"Attainment" (*upasampadā*) means acquisition. "The complete purification of one’s own mind" (*sacittapariyodapanam*) is the illumination of one's own mind;

however, that occurs through Arahantship. Thus, having abandoned all evil by means of the restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*), [one proceeds] by means of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
"Having accomplished what is wholesome, the mind should be purified by the fruit of Arhatship"—this is the teaching, the exhortation, and the instruction of the Buddhas.
In the third verse, "non-reproach" (*anūpavāda*) means not reproaching anyone with speech. "Non-injury" (*anūpaghāta*) means not causing injury with the body.
Regarding the *Pātimokkha*: that which is the *Pātimokkha*—the supreme, the most excellent, the highest virtue—or else, it protects (*pāti*) one from various misfortunes.
It is called *pātimokkha* because it liberates one from the fears of miserable rebirths (*duggatibhaya*), or because it protects one [from such fears], thus it is termed "liberation" (*mokkha*).
And within that *pātimokkha*, there is restraint (*saṃvara*). "Knowing the proper measure" (*mattaññutā*) means knowing the right amount in terms of receiving and using [alms-food].
"A secluded lodging" (*pantañca sayanāsanaṃ*) means a dwelling place free from social contact. In this regard, by two alone...
It should be understood that by means of these requisites, contentment with the four requisites is illustrated. "This is the teaching of the Buddhas" means that not reproaching others,
not harming others, restraint according to the Pātimokkha, moderation in receiving and using [requisites],
and resorting to secluded lodgings for the sake of mastery over the eight attainments— this is the teaching, the exhortation, and the instruction of the Buddhas.
Furthermore, it should be understood that these are the verses for reciting the Pātimokkha common to all Buddhas.
This concludes the detailed exposition according to the legend (*apadāna*) of the Blessed One Vipassī, up to this point: "This [recitation] belongs to the Tathāgata alone... [Devatārocanavaṇṇanā 91].

Having thus explained the state of having well-penetrated the element of phenomena (*dhammadhātu*) by saying, "O monks, the element of phenomena has been well-penetrated," he now spoke the words beginning with "Once upon a time...
in order to explain the report from the deities, which was stated as: "The deities also reported this matter to the Tathāgata."
Therein, "in the Subhagavana" means in the forest of that name. "At the foot of the king of sāla trees" means at the base of the foremost tree of the forest.
"Having dispelled sensual desire" means having dispelled it by way of uprooting it through the path of the non-returner (*anāgāmimagga*).
And just as for Vipassī, so too did deities announce that the holy life had been lived in the dispensation of the remaining Buddhas; however, the Pāḷi [text] is [given] for Vipassī.
And they have come by virtue of our Blessed One.
Therein, because they do not diminish nor fall away from their own attainment, they are called *Avihā*. Because they do not torment any being, they are called *Atappā*.
Because they are beautiful to behold, handsome, and serene, they are called *Sudassā*. They see clearly; this is their beauty.

Or, because it is "well-seen," it is Sudassī. Furthermore, because they are the eldest in all virtuous qualities and in the excellence of existence, and there is no one younger among them, they are Akaniṭṭhā.
Here, the sections for recitation (*bhāṇavāra*) should be brought together. For in this sutta, by way of the legend (*apadāna*) of the Blessed One Vipassī—
Three recitation sections (bhāṇavāra) have been stated. And just as it was for Vipassī, so too it has been stated by way of the legends (apadāna) for Sikhī and the others;
however, the Pāḷi has been abbreviated. Thus, by way of the seven Buddhas, twenty-one recitation sections were spoken by our Blessed One.
Likewise by the Aviha devas; likewise by the Atappa devas; likewise by the Sudassa devas; likewise by the Sudassī devas; likewise by the Akaniṭṭha devas.

The entire work consists of one hundred and twenty-six recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*). Within the word of the Buddha contained in the Three Piṭakas, there is no other discourse (*sutta*) of such an extent as this;
therefore, it should be understood that this discourse is known as the "King of Discourses" (*Suttantarāja*).
Following this, he spoke the passage beginning with "Thus, monks," introducing both types of connection (*anusandhi*). All of that is quite clear.
Thus ends the commentary on the Mahāpadāna Sutta in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya. 2.
The commentary on the Mahānidāna Sutta.
Commentary on the Nidāna: 95. “Thus have I heard... in the Kuru country” refers to the Mahānidāna Sutta. Herein, this is the commentary on the words not [already] explained.
“He dwells among the Kurus”: the Kurus were princes of the realm; the name for their single inhabited district is used here by way of conventional designation (*ruḷhīsaddena*).
It is called "Kuru. In that Kuru country, the commentators (aṭṭhakathācariyā), however, have said:

during the time of King Mandhātu, the people of the three continents, having heard that Jambudīpa was "the land of birth for supreme humans such as Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, Great Disciples, and Wheel-turning Monarchs—the most excellent continent, exceedingly delightful," [were moved by] King Mandhātu the Wheel-turner.
Accompanying him as he traveled through the four continents with the Wheel-Treasure at his head, they arrived.
Then the King asked the General-Treasure: "Is there indeed any place more delightful than the human world? "Why do you ask this, O Lord?
Do you not see the majesty of the moon and the sun? Is it not their very abode?"
"Is there anything more delightful than this? The King, preceded by the Wheel-Treasure, went there.
Upon hearing that "Great King Mandhātu has arrived," the Four Great Kings thought, "This king is of great psychic power and great majesty;
he cannot be resisted through war," and they offered up their own kingdoms to him. Having accepted them, he asked again: "Is there indeed..."
“Is there a place more delightful than this?
Then they described to him the Tāvatiṃsa heaven: “Your Majesty, the Tāvatiṃsa heaven is more delightful than this.
There, these four Great Kings stand as attendants at the gate of Sakka, the King of the Devas.”
Sakka, king of the gods, is of great psychic power and great majesty;

these are his places of enjoyment: the Vejayanta Palace, a thousand yojanas in height; the Sudhamma Assembly Hall of the gods, five hundred yojanas in height; the Vejayanta chariot, one hundred and fifty yojanas long;
likewise the elephant Erāvaṇa; and the Nandana Grove, adorned with a thousand celestial trees.
"The Cittalatā grove, the Phārusaka grove, the Missaka grove, and the Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree, which is one hundred yojanas in height;
beneath it is the Paṇḍukambala stone, sixty yojanas long, fifty yojanas wide, and fifteen yojanas high, the color of a jaya-flower,
whose softness allows half the body of Sakka to sink into it when he sits down."
Having heard that, the king, desiring to go there, launched the Wheel-Treasure. It halted in the air together with the fourfold army.

Then, descending from the midpoint between the two heavenly worlds, the Wheel-Treasure alighted upon the earth together with the fourfold army headed by the Counsellor-Treasure. The king alone [proceeded] to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
He arrived. Upon hearing that Mandhātā had come, Sakka went out to meet him and said, "Welcome, Great King!
All is yours, Great King! Command, Great King!

Having spoken thus, he divided his kingdom into two portions and gave one portion to him along with the celestial nymphs. As soon as the king was established in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, his human nature vanished.

His divine state vanished and he appeared [as a human]. It is said that when he was seated with Sakka upon the Pandukambala stone, no difference could be perceived between them even in the twinkling of an eye.
Failing to discern this, the devas were bewildered by the lack of distinction between Sakka and him.
While experiencing celestial splendor there, he remained until thirty-six Sakkas had arisen [and passed away].

Having ruled the kingdom for some time, Cutā died while still unsatiated with sensual pleasures; having passed away from there, he was reborn in his own pleasure garden, where his body, struck by wind and sun, met its end.
But when the Wheel-treasure (cakkaratana) had once again been established upon the earth, the Counsellor-treasure (pariṇāyakaratana) [addressed] Mandhātu on a golden tablet.
Having had sandals carved, he ruled his kingdom with this [inscription]: "This is the kingdom of Mandhātā.
Then those people who had come from the three continents, being unable to return, approached the Jewel of the Counsellor and petitioned him, saying: "Sire, we came through the majesty of the King;
now we are unable to go back. Grant us a place to dwell. He gave each of them—
She gave away the countryside. There, the region inhabited by people who had come from Pubbavideha received the name "the kingdom of Videha" through that very same former designation;
the region inhabited by people who had come from Aparagoyāna received the name "the western province";
and the region inhabited by people who had come from Uttarakuru received the name "the kingdom of Kuru."
However, when referring to many villages, market towns, and so forth, the plural number is used. Therefore it is said: "He dwells among the Kurus.
Regarding the term *Kammāsadhamma*, which is a market town (*nigama*) of the Kurus, some explain the meaning here by changing the letter *dha* to *da*.
[They say: "Kammāsadammo" means "one who has tamed (*damito*) Kammāsa. "Kammāsa" refers to Kammāsapāda (also known as Porisāda).
It is said that at the place where his foot had been pierced by a thorn, as the wound healed, it became like the wood-apple tree (*citradāru*);
therefore, he was known as Kammāsapāda. And in that place, he was tamed—that is, restrained from his state as a man-eater—by whom?
By the Great Being. In which Jātaka? Some say in the Mahāsutasoma Jātaka. These...
However, the elders say it was the Jayaddisa Jātaka. For at that time, the Great Being tamed Kammāsapāda. As it is said:
"When I was the son of Jayaddisa, the legitimate heir of the lord of the kingdom of Pañcāla."
"Having desisted from taking life, I liberated my father;
I also won over Kammāsapāda.
Some, however, explain the meaning using the letter *dha* instead. It is said that among the inhabitants of the Kurū country, there was a custom (*kuruvatta-dhamma*).
The *kammāsa* tree grew there; therefore, because the Dhamma was born in that place, it is called "Kammāsadhamma.
This is also the name of the market town (*nigama*) situated there. Why was it not expressed using the locative case? Because it was not a dwelling place.
It is said that in that market town, the Blessed One had no specific dwelling place known as a monastery (*vihāra*). From the market town...
However, having departed, there was a great forest grove on a certain delightful piece of ground well-supplied with water;
there the Blessed One dwelt, making that market town his alms-resort village. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood thus:
“He dwells among the Kurus; Kammāsadhamma is the name of a market town of the Kurus, and he has made that his alms-resort village.”
“Venerable” (āyasmā) is a term of endearment; it is a term of respect. “Ānanda” is the name of that elder.
“To one side” (ekamantaṃ) is an indication of the locative case—as in such expressions as “the moon and sun revolve unevenly”—therefore, the meaning here should be understood as:
he sat down in such a way that he was seated to one side. [The suffix -m-] has the sense of the locative.
This is a term of respectful address; "sat down" means he sat near. For the wise, having approached one who is worthy of honor, sit to one side out of skill in the use of seats.
And since he was one among them, he therefore sat to one side.
But how does one sitting to one side sit? By avoiding the six faults of sitting. Namely as follows:
—too far away, too close, in the wind, on high ground, directly in front, or directly behind.
For if one sits too far away and wishes to speak, one must speak in a loud voice.
If one sits too close, one causes physical contact. If one sits in the wind, one is troubled by the odor of the body. If one sits on high ground...
He manifests a lack of respect. If he sits too close and wishes to look [at the Blessed One], he must gaze with eye-to-eye contact;
if he sits too far back and wishes to look, he must turn his neck to see.
Therefore, having circumambulated the Blessed One three times and paid him due homage, these...
Having avoided the six faults of sitting, the Venerable Ānanda, the keeper of the Dhamma-treasury, sat down to one side.

He did so by entering into the midst of the six-colored rays of the Buddha, as if plunging into clear lac juice, as if donning a golden robe, and as if entering the center of a canopy made of garlands of red lotuses.
Thus it is said: "He sat down to one side."
At what time and for what reason did this venerable one approach the Blessed One?
It was at the evening hour, for the purpose of asking a question concerning the nature of conditions (*paccayākāra*).

On that day, it is said, this venerable one had wandered for alms through the village of Kammāsadhamma—like one depositing a thousand pieces of gold at every door for the sake of gathering a following—and had returned from his almsround.
Having performed the duties toward the Teacher, when the Teacher had entered the fragrant chamber,
he paid homage to the Teacher and went to his own daytime resting place. After his pupils had performed their duties and departed,
he swept the resting place, spread out his leather mat, took water from his water-pot, cooled his hands and feet with the water, and sat cross-legged.
Sitting with his legs crossed, he attained the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala-samāpatti*).

Then, emerging from that attainment by means of a predetermined time, he directed his knowledge toward the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*). Starting from the beginning—"with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise"—he proceeded to the end;
starting from the end, he proceeded to the beginning; starting from both ends, he proceeded to the middle; and starting from the middle, [he proceeded to the ends].
Traversing both ends, he comprehended the mode of conditionality (*paccayākāra*) three times by way of twelve steps.
As he was thus comprehending it, the mode of conditionality became clear and appeared to him as plain as an open palm.
Then he thought: "This mode of conditionality has been described by all the Buddhas as 'profound and appearing profound.'"
"It has been explained; yet for me, as a disciple established in partial knowledge, it appears clear, manifest, and evident.
Does this appear so clear only to me, or to others as well?
Then it occurred to him: "Come now, I shall take this question and ask the Blessed One; surely for me..."
The Blessed One, having taken up this occasion for instruction, will expound a discourse on the Suttantas as if lifting up Mount Sineru with his fingertips.

For when the Buddhas encounter these four matters—the formulation of the Vinaya, the distinctions between planes, the causal relations of conditions, and the distinctions between time-periods—their thundering becomes great and their wisdom penetrates deeply; such is the nature of the Buddha-wisdom.
“Greatness is manifest; the teaching is profound, struck by the three characteristics, and connected with emptiness.
Although he usually approaches the Blessed One even a hundred or a thousand times in a single day, he does not do so without cause or reason;
yet on that day, having taken up this question—“This elephant of the Buddha’s scent... [he approached].
Thinking, "Approaching the elephant of the Buddha, I shall hear the cry of the trumpeting of knowledge; approaching the lion of the Buddha, I shall hear the lion’s roar of knowledge;

approaching the thoroughbred horse of the Buddha, I shall behold the stride of the steps of knowledge," he rose from his daytime seat, shook out his leather mat, took it with him, and approached the Blessed One in the evening.
Thus it is said: "Approaching in the evening for the purpose of asking a question concerning the nature of conditions."
Regarding the phrase "how deep": here the word *yāva* (as far as/how) signifies the exceeding of a measure;
it means "deep beyond measure," that is, "extremely deep. Regarding "appearing deep": it means that being indeed deep, it appears as such; it is seen.
For one thing may be shallow yet appear deep, like old water of a dark color due to rotten leaves and so forth. Even though that [water] is only knee-deep...
It appears as if it were six *pauruṣa* [in depth]. One part is deep but appears shallow, like the clear water of the Maṇi-Gaṅgā;
for even though it is six *pauruṣa* deep, it seems as if it were only knee-deep. Another part is shallow and appears shallow, like water in a bowl or similar vessels.
One part is deep and appears deep, like the great ocean at the base of Sineru.
It is like water. Thus, water alone receives four names. But this is not the case with dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*);
for it receives only one name: "profound and appearing profound.
Even though it is of such a nature, yet it appears to me as if it were shallow and easy to grasp—this, venerable sir, is wonderful, this is marvelous!
"Venerable Sir," he said. Having thus expressed his own astonishment and asked the question, he sat down in silence.

When the Blessed One heard his words, [he thought]: "Ānanda is like one stretching out his hand to grasp the peak of existence, like one striving to cut through Sineru and extract its marrow, or like one wishing to cross the great ocean without a ship."
Thinking, "He speaks of a question within the Buddha’s domain as if it were easy for himself, like one who strives to turn over the earth in order to take its essence;
I shall explain its profound nature," he said, "Mā heva... and so forth. Therein, *mā heva*:

the syllable *ha* is merely an expletive; the meaning is "do not speak thus. And this word *mā heva* was spoken by the Blessed One both while encouraging the Venerable Ānanda and while discouraging him.
Commentary on the Exaltation:
Therein, while exalting him—“Ānanda, you possess great wisdom and lucid knowledge; therefore, even though dependent origination is profound, it appears to you as if it were shallow.
However, one should not perceive it as shallow for others; it is indeed profound.”
And it has a profound appearance. Regarding this, they cite four similes.

It is said that when a great wrestler—who had been nourished on the essence of excellent food for six months, who had practiced with wrestling-stones, and who was going to the arena at the time of a festival—was shown a wrestling-stone along the way, he asked, "What is this? When told, "It is a wrestling-stone," he said, "Bring it here!"
"Later on. When it was said, "I am not able to lift it," he went there himself and asked, "Where is this heavy spot?
Having lifted two rocks with both hands and thrown them like play-balls, he departed.

In that regard, although the wrestler’s wrestling-stone is light, it should not be said that it is light compared to others. [For] the wrestler has been nourished for six months by the essence of excellent food.
For the Venerable Ānanda had fulfilled his aspiration for a hundred thousand aeons;
just as a wrestler’s wrestling stone is light due to his great strength, so too was dependent origination shallow for the Elder due to his great wisdom,
though it cannot be said that it was shallow for others.
In the great ocean there are four kinds of fish measuring four thousand yojanas each:

the fish named *timi* measuring two hundred yojanas, the *timiṅgala* measuring three hundred yojanas, the *timiṅgila* measuring four hundred yojanas, and the *timirapiṅgala* measuring five hundred yojanas; then *ānanda*, *timinandana*, *ajjhāroha*, and the *mahātimi*.
Among these, they usually refer to it by the name *timirapiṅgala*. It is said that its right ear—
As he moved, the water in an area of five hundred yojanas was stirred. Likewise his left ear; likewise his tail;

likewise his head. But when he had moved both ears, struck the water with his tail, and began to sport by tossing his head back and forth, the water in an area of seven or eight hundred yojanas became like a pot placed on a stove and set over the fire.
The water boils as if it were a small amount of water; over an area of three hundred yojanas, the water is not even able to cover one's back.
He would say: "They say this great ocean is deep, deep indeed! Where is its depth?
We do not find even enough water to cover our backs. In that regard, for the Timirapiṅgala fish who has attained such a body...

"Just as it cannot be said that the great ocean is shallow because it is shallow for small fish, even so, although dependent origination is shallow for an elder endowed with wisdom, it cannot be said to be shallow for others.
And the king of supaṇṇas is one hundred and fifty yojanas long; his right wing is fifty yojanas."
His left wing is sixty yojanas in length, his neck thirty yojanas, his mouth nine yojanas, and his feet twelve yojanas.
When he begins to display the wind of the supaṇṇa, even a space of seven or eight hundred yojanas is not sufficient.
He would say: "They say this space is infinite, infinite; how can it be infinite?"
"We do not even find a place to stretch out our wings and flap them.
In this context, just as the sky is said to be limited for the king of the garuḍas who has attained his body, yet it cannot be said that it is limited for other small birds;
even so, dependent origination is said to be shallow for the Elder who has attained wisdom, yet it cannot be said that it is shallow for others as well.
As for Rāhu, the lord of the asuras, he measures four thousand eight hundred yojanas from the soles of his feet to the tips of his hair.
The distance between his two arms is twelve hundred yojanas; his thickness is six hundred yojanas.
The palms of his hands and the soles of his feet are three hundred yojanas each, as is his mouth. Each joint of his fingers is fifty yojanas.
Likewise the space between his eyebrows. His forehead is three hundred yojanas wide. His head is nine hundred yojanas high.
When he has entered the great ocean, the deep water reaches only up to his knees. He would say: "They say this great ocean is deep, deep;
but where is its depth? To us it is no more than knee-deep."
“...we cannot find water. In that regard, for Rāhula who was endowed with physical power, the great ocean was shallow;
yet it cannot be said that it was shallow for others. In the same way, for the Elder who was endowed with wisdom, dependent origination was shallow;
yet it cannot be said that it was shallow for others as well. With reference to this meaning, the Blessed One said: “Do not say so, Ānanda...”
He said, “Do not speak thus, Ānanda.

For to the Elder, even the profound dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) appeared as shallow for four reasons. What are these four? Because of the excellence of his past spiritual support (pubbūpanissaya), because of his dwelling at a sacred ford (titthavāsa), because of his being a stream-enterer (sotāpanna), and because of his great learning (bahussuta).
This is the discourse on the excellence of his past spiritual support.
It is said that one hundred thousand aeons ago, a Teacher named Padumuttara appeared in the world.
His city was called Haṃsavatī; his father was King Ānanda, and his mother was Queen Sumedhā. The Bodhisatta was a prince named Uttara.
On the very day his son was born, he made the Great Renunciation, went forth into homelessness, and applied himself to the supreme effort.
Having gradually attained omniscience and uttered the inspired utterance (udāna), “Through many births in saṃsāra...,” he spent seven days on the seat of enlightenment (bodhipallaṅka).
Then, thinking, “I shall set my foot upon the earth,” he extended his foot. Thereupon, the earth split open and a great lotus rose up.
Its central petals were ninety cubits long, its filaments thirty cubits, and its pericarp—
The dust was twelve cubits high and the quantity was equal to nine water-jars.
The Teacher, however, was fifty-eight cubits in height.
The distance between his two arms was eighteen cubits, his forehead was five cubits, and his hands and feet were eleven cubits each. Of that [eleven-cubit] hand...

As soon as his foot merely stepped upon the twelve-cubit navel-circle (*kaṇṇikā*), dust the size of nine water-jars rose up and, having ascended to a height of fifty-eight cubits, was scattered over the area like powdered blue vitriol (*manosilā*).
From that time on, the Blessed One became known simply as Padumuttara. Devila and Sujāta were his two chief disciples (*aggasāvaka*), and Amitā and Asamā were his two [chief female disciples].

The chief female disciple was [named] Sumana. His attendant was named Upaṭṭhāka. While bestowing his paternal care, the Blessed One Padumuttara dwelt in the capital city of Haṃsavatī with a retinue of one hundred thousand bhikkhus.
His younger brother was Prince Sumanakumāra. From Haṃsavatī, the king [sent him] two hundred and twenty yojanas away...
He gave him the village of Bhogagāma as a fief. From time to time, he would come and see both his father and the Teacher.
Then one day, the border region rose in revolt. Sumana sent word to the king: "The border region has revolted. The king replied:
"Why was I appointed by you to that place? He departed, quelled the bandits, and reported: "The country is pacified, Your Majesty."
He sent it to the king. The king, being delighted, said, "May my son come quickly.
He had about a thousand ministers. On the way, he consulted with them: "My father is pleased;
if he grants me a boon, what should I take? Then some of them said to him, "Take an elephant; take a horse; take a chariot..."
"Take [the kingdom]! Take the realm! Take the seven treasures! they said. Others said:
"You are the sons of the Lord of the Earth; wealth is not difficult for you to obtain. Yet even all this that has been acquired must be abandoned when departing;
only merit is what one takes with one when going. Therefore, while the gods are offering you a boon, [you should spend] these three months [serving] the Blessed One Padumuttara."
“Take the boon for attending upon me. He thought, “You are my virtuous friends; this intention was not mine, but was instilled by you.

I shall do so. Having gone and paid homage to his father, and being embraced by his father who kissed him on the head, he said, “I grant you a boon, my son,” to which he replied, “Excellent, Great King!”
“Great King, I wish to make my life fruitful by serving the Blessed One for three months with the four requisites;
grant me this very boon,” he said. When [the king] replied, “It is not possible, dear son; choose another boon,” he said, “Your Majesty, there are indeed only two kinds of speech for kshatriyas:
grant me this one, for I have no need for anything else. “Dear son, the minds of Buddhas...”
"It will be difficult to know; if the Blessed One does not wish for it, what will happen even if it is given by me?
He thought, "Very well, Your Majesty, I shall read the mind of the Blessed One," and went to the monastery.
At that time, having finished his meal, the Blessed One had entered the fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭi). He [stood] in the assembly hall.
He went into the presence of the monks who were sitting together. They said to him, "Prince, why have you come?
"To see the Blessed One; show me the Blessed One. "Prince, we do not get to see the Teacher whenever we wish.
"But who, venerable sirs, does get to see him? "The Elder named Sumanatthera, Prince."
“Where is the elder, venerable sir? Having asked where the elder was sitting, he went there, paid homage, and said, “Venerable sir, I wish to see the Blessed One; please show him to me.
The elder said, “Come, Prince,” took him by the hand, placed him in the courtyard surrounding the Perfumed Chamber, and ascended into the Perfumed Chamber himself. Then the Blessed One—
“Sumanas, why have you come? he asked. “Venerable sir, I have come to see the Blessed One,” replied the prince.
“In that case, monk, prepare a seat. The elder prepared a seat, and the Blessed One sat down on the seat that had been prepared.
The prince paid homage to the Blessed One and offered him hospitality. “When did you arrive, prince? he asked.
“Venerable sir, when you had entered the fragrant chamber, the monks sent me to the Elder’s presence, saying:
‘We do not get to see the Blessed One whenever we wish. Yet the Elder showed himself to us with a single word.
Venerable sir, I think the Elder is a favorite of yours. “Yes, prince, he is a favorite.”
“This monk is my follower,” [the boy said]. “Venerable sir, what must one do in the teaching of the Buddhas to become a favorite?
“Having given gifts, having undertaken moral discipline, and having performed the Uposatha observance, young man.
“Blessed One, I wish to become a favorite in the Buddha’s teaching like the Elder; please accept my invitation for the three-month rains residence. The Blessed One—

—“Is there indeed any purpose to be gained by going there? Having observed this and seen that there was, he said, “In empty dwellings, Prince, the Tathāgatas find delight. The prince said, “Understood, Blessed One;
understood, Sugata,” and added, “Venerable Sir, I shall go first and have a monastery built; then, when I have sent for them, you may come together with a hundred thousand bhikkhus.”
Having obtained his promise with the words, "Come," he went into the presence of his father and said, "Your Majesty, I have received a promise from the Blessed One;

when I have sent for him, you should dispatch the Blessed One. Having paid homage to his father and departed, he had monasteries built every yojana along the way, traveled a distance of one thousand two hundred yojanas, and while searching for a site for a monastery in his own city, he found one.

Having seen a beautiful park belonging to a householder, Sobhana purchased it for one hundred thousand [pieces of gold], and after spending another hundred thousand, he had a monastery constructed there.
Having built a fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭi) for the Blessed One and huts, caves, and pavilions for the other monks to use as night-quarters and day-quarters,
and having completed the surrounding walls and the gateway tower, he went into the presence of his father.
He sent word: “My task is finished; please send the Teacher.
After the King had fed the Blessed One, he said: “Blessed One, Suman’s task is finished; he awaits your arrival.
Then the Blessed One, accompanied by a retinue of one hundred thousand bhikkhus, stayed in monasteries at intervals of one league each.
He arrived. Hearing that the Teacher had come, the prince went out a league to meet him, honored him with garlands and other offerings, and having led him into the monastery, said:
“This garden named Sobhana was purchased by me for a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] and constructed for a hundred thousand; accept it, O Great Sage.”
He had the monastery assigned [to the Sangha]. On the day of the commencement of the rains retreat, after giving an offering, he summoned his own children, wife, and ministers, and said:
"This Teacher has come from afar to our presence; for Buddhas are indeed reverent toward the Dhamma, not toward material things.
Therefore, for these three months, wearing only two robes and observing the ten precepts—"
“Having taken this vow, I shall dwell right here; you, however, should continue to give alms for three months in this very manner to the hundred thousand who have destroyed the taints.
Thus he dwelt in a place very close to the dwelling of the Elder Sumanas, and [observed] whatever service the Elder performed for the Blessed One...
Having seen all that he was doing, he thought, "In this place, this elder is exclusively beloved; it is fitting for me to aspire to his very position.
Then, as the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā) drew near, he entered the village and gave a great almsgiving for seven days.
On the seventh day, having placed his three robes at the feet of one hundred thousand bhikkhus, he [addressed] the Blessed One.

Having paid homage, he said: "Venerable sir, from the time I began having monasteries built at intervals of one *yojana* along the road, whatever merit I have performed was not done aspiring for the state of Sakka, nor the state of Māra, nor the state of Brahmā;
rather, it was done aspiring for the position of being an attendant to the Buddha. Therefore, I too—"
“Blessed One, may I become an attendant to a Buddha in the future, just like the Elder Sumanā,” he said, and prostrating himself with the fivefold salutation, he paid homage.
The Blessed One, observing—“This is the mind of a noble son; will it indeed succeed?”—knew:
“In the future, after one hundred thousand aeons from now, a Buddha named Gotama will arise, and he shall be that very Buddha’s attendant. Thus he understood.
“May all that you desire and pray for be fulfilled;
may all your intentions be realized, like the moon on the fifteenth day.
Having heard this, the prince thought, “The Buddhas indeed speak without duplicity,” and on the very second day, he [went] to him.
He followed closely behind the Blessed One as if carrying his bowl and robe.
Having given alms for a hundred thousand years during that dispensation of a Buddha, he was reborn in the heavenly realms.

Furthermore, during the time of Kassapa Buddha, while the Elder was wandering for alms, he offered his upper garment to hold the bowl and thus made an offering. Having been reborn in the heavenly realms once again—

Passing away from there, he became the King of Bārāṇasī. Having built leaf-huts for eight Paccekabuddhas and provided them with jeweled water-vessels, he attended upon them with the four requisites for ten thousand years.
These are well-known places. Furthermore, while giving gifts for a hundred thousand kappas, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven together with our Bodhisatta.
Passing away from there, he took rebirth in the house of the Sakyan Amitodana;
having gradually undertaken the Great Renunciation and attained Perfect Enlightenment, he came to Kapilavatthu on his first journey;
then, as the Blessed One was departing from there, after the princes had gone forth for the sake of becoming the Blessed One’s retinue, [he] departed along with Bhaddiya and the others.

Having gone forth in the presence of the Blessed One, after hearing a discourse on the Dhamma from the Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta, he was soon established in the fruit of stream-entry. Thus this Venerable One was endowed with a prior supportive condition;
and by virtue of that attainment of a prior supportive condition, even the profound dependent origination appeared to him as if it were shallow.
Commentary on "Dwelling at a Sacred Site" (*titthavāsa*):
"Dwelling at a sacred site" refers to the repeated learning, hearing, questioning, and memorizing [of the Dhamma] in the presence of one's teachers.
This was exceedingly pure for the Elder; therefore, even this profound dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) appeared to him as if it were shallow.
The mode of conditionality (paccayākāra) appears quite clearly to those who have attained stream-entry (sotāpanna), and this venerable one is a stream-enterer.
Furthermore, the delimitation of name-and-form (nāmarūpa-pariccheda) becomes as evident to those of great learning as a bed and chair in a four-cubit room when a lamp is burning;
and this venerable one is the foremost among those of great learning, and by the power of his vast knowledge, even that which is profound...
The mode of conditionality appeared as clear as if it were laid out before one's eyes.

Regarding the profundity of dependent origination: therein, dependent origination is said to be profound by way of four aspects—profundity of meaning, profundity of phenomena, profundity of teaching, and profundity of penetration.

In this context, the meaning of the arising and full manifestation of aging-and-death through the condition of birth is profound; ... [and so on] ... the meaning of the arising and full manifestation of volitional formations through the condition of ignorance is profound—this is profundity of meaning (*atthagambhīratā*).

The meaning of the conditionality of volitional formations for ignorance is profound; ... [and so on] ... the meaning of the conditionality of aging-and-death for birth is profound—this is profundity of phenomena (*dhammagambhīratā*).
In some suttas, dependent origination is taught in forward order (*anuloma*); in some, in reverse order (*paṭiloma*); in some, ...
This is the profundity of the teaching: that it proceeds in forward order, in reverse order, or in both forward and reverse order;

starting from the middle in some instances; that in some cases it consists of three joints and four compendiums, in some cases two joints and three compendiums, and in some cases one joint and two compendiums.

Furthermore, the meaning of ignorance is profound in its aspect of non-knowing, non-seeing, and non-penetration of the truths; the meaning of volitional formations is their constructing, accumulating, and being accompanied by or devoid of lust;

the meaning of consciousness is its emptiness, lack of agency, and manifestation as rebirth-linking without transmigration; the meaning of name-and-form is their simultaneous arising, their analysis and non-analysis, and their bending and being bent;

the meaning of the six sense bases is their predominance, their nature as doors to the world, their field, and their state as subjects; and the meaning of contact is touching, collision, conjunction, and meeting.
The meaning of feeling (*vedanā*) is the state of experiencing the flavor of the object, whether as pleasure, pain, or neutrality, and the state of being felt;

the meaning of craving (*taṇhā*) is the state of delighting in and clinging to, like a river, a creeper, a stream of craving, or an ocean of craving that is difficult to fill; the meaning of clinging (*upādāna*) is the state of grasping, seizing, adhering, and misapprehending, which is difficult to transcend;

the meaning of becoming (*bhava*) is the state of accumulating and forming volitional formations, and of casting one into the various wombs, destinies, stations, and abodes; and the meaning of birth (*jāti*) is the state of being born, fully born, descended, produced, and manifested.
"The meaning of the destruction, passing away, breaking up, and transformation of aging-and-death is profound.
Thus, that which is the intrinsic nature of ignorance and the rest—that penetration by which ignorance and the others are penetrated according to their own essential characteristics—is "profound";
this is to be understood as profundity of penetration. All of this appeared to the Elder as if it were shallow. Therefore—
The Blessed One, encouraging the Venerable Ānanda, said, “Do not say so,” and so forth. This is the intended meaning here:
“Ānanda, you possess great wisdom and lucid knowledge; therefore, even though dependent origination is profound, it appears to you as if it were shallow.
For this reason, do not speak thus, thinking: ‘Does this appear shallow only to me, or does it appear so to others as well?’”
Commentary on the Disparagement:

As for what was said, "disparagingly," this is the intended meaning: Ānanda, do not speak thus, saying, "And yet, to me, it appears as something quite superficial. For if this [Dhamma] were indeed superficial to you...
