"It appears so; why is it that you did not become a stream-enterer through your own natural capacity, but instead realized the path of stream-entry by relying solely on the method given by me?
Ānanda, this Nibbāna itself is profound, yet for you the principle of conditionality (paṭiccasamuppāda) has become shallow;
so then, why [did you not realize] the gross fetter of sensual lust, the fetter of aversion, and the gross underlying tendency to sensual lust?"
Having eradicated these four defilements—the underlying tendency toward aversion—do you not realize the fruit of the once-returner?
Having eradicated those same four defilements when they have subsisted as mere subtle residues, do you not realize the fruit of the non-returner?

[And having eradicated] these eight defilements: the five fetters beginning with attachment to the form realm, the underlying tendency toward attachment to existence, the underlying tendency toward conceit, and the underlying tendency toward ignorance...
Having eradicated [the defilements], why do you not realize Arhatship?

And why do you not penetrate the disciple’s knowledge of the perfections (sāvakapāramiñāṇa), like Sāriputta and Moggallāna, who fulfilled the perfections for one incalculable aeon plus a hundred thousand aeons? For two incalculable aeons plus a hundred thousand aeons...
Why do you not penetrate the knowledge of private enlightenment (*paccekabodhi-ñāṇa*), like the Paccekabuddhas who have fulfilled the perfections? Or,
if this [knowledge] appears to you in its entirety as something superficial,

then why do you not realize the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), like the Buddhas who have fulfilled the perfections for four, eight, or sixteen incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya*) plus a hundred thousand aeons?
Why do you have no interest in these special attainments? Behold how far you have failed!
You, a disciple established in mere partial knowledge, say of the extremely profound nature of conditions, "It appears plain to me.
This statement of yours contradicts the teaching of the Buddhas; for by a monk such as you, [the teachings] of the Buddhas...
"It is appropriate that you speak in opposition to my discourse.
"Is it not true, Ānanda, that four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons have passed while I was striving to penetrate the nature of conditions?
And for the sake of penetrating the nature of conditions, nothing was given to me..."
There is no such thing as "giving," nor is there any such thing as "a perfection not yet fulfilled.
Yet, while I was dispersing the forces of Māra as if they were effortless—thinking, "I shall penetrate the nature of conditions"—this great earth did not shake even two finger-breadths.
Likewise, while I was accomplishing the knowledge of past lives during the first watch of the night and the divine eye during the middle watch, [it remained still]. During the last watch...

But at the time of the powerful dawn, as soon as I saw that "ignorance is a condition for volitional formations in nine ways," the ten-thousandfold world system shook like a bronze gong struck by an iron rod, emitting hundreds and thousands of roars;
it trembled like drops of water on a lotus leaf struck by the wind. Thus profound...
And this dependent origination, Ānanda, appears profound. Because of the non-awakening to this Dhamma... [as before] ...he does not transcend suffering.
"To this Dhamma" means to this Dhamma of conditions. "Non-awakening" means not awakening by way of full understanding through knowledge (*ñātapariññā*).
"Non-penetration" means not penetrating by way of full understanding through investigation and abandonment (*tīraṇappahānapariññā*). "Become like a tangled skein" means a skein...

They have become as if thrown into confusion. Just as a weaver’s thread that has been poorly laid out and gnawed by mice becomes tangled here and there, making it difficult to coordinate the tip with the tip or the end with the end—thinking "this is the tip" or "this is the end"—in the very same way, beings who stumble over this system of conditions (paccayākāra) become confused and utterly bewildered. They do not...

They are able to straighten that mode of conditionality (*paccayākāra*). In this regard, while it might be possible to straighten a tangled thread by applying personal effort (*paccatta-purisakāra*), there are no beings other than the two types of Bodhisattas who are capable of straightening the mode of conditionality through their own inherent nature (*dhammatā*).
Just as a tangled thread, when treated with sour gruel and carded with a comb...
Just as a ball struck here and there becomes knotted and entangled, so too these beings,
having stumbled among the conditions and being unable to straighten them out, become confused and entangled by way of the sixty-two views.
For whoever relies upon views, all are indeed unable to straighten out the mode of conditions.
"Born from a nest-fiber" (*kulāgaṇṭhika-jāta*): "nest-fiber" (*kulāgaṇṭhika*) refers to the thread used by a weaver. Some say that *kulā* is the name for a bird;

its nest (*kulāvaka*) is also [meant], according to some. For just as it is difficult to bring either of these two together—end with end or root with root—so too should this be construed according to the previous method.
"Muñjapabbajabhūtā" means they have become like muñja grass and pabbaja grass.
Just as when those grasses have been pounded and made into rope, it is difficult— once the rope is worn out and fallen somewhere—

to take hold of them and match tip with tip or root with root, saying "this is the tip of this grass" or "this is the root of that," so too, even that [effort] depends on individual personal exertion (*paccattapurisakāra*).

It might be possible to make it straight by applying force; however, with the exception of the two Bodhisattvas, there are no other beings capable of making the mode of conditions (paccayākāra) straight by their own nature.

Thus, this generation, unable to make the mode of conditions straight, becomes knotted by way of speculative views (diṭṭhigata) and [falls] into the states of loss, the miserable destinations, and the abyss.
One does not transcend saṃsāra.
In this context, "state of loss" (apāya) refers to the realms of hell, the animal womb, the sphere of hungry ghosts, and the host of asuras.

Indeed, all of these are called "states of loss" because they lack the "wealth" (aya) known as prosperity. Likewise, they are called "bad destinations" (duggati) because they are the destination of suffering. They are [also] devoid of the excellence of happiness.
Because of falling down, it is called a "fall" (*vinipāta*).
But the other is described thus: "The uninterrupted succession of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases as they proceed is called *saṃsāra*."
All of this does not transcend, nor does it go beyond that. Rather, by repeatedly undergoing death and rebirth— from death to rebirth, and from rebirth to death—
one wanders through the three realms of existence, the four modes of birth, the five destinations,
the seven stations of consciousness, and the nine abodes of beings, like a ship tossed by the wind upon the great ocean or like [beads] on a machine.
And like a yoked ox, it merely wanders about. Thus, it should be understood that the Blessed One spoke all this in order to inspire confidence in the Venerable Ānanda.
96. Commentary on Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda):
Now, since this sutta begins with the words, "Deep, Ānanda, is this dependent origination," and "It is like a tangled skein," [the following is explained].

And since it is bound together by only two phrases, therefore, beginning the teaching with the sequence, "Ānanda, this dependent origination is profound," he said, "With this as condition, there is aging-and-death," and so forth, for the purpose of showing the profundity of the mode of conditions.
In this regard, the meaning is as follows: the condition for this aging-and-death is...
"Ānanda, when a wise person is asked: 'This is a specific condition; therefore, because of this specific condition, there is aging and death. Does aging and death have a condition?

From what condition does aging and death come to be?'—then, just as one must remain silent when a question is set aside because it is to be left unanswered, such as when it is said, 'The soul is the same as the body,' so too should he remain silent."

Or rather, it should be said: "This was left undeclared by the Tathāgata. Not proceeding in that manner, just as when it is asked, "Is the eye eternal or non-eternal?", it must be stated with absolute certainty that it is non-eternal, so too it should be stated with absolute certainty that "it exists.
Furthermore, with what condition is aging-and-death? What indeed is that condition from which aging-and-death arises?
When it is said, "It comes to be," one must say, "With birth as condition, aging-and-death"; this is the meaning of what should be stated.
This same method applies to all the terms.
As for the statement, "With name-and-form as condition, contact," this is because when "with the six sense bases as condition" is stated, [contact] refers to eye-contact and so forth.

There is the grasping of only those resultant contacts (*vipāka-saṃphassā*). And here, wishing to show both what is already included by the phrase "conditioned by the six sense bases" (*saḷāyatana-paccayā*) and what is not yet included—the specific distinction of the conditionally arisen, as well as another specific condition for contact that exceeds the six sense bases—it should be understood that [this] has been stated. By this section, however...
"What was spoken by the Blessed One? "The source of the conditions was spoken.
For this discourse is called the *Mahānidāna* (Great Source) because it was spoken having made the conditions free from tangles and free from knots.
Now, in order to show the state of being a condition for each of those respective conditions—as it truly is, not otherwise, and not differently—[the following is said:]
He said, "It has indeed been said: 'With birth as condition, aging-and-death comes to be,'" and so forth.
In this context, "by way of method" means by way of cause. "In every way, entirely; in every manner, completely"—these are two particles. Their meaning is:

"If, in every aspect, all [aging-and-death] were not to exist in every way, that is, by their own intrinsic nature, through the name of birth. The meaning should be understood in this same manner for existence (*bhava*) and the other factors as well.
"Of anyone" (*kassaci*) is an indefinite expression, meaning "of anyone among gods and so forth.
"Anywhere" (*kimhici*) is likewise an indefinite expression, meaning "in any of the nine states of existence, such as the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) and others.

"That is to say" (*seyyathidaṃ*) is a particle used for the purpose of analyzing an unspecified matter that has been set forth; its meaning is: "I shall analyze the meaning of what was stated as 'of anyone anywhere.'"
Then, analyzing it, he said: “Of the gods, for the state of being a god,” and so forth.
Therein, “of the gods, for the state of being a god” means that which is this birth of aggregates for the divine state of the gods—that birth of aggregates by which gods are called “gods.
For if birth were entirely non-existent, one should understand the meaning in all instances according to this method.
And here, "gods" (*deva*) refers to gods by rebirth (*upapatti-deva*). "Gandhabbas" refers specifically to deities inhabiting roots, trunks, and so forth.

"Yakkhas" are non-human beings (*amanussa*). "Bhūtas" are any beings whatsoever that have been born. "Birds" (*pakkhin*) are any creatures whatsoever that possess wings of bone, wings of skin, or wings of feathers.
"Reptiles" (*sarīsapa*) are any creatures whatsoever that move by crawling along the ground. "Of those various... refers to them.

Of those [beings], such as the gods and gandhabbas. "For their sake" means for the state of being a god, a gandhabba, and so forth. "With the cessation of birth" means with the disappearance of birth; the meaning is the absence of birth.
All terms beginning with "cause" (hetu) are indeed synonyms for reason (*kāraṇa*).
For a reason is called a "cause" because it moves toward (*hinoti*) and proceeds toward its own fruit. Because it brings that fruit near—saying, "Come, take this"—it is so called.

Because it causes one to crave, it is therefore the "source" (*nidāna*). Because the fruit arises and originates from that, and because it proceeds and occurs dependent upon that, it is called both the "origin" (*samudaya*) and the "condition" (*paccaya*).
This same method applies everywhere. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "that which is called birth" (*yadidaṃ jāti*):
here, *yadidaṃ* is a particle. Its meaning should be understood according to the grammatical gender in all instances. Here—
However, the meaning of this [phrase] is: "that which is this birth. For birth is a condition for aging-and-death by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*).
99. Regarding the section on existence (*bhava*): by the phrase "what indeed," the delimitation of the sphere is established.

Therein, "existence in the sense-sphere" (*kāmabhava*) should be understood as extending downward to the limit of the Avīci hell and upward including the Paranimmitavasavatti devas. This method applies to the existence of rebirth (*upapattibhava*).
But here, it is appropriate to speak of the *kamma*-existence (*kammabhava*). For that [craving] is a condition for birth solely by way of the extreme limit of decisive support (*upanissaya*).
It should be understood that even in the sections beginning with "clinging" (*upādāna*), the delimitation of the scope is accomplished by this phrase, "What indeed... (Dhp 238). 100.

Regarding "with clinging as condition, existence (*bhava*)," here, sense-pleasure clinging (*kāmupādāna*) is a condition for all three types of *kamma*-existences and for all three types of rebirth-existences (*upapattibhava*).
In the same way, the remaining [links] should also be understood; thus, by way of the condition of clinging (*upādāna-paccaya*), twenty-four types of existence (*bhava*) are to be known.
In the direct sense (*nippariyāya*), twelve types of kamma-existence (*kammabhava*) are found here.

Their respective clingings (*upādāna*) are conditions for them both by way of co-nascence (*sahajāta-koṭi*) and by way of decisive support (*upanissaya-koṭi*). 101. Craving for form (*rūpa-taṇhā*) is craving with form as its object. This same method applies to craving for sound (*sadda-taṇhā*) and the others. Furthermore, this craving is a condition for clinging both by way of co-nascence and by way of decisive support.

102. "This is the condition for craving, namely, feeling": here, resultant feeling acts as a condition for craving by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*); other [types of feeling] act in other ways as well.

103. Having thus far shown the prior craving that constitutes the root of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), the Blessed One now proceeds with nine phrases, like one who strikes a person on the back or seizes them by the hair and drags them away from the path while they cry out again and again.
Showing craving as it manifests in active conduct, he said: “Thus, Ānanda, dependent upon feeling there is craving,” and so forth.
In this context, “craving” (taṇhā) refers to two types of craving: craving for seeking (esanatāṇhā) and craving for what has been sought (esitattāṇhā).

That craving by which one, having set out upon paths such as those of goats or carts, seeks and searches for wealth, is called craving for seeking. That [craving] which [arises] toward those things already sought and searched for...
Craving for what has been obtained is called "craving for the sought. Both of these are designations for craving in its active manifestation (*samudācāra-taṇhā*).
Therefore, this twofold [craving] is called "craving dependent upon feeling. "Seeking" (*pariyesanā*) refers to the seeking of objects such as forms;
for that occurs when craving exists. "Gain" (*lābha*) is the acquisition of objects such as forms; for that occurs when seeking exists.
It exists. Furthermore, analysis is fourfold by way of knowledge, craving, views, and thought.
Among these: “One should know the analysis of pleasure; having known the analysis of pleasure, one should devote oneself to internal pleasure”—this is analysis as knowledge.
“Analysis means two kinds of analysis: analysis of craving and analysis of views. Thus it has been handed down.
The determination of craving consists of the one hundred and eight modes of the wandering of craving. The determination of views consists of the sixty-two views.
However, in this sutta—“Desire, O Lord of Devas, has its source in applied thought”—it is applied thought itself that is presented as the "determination" here.
For once one has obtained gain, it is by means of applied thought alone that one determines whether it is desirable or undesirable, beautiful or ugly.
—“This much will be for the sake of the object of visible form; this much for the sake of the objects of sound and so forth;
this much will be mine; this much will belong to another; this much I shall enjoy;
this much I shall store away. Therefore it is said: “In dependence on gain, there is discrimination.”
"Chandarāga": thus, in regard to an object thought over by an unwholesome thought, both weak lust and strong lust arise;
for here, this is craving (*taṇhā*). "Chanda" is a designation for weak lust. "Clinging" (*ajjhosa*) is a strong determination in the form of "I" and "mine.
"Possession" (*pariggaha*) is the act of grasping by way of craving and views.
*Macchariya* means the inability to endure sharing with others. For this very reason, the ancients explain its etymological meaning thus:
"It is called *macchariya* because it functions with the thought: 'May this wonder be mine alone; may it not be a wonder for others.
*Ārakkha* means guarding thoroughly by means of locking doors, sealing chests, and so forth.
It is called *adhikaraṇa* because it "gives rise to" (*adhikaroti*); this is a name for a cause. *Ārakkhādhikaraṇa* is a neuter noun in the abstract sense;
the meaning is "for the sake of protection. Taking up a staff for the purpose of restraining others is "taking up a staff" (*daṇḍādāna*).
Taking up a sword with a single edge and so forth is "taking up a sword" (*satthādāna*). "Quarrel" (*kalaha*) refers to both quarrels of body and quarrels of speech.
The former and former [instances] are conflict (*viggaha*); the latter and latter are dispute (*vivāda*). "Tuvaṃtuvaṃ" refers to speech characterized by a lack of respect.

112. Now, in order to show that craving which manifests in such ways even by way of reverse order, he again begins the teaching with "the basis of guarding" (*ārakkhādhikaraṇa*) and thus concludes the discourse.
Therein, "craving for sensual pleasures" (*kāmataṇhā*) refers to that which has arisen by way of lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure.

Craving for form and so forth. Craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*) is lust accompanied by the view of eternalism (*sassatadiṭṭhi*). Craving for non-existence (*vibhavataṇhā*) is lust accompanied by the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*).
These two states are the craving that is the root of the round of existence (*vaṭṭamūla-taṇhā*) and the craving that is active manifestation (*samudācāra-taṇhā*); these are the two states.

"By way of a dyad" means that although they have reached a single state by virtue of having the characteristic of craving, they are divided into two portions according to the root of the round and its active manifestation within feeling.
They have a single convergence (*ekasamosaraṇā*); the meaning is that they have a single condition by way of feeling as a condition. For convergence is threefold:
convergence of descent (*osaraṇasamosaraṇa*), convergence of co-nascence (*sahajātasamosaraṇa*), and convergence of condition (*paccayasamosaraṇa*).
Among these, the statement, “Now, all those become convergences of sensual desire,” refers to what is called convergence of descent. “Rooted in desire... [etc.]...
"Friends, these states have contact as their origin and converge in feeling"—this is called "convergence by way of co-nascence.
However, "feeling has a single convergence through the pair"—this should be understood as "convergence by way of condition.
(113) "Eye-contact," and so forth—all these are exclusively resultant contacts. Among them, setting aside the four supramundane resultant contacts...
The remaining thirty-two [types of] contact occur. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "that which is called contact," here contact is a condition for feeling in many ways.
(114) In such passages as "by whatever modes, Ānanda," etc., "modes" (*ākāra*) refers to the mutually dissimilar intrinsic natures of feeling and the other [mental factors].

When these very [natures] are clearly demonstrated, they lead to their respective specific meanings; thus they are "signs" (*liṅga*). This is because they are the causes for the discernment of each [respective object].
These are the signs (*nimittāni*). They are called "indications" (*uddesā*) because they are to be pointed out in such and such a way. Therefore, this is the meaning here:

"Ānanda, by whatever modes... [as before] ...by whatever indications there is the designation (*paññatti*) of the name-body (*nāmakāya*), that is, of the collection of names—namely, when there is the indication 'feeling' (*vedanā*) in regard to the mode of feeling, the characteristic of feeling, and the sign of feeling;
and when there is the indication 'perception' (*saññā*) in regard to the mode of perceiving..."
When there is the designation "perception" (saññā) with respect to the mode of perceiving, the characteristic of perceiving, and the sign of perceiving;
when there is the designation "volition" (cetanā) with respect to the mode of intending, the characteristic of intending, and the sign of intending;

and when there is the designation "consciousness" (viññāṇa) with respect to the mode of cognizing, the characteristic of cognizing, and the sign of cognizing—then there arises the description of the "mental body" (nāmakāya) as "this is the mental body. Among those causes for the description of the mental body...
"Even in the absence of feeling and the other [mental factors], and in the absence of the modes [of perception] and so forth, would verbal contact be discerned in the material body?

That mental contact—which arises at the mind-door having made the four aggregates its basis and which is synonymous with verbal contact—would that be discerned in the material body? Could it arise by making the five sensitive organs its basis?"

Then the Venerable Ānanda, not accepting the arising of that [consciousness] from the form-body— just as the arising of a mango fruit does not occur from a rose-apple tree when mango trees are absent—
said, "Certainly not, Bhante. In the second question, he spoke by way of a summary,

defining "form" (rūpa) through its mode of being affected (ruppanākāra), its state of being affected (ruppana), its characteristic mark of being affected (ruppanaliṅga), and its sign of being affected (ruppananimitta), as well as by way of its modes and so forth.
The meaning should be understood as follows: "Contact through resistance" (*paṭighasamphassa*) is contact that arises having made the resistant form-aggregate (*rūpakkhandha*) its basis.

Here too, just as one would not expect a rose-apple fruit to arise from a mango tree when no rose-apple tree exists, the Elder, not accepting its arising from the mental body (*nāmakāya*), said, "Certainly not, Bhante."

The third question is stated by way of both [the mango and the rose-apple]. Therein, the Elder, refusing to accept the arising of both types of contact in the absence of name-and-form—just as one would not accept the arising of mangoes and rose-apples in the sky—said, "Certainly not, Bhante.

Having thus shown the specific conditions for each of the two contacts, he now began the fourth question with the words, "By whatever modes, Ānanda," in order to show that both of them, without distinction, have name-and-form as their condition. That is to say:
"Name-and-form": the meaning is that this which is name-and-form, this which is name-and-form in all six doors, is the very cause, the very condition.
For in the eye-door and the others, the eye and so forth, as well as visible forms and other objects, are "form," while the associated aggregates are "name";
thus, even this fivefold contact has name-and-form as its condition. This is also the case in the mind-door.
That which is the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*) and whatever form serves as the object—this is "form" (*rūpa*).

Those states that are associated [with consciousness] and whatever non-material phenomenon (*arūpa*) serves as the object—this is called "name" (*nāma*). Thus, mental contact (*manosamphassa*) should be understood as having name-and-form as its condition for contact.
Furthermore, name-and-form acts as its condition in many ways.
115. “Will you not descend? means: having entered, will you not proceed by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), as if it were already occurring?

“Will you coalesce? means: in the absence of rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhiviññāṇa*), will the remaining pure name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) proceed within the mother’s womb by way of coalescing—that is, becoming mixed—into the state of the embryo (*kalala*) and so forth? “Having descended, will you emerge? means...
"Having descended by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), you will depart by way of death (*cuti*"; the meaning is that you will cease).
Furthermore, that cessation of his does not occur through the cessation of that very same consciousness, nor through the cessation of the second or third [moments];
for thirty kamma-born material phenomena arise simultaneously with the rebirth-linking consciousness. And while those [material phenomena] remain...
Sixteen bhavaṅga-consciousnesses arise and cease.
During this interval, there is no obstacle for the child who has received rebirth-linking, nor for his mother; for this is called the "unoccupied period" (anokāsa).
However, if the material phenomena co-arising with the rebirth-linking consciousness are able to provide the condition for the seventeenth bhavaṅga, then the course of existence (pavatti) begins.
The continuity proceeds; the lineage is maintained. But if they are not able [to do so], the continuity does not proceed, the lineage is not maintained, and what is called "falling away" occurs.
With reference to that, it is said: "Having fallen away, you will fall away further.
"Itthattāya" means "to this state of being," that is, to the state of the five aggregates being thus complete. "Of one who is still young..."
"Are they? means "Are they present? as in the case of a dull and foolish person who is present.

"Will they be cut off? means "Will they be interrupted?"—that is, when consciousness is cut off, will mere name-and-form (nāmarūpa) arise and then undergo growth by way of the first stage of life, increase by way of the middle stage, and reach fullness by way of the final stage? Will they indeed attain these?
The meaning is: "Will you indeed attain growth, increase, and abundance by reaching ten years, twenty years, a hundred years, or even a hundred thousand years?

Therefore, "Come now, Ānanda," [he said], because [the Blessed One] was [independent] even at the time of taking rebirth-linking in the mother's womb, during the dwelling in the womb, and upon emerging from the womb.
Even at a time such as ten years after the commencement [of the cycle], consciousness alone is its condition;
therefore, this very thing is the cause, this is the condition for name-and-form, namely, consciousness. For just as a king, while restraining his retinue, might say:
"Who made you the viceroy? Who made you the commander-in-chief? Was it not by me? For if I were not acting..."
"By your own nature you might become a viceroy or a commander-in-chief; we would know your strength.
In this very way, consciousness is the condition for name-and-form. In terms of its meaning, it is as if name-and-form were saying:
"Who made you 'name,' you 'form,' and you 'name-and-form'? Was it not made by me? For if [it were] in me..."
"If you were to take rebirth in a mother's womb after having been a pure attendant, you would possess either name, or form, or both name-and-form;
we would know your power. Furthermore, this consciousness is a condition for name-and-form in many ways.
116. "The origin and arising of the mass of suffering" means the arising of the heap of suffering. "That is to say, name-and-form" refers to this very name-and-form.
This is the cause, this is the condition. For just as royal officials, while restraining the king, might say:

"By whom was 'king' made for you? Was it not made by us? For if we did not stand in the position of viceroy and in the position of commander-in-chief, you would be king all alone; let us see your kingship!"—even so it is with name-and-form.
In terms of its meaning, consciousness itself seems to say: "By whom was this rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhiviññāṇa) made?

Was it not made by us? For if you were to exist as so-called rebirth-linking consciousness without depending upon the three aggregates and the heart-base, we would see your state as rebirth-linking consciousness. And yet, this name-and-form (nāmarūpa) [depends] on consciousness...
It is a condition in many ways.

To this extent—namely, when name-and-form is a condition for consciousness and consciousness is a condition for name-and-form, as these two proceed by way of mutual condition—to this extent one might be born...
[and so on] ...or arise; thus do birth and the other [stages of suffering] come to be.
Or, they would be known through successive deaths and rebirths.

"The path of designation" (*adhivacanapatha*) refers to the path of conventional usage that proceeds by depending on the mere word, without perceiving the actual referent—for example, [calling someone] "Sirivaḍḍhaka" or "Dhanavaḍḍhaka.
"The path of etymological derivation" (*niruttipatha*) is as follows: one who remembers is "mindful" (*sato*); one who understands clearly is...
The "path of designation" (*paññatti-patha*) is the way of conventional expression proceeding by way of citing reasons, such as "one who is fully aware" (*sampajāno*), and so forth.

The "path of description" (*paññatti-patha*) is the way of conventional expression proceeding by way of making known various aspects, such as "wise, competent, intelligent, clever, one who has refuted the doctrines of others," and so forth.
Thus, by these three terms, it is the aggregates themselves that constitute the basis for these designations and the rest.
It has been explained. "The sphere of wisdom" (*paññāvacara*) means that which is to be traversed and known by wisdom. "The round turns" (*vaṭṭaṃ vattati*) means the round of saṃsāra turns.

"This state" (*itthatta*) means this condition; this is a name for the pentad of aggregates (*khandhapañcaka*). "For the purpose of making known" (*paññāpanāya*) means for the purpose of the designation of names (*nāmapaññatti*);
that is, for the purpose of the designation of names such as "feeling," "perception," and so forth, since even the pentad of aggregates is made known up to this point.
The meaning is as follows: "That is to say, name-and-form together with consciousness. This means that this name-and-form proceeds together with consciousness by way of mutual conditionality;
this much is what is intended. This, then, is the statement of the exposition here. [End of] the commentary on the designation of a self.
117. Thus the Blessed One, having shown the connection for the passage, "Ānanda, this dependent origination is deep and it appears deep," now began the teaching beginning with "And to what extent...
in order to show the connection for the passage, "[beings] born like a tangled skein.
Therein, regarding the phrases "For, Ānanda, one who holds a limited self as having form," and so forth:
He who grasps the unextended kasiṇa-sign as "self" describes it as material and limited.
But he who is a master of various kasiṇas describes it sometimes as blue and sometimes as yellow.
He who grasps the extended kasiṇa-sign as "self" describes it as material and infinite. Or again, he who [grasps] the unextended...
Having discarded the kasiṇa sign, one perceives either the area touched by the sign, or the four aggregates occurring therein, or even consciousness alone among them, as the self;
such a person describes the self as formless and limited.
Or, having discarded the expanded sign, one perceives either the area touched by the sign, or the four aggregates occurring therein... [and so on].
Or he grasps consciousness alone as the self, and he proclaims it to be formless and infinite.
118. Regarding the phrase "In this regard, Ānanda": here, "in this regard" refers to among those four types of speculative theorists. "Even now" means right now, and not beyond this.
This is stated by way of annihilationism. "Or existing there" means existing there in the next world.

This was said by way of eternalism (*sassata*). Or, "being otherwise" (*atathaṃ*) means being of a nature that is not such (*atathasabhāvaṃ*). "For the sake of being thus" (*tathattāya*) means for the state of being thus (*tathabhāvāya*).
"I shall make it suitable" (*upakappessāmi*) means I shall accomplish it. By this, he shows the dispute. For the annihilationist (*ucchedavādī*) [says]:
"The self of the eternalist, though being otherwise and possessing a nature other than annihilation, must be made thus—that is, of a nature of annihilation."
The eternalist thinks: "I will assist him, and having made him understand the doctrine of eternalism, I will lead him to adopt the doctrine of annihilationism.
The annihilationist also thinks: "Though my self is not such, being by nature non-eternal, I will assist it for the sake of its reality and for the sake of its state of eternity;
and having made him understand the doctrine of annihilationism, I will lead him to adopt the doctrine of eternalism."
"Being thus" means being in such a state as those who describe the self as having form and limited. "Having form" refers to one who has attained the meditation on the form-kasina.
"The view that the self is limited underlies" means that this view—that the self is limited—underlies [consciousness].
However, it does not underlie in the manner of a creeper or a vine; rather, it should be understood as underlying in the sense of being unabandoned.
"It is enough with this talk"—it is appropriate to say that such a view underlies that person. This same method applies everywhere.
Here, however, "one who is formless" (arūpin) should be understood to mean either "one who has attained the formless kasiṇas" or "one whose sphere is the formless aggregates.
Up to this point, there are four types of those who have attained [the jhānas], four types of their pupils, and four types of rationalists, along with their pupils.
"Four" refers to the sixteen proponents of views who regard [the self] as the self.

Having thus shown those who designate a self, [the text] now shows those who do not designate one, in order to explain the non-designation of a self. 119. Thus, having shown those who designate a self, it now shows those who do not designate one.
He said, beginning with, “And to what extent, Ānanda...”? Who, then, do not describe [the self]? First of all, all noble persons (ariyapuggala) do not describe it.
And those who are very learned—whether they are bearers of the Three Piṭakas, bearers of the Two Piṭakas, or bearers of the One Piṭaka;
even a person who has mastered the recitation of the Dhamma after having thoroughly analyzed even a single Nikāya, or one who has begun insight (vipassanā)—none of them describe it.

They do not designate them at all. For regarding these, their knowledge is simply "counterpart kasiṇa" in the case of a counterpart kasiṇa, and "formless aggregates" in the case of the formless aggregates.
This concludes the commentary on the contemplation of self.
121. Having thus shown those who do not designate [the self], he now speaks the passage beginning with "And to what extent, Ānanda...

in order to show those who do designate it. Since they designate it by way of viewing through the lens of views (*diṭṭhi*), and that viewing of theirs exists because the twenty-based personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) has not been abandoned, he therefore spoke this again to demonstrate that twenty-based personality-belief.

Therein, by the phrase "or feeling," the personality-view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) based on the aggregate of feeling is explained. By the phrase "my self is without feeling," that based on the aggregate of form is explained.
By the phrases "my self feels" and "for my self has the nature of feeling," those based on the aggregates of perception, mental formations, and consciousness are explained.
For these three aggregates, being associated with feeling, [are included therein].
He feels. And this nature of feeling is inseparable from his own being.
122. Now, pointing out the fault therein, he said: "In that regard, Ānanda," and so forth. Therein, "in that regard" means among those three types of speculative theorists (*diṭṭhigatika*).
"At whatever time, Ānanda," and so forth: whichever person regards whichever feeling as the self (*attā*), [that is the case].
This was said for the purpose of showing such faults as that each thing exists at one time and does not exist at another. 123.
They are *anicca* (impermanent) because, having existed, they cease to be. They are *saṅkhata* (conditioned) because they are made by coming together and uniting through various causes.
They are *paṭiccasamuppanna* (dependently arisen) because they have arisen precisely through the correct cause, in dependence upon this or that condition.
"Khaya," and so forth, are all synonyms for dissolution (*bhaṅga*). For that which dissolves also perishes (*khīyati*), passes away (*vayati*), fades away (*virajjhati*), and ceases (*nirujjhati*);
therefore, it is said "subject to destruction" (*khayadhamma*), and so on.
"Byagā me" means "byagā" [is derived from] "vi-agā"; the meaning is "my self has gone away, has ceased. But why [is this said] of one and the same person in all three [times]?
Regarding the times: "This is my self"—if that were so, what then would not exist?
For one who holds such views, there is no stillness at all, like a stump cast upon a heap of chaff; like a monkey in the forest, he grasps one thing and lets go of another.
Thus, specifically regarding that which is impermanent and interspersed with pleasure and pain, he regards each particular feeling as the self.

If one regards feeling—whether it be impermanent, pleasant, or painful—as the self without making distinctions, then one regards the self as something mixed with the nature of arising and passing away.
For feeling is indeed threefold and possesses the nature of arising and passing away;
yet he regards that very feeling as the self. Thus, for him, the self becomes impermanent, and at a single moment...
There is the arising of many feelings. Yet he allows that this [self] is impermanent; for there is no arising of many feelings at a single moment.
It is with reference to this meaning that it was said: "Therefore, Ānanda, on account of this, it is not acceptable to regard feeling as 'my self.'"
124. "But where, friends," means: where in the pure aggregate of form there is no feeling whatsoever.
"Would there [be]? means: would the conceit "I am" arise in that palm-leaf fan or window which is devoid of feeling?
"Therefore, Ānanda," means: because the pure aggregate of form, having arisen, thinks "I am."
He does not say so; therefore, the meaning is that even by this [method], this is not acceptable.

"Could it be that 'this I am' would exist there?"—could it be that among those three aggregates, which are phenomena consisting of feeling, even a single phenomenon could be designated as "this is indeed I"?
Or else, when those three aggregates have ceased along with the cessation of feeling...

The meaning is: "Would [the thought] 'I am this' or 'I am' arise? Then the Venerable Ānanda, not accepting that—just as one would not accept the sharpness of a rabbit's horn—said, "Certainly not, Bhante.
What has been stated by this much? The discourse on the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭakathā*) has been stated. For the Blessed One, while speaking the discourse on the cycle of existence...

In some places he speaks under the heading of ignorance (*avijjā*), in some places under the heading of craving (*taṇhā*), and in some places under the heading of views (*diṭṭhi*). Regarding this, it is said:
"Bhikkhus, no prior limit of ignorance is discerned, such that one could say: 'Before this, ignorance did not exist;
then afterwards it came into being. Thus, bhikkhus, it is said. And yet, ignorance is discerned to have this specific condition."
Thus it was spoken under the heading of ignorance (*avijjā*). “Bhikkhus, no prior limit is discerned for the craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*), such that one could say:
‘Before this, there was no craving for existence; after this, it came into being. Thus, bhikkhus, it is said.
And yet, craving for existence is discerned through its specific condition (*idappaccaya*). Thus it was spoken under the heading of craving (*taṇhā*). “The prior limit...”
“Monks, no limit to the view of existence is discerned, such that one could say: ‘Before this, the view of existence did not exist, and afterwards it came into being.
Thus, monks, it is said. And yet, the view of existence is discerned through its specific condition.
In this way, it was spoken from the standpoint of views; here too, it is spoken from the standpoint of views.
For one who holds wrong views, having grasped at feelings such as pleasure as "self," wanders constantly and continuously—
like a ship tossed by the wind upon the great ocean— as he passes away from here and there and is reborn in all states of existence,

wombs, destinies, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings, due to the influence of egoism, possessiveness, and dogmatic adherence; he is not even able to lift his head out of the round of existence.

126. Thus, having explained the round (*vaṭṭa*) by means of this much of a discourse to the one who had gone astray regarding the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*) and was caught in false views, the Blessed One now, while explaining the turning away from the round (*vivaṭṭa*), spoke the passage beginning with "But when, Ānanda, a bhikkhu...
Because the Blessed One is skilled in teaching, he did not address a person distracted by new construction work and the like who had neglected their meditation subject;
rather, he began [the discourse] with reference to a person who is a practitioner, one who dwells in the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).
He said, "He does not regard feeling as self," and so forth.
For such a bhikkhu—whatever form there is, whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle;
inferior or superior; far or near—he defines all that form as impermanent: this is one mode of comprehension (*sammasana*).

Because it proceeds with respect to all phenomena by way of the knowledge of comprehension (*sammasana-ñāṇa*)—which is described in such a manner as, "He defines [them] as suffering: this is one comprehension; he defines [them] as non-self: this is one comprehension"—he does not regard feeling as self, nor anything else.
Not regarding anything in this way, he does not cling to anything in the world. Thus, regarding the various classifications such as the aggregates and the world...
In the world, among phenomena such as form and the rest, he does not cling to even a single phenomenon as "self" or as "belonging to self.
Not clinging, he does not tremble; thus, by not clinging, he does not tremble through craving, views, or conceit.
Being without trembling—being one who does not tremble—he personally attains final nibbāna; that is, by means of his own personal nibbāna from the defilements.

He attains final Nibbāna. Furthermore, the passage beginning with "Birth is destroyed" is spoken for the purpose of showing the occurrence of his reviewing knowledge once he has thus attained final Nibbāna.
"Such is his view" means that whatever view belongs to the Arahant who is liberated in such a way, that is his view.
There is also the reading "itissa diṭṭhī," which means: "Whatever Arahant is liberated in such a way, such is his view. "That is not fitting" means that it is not appropriate.
Why? Because if that were the case, it would have to be said that "the Arahant knows nothing at all";
yet it is not appropriate to say of an Arahant who is liberated through such knowledge that he "knows nothing. For this very reason, at the conclusion of each of the four methods, he says:
"For what reason? and so forth.
In this context, "to the extent of designation" (*adhivacana*) means whatever conventional expression exists that is designated as such.

"To the extent of the range of designation" (*adhivacanapatha*) means whatever range of designation there is, whether it be the aggregates (*khandha*), the sense bases (*āyatana*), or the elements (*dhātu*).
This same method applies everywhere. "The domain of wisdom" (*paññāvacara*) refers to the pentad of aggregates which is to be traversed by wisdom. "Having direct knowledge of that" (*tad-abhiññā*)...
Having understood that. What has been shown by the Blessed One by this much? The connection has been shown, just like that of a tangled skein. 127.
Now, as for the one who was called "he does not describe," because he is one liberated-in-both-ways as he goes along and goes along—
And as for the one who is said to "not regard [anything]," because he is called "liberated by wisdom" (paññāvimutta) as he goes along and goes along,
the Blessed One spoke the passage beginning with "Seven, Ānanda, are these stations of consciousness" in order to show both the conclusion and the name of those two monks mentioned previously.
In this context, "beings" (*satta*) is stated by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*); however, according to the *Saṅgītisutta*, four [stations] will follow by way of objects (*ārammaṇa*).
"Consciousness abides herein" (*viññāṇaṃ tiṭṭhati ettha*) is thus "station of consciousness" (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*); this is a designation for the foundation of consciousness.
"And two bases" (*dve ca āyatanāni*) refers to two places of dwelling. For here, "base" (*āyatana*) is intended in the sense of a place of dwelling (*nivāsaṭṭhāna*).
For he himself will say: "The base of non-percipient beings and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are the second.

But why is all this included? For the purpose of exhausting the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*). Indeed, the round of existence is not exhausted by way of the mere stations of consciousness or the mere bases;
rather, it is exhausted by way of the realms of existence (*bhava*), matrices (*yoni*), destinations (*gati*), and abodes of beings (*sattāvāsa*).
Therefore, all of this has been included.
Now, analyzing that meaning in its proper sequence, he said: "What are the seven? and so forth.
In that context, *seyyathāpi* is a particle used in the sense of illustration; the meaning is "just as humans. For in immeasurable world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), there are immeasurable...
Among human beings, there are no two who are exactly alike in terms of their complexion, stature, and so forth.
For even those twin brothers who may be identical in complexion or stature still possess distinctions in their ways of looking forward or aside, speaking, laughing, walking, standing, and so on.
Therefore, they are said to be "of diverse bodies. However, their rebirth-consciousness (*paṭisandhi-saññā*) may even be three-rooted (*tihetuka*).

They possess both double-rooted and rootless consciousness; therefore, they are called "those with diverse perceptions. "And some gods" refers to the six classes of sense-sphere gods (*kāmāvacara-deva*).

For among them, the body of some is blue, while that of others is yellow or other colors. Their perception, however, is either double-rooted or triple-rooted; there is no rootless perception among them.
"And some beings in states of deprivation" refers to those excluded from the four lower realms, such as Uttaramātā.
The yakkhinīs Piyaṅkaramātā, Phussamittā, Dhammaguttā, and others such as these, as well as other *vemānika* (intermediate) *petas*.
For their bodies are diverse, appearing with yellow, white, black, tawny, or dark-brown complexions, and in terms of being emaciated, stout, short, or tall;
and their perception is likewise diverse, like that of humans, occurring by way of being double-rooted, triple-rooted, or rootless. Furthermore, they...
They do not possess great power like the gods, nor do they have little power like poor humans; they dwell oppressed by suffering, with food and clothing difficult to obtain.

Some are afflicted during the dark fortnight and find happiness during the bright fortnight; thus, because they have fallen from the heights of happiness, they are called "those who have fallen" (*vinipātika*).
However, among them, those who possess three roots of merit also experience the realization of the Dhamma.
For the yakkhinī Piyaṅkaramātā, having heard the Elder Anuruddha reciting the Dhamma at the time of dawn, said:
“Do not make a sound, Piyaṅkara! The bhikkhu is reciting verses of the Dhamma.
Even if we were to understand a single verse of the Dhamma, it would lead to our welfare.”
“Let us exercise restraint toward living beings, let us not speak falsehood even knowingly;
let us train ourselves in our own virtue, so that we may be released from the womb of a *pisāca*.
Having thus exhorted her son, she attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*) on that very day. But Uttara’s mother, upon merely hearing the Blessed One’s Dhamma, became a stream-enterer.
"Brahmakāyika" refers to the Brahmapārisajja, Brahmapurohita, and Mahābrahma deities.

"First-arisen" means that all of them are produced by the first jhāna. Among them, the Brahmapārisajjas are produced by a limited degree [of the first jhāna], and their lifespan is one-third of an eon (kappa).
The Brahmapurohitas are produced by a medium degree, and their lifespan is half an eon.
Their lifespan is [one] eon, and their bodies are more expansive. For the Mahābrahmās, their lifespan is one eon, but their bodies are even more expansive.
Thus, due to the diversity of their bodies and the unity of their perception by way of the first jhāna, they should be understood as "those with diverse bodies and unified perception."

And as it is for them, so it is for beings in the four woeful states. For in the hells, the personal body (attabhāva) of some is a quarter-league (gāvuta), of some half a league (aḍḍhayojana), and of some a full league (yojana);
but Devadatta was born with a body a hundred leagues long.
Among animals too, some are small and some are large. In the realm of the hungry ghosts (pettivisaya) as well, some are sixty cubits (hattha) tall and some are seventy cubits tall.
Some are eighty cubits tall, some are beautiful, and some are ugly. Likewise, there are the black-skinned *asuras*.

Furthermore, among them are the so-called long-backed *petas*, who can even reach sixty *yojanas* in height. As for their perception, however, it is exclusively the rootless (*ahetuka*) unwholesome-resultant (*akusalavipāka*) for all of them.
Thus, those belonging to the states of deprivation are reckoned as "those with diverse bodies and uniform perception."
"Ābhassara" means that from their bodies light radiates and flows forth as if it were breaking off and falling away like the flame of a torch;

thus they are called "Ābhassara. Among them, those who have been reborn after developing the second and third jhānas to a limited degree according to the fivefold method are called Parittābhā (Limited Light);
their lifespan measure is two eons. Having developed [the jhāna] to a middling degree...

Those reborn there are called the Appamāṇābhas (Immeasurable Radiance); their lifespan is four *kappas*. Having developed [the meditation] to a superior degree, those reborn there are called the Ābhassarā (Radiant); their lifespan is eight *kappas*.

Here, however, all of them are included according to the highest limit. For the bodies of all of them are of one and the same appearance, while their perception is without applied thought and consists of sustained thought only.
"Either with applied thought and sustained thought, or without applied thought and sustained thought"—this is the distinction.
"Subhakiṇha" means strewn or scattered with beauty; the meaning is that they are a single, solid mass due to the color of the radiance of their bodies.
For their radiance does not go forth by breaking off in fragments like that of the Ābhassara devas. However, in the *Pañcakanaya* [system]...

By means of the low, middling, and superior fourth jhāna, beings are reborn as those known as the Parittasubhas, Appamāṇasubhas, and Subhakiṇhas, with lifespans of sixteen, thirty-two, and sixty-four eons respectively.

Thus, it should be understood that all of them possess a single body and, through the perception of the fourth jhāna, possess a single perception. The Vehapphalas likewise [possess] only the fourth station of consciousness.

They partake [of existence]. Non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*), due to the absence of consciousness, do not enter into this classification; they are included among the abodes of beings (*sattāvāsa*).
The Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*) belong to the side of evolution (*vivaṭṭa*); they are not present at all times.

Even for a hundred thousand eons or an incalculable eon (*asaṅkhyeyya*), they do not arise when the world is empty of Buddhas. It is only within the interval of sixteen thousand eons that Buddhas appear.
They arise; they are like the site of the Bhagavā’s turning of the Wheel of Dhamma at Khaṇḍavaṭṭa.
Therefore, they belong neither to the stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*) nor to the abodes of beings (*sattāvāsa*). However, the Elder Mahāsīva said:
"But that abode of beings, Sāriputta, is not easily found which has not been inhabited by me during this long period of time, with the exception of—"
By means of this sutta, "by the Suddhāvāsa devas," he states that even the Suddhāvāsas belong to the fourth station of consciousness and the fourth abode of beings;
since this cannot be contradicted by the sutta, it is accepted.
The meaning of "with the complete cessation of perceptions of form," and so forth, has been explained in the Visuddhimagga. However, as for the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception...

Just as with perception, so too because of the subtlety of consciousness, it is neither "consciousness" nor "non-consciousness. Therefore, instead of speaking of them among the stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*), they are spoken of among the bases (*āyatana*).
128. "Therein" means in those stations of consciousness. "And he understands that" means he understands that station of consciousness.
And he understands its arising by way of the method beginning, "With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of form," and so forth.
And he understands its passing away by way of the method beginning, "With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of form," and so forth.
He understands its gratification as that pleasure which arises dependent on form... [and so on] ...dependent on consciousness.
"Pleasure and joy—this is the gratification of consciousness": thus he understands its gratification. "The danger" means: whatever form...
[and so on] ...whatever consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger of consciousness;
thus he understands its danger. "The escape" means: the removal of desire and lust regarding form... [and so on] ...regarding consciousness.
"The abandoning of desire and lust—this is the escape from consciousness. In this way, he understands its escape.
"Is it fitting for him? means: is it appropriate for that bhikkhu to delight in that station of consciousness as "I" or "mine" by way of craving, conceit, and views?
This should be understood in the same manner in all instances. However, where...
Where there is no form, there [the arising] should be applied by way of the four aggregates; where there is no consciousness, there it should be applied by way of one aggregate.
Furthermore, the phrase "from the arising of nutriment, from the cessation of nutriment" should be applied here.
"When, Ānanda, a bhikkhu" means: when, Ānanda, a bhikkhu. "Liberated through non-clinging" means: liberated from the four types of clinging.

"Released without grasping. "Released by wisdom" (*paññāvimutta*) means released by means of wisdom. The meaning is: having not yet realized the eight liberations, one is released by the power of wisdom alone, having brought about the non-occurrence of both the mental body (*nāmakāya*) and the physical body (*rūpakāya*).

This [type of person] is fivefold: the dry-insight practitioner (*sukkha-vipassaka*), and those who have attained Arhatship while established in any one of the first jhānas and so forth. As it is said:
And this was said: "What kind of person is one liberated by wisdom?
Here, a certain person does not dwell having personally realized the eight liberations with the body, but having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed.
This is called a person liberated by wisdom."
Commentary on the Eight Liberations (Aṭṭhavimokkhavaṇṇanā) 129.
Having thus shown the conclusion and the name of one bhikkhu, [the Blessed One] spoke the passage beginning with "These eight, indeed," in order to show that of the other.
Therein, in what sense is it called a "liberation" (*vimokkha*)? It is in the sense of being resolved upon (*adhimuccana*). But what is this [resolution]?

What is the meaning of "resolute confidence" (*adhimuccana*)? It is the sense of being thoroughly liberated from opposing states; it is the sense of being thoroughly liberated by way of delighting in the object.
What is meant is that its occurrence upon the object is free from apprehension and unrestrained, like a child lying on his father’s lap with all his limbs relaxed.
However, this meaning does not exist in the final liberation (*vimokkha*).
It exists in all the preceding [meditations].

Regarding the phrase "possessing form, he sees forms": here, "possessing form" (*rūpī*) means that there is within him a form-meditative absorption (*rūpa-jhāna*) produced by way of the blue kasiṇa and so forth with respect to internal things such as hair;
thus, because he has that, he is "possessing form. "He sees forms externally" refers likewise to the external.
One sees forms such as the blue kasiṇa with the eye of jhāna.
By this, the four fine-material-sphere jhānas of a person who has produced jhāna upon kasiṇas based both internally and externally are shown.
"Perceiving no form internally" means not perceiving form internally; that is to say, one who has not produced fine-material-sphere jhāna regarding one's own hair and so forth. By this—
The fine-material-sphere jhānas are shown for a person who, having performed the preliminary work externally, has produced jhāna externally.
By the phrase "he is intent upon the beautiful," the jhānas based on the color-kasinas—such as blue and so forth—which are perfectly pure, are shown.
Although there is no mental application (ābhoga) of "beautiful" within the actual absorption (appanā), that which is the pure, beautiful kasina-object [is intended].

Because he dwells having performed [this meditation] and thus comes to be described as "one who is intent upon the beautiful," the teaching is presented in this way. However, in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, it is asked: "How is it that one is intent upon the beautiful? This is the liberation.
Here, a bhikkhu dwells pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness... [and so on]... because loving-kindness has been developed."
"Beings become non-repulsive. One dwells having pervaded one direction with a mind accompanied by compassion... [and so on] ...accompanied by sympathetic joy...
[and so on] ...accompanied by equanimity. Because equanimity has been developed, beings become non-repulsive. Thus, being intent upon the beautiful itself—this is called liberation," it is said.
Regarding "all perceptions of form," and so forth— all that ought to be said has already been stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.
"This is the eighth liberation" means that because of the complete purification and liberation of the four aggregates,
this is called the eighth and supreme liberation.
130. *Anuloma* means from the beginning up to the end. *Paṭiloma* means from the end back to the beginning.
*Anulomapaṭiloma* is stated with reference to the movement here and there without stopping, due to the extreme proficiency in the attainments (*samāpatti*).
*Yatthicchakaṃ* (wherever desired) is an indication of place; in whichever place—
"He desires. "As much as he desires" is an illustration of the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*); it means whichever attainment he desires.
"For as long as he desires" is an illustration of the delimitation of duration; it means for whatever length of time he desires. "He enters" means he enters into that respective attainment.
"He emerges" means having arisen from that, he remains.

"Both-ways-liberated" means liberated by way of two parts: liberated from the material body through the formless attainments, and liberated from the mental body through the Path. And this has been said:
"Just as a flame cast by the force of the wind, O Upasīva (said the Blessed One), goes out and no longer enters into reckoning;"
"Thus the Sage, liberated from the group of names,
reaches the goal and does not enter into reckoning.
Now, this one who is liberated both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta), having emerged from any one of the spheres such as the base of infinite space, attains Arahantship.
And there is the fifth type, who, having become a non-returner, emerges from cessation and attains Arahantship. However, some maintain:

"Since the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere has two factors accompanied by equanimity, and the immaterial-sphere jhānas are likewise, one who attains Arahantship after emerging from the fourth fine-material-sphere jhāna is also 'liberated both ways' (ubhatobhāgavimutto)."

This question on liberation in both ways, however, having arisen previously at the Lohapāsāda, reached its final determination only after a long time, based on the commentary of the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷasumana.
It is said that in the Girivihāra, a pupil of the Elder heard this question from the mouth of a certain alms-collector and said: "Friend, at the Lohapāsāda, our teacher..."
"Never before has anyone heard the Dhamma praised in such a way. "But what did the Elder say, venerable sir? [He replied:

"Although the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere possesses two factors and is accompanied by equanimity, and thus suppresses the defilements, it nevertheless operates within the range where the defilements grow—that is, in the vicinity of the defilements.
For these so-called defilements, in the five-aggregate existence, [arise] from among the blue and other colors..."
They operate by depending upon an object, and that object does not transcend the fine-material-sphere jhāna.

Therefore, it is only one who, having entirely turned away from the material, suppresses the defilements by means of the immaterial-sphere jhāna and attains Arahantship, who is "liberated in both ways.
This is what the Elder said, friend. Having said this, he cited this Sutta:

“And what kind of person is one liberated-in-both-ways? Here, a certain person dwells having personally realized the eight liberations with the body, and having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed. This is called a person liberated-in-both-ways.
And by this liberation-in-both-ways, Ānanda—meaning from this liberation-in-both-ways. The rest is clear everywhere.
Thus ends the commentary on the Mahānidāna Sutta in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya. 3.
The commentary on the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta.
131. *Evaṃ me sutaṃ* (Thus have I heard): this is the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta.
Herein is the word-by-word commentary: *Gijjhakūṭe*: "At Vulture Peak. Vultures dwelt upon its peaks, or its peak was like that of a vulture;

thus it is called Gijjhakūṭa. At that Gijjhakūṭa. *Abhiyātukāmo*: "Desiring to go forth" means desiring to go for the purpose of overcoming. *Vajjī*: "The Vajjis" refers to the Vajjian kings. *Evaṃmahiddhike*: "Of such great power."
"Endowed with such great royal power"—by this he spoke of their state of being united.
"Possessed of such great majesty"—by this he spoke of their training in the arts of elephant-riding and so forth, with reference to which it was said:
"Truly well-trained are these Licchavi youths, truly well-disciplined are they."
"O Licchavi youths, how is it that they will shoot arrows through the narrow slit of a palm leaf, one after another, without missing?
"I shall cut off" means "I will sever. "I shall cause to perish" means "I will destroy; I will bring to non-appearance. "Calamity and ruin":
here, "not right" (*na ayo*) is *anayo*; this is a name for lack of prosperity.
"Calamity" (*byasana*) means that which scatters and distracts both welfare and happiness; this is a term for the loss of relatives and so forth.
"I will lead them away" (*āpādessāmi*) means "I will cause them to fall [into calamity].
Thus, it is said, while standing, sitting, and so on, he speaks only of this talk of war, saying, "Be prepared to depart," and so forth.

He ordered an army. Why? It is said that along the Ganges, for half a *yojana* from a certain port town, the authority belonged to Ajātasattu, and for another half *yojana*, it belonged to the Licchavis.
The meaning is that this was the boundary where their respective jurisdictions met.
Moreover, valuable goods were brought down from the foot of the mountains there. Hearing of this, Ajātasattu thought, "I shall go today; I shall go tomorrow."
While he was still deliberating, the Licchavi kings, acting in unison and in harmony, went ahead and took everything.
When Ajātasattu arrived later and learned of this occurrence, he departed in a state of anger. They did exactly the same thing again the following year.
Then, having become filled with powerful resentment, he acted in this manner at that time.
Then he thought: "A battle with a multitude is indeed a grave matter; there is not even one futile blow [in such a conflict].
However, by acting after consulting with a single wise man, one remains free from fault. And there is no wise man equal to the Teacher.
The Teacher is residing at the Dhura Monastery not far away; well then, I shall send someone and ask him. If—"
“There will be some purpose for my going; the Teacher will remain silent, but if there is no purpose, he will say, ‘What is the point of the king going there?
Thus he dispatched the brahmin Vassakāra. The brahmin went and reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Therefore it is said: “Then the king... [omitted] ...I shall cause him to be led away.”
Commentary on the Factors Leading to the Decline of a King: 134.
"Fanning the Blessed One": The Elder, abiding by the head of his duty, fanned the Blessed One;
yet for the Blessed One, there was neither cold nor heat. Having heard the words of the brahmin, the Blessed One did not address him further.
Desiring to consult with the Elder, he said, "What have you heard, Ānanda? and so forth.
"Frequent assemblies" means that even those who assemble three times a day, or who assemble from time to time, are indeed those who hold frequent assemblies.
"Those who assemble often" refers to those who think: "We assembled yesterday, we assembled the day before, and again today—for what purpose [have we gathered]?"
They are said to be "frequent in assemblies" when they meet often without failing to reach a conclusion, thinking, "Let us assemble. "For as long as" means for whatever length of time.
"Only growth, Ānanda, is to be expected for the Vajjis, not decline"—for if they do not assemble frequently, they do not hear the message brought from all directions and intermediate points;
consequently, [they fail to know] whether the boundary of such-and-such a village...

If they do not know that "the boundaries of the towns are in turmoil" or "bandits have taken possession of such-and-such a place," the bandits, perceiving that "the kings are negligent," strike at the villages, towns, and so forth, and destroy the countryside. In this way, there is a decline for the kings.
However, by meeting together frequently, they hear of various occurrences; then, by dispatching forces, they crush their enemies.
Even the thieves think, “The kings are vigilant; it is not possible for us to roam about in bands,” and so they break up and flee.
In this way, there is growth for the Vajjis. Therefore it was said: “Growth alone, Ānanda, is to be expected for the Vajjis, not decline.
In this context, “to be expected” (pāṭikaṅkhā) means that which is to be desired, or rather, that which is to be regarded as certain to happen.

Regarding the passage beginning with "assembled" (*samaggā*): when the assembly drum has been sounded, those who cause a distraction by thinking, "I have business today," or "I have a ceremony," are said not to assemble as a harmonious group.

However, upon merely hearing the sound of the drum, even those eating, adorning themselves, or putting on their robes—even if they are half-eaten or half-adorned—while in the act of putting on their robes...
When they assemble together, they are said to have assembled in harmony.

However, once assembled, if after deliberating and consulting, they perform their duties and then depart from the assembly as a single body without rising [to leave], they are not said to have risen in harmony.
For when they have thus risen, those who depart first think: "We have heard only the preliminary talk; now the formal discussion will take place."
But those who emerge from one side are said to emerge in concord.

Furthermore, having heard that "in such-and-such places the village boundaries or town boundaries are crowded and beset by thieves," and when it is asked, "Who will go and perform this crushing of enemies?
they say, "I first! I first! and go; even these are emerging in concord.

...by name. However, while one king’s administration was failing, although the other kings sent their sons and brothers and supported his administration, they did not say to the visiting king, "Go to such-and-such a house;
go to such-and-such a house," nor did they all welcome him together as one when that one king encountered a festival, a disease, or some other similar misfortune.
When pleasure or pain arises, even though all [the people] there act as companions to one another, they are said to perform what ought to be done in harmony.
Regarding the phrases "not laid down" and so forth: when they cause taxes, tributes, or fines that were not previously established to be brought in, they are said to "lay down what was not laid down.
However, when they fail to bring in what has come down by way of ancient custom, they "abolish what was laid down."

They are called "thieves" because, when a person is caught and brought before them, they do not investigate but instead hand down punishments of mutilation or execution; thus, they do not act by adopting the ancient Dharma of the Vajjis.
As these men establish what was not previously established, people oppressed by new taxes and such things say, "We are utterly afflicted;
who will live under their dominion? and having entered the borderlands, they become bandits.
Or, having become accomplices with thieves, they raid the countryside.
As they destroy established order and fail to collect taxes and other dues handed down through tradition, the treasury declines.

Consequently, the elephants, cavalry, infantry, and female attendants, unable to receive their regular rations as prescribed, decline in both vigor and strength. They become neither capable of combat nor fit for service.
When people in the kingdom do not adhere to the ancient Vajjian laws, they become angry, thinking:
"They have treated our son, father, or brother as a thief when he was no thief, and have cut him down or destroyed him.
Thus, having entered the borderlands, they become thieves or allies of thieves and strike at the countryside; in this way, there is decline for kings. This is what has been prescribed.
But when they establish [the laws], people—rejoicing and delighted that "the kings are acting exactly according to tradition"—carry out their occupations such as agriculture and trade.
Because they do not abolish what has been established and they collect the traditional taxes and duties, the treasury increases;
consequently, the elephants, horses, infantry, harem women, and so forth, receive their regular allowances as prescribed.
They are endowed with strength and power, capable both of enduring battle and of performing service. Regarding the phrase "the ancient Vajjian custom":
it is said that in former times, when the Vajjian kings were presented with someone brought before them as "this is a thief," they would not say, "Seize this thief!
but instead handed him over to the chief judges. Having investigated the case, if...
If he is not a thief, they release him. If he is a thief, he says nothing himself and hands him over to the judges. If they too determine that he is not a thief, they release him;

if he is a thief, they hand him over to the experts in legal procedure (*suttadhara*). They too, having deliberated, if he is not a thief, release him; if he is a thief, they hand him over to the eight clansmen (*aṭṭhakulika*).
They too, having done exactly the same, hand him over to the commander-in-chief (*senāpati*), and the commander-in-chief to the viceroy (*uparāja*).
The viceroy [reports] to the king; having investigated the case, if the man is not a thief, the king releases him.

But if he is a thief, the king causes the genealogical register (*paveṇīpotthaka*) to be read. In that [register], it is written: "For whoever has committed such-and-such an act, this is the punishment.
The king, having compared the man's deed with that [record], inflicts a punishment appropriate to it. Thus, this is the ancient Vajjian law.
When they conduct themselves according to these observances, people do not find fault with them, thinking: "The kings are performing their duties according to ancient tradition;
there is no fault in them, but rather the fault is our own. Thus, being heedful, they carry out their tasks.
In this way, there is growth for the kings. Therefore it was said: "O Ānanda, only growth is to be expected for the Vajjis, not decline."
"Honoring" means that whatever honor they perform for them, they do it beautifully. "Revering" means they act by establishing a sense of respect.
"Loving" means they hold them dear with their minds. "Worshiping" means they show acts of prostration.
"Thinking [their words] should be heard" means going to attend upon them two or three times a day and [listening to] their discourse.

They think it should be heard and believed. In this regard, those who do not perform honors and services for such elderly kings, nor go to attend upon them for the sake of receiving instruction, are neglected by them;
being left without counsel and addicted to play, they fall away from their kingdom. But as for those who act accordingly, the elderly kings—
“They explain the ancient tradition, saying: ‘This should be done; this should not be done.
Even when they have entered into battle, they show them the proper method, saying: ‘One should enter thus; one should withdraw thus.
Being thus instructed by them and practicing according to that instruction, they are able to maintain the royal lineage. Therefore it was said: ‘Only growth…’”
“Ānanda, it is to be expected for the Vajjis that they will not decline.
“Noble women” means the matrons of noble families. “Noble maidens” means their daughters who have not yet been married.

Regarding the phrase “having dragged away and overpowered,” here “dragged away” (*okkassa*) or “overpowered” (*pasayha*) is a name for the very act of overpowering. Some also read it as “having raised up” (*ukkassa*).
In this context, *okkassa* means having dragged down or pulled away. *Pasayha* means having overcome or overwhelmed;
such is the literal meaning of the words. For those acting in this way toward the people in their conquered realm, [the people think]:
"These kings, by force, [seize] even our sons and mothers from our homes, and even our daughters whom we raised by removing spit, mucus, and so forth with our own mouths..."
Having seized them, they keep them in their own homes. Thus, becoming angry, they enter the borderlands and, acting as bandits or bandit-associates, they plunder the countryside.

However, for those who do not act in this way, the people within the realm remain free from anxiety and, performing their own duties, increase the royal treasury. In this manner, the increase and decrease [of the kingdom] are to be understood.
"The Vajjian shrines" (*vajjicetiya*) refers to spirit-haunted sites that received the name "shrines" (*cetiyāni*) in the sense of being venerated by the Vajjian kings in the Vajjian realm.
"Internal" means situated within the city; "external" means situated outside the city.
"Previously given" means given in the past; "previously performed" means performed in the past. "They will not let them fall into ruin" means without letting them fall into ruin.
They will act exactly as they have always done; for when people fail to pay the righteous tax, the deities do not provide well-ordered protection.
Although they are unable to produce suffering that has not yet arisen, they cause coughs, headaches, and other ailments to increase once they have arisen;
and when war breaks out, they do not stand as allies. However, for those who do not let the tax fall into neglect, the deities provide well-ordered protection.
Even if they are unable to produce happiness that has not yet arisen, they eliminate coughs, headaches, and other ailments that have already arisen;
thus they act as companions at the head of the battle. In this way, increase and decrease should be understood here.
Regarding the phrase "righteous protection, defense, and guardianship," it is protection itself that ensures what is undesired does not occur.
It is an "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*) because it acts as a barrier. It is "protection" (*gutti*) because it guards [the property] so that it does not perish according to one's wish.
In this context, guarding by surrounding with a military force is not what is called the "righteous protection, obstruction, and guard" for those who have gone forth.
Rather, it is when they do not cut down trees in the monastery grove, do not punish those guilty of offenses, and [do not pollute] the lotus ponds...
When fish do not take [the bait], such an action is called a righteous protection, shield, and guard.
