By the phrase "how they might not come in the future," he asks about the activity of their minds—that is, the continuum of their mental states as it has thus been established.
In this regard, those who do not desire the arrival of future Arahants are faithless and lack confidence.
When renunciants arrive, they do not go out to meet them; having gone, they do not see them;
they do not offer hospitality; they do not ask questions; they do not listen to the Dhamma; they do not give gifts;
they do not listen to the words of appreciation; they do not provide a place for them to stay. Then their ill repute spreads: "So-and-so..."
“King Nāma is faithless and lacks confidence; when renunciants arrive, he does not go out to meet them...
[and so on] ...he does not provide a place for them to stay. Having heard this, the renunciants did not travel through his city gates, and even those who were traveling did not enter the city.
Thus, there was simply no arrival of arahants who had not yet come, and for those who had already arrived—

When there is no comfortable dwelling, even those who have come without knowing [the situation] think, "We came thinking we would stay," but then, [realizing], "In this manner of these kings, who will be able to live here?
they depart and go away. Thus, with those who had not yet come failing to come, and those who had already come living in suffering, that region becomes uninhabitable for renunciants. From that...
There is no protection from deities; when there is no protection from deities, non-human beings find an opportunity.

When non-human beings are prevalent, they cause diseases that have not yet arisen to arise, and there is no arrival of merit based on seeing those who are virtuous or asking them questions and so forth.
Conversely, however, there arises the bright side (sukkappakka), which is the opposite of the aforementioned dark side (kaṇhapakka).
"In this way, increase and decrease are to be understood here.
(135) "They burn one another"—the Blessed One said this in order to demonstrate the manner in which he had previously taught this "Sevenfold [Discourse] on the Vajjīs" to the Vajjīs.
Therein, "at the Sārandada Shrine" means at the monastery bearing that name. It is said that before the Buddha had appeared, there [was] Sārandada’s...
The dwelling place of the *yakkha* became a shrine (*cetiya*). Then they had a residence for the Blessed One built there;
because it was constructed at the Sārandada Shrine, it came to be known simply as the Sārandada Shrine.
"Akaraṇīyā" means things that should not be done, i.e., things that should not be undertaken. "Yadidaṃ" is a mere particle. "Yuddhassa" is used in the sense of the instrumental case.
The word *sāmivacanaṃ* means that it is not possible to capture [the enemy] through direct combat. "Except for by means of conciliation" (*aññatra upalāpanāya*) means excluding conciliation.
"Conciliation" (*upalāpanā*) refers to making a gesture of reconciliation by sending elephants, horses, chariots, gold, silver, and so forth, saying, "Enough with this dispute; let us now be united.
For by making such a gesture of reconciliation, it is possible to capture them solely through trust.
"Meaning. "Except for causing a breach of friendship" means setting aside the breaking of friendships.
By this, he shows that even by creating a mutual rift, it is possible to capture them. Having grasped the underlying method in the Blessed One’s discourse, the brahmin spoke thus.
But did the Blessed One not know that the brahmin had grasped the method through this discourse? Yes, he knew. Knowing...
Why did he speak? Out of compassion. For it occurred to him: "Even if I do not tell him, he will go in a few days and seize them all.
But if I tell him, he will seize them in three years by causing a schism among those who are united.
Even this much [time] is better for life; for while living for this long, they will perform merit that serves as their own support."
"Having rejoiced" means having rejoiced with the mind. "Having expressed approval" means having expressed approval with speech, saying, "How well spoken indeed is this by the Blessed One Gotama!
He departed, having gone into the presence of the king. Then the king asked him, "What did the Teacher say, Master?
He replied, "Just as it is not possible for anyone, O sir, to [contradict] the word of the ascetic Gotama..."
“However,” he said, “they can be captured either by means of deception or by causing a schism.
Then the king asked him, “If we capture them through deception, our elephants, horses, and other assets will be lost; therefore, I shall capture them by means of a schism.
What shall we do? [The man replied,] “In that case, Great King, you should initiate a discussion regarding the Vajjis in the assembly. Then I—”
—“What use have you, Great King, for them? Let these kings live by performing their own work, such as agriculture and trade,” having said this, I shall depart.
Then you may say, “Why indeed, sir, does this brahmin oppose the talk that has arisen concerning the Vajjis?
And during the day, I shall send a gift to them; that too—
"Having had me seized, and having charged you with my crime, do not subject me to imprisonment, flogging, or other such punishments;
simply shave my head and have me led out of the city. Then I said: "I had the ramparts and moats built around your city;
it is said that I know the weak spots and the shallow and deep places. Before long now, straightway—"
“I shall do it,” he will say. Upon hearing that, you should say, “Let him go. The king did everything accordingly.
When the Licchavis heard of his departure, they said, “That brahmin is a rogue; do not let him cross the Ganges.
There, when some said, “It seems he was treated this way because he spoke about us,” [the others replied], “By him—”
“Indeed, friend, let him come,” they said. He went and, seeing the Licchavis, was asked, “Why have you come?

and he reported the matter to them. The Licchavis said, “It is not right to impose such a heavy penalty for so slight a matter,” and asked, “What office do you hold there? “I am the minister of justice,” he replied. At that very moment—
"Let him hold that office. He administered justice even more effectively, and the princes learned their craft under his guidance.
Having established his reputation for virtue, one day he took a Licchavi aside and asked, "Are the boys plowing?
"Yes, they are plowing. "With two oxen yoked? "Yes, with two oxen yoked. "Is this much..."

Having spoken thus, he turned back. Then another person asked him, "What did the teacher say? and not believing what was told by him, said, "He does not speak to me according to reality," and so he broke with him.
On another day, the brahmin led a certain Licchavi aside, asked him, "With what sauce did you eat? and having done so, he turned back. He too—
Another, having been questioned, did not believe him and likewise broke away.
On another day, the brahmin led one Licchavi aside and asked, "It is said that you are extremely poor. When asked, "Who says so? he replied, "A certain Licchavi named so-and-so.
Leading yet another aside, he asked, "It is said that you are of a timid nature. When asked, "Who says so? [he replied as before].
"Such-and-such a Licchavi. Thus, even though it had not been told by one person to another, he spoke it to others;
and within three years, having caused those kings to break with one another so that they would no longer travel along the same road, he had the assembly drum beaten.
The Licchavis, being told, "Let the lords assemble! Let the heroes assemble! did not assemble.
The Brahmin sent a message to the king, saying, "This is the time now; let him come quickly.
Upon hearing this, the king had the drum for the army beaten and set out. When the people of Vesālī heard of it, they beat their drums, saying, "We will not allow the king to cross the Ganges.
Hearing that as well, [the Licchavis] said, "Let the brave kings go," and so forth, and did not assemble.
“We will not allow them to enter the city; we shall stand with the gates closed,” they proclaimed, and had the drum beaten. Not even a single person assembled.
Having entered through the gates exactly as they were left open, he brought them all to ruin and misfortune and departed.
*Commentary on the Factors of Non-Decline for Monks*

136. Then the Blessed One, having gathered [the monks]—in the phrase beginning with "not long after they had departed," etc.—having sent those possessing psychic power (*ṛddhimant*) to the distant monasteries and having gone himself to the nearby monasteries, he gathered them together, saying: "Gather, venerable ones; the Blessed One desires your assembly.
Regarding the term *aparihāniya*: it means that which causes non-decline, that which serves as a cause for growth. Regarding the *dhamma*...
"I shall teach," he thought, "making it as clear as if one were raising a thousand moons and a thousand suns, or as if lighting a thousand oil lamps inside a house with four walls.
In this context, "frequent assemblies" is exactly the same as what was stated in the *Vajjiputta Sutta*. And here too, "frequently"—
Not being assembled together, they do not hear the messages arriving from various directions. Consequently, they do not know such things as: "The boundary of such-and-such a monastery is in disorder;
the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies have been suspended; in such-and-such a place, monks are performing medical treatments, acting as messengers, and so forth;

they are full of requests and maintain their livelihood through the giving of flowers and similar means. Furthermore, even wicked monks, perceiving that "the Saṅgha of monks is negligent," [take advantage of the situation].
When they have become a mass [of corruption], they cause the Teaching to decline. However, when they assemble frequently, they hear of various occurrences;
then, by dispatching the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, they straighten the boundaries (sīmā) and ensure that the Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, and other rites are carried out.
In places where wrong livelihood is prevalent, they dispatch those belonging to the Noble Lineage (ariyavaṃsaka) and cause the discourse on the Noble Lineage to be taught. As for wicked bhikkhus—
The holders of the Vinaya cause disciplinary measures to be imposed; even wicked bhikkhus, thinking, "The Saṅgha of bhikkhus is vigilant;
it is not possible for us to wander about in a faction," break away and flee. In this way, the decline and growth [of the Saṅgha] are to be understood here.

Regarding the terms *samagga* (united) and so forth, a formal agreement (*katikavatta*) may be made for the purpose of maintaining a cetiya, or for the purpose of roofing the Bodhi-house or the Uposatha hall.
Or, out of a desire to postpone [the meeting] or a desire to give instruction— when the gong or bell has been struck with the words,

"Let the Saṅgha assemble"— those who cause a distraction by saying, "I have work on my robes," "My bowl must be fired," or "I have building work to do," are said not to assemble in concord. However, setting all that aside...
When they assemble all at once, each thinking, "I shall go first! I shall go first!", they are said to have assembled in harmony.
Once assembled, however, having deliberated and consulted together, and having done what was to be done, they do not rise up separately;
thus they are said to have risen up in harmony. For among those who have risen up in this way, those who depart first think as follows:
“We have heard only outside talk; now there will be a formal deliberation. However, when they rise all at once, they are said to rise in concord.

Furthermore, having heard that “in such-and-such a place the monastery boundary is confused and the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies have been suspended, and in such-and-such a place wicked monks who perform medical treatments and the like are prevalent,” [one might wonder]: “Who shall go to them?”
When it is said, "He will impose a censure," they say, "I first! I first!
and even as they go, they are said to be rising in harmony.
But upon seeing a visitor, instead of saying, "Go to this cell, go to that cell; who is this? [they rise together].
Even though all were performing their duties—seeing that his bowl and robe were worn out, they sought a bowl and robe for him during his alms-round;

seeing he was ill, they sought medicine for him; and even when he was sick and without a protector, instead of saying, "Go to such-and-such a cell, go to such-and-such a cell," they looked after him each in their own cell—one [monk] remained behind, lagging behind.
There is the case where they form a faction; having won over a wise bhikkhu and having had him overturn that factional rule, they perform the duties of the Saṅgha in concord.
Regarding the phrases "what has not been laid down" and so forth: those who establish a new, unrighteous agreement or training rule are said to be establishing "what has not been laid down."
They are said to "lay down rules," like the monks at Sāvatthī in the case of the *purāṇasanthatavatthu*.

They are said to "abolish what has been laid down" by teaching a doctrine that is contrary to the Dhamma and contrary to the Vinaya, like the Vajjiputtakas of Vesālī one hundred years after the Parinibbāna of the Blessed One.
Furthermore, those who intentionally transgress minor and secondary offenses regarding the rules as they have been laid down...
They are said not to live in accordance with the training rules they have undertaken, like Assaji and Punabbasuka. However,
by not binding themselves to new agreements or training rules, but illuminating the teaching through the Dhamma and Vinaya,
not abolishing the minor and lesser training rules, not enacting what has not been enacted, and not abolishing what has been enacted—
They are said to live having undertaken the training rules as they have been laid down, like the Venerable Upasena and the Venerable Yasa Kākaṇḍakaputta.
"Let the Sangha hear me, friends: we have training rules that have passed into the hands of householders; even householders know them."
‘This is permitted for you, recluses, sons of the Sakyan; this is not permitted for you.
For if we were to abolish the minor and lesser training rules, there would be those who would say:
‘The training rule for the disciples was laid down by the recluse Gotama as a smoke-bannered proclamation; as long as their Teacher remained, so long did they [abide by them].’”
“They trained in the training rules. Since our Teacher has attained final Nibbāna, they no longer train in the training rules.

“If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha not lay down what has not been laid down, let it not abolish what has been laid down, and let it proceed by undertaking and practicing the training rules exactly as they have been laid down.”
And like the Venerable Mahākassapa when he established this *tanti* (textual tradition). "Only growth" (*vuddhiyeva*) means only increase through qualities such as virtue (*sīla*), and not decline.

"Elders" (*therā*) refers to those who have attained stability and are endowed with the qualities that constitute the state of an elder. "Knowing many nights" (*rattaññū*) means those who know [the duration of] many nights.
"Long-ordained" (*cirapabbajitā*) means those for whom it has been a long time since their going forth. They stand in the position of a father to the Saṅgha.

The Saṅgha is the father. Because they stand in the place of a father, they lead the Saṅgha forward; being its forerunners, they cause it to proceed in the three trainings, and thus they are the "leaders of the Saṅgha" (saṅghapariṇāyakā).
Those who do not perform services such as honoring them, and who do not attend upon them two or three times for the sake of receiving exhortation—
They, too, do not give them instruction, do not speak of the traditional lineage, and do not teach them the essential discourses on the Dhamma.

Thus, being neglected by those [elders] regarding the aggregates of virtue and so forth, as well as the seven treasures of the noble ones and other such qualities, they fall away from them. However, those who perform services for them and attend upon them—
They too give them instruction: "In this way you should advance; in this way you should retreat; in this way you should look ahead;
in this way you should look around; in this way you should bend your limbs; in this way you should stretch them;
in this way you should carry your outer robe, bowl, and inner robes. Thus they speak on the traditional lineage and the essential discourse on the Dhamma.
They train them and instruct them by means of the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) and the ten topics of discourse (kathāvatthu).

Standing firm in their instruction, they increase in virtues such as moral discipline (sīla) and attain the goal of recluseship (sāmaññattha). In this way, decline and growth are to be understood here.
"Punabbhava" means rebirth; that which has rebirth as its nature (sīla) is "ponobbhavika," meaning it brings about rebirth.
This is the meaning; therefore, [it is said] "of renewed existence. Regarding the phrase "they do not come under its power":
here, those who, for the sake of the four conditions, wander from village to village following after their attendants, are said to come under the power of that craving;
others are said not to come under its power. In that regard, the decrease and increase are indeed manifest.
“In forest-dwelling places” means in dwellings located at least five hundred bow-lengths from the village. “With longing” means with craving and attachment.

For even if one has attained jhāna while staying in a lodging near a village, as soon as one emerges from it, one hears the sounds of women, men, girls, and so forth, by which even the distinction one has attained begins to decline.
But in the forest, having slept and just awakened, one hears [the sounds] of lions, tigers, peacocks, and the like.
He hears the sound, and by means of it, having attained forest-rapture (*araññaka-pīti*) and contemplating that very [sound], he establishes himself in the supreme fruit (*aggaphala*).
Thus the Blessed One praises even one who is sleeping in the forest over a monk who has entered and remains in meditative absorption (*jhāna*) in a village lodging.
Therefore, for that specific purpose, he said: "They will have regard for forest lodgings."
"They will establish mindfulness within themselves" means they will establish mindfulness within their own internal selves.
"Good-natured" means those of a pleasant character. Here too, the resident monks who do not wish for the arrival of their fellow celibates are faithless and lack confidence.
[They neglect] such duties as going out to meet visiting bhikkhus, receiving their bowls and robes, preparing seats, and holding fans.
They do not perform it, and then their ill-repute arises: "The monks living in such-and-such a monastery are faithless and lacking confidence;
they do not perform the duties and services for those who have entered the monastery. Hearing this, even those who have gone forth will not enter the monastery, even when passing by its gate.
Thus, there is simply no arrival of those who have not yet come. But as for those who have already arrived...

If there is no comfortable living, even those who have come without prior knowledge will think, “We came thinking we would stay, but with these resident monks acting in this manner, who will stay? and they depart.
Thus, that monastery becomes a place where other bhikkhus do not dwell. Consequently, the residents miss the opportunity to see those who are virtuous.

Those who do not obtain the dispelling of doubt, nor an instructor of conduct, nor the hearing of the sweet Dhamma, neither grasp the Dhamma they have not yet grasped, nor perform the recitation of what they have already grasped. Thus, for them there is only decline, not growth.
But those who desire the arrival of their fellow celibates (sabrahmacārīs) are faithful and confident; toward the fellow celibates who have arrived—
Having gone out to meet them and performed other services, they prepare lodgings and offer them;
having accepted these, the monks enter for alms, dispel their doubts, and obtain the hearing of the sweet Dhamma. Then their reputation rises:
“The monks of such-and-such a monastery are thus faithful, confident, perfected in conduct, and supportive. Hearing this, the monks...
They come even from afar, and the resident monks perform the duties for them.
Having arrived nearby, they pay homage to the more senior guests and sit down; they take a seat near a junior guest and sit down. Having sat down, they ask:
"Will you stay in this monastery, or will you depart? If he says, "I will depart," [they reply]: "The lodging is suitable..."
Saying things such as, “Almsfood is easily obtained,” they do not allow [the newcomers] to depart.

If there is one who is a master of the Vinaya, they recite the Vinaya in his presence. If there is one who is a master of the Suttantas and so forth, they recite those various teachings in his presence.
By abiding by the exhortation of the visiting elders, they attain arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*). Thus it is with the visitors.
“We came thinking, ‘We shall stay for one or two days,’ but because of the pleasantness of living here, we shall stay for ten or twelve years”—those who speak thus;
in this way, the decrease and increase [of time] are to be understood here. 137.

In the second set of seven, they have work as their delight (*ārāma*), thus they are "delighting in work" (*kammārāmā*). They rejoice in work, thus they are "rejoicing in work" (*kammaratā*). They are devoted to the delight in work (*kammārāmatamanuyuttā*).
Engaged, thoroughly engaged, and devotedly engaged. In this context, "work" refers to tasks that ought to be done. Namely:

the sorting of robes, the making of robes, providing support, needle-cases, alms-bowl bags, waistbands, girdles, water-strainers, foot-wipers, and the making of brooms and so forth. For some indeed perform these...
One who performs these [other tasks] throughout the entire day is the one referred to by this prohibition. However, he who performs these very tasks at the time they are to be done—
taking the recitation at the time for recitation, rehearsing at the time for rehearsal, performing the duties in the shrine courtyard at the time for those duties,
and applying attention at the time for attention— is not called "one who delights in work."

Regarding the phrase "not delighting in talk": here, one who spends both day and night merely engaged in conversation and chatter by way of descriptions of women’s beauty, men’s beauty, and so forth, does not set limits to such talk;
this is what is called "delighting in talk. However, one who spends the day and night expounding the Dhamma and answering questions is indeed one who has little talk regarding talk.
He is indeed one who observes the limits. Why? Because it has been said: "When you have gathered together, monks, two things are to be done:
either a discourse on the Dhamma or noble silence.
Regarding the phrase "not delighting in sleep": here, one who—even while walking, sitting, or lying down—is overcome by sloth and torpor and simply sleeps; [that person is so described].

This is what is called "delighting in sleep. However, when one's mind sinks into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) due to the physical exhaustion of the body composed of the four great elements, this is not "delighting in sleep.

For this very reason, he said: "I recall, Aggivessana, that in the last month of summer, after my meal and having returned from my alms round, I would spread out my outer robe folded fourfold and lie down on my right side, mindful and clearly comprehending, to fall asleep."

Regarding the phrase "not delighting in company": here, one who dwells in close association—such as being a companion to one person, a third to two, or a fourth to three—and does not find satisfaction in solitude, is one who delights in company.
However, it should be understood that one who finds satisfaction in solitude throughout the four postures is not one who delights in company.
"Of evil desires": herein, those who possess the desire for unworthy esteem—being immoral—are called "of evil desires.

"Of evil friends," etc.: those whose friends are evil are "of evil friends. "Of evil companions": those whose companions are evil throughout the four postures (*iriyāpatha*) are "of evil companions. "Inclined toward evil": because they are bent, sloped, and prone toward evil, they are "inclined toward evil.
"By a mere trifle": by a low, insignificant, or trifling thing. "In the interval": in this interval, without having yet attained *arahantship*.
“Vosānaṃ” means the state of completion—the withdrawal [thinking] “enough with this much,” or the state of having fulfilled one’s task.

This is what is meant: “As long as they do not fall into complacency because of mere purity of virtue, or mere insight, or mere jhāna, or the mere state of being a stream-enterer, or the mere state of being a once-returner, or the mere state of being a non-returner, so long...”
“Only growth, monks, is to be expected for the bhikkhus, not decline.
138. In the third set of seven, “faith” (*saddhā*) refers to those endowed with faith. Therein, faith is fourfold:
faith as a coming-into-being, faith through realization, faith as serene confidence, and faith as conviction. Among these, faith as a coming-into-being belongs to the omniscient Bodhisattvas.
There is faith of realization belonging to noble persons (*ariyapuggala*). When it is said, "The Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha," the clarity that arises is faith of clarity (*pasādasaddhā*).
Faith consisting in conviction after having resolved and determined is faith of resolution (*okappanasaddhā*). Both these two kinds of faith are intended here.
For one endowed with such faith becomes "liberated by faith" (*saddhāvimutta*), like the Elder Vakkali. Indeed, his duty at the shrine precinct (*cetiyāṅgaṇavatta*)—
Or else, he performs the duties pertaining to the circle of enlightenment. He fulfills all the duties, such as the duties toward one’s preceptor and the duties toward one’s teacher.
“Conscientious” means his mind is endowed with *hiri*, which has the characteristic of loathing evil. “Moral dread” means he is possessed of *ottappa*, which has the characteristic of fearing evil.
Regarding the term "learned" (*bahussuta*): here there are two kinds of learned ones—the learned in the scriptures (*pariyatti*) and the learned through realization (*paṭivedha*).
The "scriptures" refers to the three Piṭakas. "Realization" refers to the realization of the Truths. In this context, however, the scriptural learning is intended.
One by whom much has been heard is "learned. Furthermore, such a person is one who releases [others] from dependence, one who attends upon the assembly, and one who instructs the bhikkhunīs.

"Learned in all respects" (*sabbatthaka-bahussuta*) is fourfold. Among these, the three types of learned ones are to be understood according to the method stated in the *Ovādavagga* of the *Samantapāsādikā* Vinaya commentary.
Those who are "learned in all respects," however, are like the Elder Ānanda; they are the ones intended here.
"Aroused in energy" (*āraddhavīriya*) refers to those whose bodily and mental energy has been aroused. Among them, those who [avoid] physical socializing...
Having dispelled [distractions] while in the four postures, they become solitary by means of the eight bases for exertion;

their physical energy is said to be "aroused. Those who, having dispelled mental entanglements, become solitary by means of the eight attainments, do not allow a defilement arisen while walking to reach the state of standing, nor a defilement arisen while standing to reach the state of sitting.
They do not allow defilements that have arisen while sitting to reach the state of lying down; rather, they suppress those defilements right where they arise.
Thus, their mental energy (*cetasika-vīriya*) is said to be "aroused. Regarding "one who possesses established mindfulness" (*upaṭṭhitasati*):
these are those who remember and recollect things done long ago and so forth, such as the Elder Mahāgātimbava-Abhaya, the Elder Dīghabhāṇaka-Abhaya, and the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷa-Abhaya.

It was like this: it is said that on the fifth day after his birth, the Elder Mahāgatimbaya-Abhaya saw a crow stretching out its beak toward auspicious milk-rice porridge and let out the sound "huṃ! huṃ!
Later, when he was an elder, being asked by the monks, "Venerable sir, from when do you have memory? he replied, "Friends, from the sound I made on the fifth day after my birth."
On the ninth day after the birth of the Elder Abhaya, the reciter of the *Dīgha Nikāya*, his mother bent down, thinking, "I shall kiss him," and her hair-ornament (*moḷi*) became loosened.
Thereupon, jasmine flowers the size of bowls fell upon the child's chest and caused him pain.
When he was at the stage of an elder, being asked, "Venerable sir, from when do you remember? he replied, "From the ninth day after my birth."
The Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷābhaya said: “In Anurādhapura, after having three gates closed and allowing people to exit through only one gate, it was possible—by asking each person, ‘What is your name?
What is your name? and then receiving their names without asking again in the evening—to do so;
thus he replied, ‘It is possible, friend. It is with reference to such bhikkhus that the phrase ‘with mindfulness established’ is stated.”
"Endowed with wisdom" means being possessed of the wisdom that discerns the arising and passing away of the five aggregates. Furthermore,
by these two terms, both right mindfulness and the wisdom of insight— which constitute the requisites for insight— are described for those bhikkhus who practice insight.
139. In the fourth group of seven, mindfulness itself is the enlightenment factor of mindfulness (*satisambojjhaṅga*).

This same method applies everywhere. Therein, the enlightenment factor of mindfulness has the characteristic of establishing; the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena has the characteristic of investigating;

the enlightenment factor of energy has the characteristic of exerting; the enlightenment factor of rapture has the characteristic of pervading; the enlightenment factor of tranquility has the characteristic of calming... [and so forth].
The enlightenment factor of tranquility has the characteristic of serenity; the enlightenment factor of concentration has the characteristic of non-distraction;
the enlightenment factor of equanimity has the characteristic of reflective discernment. "They will develop" means:

by arousing the mindfulness enlightenment factor through four causes, by arousing the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor through six causes, and by arousing the energy enlightenment factor through nine causes.
The meaning is that they will increase by arousing the enlightenment factor of mindfulness through ten causes, the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena through seven causes,

the enlightenment factor of energy through eight causes, the enlightenment factor of rapture through ten causes, the enlightenment factor of tranquility through seven causes, the enlightenment factor of concentration through ten causes,
and the enlightenment factor of equanimity through five causes. By this [it is shown] those associated with the path and fruit of insight.
He taught the factors of enlightenment (sambojjhaṅga) as a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane.
140. In the fifth group of seven, "perception of impermanence" (aniccasaññā) refers to the perception that arises together with the contemplation of impermanence.
The same principle applies to the perception of non-self (anattasaññā) and the others. These seven are also mundane insights (vipassanā). "This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely..."
According to the manner in which it is stated, “The stilling of all formations, dispassion, cessation,” it should be understood that two [types of giving] here are supramundane as well.
141. In the group of six, “loving-kindness bodily action” refers to bodily action to be performed with a mind of loving-kindness.
The same method applies to vocal action and mental action as well. These, however, are presented from the perspective of monks, yet they are also found among laypeople. For monks...
The fulfillment of the duties of proper conduct with a mind of loving-kindness is called bodily action of loving-kindness.

This includes such acts as going to see a cetiya, going to pay homage at the Bodhi tree, or going to invite the Saṅgha; and upon seeing a bhikkhu who has entered a village for alms, going out to meet him, receiving his bowl, preparing a seat, and following him on his departure.
Loving bodily action (*mettā-kāyakamma*) is as follows:

establishing the training rules for conduct and discipline for the monks with a mind of loving-kindness, teaching them meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*), giving Dhamma teachings, and even the entire word of the Buddha contained in the Three Piṭakas—this is called loving verbal action (*mettā-vacīkamma*). [As for] householders, [saying] "We are going to pay homage at the cetiya,"...
"Let us go to pay homage to the Bodhi tree; let us listen to the Dhamma; let us perform offerings of lamps, garlands, and flowers;
let us undertake and practice the three types of good conduct; let us provide alms-food by ticket and other such gifts; let us provide the rains-retreat offerings;
today we shall provide the four requisites for the Saṅgha; having invited the Saṅgha, prepare hard foods and other offerings."

When one says, "Prepare the seats," "Set out the drinking water," "Go forth to meet the Saṅgha and bring them here," "Seat them on the prepared seats," or "Perform services with a sense of devotion and enthusiasm," such speech is called verbal action of loving-kindness (*mettā-vacī-kamma*).
Furthermore, when one rises early in the morning for the bhikkhus, attends to their physical needs, performs duties such as the *cetiyāṅgaṇa* (shrine-yard) observances, and sits in a secluded place—
Thinking, “May the bhikkhus in this monastery be happy, free from enmity, and free from affliction,” while seated there, is what is called loving-kindness as mental action.
Thinking, “May the laypeople be happy, free from enmity, and free from affliction,” is what is called loving-kindness as mental action.
“Both openly and in private” means both in their presence and in their absence. In that regard, assisting novices with tasks such as robe-making is [loving-kindness].
“Face-to-face loving bodily action” refers to [acts such as] washing the feet of the elders, paying homage, and fanning them.
Furthermore, all forms of respectful service (*sāmīcikamma*) toward the elders—such as washing their feet, prostrating, and offering fans—is called face-to-face loving bodily action.

“Behind one’s back loving bodily action” refers to the act of putting away wooden utensils and the like that have been poorly placed by both oneself and others, doing so without showing contempt for them, just as if one had placed them poorly oneself.
Addressing someone directly by saying, "The Elder Deva" or "The Elder Tissa," is what is called loving verbal action in their presence (*sammukhā mettā-vacīkamma*).
However, when they are not present in the monastery, asking about them and saying, "Where is our Elder Deva? Where is our Elder Tissa?
When will he perhaps arrive?"—such speech of endearment is what is called loving verbal action in their absence (*parammukhā mettā-vacīkamma*).
Opening eyes that are moistened and lubricated with the oil of loving-kindness (*mettā*), and gazing with a serene face,
is called mental action of loving-kindness in the presence (*sammukha*). The Elder Deva’s mental attention, "May the Elder Tissa be healthy,
may he be free from illness," is called mental action of loving-kindness in the absence (*parammukha*).

"Gains" refers to requisites such as robes that have been obtained. "Righteous" means acquired through the practice of alms-gathering in accordance with the Dhamma and justice, having abandoned wrong livelihoods such as hypocrisy and the like.

"Even down to what is contained merely in the bowl" means, at the very least, even the amount of two spoonfuls of alms-food that has fallen within the bowl and is included therein. "One who enjoys without apportioning" means...
In this context, there are two kinds of "apportionment" (paṭivibhatta): apportionment of material goods (āmisappaṭivibhatta) and apportionment of persons (puggalappaṭivibhatta).
Therein, the mental division [of one's thought] such as, "I will give this much, I will not give that much," is called apportionment of material goods.
However, the mental division [of one's thought] such as, "I will give to such-and-such a person, I will not give to such-and-such a person," is apportionment of persons.
...so it is called. One who, without doing either of those two, eats what has not been shared out is called "one who enjoys what is unshared.
Regarding the phrase "one who shares enjoyments with virtuous fellow-practitioners," this is the characteristic of one who shares enjoyments:
whatever excellent thing is obtained, that very thing is not sought from householders through the means of trading profit for profit.

He gives it, but does not consume it himself; and when receiving it, he should take it with the thought, "Let it be shared by the Saṅgha," strike the bell, and consume it as if it were the property of the Saṅgha.
Now, who fulfills this duty of courtesy (*sāraṇīya-dhamma*), and who does not fulfill it? First of all, one who is immoral (*dussīla*) does not fulfill it; for indeed—
The virtuous take what belongs to him. However, one who is pure in virtue fulfills the duties (*vatta*) without breaking them. Herein, this is the duty:

for if one gives to a mother, a father, a teacher, or a preceptor by making it a specific designation, he is merely giving what ought to be given; it does not constitute the "duty of courtesy" (*sāraṇīya-dhamma*), but rather is called "tending to an impediment. This is the duty of courtesy.

Indeed, it is appropriate only for one who has no impediments regarding the robe. However, when distributing specifically designated robes, they should be given to the sick, the attendants of the sick, newcomers, those departing, and to a newly ordained monk who does not know how to take up the outer robe and bowl.
Having given these, the remainder should be distributed starting from the seat of the senior elder; rather than giving small portions to everyone, each person should be given as much as they take.
If there is nothing remaining, one should again go for alms; then, starting from the senior’s seat, whatever is excellent should be given, and the remainder may be consumed.
Because of the words "by those who are virtuous," it is even permissible not to give to one who is immoral.
However, this duty of courtesy (*sāraṇīya-dhamma*) is fulfilled by a well-trained assembly, not by an untrained assembly.
For in a well-trained assembly, one who obtains something from elsewhere does not take it; even if one does not obtain anything from elsewhere, one takes only what is moderate, not more than that.

Yet this quality of courtesy (sāraṇīyadhamma) is fulfilled only after twelve years of giving whatever is obtained by wandering for alms again and again, and not before that. For if, in the twelfth year—
The Elder of the Saṅgha, having placed the alms-bowl filled with the *sāraṇīya-dhamma* food in the hall of seats, goes to bathe.
When asked, "Whose bowl is this?", and it is replied, "It belongs to the one who fulfills the *sāraṇīya-dhamma*," [the Elder] says, "Bring it here.
Having then distributed and eaten all the alms-food, he sets down the empty bowl. Then that bhikkhu [returns and finds] the empty...
Upon seeing the bowl, he gives rise to dejection, thinking, "They have used it up without leaving anything for me.

Thus, the *sāraṇīya-dhamma* (the practice of mutual recollection) is broken, and one must fulfill it again for twelve years. This is similar to the probation (*parivāsa*) imposed on members of other sects;
once a breach has occurred, it must indeed be fulfilled all over again. But he who thinks: "It is a gain for me, it is a great fortune for me, that..."
When his fellow celibates enjoy what has come into his bowl even without asking for permission, he gives rise to gladness; that is called "fulfilled.
For one who has thus fulfilled the quality of conciliation, there is neither envy nor stinginess. He becomes dear to people and easily obtains the requisites.
Even when what is placed in his bowl is given away, it is not exhausted, and in the place where divisible goods are kept—
One obtains the best goods; or when danger or famine arrives, the deities exert themselves on one's behalf.
Here are some examples: it is said that the Elder Tissa, a resident of Senagiri, lived near Mahāgirigāma.
Fifty great elders, while traveling to Nāgadīpa to pay homage at the Cetiya, were wandering for alms in Girigāma.
Having received nothing at all, they departed. But as the Elder was entering, he saw them and asked, "Venerable sirs, did you receive anything?
"We wandered about, friend," they replied. Knowing that they had received nothing, he said, "Venerable sirs, please stay right here until I return.
"Friend, we are fifty men and have not obtained even enough oil for a single bowl," they said.
"Venerable sir, the resident monks are capable; even if they do not receive alms, they know the path and the common areas.
The elders waited. The elder entered the village. At the very house where he was to stay, a great female lay devotee had prepared milk-rice and stood watching for the elder.
Then, as soon as the elder reached the door, she filled his bowl and gave it to him.
Taking it with him, he went into the presence of the elders and said to the senior of the Saṅgha, "Venerable sir, please accept this.
The elder thought, "We so many have received nothing at all, yet this man has come back so quickly after taking it; what could this be?
He looked toward the faces of the others. By the very manner of his look, the elder understood and said, "Venerable sir, this is almsfood obtained righteously and equitably."
"Take it without hesitation," he said, and starting from the beginning, he gave as much as they desired to everyone, and then he himself ate as much as he required.
Then, at the conclusion of his meal, the elders asked him: "Friend, when did you penetrate the supramundane Dhamma?
"Venerable sirs, I have no supramundane Dhamma. "Friend, do you possess the jhānas? "Venerable sirs, I do not possess even those."
“Is it not a marvel, friend? “It is a quality that inspires recollection, venerable sir, which I have fulfilled.
From the time that quality was fulfilled by me, even if there were a hundred thousand bhikkhus, what is in my bowl would never be exhausted.
Having heard this, they said: “Excellent, excellent, good man! This is worthy of you. This, first of all, is [the account of] “what is in the bowl.”
The background story for the phrase “it does not exhaust” is as follows:
This very elder, having gone to the place of almsgiving during the Great Offering of Mount Goods (*giribhaṇḍa-mahāpūjā*) at Cetiyapabbata, asked, “What excellent goods are there in this place?
[They replied,] “Two robes, venerable sir. [He said,] “These shall come to me.”
Having heard this, the minister informed the king: "A certain youth has spoken thus.
[The king] said, "Such was the thought of the youth, but fine garments are suitable for the great elders," and set them aside, thinking, "I shall give them to the great elders.
When the Saṅgha of monks stood in order and he began to distribute them, even though those garments had been placed upon his head, they fell from his hand.
They did not mount [the throne]. Others mounted it. But at the time of giving the gift to the youth, he had already mounted the hand [of the throne].

Having let him down from his hand, the king looked at the face of the minister, seated the youth, gave the gift, dismissed the Saṅgha, and sat down beside the youth, saying: "Venerable sir, when did you penetrate this Dhamma? He—
“Even by way of a figurative expression, when speaking of what does not exist, you said: ‘Great King, I have no supramundane Dhamma.
Was it not so, venerable sir, that you spoke previously? “Yes, Great King, I am one who fulfills the qualities of endearment (*sāraṇīya-dhamma*).
From the time I fulfilled those qualities, the finest goods reached me in the place where the goods to be distributed were kept. “Excellent, excellent!”
"Venerable sir, this is worthy of you," she said, and after paying homage, she departed.
This is the story concerning the passage: "The finest goods reach the place where the goods intended for distribution are kept.
However, during the time of the Brahmin Tissa’s threat, the inhabitants of Bhātaragāma fled without even informing the Elder Nun Nāgā. The Elder Nun...
At the time of dawn, she said to the young bhikkhunīs, “This village is exceedingly quiet; wait here for a moment.
They went and, having ascertained that everyone had departed, returned and informed the elder nun. Having heard this, she said, “Do not worry about their departure;
apply yourselves instead to your own recitation, questioning, and systematic reflection.”

Having said, "Please do so," she put on her robes at the time for the alms-round and stood at the village gate at the foot of a *nigrodha* tree with eleven other bhikkhunīs, herself being the twelfth.
The deity dwelling in that tree gave alms-food to all twelve bhikkhunīs and said, "Venerable ladies, do not go elsewhere;
come here always. Now, the Elder’s younger brother was Nāgatthera.
There was a man who, thinking, "This is a great danger; it is not possible to subsist here, I shall go to the other shore," set out from his own dwelling place with himself as the twelfth man.
Seeing the elder nun, he thought, "I will go [with her]," and arrived at the brother's village.
Hearing that "the elders have arrived," the elder nun went into their presence and asked, "What is it, noble sir? He—
She explained that situation to her. She said, “Stay in the monastery for just one more day today; you may depart tomorrow.
The elders went to the monastery.
On the following day, the elder nun, having walked for alms at the foot of a tree, approached the elder and [offered] this alms-food.
“Eat it,” he said. The Elder replied, “It will suffice for the elder nun,” and remained silent.
“Dear one, this almsfood is lawful; eat it without anxiety. “It will suffice for the elder nun,” [the other] said.
She took the bowl and threw it into the air. The bowl remained suspended in the air. The Elder said, “Even though it remains at the height of seven palm trees, it is still the meal of a bhikkhunī.”
Having said, "Elder," he added: "Fear does not exist at all times;

when fear has subsided, if I am reproached in my mind while speaking of the Noble Lineage, saying, 'O alms-collector, you spent your time eating the food of a bhikkhunī,' I shall not be able to remain steadfast.
Therefore, be heedful, Elders! and he set out upon the path.
The tree deity also stood there thinking, "If the elder eats the almsfood from the hand of the elder nun, I will not turn him back; but if he does not eat it, I will turn him back.
Seeing the elder's departure, she descended from the tree and said, "Venerable sir, give me the bowl," and having taken the bowl, she led the elder to the very foot of the tree.

Having brought him, prepared a seat, given him almsfood, and having requested him to wait until his meal was finished, she attended upon twelve bhikkhunīs and twelve bhikkhus for seven years. This is the basis for the statement, "Devas exert themselves [to provide assistance].
For there, the Elder Nun fulfilled the qualities that are conducive to affection.

Regarding the terms *akhaṇḍāni* and so forth: if, among the seven classes of offenses, one has broken a training rule either at the beginning or at the end, one's virtue is called "broken" (*khaṇḍa*), like a garment torn at the edge.

However, for one who has broken it in the middle, it is called "perforated" (*chidda*), like a garment with a hole in the center. Furthermore, for one who has broken two or three [rules] in succession...
When they are broken on the back or the belly, it is called "spotted" (*sabala*), like a cow that has a different color—such as black, red, or another hue—arisen in those places.
But when there are variegated specks of a different color here and there, it is called "speckled" (*kammāsa*), like a cow. However, for one whose [faculties] are entirely unbroken, those virtues...
They are called "unbroken, flawless, unspotted, and unblemished.

Furthermore, they are "free" because they liberate one from the slavery of craving and establish one in the state of freedom. They are "praised by the wise" because they are commended by the Buddhas and other wise ones.
They are "unadhered-to" because they cannot be adhered to by anyone through craving or views, such that one could say, "You have previously fallen into this."
Because they cannot be transgressed and are not subject to attachment, and because they lead to access concentration or absorption concentration,
they are called "conducive to concentration.
"They will dwell having attained commonality in virtue" means together with those bhikkhus dwelling in various directions and regions.

They will dwell having attained a state of virtue that is equal. For the virtue of stream-enterers and others remains exactly the same as the virtue of other stream-enterers and others, even when they dwell in the midst of the ocean or in the world of the devas; there is no difference in the virtue of the Path.
It is with reference to this that it was said.
"This view" refers to right view associated with the Path. "Noble" means faultless. "Leads out" means it is conducive to deliverance.
"For one who acts accordingly" means for one who practices in such a manner. "For the destruction of all suffering" means for the purpose of the total exhaustion of all suffering.
"Having entered upon the commonality of view" means they will dwell having attained a state of identical view. "Only growth" means that for those dwelling in this way, there is only growth.
"It is to be expected for monks, not their decline.
(142) "This very thing is abundant": because he is close to final Nibbāna, when advising the monks, he repeatedly delivers this very same discourse on the Dhamma.
"Thus is virtue" means: such is virtue; this much is virtue. Herein, there is the virtue of the fourfold purification (*catupārisuddhisīla*).
Virtue is one-pointedness of mind, which is concentration; insight is wisdom, which is to be understood as wisdom (*paññā*).
Regarding the phrases "perfumed by virtue" and so forth: it is by standing upon that very virtue that one generates the concentration of the path and the concentration of the fruit.

That [virtue] is thus perfumed by that virtue and becomes of great fruit and great benefit. It is by standing upon that concentration that one generates the wisdom of the path and the wisdom of the fruit.

When that wisdom is cultivated by means of that concentration, it becomes of great fruit and great benefit. Standing upon that wisdom, one generates the path-consciousness and the fruition-consciousness;
when cultivated by that [wisdom], it is rightly liberated from the taints.
"As long as they please" means that for the Buddhas there is no such thing as dissatisfaction or agitation; it means according to their liking, according to their inclination.
But it is said: *Āyāma* means "come, let us go. There is also the reading *ayāma*, which has the same meaning: "let us go.
The Blessed One addresses the Elder Ānanda because of his status as one who dwells in his immediate presence. The Elder, however, announces to the monks: "Friends, take up your bowls and robes;
the Blessed One wishes to go to such-and-such a place."
144. The journey to Ambalaṭṭhikā is self-evident. Furthermore, the passage beginning with “Then the Venerable Sāriputta” has been explained in detail in the *Sampasādanīya Sutta*.
148. Regarding the description of the dangers of immorality:
“In Pāṭaligāma, a rest-house” (*āvasathāgāra*) refers to a lodging for guests. It is said that in Pāṭaligāma there was always...
The associates of two kings came and, having driven people out from their homes and families, stayed for a month or even half a month.
Those people, being constantly harassed, thinking, "There will be a place to stay when they arrive," built a large hall in the middle of the city;
in one part of it was a place for the storage of goods, and in another part...
They made it their place of residence. Upon hearing that "the Blessed One has arrived," they thought: "Even if we had to go ourselves, the Blessed One might have to be brought [to us];
yet he has reached our own dwelling place of his own accord. Today, we shall have auspicious blessings recited for the Blessed One at the guest house.
It was for this very purpose that they approached. Therefore, they spoke thus: "To where the guest house is..."
They, it is said, thinking—“Buddhas are indeed inclined toward the forest and delight in the forest;
they might or might not wish to dwell within a village”—had come without attending to the guest-house, being unaware of the Blessed One’s intention.
Now, having understood the Blessed One’s intention, they approached the guest-house with the thought, “We shall go ahead and attend to it.”
"Sabbasantharin" means: I spread [the seat] in such a way that it is entirely covered.
149. "Dussīla" means one who is without virtue, devoid of virtue. "Sīlavipanna" means one whose virtue has failed, one whose restraint is broken. "Pamādādhikaraṇa" means on account of negligence.
And this sutta is presented with reference to householders, yet it certainly applies to those who have gone forth as well. A householder...
For by whatever craft one maintains one’s livelihood— whether by agriculture or by trade— if one is negligent through such acts as the taking of life,
one will be unable to carry out those tasks at the proper time, and thus even one’s capital will be lost. Furthermore,
by committing the taking of life or theft and so forth during the festival season, one incurs a great loss of wealth by way of punishment.
One who has gone forth but is immoral, due to negligence, suffers loss in terms of virtue, the word of the Buddha, meditative absorption, and the seven treasures of the noble ones.

He sits down embarrassed, with shoulders slumped and head bowed, scratching the ground with his fingernail; whereas one who is confident...
He is unable to speak. Even when he has gone forth, he approaches with fear, thinking, "Many monks have assembled;

Thus, being apprehensive, he is unable to speak with confidence. But another person, though immoral and arrogant—
He wanders about as if [possessed], yet he too becomes dejected because of his own disposition.
"He dies deluded": for when he lies upon his deathbed, the place where he undertook and engaged in unvirtuous deeds comes into his field of vision;
opening his eyes, he sees this world, and closing them, he sees the world beyond. To him—

“Sunidha and Vassakāra” refers to two brahmins, Sunidha and Vassakāra; they were the chief ministers of Magadha.

"As a bulwark against the Vajjis" means for the purpose of cutting off the source of income for the royal families of the Vajjis. "In groups of a thousand" means by way of individual units of a thousand.

"By the thousands. "Sites" means house-sites. "The minds incline toward constructing dwellings" means that the minds of those who recite the science of site-selection (*vatthuvijjā*) incline toward constructing the dwellings of kings and royal ministers.

"Here is a spirit-grasping, here is a ghost-grasping, or there is a stone or a stump," they see.
Then, having recited their craft-mantras, they construct [the dwellings] as if consulting with deities.
Or else, deities taking possession of their bodies direct their minds toward constructing dwellings in various places. They [fix] stakes at the four corners.

(154) A *uḷumpa* is made by hewing logs to form rafts for the purpose of crossing to the other shore. A *kulla* is made by binding together creepers and the like.

In the verse beginning with “Those who cross the ocean,” the term “ocean” (*aṇṇava*) is a designation for a body of water that is, at the very least, one *yojana* in depth and breadth. Here, however, it is intended as a river.
This is what is meant: those who cross the deep and wide river of craving (*taṇhā*) [cross] the bridge known as the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*).

Having made [a raft], people bind together a raft even when they wish to cross over this mere trifle, without touching the marshes or the low-lying places filled with water. But the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddha,

Wherever there are such monks among any [people], they...
The meaning is: "They should enter the rains retreat here and there. Why did he say this? It was for the sake of their comfortable dwelling.
For in the village of Veḷuva, there was no sufficient lodging and alms were scarce; however, around Vesālī there were many lodgings and alms were easily obtained.
That is why he spoke thus. But why did he not dismiss them, saying, "Go as you please"?
Out of compassion for them. It occurred to him thus: "I shall pass away after remaining for only ten months.
If these people go far away, they will not be able to see me at the time of my Parinibbāna.
Then they might think: 'The Teacher, while passing away, did not give us even so much as a token of remembrance; had he known [otherwise], he would not have gone so far.'"

[He thought,] "We might have to stay [here]," and thus he would have felt remorse. However, because those living all around Vesālī would come eight times a month to hear the Dhamma and receive the advice of the Sugata, he did not dismiss them.
164. *Khara* means harsh. *Ābādha* means a disease of a contrary nature. *Bāḷhā* means powerful. *Māraṇantikā* means ending in death.
"Capable of bringing him to the very brink of death. "He endured with mindfulness and clear comprehension":
having established mindfulness well and delimited [the situation] with wisdom, he endured it. "Without being distressed":
not turning this way and that in accordance with the sensations, he endured it without being oppressed or pained. "Without informing": without letting [them] know.
"Without having taken leave" means without having asked for permission, that is, without having given instruction and exhortation.

"By means of energy" refers both to the energy of the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga-vīriya*) and the energy of the attainment of fruition (*phala-samāpatti-vīriya*). "Having diverted" means having suppressed.

Regarding the term "life-formations" (*jīvitasaṅkhāra*): here, life itself is a life-formation; it is that by which life is formed—that is, by which life, when being severed, is joined back together and maintained.
Thus, the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) is also a formation of life (*jīvitasaṅkhāra*). That is what is intended here.
"Having resolved" means having resolved and having set it in motion; the brief meaning here is:
"One should enter the attainment of fruition which is capable of establishing life. But did the Blessed One not enter the attainment of fruition prior to this? He did enter it. However, that—
Momentary attainment (*khaṇika-samāpatti*). Momentary attainment suppresses feeling only during the state of attainment itself;
as soon as one has emerged from that attainment, feeling again overwhelms the body, just as water overflows when a log or a stone is thrown into it and the moss is cut away.
However, that which [remains] regarding the sevenfold materiality and the sevenfold immateriality is silent.
Having made it free from tangles, the attainment entered by way of great insight suppresses [the defilements] thoroughly.
Just as when a man has plunged into a lotus pond and thoroughly churned up the moss with his hands and feet, the water takes a long time to cover it over again;
even so, for one who has emerged from that state, feeling arises only after a long time. Thus said the Blessed One.

On that day, as if establishing fresh insight upon the Great Enlightenment Seat (mahābodhipallaṅka), he rendered the sevenfold set of form and the sevenfold set of the formless free from thicket and tangle;
having integrated them through fourteen modes, he suppressed feeling by means of great insight (mahāvipassanā) and entered into meditative attainment (samāpatti), resolving:
"May [feeling] not arise for ten months. Feeling was thus suppressed by attainment.
He did not even emerge for ten months.
"Recovered from illness" means that having been ill, he has emerged again. "As if become sweet" means having become heavy and stiff, like a man impaled on a stake.
"They do not spread" means they do not manifest, nor do they appear in various forms.
“They do not stand firm; even the teachings do not occur to me” means he indicates that the teachings such as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) were no longer clear to him.
However, the Elder was well-versed in the textual teachings (tantidhamma). “He does not utter them” means he does not give his final exhortation;
it is with reference to this that he speaks.
165. "Neither internal nor external" means doing neither with respect to the Dhamma nor with respect to the person.
For one who thinks, "I will not teach this much Dhamma to another," makes the Dhamma internal;
one who thinks, "I will teach this much to another," makes the Dhamma external; and one who thinks, "I will teach this to this particular person..."
But by thinking [of someone], one makes that person "internal. By thinking, "I will not teach this to him," one makes that person "external. The meaning is: he taught without doing so.

"The teacher’s fist" (ācariyamuṭṭhi) refers to what is known as the "teacher’s fist" among outsiders; it is like when, having not told anything to anyone during their youth, they lie on their deathbed in their final days.
They speak to their own beloved pupil; likewise, it shows that for the Tathāgata there is nothing whatsoever held back—
like something clenched in a fist with the thought, "I will speak of this in my final place at the time of my passing" or "I will preserve it"— saying,
"I [shall lead] the community of bhikkhus," meaning either "I alone shall lead the community of bhikkhus" or "I am its presiding head."
"Uddesiko" means one who has "uddesa" (recitation/assignment) in the sense of being designated. The meaning is:
"May the Saṅgha of bhikkhus designate me alone and look toward me; let them not exist after my passing, or let there be whoever they may be"—it is not so.
This is because envy and avarice were destroyed right on the seat of enlightenment (bodhipallaṅka); therefore, it is not so.
It exists. "What is it? refers to that which [exists]. "Eighty years old" means eighty years of age;

this is stated for the purpose of indicating the arrival at the final stage of life. "By means of repairs mixed with binding" means by means of repairs mixed with binding, such as binding the arms and binding the wheels.
"He maintains himself" means he maintains himself as if by means of repairs mixed with binding, like an old cart. By means of the binding of the fruit of Arhatship, the four postures are maintained.
This shows that it occurs for the Tathāgata.
Now, in order to clarify this meaning, he said: "At whatever time, Ānanda," and so forth. Therein, "all signs" refers to the signs of form and so on.
"Some feelings" refers to mundane feelings. Therefore, Ānanda, [he said] because...
He shows this by saying: "By means of this dwelling in the attainment of fruition, there is comfort; therefore, you too should dwell in this manner for that very purpose.
"Be islands unto yourselves" means: dwell having made yourself an island and a support, just like an island in the great ocean.
"Be refuges unto yourselves" means: be those who have only yourselves as their destination, not others. The same applies to the phrases "be islands of the Dhamma" and "be refuges in the Dhamma."
This is the method. *Tamatagge* means "at the very top of darkness. The letter *ta* is used here due to the requirements of metrical euphony (*padasandhi*).
This is what is meant: "These are the very tops of darkness; thus they are 'tamataggā'.
Having thus severed every bond of darkness, Ānanda, these bhikkhus of mine will be exceedingly supreme in the highest state. They will stand at the very pinnacle of all those who desire training.
"All those bhikkhus, having the four foundations of mindfulness as their domain, will be foremost"—with these words, he concludes the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship.
The commentary on the second recitation section is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Radiance of the Sign.
166. "He entered Vesālī for alms"—when did he enter it? It was at the time when he had departed from Ukkacela and gone to Vesālī.
It is said that after the Blessed One had completed the rains retreat, he left Veḷuva Village with the intention of going to Sāvatthī;
returning by the same path he had come, he eventually reached Sāvatthī and entered the Jeta Grove. The Dhamma Generalissimo [Sāriputta] [regarding] the Blessed One...

Having demonstrated his duties, he went to his daytime resting place. There, after demonstrating his duties to his resident pupils, once they had departed, he swept the resting place, spread out his leather mat, washed his feet, sat down cross-legged, and entered the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
Then, when he emerged from that state at the predetermined time, this reflection arose in him:
The thought arose: "Do the Buddhas pass away first, or do the chief disciples?
Then, knowing that "the chief disciples pass away first," he examined his own life-force (*āyusaṅkhāra*). He knew: "Only seven days remain of my life-force.
Then he considered: "Where shall I pass away? Thereupon [he reflected]: "Rāhula has passed away among the Tāvatiṃsa gods..."
While reflecting again, "The Elder Aññāsikoṇḍañña [attained parinibbāna] at the Chaddanta Lake;
where shall I attain parinibbāna?", he brought to mind his mother: "Even though my mother was the mother of seven Arhats, she lacked faith in the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha.
Does she have the necessary potential (upanissaya), or does she not? Having thus reflected, he—
Seeing the decisive support for the path of stream-entry, and looking to see for whom the realization would come through his teaching, he perceived:
"It will be through my own teaching of the Dhamma, and not through anyone else's. However, if I were to remain inactive, there would be those who would say of me:
'The Elder Sāriputta is a refuge even for the rest of the people; for thus it is with him—'"
On the occasion of the teaching of the *Samacitta Sutta*, one hundred thousand million deities attained *arahantship*. There is no counting the number of deities who penetrated the three lower paths.
In other instances as well, numerous realizations (*abhisamaya*) are seen.
Even by merely gladdening their hearts there, eighty thousand families were reborn in the heavenly realms. Now, he [the Buddha] was unable to take even a mere glance at his own mother’s desire.

“I was not able,” he said. Therefore, having resolved, “Having freed my mother from wrong views, I shall attain final nibbāna right here in the birth-chamber,” he thought, “This very day, having obtained the Blessed One’s permission, I shall depart,” and addressed the Elder Cunda:
“Friend Cunda, give notice to our assembly of five hundred bhikkhus: ‘Friends, take [these robes]…’”
“Take up your bowls and robes; the Dhamma-Senāpati wishes to go to Nāḷakagāma. The Elder did accordingly.
The monks, having tidied their lodgings and taken their bowls and robes, came into the presence of the Elder.
The Elder, having tidied his own lodging and swept the day-quarters, stood at the door of the day-quarters looking toward the day-quarters—
“This is now the final sight of you; there will be no coming back again,” he said, as he approached the Blessed One surrounded by five hundred bhikkhus, paid homage, and spoke thus:
“Now I shall be severed, O Lord of the World, Great Sage!”
There is no coming or going; this is my final salutation.
My life is short; after seven days from now, I shall cast off this body like the laying down of a heavy burden.

“Venerable sir, let the Blessed One grant me leave; let the Sugata grant me leave; the time for my final Nibbāna has come, and the life-faculty has been relinquished. For the Buddhas, however, when it is said, “Enter final Nibbāna,” they are as it were praising death; whereas when it is said, “Do not enter final Nibbāna,” they are as it were praising life. Thus, when the Blessed One said, “Let the Blessed One grant me leave,” he was as it were praising life. And because the Blessed One granted him leave, he did not enter final Nibbāna at that moment. But when the Blessed One said, “The time for your final Nibbāna has come,” he was as it were praising death. And because the Blessed One did not grant him leave, he entered final Nibbāna at that very moment. Therefore, it is said: “The time for my final Nibbāna has come, and the life-faculty has been relinquished. Furthermore, this was said by way of praise for the Blessed One’s power, thinking: “The Blessed One has such power that if he so desired, he could extend his life-span even for a world-cycle, yet he does not do so; rather, he relinquishes the life-faculty and enters final Nibbāna. This is the meaning. Now, the Blessed One, having thus spoken, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. At that time, the Venerable Mahākassapa was standing before the Blessed One, fanning him. Then the Venerable Mahākassapa said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, why has the Blessed One risen from his seat so soon? “Kassapa, I have granted leave to Sāriputta, saying: ‘Let the Blessed One grant me leave; let the Sugata grant me leave; the time for my final Nibbāna has come, and the life-faculty has been relinquished. “But, venerable sir, did you say ‘final Nibbāna’? “Yes, Kassapa. “Venerable sir, if the Blessed One had said, ‘Enter final Nibbāna,’ the world would have been plunged into darkness. If the Blessed One had said, ‘Do not enter final Nibbāna,’ the world would have been filled with light. It is a gain for us, venerable sir, a great gain for us, venerable sir, that we have obtained the sight of Sāriputta, who was like a second Teacher to the Blessed One. “It is a gain for you, Kassapa, it is a great gain for you, Kassapa, that you have obtained the sight of Sāriputta, who was like a second Teacher to me. Then the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākassapa has said: ‘If the Blessed One had said, “Enter final Nibbāna,” the world would have been plunged into darkness. If the Blessed One had said, “Do not enter final Nibbāna,” the world would have been filled with light. “Ānanda, it is just as Mahākassapa has said. If I had said, ‘Enter final Nibbāna,’ the world would have been plunged into darkness. If I had said, ‘Do not enter final Nibbāna,’ the world would have been filled with light. Ānanda, Sāriputta was possessed of four wonderful and marvelous qualities. What four? Ānanda, just as the moon is possessed of four wonderful and marvelous qualities—namely, its disc is clear, its rays are cool, it dispels the darkness of night, and it illuminates the four quarters—so too, Sāriputta was possessed of these four wonderful and marvelous qualities. What four? His mind was clear, his wisdom was cool, he dispelled the darkness of ignorance, and he illuminated the four assemblies. Ānanda, Sāriputta was possessed of these four wonderful and marvelous qualities. Then the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is a gain for us, a great gain for us, venerable sir, that we have obtained the sight of Sāriputta, who was like a second Teacher to the Blessed One. “It is a gain for you, Ānanda, it is a great gain for you, Ānanda, that you have obtained the sight of Sāriputta, who was like a second Teacher to me. Then the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, where shall the Venerable Sāriputta be reborn? “Ānanda, Sāriputta has attained final Nibbāna. “But, venerable sir, where has the Venerable Sāriputta attained final Nibbāna? “Ānanda, Sāriputta has attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue.

“Venerable sir, it is a gain for us, a great gain for us, venerable sir, that the Venerable Sāriputta has attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue. “Indeed, Ānanda, it is a gain for you, a great gain for you, Ānanda, that Sāriputta has attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue. For, Ānanda, those disciples who possess the four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) and have reached the perfection of analytical knowledge, they are reckoned as the foremost among them, and Sāriputta was one of them. Those disciples who possess the six supernormal powers (abhiññā) and have reached the perfection of supernormal powers, they are reckoned as the foremost among them, and Sāriputta was one of them. Those disciples who possess the three true knowledges (vijjā) and have reached the perfection of true knowledge, they are reckoned as the foremost among them, and Sāriputta was one of them. Those disciples who possess the four paths and fruits and have reached the perfection of the path and fruit, they are reckoned as the foremost among them, and Sāriputta was one of them. Those disciples who possess the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and have reached the perfection of the foundations of mindfulness, they are reckoned as the foremost among them, and Sāriputta was one of them. Those disciples who possess the four right endeavors (sammappadhāna), the four bases of psychic power (iddhipāda), the five faculties (indriya), the five powers (bala), the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), and the Noble Eightfold Path (ariya-aṭṭhaṅgika-magga), and have reached the perfection of these, they are reckoned as the foremost among them, and Sāriputta was one of them. Therefore, Ānanda, it is a gain for you, a great gain for you, Ānanda, that Sāriputta has attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue. Then the Venerable Ānanda, having paid homage to the Blessed One, keeping him on his right, went to the Venerable Sāriputta’s dwelling. Upon arrival, he entered the dwelling and saw the Venerable Sāriputta’s body lying on a bed covered with a white cloth. Seeing this, he sat down on a seat to one side and lamented: “Too soon has the Venerable Sāriputta passed away! Too soon has the Venerable Sāriputta passed away! Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, having paid homage to the Blessed One, keeping him on his right, went to the Venerable Sāriputta’s dwelling. Upon arrival, he entered the dwelling and saw the Venerable Sāriputta’s body lying on a bed covered with a white cloth. Seeing this, he sat down on a seat to one side and lamented: “Too soon has the Venerable Sāriputta passed away! Too soon has the Venerable Sāriputta passed away! Then the Venerable Mahākassapa, having paid homage to the Blessed One, keeping him on his right, went to the Venerable Sāriputta’s dwelling. Upon arrival, he entered the dwelling and saw the Venerable Sāriputta’s body lying on a bed covered with a white cloth. Seeing this, he sat down on a seat to one side and said to the Venerable Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, why are you lamenting? Friend Moggallāna, why are you lamenting? The nature of conditioned things is such that they are impermanent, subject to change, and bound to end. That which has arisen, that which has come to be, that which is conditioned, that which is dependently originated—that being subject to decay, how could it not pass away? It is impossible that what is
If they were to speak [of his passing], those with wrong view would attribute fault to him by saying he was describing the virtues of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*);
therefore, he said neither of these two things. For this reason, the Blessed One asked him: “Where, Sāriputta, will you attain final Nibbāna?
When he replied, “Venerable Sir, there is a village called Nāḷaka in Magadha where I was born; there I shall attain final Nibbāna,” [the Buddha said: “For whom... [it is not possible].”
"Now, Sāriputta, you should consider it time; for now, it will be difficult for your elder and younger brothers to see such a bhikkhu as yourself, so teach them the Dhamma.
The Elder, perceiving that "the Teacher expects me to give a teaching of the Dhamma preceded by a display of supernormal power," said:

Having paid homage to the Blessed One, he rose up to the height of a palm tree, then descended again and, having paid homage to the Blessed One once more, stood in the sky at the height of seven palm trees.
Displaying his supernormal powers, he taught the Dhamma. The entire city gathered together.
The Elder descended, paid homage to the Blessed One, and said, "It is time for me to depart, Bhante. The Blessed One [addressed] the General of the Dhamma...
"I shall cause you to practice," he said, and rising from his Dharma-seat, he went toward the Perfumed Chamber and stood upon the jeweled slab.
The Elder circumambulated him three times, paid homage at four places, and said:
"Lord, in a past incalculable aeon plus one hundred thousand aeons, you fell at the feet of the Perfectly Enlightened One Anomadassi and obtained the vision of you."
"I made this aspiration. That aspiration of mine has been fulfilled; you have been seen by me—this is my first sight of you, and this is my last sight of you.

There will be no further sight of you. Having said this, and having raised his hands in a brilliant añjali with the ten fingers joined together, he withdrew while facing them as long as they remained within the range of his vision, saying: "From this point on, by way of death and rebirth..."
“There is no coming and going at any place whatsoever. Having paid homage, he departed.
A great earthquake occurred, bounded by the waters. The Blessed One said to the monks standing around him, “Follow your eldest brother, monks.
The monks followed him as far as the gateway. The Elder said, “Stop!”
“Friends, be heedful,” he said, and having made them turn back, he departed with his own retinue alone. The people followed after him, lamenting:
“Formerly, the noble one used to go on tours of return; this departure, however, is not for a return.
They too he made turn back, saying: “Be heedful, friends; such indeed is the nature of conditioned phenomena.”
Then the Venerable Sāriputta, providing assistance to people along the way for seven days, arrived at Nāḷakagāma in the evening and stood at the village gate at the foot of a banyan tree.
Now, a nephew of the elder named Uparevata, who was going out of the village, saw the elder, approached him, paid homage, and stood there. The elder—
He said to her, "Is your grandmother at home? "Yes, venerable sir," she replied. "Go and inform them of our arrival here.
