When they ask, "For what purpose have you come? say, "It seems that today there will be a festival in the village for one day;
please prepare the birth-chamber and find a place for five hundred bhikkhus to stay. She went and said, "Grandmothers..."
“My maternal uncle has arrived,” he said. “Where is he now? “At the village gate.
“Is he alone, or is anyone else with him? “There are five hundred bhikkhus. “For what reason have they come? He reported the matter to her.
The brahmin lady thought, “Why indeed does he have so many people prepare a dwelling place? Having gone forth in his youth, in his old age—”
Thinking, "I wish to become a householder," she had the birth-chamber cleaned, prepared a dwelling place for five hundred bhikkhus, lit oil-lamps, and sent word to the Elder.
The Elder, together with the bhikkhus, ascended the palace. Having ascended, he entered the birth-chamber and sat down.
Sitting down, he dismissed the monks, saying, "Go to your own dwelling places.
As soon as they had departed, a severe illness arose in the Elder; mortal pains of dysentery set in, such that one vessel would enter [his body] while another would exit.
The brahmin woman thought, "The condition of my son does not please me."

He stood leaning against the door of his own dwelling-cave. The Four Great Kings, looking about for where the Dhammasenāpati was staying, saw him lying on the bed of final passing away in the birth-chamber at Nāḷakagāma, and thinking, “We shall go to see him for the last time,” they approached, paid homage, and stood there.
The Elder asked, “Who are you?”—“We are the Great Kings, venerable sir.”
"Why have you come? "We have come to be attendants to the sick. "Very well, there is already an attendant;
go, you," he dismissed them. After they had departed, Sakka, Lord of the Devas, arrived by that same route;
after he had gone, Suyāma and the others, as well as Mahābrahmā, came. The Elder dismissed them in the very same manner.
Having seen the arrival and departure of the deities, the brahmin woman thought, "Who are these who come, pay homage to my son, and depart?
She went to the door of the elder’s cell and asked, "Dear Cunda, what is the news?
He explained the matter to her and said, "Venerable lady, the great lay devotees have arrived. The elder asked, "Why at this unusual hour?"
He asked, "Have you come? She replied, "Yes, dear, I have come to see you. He then asked, "Dear, who came first?
"The four Great Kings, dear," she said. "Dear, are you greater than the four Great Kings? "These laywomen, dear, are like mere monastery attendants;
from the moment our Teacher took conception, they have stood with swords in hand [to protect him]."
"Having offered the sacrifice, they established a protection. "Father, when they had gone, who arrived? "Sakka, the lord of the gods.
"Father, are you greater even than the king of the gods? "O lay follower, he is like a novice monk collecting alms;
he descended from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven at the time our Teacher descended, having taken his bowl and robes. "Father, when he had gone..."
"Who is it that has come, shining as if on fire? "Upāsikā, this one is your Teacher, the Blessed One, who is called Mahābrahmā.
"My dear, are you greater than even the Blessed One, the Mahābrahmā? "Yes, Upāsikā;
it is said that on the day our Teacher was born, these four Mahābrahmās received the Great Man with a golden net."
Then, as the brahmin woman was thinking, "Such is the power of my son;
what kind of power must the Blessed One, my son’s Teacher, possess?", five-colored rapture suddenly arose and pervaded her entire body.
The Elder thought, "My mother has experienced joy and gladness; now is the time for a teaching of the Dhamma."
Having reflected, he asked, "What are you thinking, Great Laywoman? She replied, "This is the quality of my son;
but what kind of qualities will this Teacher possess? This, Father, is what I am reflecting upon. [He said:
"Great Laywoman, at the moment of my Teacher's birth, at his Great Renunciation, at his Perfect Enlightenment, and at the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, the ten-thousandfold world-system..."
"Kampittha, there is indeed no one equal to the Blessed One in virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Having thus spoken at length, he delivered a Dhamma teaching connected with the qualities of the Buddha.
At the conclusion of the Dhamma teaching, the brahmin woman, having established herself in the fruit of stream-entry, said to her son:
“Father Upatissa, why did you act thus? Why have you not given me such an ambrosia for all this time?
The Elder, thinking, “I have now given the maintenance fee to my mother, the brahmin lady Rūpasārī;
this much will suffice,” dismissed the brahmin lady, saying, “Go, Great Laywoman,” and then asked, “Cunda, what is the time?”
He said, "It is the time of the strong dawn, venerable sir. "In that case, assemble the community of bhikkhus," [the Buddha said].
"The community has assembled, venerable sir," [he replied]. "Having lifted me up, have Cunda sit down.
Having lifted him up, he had him sit down. The Elder addressed the bhikkhus: "Friends, for forty-four years you have been wandering with me. Whatever..."
“If there is anything bodily or verbal of mine that you do not approve of, forgive it, friends.
“Venerable sir, for us who wander never leaving you, as if you were our very shadow, there is nothing whatsoever that we do not approve of; rather, please forgive us,” they said.
Then, as the crest of dawn appeared, the Elder, making the great earth resound, [attained parinibbāna] through the attainment of the remainderless element.
He attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna. Many gods and humans paid honor to the Elder at the time of his final Nibbāna.
Venerable Cunda took the Elder’s bowl and robes, as well as the water-strainer for the relics, and having gone to Jetavana, he took the Elder Ānanda and approached the Blessed One.
The Blessed One took the water-strainer for the relics together with the five [hundred monks].
Having praised the Elder’s virtues with hundreds of verses and having had a relic-stupa constructed, he gave notice to the Elder Ānanda for the purpose of traveling to Rājagaha.
The Elder announced this to the monks. The Blessed One, surrounded by a great community of monks, went to Rājagaha.
When they arrived there, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna attained final nibbāna. The Blessed One [took] his relics...
Having taken [the relics] and had a stupa constructed, he departed from Rājagaha and, proceeding by stages toward the Ganges, arrived at Ukkacela.

There, seated on the bank of the Ganges surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he taught a discourse concerning the final nibbāna of Sāriputta and Moggallāna; then, departing from Ukkacela, he went to Vesālī.
When things had thus transpired, the Blessed One dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe, and entered Vesālī for alms;
this is the sequential account here.
"A sitting mat" refers here to a piece of leather. "Udena Shrine" means at the site of the shrine of the yakkha Udena.
"What kind of dwelling" is what is said. This same method applies to the [meditations] beginning with those of the Gotamakas.
"Developed" means increased. "Cultivated" means done repeatedly. "Made a vehicle" means made like a yoked vehicle. "Made a foundation" means made like a foundation in the sense of being a support.
"Established" means resolved upon. "Perfected" means accumulated on all sides and well-increased. "Well-commenced" means properly undertaken.
Having spoken thus without restriction, he spoke the words beginning with "Indeed, for a Tathāgata... in order to show it again by way of restriction.
And here, "for an eon" (*kappa*) means for the duration of a lifespan. He would remain, fulfilling whatever measure of human lifespan exists at that particular time.
Or "for the remainder of an eon" means more than the hundred years mentioned as "little or more."
Or rather, the Elder Mahāsīva said: "For Buddhas, there is no such thing as thundering out of place.

Just as he suppressed the fatal sensation that arose in the village of Veḷuva for ten months, so too, by repeatedly entering that attainment and suppressing it for ten months at a time, he could have remained throughout this entire auspicious aeon (bhaddakappa). Why, then..."
Is it not the case that he does not remain? For the body subject to grasping is overcome by decrepitude and the like;

yet the Buddhas, without falling into a state of decrepitude and so forth, attain final nibbāna at the end of the fifth portion of their lifespan, precisely while they are still beloved and pleasing to the multitude.
Furthermore, when the great disciples who have awakened after the Buddha have attained final nibbāna, he must remain all alone, like a single tree stump, even though surrounded by young novices.
Or else, he might think, "Oh, how contemptible is the assembly of the Buddhas! and thus fall into a state of disparagement. Therefore, he did not remain standing.
Even when this was said, it was not accepted; in the Aṭṭhakathā, only this [explanation], "a full lifespan," has been fixed.
As for the phrase "as his mind was obsessed by Māra," here *yathā* is merely a particle (*nipāta*). Just as by Māra...
The meaning is that just as no other ordinary person (*puthujjana*) whose mind is obsessed and overwhelmed would be able to penetrate [the truth], even so he was unable to penetrate it.
For what reason? Because Māra obsesses the mind of one who has not entirely abandoned all twelve distortions (*vipallāsa*). In the Elder, however, four distortions remained.
Because they have not been abandoned, Māra obsesses his mind.
But what does he do when he causes that obsession? He displays a terrifying visible object or makes a terrifying sound audible;
then, upon seeing or hearing it, beings lose their mindfulness and their mouths go agape. Having thrust his hand into their mouths—
It crushes the heart. Thereupon, they remain unconscious. But how could this [being] thrust its hand into the Elder’s mouth?
It merely displays a terrifying object. Having seen that, the Elder did not penetrate the radiance of the sign.
The Blessed One, though already knowing, asked: “For what purpose did you address him up to three times? [The Elder replied: “Let it be, sir.”
When he had thus entreated, [the Buddha said], "Venerable sir, Blessed One," [the reply was] "This misdeed is yours alone;
this transgression is yours alone," in order to lighten his grief by laying the blame upon him. This is the commentary on the discourse regarding the request for death.
168. Regarding the phrase "Māra the Evil One" (*māro pāpimā*): here, *māra* is so called because he "kills" (*māreti*) by leading sentient beings toward what is harmful.
*Pāpimā* is a synonym for that same being; indeed, because he is possessed of evil qualities (*pāpadhamma*), he is called "the Evil One.

His other names are also *Kaṇha*, *Antaka*, *Namuci*, and *Pamattabandhu*. Furthermore, as for the words "spoken by him," this refers to [the teaching] following the Blessed One’s attainment of full enlightenment.
On the eighth week, having come to the very seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), he said: "Blessed One, that purpose for which you fulfilled the perfections (pāramī) has been attained by you;
omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa) has been realized. What is the use of wandering through the world?
Having spoken thus, just as he does today, he entreated: "Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One now attain final nibbāna. The Blessed One replied to him: "No..."
Having said, "He spoke thus," and so forth, he rejected [the proposal]. With reference to that, he said, "But this was spoken, venerable sir," and so on.
In that context, "learned" (*viyatta*) means learned by way of the Path. Likewise, "disciplined" (*vinīta*) and "confident" (*visārada*).
"Much-heard" (*bahussuta*) means those who have heard much regarding the Three Piṭakas; thus they are "much-heard. "Bearers of the Dhamma" (*dhammadhara*) means they retain that very Dhamma.

Alternatively, they are both "learned in the scriptures" (*pariyatti-bahussuta*) and "learned through realization" (*paṭivedha-bahussuta*). Because they retain the teachings of both the scriptures and realization, they are "bearers of the Dhamma" (*dhammadhara*);

this is how the meaning should be understood here. "Practicing in accordance with the Dhamma" (*dhammānudhammapaṭipanna*) means practicing the Dhamma of insight (*vipassanā*) which is the "conformity-Dhamma" (*anudhamma*) to the Noble Dhamma.
"Practicing with propriety" (*sāmīcippaṭipanna*) means practicing the appropriate course of conduct.

"Those who have entered upon the path. "Practitioners of the Dhamma" means those whose nature is to practice in accordance with the Dhamma. "Their own teacher's doctrine" refers to their own master’s teaching.
All terms beginning with "they will proclaim" are synonyms for one another. "With the Dhamma" means with words that possess a logical basis and a supporting reason.
"With a demonstration" means until they teach the Dhamma by making it lead to liberation.
"Brahmacariya" refers to the entire holy life of the Dispensation as comprised within the three trainings.

"Iddha" means successful by way of the flavor of meditative absorption (*jhāna*). "Phīta" means having reached growth by way of the attainment of the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), like a tree in full fruit and blossom.
"Vitthārika" means extensive by way of being established in various directions and regions. "Bāhujañña" means [known] by many people.
"Known and penetrated" means by way of the realization of the great multitude. "Became widespread" means it reached a state of broad expansion in every respect.
How so? "Well-proclaimed as far as gods and humans" means that all those of a discerning nature—both gods and humans—who exist, have well proclaimed it.
"Free from anxiety" means being without attachment. For you, O Evil One, have been wandering about since the eighth week after [my enlightenment], crying out:
"Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One now attain final Nibbāna; let the Sugata now attain final Nibbāna! From this day forward, be devoid of hope;
do not exert yourself for the sake of my final Nibbāna—thus he says.
Commentary on the Relinquishing of the Life-Force (Āyusaṅkhāra): 169.

"Mindful and clearly comprehending, he relinquished the life-force" means that having established mindfulness well and delimited [the duration] with knowledge, he released and abandoned the life-force.
In this regard, the Blessed One did not relinquish the life-force as one might throw a clod of earth with the hand.
He relinquished [the attainment], having entered into meditative absorption for only three months; thereafter, he gave rise to the thought, "I shall not enter it again.
It is with reference to this that it is said, "he relinquished" (*ossaji*). There is also a reading, "he released" (*ussajji*).
A "great earthquake" (*mahābhūmicālo*) is a massive shaking of the earth. At that time, it is said, the ten-thousandfold world system trembled. "Terrifying" (*bhiṃsana*) means causing fear.
"And the divine drums resounded" means the celestial drums resounded; the sky thundered with a dry roar; lightning flashed out of season;
and a momentary rain fell—this is what is meant.
"He uttered an inspired utterance": why did he utter it? Someone might say: "The Blessed One followed closely behind [the monk]..."
“‘Enter final Nibbāna, venerable sir! Enter final Nibbāna, venerable sir!’—thus, tormented by fear, he relinquished the life-formations.
[The Buddha said: “Let there be no occasion for that; for one who is terrified, there is no such thing as an inspired utterance (udāna).
To illustrate this, he uttered an inspired utterance released through the force of joy.
In this context, "measured" (*tula*) means that which has been weighed and delimited because it is directly perceptible even to all beings, including dogs and jackals. What is that?
It is kamma of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*). "Immeasurable" (*atula*) means that there is no other worldly kamma similar to it, nor is there anything equal to it.

What is that? It is sublime kamma (*mahaggata-kamma*). Alternatively, the sense-sphere and fine-material-sphere (*rūpāvacara*) kamma is "measured," while the immaterial-sphere (*arūpāvacara*) kamma is—
*Atulaṃ*: either that which has a small result is *tulaṃ*, while that which has a great result is *atulaṃ*. *Sambhavanti*: being the cause for becoming;
the meaning is "that which forms a mass" or "that which forms a heap. *Bhava-saṅkhāraṃ*: that which conditions renewed existence.
*Avassajī*: he relinquished. *Munī*: the Buddha-muni. *Ajjhattarato*: one who delights in his own internal [nature]. *Samāhito*: by way of access and absorption concentration.
"Composed. "He shattered like armor": he shattered it as if it were armor. "Born of himself": the defilement arisen within himself.

This is what is meant: "He cast off that which is called 'becoming' (sambhava) in the sense of having fruition, and 'formations of becoming' (bhavasaṅkhāra) in the sense of constructing existence—that is, mundane karma consisting of the weighing and the weighed. At the head of the battle, a great warrior [shatters] his armor..."
"Having become inwardly delighted and concentrated, he shattered the defilement that arises from oneself as if it were [shattering] a vessel.

Alternatively, *tulam* means weighing or examining. *Atulañ ca sambhavam* refers to both Nibbāna and the source of existence (*sambhava*). *Bhava-saṅkhāram* means the volitional formations leading to existence.
*Avassaji muni* means "the Sage abandoned [them]," [realizing]: "The five aggregates are impermanent; the cessation of the five aggregates..."

Weighing it in this manner—“Nirvana is permanent,” and so forth—the Buddha-Muni, seeing the danger in existence (*bhava*) and the benefit in Nirvana, abandoned that karma which is the formative force of existence and the root of the aggregates by means of the Noble Path that brings about the destruction of karma, as described in the words: “It leads to the destruction of karma. How so? Being inwardly delighted and concentrated...
He shattered the net of all defilements—which had arisen within himself and was named "self-arisen" because it originates in the self—just as one might break through armor.

For he was delighted in the internal by way of insight (*vipassanā*) and concentrated by way of serenity (*samatha*). Thus, starting from the preliminary stage, by the power of serenity and insight, he stood having completely enveloped his personal existence (*attabhāva*) as if with armor;
that net of all defilements, which had arisen within himself, was thus destroyed.
He broke [the barriers]. Because there is an absence of defilements (*kilesa*), an action performed [by one] is called "rendered useless" (*avassattha*) due to its lack of rebirth-linking;
thus, he abandoned action through the abandoning of defilements. Furthermore, for one whose defilements are abandoned, there is no such thing as fear.

Therefore, it should be understood that he relinquished the life-formations (*āyusaṅkhāra*) while entirely free from fear, and uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*) for the purpose of making known his state of fearlessness.
The Explanation of the Great Earthquake (Mahābhūmicālavaṇṇanā) 171.
Regarding the phrase "when great winds blow": at whatever time or on whatever occasion great winds blow, even as they blow, there arise what are called "uplifting winds.
As they blow, [they stir] that which is nine hundred and sixty thousand *yojanas* thick.
They cut off the wind that supports the water; consequently, the water falls into space, and as it falls, the earth falls.
Again, the wind, by its own power, binds and seizes the water as if drawing it into a bellows;
then the water rises up, and as it rises, the earth rises up. Thus, the water—
It causes the earth, which has been shaken, to shake. And this shaking continues even until the present day;
however, because of its density, the rising and falling are not perceived.

"Of great power (mahiddhika) and great majesty (mahānubhāva)": he is "of great power" due to the greatness of his success (*ijjhanassa mahantatāya*), and [he is "of great majesty"] due to the greatness of what is to be experienced.
"Of great power. "Limited" means weak; "immeasurable" means strong.

"He makes this earth tremble" means that having produced supernormal power (*iddhi*), he causes the earth to tremble—either to inspire awe, like Mahāmoggallāna, or to investigate, like the novice Saṅgharakkhita, who was the nephew of the Elder Mahānāga.
It is said that this venerable one [did so] from the very moment his hair was cut.
Having attained arahantship, he thought: "Is there any bhikkhu who, on the very day of his going forth, has attained arahantship and caused the Vejayanta Palace to tremble?

Then, realizing that there was no such person, he thought, "I shall cause it to tremble. Standing upon the summit of the Vejayanta Palace by means of the power of higher knowledge (*abhiññā*), he struck it with his foot, but was unable to make it tremble. Then he...
The female dancers of Sakka said, "Son Saṅgharakkhita, you wish to shake the Vejayanta Palace with a head that has a putrid odor;
dear one, the palace is well-established, how will you be able to shake it?
The novice thought, "These deities are playing with me, but I have not obtained my teacher."
Thinking, "Where indeed is my teacher, the Elder Sāmuddikamahānāga?

and reflecting upon it, he learned that the elder had created a water-cave in the great ocean and was sitting there for his midday rest. Having gone there and paid homage to the elder, he stood before him.
Then the elder said to him, "What is this, dear Saṅgharakkhita? Have you entered into battle without having trained? To which he replied, "I could not."
"Father, will you shake the Vejayanta Palace? he asked. "I could not find my teacher, venerable sir," he replied. Then the Elder said to him:
"Father, if someone like you cannot shake it, who else will? Have you ever seen, father, a lump of cow dung floating on the surface of water?
Father, when they bake a cake in a pan, they cut it away along the edges."
“Know it by this simile,” he said. He replied, “It will suffice, venerable sir; this much will do.
Having spoken thus, he resolved that water should fill the space occupied by the palace, and then departed toward the Vejayanta Palace.
When the daughters of the gods saw him, they said, “Having gone away once out of shame, the novice is coming back again; he is coming back yet again!”
They spoke thus. Sakka, the king of the gods, said: “Do not speak with my son;
he has now found a teacher, and in an instant he will cause the palace to tremble. The novice also struck the pinnacle of the palace with his big toe.
The palace tilted in all four directions. The devas cried out: “Support it, dear one! Support the palace!”
“Father, give it a firm foundation for the palace,” they cried out. The novice, having set the palace in its proper place, stood upon the roof of the palace and uttered this inspired utterance:
“Today I have gone forth; today I have attained the destruction of the taints.”
"Today I shake the palace; oh, how sublime is the Buddha!
Today I have gone forth... oh, how sublime is the Dhamma!
Today I have gone forth... oh, how sublime is the Saṅgha!"
Regarding what should be said concerning these other six earth-quakes, it has already been stated in the *Mahāpadāna*.

Thus, among these eight earth-quakes: the first was due to the disturbance of the elements; the second, through the power of psychic potency (*iddhānubhāva*); the third and fourth, through the splendor of merit (*puññateja*);
the fifth, through the splendor of knowledge (*ñāṇateja*); the sixth, by way of the giving of applause (*sādhukāra*); and the seventh, through the state of compassion (*kāruññabhāva*).
The eighth was by means of weeping. When the Great Being was descending into his mother’s womb and when he was emerging from it, the earth shook due to the power of his merit.
At the time of his full enlightenment, having been struck by the power of his knowledge, it shook.

At the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, established in the state of approval, it shook as it gave its assent. At the relinquishing of the life-force, established in the state of compassion, [it shook].
It shook because it could not endure the agitation of the mind; it shook because it was overwhelmed by the force of weeping at the final passing away (*parinibbāna*).

However, this meaning should be understood in terms of the earth-deity (*pathavī-devatā*), for this does not apply to the great primary element of earth (*mahābhūta-pathavī*), since it is insentient (*acetana*).
Regarding the phrase "These, Ānanda, are the eight causes," here "these" (*ime*) is the demonstrative indicator (*niddiṭṭha-nidassana*). And up to this point, the Venerable [Ānanda]—
Ānanda perceived: "Surely today the Blessed One has relinquished the life-formations.
But the Blessed One, although aware that this had been perceived, spoke the words beginning with "These eight," etc., without giving him the opportunity, while summarizing other groups of eight.
Commentary on the Eight Assemblies:
172. In that regard, "an assembly of many hundreds of kṣatriyas" refers to gatherings such as those with Bimbisāra, his kinsmen, or the Licchavis;
moreover, such assemblies are found even in other world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*). "Previously conversed" means that exchange of greetings and conversation had previously taken place.
"Discussion" refers to discussion regarding the Dhamma that had also been undertaken previously. "Whatever their appearance may be" means that they may be white-skinned, and so forth.
Whether they be black or of mottled complexion, the Teacher is indeed golden-hued. This, however, is said with reference to his physical form.
And as for that form, it appears to them exactly as it is; yet the Blessed One does not become like a barbarian, nor does he appear as one wearing earrings of loosened gems;
he sits in the very garb of a Buddha. But they [perceive him] as having a form identical to their own.
They see [him]. Whatever their own voices may be—even if they are broken-voiced, gurgling-voiced, or crow-voiced—the Teacher’s voice is like the Brahmā-voice.
However, this was said with reference to another language (bhāsantara).
For even if the Teacher speaks while seated upon a royal throne, they think, "Today the king speaks with a sweet voice. When he has finished speaking and departed...
But when they saw the King return to the Blessed One, the inquiry arose: "Who indeed is this?

In that context, regarding the phrase "Who indeed is this," even as they were investigating—thinking, "In this very place, who is this person who has just now appeared speaking in a sweet manner in both the Magadhi and Sinhala languages—is he a god or a human?"—they did not [recognize him].
The meaning is "knowing. But for what purpose does he teach the Dhamma to those who do not know it in this way? For the sake of *vāsanā* (mental impression).
For even the Dhamma heard in such a manner becomes a condition for the future; thus, he teaches with reference to the future.
[He taught] to the assembly of several hundred brahmins and others by means of the encounters with Soṇadaṇḍa, Kūṭadaṇḍa, and so forth, as well as by means of other world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).
And their arising should be understood.
For what purpose did the Blessed One bring forward these eight assemblies? It was solely for the purpose of demonstrating his state of fearlessness.
Having brought them forward, he said: "Ānanda, even when approaching these eight assemblies and teaching the Dhamma, the Tathāgata..."
"There is neither fear nor trepidation; who indeed would be fit to conceive the notion that the Tathāgata might be afraid upon seeing Māra alone?
Fearless, Ānanda, the Tathāgata, undaunted, mindful and clearly comprehending, relinquished the life-formations.
*Commentary on the Eight Bases of Mastery* (Aṭṭha-abhibhāyatana-vaṇṇanā)
173. "Spheres of mastery" (*abhibhāyatana*) means causes for mastering. What do they master? Both adverse states (*paccanīkadhamma*) and objects (*ārammaṇa*).
For they master adverse states by way of being their opposites, and they master objects through the person's preeminence in knowledge (*ñāṇuttariyatā*).
In the phrases "perceiving forms internally," etc., one is "perceiving forms internally" by way of preliminary work (*parikamma*) upon internal forms.
It is called [the preliminary work]. For when one performs the preliminary work on the blue, one does so upon the hair, the bile, or the pupil of the eye.
When performing the preliminary work on the yellow, one does so upon the fat, the skin, the backs of the hands and feet, or the yellow parts of the eyes.
When performing the preliminary work on the red, one does so upon the flesh, the blood, the tongue, or the red parts of the eyes.
Or he does it. When performing the preliminary work (*parikamma*) on the white, he does it on the bone, or the teeth, or the nails, or the white parts of the eyes.
But that [white] is not truly blue, truly yellow, truly red, or truly white; it is simply impure.
"One sees forms externally" refers to one for whom such preliminary work has arisen internally, and the sign (*nimitta*)...
But externally; thus, by way of internal preliminary work (*parikamma*) and external absorption (*appanā*), one is said to be:
“Perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally. “Limited” (*parittāni*) means unextended.

“Beautiful or ugly” (*suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni*) means they are either beautiful or ugly. It should be understood that this base of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) is spoken of specifically in terms of being limited.

"He overcomes them" means: just as a person who has eaten his fill, having received only a spoonful of food, gathers it together thinking, "What is there to eat here? and makes it into a single mouthful;
even so, a person of superior knowledge with clear wisdom thinks, "What is there to attain in this limited object? This is not for me."
"Having overcome those forms as 'a burden,'" he enters into attainment; the meaning is that he reaches absorption (*appanā*) in this very moment with the mere arising of the sign (*nimitta*).
By the words "I know, I see," his mental application (*ābhoga*) is described. And that [application] belongs to one who has emerged from attainment, not while within the attainment itself.
"He is percipient thus" refers both to the perception of mental application and to the perception of the jhāna.

He perceives thus. For he possesses the perception of mastery even while within the attainment (*samāpatti*), but the perception of directed attention (*ābhoga*) belongs only to one who has emerged from the attainment.
"Immeasurable" means having increased in measure; the sense is that they are vast. Regarding the word "having mastered": here, just as...
Just as a gluttonous man, having received an extra portion of food, thinks, "Let there be more; what will this do for me?
and does not regard it as significant, so too a person supreme in knowledge, possessing clear wisdom, thinks, "What is there here to enter into?
This is not immeasurable; I have no burden in achieving one-pointedness of mind."
Having mastered these, he attains absorption; the meaning is that he reaches absorption right here simultaneously with the arising of the sign.
"Perceiving the formless internally" means being devoid of the preparatory perception regarding internal forms, either due to not having obtained them or due to having no need for them.
"One sees forms externally" refers to one for whom both the preparation and the sign have arisen only externally.
Thus, by means of both external preliminary work (*parikamma*) and absorption (*appanā*), one is said to be "percipient of the formless internally while seeing forms externally.
The rest here follows the same method as described for the fourth base of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*).

Among these four, the limited [objects] are presented according to the temperament of one dominated by applied thought (*vitakkacarita*), while the immeasurable [objects] are presented according to the temperament of one dominated by delusion (*mohacarita*).
"Golden" is by way of one whose temperament is dominated by hatred; "ugly" is by way of one whose temperament is dominated by lust. For these [objects] are suitable for them.
And that suitability for them has been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga* in the section on the description of temperaments (*caritaniddesa*).

In the context of the fifth base of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) and so forth, the term "blue" is stated as a comprehensive inclusion of all [shades], whereas "blue-colored" is stated by way of the specific color itself.
"Blue in appearance" means by way of their visible aspect; it is said that they appear as unblended colors, being seen as purely blue due to the absence of other cognitions and marks.
"Blue in luster," however, is said by way of their radiance;
the meaning is that they have a blue luster, being endowed with blue effulgence. By this, he shows their purity. It is precisely by way of their pure color...
For these four bases of mastery (abhibhāyatana) have been taught. Regarding "umāpuppha" (flax flower):
this flower is glossy and soft, and even when being seen, it remains blue. However, flowers such as the girikaṇṇikā are white in their constituent elements (dhātu) even when being seen.
Therefore, only this [blue flax flower] was taken, and not those others. "Bārāṇaseyyaka" means originating from Bārāṇasī. In that regard—
It is said that the cotton was soft, the spinners were skilled, and the weavers were expert; the water used was pure and smooth.
Therefore, that cloth was polished on both sides; it appeared smooth, soft, and glossy on both surfaces.
The meaning of the phrases beginning with "yellow" (*pītāni*) should be understood in this same manner. When one is acquiring the blue kasiṇa (*nīlakasiṇa*), in the blue...
"He grasps the sign in a flower, or in a cloth, or in a color-element," and so forth;
furthermore, the entire procedure for making the kasiṇa, the preliminary work (parikamma), and the method for absorption (appanā) have already been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.

These eight bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) have also been brought forward solely for the purpose of demonstrating the state of fearlessness. It is said that after saying these things, he spoke as follows:
“Ānanda, even for a Tathāgata who enters and emerges from such attainments as these, there is no fear or trepidation.
Who, indeed, would be fit to conceive the notion that the Tathāgata might be afraid upon seeing Māra alone?
Fearless, Ānanda, the Tathāgata—undaunted, mindful, and clearly comprehending—relinquished the life-formations.”

Commentary on the Eight Liberations (Aṭṭhavimokkhavaṇṇanā) 174. The discussion on the liberations is indeed of clear meaning. These eight liberations have been brought forward solely for the purpose of demonstrating the state of fearlessness.
Having said this, it is further stated: "Ānanda, even for one who enters and emerges from these attainments..."
“And for the Tathāgata there is no fear or trepidation... [etc. ...he relinquished it. 175.

Now, even here, the Blessed One, without giving Ānanda an opportunity to speak, began another teaching in the manner of the passage beginning with “At one time... Therein, “the first after his full enlightenment” means during the very first eight days after he had become fully enlightened.
177. “Relinquished” (*ossaṭṭha*) means abandoned or set aside; having said this, he remarked: “Therefore, this ten-thousandfold world-system trembled.”
The Discourse on Ānanda’s Request (Ānandayācanakathā) 178. *Alam* is a word of refusal. *Bodhim* refers to the penetration of the knowledge of the four paths.
When he says, *saddahasi tvam*, he means: "Do you have faith in that which has been spoken by the Tathāgata? Therefore, *tasmātihānanda* means: because of this statement...
"Because you have faith, it is shown that this misdeed belongs to you alone.
(179) "On one occasion..."—the Blessed One said this to show: "It was not only here that I addressed you;
on another occasion as well, having addressed you, I produced a gross sign, yet even that was not penetrated by you. This fault is yours alone."
Thus, for the purpose of dispelling sorrow, he began in various ways to attribute faults to the Elder himself.

(183) “From those who are dear and beloved”: this refers to mother, father, brother, sister, and so forth; through birth there is change, through death there is separation, and through becoming there is alteration.
“How can that be found here? means: because of all those who are dear and beloved...

There is a difference in nature; therefore, even after fulfilling the ten perfections, attaining full enlightenment, setting in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, displaying the Twin Miracle, and descending from the heavens, it is impossible that the body of the Tathāgata—which is born, become, conditioned, and subject to dissolution—should not eventually perish. This state of affairs does not exist.
"Even by weeping and even by crying out, it is not possible to recover that cause. "He will swallow it back again" means:
indeed, he will swallow back again that which has been cast out and vomited. "As this holy life" means:
as this holy life of the Dispensation, which comprises the three trainings.
"Enduring" means capable of withstanding the journey. "Long-lasting" means long-lasting by way of its prolonged duration.
The entire passage beginning with "the four foundations of mindfulness" is explained solely in terms of both the mundane and the supramundane.

Furthermore, the detailed exposition of these factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyā dhammā) in all their aspects is found in the *Visuddhimagga*, in the section on the purification by knowledge and vision of the way (*paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi*).
Thus it was said. The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the third recitation section is finished.
The commentary on the "Elephant’s Look Back" (Nāgāpalokita) is concluded.
186. Regarding "the backward glance of a nāga": for while the bones of the Paccekabuddhas stand with their ends touching end to end like the tips of hooks, it is not so for the Buddhas.
For the Buddhas, however, they remain joined together like links of a chain;
therefore, when looking back, it is impossible to turn the neck. Just as...
However, when a noble elephant wishes to look toward the rear, it turns its entire body; such is the manner in which one must turn.

But as for the Blessed One, while standing at the city gate with the thought "I shall look toward Vesālī" having just arisen in his mind—[the people thought]—"The Blessed One, by you who have fulfilled the perfections for many thousands of millions of eons, has never even turned his neck..."

Thinking, "The formal act of seeking permission has been performed," this earth turned like a potter’s wheel and caused the Blessed One to face toward the city of Vesālī; it was with reference to this that it was said.
But is it not the case that [the Buddha visited] not only Vesālī, but also Sāvatthī, Rājagaha, Āḷandā, Pāṭaligāma, Koṭigāma, and Nādikā?
Why did he not look back with a "Nāgāpalokita" (the elephant’s backward glance) at each place as he was departing from each one, seeing them all for the last time?
Because it would not have been extraordinary. For it is not considered extraordinary for one who turns back and looks at each place;
therefore, he did not look back. Furthermore, the kings of Vesālī were near their destruction; they were destined to perish after three years more.
Having made a shrine named Nāgāpalokita at the city gate, they will worship it with perfumes, garlands, and so forth;
thinking, "That will lead to their welfare and happiness for a long time," he looked back out of compassion for them.

"One who brings an end to suffering" means one who brings an end to the suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*). "Possessed of eyes" means possessed of the five kinds of eyes. "Parinibbūta" means parinibbūta through the parinibbāna of the defilements (*kilesa*).

Commentary on the Four Great Authorities (Catumahāpadesavaṇṇanā): 187. *Mahāpadesa* means "great occasion" or "great reference. The meaning is: those great reasons which have been spoken by referring to the Buddha and others, who are great and great. 188.
*Neva abhinanditabbaṃ* means that one should not even listen to it beforehand by giving a cry of approval (*sādhukāra*) with a joyful and satisfied heart.
For when this has been done, if he is later told, "This does not agree," he will say, "Was this doctrine [dhamma] true before, and now it is no longer the doctrine?
and thus he does not relinquish his tenet. "It should not be rejected" means that one should not say beforehand, "What is this fool saying?
For if such a thing were said, he would not even speak what is appropriate to say. Therefore he said: "Without approving..."
"Without disparaging. "Words and phrases" means the syllables (byañjana) that constitute the words (pada). "Having thoroughly mastered" means having properly grasped it, thinking:
"In this place the text (pāḷi) was spoken; in this place the meaning (attha) was spoken; in this place the connection (anusandhi) was explained;
in this place the sequence (pubbāpara) was explained. "They should be compared with the Sutta" means they should be brought down into the Sutta.
"Things to be pointed out in the Vinaya" means things to be reconciled with the Vinaya. And here, "sutta" refers to the Vinaya;
as it is said: "Where was it prohibited? At Sāvatthī, in the Suttavibhaṅga. "Vinaya" refers to the Khandhaka;
as it is said: "In the Vinayātisāra. In this way, even the entire Vinaya Piṭaka is not exhausted [by these categories].
Furthermore, the *Ubhatovibhaṅga* is the *Sutta*, while the *Khandhaka* and *Parivāra* are the *Vinaya*; thus, the *Vinaya Piṭaka* is comprised.
Alternatively, the *Suttanta Piṭaka* is the *Sutta* and the *Vinaya Piṭaka* is the *Vinaya*; thus, only two *Piṭakas* are comprised.
Or again, the *Suttanta* and *Abhidhamma Piṭakas* are the *Sutta* and the *Vinaya Piṭaka* is the *Vinaya*; thus, in this way as well, the three *Piṭakas* are comprised.
They have not yet been exhausted. For there exists the word of the Buddha known as "not included in the Suttas" (Asutta-nāmaka), namely:
the Jātaka, the Paṭisambhidā, the Niddesa, the Suttanipāta, the Dhammapada, the Udāna, the Itivuttaka, the Vimānavatthu, the Petavatthu, the Theragāthā, the Therīgāthā, and the Apadāna.
But the Elder Sudinna, maintaining that "there is no word of the Buddha that is not included in the Suttas," refuted all [of the opponent's arguments] and said:
"The three Piṭakas are the Sutta; however, the Vinaya is the *kāraṇa* (the underlying reason). Then, demonstrating that reason, he cited this Sutta:
"Those qualities, Gotamī, which you might know to lead to passion and not to dispassion..."
They lead to bondage, not to liberation; they lead to accumulation, not to diminution; they lead to great desire, not to fewness of wishes;
they lead to lack of contentment, not to contentment; they lead to social entanglement, not to seclusion;
they lead to laziness, not to the arousal of energy; they lead to being difficult to support.
They do not lead to being easy to support. You should categorically hold, Gotamī, that: "This is not the Dhamma; this is not the Vinaya;

this is not the Teacher’s instruction. But those teachings you should know, Gotamī, which lead to dispassion and not to passion, which lead to detachment and not to bondage, and which lead to diminution—
They do not lead to accumulation, but to fewness of wishes, not to great desire;
they lead to contentment, not to discontent; they lead to seclusion, not to socializing; they lead to the arousal of energy, not to indolence;
they lead to being easy to support, not to being difficult to support. You may hold this with absolute certainty, Gotamī.
—‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction.

Therefore, they should be verified within the word of the Buddha contained in the Three Piṭakas as Sutta; they should be reconciled within the Vinaya as that which effects the subduing of passion and so forth.
This is the meaning here. ‘They do not descend into the Sutta’ means that they do not appear anywhere in the sequence of the Sutta.

The meaning is that they are recognized as having come from one of the *Guḷha-Vessantara*, *Guḷha-Ummagga*, *Guḷha-Vinaya*, or *Vedalla-Piṭaka* after removing the outer covering without having arrived [at them directly].
For those things which have come down in this way, if they are not recognized as being for the discipline of passion and so forth, they are not to be discarded.
Therefore it was said: "Thus, monks, you should discard this. By this method...
The meaning is to be understood in every respect.
"Monks, you should uphold this as the fourth great authority"—this means you should uphold this as the fourth basis for the establishment of the Dhamma.
However, on this point, this supplementary matter should be understood: the four great authorities are found in the *Sutta* and the *Khandhaka*.
The four great authorities, the four ways of answering questions, the discourses, what is in conformity with the discourses, the teachers’ tradition, one’s own reflection, and the three councils.

In this regard, when a dispute arises concerning the Dhamma and the Vinaya as to whether "this is the Dhamma" or "this is the Vinaya," these four great authorities are the standard. Whatever therein accords [with them] should be accepted; the other should not be accepted, even if it is proclaimed with loud cries.
When a decision regarding what is allowable and what is not allowable has arisen—namely, "This is allowable;

this is not allowable"—the four great authorities (mahāpadesa) stated in the Khandhaka according to the method beginning with, "Monks, whatever has not been prohibited by me as 'this is not allowable,' if it conforms to what is not allowable and contradicts what is allowable, that is not allowable for you," are the standard. Of these:
The discussion on legal determination (*vinicchaya*) is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*. Therein, according to the method explained, one should reach a definitive conclusion as follows:
"Whatever conforms to what is allowable (*kappiya*) is itself allowable; the other is unallowable (*akappiya*).
[This concerns] a question to be answered categorically, a question to be answered analytically, and a question to be answered with a counter-question.
“The question is to be set aside”—these are called the four ways of answering questions. Among these, when asked, “Is the eye impermanent?
one must answer with absolute certainty: “Yes, it is impermanent. This same method applies to the ear and the other sense organs. This is the question to be answered categorically.
When asked, “Is that which is called ‘impermanent’ the eye alone? one should say: “It is not the eye alone; the ear is also impermanent, the nose is also...”
It should be answered by analyzing it as follows: "Is it impermanent? This is a question to be answered by analysis (*vibhajjabyākaraṇīyo pañho*).
When asked, "Is the ear as it is the eye, and the eye as it is the ear?", one should counter-question, "In what sense do you ask?
If he says, "I ask in the sense of seeing," one should answer, "No. But if he says, "I ask in the sense of being impermanent," [one should answer, "Yes"].
When this is said, it should be answered "Yes. This is a question to be answered by way of counter-question. However, when asked such things as "Is that soul the same as the body?
one should set it aside, saying, "This was left undeclared by the Blessed One. This question is not to be answered. This is a question to be set aside.
Thus, when a question arrives in such a manner, these four ways of answering questions are the standard.
By means of these [categories], that question should be answered.

Regarding the *sutta* and so forth: "Sutta" refers to the three Piṭakas contained within the three Councils (*saṅgīti*). "Suttānuloma" refers to what is concordant with the Suttas and what is appropriate.
"Ācariyavāda" refers to the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). "Attanomati" refers to an understanding attained through the grasping of the underlying method (*nayaggāha*).
One's own inspired thought (*paṭibhāna*). In this regard, a Sutta is not to be contradicted; one who contradicts it contradicts the Buddha himself.

However, a practice that is in conformity (*anuloma*) must be accepted only if it accords with the Sutta, and not otherwise. The teaching of the teachers (*ācariyavāda*) is also to be accepted only if it accords with the Sutta, and not otherwise.
One's own opinion (*attanomati*), however, is the weakest of all; even that [must be accepted] only if it accords with the Sutta.
Only those [texts] that are consistent with the [authentic tradition] should be accepted, not others.

As for these three councils—the one of five hundred, the one of seven hundred, and the one of a thousand—it is only the discourses (sutta) recorded therein that are authoritative; other texts, being censurable discourses, should not be accepted.
For even if certain words and phrases seem to fit there, they should be understood as neither descending into the Sutta nor appearing in the Vinaya.
Commentary on the Discourse Concerning Cunda the Smith’s Son (Kammāraputtacundavatthu). 189.

"Of the smith’s son" means of the son of a goldsmith. It is said that he was a wealthy man with a large household who, upon his very first sight of the Blessed One, became a stream-enterer; having built a monastery in his own mango grove, he offered it to the Buddha. Regarding that...
It was said with intentional meaning: "in the mango grove.
"Sūkaramaddava" refers to the flesh from the body of a single, prime-aged boar, neither too young nor too old.
It is said that this meat is both tender and succulent; the meaning is that he had it prepared and well-cooked. Some [say]...

They say: "But 'sūkaramaddava' is a name for a method of cooking soft rice with the broth of the five products of the cow, just as 'cow-drinking' (*gavapāna*) is a name for a type of cooking. Some say: "'Sūkaramaddava' is a method of elixir (*rasāyana*);
it appears in the science of elixirs, and Cunda [prepared it] thinking, 'May there not be a final passing away (*parinibbāna*) of the Blessed One.'"
"The elixir has been prepared. Now, as for that, the deities added vital essence (*ojā*) from the four great continents surrounded by two thousand islands.
For what purpose does he utter this "Lion's Roar" (*sīhanāda*)? It is for the sake of clearing away the reproaches of others.

For those who might say, "He did not give the leftovers from his own consumption to either the monks or to human beings, but had them buried in a pit and thus wasted them"—it is to refute such claims.
Having heard this, thinking, "There will be no opportunity for [further] speech," he roars the lion’s roar in order to release others from blame. 190.
Regarding the phrase "after eating the *sūkaramaddava*": it arose after he had eaten, but not on account of the eating itself.
For if it had arisen in one who had not eaten, it would have been excessively severe; however, because he had eaten such succulent food, [it was otherwise].
His bodily pain was slight; for that reason, he was able to go on foot. "While purging" means while his blood was frequently flowing out in discharge.

"He said" refers to what he spoke thus for the sake of attaining final nibbāna at the place of his own choosing. Furthermore, it should be understood that these are verses established by the Elders who compiled the Dhamma.
The Commentary on Fetching Water (Pānīyāharaṇavaṇṇanā) 191.

*Iṅgha* is an indeclinable used in the sense of an exhortation. *Acchodakā* means having clear water. *Sātodakā* means having sweet water. *Sītodakā* means having cool water. *Setakā* means free from mud. *Suppatitthā* means having beautiful landing places.
The Commentary on the Story of Pukkusa the Malla’s Son.
192. His name was Pukkusa; he was the son of a Malla king. It is said that the Mallas ruled by turns;
as long as their turn did not arrive, they engaged in trade.
This man, also engaging in trade, had five hundred carts yoked and traveled with the wind blowing from behind and the wind blowing against him from the front.
Having sent the caravan leader ahead, he himself followed behind. At that time, however, the wind was blowing from behind;
therefore, having sent the caravan leader ahead and seated himself in a vehicle adorned with all kinds of jewels, he departed from Kusinārā and set out on the road, thinking, "I shall go to Pāvā.
Thus it is said: "He was traveling along the highway from Kusinārā to Pāvā."
Āḷāra was his name. It is said that he had long, reddish-brown eyes, and for that reason his name became Āḷāra.
Kālāma was his clan. "Yatra hi nāma" means "he who indeed. "Neva dakkhati" means "he did not see.
Because it is joined with the word *yatra*, this is stated in reference to the future. For such is the grammatical characteristic (*saddalakkhaṇa*) in these types of passages.
193. “Niccharantīsu” means while they are moving about. “Asaniyā phalantiyā” means while the thunderbolt is crashing with a great roar, as if it were splitting;

for there are nine kinds of thunderbolts: the unconscious (*asaññā*), the cross-eyed (*vicakkā*), the shimmering (*saterā*), the gurgling (*gaggarā*), the monkey-head (*kapisīsā*), the fish-wriggler (*macchavilolikā*), the cock (*kukkuṭakā*), the staff-jewel (*daṇḍamaṇikā*), and the dry-thunderbolt (*sukkhasanī*). Among these, the “unconscious” one is unconscious...
It performs various actions. *Vicakkā* flies making a single wheeling circle. *Saterā* falls fluttering like a bird.
*Gaggarā* falls with a gurgling sound. *Kapisīsā* acts like a monkey tossing up its eyebrows.
*Macchavilolikā* acts like a darting fish. *Kukkuṭakā* falls fluttering like a cock. *Daṇḍamaṇikā* acts like a plough.
It falls. *Sukkhāsanī* means it clears away the place where it has fallen.
*Deve vassante* means while it is raining, having thundered with a dry peal [of lightning] at intervals. *Ātumāyaṃ* means I dwell depending on Ātumā.
*Bhusāgāre* means in a threshing-floor shed. *Ettheso* means for this reason this great multitude of people has assembled.
"Where were you? means "In what place were you? "That you, venerable sir" means "You yourself, venerable sir.

(194) "Golden-colored" means having the color of refined gold (*siṅgī-suvaṇṇa*). "A pair of polished [robes]" means a pair of smooth cloths; the meaning is a pair of fine cotton garments (*saṇha-sāṭaka*).
"To be worn" means that it should be worn by me from time to time; the meaning is that it should be put on. It is said that...
Thus, having worn it on such a festive day, he would set it aside for the rest of the time.
This was said with reference to that most excellent pair of auspicious garments. "Out of compassion" means out of regard for me.
"Clothe [me]" is a formal expression; the meaning is: "Give one to me and one to Ānanda. But did the Elder take them? Yes, he took them.

Why? Because his duty had reached its culmination. For although he had rejected such gains as these and entered upon the role of an attendant, that duty of his as an attendant had reached its peak; therefore, he accepted them.
And those who might say: "I suppose Ānanda was unsuccessful, for having attended him for twenty-five years, he has gained nothing"—[this would be their view].
“...was previously obtained by him from the presence of the Blessed One. He accepted [the offering] even for the sake of cutting off their opportunity for speech.
Moreover, the Blessed One knew: “Even though Ānanda accepts it, he will not keep it for himself; he will offer it to me alone.
But when the son of the Mallas honors Ānanda, the Saṅgha as well will have been honored; thus, for him—”
“He shall become a great mass of merit,” [the donor thought], and he gave one [robe] to the Elder. The Elder, for that very reason, accepted it.
“With a discourse on the Dhamma” means with a discourse of thanksgiving regarding the robes.
“Offered to the Blessed One’s body” means made to adhere to him by way of being worn as an inner and outer robe. The Blessed One, from that—
He wore one [robe] and draped the other over his shoulders.
"Like a spent ember" means that just as a spent ember glows only from within and has no radiance on the outside, so too it appears with its radiance concealed externally; this is the meaning.
"In these two times, Ānanda"—why is it so only in these two times? It is because of the specific nature of the nutriment.
And with powerful joy. For on these two occasions, the deities throughout the entire *cakkavāḷa* infuse the food with nutritive essence (*ojā*).
That refined food, having entered the stomach, produces a state of clarity.

Because of the clarity of the matter produced by nutriment, the six faculties, with the mind as the sixth, shine forth exceedingly. And on the day of his full enlightenment—“that which had been accumulated over many hundreds of thousands of millions of eons...”
As he reflects, "Today my mass of defilements has been abandoned," powerful joy arises;
his mind becomes serene. When the mind is serene, the blood becomes serene; when the blood is serene, the six faculties, with the mind as the sixth, shine forth exceedingly.
On the day of his parinibbāna as well, [he thought]: "Today, indeed, I have—by means of many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas—"
As he reflects, "I shall enter the city called the Great Nibbāna of the Deathless," powerful joy arises;
his mind becomes serene; when the mind is serene, the blood becomes serene;
when the blood is serene, the six faculties, with the mind as the sixth, shine forth exceedingly. Thus, by means of this specific nutriment and that powerful joy, in these two—
It should be understood that "it was thus at those times. "In the vicinity" means in the Sāla grove where [the road] turns from the east.
"Between the twin Sāla trees" means in the middle of the twin Sāla trees.
The verse beginning with "Golden-hued" was placed [there] at the time of the communal recitation (saṅgīti).

196. Regarding the phrase "having bathed and drunk": it is said that at that time, while the Blessed One was bathing in the river, the fish and turtles within the river, as well as the groves on both banks, all became golden in color.
"The mango grove" refers to a mango grove on the bank of that very same river. "To the venerable Cundaka": it is said that at that moment, the Elder Ānanda [was wearing] a water-cloth...
Pressing on, he followed; the Elder Cunda was nearby. The Blessed One addressed him.
The verses beginning with "Having gone to the Kakudha river" were established at the very time of the Council (saṅgīti).
Therein, "the Dhamma that has proceeded here" means the Dhamma that has proceeded here in the Dispensation (sāsana) of the Blessed One—the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dhamma (dhammakkhandha).
The meaning is "proceeding. "He sat down in front" means he sat down right before the Teacher. At this point, the Elder had arrived.
Then, to the Venerable Ānanda who had thus arrived, the Blessed One addressed him: 197.
"Lost gains" means those gains which consist of the benefits of giving for others; these are "lost. "Ill-gotten" means...
Even human birth, though obtained through a distinction of merit, is a difficult attainment. "Of whom you" means "of you.
Who knows whether it was with husks or too overcooked? Having consumed whatever kind of final alms-food it may have been, the Tathāgata attained Parinibbāna;
surely, what was given to him must have been either this or that. "Gains" refers to the benefits of giving, both pertaining to the present life and to future lives.
"It is a gain! It is well-gained for you that you have attained this human state. "They bear equal fruit" means they are identical in fruit in every respect.
But surely, when the Tathāgata ate the alms-food given by Sujātā and attained full enlightenment, he consumed it at a time when he still possessed lust, hatred, and delusion;
whereas this food given by Cunda was consumed at a time when he was free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion. Why is this so?
Are these equal in their fruit? They are equal by way of the equality of final Nibbāna, the equality of meditative attainment, and the equality of recollection.
For the Blessed One, having consumed the alms-food given by Sujātā, attained final Nibbāna through the element of Nibbāna with residue remaining;
and having consumed what was given by Cunda, he attained final Nibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without residue remaining.

Thus, they are equal in fruit even through the equality of their final *parinibbāna*. On the day of his full awakening (*abhisambodhi*), he entered twenty-four hundred thousand million meditative attainments (*samāpatti*);
on the day of his *parinibbāna*, he likewise entered all of them—thus, they are equal in fruit even through the equality of their meditative attainments.
And later, Sujātā heard: "This is not, it seems, a tree deity; this is surely a Bodhisatta."
“Having consumed that alms-food, it is said, he awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment; for seven days and seven nights, it is said, his sustenance was provided by that.
Upon hearing this, as she recollected, “What a gain for me!”, a powerful surge of joy and gladness arose within her.
And later, for Cunda as well, [the thought occurred]: “It is said, this was my final alms-food.”

Having heard, "He has been given; indeed, the head of the Dhamma was taken by me; having consumed my alms-food, the Teacher has attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue," a powerful joy arose in him as he recollected, "What a gain it is for me!
Thus, it should be understood that they have equal results even through the equality of such recollection.
"Leading to fame" means leading to a retinue. "Leading to lordship" means leading to the state of being the eldest or preeminent.
"From self-restraint" means for one who restrains himself by means of the restraint of virtue (*sīla*); the meaning is: for one established in self-control (*saṃvara*).
"Enmity does not accumulate" means that the fivefold enmity does not increase. "And the skillful man abandons evil" means that the skillful person, endowed with wisdom...
By means of the Noble Path, he abandons evil, wretched, and unwholesome states without remainder.

"Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished" means that having abandoned this evil, he is extinguished by the extinction of defilements (kilesanibbāna) through the destruction of lust and the other [afflictions].
Thus, perceiving both Cunda’s merit and his own perfection as one worthy of offerings (dakkhiṇeyya), he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna).
The commentary on the fourth recitation section is finished.
Commentary on the Twin Sāla Trees (198):
Regarding the phrase "together with a great community of bhikkhus," there is no limit to the number of bhikkhus here. At the village of Veḷuva...

Indeed, from the time of the suppression of his pain onwards, when it was heard that "the Blessed One will soon attain final Nibbāna," not even a single bhikkhu among those who had come from here and there departed; therefore, the Saṅgha became beyond counting.
Regarding the phrase "Upavattana, the Mallans’ Sal Grove": just as [from the river Kalamba] by way of the gate of the Royal Mother’s Monastery...
One must go to the Thūpārāma; likewise, from the western bank of the Hiraññavatī River, there is the Sālavana Garden.
Just as the Thūpārāma is situated relative to Anurādhapura, so is that [garden] situated relative to Kusinārā.
Just as the road entering the city through the southern gate from the Thūpārāma goes facing east and then turns northward, so it is from the garden to the Sālavana.
Having gone facing east, it turned back toward the north; therefore, it is called "Upavattana" (the Turning Back).
Between the twin *sāla* trees, at the northern head, there was indeed one row of *sāla* trees at the head-end of that couch and one at the foot-end.
There too, one young *sāla* tree stood near the head-end and one near the foot-end.
Furthermore, it is said that the twin *sāla* trees were so called because they stood with their roots, trunks, branches, and leaves intertwined with one another.
"Prepare a couch," he said, referring to the royal couch that was kept in that park;
having had that very one prepared, the Elder gave it to him.
“I am weary, Ānanda, I shall lie down,” said the Tathāgata.
For to the Tathāgata there were these [elephants]: Gocari, Kaḷāpa, Gaṅgeyya, Piṅgala, Pabbateyyaka, Hemavata, Tambo, Mandākinī, and Uposatha.
"And Chaddanta as the tenth—these are the supreme among elephants.
Herein, the strength of ten ordinary elephants, which is reckoned as their range of action (*gocara*), is the strength of one *kaḷāpa*.
Thus, by a calculation increasing tenfold, the strength of ordinary elephants amounts to a measure of a thousand million (*koṭisahassa*). That—
From the moment he had consumed all of Cunda’s alms-food, his strength was completely exhausted, like water poured into a leaking jar.
Kusinārā is three *gāvutas* from the city of Pāvā;
even as he traveled with great effort, sitting down at twenty-five places along the way, by the time the sun set, he reached there.
At the time of twilight, the Blessed One entered the Sāla grove. Thus, disease comes along, crushing all health.
As if to demonstrate this matter, speaking words that inspire a sense of spiritual urgency in the entire world, he said:
"I am weary, Ānanda; I shall lie down."
But why did the Blessed One come here with such great effort; was it not possible for him to attain final nibbāna elsewhere?
It is not that it is impossible to attain final nibbāna anywhere; however, he came here for three reasons.
For the Blessed One saw it thus: "If I were to attain final nibbāna elsewhere, the occasion for the discourse on Mahāsudassana would not arise."

"But when I am attaining final nibbāna at Kusinārā, I shall teach— adorned with two recitations— that prosperity which I was to experience in the world of the devas but instead experienced right here in the human world; having heard that,
many people will think that they too should perform wholesome deeds."
Furthermore, he saw this: "If I were to attain final Nibbāna elsewhere, Subhadda would not see me;
he is one who can be guided by a Buddha, not by a disciple, and the disciples would not be able to train him.
But if I attain final Nibbāna at Kusinārā, he will approach me and ask a question, and at the conclusion of the answer to his question, having established himself in the refuges—"

“Having received the going-forth and the full ordination in my presence, and having taken up a meditation subject, he will attain arahantship while I am still living and will become my final disciple.
Furthermore, he sees: “If I were to attain final nibbāna elsewhere, there would be a great quarrel over the distribution of my relics.”
"It appears as red as a river. When the Blessed One has attained final nibbāna at Kusinārā, the brahmin Doṇa will settle that dispute and distribute the relics.
For these three reasons, it should be understood that the Blessed One came here with such great effort.
Regarding "the lion’s posture": there are four postures—the posture of those who indulge in sensual pleasures, the posture of hungry ghosts, the lion’s posture, and the Tathāgata’s posture.

In this context: “Monks, for the most part, beings who enjoy sensual pleasures lie on their left side”—this is the reclining posture of those who enjoy sensual pleasures. For among them, there are generally none who lie on their right side.

“Monks, for the most part, hungry ghosts lie on their backs”—this is the reclining posture of hungry ghosts. Because they have little flesh and blood, hungry ghosts are composed of a tangled mass of bones; they are unable to lie on one side and thus lie only on their backs.
“Monks, Sīha, the king of beasts, makes his bed on his right side... [and so on] ...he becomes joyful.”
This is the lion’s posture. For the lion, king of beasts, being pre-eminent in vigor, places his two forefeet in one place and his hind feet in another;

having tucked his tail between his thighs and observed the positions where his forefeet, hind feet, and tail rest, he places his head upon the tops of his two forefeet and lies down. During the day...
Even when waking from sleep, he does not wake up startled; rather, lifting his head, he observes the place where his front feet and so forth were positioned.

If anything has been displaced from its position, he becomes dissatisfied, thinking, "This is not worthy of your birth or your courageous nature," and remains lying right there instead of going out for alms.
He departs. But when [the prey] remains without having been abandoned, he— delighted and joyful, thinking, "This is worthy of your birth and your courageous nature"—
rises up, stretches with the stretch of a lion, shakes his mane, roars the lion’s roar three times, and departs for his range.

“Furthermore, the posture of the fourth jhāna is called the reclining posture of the Tathāgata. Among those, it is the lion’s posture that is mentioned here. For this is indeed called the supreme posture because it is a bodily posture characterized by intense fiery energy (*tejo*).

“Placing foot upon foot” means placing the left foot upon the right foot. “Having placed it down” (*accādhāya*) means having placed it down excessively—that is, having set it down slightly beyond [the other].
For if the ankle were to touch the ankle, or the knee the knee, pain would arise repeatedly.
The mind is not one-pointed, and the bed becomes uncomfortable. However, by placing [the limbs] so that they do not touch one another, no painful sensation arises;
the mind becomes one-pointed, and the bed becomes comfortable. Therefore, he lay down in this manner.
But because he had already entered upon the posture for lying down, the phrase "having attended to the perception of rising" is not mentioned here.

In this context, non-exertion should be understood as being due to physical exhaustion; however, because of his sleepiness, there was no opportunity for the Blessed One’s life-continuum (bhavaṅga) during that night.

For in the first watch he gave a Dhamma teaching to the Mallas, in the middle watch he [conversed with] Subhadda, in the last watch he exhorted the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and at the break of dawn he attained final Nibbāna.
"Sabbaphāliphullā" means they were all in full bloom on every side; from the roots up to the tips, they were covered in blossoms.
And it was not only the twin *sāla* trees that were so; indeed, all the trees were in full bloom.
Not only in that very park, but throughout the entire ten-thousandfold world-system (*dasasahassacakkavāḷa*), the flowering trees put forth their flowers.
They took [the fruits]; those trees bearing fruit took their fruit. On the trunks of all the trees, trunk-lotuses blossomed;
on the branches, branch-lotuses; on the creepers, creeper-lotuses; and in the sky, sky-lotuses blossomed. Lotus-stalks burst forth from the surface of the earth.
The entire great ocean became covered with five-colored lotuses, extending for three thousand yojanas.
The Himalayas became exceedingly beautiful, like a mass of peacock feathers bound together in a dense cluster, like a continuous garland of *gavacchika* flowers,
like a floral head-ornament (*pupphavaṭaṃsaka*) firmly pressed and tied, and like a flower-basket filled to the brim.
As they were scattering [flowers] over the body of the Tathāgata, those twin *sāla* trees had their trunks, branches, and boughs shaken by the earth-deities.
They scatter over the body of the Tathāgata; the meaning is that they strew flowers upon the body. "They overspread" (ajjhokiranti) means they scatter as if covering it completely.
"They scatter abundantly" (abhippakiranti) means they scatter repeatedly and again and again.
"Divine" (dibbāni) means those produced from the Nanda lotus-pool in the world of the gods; they are golden-colored and have petals the size of a ceremonial parasol.

They gather dust the size of a large gourd. Not only Mandārava flowers, but other divine blossoms as well—such as those from the Pāricchattaka and Koviḷāra trees—are filled into golden caskets by deities stationed at the rim of the world-system, in the City of the Thirty-three, and in the Brahma-world; these then fall from the sky. [This occurs] for the Tathāgata.
The bodies, coming from within without being scattered, showered the Tathāgata’s very body with lotus-pollen and saffron powder.
"Divine sandalwood powders" refers to the sandalwood powders suitable for the deities.
And these were not only those suitable for the deities, but also those suitable for the nāgas, supaṇṇas, and humans. Furthermore, it was not only sandalwood powders that were used.
Powders of all kinds of divine fragrances, such as black aloe-wood and red sandalwood;

and powders of yellow orpiment, collyrium, gold, and silver—all these various preparations of divine perfumes—were brought by deities stationed at the rim of the world-system and other locations, who filled them in golden and silver caskets.
Without scattering anything along the way, they showered them directly upon the body of the Tathāgata alone.
"Even divine musical instruments" refers to the instruments used by the deities. It should be understood that not only those,
but all the musical instruments of the gods, nāgas, supaṇṇas, and humans throughout the ten thousand world-systems— classified as stringed, covered with leather, solid, and hollow—
gather together in a single world-system and resound in the sky.
"Even celestial songs were sung. It is said that these deities known as Varuṇa and Vāraṇa are long-lived gods;

having heard, "The Great Man, being born on the human path, will become a Buddha," they began stringing garlands, thinking, "We shall take him away on the day he takes rebirth. While they were still stringing them, [they heard: "The Great Man has entered his mother’s womb..."
Having heard, "He has been born," they were asked, "Whose [child] are you weaving? and they replied, "It is not yet finished; we shall take it on the day he emerges from the womb.
Again, having heard, "He has emerged," they said, "We shall go on the day of the Great Renunciation.
After living at home for twenty-nine years, [they thought], "Today he has gone forth on the Great Renunciation."

Having heard, "He will go on the day of his full enlightenment," [they set out]. Having practiced austerities for six years, and having heard, "Today he has attained full enlightenment," they thought, "We shall go on the day of the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma.
And having heard, "After spending seven weeks at the Seat of Enlightenment, he went to Isipatana and turned the Wheel of Dhamma," they thought, "We shall go on the day of the Twin Miracle."
Hearing, "Today the Twin Miracle will be performed," they thought, "We shall go on the day of the Descent from Heaven.

Hearing, "Today the Descent from Heaven will take place," they thought, "We shall go when the life-faculty is relinquished. Hearing, "Today the life-faculty has been relinquished," they thought, "It is not yet finished;
we shall go on the day of the Parinibbāna. Hearing, "Today, between the twin *sāla* trees, the Blessed One..."
Having heard, "With mindfulness and clear comprehension, he has assumed the lion’s posture on his right side; at the time of the powerful dawn, he will attain final Nibbāna.
To whom, then, should you offer gifts? they thought: "What is this? On this very day he took rebirth in a mother’s womb;
on this very day he emerged from his mother’s womb; on this very day he made the Great Renunciation; on this very day he became a Buddha..."
‘Today he was born; today he set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion; today he performed the Twin Miracle; today he descended from the world of the gods;
today he relinquished the life-force; and today, it is said, he will attain final Nibbāna.
Surely he ought to have remained for at least the duration of a meal of rice-gruel on the second day—for one who has attained Buddhahood after fulfilling the ten perfections!
Thinking, “This is improper,” they arrived while still carrying their unfinished garlands; finding no space within the Cakkavāḷa,
they hung from the rim of the Cakkavāḷa and, running along that very rim, grasped one another by hand and by neck,
and [recited] the thirty-two marks of a Great Man with reference to the Three Jewels.

Having sung songs concerning the six-colored rays, the ten perfections, the five hundred and fifty Jātaka tales, and the fourteen Buddha-knowledges, they cry out at the conclusion of each, “Of great fame!
Of great fame! It is with reference to this that it was said:
“Even divine songs resound in the sky as an offering to the Tathāgata.”

199. But the Blessed One, while lying on his right side between the twin sāla trees, saw the great enthusiasm of the assembly gathered from the surface of the earth up to the rim of the world-system, and from the rim of the world-system up to the Brahma-world;
having seen this, he informed the Venerable Ānanda. Thus it was said: "Then..."

The Blessed One [addressed] the Venerable Ānanda... [as before] ... "for the worship of the Tathāgata. Having thus displayed such great honor, he said, "Not by this alone, Ānanda," and so forth, showing that even by that he had not been truly honored.
This is what is meant: "Ānanda, when I was lying at the feet of Dīpaṅkara, having brought together eight qualities..."
"When I made my resolution (abhinīhāra), it was not made for the sake of garlands, perfumes, music, or song;
nor were the perfections (pāramiyo) fulfilled for this purpose. Therefore, I am not truly honored by this offering.
But why did the Blessed One, elsewhere, accept even a single *umā* flower when it had been offered after reflecting upon the qualities of a Buddha?
Having praised the fruit of worship as being even beyond the scope of a Buddha’s knowledge, why does he here refuse such a great offering?
It is for the sake of favoring the assembly and out of a desire for the long endurance of the Dispensation.

For if the Blessed One had not refused it in this way, in the future, when the time for virtue comes, they would not fulfill their virtue; and when the time for concentration comes, they would not fulfill their concentration.
They will not bring them to fulfillment; they will not cause the embryo of insight (vipassanā-gabbha) to take root in the place where insight should arise.

Having encouraged their attendants, they will dwell performing only material offerings. Indeed, this kind of material offering is incapable of sustaining the Dispensation for even a single day or the duration of a single meal of rice-gruel. For even a thousand monasteries like the Mahāvihāra—
