Even a thousand cetiyas equal to the Mahācetiya are not able to sustain the Dispensation; rather, it belongs only to him by whom the appropriate deed has been performed.
Right practice, however, is the worship befitting the Tathāgata.
For that was indeed what he aspired to, and it is capable of sustaining the Dispensation; therefore, pointing this out, he said, "Ānanda, whoever... and so forth.
In this context, "one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma" means one who has entered upon the preliminary practice that is the "conformity" (*anudhamma*) to the ninefold supramundane Dhamma.
Furthermore, because that very practice is appropriate, it is called "proper conduct" (*sāmīcī*). One who has entered upon that proper conduct is "one who practices properly" (*sāmīcippaṭipanna*).
One who lives out and fulfills that very conformity—which is termed the preliminary practice—is "one who lives in accordance with the Dhamma" (*anudhammacārī*).

The "practice of the prior stage" (pubbabhāgapaṭipadā) should be understood as the right practice extending from virtue, the rules of conduct, and the undertaking of ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), up to the stage of the lineage (gotrabhū).

Therefore, a bhikkhu who, being established in the six things not to be despised, transgresses the prescribed rules and maintains his life through improper search (an-esanā) is not one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma. But he who [observes] all that has been prescribed for himself...

One who does not transgress even in the slightest the training rule—the Victor’s boundary, the Victor’s limit, the Victor’s black thread—is said to be "one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma.

The same principle applies to a bhikkhunī. As for a lay follower (upāsaka) who, having undertaken the five enmities and the ten courses of unwholesome action, persists in them and applies himself to them, he is not one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma.
But he who fulfills the three refuges, the five precepts, and the ten precepts;
who observes the eight Uposatha days of the month; who gives gifts; who performs worship with perfumes and flowers; who attends upon his mother and father;
and who attends upon righteous recluses and brahmins—this person is called one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma.
The same method applies to a female lay follower as well.
"With supreme worship" means with the highest form of worship. For this is called non-material worship; it is capable of sustaining my dispensation.
Indeed, as long as these four assemblies worship me with this [worship], so long will my dispensation endure in the midst [of the world].
It shows that he will shine like the full moon in the sky.
[Commentary on the Elder Upavāṇa, 200.
"He drew back" means he removed it. "Go away" means depart. With that single word, the elder set down his palm-leaf fan.
He stood to one side. The passage beginning with “attendant” (*upaṭṭhāka*) is said with reference to his status as an unappointed attendant during the First Enlightenment.
When the Elder had spoken thus, “Venerable sir, this is the venerable Upavāṇa,” Ānanda perceived that Upavāṇa possessed a state of defilement.
Thinking, “I shall now explain his faultless nature,” the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with “Ānanda, for the most part.”
In this context, the phrase "for the most part" is stated with reference to the state of being excluded for both the non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*) and the formless deities (*arūpadevatā*).

"Unfilled" (*apphuṭo*) means untouched or unoccupied. It is said that in a space only the size of a hair-tip near the Blessed One, ten highly influential deities each stood, having manifested subtle bodies. Beyond them...
Twenty each. Beyond them, thirty each. Beyond them, forty each. Beyond them, fifty each.
Beyond them, sixty deities stood, sixty in each group.
They did not obstruct one another with hand, foot, or cloth; there was no need for them to say, "Move aside for me! Do not touch me!"
There was no [obstruction]. Those deities, having become ten, twenty, thirty, forty, or even fifty, stood within the space of a needle’s point without obstructing one another;
they were exactly as described. "Ovārento" means "blocking. It is said that the Elder was naturally large of body, resembling a young elephant.
Thus, having put on the rag-robe (*paṃsukūlacīvara*), it appeared as if it were too large.
"To see the Tathāgata"—thus they complained, being unable even to see the Blessed One’s face.
But were they not able to see the Elder by looking through him? Yes, they were not able; for devas [cannot see] an ordinary person (*puthujjana*).

They were able to see through [the wall], but not those whose taints were destroyed (khīṇāsava). Furthermore, because of the Elder’s great authority and the excellence of his fiery power (tejos), they were not even able to approach him.
But why was it that only this Elder possessed such fiery power, and not other Arahants?
It was because he had been the guardian deity of the stupa of Buddha Kassapa.

It is said that when the Perfectly Enlightened One Vipassi had attained Parinibbāna, they constructed a single stupa for his relic-body, which resembled a solid mass of pure gold; for the Buddhas of long lifespan have but one stupa.
People performed the function of clay there with golden bricks—one span in length, a cubit in width, and two finger-breadths in thickness—and with yellow orpiment and red arsenic.
Having accomplished the purpose of water with sesame oil, they raised [the mound] to the extent of one *yojana*.

Then the earth-dwelling deities raised it to the extent of one *yojana*, then the space-dwelling deities, then the heat-cloud deities, then the rain-cloud deities, then the deities of the Four Great Kings, and then the Tāvatiṃsa deities raised it to the extent of one *yojana*; thus the shrine became seven *yojanas* high.
It happened thus: when people arrived carrying garlands, perfumes, garments, and other offerings, the guardian deity took them and worshipped the cetiya even as they were looking on.
At that time, this elder, having been a wealthy brahmin, had gone there taking a single yellow garment. The deity [took that from him].
Taking the cloth from his hand, he made an offering at the cetiya. Seeing this, the brahmin, with a mind full of faith, made an aspiration:
"In the future, may I also become a protective deity at the cetiya of such a Buddha.
When he passed away from there, he was reborn in the world of the gods. As he was wandering through the realms of gods and humans, the Blessed One Kassapa appeared.
Having arisen in the world, he attained final Nibbāna. He too had only a single relic-body. Taking that, they constructed a *cetiya* one league in extent.
Having become a protective deity there, when the Dispensation had disappeared, he was reborn in the heavenly realm;
passing away from there during the time of our Blessed One, he took rebirth in a great family, went forth, and became a monk.
He attained arahantship. Thus, because he came as a protective deity for the cetiya, the Elder should be understood as one who is preeminent in spiritual power (*tejussada*).
"The deities, Ānanda, are complaining" means: "Ānanda, the deities are complaining; it shows that there is no fault whatsoever in my son.
Why did he ask, "But of what nature [are they], venerable sir"? Because the Blessed One said to you, "The deities are complaining."
"Speak," [the Blessed One said]. "But in what state do you attend to them? Do you endure their final nibbāna?
Thus he asks. Then the Blessed One, saying, "I do not speak of a cause for enduring," spoke the words beginning with "Peaceful is Nanda...
to show that they do not endure it.
In that context, "perceiving earth in space" means having fashioned earth in space and perceiving it as earth there.
"Wailing" means crying out. "Falling headlong" means falling from here or there as if cut in the middle.
"Whirling" means whirling about and returning to the very place where they fell. "Revolving" means [from the place where they fell]...

They go moving on their sides. Moreover, even when they stretch out two feet and turn around once toward the front, once toward the back, once to the left, and once to the right, they are said to be "turning over" (*āvaṭṭanti*) and "rolling over" (*vivaṭṭanti*).
"Ānanda, there are deities who perceive earth upon the earth"—it is said that these natural-earth deities are unable to support [the weight].
He was unable to do so. Therein, the deities sank down like the Brahmā Hatthaka. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Hatthaka, manifest a gross physical form. Thus, this was said with reference to those deities who fashioned earth upon the earth: "perceiving earth in the earth."

"Free from passion" means those who have abandoned mental distress; they are like stone pillars, non-returners whose taints are destroyed. Commentary on the Four Arousing Places (Catusaṃvejanīyaṭhānavaṇṇanā): 202. "Those who have completed the rains residence":
it is said that during the time of the Buddhas, monks would assemble at two specific times: when the rains residence was drawing to a close...

It was for the purpose of taking up a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) at the commencement of the rains retreat, and for those who had completed the rains, for the purpose of announcing the special attainments produced through their application to the meditation subjects they had taken up.

And just as it was during the time of the Buddha, so too on the island of Tambapaṇṇi, the monks from the west of the Gaṅgā assembled at the Lohapāsāda, while the monks from the east of the Gaṅgā assembled at the Tissa Mahāvihāra. Among them, those from the west of the Gaṅgā...
The monks, having taken refuse-rakes and brooms, returned and assembled in the Great Monastery.
Having performed the plastering work at the shrine, they established the custom: "Having completed the rains retreat, you must come and assemble in the Loha-pāsāda.
They dwelt in comfortable locations, and when the rains retreat was over, they returned to the Loha-pāsāda to the assembly circle of the five Nikāyas, for those...
Those for whom the *pāḷi* was familiar recited the *pāḷi*; those for whom the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) was familiar recited the commentary.
If anyone corrupted either the *pāḷi* or the commentary, they would investigate him, asking, "From whom did you receive this?
and having corrected it, they made him learn it again. Those living on the far side of the Gaṅgā did exactly the same at the Tissamahāvihāra. Thus, in both places...
When the monks have assembled at the proper times, those who had previously gone out after taking up a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) return in order to report their spiritual progress;
it is with reference to such individuals that he says, "Venerable sirs, those who have completed the rains retreat," and so forth.
*Manobhāvanīya* means "cultivated" or "honored by the mind. Alternatively, it refers to those who cultivate—that is, increase—their own minds [by removing] the stains of passion and the like.
"They carry away" means "they treat such [a person] as such. It is said that the Elder, being perfect in his duties, would not sit down stiffly upon seeing an elder monk;
rather, he would go out to meet him, take the umbrella, bowl, and robes from his hands, strike the seat to clear it, and offer it to him.
Then, having performed the duties for him while he was seated there, he would attend to the lodging and offer it back to him.
Seeing a newly ordained monk, he did not sit in silence, but stood nearby and performed the proper duties (*vatta*).
Desiring that his practice of these duties should never decline, he spoke thus.
Then the Blessed One thought: "Ānanda thinks, 'I shall not obtain the sight of those who are worthy of esteem (*manobhāvanīya*'); well now, [let me grant him this]."

Thinking, "I shall point out the place for seeing those monks who are to be cherished by the mind, where one dwelling [there] will obtain the sight of such monks without having to wander here and there," he said,

"These four kinds of persons," and so forth. In that context, "of the faithful" means of one whose mind is clear toward the Buddha and others, who is endowed with proper conduct, and from whom [the opportunity] begins at dawn.
All the observances (*vatta*), such as those pertaining to the courtyard of the shrine (*cetiyaṅgaṇa*), are seen to have been performed.

"Worthy of being seen" means they are fit to be seen and should be visited for the purpose of seeing them. "Arousing spiritual urgency" means they produce a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). "Places" (*ṭhāna*) means causes, or simply specific locations.
The phrase "whosoever" is stated for the purpose of showing that this pilgrimage to the shrines (*cetiyacārikā*) serves as a guide. In that regard, the pilgrimage to the shrines...
Regarding those who "wander about"— that is, those who wander about there and there sweeping the grounds of the cetiya, washing the seats, or sprinkling water at the Bodhi tree—

it need not even be said of them that they will, having set out with a devout mind thinking, "We shall worship the cetiya," die along the way and nevertheless be established in heaven without obstacle; this is what is being shown.
Commentary on the Discourse of Ānanda’s Question (203):
"Non-seeing, Ānanda. This shows that non-seeing of women is the supreme practice in this regard.
For a bhikkhu who has closed the door and is sitting in his lodging does not see a woman even if she has come and is standing at the door.
As long as he does not see [the object], greed does not arise in him at all and his mind does not waver.

But when there is seeing, both of these occur for him. Therefore he said: "Non-seeing, Ānanda. When there is seeing—meaning, when there is seeing in places such as where one has approached to receive alms—how, O Blessed One, should one practice? How should one act when there is seeing?

He asked. Then the Blessed One considered that it would be better to speak with either the man standing there who, having taken up a sword, said, "If you speak with me, I shall strike off your head right here," or with the female yakṣī standing there who said, "If you speak with me, I shall have your flesh minced and eaten right here.
For [it is better] for the sake of a single individual existence...
Because of that, there is ruin, not the experience of boundless suffering in the states of misery. But when there is conversation and talk with women, intimacy arises;
when there is intimacy, an opportunity for corruption arises; one whose mind is corrupted meets with the ruin of virtue and becomes a filler of the states of misery.
Therefore he said, "no conversation. And this has also been said:
“One may converse with one who has a sword in hand, one may even converse with a *pisāca* demon;
one may even approach a venomous snake whose bite brings death—
but one should never, ever, converse alone with a woman.”

"But by addressing [her]" means: if a woman asks about the day, requests moral precepts (*sīla*), desires to hear the Dhamma, asks a question, or there is some task to be performed for her by those who have gone forth—on such occasions, if one does not address her, people will say, "This man is mute;
this man is deaf; he sits with his mouth closed as if he has just finished eating."
Since he speaks thus, it is necessary that one must address him. But [the questioner] asks: "How, then, should one proceed when addressing him?
Then the Blessed One said: "Come, monks, maintain the thought of a mother toward those who are like mothers;
maintain the thought of a sister toward those who are like sisters; maintain the thought of a daughter toward those who are like daughters."
It was with reference to this exhortation that he said, "Ānanda, mindfulness should be established.

"Be unburdened" means: be free from the bonds of anxiety and be without worldly striving. "Strive for the essential goal" means: strive for the supreme goal, which is Arhatship. "Devote yourselves" means:
apply yourselves to the practice for the sake of attaining that. "Be heedful" means: do not lose mindfulness regarding that.
“By means of the application of ardor and energy, you should dwell as ardent ones, with minds sent forth and directed by self-exertion through indifference toward both body and life.
“But how, venerable sir, should we proceed? they asked—the wise kṣatriyas and others. “Surely they will question me:
‘Venerable Ānanda, how should one proceed regarding the Tathāgata’s body?’”
He asks, "How shall I give them an answer? "With unwashed cloth" means with new Kāsika cloth.
"With beaten cotton" means with well-beaten cotton. For because Kāsika cloth is so fine, it does not absorb oil, whereas cotton does;
therefore he said, "with beaten cotton. "Of iron" means of gold; for [the word] *ayasa* refers to gold.
Here, "venerable" (ayasma) is intended.
Regarding the description of persons worthy of a stupa (thūpāraha-puggalavaṇṇanā):
as for the phrase "a wheel-turning monarch" (rājā cakkavattī), why is it that the Blessed One [mentions] a king who has passed away after living in the midst of the household?
[The Buddha] permits [the offering of] a stupa for one who is an arahant, but not for a virtuous worldling (puthujjana) bhikkhu. Why?
Because it would not be extraordinary. For if stupas were permitted for worldling bhikkhus, there would be no room for stupas even on the island of Tambapaṇṇi, let alone in other places.
Therefore, thinking, "They will become commonplace," he does not permit it. Only a single wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti) arises at one time.

Therefore, his stupa becomes marvelous. However, it is indeed appropriate to pay great honor even to an ordinary person (puthujjana) who possesses virtue, just as one does for a bhikkhu who has attained final Nibbāna.
— The Description of the Marvellous Qualities of Ānanda.

207. "They dwell here": by "monastery" (*vihāra*), a circular hall (*maṇḍalamāla*) is intended; having entered that. "The monkey-head" (*kapisīsa*) is the knob of the bolt fixed at the top of the door-posts. "He stood weeping":
it is said that the venerable one thought, "The Teacher has described to me a dwelling place that inspires spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*);
he has described the purposefulness of visiting the shrines (*cetiyacārikā*); [and] the question regarding how one should behave toward women..."
“[The Buddha] has been dismissed; his conduct regarding his own body has been declared; the four [types of persons] worthy of a stupa have been explained;
surely today the Blessed One will attain final Nibbāna. As he was reflecting thus, a powerful dejection arose within him.
Then it occurred to him: “Weeping in the presence of the Blessed One is unseemly; let me go to a secluded place and diminish my grief.”
“I shall do so,” he thought, and he did accordingly. Therefore it is said: “He stood weeping. “Ahañca vatamhi” means “Indeed, I am [such a one]”;
there is also the reading “ahaṃ vatamhi. “He who is compassionate toward me” means he who has compassion for me and instructs me:
“From tomorrow onwards, to whom shall I give water for washing the face? To whom shall I [give water for washing] the feet?”
"I shall wash [my feet]; for whom shall I attend to the lodgings; having taken whose bowl and robes shall I wander?"—thus he lamented much.
"He addressed" means that, not seeing the Elder among the community of monks, he addressed him.
"With a friendly bodily action" means with a bodily action such as offering water for washing the face, which proceeds from a mind of loving-kindness (*mettā*).
"By what is beneficial" means by that which is performed with the thought of what is truly beneficial. "By happiness" means by happiness and joy itself;
the meaning is not by one who is suffering or dejected. "By non-duality" means by that which is performed without making two divisions.

For just as one person performs [an act] only in the presence of another and not behind their back, while another performs it only behind their back and not in their presence—thus, it is by that which is performed without such a distinction.

It has been said. "By the immeasurable" means by that which is devoid of measure. For it shows that even the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) is too narrow, even the peak of existence (*bhavagga*) is too low, and that the bodily action performed by you alone is vast.
"By loving verbal action" means by verbal action such as announcing the time for washing the face, etc., which proceeds from a mind of loving-kindness (*mettā*).

Moreover, even the words "Well said, Bhante," uttered after hearing the exhortation, constitute a loving verbal action (*mettaṃ vacīkamma*). By a loving mental action (*mettena manokammena*) means by the mental action performed as follows:
having attended to one’s physical needs at the proper time and sat down in a secluded place, one thinks, "May the Teacher be free from illness, free from affliction, and happy.
"You have performed merit" means you have fulfilled your aspiration for a hundred thousand aeons.
He shows this by saying, "You have performed merit. He means: "Do not, on account of this much, become confident and fall into negligence; rather, apply yourself to striving.
For one who applies himself in this way, you will quickly become free from taints; you will attain Arahantship at the time of the Dhamma-saṅgīti.
For service rendered to one such as I never goes in vain. Thus he shows it.

Having spoken thus, as if stretching out the great earth, as if expanding the sky, as if lowering the Cakkavāḷa mountains, as if lifting up Mount Sineru, and as if grasping the Great Rose-apple Tree by its trunk and shaking it, the Blessed One began to speak of the virtues of the Venerable Ānanda.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "In that regard, those who..."
Why was it not said, "O monks, [there is no other Buddha] at present"? Because there is no other Buddha.
By this very fact, it should be understood that "there is no other Buddha even within the limits of a world-system (cakkavāḷa). "Wise" (paṇḍita) means competent.
"Intelligent" (medhāvī) means skilled in the aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), bases (āyatana), and so forth.

209. "A company of bhikkhus approaches Ānanda for the sake of seeing him" refers to those who, desiring to see the Blessed One, approach the Elder, as well as those who come having heard of the Elder's virtues, thinking:
"The Venerable Ānanda is indeed all-beautiful, handsome, lovely to behold, learned, and an ornament to the Saṅgha.
It is with reference to them that it is said, "A company of bhikkhus approaches Ānanda for the sake of seeing him."

It has been said. This same method applies everywhere. "Attamanā" means "with hearts satisfied," that is, with minds joyful because hearing [the news] coincides with their desire, even though they have not yet met in person.
"Dhamma" refers to such a form of friendly greeting as: "Friend, I hope you are well; I hope you are getting by; I hope you are performing your work with wise attention;
I hope you are fulfilling the duties toward your teachers and preceptors. In that regard, concerning the bhikkhunīs:
—“Sisters, do you conduct yourselves having undertaken the eight *garudhammas*? This too is a point of distinction.
When lay followers (*upāsakas*) arrive, he does not offer such greetings as, “Lay follower, I hope your head or limbs are not aching; I hope your sons and brothers are healthy.
Rather, he greets them thus: “How is it, lay followers, with regard to the three refuges and the five...”
“Guard your moral precepts; observe the Uposatha on eight days of the month; fulfill your duty of service toward your mother and father;
and support righteous recluses and brahmins. This same method applies to female lay followers as well.
Now, drawing a comparison between the Elder Ānanda and a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti), he said: “Bhikkhus, these four... and so forth.
In this context, "khattiyas" refers to those of the khattiya caste, both those who have been consecrated and those who have not.

It is said that upon hearing reports of his virtues—namely, "The so-called Wheel-Turning Monarch (cakkavatti) is handsome, beautiful to behold, inspiring, traveling through the sky, ruling the kingdom as a righteous king of Dhamma"—they were delighted, thinking, "To hear of him is equal to seeing him. "He speaks" means while conversing.
To the kshatriyas he offers greetings, saying: “How, dear sirs, do you fulfill the duties of kings? Do you protect your ancestral lineage?
To the brahmins, however, he offers greetings, saying: “How, teachers, do you recite the mantras? How do the students learn the mantras?
Have you received sacrificial fees, robes, or the Kapila cow? To the householders...
“Father, is there no oppression from the royal family by means of punishment or force?
Does the rain fall properly from the sky, and do the crops flourish?”—in this way he performs a friendly greeting. Toward the ascetics:
“Venerable sirs, are the requisites for those gone forth easy to obtain? Do you not neglect the duties of an ascetic?”—in this way he performs a friendly greeting.
Commentary on the Teaching of the Mahāsudassana Sutta: 210.
*Khuddakanagaraka* means in a small town that is merely a semblance of a city and is cramped. *Ujjaṅgalanagaraka* means in a town situated in a desolate or uneven region.
*Sākhānagaraka* means just as the branches of trees are called "small," so too [is this town].
In small towns that are like branches of other great cities. "Khattiya mahāsālā" refers to great khattiyas who have attained the status of great khattiya wealth.
This same method applies everywhere.
Among them, those called "khattiya mahāsālā" are those who have buried and deposited a hundred crores or even a thousand crores of wealth.
A single cartload of kahāpaṇas goes out for their daily expenses, and two carts enter in the evening.
Those called wealthy brahmins have eighty koṭis of wealth stored up; a single jar of kahāpaṇas goes out for their daily expenses, and one cart enters in the evening.
Those called wealthy householders have forty koṭis of wealth stored up.
“...there is a daily expenditure of five kahāpaṇas, and a jar [of provisions] enters in the evening.
“Do not say so, Ānanda; do not say so, Ānanda. This should not be called a ‘small town.
For I could describe the prosperity of this very city by saying: ‘Many times, standing and sitting, with great...”
Having said, “He has come here through great exertion and great prowess,” he spoke the passage beginning with “In former times.
“Subhikkhā” means well-supplied with various kinds of food and edibles. “With the sound of elephants”: when one elephant makes a sound, eighty-four thousand elephants make a sound;
thus it was never devoid of the sound of elephants, and likewise of the sound of horses. Furthermore, those who possess merit here—
Beings wander through the streets following one another in chariots yoked with four horses;
thus, it is never devoid of the sound of chariots. Furthermore, drums and other musical instruments are constantly played there;

thus, it is never devoid of the sounds of drums and so forth. In this context, "the sound of *saṃma*" refers to the sound of a bronze gong (*kaṃsatāḷa*). "The sound of hand-clapping" (*pāṇitāḷa*) refers to...
The sound of square wooden clappers struck with the hand—some also call it the sound of a *kuṭabherī* drum—is heard:
"Bathe! Drink! Eat!"—that is, "Bathe! Drink! Eat! This, however, is the summary here:
by this tenth sound, "Eat, sirs!", it is not devoid of noise; it is a place where the sound is never interrupted. Just as in other cities...
"Throw away the rubbish! Take up the spades! Take up the baskets! We shall go on a journey!
Take up the bags of rice! Take up the bags of cooked food! Prepare your shields, weapons, and so forth!"—such were the sounds [heard there], but he shows that it was not like this here.

Having said, "By the tenth sound," and having concluded the entire Mahāsudassana Sutta with the words, "Ānanda, the royal capital Kusāvatī was surrounded by seven walls," he said, "Go now, Ānanda," and so forth.
In that context, "approach" (*abhikkamatha*) means "go toward," that is, "come hither. But how did they [know] the Blessed One’s arrival?
"Do they not know? "They do know. There is a great clamor wherever the Buddhas go;

they have not come because they were occupied with some business. Thinking, 'When they arrive, they will arrange and assign places for the standing and sitting of the Saṅgha of monks,' the Blessed One sent them [the message] even though it was not the usual time."
Commentary on the Homage to the Mallas (Mallānaṃ vandanāvaṇṇanā) 211.
Regarding the phrase “And for us” (*amhākañca no*): here, *no* is merely a particle (*nipātamattaṃ*). “Afflicted by suffering” (*aghāvino*) means those in whom suffering has arisen.
“Dejected” (*dummanā*) means unhappy. “Overcome by mental distress” (*cetodukkhasamappitā*) means overcome by grief (*domanassa*). “From family to family” (*kulaparivattaso kulaparivattaso*).
"Setting aside" means having set aside each individual household rotation (*kulaparivatta*) and each household group (*kulasaṅkhepa*) separately, according to their respective streets and lanes. —
The Explanation of the Story of the Wanderer Subhadda.
212. "The wanderer named Subhadda" refers to a covered-wanderer who had gone forth from a prominent family of northern brahmins.
"One of a doubting nature" means one of a skeptical disposition. But why did it happen to him only today? It was because of such a supporting condition (*upanissaya*).
It is said that formerly, at a time when they were performing meritorious deeds, there were two brothers. They cultivated their crops together. There, the elder brother—
“I must give the gift of the first-fruits nine times during a single harvest,” he thought.

At the time of sowing, having given the seed-money, at the time of the crop’s growth, he consulted with his younger brother, saying, “At the time of growth, we shall cut open the stalks and give them.
The younger brother said, “Do you wish to destroy the young crop? The elder brother [perceived] the younger brother’s refusal to comply.
Having recognized this, she divided the field; from her own portion, she split open the ear of grain, extracted the milk, and mixed it with ghee and fresh butter to give it to him.

At the time of threshing, she had the best of the threshed grain prepared for him; at the time of winnowing, the best of the winnowed; at the time of binding into bundles, the best of the bundles; at the time of sheaves, the best of the sheaves;

at the time of the threshing floor, the best of the threshing floor; at the time of the granary, the best of the granary; and at the time of the storehouse, the best of the storehouse—thus, for each harvest.
The eldest gave nine first-fruits offerings; the youngest, however, having set aside [the best portion], gave them.

Among them, the eldest became the Elder Aññāsikoṇḍañña. The Blessed One, looking about [and thinking], "To whom indeed should I first teach the Dhamma?", saw that Aññāsikoṇḍañña had given nine first-fruits offerings during a single harvest, and [considered] this foremost Dhamma...
"I shall teach him the Dhamma," he thought, and so he taught the Dhamma first of all. Together with eighteen koṭis of Brahmās, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry.

But the younger brother, having been left behind because his gift had been given later, desired to see the Teacher at the very time of the Teacher’s final Nibbāna, thinking thus: "I wish to see the Teacher."
"Do not harass the Tathāgata," the Elder said, thinking: "These are called 'adherents of other sects' who grasp only at their own positions;

if the Blessed One speaks much for the sake of making them relinquish theirs, there will be harassment of his body and speech, and the Blessed One is already naturally fatigued. The wanderer [said]: "This is not for me..."
“A bhikkhu makes way; however, one who has need must follow and cause it to be done.
Following the elder, he spoke thus a second and a third time.
213. “He heard” means that while standing at the door of the hemp-cloth, he heard with his natural hearing; and having heard, moreover—
Because he had come with great effort for the sake of Subhadda alone, [the Buddha] said, "Enough, Ānanda," and so forth.
In that context, *alaṃ* is a particle used in the sense of prohibition. *Aññāpekkho vā* means "desiring to know. *Abbhaññiṃsu* means they understood exactly according to their own declaration.
This is what is meant: if their declaration were leading to liberation (*niyyānika*), then all...
Whether they have directly known it or not, they have not; therefore, whether their declaration is leading or not leading—this alone is the meaning of that question.

Then the Blessed One, having rejected [the question] with the words "Enough," because there was neither purpose nor occasion in stating its lack of leading quality, taught the Dhamma itself. For in the first watch...

Having taught the Dhamma to the Mallas during the middle watch, and having exhorted the Saṅgha of bhikkhus during the last watch, the Blessed One has come thinking, "I shall attain final Nibbāna at the time of the powerful dawn. 214.
"Not even a single ascetic is found there": first, not even a stream-enterer ascetic is found there; second—
The meaning is that there is no once-returner ascetic there, no third non-returner ascetic, and no fourth arahant ascetic.
Having spoken of this in general terms in the previous teaching with the words "In this [teaching]," he now speaks while specifying his own dispensation:
"The doctrines of others are empty of ascetics. This refers to those four who have undertaken insight meditation for the sake of the four paths.
The doctrines of other teachers are empty, hollow, and void because they lack the twelve ascetics—namely, the four who stand on the path and the four who stand in the fruit.

And as for these, Subhadda, these twelve bhikkhus would dwell rightly; herein, one who has entered the stream (sotāpanna) is said to dwell rightly when, having explained to another the state he has attained, he establishes that other person as a stream-enterer.

This same method applies to the once-returner and the others. One who stands on the path of stream-entry, while causing another to stand on the path of stream-entry, is said to "dwell rightly. This same method applies to those standing on the remaining paths.

One who has begun insight meditation for the sake of the path of stream-entry, having explained his own familiar meditation subject to another who has also begun insight meditation for the sake of the path of stream-entry—

One who practices thus is said to "dwell rightly. This same method applies to those who have begun insight meditation for the sake of the remaining paths. It is with reference to this that he said, "They would dwell rightly.
"The world would not be empty of Arahants" means it would be as densely packed as a grove of reeds or a thicket of rushes.
"At twenty-nine years of age" means having reached the age of twenty-nine. In the phrase "whom [I] went forth," the word *yaṃ* is a mere particle.
"Seeking what that is wholesome? means seeking and searching for "what is wholesome.
In this context, "what is wholesome" refers to omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*); thus, the meaning is "seeking that.
"Since I" shows that from the time I went forth until now, more than fifty years have passed. "Of the methodical Dhamma" (*ñāyassa dhammassa*)...
Of the noble path-dhamma. "Practicing partially" means proceeding on a partial portion of the path of insight (*vipassanāmaggapadesa*).
"Outside of this" means outside of my teaching. "There is not even a recluse" means there is not even one who practices insight partially;
it is said that there is not even a first recluse, a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*).

"Ye ettha" means: "Those of you who here in this Dispensation have been consecrated by the Teacher in his presence with the consecration of a resident pupil (antevāsika)—for you it is a gain, for you it is well-acquired.
It is said that in external systems, when a teacher says to a resident pupil, "Ordain this one;
instruct this one; teach this one," he is thereby established in the teacher’s own position.
Because he was so, these gains accrued to him: "Ordain this one; instruct this one; advise this one.
Subhadda spoke thus to the Elder as well, having taken up that very same external doctrine.
How did he obtain [them]? It is said that the Elder led him aside and, with water from his own water-pot...

Having moistened his head, he taught him the meditation subject of the five skins; then, having shaved off his hair and beard, clothed him in saffron robes, and granted him the refuges, he brought him into the presence of the Blessed One. The Blessed One ordained him and assigned him a meditation subject.
Having taken that, he established a walking path at the edge of the park and, striving and exerting himself, practiced it.
Increasing his insight (*vipassanā*), he attained *arahantship* together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*). Having returned and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down.
With reference to him, it was said: "Not long after his full ordination... and so forth.
Furthermore, the compilers of the Council state that he was the last of the Blessed One’s personal disciples (*sakkhisāvaka*). In this regard, whoever...
Having gone forth while the Blessed One was still living, he later receives full ordination (*upasampadā*), takes up a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), and attains *arahantship*;
or, having received full ordination while the Blessed One was still living, he later takes up a meditation subject and attains *arahantship*;
or, having taken up a meditation subject while the Blessed One was still living, he later attains *arahantship* itself.
He attained [the goal], being the very last disciple to become a witness (sakkhisāvaka).
Furthermore, he went forth and received full ordination while the Blessed One was still living, and having taken up a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), he reached Arahantship.
The commentary on the fifth recitation section is finished.
The Commentary on the Tathāgata’s Final Words: 216.
Now, he began the exhortation to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus; to show this, the passage beginning with “Then the Blessed One” was spoken.
Therein, “taught and laid down” means that both the Dhamma and the Vinaya were taught and laid down.

"And what is called 'laid down' means established or set forth. 'That Dhamma and Discipline shall be your teacher after my passing' means that this Dhamma and Discipline shall be your teacher once I am gone.
For while I was still present, I [established]: 'This is light; this is heavy; this is curable; this is incurable;
this is an offense of worldly transgression; this is an offense of formal rule; this is an offense..."
“This offense is cleared in the presence of an individual; this offense is cleared in the presence of a group; this offense is cleared in the presence of the Saṅgha.
Thus, when a matter has been introduced according to the seven classes of offenses, the Vinaya—consisting of the two Vibhaṅgas together with the Khandhaka and Parivāra—has been taught.
That entire Vinaya Piṭaka shall be for you after I have attained final Nibbāna.
He will accomplish the Teacher’s work.

And while I remain, [I shall do so] by way of this or that aspect: "These are the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path."
Having analyzed these phenomena again and again, the Sutta Piṭaka has been taught;
that entire Sutta Piṭaka, once I have attained final Nibbāna, will fulfill for you the role of a Teacher. And while I was still present, it was said:
"These are the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the four truths, the twenty-two faculties, the nine causes..."
There are four nutriments, seven contacts, seven feelings, seven perceptions, seven volitions, and seven consciousnesses.
Regarding those as well, one discerns these phenomena: “So many are of the sense sphere, so many are of the fine-material sphere, so many are of the immaterial sphere;
so many are included [within the mundane], so many are not included; so many are mundane, so many are supramundane. It is by means of such phenomena that one discerns.

Having analyzed and further analyzed it, I have taught the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, adorned with twenty-four great treatises (*mahāpaṭṭhāna*) and infinite methods (*anantanaya*). After I have attained final Nibbāna,
this entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka will fulfill for you the role of a Teacher.

Thus, all of this—from the time of his full enlightenment until his final nibbāna—spoken and uttered over forty-five years, has become a great classification consisting of "the three Piṭakas, the five Nikāyas, the nine Aṅgas, and eighty-four thousand divisions of the Dhamma.
Thus these eighty-four thousand divisions of the Dhamma endure; I...
"I alone shall attain final Nibbāna. Now, I alone am advising and instructing you;
but when I have attained final Nibbāna, these eighty-four thousand sections of the Dhamma shall advise and instruct you.
Thus the Blessed One, demonstrating many reasons, instructed them, saying, "He shall be your teacher after my passing," and further [foretold] their future conduct.
He said, "As for how he shows [this]," and so forth.
In that context, *samudācaranti* means they speak or address [one another]. "By name or by clan" means:
rather than saying "the junior ones," they address them by name such as "Tissa" or "Nāga," or by clan such as "Kassapa" or "Gotama," or as "Friend Tissa."
"Friend Kassapa"—thus one may address him with the term "friend. Or else, as "Venerable Sir" (*bhante*) or "Worthy One" (*āyasmā*), one may address him as "Venerable Sir Tissa" or "Worthy Tissa.
Regarding the phrase "let him eradicate," it means: "if he so desires, let him eradicate; if he wishes, he might eradicate.
Why, then, instead of stating it categorically as "eradicate," is it expressed using a conditional formulation?
“Did he set it aside? Yes; because he had perceived the strength of Mahākassapa. For the Blessed One saw:
“Even if you say ‘abolish them,’ Kassapa will not abolish them at the time of the recitation. Therefore, he set it aside by way of a formal resolution (*vikappa*).
In this regard, some elders said: “Excluding the four *pārājika* rules, the rest are minor and secondary rules,” and so forth.

According to this method, the discussion on the minor and lesser rules (khuddānukhuddaka-kathā) was indeed included in the Council of Five Hundred; the detailed analysis of this matter is also stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*.
However, some say that when King Milinda asked, "Venerable Nāgasena, what is the minor rule? What is the lesser rule? he replied:
"Great King, an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is the minor rule; an offense of wrong speech (dubbhāsita) is the lesser rule."
Because it was so stated, the Elder Nāgasena knew what were the minor and lesser rules. But Mahākassapa, not knowing that, said: "Let the Saṅgha hear me, friends:
our training rules have passed into the hands of householders, and even householders know:
'This is permitted for you, the recluses, sons of the Sakyans; this is not permitted for you. If we [were to abolish] the minor and lesser rules..."
"We shall abolish the training rules, so that there will be those who say: 'The training rules for the disciples were laid down by the ascetic Gotama only for a limited time;
as long as their Teacher remained, they trained in these rules, but now that their Teacher has attained final Nibbāna, they no longer train in these rules. If it is the Sangha's [wish]..."

"It is the proper time for the Saṅgha not to ordain what has not been ordained, not to abolish what has been ordained, and to practice by undertaking the training rules exactly as they have been ordained. This is the motion (*ñatti*).
Thus he announced the formal act (*kammavācā*). That should not be understood in that way; for the Elder Nāgasena said: "An opportunity for the opponent..."
"Do not let it be so," he said. The Elder Mahākassapa then recited the formal motion (kammavācā), saying, "I shall not abolish even minor and lesser offenses.
The discussion on the *brahmadaṇḍa* (the censure of being excluded from the Saṅgha) has also been explained in the *Samantapāsādikā*, as it is included in the *Saṅgīti*.
"Doubt" (*kaṅkhā*) means perplexity. "Uncertainty" (*vimati*) is the inability to reach a decision, such as: "Is he a Buddha, or is he not a Buddha?"

“If anyone should have a doubt as to whether it is the Dhamma or not the Dhamma, whether it is the Saṅgha or not the Saṅgha, whether it is the Path or not the Path, or whether it is the Practice or not the Practice—I say to you: ‘Ask, monks! This is the summary of the meaning here. Even out of reverence for the Teacher...
"You should ask" means: "We have gone forth in the presence of the Teacher; even our four requisites belong to the Teacher alone.
We ought not to harbor doubt for so long, and on this final day we should not entertain doubt.
If you do not ask out of such reverence for the Teacher, [the Buddha says]: "Monks, let a companion inform his companion."
"Whosoever among you has a personal acquaintance or a close friend who is a bhikkhu, let him inform that bhikkhu:
'I shall speak to this bhikkhu; having heard his account, all of you will become free from doubt.

Thus he shows it. 'Thus with confidence' means: 'In this way, I have faith,' is the meaning. 'Knowledge itself' means: the very knowledge that makes the state of being free from doubt directly manifest."
In this context, the meaning is that for the Tathāgata there is not even a mere matter of faith.

"Of these, Ānanda" refers to these five hundred bhikkhus sitting within the enclosure. "Whoever is the last" refers to one who is last by way of spiritual qualities; he said this with reference specifically to the Elder Ānanda.
"Accomplish it through diligence" means you should accomplish all duties by not being separated from mindfulness. Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Lying upon his deathbed at the time of his parinibbāna, he bestowed all the exhortations given over forty-five years by condensing them into a single phrase on heedfulness.
"This was the Tathāgata’s final word"—this, however, is the statement of those who compiled the Council (the Saṅgītikārakas).
This concludes the commentary on the account of the parinibbāna.
219. Hereafter, in order to show that which the Blessed One did as preparation for his final *parinibbāna* before passing away, it is said:
"Then the Blessed One entered the first *jhāna*," and so forth. In this context, the question "Venerable sir, has he attained *parinibbāna*?

is asked by one who, having seen the absence of inhalation and exhalation in the Blessed One who had entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), inquired about him. The Elder replied, "No, friend."

How does he know this? It is said that the Elder, entering each successive meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) together with the Teacher, proceeded as far as the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*).
There, he knew: "Now the Blessed One has entered cessation (*nirodha*); and within cessation, there is no such thing as passing away."
Then the Blessed One, having emerged from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, entered the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception...
[pe] ...having emerged from the third jhāna, he entered the fourth jhāna.
In this context, the Blessed One entered the first jhāna in twenty-four instances, the second jhāna in thirteen instances, and likewise—
He attained the third jhāna. In fifteen instances, he attained the fourth jhāna.

How so? First, he attained the first jhāna in these twenty-four instances: the ten kinds of foulness (asubha), the thirty-two aspects (dvattiṃsākāra), the eight kasinas, the four divine abidings of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna), and the delimited space (paricchedākāsa). However, setting aside the thirty-two aspects...
He attained the second jhāna in the ten foul objects (*dasasu asubhāni*) and the remaining thirteen [meditation subjects], and he attained the third jhāna in those very same subjects.

However, in fifteen places—namely, the eight kasinas, the sublime abode of equanimity (*upekkhā-brahmavihāra*), mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*), the space of delimitation (*paricchedākāsa*), and the four formless states (*catūsu arūpesu*)—he attained the fourth jhāna. And this too is merely a summary account. [The city of] Nibbāna...
But as the Blessed One, the Lord of Dhamma, was entering [the city], he entered all twenty-four million meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
Having experienced the bliss of all these attainments, as if embracing his kinsmen while departing for a foreign land, he entered [the city].
Immediately after emerging from the fourth jhāna, the Blessed One attained final nibbāna (*parinibbāyi*); here, "immediately after the jhāna" means—

"Immediately after reviewing" refers to two kinds of immediacy (*samanantara*). Therein, for one who has emerged from jhāna and entered the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), attaining final nibbāna right there is called "immediacy following jhāna.
For one who, having emerged from jhāna, reviews the factors of jhāna and then enters the life-continuum, attaining final nibbāna right there is called "immediacy following review. These also...

Two [moments] are immediately consecutive. However, the Blessed One, having entered into jhāna, emerged from jhāna, and reviewed the factors of jhāna, attained final nibbāna through the indeterminate life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅgacitta) with respect to the truth of suffering.
For all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, or noble disciples—even down to an ant—everyone [attains final nibbāna] by means of the indeterminate life-continuum consciousness alone.
“They pass away by means of the truth of suffering. The great earth-tremors and so forth are to be understood according to the method already stated.

220. “Beings” (*bhūtā*) means sentient beings (*sattā*). “Peerless” (*appaṭipuggalo*) means devoid of any rival person. “Attained to power” (*balappatto*) means one who has attained the tenfold power of knowledge. 221.

“Subject to arising and passing away” (*uppādavayadhammino*) means having the inherent nature of arising and passing away. “Their subsiding” (*tesaṃ vūpasamo*) means the subsiding of those conditioned formations; the meaning is that the unconditioned Nibbāna alone is happiness.
222. "There was no inhalation or exhalation" means that his inhalation and exhalation had ceased. "Unshaken" (*anejo*) means unshaken by the lack of *ejā*—that is, by craving (*taṇhā*).
"Aiming for peace" (*santiṃ ārabbha*) means aiming at, depending upon, and referring to *nibbāna* without remainder (*anupādisesa*).
"When he passed away" (*yaṃ kālamakārī*) means when he made an end to his time. This is what is meant: "Friend, my Teacher, the Buddha-Muni, [thinking] 'I shall go to peace'..."
"He passed away while intent upon peace; for him whose mind was thus established and who was such a one (tādin), inhalation and exhalation have now ceased—they do not exist, they do not proceed.
"Without dejection" means with a mind that is not depressed, not contracted, but rather fully blossomed. "He endured the sensation" means he bore the sensation...
He consented; he did not follow after his feelings, nor did he roll about here and there.

"Liberation" (vimokkha) means that by means of some state, there arose an unobstructed liberation, a complete arrival at the state of non-designation (appaññatti-bhāva), like the extinguishing of a lamp. 223.

"Then there was..."—this refers specifically to the earthquake mentioned below as occurring "simultaneously with the Parinibbāna. For that [earthquake] was hair-raising and terrifying. "Endowed with the excellence of all modes" means endowed with every excellent quality.
224. "Those who have not yet abandoned passion" refers to both worldlings (*puthujjana*) and stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) and once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*).

For in them, mental distress (*domanassa*) has not been abandoned; therefore, they too weep, raising their arms. Placing both hands upon their heads and weeping—all this is to be understood in the same manner as previously described.
225. "They lament" means: "The noble ones themselves are unable to endure [this suffering]; how then will they comfort other people?"
They spoke and complained: "Venerable sir, in what manner does the Venerable Anuruddha attend to the deities?
"Venerable sir, in what manner does the Venerable Anuruddha observe the deities? Are they enduring the Teacher’s final passing away?
Then, for the purpose of showing their state, the Elder said, "Peaceful are they," and so forth. That has already been explained. "The remainder of the night..."
Because he attained final nibbāna early in the morning, the remainder of the night was the "minor watch" (cullakaddhāna). Regarding the phrase "with a discourse on the Dhamma":

there is no such thing as a separate, distinct discourse on the Dhamma; rather, it means: "Friends, in this world including the devas, even for the Teacher who is peerless, this King of Death feels no shame; how much less, then, would he feel shame before the common people of the world?"
They spent their time in such discourse connected with death. Indeed, while they were engaged in that conversation, the dawn broke in just a moment.
Then, upon seeing the rising of the dawn, the elder said this to the elder: "By what very purpose... [He asked: "Of what kind?"
"Should there be honor with garlands, perfumes, and so forth at the place of the Parinibbāna? What kind of seating arrangement should there be for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus?
What kind of solid and soft food should there be?"—thus, they were occupied solely with that which must be done upon hearing of the Blessed One’s state of having attained Parinibbāna.
**Commentary on the Worship of the Buddha’s Relics** 227.

“And all the musical instruments” means all the musical equipment. “Assemble them” means: having caused the drum to be beaten, collect them. They did exactly so. “In the maṇḍala-pavilion” means in the cloth-canopy pavilion. “Preparing” means making ready.
“From the south to the south” means from the southern direction of the city toward the southern direction. “On the outside” [is the meaning].
"Outside" means having carried it out through the exterior side of the city without bringing it inside the city. "To the south of the city" means:

having placed it in a location similar to the southern gate of Anurādhapura and having paid it honor and respect, [they thought], "We shall cremate it in a place like the Jeta Grove"—this is the meaning.
228. "The eight chief Mallas" refers to the eight Malla kings, who were in their middle years and endowed with great strength.
"Having washed their heads" means having rinsed their heads and bathed. Regarding "the venerable Anuruddha":
since it was well known that the Elder alone possessed the divine eye, they asked the Elder—even though other great elders were present—thinking, "He will explain this for us in a way that is clear."
"But how, venerable sir, is it that you know the intention of the deities? "Venerable sir, we indeed know our own intention;
but how do you ask about the intention of the deities? The Elder, first showing them their own intention, said, "But for you," and so forth.
"The Makuṭabandhana Shrine" refers to the auspicious hall for the adornment of the Malla kings.
This is its name. However, in the sense of being honored (*cittīkata*), it is called a "shrine" (*cetiya*).

Regarding the phrase "as far as the joints, the refuse-heaps, and the narrow passages": here, "joints" (*sandhi*) refers to the structural joints of a house; "refuse-heaps" (*samala*) refers to the drainage pipes for heaps of excrement;
and "narrow passages" (*saṅkaṭīra*) refers to rubbish heaps. "With divine and human dances" refers to those of the deities above.
Dances took place below the humans; the same applies to songs and so forth.
Moreover, they proceeded honoring and worshipping, with humans amidst the deities and deities amidst the humans.
When the Blessed One’s body was being carried thus through the middle of the city, Mallikā—named so after the Mallan general Bandhula—[was there].
Hearing that they were bringing the Blessed One’s relics, she had the Great Garland ornament— resembling Visākhā’s own jewelry— which she had kept without using since her husband’s death,
brought out. Thinking, “With this I shall honor the Teacher,” she had it melted down,
washed it with scented water, and stood at the gate.
It is said that those ornaments belonged to those two women and to the thief Devadāniya; thus, they were found in exactly three places.
When the Teacher’s body reached the gateway, she said, "Take them down, dear ones, from the Teacher’s body," and fastened those ornaments upon the Teacher’s body.
Fastened from the head down to the soles of the feet, they remained there.
The Blessed One’s golden-hued body, adorned with a magnificent ornament made of the seven precious gems, shone exceedingly.
Seeing this, she, with a heart full of faith, made this aspiration:
“For as long as I wander in saṃsāra, may I have no need for separate ornaments; may my body always remain as if it were naturally adorned.”
Then, having lifted up the Blessed One with a great palanquin made of the seven precious gems and carried him out through the eastern gate,
they deposited the Blessed One’s body there at the Mallas’ Shrine called Makutabandhana, located to the east of the city.
The Commentary on the Story of the Elder Mahākassapa:
231. From Pāvā to Kusinārā: Having wandered for alms in the city of Pāvā, he set out on the highway with the intention, "I shall go to Kusinārā.

Regarding the phrase "he sat down at the foot of a tree": why is it not stated here that he was there for his midday rest (*divāvihāra*)? Because he did not sit there specifically for the purpose of his midday rest.
For all the monks who were the Elder’s attendants had been brought up in comfort and possessed great merit.
At midday, as they walked on foot over ground that was like a red-hot stone, they became exhausted. Seeing them, the Elder thought:
"The monks are weary, yet the place we must go is not far; let us rest for a short while and allay our fatigue."

Thinking, “I will go to Kusinārā at the time of evening and see the One of Ten Powers,” he descended from the road, spread his outer robe at the foot of a certain tree, cooled his hands and feet with water from his water-pot, and sat down.
His attendant monks also sat at the foot of the tree and applied themselves to practice through wise attention. Of those three...
They sat down reciting the praises of the jewels. Thus, because they were seated for the purpose of dispelling their distress, it is not called "the midday rest.

"Taking a mandārava flower" means taking a flower as large as a great alms-bowl, placing it on a visiting staff, and holding it like an umbrella. "He saw" means he saw him approaching from afar. And having seen him, he thought:
"This mandārava flower is visible in the hand of the Ājīvaka; and this is not [found] at all times on the path of men."

It is visible; however, when someone possessing psychic power (*iddhimā*) performs a transformation of psychic power (*iddhi-vikubbana*), it occurs during such events as the descent of the Omniscient Bodhisatta into his mother’s womb.
But today no one has performed a transformation of psychic power;
my Teacher has not descended into his mother’s womb, nor is he emerging from the womb, nor is there his full enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*) today.
“It was not the Turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, nor the Twin Miracle, nor the Descent from Heaven, nor the relinquishing of the life-faculty.
My Teacher is old; he must surely have attained final Nibbāna.
Then, having resolved, “I shall ask him,” while still seated, he thought: “If I were to ask while remaining seated, it would be improper toward the Teacher...”
Thinking, “Disrespect will have been shown,” he rose up, moved away from his standing place, and—
like a six-tusked king of elephants donning a jeweled skin— put on the cloud-colored rag-robe given by the One of Ten Powers.
Joining his ten fingers in a resplendent añjali and placing it upon his head, he stood facing the Ājīvaka with the reverence he had for the Teacher.
“Friend, do you know our Teacher? he asked. Now, did he ask because he did not know whether the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, or because he did know?

Some say that the knowledge of those whose taints are destroyed is dependent upon an act of attention (*āvajjana*); therefore, because he had not applied his attention, he asked as if he did not know.

Others say that the Elder was one who frequently entered meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), and was constantly in retreat houses, pavilions, and so forth, during his night and day standing-meditations.

He sustained himself by the power of meditative attainment alone; even upon entering a village belonging to a family, he would enter a meditative attainment at the gate and, only after emerging from that attainment, would he accept alms.
It is said that the Elder intended to bring great benefit to the people through this final existence, thinking:
"Those who give me alms or honor me with perfumes, garlands, and so forth..."
"May that [merit] be of great fruit for those who perform it"—thus he acts.
Therefore, they say that he does not know because of his abundance of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), and thus asks while being ignorant; but that should not be accepted.
For there is no cause here for ignorance. The Teacher’s Parinibbāna was a distinguished event, marked by such things as the shaking of the ten-thousandfold world system.
By means of signs. Now, among the Elder’s assembly, some monks had previously seen the Blessed One, while others had not.
Of those who had seen him, they were still desirous of seeing him; and of those who had not seen him, they too were desirous of seeing him.
Thereupon, those who had not seen him went out of an excessive desire to see him, [asking], "Where..."
If they were to ask, "Where is the Blessed One? and hear that he has attained final Nibbāna, they would be unable to sustain themselves.
Casting aside their robes and bowls, clad in a single garment, poorly dressed, or improperly robed, they would weep while beating their breasts.
Then people there would say: "These rag-robe wearers who came with the Elder Mahākassapa have themselves become like women."
“They are weeping; will they comfort us?”—thus they will point out my fault. But this is a vast, empty wilderness; here there is no fault in people weeping however they may.
Thinking that even sorrow becomes diminished upon hearing [the news] earlier, he asked while already knowing, for the purpose of arousing mindfulness in the bhikkhus.

"Today the ascetic Gotama has attained final Nibbāna" means that today the ascetic Gotama has been completely extinguished for seven days. "From there" means from the place where the ascetic Gotama passed away.
232. "Subhadda by name, an elder who went forth late in life": "Subhadda" is his name; he is called "an elder who went forth late in life" because he entered the religious life in his old age.
But why did he speak thus? Out of resentment toward the Blessed One. It is said that this man—
In the Khandhaka, regarding the account at Ātumā: a barber who had gone forth in old age,
having heard that the Blessed One was coming from Kusinārā together with one hundred and twenty-five bhikkhus to Ātumā— having himself gone forth long ago—
thought, "When he arrives, I will prepare rice-gruel for him," and spoke thus to his two sons who were standing on the level of novice monks.
— “It seems, dear ones, that the Blessed One is coming to Ātumā together with a great Saṅgha of monks, numbering twelve hundred and fifty.
Go, dear ones, taking your barber’s equipment, and wander from house to house with a measuring scoop,
collecting salt, oil, rice, and solid food for the Blessed One.”
“We will give a drink of rice-gruel to whoever comes. They did so.
When people saw those boys—so charming and eloquent—they would make them do it whether they wished to or not.
Once it was done, they would ask, “What will you have, dear ones? and they would reply, “Nothing else for us.”
"But our father was a friend of the Blessed One; when he arrives, he wishes to give an offering of rice gruel.
Having heard this, the people gave everything they were able to bring without further deliberation. Even for what they could not obtain themselves, they sent it by means of other men.
Then, when the Blessed One had come in person and entered the straw hut, Subhadda arrived in the evening.
Having gone to the village gate, he addressed the people: "Lay followers, I do not expect anything else from you;
the rice and other provisions brought by my children are sufficient for the Saṅgha. Give me manual labor.
Saying, "Take this and that," he had all the requisites brought and [set up] cooking stoves in the monastery.
Having had one black *kāṣāya* robe made, he put it on and draped another of the same kind over it;
then, wandering all night long with the words "Do this! Do that!", he spent a hundred thousand [pieces of money] and had *bhojja-yāgu* and honey-balls prepared.
*Bhojja-yāgu* is rice-gruel to be drunk after eating; in it were ghee, honey, molasses, fish, meat, and the juices of flowers and fruits.
Whatever was called "hard food," he put it all in; it became fragrant and suitable for anointing the heads of those wishing to play.
Then the Blessed One, having attended to his physical needs at an early hour, set out toward Ātumā with the community of monks to wander for alms.
People informed him: "The Blessed One is entering the village for alms."
“For whom was the rice-gruel prepared by her? He, still wearing the same black robes as he had put on, took the serving spoon and ladle in one hand;
then, like Brahmā, he placed his right knee upon the ground, paid homage, and said:
“Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One accept my rice-gruel.”

Then, according to the method set forth in the Khandhaka—that "Tathāgatas, though already knowing, ask questions"—the Blessed One questioned him and, having heard his reply, rebuked that elder who had gone forth late in life.

On that occasion, he laid down two training rules: the rule concerning the undertaking of what is unallowable and the rule concerning the carrying of a razor-case. Then he said: "Monks, for many millions of eons..."
"Those who seek food have spent their time merely searching; however, this food of yours has been acquired through an improper means and is not allowable.
For those who consume it, many thousands of future existences will arise only in the states of misery.
Go away; do not take it! Having said this, he set out toward his alms-round. Not a single monk took anything at all.
Subhadda, being dissatisfied, wanders about thinking, "I know everything. If he does not wish to accept [the food], one should send word to inform him.
This so-called "cooked food" would last at most seven days even if it remained for the longest time;
indeed, this would have been sufficient for me for as long as my life lasted. He has ruined everything; he wishes me harm—thus [he thought] regarding the Blessed One.
Having harbored resentment toward the One of Ten Powers, he was unable to say anything while [the Buddha] was still alive. For it had occurred to him:
"This is a Great Man who has gone forth from a noble family; if I say anything at all, he will surely rebuke me.
But now, having heard that "The Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna," he spoke thus, as glad and joyful as one who has found relief after being gasping for breath.
When the Elder heard this, he felt as if a blow had been struck to his heart and as if a dry thunderbolt had fallen upon his head; a sense of spiritual urgency arose within him:
"The Blessed One has been completely extinguished for only seven days, yet today his golden-hued body still remains intact!
Alas, such a great mass of evil has so quickly accrued to one who has striven with such hardship to fulfill the Dispensation of the Blessed One!"

“A thorn has arisen; indeed, if this evil man continues to grow, he will find other companions like himself and it will be possible for him to cause the Dispensation to decline. Then the Elder thought:
“If I were to have this old man clothed here in rags and have him covered with ashes...”

"I shall have it removed; otherwise, people will point out our fault, saying, 'While the body of the ascetic Gotama was still alive, his disciples were already quarreling over it. For now, I shall endure it.
Indeed, the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One is like a heap of flowers not yet gathered. In that regard, just as flowers struck by the wind..."

Whether they go here or there, as time passes under the influence of such evil persons, one or two training rules will be lost from the Vinaya; one or two sections of questions will be lost from the Sutta;
and one or two levels of existence will be lost from the Abhidhamma. Thus, in due course, when the root is lost, they will become like demons.
"We shall become so; therefore, we will compile the Dhamma and Vinaya.
For when this is done, this Dhamma and Vinaya will remain unshakable, like flowers gathered firmly by their stalks.
It was for this purpose indeed that the Blessed One came out three *gāvutas* to meet me and conferred the full ordination upon me with the three exhortations."
He gave [it]; having removed it from his body, he performed a change of robes upon his person;

and waving his hand in the air while explaining the practice that resembles the moon, he spoke making me a witness with his own body, and three times he entrusted the entire inheritance of the Dispensation to me.
While a monk such as I remains, this evil one shall not obtain growth within the Dispensation. Until—
Non-Dhamma does not shine forth, and Dhamma is not obstructed. Non-Vinaya does not shine forth, and Vinaya is not obstructed.
Those who speak non-Dhamma are not powerful, and those who speak Dhamma are not weak;
those who speak non-Vinaya are not powerful, and those who speak Vinaya are not weak. Therefore, I shall recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya together.
"Then the monks, each taking what is sufficient for himself, will discuss what is allowable and what is not.
Thereupon this evil one will bring upon himself his own refutation; he will no longer be able to lift up his head, and the Dispensation will become powerful and flourishing."

Thinking, "I must not tell anyone that such a thought has arisen in me," he reassured the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Therefore it was said: "Then the Venerable Mahākassapa... [omission] ...this is impossible. 233. *Citakaṃ*:
a funeral pyre made of sandalwood measuring one hundred and twenty cubits (*ratana*). *Āḷimpessāmā* means we shall cause the fire to be kindled. *Na sakkonti āḷimpetuṃ*:
even eight, sixteen, or thirty-two men were unable to set it ablaze, though they used pairs of torches held together.
Even though they took palm-leaf fans and fanned [the fire], and blew with bellows, performing various efforts, they were simply unable to make the fire catch.
"The intention of the deities" means that those deities, it is said, were the very deities who served the Elder.
For among the eighty great disciples, eighty thousand families who had gained confidence in their hearts became their attendants in the heavenly realm.

They were reborn there. Having gained confidence in the Elder, those deities who had been reborn in heaven, not seeing the Elder at that assembly, thought, "Where indeed is our family preceptor, the Elder?
Seeing him traveling along the road, they made this resolution:
"May the funeral pyre not ignite until our family preceptor, the Elder, has paid his respects."
When people heard this, they said: "Friends, it is said that a bhikkhu named Mahākassapa is coming with five hundred bhikkhus, thinking, 'I shall pay homage at the feet of the One of Ten Powers.
It is said that until he arrives, the funeral pyre will not ignite.
What kind of bhikkhu is he? Is he dark or fair, tall or short? When such a bhikkhu stands before us, what [can we do]?"
“[This is] the Parinibbāna of the One Possessing the Ten Powers,” some said, and went out to meet him with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings in their hands.
Others, having decorated the streets, stood waiting and looking toward the path of his arrival.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa approached Kusinārā... [and] paid homage with his head. It is said that the Elder [approached] the funeral pyre.
Having performed a circumambulation, he observed while reflecting: "The head is in this place;

the feet are in this place. Then, standing near the feet, he attained the fourth jhāna based on direct knowledge (abhiññā), and emerging from it, [he saw] the feet of the One Possessing Ten Powers, adorned with the mark of the wheel featuring a thousand spokes, together with the cotton cloths.
He made this resolution: “May these five hundred pairs of garments, the golden bowl, and the sandalwood bier, being divided into two parts, rest upon my head, the highest part of my body.

Simultaneously with the thought of his resolution, those five hundred pairs of garments, having been divided into two, emerged from beneath his feet like the full moon from between the clouds. The Elder [placed them] upon his head, which resembled a blooming red lotus.
Stretching out his hand, he firmly grasped the Teacher’s gold-colored feet as far as the ankles and placed them upon his own noble head.
Thus it is said: “He paid homage at the Blessed One’s feet with his head.
When the great multitude saw that marvel, they let out a great shout all at once and honored him with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings.

He paid homage according to his inclination. But when the Elder, the great multitude, and those five hundred bhikkhus had thus paid homage, there was no further need for a formal resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*).

By the power of the natural resolution alone, the Blessed One’s lacquer-colored soles of the feet were released from the Elder’s hands and remained in their original position upon the sandalwood logs and other materials, without moving at all.

They remained established; they stayed exactly where they were. For when the Blessed One’s feet emerged or entered [the earth], not even a thread of cotton, a weft-thread, a drop of oil, or a block of wood moved from its place.
Everything remained exactly as it was. But when he had risen and [the sun] had set...
When the feet of the Tathāgata had vanished like lightning and like the sun, the great multitude wailed with a great cry;
their compassion was even greater than at the time of the Parinibbāna itself.

As for the statement that "the funeral pyre of the Blessed One ignited by itself," this was said because no one was seen attempting to ignite it. However, through the power of the devas, it ignited all at once from every side.
235. "Only the bodily relics remained" means that because they previously existed as a single solid mass, it was called a "body" (*sarīra*).

Now, because they are scattered, it is said "bodily relics" (*sarīrāni*); the meaning is that the *dhātu*s (relics) remained, resembling jasmine buds, like polished pearls, and like gold. For the body of Buddhas with long lifespans is like a mass of gold.
There is only one [Buddha]. However, the Blessed One thought: "I shall not remain for long; I will attain final Nibbāna.

My teaching has not yet been spread everywhere. Therefore, even after I have attained final Nibbāna, let the great multitude, having taken even a relic the size of a mustard seed and having built a cetiya in their respective dwelling places, become destined for heaven by honoring it."
He resolved upon the dispersal of the relics. Now, how many of his relics were dispersed and how many were not?
These seven relics—the four canine teeth, the two collar-bones, and the cranial protuberance—were not dispersed; the remainder were dispersed.
Among them, the smallest relic was the size of a mustard seed, while the great relic in the center was the size of a split grain of rice.
"Extremely large, [yet] the size of a split mung-bean in the middle.
"Streams of water": streams of water the size of an outstretched arm, or the size of a shank, or even the size of a palm trunk, fell from the sky and extinguished it.
"From the water-palmyra trees": this was said with reference to the *sāla* trees standing surrounding [the fire].
For from the gaps between the branches of those [trees] as well, streams of water issued forth and extinguished [the fires].
The Blessed One’s funeral pyre was vast; even after splitting the earth all around it, columns of water the size of plowshares, resembling crystal ornaments, rose up and took hold of the pyre itself.
"With scented water" means having filled golden jars and silver jars [with it].

"With various kinds of scented water brought [for the purpose]. "They extinguished" means: having scattered it with golden and silver eight-handled fans, they extinguished the sandalwood funeral pyre.
And while the pyre was burning, from the gaps between the branches and the spaces between the canopies of the *sāla* trees standing surrounding it—
Flames burst forth from between the leaves; there is no leaf, branch, or flower that is not consumed by fire.

Even the termites and monkeys move only within the midst of the flames. This is like a discourse on the Dhamma concerning streams of water falling from the sky, streams of water issuing from *sāla* trees, and streams of water emerging after splitting the earth.
...the measure. Then, having extinguished the funeral pyre in this manner, the Malla kings had the fourfold fragrant preparations prepared in the assembly hall (*santhāgāra*);

they scattered flowers with parched grain as the fifth; they tied a canopy of cloth above, inlaid it with golden stars and the like, and hung down there garlands of perfumes, flower wreaths, and jewel necklaces, [extending] from the assembly hall as far as the place called the Diadem-Binding (*makuṭabandhana*).
The auspicious Sāla hall for the consecration of the Sīsa tree was prepared: on both sides, a fence of reed-mats was constructed;
above, a canopy of cloth was fastened and adorned with golden stars and the like; there, fragrant garlands, flower garlands, and jewel garlands were suspended;
bamboo poles the color of precious gems were used to hoist five-colored banners; and around the perimeter, wind-banners were displayed.
Having surrounded the area and well-swept the streets, they set out plantain trees and full water-pots, lit staff-lanterns,
and placed the golden casket containing the relics upon the back of a decorated elephant. Honoring it with garlands, perfumes, and other offerings,
