and performing excellent dances, they brought it into the city and placed it upon a couch made of sarabha wood in the assembly hall.

They held it [over him], except for the white parasol above. Having done this—“Then the Mallas of Kusinārā, having made a lattice-work of spears in the assembly hall, kept the Blessed One’s remains there for seven days”—all of this should be understood.
In that context, “having made a lattice-work of spears” means having had it surrounded by men holding spears in their hands. “A rampart of bows” means...
First, they had elephants circle about, striking trunk against trunk; then horses, neck against neck;
then chariots, tip of pole against tip of pole; then warriors, arm against arm.
Around the perimeter of these, they had bows circle about, striking tip against tip. Thus...
They established a guard for a distance of one *yojana* all around, making it as if covered with armored cow-hides for seven days.
It is with reference to this that it was said: “Having had a rampart of bows constructed.
But why did they do so? For during the two preceding weeks, they had [reserved] a place for the standing and sitting of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
While they were preparing hard food and soft food and arranging for excellent festivities, they found no opportunity [to attend].
Then it occurred to them: "We shall enjoy these seven days of excellent festivities;
however, it is possible that someone might come and take the relics while we are inattentive. Therefore, let us establish a guard."
"Let us play. They did exactly so. 236.
"The king heard"—how did he hear it? It is said that his ministers first heard of it and reflected upon it.
“The Teacher has indeed attained final nibbāna; he cannot be brought back again.
However, there is no one equal to our king in ordinary faith. If he hears this in this very manner, his heart will burst.
Moreover, the king must be protected by us. Having said this, they brought three golden bowls filled with the four sweet substances.
Having filled [the vessel] and gone into the presence of the king, they said this: “Your Majesty, we have seen a dream;
to counteract it, it is fitting for you to put on a fine linen double-garment such that only the space of the nostrils is visible, and then lie down upon a drona-measure of the four sweets.
Having heard the words of the ministers who act for his welfare, the king said, “So be it, dear ones.”
Having accepted [the request], he acted accordingly.

Then one minister, having removed his ornaments and disheveled his hair, turned toward the direction where the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, raised his hands in añjali, and said to the king: "Your Majesty, there is no being whatsoever who can escape death."
“That Blessed One, our Teacher, the increaser of our lifespan, the shrine-ground, the field of merit, the one who sprinkles the consecration—He has attained final Nibbāna at Kusinārā.
Upon hearing this, the king fainted; he emitted steam from a bowl of the four sweets.
Then, lifting him up, they laid him down in a second bowl. Having regained consciousness once more, he said: “Sirs, ...”
“What do you say? he asked. “The Teacher, Great King, has attained final Nibbāna,” they replied.
The king fell unconscious once more, and from the bowl of the four sweet substances, steam was released. Then, lifting him up from there as well, they laid him down in the third bowl.
Regaining consciousness again, he asked, “Dear ones, what do you say? “The Teacher, Great King, has attained final Nibbāna,” they replied.
The king fell unconscious once more; then, having lifted him up and bathed him, they poured water from jars over his head.

Having regained consciousness, the king rose from his seat, scattered his jewel-colored hair—which was perfumed with fragrances—over his back which was like a golden slab, and struck his chest with his hand.
With his well-rounded fingers, which were the color of coral sprouts, he [grasped] that which was the color of a golden *bimbi-saka* fruit.
Seizing him as if sewing his chest together, he entered the middle of the street in the guise of a madman, lamenting;
surrounded by adorned dancers, he departed from the city, went to Jīvaka’s Mango Grove, and having looked toward the spot where the Blessed One was seated and teaching the Dhamma, he thought:
"The Blessed One is omniscient; did he not sit in this very place and teach the Dhamma?"
“You dispelled the dart of my sorrow; you extracted the dart of my grief.
I have gone to you for refuge, yet now you do not even grant me a reply, Blessed One!

Having lamented thus again and again, he continued, “Is it not true, Blessed One, that on another occasion at such a time, [you said], ‘Accompanied by a great community of monks, you shall wander on tour across the surface of Jambudīpa’?”
"I used to hear you say, 'Go forth! but now I hear you speak of conduct that is unbecoming and improper for you.
Having spoken these and other such words, she recollected the virtues of the Blessed One with about sixty verses and thought: "It will not be accomplished by my mere lamentation;
I shall have the relics of the One Possessed of Ten Powers brought here. Thus she heard. And having heard this, because of her state of unconsciousness and so forth, [she fainted].
At the conclusion, he dispatched a messenger. With reference to that, the passage beginning with "Then the king" was spoken.
In this context, "he dispatched a messenger" means he sent both a messenger and a letter. Having sent them, [thinking], "If they give it, that is well;
if they do not give it, I shall take it by means of force," he arrayed his fourfold army.
He too had indeed set out. And just as Ajātasattu did, so too the Licchavis and others sent messengers and themselves set out with a fourfold army.
Among them, the Pāveyyakas lived in a city only three *gāvutas* distant from Kusinārā, being closer to it than all the others;
the Blessed One also went to Kusinārā only after entering Pāvā. Now, why [did he do so]?
If you ask why they did not arrive earlier: these kings had large retinues, and as they were forming their great entourages, they arrived later.

When all those inhabitants of the seven cities had come and surrounded the city of Kusinārā, saying, "Give us either the relics or battle," they said this to the Saṅgha and the assembly: "This Blessed One was ours..."
They gave this reply: "Gāmakkhetta. It is said that they spoke thus:
"We did not send the Teacher's message, nor did we go and bring it back. Rather, the Teacher himself came, sent the message, and had us summoned.
Furthermore, whatever jewel arises within your village territory, that is not [yours]."
"Give it to us! In the world with its gods, there is no jewel equal to the Jewel of the Buddha;
having obtained such a supreme jewel, we will not give it up. It is not only you who have drunk milk from your mother’s breast—we too have drunk milk from our mother’s breast.
You are not the only men—let us also be men! Thus they spoke to one another, asserting their sense of self.
Having sent back their reply, they let out mutual roars of pride. But had there been a battle, victory would have belonged to the people of Kusinārā alone. Why?
Because the deities who had come for the purpose of worshipping the relics became their partisans.
However, in the Canon it says: "The Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna within our village territory; we will not give [the relics] away."
“Let us give a portion of the Blessed One’s relics”—this much was said.
When this had been spoken, the brahmin Doṇa—having heard this dispute of theirs, thought:
“These kings are quarreling over the place where the Blessed One attained final nibbāna; this is indeed not fitting. Enough of this!”
Thinking, "I shall settle this by means of a debate," he went to those assemblies and groups and said this. What did he say?

Standing on elevated ground, he uttered what is called the "Donagajjita" (the Roar of the Don), consisting of two recitation sections. Regarding that, in the first recitation section, they did not understand even a single word.
At the conclusion of the second recitation section, [they thought]: "This sound is like that of a teacher!"
“The sound is like that of a teacher,” they all said, and they became free from fear.
It is said that among those born in noble families on the plains of Jambudīpa, there was generally no one who was not his pupil.
Then, having heard their words and perceiving that they were silent and free from fear, he spoke again, saying, “Listen, sirs! and recited these two verses.
In that context, "our Buddha" means our Buddha. Even before reaching the stage of Buddhahood, while fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs),

he was [known as] Khantivāda during his time as the ascetic Khantivāda, Dhammapāla during his time as Prince Dhammapāla, Chaddanta during his time as the elephant Chaddanta, Bhūridatta during his time as the royal nāga Bhūridatta, Campeyya during his time as the royal nāga Campeyya,
Saṅkhapāla during his time as the royal nāga Saṅkhapāla, Mahākapi during his time as the Great Monkey, and in many other such births.

Without harboring anger toward others, he practiced only patience; he praised patience alone. How much more so now that he has attained the characteristic of equanimity (*tādilakkhaṇa*) regarding both the desirable and the undesirable!
In every respect, our Buddha was one who spoke of patience;
for one such as him, it is certainly not fitting that there should be any physical conflict or injury to the body of the Supreme Person. Thus, "it is not fitting" means it is not good.
"Indeed, this is good. "Regarding 'in respect of the body' (sarīrabhāge)": it means for the sake of dividing the body, that is, as a cause for the partitioning of the elements (dhātu).
"'There might be a clash'": it is said that a clash of weapons must not be allowed to happen.
"'May all you worthy ones be united'": may all you worthy ones be united; do not be divided. "'In harmony' (samaggā)": by means of the body...
“Be united in mind, speech, and action; be of one accord and in harmony. ‘Rejoicing together’ means you should be mutually affectionate even in your hearts.
‘Let us divide into eight portions’ means let us divide the relics of the Blessed One into eight parts.
‘Of the Visionary One’ refers to the Buddha, who possesses the five kinds of vision. It is not only you who have faith, but the great multitude as well.”
Having stated many reasons why not even one among them was unfit to receive [a portion], he persuaded them.
"Having assented to those communities and groups" means having given his word to those various communities and groups who had assembled from here and there.
"Having divided the relics of the Blessed One into eight equal and well-portioned shares" means...
The sequence here is as follows: it is said that Doṇa, having given his consent, had the golden casket opened.
The kings arrived and, standing right by the casket, saw the relics which were golden in color; they thought: "The Blessed One was omniscient;

formerly we [beheld] your body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, inlaid with the six-colored rays of a Buddha, and resplendent with the brilliance of the eighty minor characteristics."
"We saw his body of golden hue; but now only the relics of golden hue remain.
This is not right for you, Blessed One," they lamented.
At that moment, the brahmin, perceiving their state of negligence, took the tooth relic and placed it within his turban.
He set them aside, and then afterwards divided them equally into eight portions with perfect symmetry.
All the relics amounted to sixteen *nāḷis* by ordinary measure; the inhabitants of each city received two *nāḷis*.
Even as the Brahmin was dividing the relics, Sakka, the lord of the devas, [thought]: "By whom, indeed, for the sake of cutting through the doubts of the world together with its gods..."
Looking at it, he thought, "The Blessed One’s right canine tooth was taken as a prerequisite for the discourse on the Four Noble Truths.
Seeing that it had been taken by a brahmin, he thought, "Even the brahmin will not be able to perform a fitting honor for this tooth;
I shall take it. Taking it from the place where it was wrapped, he placed it in a golden casket, brought it to the world of the gods, and enshrined it at the Cūḷāmaṇi Cetiya.
The Brahmin, too, having divided the relics but not seeing his own tooth—since it had been taken by theft—was unable even to ask, "By whom was my tooth taken?
Seeing that he was being blamed for his own fault, thinking, "Did you not yourself divide the relics?
Did you not know from the very beginning that your own relic existed?"—he said, "As for me..."
He was unable even to say, "Give me a portion.
Then, thinking, "This golden urn, too, has become a relic-receptacle, for by it the relics of the Tathāgata were measured; I shall build a stupa for this," he said, "Sirs, please give me this urn."
The Moriyas of Pippalivana, like Ajātasattu and the others, dispatched messengers and set out prepared for battle.
Regarding the description of the honoring of the relic-stūpa:
"In Rājagaha, he built a stūpa for the Blessed One’s bodily relics and held a great festival. How did he do so? From Kusinārā...
Having had a level road, eight usabhas wide, constructed all the way to Rājagaha— a distance of twenty-five yojanas—
just as the Malla kings had performed worship between the Makuṭabandhana and the Santhāgāra,
he likewise had such worship performed along the entire twenty-five-yojana road for the sake of the world’s lack of weariness everywhere.
Having displayed them in the marketplace and placed the relics in a golden casket, he had it enclosed within a lattice-work of spears;
then, he caused the people within his own realm, measuring five hundred yojanas in circumference, to assemble.
Taking those relics, they departed from Kusinārā, playing delightful music as they went, wherever golden-hued flowers appeared.
As they proceeded, they placed relics here and there and made offerings.
When those flowers were exhausted, they would travel on; and when the front of the chariot reached the rear part, for seven days they performed excellent festivities.
Thus, seven years, seven months, and seven days passed as they were bringing back the relics.
The holders of wrong view, lamenting, “Since the time of the Parinibbāna of the ascetic Gotama, we have been oppressed by this woman who has been enjoying herself to her heart’s content;
all our businesses have been ruined,” became corrupted in mind and were reborn in the states of misery, numbering eighty-six thousand.
The Arahants, having directed their attention and seen that the great multitude had been reborn in the states of misery due to their corruption of mind, [acted accordingly].

Thinking, “We shall cause Sakka, the king of the gods, to devise a means for bringing forth the relics,” they went into his presence, announced the matter, and said, “Great King, please devise a means for bringing forth the relics.
Sakka replied, “Venerable sirs, there is no ordinary person equal in faith to Ajātasattu;
he will not do my bidding. However, one who resembles a physician for Māra—”
"I shall manifest a terrifying sight, I shall raise a great clamor, and I shall cause possession by a *yakkha*, seizure, vomiting, and fever;
you should say, 'Great King, malevolent spirits are angry; have the relics brought forth!
and thus he will have them brought. Then Sakka did all of that.
The elders also approached the king and said, "Great King, non-human beings are enraged; have the relics brought forth.
The king replied, "Venerable sirs, my heart is not yet satisfied; nevertheless, let them be brought.
On the seventh day, the relics were brought. Having taken the relics thus brought, [they established] a stupa in Rājagaha.
And they held a great festival. The others also, having brought [relics] according to their respective strength, erected stūpas and held festivals in their own places.

"Thus it was in the past"—thus did the compilers of the Council later say that this distribution of the relics and the construction of the ten stūpas had occurred in Jambudīpa in the past. But when the stūpas were thus established, the Elder Mahākassapa...
Seeing an obstacle to the relics, he approached King Ajātasattu and said, "Great King, it is fitting that you establish a single relic repository.
"Very well, venerable sir, let me first undertake the work of enshrining; but how shall I bring back the remaining relics?
"Great King, the bringing of the relics is not your burden; it is our burden. "Very well."
“Venerable sir, please bring the relics; I shall establish a reliquary for them.

The Elder brought all the relics, setting aside only those portions intended for the service of various royal families. However, in Rāmagāma, the *nāgas* took possession of the relics, so there was no obstacle to them.
[He thought: “In the future, in the island of Laṅkā, at the Mahāvihāra, within the Mahācetiya...”

Thinking, "They will deposit [the relics]," they did not bring them from there; instead, having brought them from the remaining seven cities, they stood in the southeastern direction of Rājagaha and resolved:
"Let whatever stone exists in this place disappear; let the earth become perfectly pure;
let no water rise up."
The king had that spot excavated; then, having had bricks made from the soil thus extracted, he caused eighty cetiyas for the great disciples to be constructed.

When people asked, "What is the king having built here? they replied, "Cetiyas for the great disciples," and no one knew of their nature as repositories for relics. However, in that location, which was eighty cubits deep—
When [the relic chamber] was completed, he had a copper-iron house built there in the Thūpārāma, equal in size to the Cetiya-hall, after having a layer of iron spread beneath it.
He then had eight caskets made of yellow sandalwood and so forth, as well as eight reliquaries.
Then, having placed the Blessed One’s relics into a casket of yellow sandalwood, he [placed] that yellow sandalwood casket into another...
The yellow sandalwood casket [was placed] in another; thus, having combined those eight yellow sandalwood caskets together by this same method,
he placed those eight caskets upon the eight yellow sandalwood stupas,
the eight yellow sandalwood stupas upon the eight red sandalwood caskets, and the eight red sandalwood caskets upon the eight red sandalwood stupas.
Eight red sandalwood stūpas were placed in eight ivory caskets; eight ivory caskets were placed in eight ivory stūpas;
eight ivory stūpas were placed in eight caskets made of all kinds of gems; eight caskets made of all kinds of gems were placed in eight stūpas made of all kinds of gems;
eight stūpas made of all kinds of gems were placed in eight golden caskets; and eight golden caskets were placed in eight golden stūpas.
Eight golden stūpas were placed within eight silver caskets; eight silver caskets within eight silver stūpas;
eight silver stūpas within eight jewel caskets; eight jewel caskets within eight jewel stūpas;
eight jewel stūpas within eight ruby caskets; and eight ruby caskets within eight ruby stūpas.
He placed eight ruby stūpas in eight masāragalla caskets; eight masāragalla caskets in eight masāragalla stūpas; eight masāragalla stūpas in eight crystal caskets;
and eight crystal caskets in eight crystal stūpas.
The uppermost Phalikacetiya of them all was the size of the Thūpārāma-cetiya;
above that he had a house made of all kinds of gems built, above that one of gold, above that one of silver, and above that a house of copper.
There, having strewn sand made of all kinds of gems, [he placed] thousands of water-born and land-born flowers.

Having scattered [the offerings], he had all these—five hundred and fifty Jātaka tales, eighty great Theras, Great King Suddhodana, Queen Mahāmāyā, and the seven co-born ones—fashioned entirely out of gold.
He had five hundred and fifty full jars made of gold and silver set up, and he raised five hundred golden banners. [He also raised] five hundred golden lamps and five hundred...
Having had silver lamps made and filled them with fragrant oil, he placed cotton wicks inside them.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa, having made the resolution: "May the garlands not wither, may the scents not perish, and may the lamps not go out," had letters engraved upon a golden plate:
"In the future, a prince named Piyadāsa shall raise the royal parasol and become King Asoka, the Dharma-King; he will cause these relics to be widely distributed."
The king, having honored [the relics] with all his ornaments, departed while closing the door from the very beginning.
Having closed the copper-iron door and tied the key-ring to the pulling-rope, he placed a great heap of jewels right there and had an inscription engraved:
"In the future, may a poor king take this jewel and perform honor for the relics."
Sakka, the king of the gods, addressed Vissakamma: "Dear son, Ajātasattu has deposited the relics;
establish a guard over them here. Having been sent, he arrived and constructed a cage of interlaced branches.
He placed wooden figures inside that relic chamber, holding swords the color of crystal, and set it revolving with a speed like the wind.
Having joined the rollers and bound them with a single axle-pin, he constructed a stone enclosure all around in the shape of a brick hall,
covered it over with a single slab, filled it with earth, leveled the ground, and erected a stone stupa upon it.
When the enshrinement of the relics was thus completed, the Elder remained for the duration of his lifespan and then attained final nibbāna.
The king also departed according to his karma, and those men likewise passed away.
Later on, a prince named Piya-dāsa raised the royal parasol and became the righteous king named Aśoka;
having taken those relics, he caused them to be distributed throughout Jambudvīpa. How so? By relying upon the novice Nigrodha.
Having gained faith in the Teaching and having caused eighty-four thousand monasteries to be built, he asked the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus:
“Venerable Sirs, I have had eighty-four thousand monasteries constructed; from where shall I obtain relics? [The Bhikkhus replied:
“Great King, we hear that there is indeed a ‘relic-treasury,’ but it is not known whether it is in such-and-such a place. The King—
Having had the shrine at Rājagaha demolished and not finding the relic, he restored it to its former state;
then, taking with him the four assemblies—the monks, the nuns, the laymen, and the laywomen—he went to Vesālī. Not finding it there either, he went to Kapilavatthu.
Not finding it there either, he went to Rāmagāma. At Rāmagāma, the Nāgas would not allow him to demolish the shrine. At the shrine—

The pickaxe fell and broke into pieces. Thus, having failed to obtain the relics even there, and having broken open the shrines at Allakappa, Veṭhadīpa, Pāvā, and Kusinārā everywhere without obtaining the relics, they restored them to their original state.
Then, returning again to Rājagaha, they convened the four assemblies and asked: "Has anyone ever heard before that in such-and-such a place..."
He asked, "Where is the deposit of the relics?
Thereupon, one elder of two hundred years said, "I do not know where the deposit of the relics is;
however, when I was seven years old, my father, the Great Elder, had me take a flower-basket and said, 'Come, novice, between such-and-such trees...'"
“There is a stone stupa; let us go there. Having gone and made offerings, he said, “It is fitting for the novices to investigate this site.
[The novices] replied, “We know only this much, Great King.
The king said, “This very spot is it,” and having had the earth removed and the stone stupa and the soil cleared away, he saw the plastered floor beneath. Then, [he saw] the plaster...
Having had the bricks removed, he gradually descended into the monastery courtyard and saw sand made of the seven precious gems and wooden figures with swords in their hands, all revolving.

Summoning the yakṣa-servants and having them perform an offering ceremony, yet seeing neither the end nor the limit [of the treasure], he paid homage to the deities and said: "I shall take these relics and [distribute] them among the eighty-four thousand..."
“I shall deposit [the relics] in thousands of monasteries and pay them honor; let not the deities create obstacles for me,” he said.
King Sakka, the lord of the gods, while wandering on his rounds, saw him and addressed Vissakamma:

“Dear son, King Asoka, the righteous monarch, has entered the monastery courtyard with the intention of removing the relics; go and remove the wooden figures. He [Vissakamma], in the guise of a young boy from Pañcacūḷagāma—
Having gone and stood before the king with bow in hand, he said, "I shall take it away, Great King. "Take it, dear one," [the king replied].
Taking an arrow, he pierced the very joint, and everything was scattered.
Then the king took the key-ring for the fastening of the drawer and saw the cluster of jewels. "In the future, a poor king will take this jewel..."
Seeing these words again—“Let him pay honor to the relics”—he became enraged and thought, “It is improper to call a king such as I a ‘poor king.
After deliberating thus again and again, he had the door opened and entered the inner chamber.
The lamps that had been lit more than two hundred and eighteen years prior continued to burn just as they were.
Blue lotus flowers appeared as if they had been gathered and placed there at that very moment; the floral canopy seemed as if it had been woven at that very moment;
and the perfumes seemed as if they had been ground and set down just that instant. Then the King, taking up a golden plate, said:
"In the future, a prince named Piya-dāsa shall raise the royal parasol and become a righteous king named Aśoka; he [shall enshrine] these relics..."
Having recited, "He will cause it to spread," he said, "Behold me, O noble Elder Mahākassapa!
and, folding his left hand, he struck with his right hand.

Leaving only a small portion of the relic for veneration at that spot, he took the remaining relics, closed the relic-chamber as it had been previously sealed, and restored everything to its original state.
Having built the stone cetiya above and established the relics within eighty-four thousand monasteries, he paid homage to the Great Elders and asked:
"Am I, venerable sirs, an heir to the Buddha’s Dispensation? "Of what are you an heir, Great King?
You are an outsider to the Dispensation. "Venerable sirs, having spent ninety-six crores of wealth, [I have established] eighty-four..."
“Having had thousands of monasteries built, am I not an heir? Who else is an heir?
“You are indeed a donor of requisites, O Great King; but he who causes his own son and daughter to go forth is called an heir to the Teaching.
He then caused his son and daughter to go forth. Then the elders said to him, “Now, Great King, you are an heir to the Teaching.”

"Thus it was in the past": this means that in the past, even the enshrinement of the relics upon the surface of Jambudīpa occurred in this manner. The compilers of the Third Council also established this phrase.
However, the verses beginning with "Eight *doṇas* of the Visionary One’s body" were spoken by the Elders in the island of Tambapaṇṇi.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīghanikāya*.
The Commentary on the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta is finished.
4. The Commentary on the Mahāsudassana Sutta:
The Description of the Royal Capital Kusāvatī.
241. Thus have I heard: this is the Mahāsudassana Sutta. Herein, this is the commentary on the hitherto unexplained passages: "made entirely of precious gems.

In this context, each brick was made of one [of these]: one of gold, one of silver, one of beryl, one of crystal, one of ruby, one of masāragalla, and one of all precious gems; this is the wall among all walls.
It was sixty cubits in height on the inside. However, some elders say: "A city must be beautiful to behold for those standing inside and looking out;
therefore, the outermost wall was sixty cubits high, and the others were successively lower. Others say:
"It must be beautiful to behold for those standing outside and looking in; therefore, the innermost wall was sixty cubits high," [and the others were successively lower].
“The rest are successively lower,” so it is said. Some say: “It must be beautiful for those looking from both inside and outside;
therefore, the wall in the middle is sixty cubits high, and on both the inside and the outside there are three tiers each, successively lower.
*Esikā* means a pillar or post. *Tiporisaṅga* means one-and-a-half times the height of a man, measured by the hand of a man of medium stature.
"Five cubits [in height]"; by that, the meaning is that the enclosure is three *porisa* long, measuring fifteen cubits. How, then, are they situated?

Along the outer side of the city, one stands leaning against each pillar of a great gate, one against each pillar of a small gate, and three each in the intervals between the great gates and the small gates. Among the rows of palm trees, those made of all kinds of jewels...
Regarding the statement that "one of the palm trees is made of gold," it should be understood that this refers precisely to the characteristics already described for the walls;

the same principle applies to the leaves and fruits as well. Furthermore, those rows of palm trees were eighty cubits in height, standing one by one within the intervals between the walls on a level ground surface covered with scattered sand.
*Vaggū* means clever and beautiful. *Rajanīyo* means capable of causing delight. *Khamanīyo* means that even when heard for a whole day, it is endured and does not cause loathing.
*Madanīyo* means that which generates pride, intoxication, and the intoxication of man.
*Pañcaṅgikassa* refers to that which is endowed with these five factors: *ātata*, *vitata*, *ātatavitata*, *susira*, and *ghana*. Among these, *ātata*...

"Struck" (*nāta*) refers to single-sided musical instruments such as drums covered with leather. "Stretched" (*vitata*) refers to those with two surfaces. "Tightly stretched" (*ātatavitata*) refers to those covered on all sides.
"Hollow" (*susira*) refers to flutes and the like. "Solid" (*ghana*) refers to cymbals and the like. "Well-tuned" (*suvinīta*) means well-adjusted by means of tightening, loosening, and so forth.
"Well-beaten" (*suppaṭitāḷita*) is for the purpose of knowing whether it remains within the proper measure.
"Of that which was well-beaten. "Accompanied by those who were highly skilled" means played by those who were clever and proficient at playing instruments.

"Gamblers" refers to those who gamble with dice. "Drunkards" refers to those intoxicated by liquor; they are the very same people as those previously mentioned, but here they are designated as such because of their repeated desire for drink.
"They entertained themselves" means they sported about, dancing while moving their hands or feet.
Commentary on the Wheel-Treasure (Cakkaratana-vaṇṇanā): 243.
"Of one who has bathed his head" means of one who has bathed with scented water together with the head. "Observer of the Uposatha" means one who has undertaken the Uposatha precepts.
"Having gone to the top of the excellent palace" means having gone to the upper part of the excellent palace after having eaten a fine meal. Of the excellent palace...
Having entered the inner chamber on the upper floor while reflecting upon the precepts, at that time the king—
having already given a great almsgiving by bestowing a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] early in the morning, having bathed his head with sixteen jars of scented water,
and having finished his breakfast— drew up his pure upper robe over one shoulder, sat cross-legged on the royal couch in the upper palace, and...
Sitting there, he sat reflecting upon his own accumulation of merit consisting of acts such as giving.

This is the natural law for all wheel-turning monarchs (*cakravartin*). While they were thus reflecting, the divine Wheel-Treasure appeared—arisen from the temperature-conditioned by the aforementioned meritorious kamma, resembling a cluster of blue sapphires, as if splitting the surface of the eastern ocean and as if adorning the sky.
It appeared. It appeared in exactly the same way for Mahāsudassana as well. This is called "divine" because it is endowed with divine power (*dibbānubhāva*).
It has a thousand spokes, thus it is "thousand-spoked" (*sahassāra*). Together with its rim and together with its hub, it is "with-rim" (*sanemika*) and "with-hub" (*sanābhika*).
It is complete in all its aspects, thus it is "perfect in every respect" (*sabbākāraparipūra*).
In this context, it is a wheel (*cakra*) and, in the sense of producing delight (*rati*), it is a jewel (*ratna*); thus, it is the "Wheel-Jewel" (*cakkaratana*).
Furthermore, that by which it is said to be "with a hub" (*sanābhika*) is made of sapphire (*indanīla*);
in its center, however, is a tube made of the finest silver (*sāra-rajata*), which shines as if laughing with a row of pure, glossy teeth, like the orb of the moon with its central void.
On both outer edges, it is enclosed by a silver band. Furthermore, on the bands surrounding its nave and rim, the demarcation lines appear clearly divided at appropriate and inappropriate places.
This, first of all, is the perfection of its nave in every respect.
Furthermore, those which were described as "the thousand spokes together with the rim" are composed of the seven precious gems and are endowed with radiance like the rays of the sun;
even their joints, the divisions of the gems, and the lines are clearly discernible as being perfectly well-proportioned.
This is the perfection of its spokes in every respect.
As for that rim by which it is called "with a rim" (*sanemika*), it is made of coral, deep red, pure, and glossy, as if mocking the splendor of the mass of rays from the rising sun.

At its joints, lines of circular demarcation appear, well-proportioned and beautiful like bands of Jambu-river gold, radiant with the hue of twilight. This is the perfection of its rim in every respect.
On the back of its rim, however, between each set of ten spokes, there is a coral handle that is hollow inside like a bamboo reed,
latticed with circular openings, and capable of catching the wind; when it is struck by the wind as if well-tuned,
its sound is as charming, delightful, lovely, and intoxicating as that of a fivefold musical ensemble.
Furthermore, above that coral shaft was a white parasol, flanked on both sides by two rows of flower garlands;
thus, with a hundred coral shafts adorned by such a surrounding rim and naves,
each accompanied by a hundred white parasols encircled by two rows of flower garlands, there were within the two central tubes of the hubs—
There are lion-faces from which two clusters of pearls hang down, as large as palm trunks, as beautiful as a mass of full-moon rays, and bordered by red woolen tassels resembling the young sun;
they seem to mock the splendor of the Ganges’ course through the sky.
As these revolve together with the Wheel-Treasure (cakraratna) in the air, the three wheels appear as if they are turning in unison.
This is its complete fulfillment in every respect.
Now, this [offering], being thus fulfilled in all aspects, occurs when people, having naturally finished their evening meal,
are seated on seats prepared at the doors of their respective houses and are engaged in conversation and discourse in the streets, crossroads, and so forth.
It was as if it were beautifying the sky with children playing upon it— neither too high nor too low, near the tops of the forest groves—
causing the ears of living beings to tingle from the distance of twelve leagues with the sweet sound of the tips of its tree branches,
and from the distance of a league with a splendor blazing from a multitude of various radiances.
As if drawing in the eyes [of all beings], as if proclaiming the power of the merit of the Wheel-turning Monarch (cakravartin), it comes forward toward the royal capital.
Then, at the mere sound of that Wheel-treasure, [the people wonder]: "From where does this sound come? To whom does this sound belong?"
As those people, their hearts directed toward him, were looking toward the eastern direction, one among them said to another:
"Behold, sirs, this marvel! Previously this full moon rose alone;
but today it has risen accompanied by its own double. For indeed, like a pair of royal swans, this pair of full moons appears in succession, one after the other."
“He is leaping up into the vault of the sky! Another said to him, “What are you saying, friend?
Have you ever before seen two full moons rising together? Is this not the sun that has risen, bearing a mass of golden rays and possessing a shaft of light like a peacock’s feather?
Another, having laughed, said to him, “Are you mad? Was it not just now—”
"The sun has set; how could it rise again following this full moon?
Surely this must be the celestial mansion of some meritorious person, resplendent with the combined radiance of many jewels.
As they all moved away, others spoke thus: "Sirs, why do you prattle so much? This is not the full moon."
"It is neither the sun nor a celestial mansion. These do not possess such glorious splendor; rather, this must be the Wheel-Treasure (cakkaratana).
While the people were thus conversing, the moon’s orb vanished and that Wheel-Treasure appeared before them.
Then, when they ask, "For whom has this arisen?", there arise those who say, "It has not arisen for anyone else;
surely it has arisen for our Great King, who has fulfilled the duties of a Wheel-turning Monarch.
Then both that great multitude and whoever else sees it all follow after the Wheel-treasure alone. And as for that Wheel-treasure—
As if wishing to announce his arrival for the sake of the king alone, he circumambulated the city seven times along the very top of the wall;
then, having paid respectful homage to the king’s inner palace, he stood as if struck by a bolt at a spot facing the northern lion-window of the palace—
a place where it was easy to offer worship with perfumes, flowers, and the like— and remained there.

While he was thus situated, the king saw a mass of radiance entering through the openings of the windows and other apertures, illuminating the interior of the palace with the brilliant luster of various colored gems; seeing this, a longing arose within him to behold it.
His attendants also approached and informed him of the matter with affectionate words. Then the king’s body was suffused with intense joy and gladness.
Having unfastened his couch and risen from his seat, he went near the lion-window;
seeing that Wheel-Treasure, he reflected upon the thought beginning with, "I have indeed heard this," and so forth. All of this occurred for Mahāsudassana exactly in the same way.
Therefore it is said: "Having seen [it], King Mahāsudassana... 'Might I perhaps be a king, a wheel-turning monarch?'"
Regarding the statement, "In that case, he is a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti)," to what extent does one become a wheel-turning monarch?
Even when the Wheel-treasure has risen into the air by only a finger’s breadth or two finger-breadths and is in motion,
in order to show what must now be done for its continued turning, he said, "Then, Ānanda," and so forth.
244. Therein, "having risen from his seat" means having risen from where he was sitting and approached the vicinity of the Wheel-Treasure (*cakraratna*).
"Taking the golden pitcher" means lifting up the golden pitcher with a spout like the trunk of an elephant.

"Immediately following, King Mahāsudassana together with his fourfold army"—for indeed, after all wheel-turning monarchs have been sprinkled with water, [the proclamation is made]: "May he conquer!"...
Immediately upon the words "Sire, the Wheel-Treasure," the Wheel-Treasure rises up into the air and sets in motion.
At the very moment it begins to turn, that king becomes known as a Cakkavatti (Wheel-turning Monarch).
Once the Wheel-Treasure has set in motion, the king, following after it, mounts the excellent vehicle of a Cakkavatti and ascends into the air. Then, for him—
Then the retinue, holding parasols, yak-tail whisks, and other items, as well as the women of the inner apartments, together with the subordinate royal commanders and others,
each accompanied by their own military forces adorned with various types of armor such as tunics and breastplates,
shining with the luster of diverse ornaments, and decorated with raised banners and flags, ascended into the air and surrounded the king.
Furthermore, for the purpose of winning over the people, the king’s officers caused drums to be beaten throughout the city streets, proclaiming:
"Sirs, our King’s Wheel-Treasure has appeared; assemble, adorned and well-attired according to your respective means!
Then the great multitude, by their very nature, abandoned all other duties at the mere sound of the Wheel-Treasure and [prepared] perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
Having gathered together as if assembled, they all rose up into the air and surrounded the king.
Indeed, whoever conceived the desire to go with the king, he too became situated in the sky.
Thus, the assembly was twelve yojanas in length and breadth. Therein, not even a single person had a mangled or broken body, nor were their garments soiled.
Or rather, there was none. For a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti) is surrounded by purity.
The retinue of a wheel-turning monarch, moving through the air like vidyādhara men, appears like jewels scattered upon a surface of sapphire.
It was exactly so for Mahāsudassana as well. Therefore it is said: “Immediately following him was King Mahāsudassana together with his fourfold army.”
Furthermore, that Wheel-Treasure moves through a region of the sky that is neither too high nor too low above the tops of the trees.
Thus, those who desire the flowers, fruits, and foliage of the trees are able to grasp them with ease;
and likewise, those standing on the ground are able to discern, "This is the king, this is the viceroy, this is the commander-in-chief."
Regarding the places and postures, whoever wishes to go by whichever means does so by that very means. Those devoted to crafts such as painting proceed while performing their respective tasks;
for just as on the earth, so too all their activities are accomplished even in the air.
Thus, having taken the retinue of the Wheel-turning Monarch, that Wheel-treasure [proceeds] by its left side.
Leaving Sineru, it proceeds across the upper portion of the great ocean to Pubbavideha, measuring seven thousand yojanas in extent.

Therein, upon a delightful region of ground that is pure, level, and well-provided with shade and water—where food and requisites are easily obtained, which is capable of accommodating an assembly of thirty-six yojanas in circumference and twelve yojanas in depth—one finds [the city]. Above that [region]...
That wheel-treasure stands as if fixed to its axle.
Then, by that sign, the great multitude descends and establishes their residence, performing all their duties such as bathing and eating according to their pleasure.
For Mahāsudassana, it was exactly the same. Therefore it is said: "In whatever place, Ānanda, the wheel-treasure comes to rest..."
There King Mahāsudassana took up residence together with his fourfold army.
When the Wheel-turning Monarch had thus taken up residence, the kings who were there, upon hearing that "an enemy's army has arrived," did not assemble their forces and prepare for battle;
for immediately upon the appearance of the Wheel-treasure, [the world was already subdued].
There is no being whatsoever who would dare to raise a weapon against that king with the perception of him as an enemy.
Such is the majesty of the Wheel-Treasure.
Indeed, by the power of the Wheel, for that king—
All enemies come under his subduing;
because he is the subduer of enemies (Arindama),
that is called the "wheel" (cakra) of that lord of men.
Therefore, all those kings, having taken gifts appropriate to their own royal splendor and power, approached that king with bowed heads;

performing worship at his feet by means of the radiance of the jewels in their crests, they responded to his command with such words as, “Come, O Great King,” and so forth. It was the same for Mahāsudassana.
They did exactly so. Therefore it was said: “And those, Ānanda, who were in the eastern direction... ‘Instruct us, Great King. In this context, *svāgataṃ* means “a good arrival.
For when one has arrived, people grieve; when he has departed, they rejoice. When one has arrived, they rejoice; when he has departed, they grieve.
You are such a one who rejoices at an arrival and grieves at a departure. Therefore, your coming—

"Welcome," it is said. When this has been said, the wheel-turning monarch does not say, "Provide such-and-such a tribute for me every year," nor does he take away the wealth of one person to give it to another.
Rather, by means of wisdom appropriate to his status as a Dhamma-king, he examines [the situation] regarding the taking of life and so forth, and with loving-kindness...

With a gentle voice, he taught the Dhamma by way of such passages as: “Behold, dear ones, this act of taking life, when practiced, cultivated, and frequently repeated, leads to rebirth in hell,” and so forth; then he gave the exhortation: “No living being should be killed,” and so on.
King Mahāsudassana did exactly the same; therefore it is said: “King Mahāsudassana spoke thus: ‘No living being should be killed... and so on.
"Eat what you have been served. But do all [the king's men] accept this advice of the king? Even among the Buddha’s followers, not all accept it;
how much less would they accept it from a king? Therefore, those who are wise and discerning accept it, while all others merely become his subordinates.
For this reason, he said, "But as for those, Ānanda... and so forth.
Then, after this advice had been given to the inhabitants of Pubbavideha and they had finished their morning meal, that Wheel-Treasure, by the power of the Wheel-turning Monarch,
rose up into the air and plunged into the eastern ocean. And as it plunged in,
the expansion of the waves subsided like a king of serpents who has withdrawn his hood upon smelling the scent of an antidote.
Having offered the sacrifice, as the water of the great ocean receded, it retreated for the distance of a *yojana* and stood within the sea like a wall of beryl.

At that very moment, as if desiring to behold the royal majesty of merit (*puññasiri*), various jewels scattered upon the surface of the great ocean came from here and there and filled that region. Then, that royal assembly...
Having seen that surface of the great ocean filled with various jewels, he takes them from his lap or other parts as he pleases;
and when the assembly has taken the jewels as they please, the Wheel-treasure turns back.
As it turns back, the assembly is in front, the king is in the middle, and the Wheel-treasure is at the rear. And that water of the ocean, as if being enticed—
As if unable to endure separation from the glory of the Wheel-Treasure, it approaches, striking continuously against the edge of its rim. Thus,
having conquered Pubbavideha as far as the eastern great ocean, the Wheel-turning Monarch,
desiring to conquer Jambudīpa as far as the southern ocean, [proceeds] by means of the direction indicated by the Wheel-Treasure.
By means of the Path, it proceeds toward the southern ocean. Mahāsudassana likewise went in that very same manner. Therefore it was said:
“Then, Ānanda, the Wheel-Treasure, having plunged into the eastern ocean and emerged from it, proceeded toward the southern direction.”
Furthermore, the manner of his proceeding as he thus advanced, his encampment, the arrival of rival kings,
their receipt of instructions, his plunging into the southern ocean, and the taking of jewels from the ocean waters as they receded—
all this is to be understood in the same manner as previously described.
Having conquered that Jambudīpa measuring ten thousand yojanas, he crossed back from the southern ocean and proceeded,
in the same manner previously described, to conquer Aparagoyāna measuring seven thousand yojanas;
having likewise completely subdued it up to its ocean boundary, he crossed back from the western ocean and [proceeded to] the eight thousand yojanas [of Uttarakuru].
Having likewise gone to conquer Uttarakuru and having similarly conquered that region as far as the ocean’s edge, he crosses back over from the northern ocean.
At this point, the sovereignty over the earth bounded by the four oceans has been attained by the Wheel-turning Monarch.
Having thus achieved victory, in order to display the glory and prosperity of his own kingdom, he and his retinue leap upward into the expanse of the sky.
Beholding the four great continents— surrounded by five hundred minor islands each, like four lotus ponds amidst a variegated forest of fully blossomed *paduma*,
*kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* lotuses— the wheel-treasure returns in due order to its own royal capital by the very path indicated by the wheel-treasure itself.
Then, that wheel-treasure stands as if adorning the gate of the inner palace.
When that Wheel-Treasure was thus established, there was no need for torches or lamps within the royal palace;
the radiance of the Wheel-Treasure alone dispelled the darkness of night. And for those who desired darkness, there was indeed darkness.
All this occurred in exactly the same way for Mahāsudassana as well. Therefore...
It is said: “Having plunged into the southern ocean... such a Wheel-Treasure (cakkaratana) appeared.
246. When the Wheel-Treasure has thus appeared, the ministers of that Wheel-turning Monarch [go to] the place where his ordinary auspicious elephant is kept.
Having had the ground leveled and made even, and having had it smeared with fragrant scents such as yellow sandalwood, he fashioned it like a celestial palace:
strewn below with various colorful and fragrant flowers, and above adorned with a canopy decorated with lovely flower garlands interspersed here and there with golden stars.
Then he exclaimed: "O King, the arrival of such a noble elephant-treasure!"
"Reflect upon this," they said. Having given a great gift and undertaken the precepts according to the method previously described, he sat down reflecting upon that excellence of merit.

Then, impelled by the power of his merit, and desiring to experience that special honor, [the Bodhisatta] came from either the Chaddanta or the Uposatha lineage, his pure white body adorned with feet, neck, and face as radiant as the orb of the rising sun.
A pre-eminent elephant, standing on seven feet, with well-proportioned limbs and members, possessing a beautiful trunk like a blooming red lotus,
endowed with psychic power like a yogi capable of traveling through the air, and resembling a silver mountain with its flanks colored by powdered emerald,
arrived and stood at that spot. Coming from the Chaddanta lineage, he was the youngest of all.
The one who comes from the family of those observing the Uposatha is the eldest of all. However, in the Pāḷi, it is stated simply as "the Nāga king Uposatha.
It is said in the Aṭṭhakathās that the one called "Nāga king" is not for anyone's use; rather, it is the youngest of all who comes.
This [king] appears to those who have fulfilled the conduct of a Cakkavatti and are reflecting in the manner prescribed for Cakkavattis.
But Mahāsudassana himself came to the place where his ordinary auspicious state-elephant was kept, had that elephant removed, and stood there.
Therefore it is said: “Furthermore, Ānanda... [as before] ...the king of elephants.
Having seen that elephant-treasure thus manifested, the elephant-keepers and others were thrilled and delighted, and with great speed—

Having gone, they informed the king. The king, arriving in great haste, saw him and, with a mind full of faith, thought, "How excellent indeed is this elephant-vehicle, were it only to become tamed! As he was thinking this, he extended his hand.
Then, like a domestic cow and calf, the elephant lowered its ears and, displaying a state of gentleness, approached the king.

The king desired to mount it. Then his attendants, understanding his intention, brought that elephant-treasure after having it equipped with a golden banner, golden ornaments, and covered with a net of gold.
Without even sitting upon it, the king ascended by means of a ladder made of the seven precious gems, his mind intent on traveling through the air.
Simultaneously with the arising of that thought, that king of elephants—
Like a royal swan, it traverses the blue expanse of the sky, which is like a mass of radiance from sapphire gems.

Then the entire royal retinue follows in the same manner as described for the movement of the wheels. Thus, the king together with his retinue, having traveled across the entire earth even before breakfast, returns to the capital.
Such is the great power of the Wheel-turning Monarch’s elephant-treasure.
It was so. For Mahāsudassana, too, it was exactly like that. Therefore it is said: "Having seen [it], for the king... it appeared. 247.
Now, when the elephant-treasure had thus appeared, the ministers of the Wheel-turning Monarch [prepared] the place for the ordinary auspicious horse-rite.
Having had the surface of the palace floor made clean and having adorned it, they, as before, roused their enthusiasm for the purpose of anticipating the king’s arrival.

He, having likewise performed acts of giving, honoring, and hospitality as before, and having undertaken the precepts and observances, sat comfortably on the palace terrace and recollected his success through merit. Then, impelled by the power of that merit, from the Sindhu breed—

He is resplendent with a mass of white autumn clouds interlaced with streaks of lightning; he has red feet and a red beak, and his body is pure, glossy, dense, and compact like a cluster of moonbeams.
Because he is endowed with a black head—black in color like a crow’s neck or a sapphire—he is called "Black-Headed" (*Kāḷasīsa*).
Because he is endowed with hair that resembles *muñja* grass, soft, round, and growing in even pairs, as if perfectly arranged and set in place, he is called "Muñja-Haired" (*Muñjakesa*).
The horse-king named Valāhaka, possessing the power of flight, arrived and alighted at that spot.
He came to Mahāsudassana just as the elephant-treasure had done. All the rest should be understood according to the same method explained for the elephant-treasure.
Referring to such a horse-treasure, the Blessed One said: "And furthermore," and so forth.
248. Now, regarding the description of the jewel-treasure:

when the Wheel-turning Monarch has thus manifested the horse-treasure, it is four cubits in height, with a circumference equal to that of a wagon’s nave, and adorned on both sides from the edge of the hub with two golden lotuses featuring strings of perfectly pure pearls emerging from them.
Adorned and surrounded by eighty-four thousand gems, that jewel-treasure comes from Mount Vepulla, spreading a splendor like that of the full moon encircled by the host of stars.
When it has thus arrived and been placed within a net of pearls, it is raised sixty cubits into the air by means of a succession of bamboo poles;
and during the night, for a distance of one league all around, it illuminates the area.
The light pervades the space, by which that entire space becomes filled with light as if at the time of sunrise.
Then, thinking it was "day," the farmers set about their plowing, the merchants opened their shops, and various craftsmen engaged in their respective works.
For Mahāsudassana, too, everything occurred exactly in that same way. Therefore it is said: "Again..."
"And furthermore, Ānanda, ...pe... the jewel-treasure appeared.
Thus, for the wheel-turning monarch to whom the jewel-treasure has thus appeared, it is the specific cause for his excellence in the pleasures of the sense-sphere.
The jewel of the woman (itthiratana) appears. Either they bring his chief queen from the Madda royal family, or she comes of her own accord from Uttarakuru through the power of merit.
As for her remaining excellence, it has been described in the Canon itself in such passages as:
"Furthermore, Ānanda, the jewel of the woman appeared to King Mahāsudassana; she was beautiful and lovely to behold. Etc.
In this context, "abhirūpā" means one who possesses a form that is superior in its complete configuration.
"Dassanīyā" means that even while being seen, she causes the eyes to close; therefore, she should be looked upon even by setting aside other duties and distractions.
"Pāsādikā" means that even while being seen, she gladdens the mind through the influence of joy. "Paramāya" means supreme, because she brings about such confidence. "Vaṇṇapokkharatāya" means...
"By beauty of complexion. "Endowed with" means possessed of. She is "handsome" because she is neither too tall nor too short;
"lovely to behold" because she is neither too thin nor too stout; "gracious" because she is neither too dark nor too pale.
She is "endowed with the highest excellence of complexion" because she surpasses human color yet has not reached the divine color. For the radiance of human complexion—
It does not issue forth externally; however, it issues forth even to a very great distance for the devas.
Furthermore, the radiance of the body illuminates an area measuring twelve cubits. Regarding its lack of excessive length and so forth:
by the first pair [of qualities], there is perfection of height; by the second pair, perfection of circumference; and by the third pair, perfection of color.
...are said. Furthermore, by these six [qualities], the absence of bodily failure is expressed; by the phrase "surpassing human appearance," bodily perfection is expressed.
"Like a tuft of cotton or a tuft of kapok" refers to a tuft of cotton or a tuft of kapok that has been beaten a hundred times and placed in clarified butter (*sappimaṇḍa*).
"Cool" means during the king's cool season. "Warm" means during the king's warm season. "Sandalwood fragrance" means...
The fragrance of fresh, well-pounded yellow sandalwood, blended with the four ingredients, wafts from his body at all times.

Regarding the phrase "the scent of blue lotuses wafts": at times of laughing and speaking, an exceedingly sweet fragrance wafts from his mouth, like that of a blue lotus blossoming at that very moment.
Furthermore, in order to demonstrate conduct befitting her physical excellence—which was endowed with perfection of form, touch, and fragrance—the passage beginning with "But she...
was spoken. In that context, she is called *pubbuṭṭhāyinī* because, upon seeing the king, she rises first from her seat as if scorched by fire.
When he is seated, she performs such duties as fanning him with a palm-leaf fan.
She who, having done [something], afterwards falls down or sits down is "one who follows behind" (*pacchānipātinī*). She who responds with the words "What shall I do for you, O Lord?
is "one who gives an affirmative reply" (*kiṃkārapaṭissāvinī*). She who conducts herself and acts only in a way that is pleasing to the king is "one who behaves agreeably" (*manāpacārinī*).
She who speaks only what is dear to the king is "one who speaks kindly" (*piyavādinī*).
Now, in order to show that "her conduct was indeed for the sake of the purification of her being, and not out of deceit," he said, "But she...
and so forth. Therein, "she did not transgress" means she did not act by overstepping [the bounds]; it is said that, setting aside the king, she did not desire any other man even in her mind.
In this context, those qualities mentioned at the beginning of her description, such as “beautiful,” and at the end,

such as “rising early,” are merely her natural (pakati) qualities. However, those qualities such as “surpassing human beauty” should be understood as having arisen through the power of past karma, manifesting from the appearance of the Wheel-Treasure onwards, based upon the merit of a Wheel-turning Monarch.
Or rather, from the moment the Wheel-Treasure appeared, she became perfected in every respect, beginning with her beauty. Therefore he said: “Such a woman-treasure appeared.
250. Now, regarding the description of the Householder-Treasure:
for the King, the Wheel-turning Monarch, once such a woman-treasure had thus appeared, there were duties to be performed concerning wealth.
The householder-treasure appears for the purpose of ensuring that [the wheel-turning monarch] proceeds according to his pleasure.
By nature he is of great wealth, born into a family of great wealth; he is a merchant-householder who increases the king’s hoards of riches.

Accompanied by the power of the wheel-treasure, there appears in him a divine eye born of the ripening of kamma, by means of which—even within the interior of the earth, within a distance of one league—[he perceives all things].
He sees a treasure; having seen that wealth, he goes with a joyful heart, entertains the king with riches, and accomplishes all his financial requirements.
He accomplished them for Mahāsudassana in exactly the same way. Therefore it was said:
"Furthermore, Ānanda... such a householder-treasure appeared."
The Description of the Jewel of the General (Pariṇāyakaratana-vaṇṇanā) 251.

When the Wheel-turning Monarch has thus manifested the Jewel of the Householder, the Jewel of the General appears, capable of managing all the king’s affairs. He is the king’s eldest son; by his very nature, he is wise.
He was learned, wise, and discerning. Relying on the power of the king’s merit, however, the knowledge of others’ minds arose in him through the power of his own karma.
By means of this, he was able to discern the mental dispositions of the twelve-league royal assembly and distinguish between what was beneficial and what was harmful to the king;
seeing his own such power, he too was filled with joy at heart.
He invited the king by instructing him in all his duties. He did exactly the same for Mahāsudassana as well. Therefore it is said:
“Furthermore... the Counsellor-treasure appeared.
In that context, “to place where it should be placed” means to appoint [him] to each respective position.

Commentary on the One Endowed with the Four Kinds of Knowledge: 252. “Samavepākiniyā” means that which causes even digestion. “Gahaṇiyā” means by the fire element born of karma. In this regard, there are two types:
one for whom food is digested as soon as it is eaten, and another for whom it remains right there, like a meal placed in a covered vessel. Both of these...
One who does not possess such a state is not endowed with even digestion. However, one for whom the desire to eat arises again at the time of the meal is endowed with even digestion.
*Commentary on the Dhamma-Pāsāda and Pokkharani*
253. "He had it made" does not mean that he had it constructed after having a drum beaten in the city and assembling a multitude of people;
rather, as soon as the thought arose in the king's mind, eighty-four thousand lotus ponds sprang up by bursting through the earth.
It is with reference to these that this was said. "With two railings" means that one was surrounded only by a boundary of bricks.
"By one [fence]" refers to the boundary delimiting the extent of the monastic cell (pariveṇa). Why did it occur to him?
It is said that one day, seeing a great crowd of people going along after having bathed and drunk, the Great Man thought: "These people are walking as if they were madmen.
If they had flowers as ornaments here [on their heads], it would be excellent. Then it occurred to him.
In that context, "blooming in all seasons" means that a flower blooms in only one season. However, he thought, "I shall act in such a way that it will bloom in all seasons.

As for "he caused to be planted": he did not have various kinds of lotus seeds and so forth brought from here and there and planted; rather, everything was accomplished for him by the mere arising of his thought. That...
The world thought, "It was planted by the king. Therefore it is said: "He caused it to be planted.
From that time forth, the great multitude went about as if sporting in a festival, adorning themselves with various kinds of garlands from both water and land.
Then the king, desiring to make the people even more thoroughly established in happiness than before, thought: "What if I were now to [provide] for these..."
Having considered the provision of comfort for the people with the words beginning, “On the banks of the lotus ponds,” he performed everything accordingly.

Therein, they bathed him: one massaged his body, another prepared the fragrant powders, another brought water for him as he bathed on the bank, and another received his garments and gave them back to him.

"He established [the festival]"—how did he establish it? Having had ornaments made suitable for both women and men, King Mahāsudassana gave a gift by setting aside everything except for the women themselves for the purpose of entertainment, and he caused a drum to be beaten, saying, "Enjoy this!
Then the great multitude came to the banks of the lotus pond.
Having bathed, changed his clothes, and anointed himself with various perfumes, he wore a garland variegated with ornaments; then, having gone to the head of the almsgiving,
whatever among the many kinds of rice gruel, cooked rice, and snacks, as well as the eight kinds of drinks,
anyone desired, that he ate and drank, and having put on fine, multi-colored linen garments, he attained prosperity.
Having experienced them, those who possess such things leave them behind; but those who do not possess them take them and go.

Even regarding elephant and horse carriages and the like, they sit upon them and travel a short distance, after which those who have no need leave them behind, while those who do have need take them and go.
Having lain down upon excellent couches and enjoyed their prosperity, those who have no need leave them behind.
Those who desire them take them and go; even after enjoying prosperity together with women, those who no longer desire them leave them behind, while those who do desire them take them and go.

And even after adorning themselves with the seven kinds of jewel ornaments and enjoying prosperity, those who no longer desire them leave them behind, while those who do desire them take them and go. That gift, too, arises again and again.
It was indeed being given. The inhabitants of Jambudīpa had no other business; they went about their lives merely consuming the king’s gifts.

Then the brahmins and householders thought: “Even though this king gives such a gift, he does not have anything brought to him, saying, ‘Give me rice and so forth,’ or ‘Give me milk and so forth. Yet it is not as if we do not [give] to the king.”
"It is appropriate for them to remain silent [thinking], 'He causes it to be brought,'" they collected much wealth and presented it to the king.
Therefore, he said: "Then, Ānanda, the brahmins and householders," and so forth.
Why did they reflect in this way? Because from some house little was brought, while from others much was brought; as that was being gathered together—
"—'Is it only from your house that beautiful things are brought, and not from my house?
Is it only in your house that there is much, and not in mine?'—in this way, even the sound of quarreling might arise; let it not arise. Thus they reflected.
"Come here, friend! means "Come here, comrade! Having bestowed a name upon the palace, they called it "Dhamma."

He gave the command. Vissakamma, however, having asked back, "O Deva, how great shall the celestial palace be?", and being told, "Let it be one *yojana* in length and half a *yojana* in width, and let it be made entirely of all kinds of gems," replied to him, "So be it;
may your word be auspicious. Having thus assented and informed the Dhamma King, he constructed it. Therein, thus—
"Bhadante tava" means "It is well for you, Ānanda. "Having heard" (paṭissutvā) means having accepted; the sense is "having spoken.

"By silence" (tuṇhībhāvena): desiring, "There will be an opportunity for me to practice the duty of a recluse," he consented by means of silence. "Made of heartwood" (sāramayo) means made of sandalwood heartwood.
257. Regarding the phrase "with two railings" (*vedikā*): here, one railing was at the top of the dome (*uṇhīsa*), and one was at the bottom, at the edge of the base.
258. "Difficult to look upon" (*duddikkha*) means difficult to behold; the sense is that it was hard to see because of the perfection of its radiance.

"It steals away" (*musati*) means it carries off [the gaze], makes it tremble, and does not allow it to remain steady. "Risen up" (*viddha*) means elevated; it refers to having become distant due to the clearing of clouds.
"Meaning": *deva* means "in the sky.
259. As for "he had it made": he did not have it made by commanding, "I am having a lotus pond made in this place; you must demolish your houses.
Rather, by the mere arising of his thought, the earth split open and such a lotus pond appeared.
"Ahosi. "With all desires" means with all desired objects; he satisfied the recluses with the requisites of a recluse, and the brahmins with the requisites of a brahmin.
The commentary on the first recitation section is finished.
Commentary on the Attainment of Jhāna:
260. "Possessed of great psychic power" means endowed with a great supernormal power (iddhi) consisting in the manifestation of eighty-four thousand lotus ponds by the mere arising of a thought.
"Of great majesty" means because of the greatness of those very things to be experienced.
"Endowed with great power. *Seyyathidaṃ* is a particle; its meaning is "of which three? Regarding *dānassa*:
it is the relinquishing of what has been acquired. Regarding *damassa*: in the Āḷavaka Sutta, wisdom is described as "taming" (*dama*).
Here, it refers to the observance of the Uposatha performed by one who tames himself. Regarding *saṃyamassa*: it is virtue (*sīla*).
The Commentary on the Former Exertions of the Bodhisatta:
His former exertion is to be understood by way of this context. It is said that in the past, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a family of householders.
At that time, while the dispensation of the living Buddha Kassapa still existed, there was an elder dwelling in the forest.
The Bodhisatta, having entered the forest by his own kamma, saw the Elder;
he approached him, paid homage, and after observing the places for sitting and walking, he asked: "Does the noble one dwell right here, venerable sir?
Upon hearing, "Yes, lay follower," he thought: "It is fitting to build a leaf-hut for the noble one right here."
Leaving aside his own work, he pounded building materials, constructed a leaf-hut, thatched it, plastered the walls with clay, fitted a door, and prepared a bed of straw;
then he sat to one side, wondering, "Will he make use of it, or will he not?
The Elder, having come from within the village, entered the leaf-hut and [sat] upon the bed of straw.
He sat down. The lay follower also came, paid homage, and sat nearby, asking, "Is the leaf-hut comfortable, venerable sir?
"It is comfortable, good sir; it is suitable for one who has gone forth. "Will you stay here, venerable sir? "Yes, lay follower," he replied.
Knowing from his manner of acceptance that he would indeed stay, [the lay follower thought], "He must come regularly to my house door."
Having made him promise, he said, "Venerable sir, grant me one boon. "Lay follower, those who have gone forth have transcended boons.
"Venerable sir, please tell me what is allowable and what is blameless. "Speak then, lay follower.
"Venerable sir, in a place where people reside permanently, they expect one's arrival on auspicious or even inauspicious occasions; they become angry if one does not come."
"Therefore, even if you go to another place where you have been invited, you must complete your meal duties only after entering my house. The Elder consented.

He spread out a mat of straw in the leaf-hut, arranged a bed and a bench, set up a backrest, placed a footstool, dug a lotus-pool, constructed a walking path, scattered sand over it, and [prepared for] the deer to come.
Seeing them strike against the wall and causing the plaster to fall, he surrounded it with a thorn hedge.
Seeing them descend into the lotus pond and agitating the water, he built up a rampart of stones within and surrounded the exterior with a thorn hedge;
then, along the inner edge of the enclosure, he planted rows of palm trees. Seeing them agitating the well-swept area of the Great Walkway (mahācaṅkama), he...
Having enclosed even the walking path with a fence, he planted a row of palm trees along the inner edge of that fence.
Having thus completed the dwelling, he provided for the Elder a triple robe, almsfood, medicine, utensils for use,
a water-strainer, a pepper-shaker, a nail-cutter, a needle, a walking stick, sandals, a water-pot, and an umbrella.
He gave him a lamp-stand, a water-strainer for removing dirt, a water-filtration cloth, a water-pot, a bowl, a platter, and whatever other articles of use belong to those who have gone forth;
there was no requisite that the Bodhisatta had not given to the Elder.
Guarding his moral precepts and observing the Uposatha, he attended upon the Elder for as long as he lived. The Elder—
Dwelling right there, he attained *arahat*-ship and attained final *nibbāna*.

The Bodhisatta, too, having performed meritorious deeds for the duration of his lifespan, was reborn in the world of the gods; passing away from there and coming to the human world, he was reborn in the royal capital of Kusāvatī and became King Mahāsudassana.
"Thus, even though merit is not very great, when performed in a worthy field..."
"It brings great fruition; therefore, that which ought to be done should be discerned by one who possesses wisdom.
"Great array" refers to a large gabled hall made of silver. Desiring to dwell there, he went [to it].
Up to this point, these are sensual thoughts (*kāmavitakka*); you must turn back from this point on, for beyond this, it is not your domain. This—
"A meditation hall, indeed; this is not a place for you to dwell. Thus he turned back those three thoughts right at the door of the gabled house.
Regarding the "first jhāna" and so forth, there is no separate requirement for the preliminary work (*parikamma*) of the kasiṇas.
If there is need for a blue kasiṇa, one uses a blue gem; if there is need for a yellow kasiṇa, gold; if there is need for a red kasiṇa...
When there is a need for a white *kasiṇa*, even when looking again and again at a red gem, only the *kasiṇa* appears as silver.
Regarding the phrases beginning with "accompanied by loving-kindness" (*mettāsahagatena*), everything that ought to be said has already been stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.
Thus, in the Pāḷi, only the four jhānas and the four immeasurables (*appamaññā*) are mentioned. However, the Great Man (*mahāpurisa*) [possesses] all...
Having produced the eight attainments and the five higher knowledges, he enters those attainments in fourteen ways— by way of forward and reverse order, and so forth—
and sustains himself solely by the bliss of attainment, just as a bee that has entered a honeycomb is sustained by the sweet nectar.
[The Description of the Eighty-four Thousand Cities, etc.]

263. "With Kusāvatī as the chief royal capital" means that the royal capital Kusāvatī was the foremost and most excellent among those cities. "The offering of food" refers to the food that was to be brought forward. 264.
Why did he think in this way—"for every hundred years, for every hundred years"? Because he became weary of the sound; for it is said, "Sound is a thorn to one who has attained meditative absorption.
Therefore, the Great Man was weary of the sound. Then, why did he think, "Let them not come"?
"Does he not speak? [The answer is: He does not speak so that they might not think, "Now the King does not see us; we shall no longer receive our regular allowance.
Thus he speaks so that such a thought might not arise in them. Commentary on the Visit of Queen Subhaddā (265):
When did this occur? It was on the day of the King’s passing away. At that time, it is said, the deities thought thus.
—“Let the king not perform the funeral rites for one who is without a protector; let him perform them surrounded by his many wives, daughters, and sons.
Then, having turned the queen’s attention toward this, they caused such a thought to arise in her.
“Yellow garments”—it is said that these were naturally pleasing to the king, therefore he said, “Put those on. “Stay right here, O Queen,” he said to the queen.
"This place called the meditation-hall is not a dwelling for you to live with; it is my place for finding the joy of meditation. Do not enter here.
Then this thought occurred to him:
"In this world, sentient beings indeed shine with great splendor at the time when death is near; therefore, this king..."
Seeing that his faculties were serene, it occurred to her: "May there not be a death for the king.
Not wishing for his death, she thought, "I shall speak of his virtues now and create an appearance of staying [with him].
Having thought this, she said, "These are yours, O King," and so forth. In that context, "generate desire" means: produce affection; take delight.
“Have regard for life; have longing for life; create attachment and craving”—this is the meaning.
Thus, O Queen, you said to me: “We women, Your Majesty, do not know the proper conduct toward those who have gone forth;
what can we say, Great King? This was said by the queen, who had thought, “This one has gone forth.”
When she had spoken thus, he said: “O Queen, you should address me in this way,” and so forth.
“Censured” means censured by Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, disciples, and other wise and learned men. For what reason?

Because dying with longing [for sensual pleasures] is the cause for being reborn within one’s own household as a spirit, a dog, a goat, an ox, a buffalo, a rat, a cock, a spider, a centipede, and so on.
268. Then, Ānanda, Queen Subhaddā, having wiped away her tears—having gone to one side, wept and wailed, and wiped away her tears—spoke thus.
269. [Regarding the phrase] “of the householder”:
why did she say this? It is said that their great prosperity was like that of Soṇa the merchant’s son and others.
It is said that for Soṇa, the merchant’s son, a single bowl of food was worth two hundred thousand [pieces of gold].
Thus, after they had eaten such food, there would arise for a moment a drowsiness from food, a stupor from food, and exhaustion from food. 271.
"At that time, wherever I dwell" means that at that time, the place where I live is but a single city; as for the remaining ones...
Sons, daughters, and so forth, as well as male and female slaves, lived there. The same principle applied to the palaces and gabled chambers.
Even regarding couches and such, he used only a single couch, while the rest became the property for his sons and others. Among the women, only one attended upon him;
the others were merely part of the retinue. As for clothing, thinking "I am wearing it," he dressed himself in only a single pair of garments.
It belongs to the one hundred and sixty thousand men, numbering eighty thousand more, who wander about surrounding him.
