By the phrase "I eat," he shows that he eats only a measure of boiled rice the size of a *nāḷika*, while the remainder belongs to the eight hundred thousand men, numbering forty thousand more, who wander about surrounding him. This is called "a single cooking for all."
Indeed, it is sufficient for ten people.

Furthermore, these eighty-four thousand cities, eighty-four thousand palaces, and eighty-four thousand gabled chambers were produced as a byproduct of a single leaf-hut. The eighty-four thousand couches were for the purpose of reclining.
The eighty-four thousand elephants, the eighty-four thousand horses, and the eighty-four thousand chariots were produced as the result of having given couches for the purpose of sitting.
The eighty-four thousand gems were produced as the result of having given a single lamp.
The eighty-four thousand lotus ponds were produced as the result of having given a single lotus pond.
They were produced as a result of the gift of eighty-four thousand women, eighty-four thousand sons, eighty-four thousand householders,
and various articles for personal use, including bowls, platters, water-pots, strainers, needles, nail-clippers,
keys, ear-cleaners, foot-stools, sandals, umbrellas, and walking-sticks. Eighty-four...
It should be understood that the eighty-four thousand cows were produced as the result of giving gifts of milk products;

the eighty-four thousand million garments for wearing and wrapping were produced as the result of giving gifts of clothing; and the eighty-four thousand pots of rice were produced as the result of giving gifts of food.

272. Thus the Blessed One, having related in detail Mahāsudassana’s prosperity from the beginning, spoke the words beginning with “passa Ānanda” while lying on his parinibbāna bed, showing that all of it was like children playing with sandcastles.
In this context, “vipariṇatā” means that through the abandonment of its original nature, it has reached a state of non-manifestation, like an extinguished lamp. Thus...
"Impermanent, Ānanda, are conditioned phenomena. Thus they are impermanent in the sense of non-existence after having come to be.

To this extent, the Blessed One—just as if a man were to build a ladder against a seven-hundred-cubit-tall *campaka* tree, climb it, take a *campaka* flower, and then descend while letting go of the ladder—likewise builds the ladder.
As if having ascended the great splendor of Mahāsudassana, which reaches many hundreds of thousands of millions of years in height, he has descended,
taking hold of the characteristic of impermanence while letting go of the ladder, as it were. For this very reason, in the past,
when King Vasabha was at Ambalaṭṭhikā on the eastern side of the Lohapāsāda, while the Dīgha-bhāṇaka Theras were reciting this Sutta...
Having heard this, he thought: "What has my noble uncle said here? He is merely describing the prosperity found in his own place of eating and drinking.

Then, at the moment it was said, "Thus, Ānanda, conditioned phenomena are impermanent," he thought, "Seeing this, the One with Vision must have spoken thus," and he contracted his left hand and [reached out] with his right hand.
Clapping his hands, with a heart full of joy, he gave his approval, saying, "Excellent! Excellent!

"In this way it is impermanent" means that, like bubbles on water and so forth, it is devoid of permanence. "In this way it is not a source of consolation" means that, like water drunk in a dream or sandalwood paste smeared [on the body], it is devoid of comfort.
"He should cast off the body" means he should discard the body. Now, as for the casting off or the tending of another's body...
"Or rather, Ānanda, it is because the Tathāgata has abandoned the defilements," he said. Having said this, he addressed the Elder again:
"The majesty of a wheel-turning monarch, Ānanda, vanishes on the seventh day after a king has gone forth into homelessness.
But for Mahāsudassana, on the very seventh day after his passing away, the walls made of the seven treasures and the palm trees made of the seven treasures [vanished]."
"The eighty-four thousand lotus ponds, the Palace of Dhamma, the Lotus Pond of Dhamma, and the Wheel-Treasure—all these disappeared.
Regarding the elephant and the other treasures, however, this is the natural law: those whose lifespan has been exhausted pass away together with it.

If there remains a residue of life, the Elephant-Treasure goes to the Uposatha elephant-herd; the Horse-Treasure goes to the Valāhaka horse-herd; and the Jewel-Treasure [goes to the Maṇikāra jewel-herd].
He goes to Mount Vepulla itself. The majesty of the Woman-Treasure vanishes.
The sight of the Householder-Treasure becomes normal once more. The discernment of the Counsellor-Treasure perishes.
"This is what the Blessed One said"—this refers to everything that the Blessed One spoke, both what is recorded in the Canon and what is not. The rest is self-evident.
Thus ends the commentary on the Mahāsudassana Sutta in the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya. 5.
The commentary on the Janavasabha Sutta.
Commentary on the *Nātikiya* and other grammatical works, §§273–275.
Thus have I heard: this is the *Janavasabha Sutta*. Herein is the commentary on the words not [previously] explained:
“In every direction, in every region” means all around, in every region. “Attendant” refers to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha.
“Among attendants. “In rebirths” means in the rebirths resulting from knowledge, wisdom, and merit. “In Kāsī and Kosala” means in Kāsī and in Kosala; the sense is:

in the kingdom of Kāsī and in the kingdom of Kosala. This method applies everywhere. However, he does not predict [the future] regarding the six kingdoms of Aṅga, Magadha, Yona, Kamboja, Assaka, and Avantī.
And among these sixteen great provinces, it is only in the first ten that [he predicts].
He explains. "The inhabitants of Nātika" means those dwelling in the village of Nātika.
"By that" means by that state of being a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) and so forth.

"Having heard" means having heard the Blessed One’s explanation of the question as he was explaining it after delimiting [the matter] with his omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*); thus, having reached a definitive conclusion regarding their status as non-returners and so forth, they [attained] that state of being a non-returner and so forth.
They were uplifted in mind. In the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), however, it is stated: "By him" means "by those Nādikans.
In this sense, the particle *na* is merely an expletive. 277.
Regarding the phrase "appearing as if praising the Blessed One": "Oh, the Buddha! Oh, the Dhamma! Oh, the Saṅgha! Oh, the Dhamma!"
"He was well-expounded"—thus he passed away while praising him in this way. "May many people have faith":
"Our father, mother, brother, sister, son, daughter, and friend—he ate with us, he slept with us, and we did such and such pleasing things for him;
it is said that he was a non-returner, a once-returner, or a stream-enterer! Oh, how wonderful!"
"Ah, well said!"—thus the great multitude might attain confidence.
278. "Gati" means the course of knowledge. "Abhisamparāya" likewise means the future course of knowledge. "Addasā kho" (he indeed saw): how many people did he see?
Twenty-four hundred thousand. 279. "Upasantapadisso" means one who sees with tranquility. "Bhātiriva" means it shines exceedingly; it radiates intensely.

"Of the faculties" means of the faculties with the mind as the sixth. "I saw them, Ānanda," he said, referring to neither ten, nor twenty, nor a hundred, nor a thousand, but exactly no more and no less than two million four hundred thousand.
*Janavasabha-yakkha-vannanā* (The Commentary on the Janavasabha Yakkha)
280. But when I saw that so many people had been liberated from suffering by relying on me, a powerful joy arose;

my mind became serene. Because of the serenity of the mind, the blood originating from the mind became serene. Because of the serenity of the blood, the six faculties, with the mind as the sixth, became serene.
Having said all this, he then spoke the words beginning with "Then, Ānanda. In that passage:

Because he became a stream-enterer after hearing the Blessed One’s discourse on the Dhamma, having become the leader of one hundred thousand and ten thousand people, he was therefore named Janavasabha.
"Seven from here" means seven times after passing away from this world of the gods; "seven from there" means seven times after passing away from that world of humans.
"Fourteen rounds of saṃsāra": this refers to all fourteen sequences of aggregates (*khandha*).

"I know my dwelling" means I know my dwelling by way of birth. "Where I formerly dwelt" means where, having entered into companionship with Vessavaṇa among the devas and having been a king among humans, I dwelt prior even to this present existence. Formerly, thus...

And because he had lived [the holy life], having now become a stream-enterer and performed much merit in the three bases, he was capable of being reborn in a higher realm through the power of that merit;
yet, due to the strength of his attachment to the place where he had lived for so long, he was reborn right here.
"And my hope is established" means: "I am a stream-enterer"—having said this, he did not pass away while remaining heedless.
"I spent [that time]. But I have now begun insight meditation for the sake of the path of the once-returner.

I dwell with such enthusiasm, thinking, 'I shall penetrate [the truth] this very day, this very day!'"—this he says to show. "From that time forward" refers to the day he became a stream-enterer upon his first sight [of the Buddha] in the Laṭṭhivana Grove.
"From that time forward, venerable sir, for a long time I have known non-falling, non-falling."

"Starting from that day, venerable sir, I recognize—meaning, I am aware of—the state of being subject to non-falling (avinipātadhammatā), which was attained through the path of stream-entry in the Laṭṭhivana grove over a long period consisting of my previous fourteen existences.
"Not wonderful" (anacchariyaṃ) means "not at all wonderful" (anu-acchariyaṃ). While reflecting again and again, [he thought]: "This indeed is wonderful..."
While traveling on some business, I saw the Blessed One on the road. This too is wonderful:
that which was heard directly from the Great King Vessavaṇa as he spoke to his own assembly is exactly as it was seen by the Blessed One.
There are two conditions: the fact of having seen him on the road, and the desire to report what was heard directly from Vessavaṇa.

The Description of the Assembly of the Gods (Devasabhāvaṇṇanā) 282. Regarding the phrase "assembled": for what reason did they assemble? It is said that they assemble for four reasons: for the purpose of gathering [the community] at the commencement of the rains retreat;

for the purpose of gathering [the community] at the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā); for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma; and for the purpose of enjoying the festival of the Pāricchattaka tree. Therein:

"Regarding 'one's own entry into the rains': on the full moon of Āsāḷhī, the gods in the two divine worlds assemble in the Sudhamma divine assembly hall and deliberate: 'In such-and-such a monastery, one bhikkhu has entered the rains;
in such-and-such a monastery, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, or a thousand bhikkhus have entered the rains.'"
"In this very place, ensure that the protection of the noble ones is well-arranged"—thus was the invitation for the commencement of the rains retreat made.

At that time as well, they assembled for this very reason. "This is their seat" means this is the seat for those four Great Kings. When they are thus seated, only then does our own seat become available.
"For whatever purpose" means for the purpose of the commencement of the rains retreat. Having reflected upon that purpose, having deliberated upon that purpose—

Having considered this for the sake of protecting the Saṅgha of monks dwelling in the forest, [the Great Kings] consulted with the four Great Kings, saying, "Provide protection here and there for the Saṅgha of monks who have settled in these places.

Having been thus addressed, the thirty-three sons of the gods speak; it is the Great Kings who are said to have spoken those words. Likewise, the thirty-three sons of the gods give instructions in return.
The others are called "words of subsequent instruction. In both instances, however, the particle *pana* is merely a grammatical filler (*nipāta*). "Not yet arrived" means not having come.

283. "Exalted" means vast and great. "Divine power" refers to that radiance of all the deities—which emanates from their garments, ornaments, celestial mansions, and bodies—that pervades twelve *yojanas*.
Furthermore, the bodily radiance of those of great merit pervades one hundred *yojanas*.
Having transcended that divine power, he says, "This is indeed a precursor for Brahmā.
Just as the dawn is the forerunner and the precursor to the rising of the sun, even so he illustrates that this is likewise a "precursor" for Brahmā.
(Commentary on the Sanaṅkumāra-kathā)
284. "Unsurpassable" (*anabhisambhavanīya*) means unattainable; the meaning is that the gods of the Thirty-three do not see it.

"Within the range of vision" (*cakkhupathe*) means within the clarity of sight or within the field of perception (*āpāthe*). It is said that he is not surmountable—that is, unattainable—within the range of the gods' vision;
he does not overcome them. For the deities below are gross compared to the deities above.
They were able to see their own forms exactly as they had been fashioned; "attainment of feeling" (*vedapaṭilābha*) means the attainment of joy.
"Now anointed in kingship" means just now anointed in kingship. This matter, however, should be illustrated by the story of Duṭṭhagāmaṇi Abhaya:
it is said that after he had conquered thirty-two Tamil kings and attained his consecration in Anurādhapura, he was filled with joy and gladness.
For a month he could not find sleep; therefore, he informed the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus, saying: "Venerable sirs, I cannot find sleep. [The Saṅgha replied:
"In that case, Great King, observe the Uposatha today. He then observed the Uposatha.
The Saṅgha went and dispatched eight Abhidhamma specialists, saying: "Recite the *Cittayamaka*. They went and...
“Lie down, Great King,” they said, and began their recitation. As he listened to the recitation, the king fell asleep.

The elders departed, thinking, “Let us not wake the king. On the second day, having awakened at sunrise, the king did not see the elders and asked, “Where are the venerable ones? [They replied: “Because you were falling asleep...”
"Knowing that they have gone. He said, "Sir, for my noble grandfather there is no medicine called 'ignorance' regarding children;
indeed, he knows even the medicine for sleep.
[He spoke] as one resembling the Gandhabba Pañcasikha. It is said that [he acted] like the Gandhabba deva-son Pañcasikha.
All deities regard their own personal existence as "mine. Therefore, Brahmā too appeared after having fashioned for himself a similar personal existence.
"He sat cross-legged" means he sat having folded his legs in the cross-legged posture.
"Relaxed" means well-liberated and unobstructed. "Intelligible" means making the meaning known. "Melodious" means sweet and soft.
"Savanīyo" means worthy of being heard, pleasant to the ear. "Bindū" means a single, compact mass. "Avisārī" means well-dispersed and not scattered.
"Gambhīro" means originating from a deep source starting from the base of the navel, not originating from the striking of the tongue, teeth, lips, palate, or throat.
For if it originates in such a way, it is neither sweet nor does it carry far. "Ninnādo" is like the sound of a great rain-cloud or a large drum.
It is like a sound accompanied by resonance. Furthermore, it should be understood here that each subsequent word is the very meaning of each preceding one.
"According to the assembly" means he makes himself understood only as many times as there are people in the assembly;

his voice reverberates only within the assembly and does not flow outside of it. The phrase beginning with "Whatever beings... is for the purpose of showing that he has practiced for the welfare of many people.
He says: "They have gone for refuge. He does not say this with reference to those who have gone for refuge in whatever way or manner;
rather, he speaks with reference to those who have taken refuge with their doubts resolved. "Filling the host of Gandhabbas" means they fill the assembly of Gandhabba devas.
Thus, from the time our Teacher appeared in the world, [they have been filling] even the six celestial worlds and so forth, like grinding flour.
He said that the assembly was so dense it was like a filled bamboo tube or a thicket of reeds and cane.
287. Regarding the commentary on the developed bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*):
"As well as these have been well-expounded by that Blessed One"—that is, as they have been well-expounded by my Teacher, the Blessed One.

...as well as being well-expounded. Regarding the term *iddhipādā* (bases of psychic power): here, it should be understood that they are "powers" (*iddhi*) in the sense of succeeding (*ijjhanatthena*), and "bases" (*pādā*) in the sense of being a foundation (*patiṭṭhānatthena*).

"By means of the abundance of powers" (*iddhipahutāya*) means by means of the sufficiency of powers. "By means of the variety of powers" (*iddhivisavitāya*) means by way of the manifestation of various powers;
what is meant is that mastery has been attained through repeated practice. "By means of the versatility of powers" (*iddhivikubbanatāya*) means by way of the transformational display of powers.
This is for the purpose of showing [the jhāna] by way of its various aspects.

Regarding the phrases "endowed with the volitional formations of striving associated with concentration through desire" (*chandasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgata*) and so forth: concentration caused by desire, or concentration in which desire predominates, is "concentration through desire" (*chandasamādhi*);

this is a designation for the concentration obtained by making the desire to act (*kattukamyatā-chanda*) the dominant influence. The formations that constitute striving are "volitional formations of striving" (*padhānasaṅkhārā*).
This is a designation for the energy of right effort that accomplishes the four tasks.

"Endowed with" means possessed of both concentration through desire and the volitional formations of striving. "Base of psychic power" (iddhipāda) is so called either in the sense of success (*ijjhana*) by way of the term for accomplishment, or by this other method:
beings succeed, prosper, and reach excellence by means of it; thus it is "success" (*iddhi*).

The meaning is that for those [states] that have reached number and are associated with the consciousness of direct knowledge, the remaining collection of consciousness and mental factors serves as the "foot" in the sense of being the basis for the volitional formations of desire-concentration (*chanda-samādhi-padhāna-saṅkhāra*). For this has been said:

"The 'basis of psychic power' (*iddhipāda*) is, for one who has become thus, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness. According to this method...
The meaning should also be understood through the synonyms.

For just as concentration obtained by making desire the dominant factor is called "concentration of desire," so too concentration obtained by making energy, mind, or investigation the dominant factor is called "concentration of investigation.
Furthermore, access concentration is the foot, and the first absorption is the psychic power; together with its access, it is [the first absorption].
The first jhāna is the "foot" (pāda) and the second jhāna is the "success" (iddhi); thus, the meaning here should be understood as "the foot" in the prior stage and "success" in the subsequent stage.
The detailed discussion on the bases of success (iddhipāda) has been set forth in the *Visuddhimagga* and the *Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā*.
However, some say: "Success is accomplished; the basis of success is unaccomplished. In order to refute their argument:

In the Abhidhamma, the section known as the *Uttaracūḷikavāra* is recited: “There are four bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*): the basis of psychic power consisting of desire (*chanda*), the basis of psychic power consisting of energy (*viriya*), the basis of psychic power consisting of mind (*citta*), and the basis of psychic power consisting of investigation (*vīmaṃsā*).
Therein, what is the basis of psychic power consisting of desire?
Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna that is leading to liberation, tending toward the abandoning [of defilements], for the sake of abandoning views—first...”
On the stage of attainment, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is difficult to practice and slow in direct knowledge.
At that time, whatever desire, longing, wish-to-act, and wholesome desire for the Dhamma there is—this is called the basis of psychic power consisting of desire;
all remaining phenomena are associated with the basis of psychic power consisting of desire. These, moreover—
They have come by way of the supramundane alone. Therein, the Elder Raṭṭhapāla brought forth the supramundane Dhamma making zeal his primary focus;
the Elder Soṇa making energy his primary focus; the Elder Sambhūta making mind his primary focus;
and the Venerable Mogharāja making investigation his primary focus.
In this context, just as among the four sons of ministers who were living in dependence on the king while aspiring to a position—
one of them, having conceived a desire for service and having understood the king’s inclination and preference,
served him day and night and, by pleasing the king, attained that position— so too should one who produces supramundane states through the predominance of zeal be understood.
But another—thinking, “Who can attend [to the king] day after day?
When a task arises, I shall satisfy him through my own exertion”—was dispatched by the king to a rebellious border region; having crushed the enemy through his exertion, he attained a high position.
Just as he did, so too should one who produces supramundane states through the burden of energy be understood.
One person thinks: "Even attending [the king] day after day, and even being covered by a breastplate of arrows, is merely a burden;

I shall win favor through the power of spells. Because he has practiced the science of the Khattavijjā, he wins the favor of the king by means of the arrangement of spells and attains a high position.
Just as he does, so too should one who produces supramundane states through the burden of the mind be understood.
Another—thinking, "What is the use of these services and such? Kings indeed grant positions to those endowed with noble birth;
if he grants one to such a person, he will grant one to me"—attains a position solely by relying on his noble birth.
Just as he did, so too should one be understood as a producer of supramundane states by relying on perfectly pure investigation and taking investigation as the primary burden.
*Anekavihitam* means manifold. *Iddhividham* means a category of psychic power (*iddhi*).
288. Regarding the commentary on the threefold attainment of the opportunity:
*Sukhassādhigamāya* means for the sake of attaining the bliss of jhāna, the bliss of the path, and the bliss of the fruit.
“Associated” (*saṃsaṭṭha*) means having a mind that is conjoined (*sampayutta*). “Noble Dhamma” (*ariyadhamma*) means the Dhamma taught by the Noble One, the Blessed Buddha.
“Hears” (*suṇāti*) means he hears it either from the presence of the Teacher or as it is being taught by monks, nuns, and others.

“Attends to it properly” (*yoniso manasikaroti*) means he attends to it by way of method, path, and cause, such as through [the contemplation of] “impermanence,” and so forth. “Proper attention” (*yoniso manasikāra*) is defined as follows: [...]* *Note: The provided source text appears to be truncated at this point.*

“Attention to means, attention to the path—attention that turns the mind toward, repeatedly turns it toward, directs it toward, attends to, and focuses upon what is impermanent as ‘impermanent,’ what is suffering as ‘suffering,’ what is non-self as ‘non-self,’ and what is foul as ‘foul’;
or attention in accordance with the truths—this is called wise attention. When this wise attention had been thus spoken of, [the Buddha asked: “What is its function?”
The meaning is "he undertakes. "Unmixed" means he dwells unmixed with both sense-objects (*vatthukāma*) and the defilements of sensual desire (*kilesakāma*).

"Happiness arises" means the happiness of the first *jhāna* arises. "Joy beyond happiness" means that for one who has emerged from attainment, joy arises repeatedly on account of the *jhāna*-happiness. "Exultant" refers to the mode of being satisfied.
“Weak rapture” (*dubbalapīti*). “Gladness” (*pāmojja*) is a more powerful rapture and joy.

“The first attainment of an opportunity” means that the first jhāna, having suppressed the five hindrances, remains having taken its own opportunity; therefore it is called “the first attainment of an opportunity.
Regarding the term “gross”: let the bodily and verbal formations be gross for now, but how are the mental formations gross?
Because they have not been abandoned. For bodily formations are abandoned by the fourth jhāna, verbal formations by the second jhāna, and mental formations by the attainment of cessation.
Thus, even though the bodily and verbal formations have been abandoned, those [mental formations] still persist;
therefore, in relation to what has been abandoned, they are called "gross" because they have not been abandoned. "Pleasant" refers to that which arises for one emerging from cessation.
The bliss of the attainment of fruition belonging to the fourth jhāna. "Joy greater than bliss" refers to the successive joy experienced by one who has emerged from the attainment of fruition.
"The second attainment of an opportunity": the fourth jhāna remains having suppressed both pleasure and pain and having taken its own opportunity;
therefore it is called "the second attainment of an opportunity. [This concludes the discussion of] the second and third jhānas.
In this context, since they are already included when the fourth category is taken, they are not mentioned separately.
Regarding the terms "wholesome" (*kusala*) and so forth: "wholesome" refers to the ten wholesome courses of action (*kamma-patha*); "unwholesome" refers to the ten unwholesome courses of action.

The pairs such as "blameworthy" (*sāvajja*) and so on should also be understood by way of these very same categories. Furthermore, all of this—both the dark (*kaṇha*) and the bright (*sukka*)—is included herein.
"And with its counterpart" means having a black-and-white counterpart. For this very nibbāna is without a counterpart.
"Ignorance is abandoned" means the ignorance that conceals the round of existence is abandoned. "True knowledge arises" means the true knowledge of the path of arahantship arises.
"Bliss" refers to both the bliss of the path of arahantship and the bliss of the fruit. "Joy beyond bliss" means...
For one who has emerged from the attainment of the fruit, there is successive mental joy. The third "attainment of an opportunity" refers to the path of arahantship;
having suppressed all defilements, it stands having taken its own opportunity. Therefore, it is called the "third attainment of an opportunity.
As for the remaining paths, they are already included once that [path] is grasped, and thus are not mentioned separately.
These three attainments of opportunity, however, should be explained in detail by way of the thirty-eight objects.

How so? Having defined all the objects according to the method stated in the *Visuddhimagga*—both by way of access (*upacāra*) and absorption (*appanā*)—the first jhāna in twenty-four instances should be called "the first attainment of opportunity. In thirteen...

Having reached the second and third jhānas in eight places, and the fourth jhāna together with the attainment of cessation in fifteen places, it should be called the "second acquisition of an opportunity.
Furthermore, the ten access-concentrations (upacāra-jhāna), which serve as the proximate cause for the Path, belong to the "third acquisition of an opportunity.
Moreover, among the three trainings, the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā) belongs to the first acquisition of an opportunity.
It should also be explained by way of the trainings (*sikkhā*): the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-sikkhā*) is the second, and the training in higher wisdom (*adhipaññā-sikkhā*) is the third.
Furthermore, in the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta*, there is the attainment of the first occasion from the minor morality up to the first jhāna;

the second [occasion] from the second jhāna up to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*); and the third attainment of an occasion from insight (*vipassanā*) up to arahantship.

It should also be explained by way of the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta*. Furthermore, it should be explained by way of the Piṭakas as follows: among the three Piṭakas, the Vinaya Piṭaka occupies the first place, the Sutta Piṭaka the second, and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka the third.
It is said that in former times, at the commencement of the rains retreat, the Great Elders would introduce this very Sutta. For what reason?

[They thought: "We shall be able to explain it by dividing it into the Three Piṭakas. For when one explains it by bringing together the Three Piṭakas, it is impossible to say that it has been poorly explained.
This Sutta is truly well-explained only when it is taught after having caused the Three Piṭakas to be analyzed.
Commentary on the Four Foundations of Mindfulness. 289.
“For the attainment of the wholesome” means for the sake of attaining both the wholesome of the path and the wholesome of the fruit;
for both of these are indeed wholesome in the sense of being blameless or in the sense of being secure. In that regard, one is rightly concentrated therein... [text continues]... in that.

Being concentrated on the internal body, he becomes one-pointed in mind. "He generates knowledge and vision regarding the external body of another" means that he sends forth knowledge from his own body toward the body of another. This same method applies everywhere.

And in all instances, by the phrase "mindfulness," it is mindfulness that grasps the body and so forth; and by the phrase "the world," it is precisely those bodies and so forth that have been grasped which constitute the world.
It should be understood that these four foundations of mindfulness are taught as a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane.
290. Commentary on the Requisites for Concentration:
Regarding the phrase "requisites for concentration," there are three kinds of requisites here: "The chariot has virtue as its requisite, jhāna as its axle, and energy as its wheels."
For here, "accessory" (parikkhāra) means an ornament. In the passage, "It is well-furnished with the seven accessories of a city," accessory means an attendant.
In the passage, "The accessory for the requisites of life in the case of illness," accessory means a provision.
But here, it is stated as "the seven accessories of concentration" by way of an accessory as an attendant.
“Parikkhatā” means surrounded. “This is called noble right concentration”:
this is called “noble right concentration” because it is surrounded by the seven factors, just as a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti) is surrounded by the seven treasures.
“Saupaniso itipi” means it is also called “with its proximate cause”; what is meant is that it is indeed accompanied by its retinue. “Of right view”...
"For one established in right view, right intention arises"—that is, right intention occurs. This same method applies to all the terms.
Furthermore, this meaning should be understood both with reference to the path and with reference to the fruit.

How so? For one established in the right view of the path, the right intention of the path arises... [and so on] ...for one established in the knowledge of the path, the deliverance of the path arises. Likewise:

For one established in right view regarding the fruit, right intention regarding the fruit arises... [and so on] ...for one established in right knowledge regarding the fruit, liberation through the fruit arises.

"Well-proclaimed" and so forth are described in the *Visuddhimagga*. "Opened" means uncovered. "Of the Deathless" means of Nibbāna. "Gates" means paths of entry. "With verified confidence" means with unshakable confidence. "Disciplined in the Dhamma" means led out by the path of true deliverance.
"This other class" refers to non-returners (*anāgāmin*); thus, it is meant that there are indeed non-returners. "Partakers of merit" means those born from a portion of merit.
"Being conscientious" means being possessed of moral dread (*ottappa*). By this, he indicates: "I am unable to determine whether one might occasionally speak falsely out of fear of lying;
however, it is not that I lack the power to determine it."

291. "What do you think of this?"—by this, he asks Vessavaṇa alone; however, he does not hold the view that "he did not have such a teacher" or "he will not have one. For there is no difference in the realization (*abhisamaya*) of all Buddhas. 292. "In his own assembly"—that is, in his own retinue.

"This holy life (*brahmacariya*)"—this refers to the entirety of the holy life consisting of the three trainings (*sikkhattaya*). The rest is self-evident. Furthermore, these phrases were established by the Elders who compiled the Dhamma (*dhammasaṅgāhakathera*).
Thus ends the commentary on the Janavasabha Sutta in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya. 6.
Commentary on the Mahāgovinda Sutta.
293. Thus have I heard: this is the Mahāgovinda Sutta. Herein is the commentary on the words not [already] explained:

Pañcasikha means one with five tufts of hair and five earrings. It is said that while he was still a youth performing meritorious deeds on the human path, at the time when he was a young boy with five tufts of hair, he became the leader of cowherds;
taking other boys with him, he [erected] a *sāla* tree [shelter] at crossroads outside the village.

Performing such meritorious deeds as digging ponds, building bridges, leveling uneven roads, and removing trees that obstruct the axles of vehicles, he wandered about until, while still young, he passed away.
That physical form of his was desirable, lovely, and pleasing; having died, he was reborn in the realm of the Four Great Kings.
Taking a lifespan of ninety thousand years, he was reborn. His physical form was three-quarters of a league in height and resembled a mass of gold.

Having adorned himself with ornaments weighing as much as a thousand carts, having anointed himself with perfumes filling nine jars, wearing divine red garments, and having fastened a golden earring of red gold and five earrings, [he appeared].
He moved about with five topknots on his back, like the treatment given to a young child; therefore, they knew him as "Pañcasikha" (Five-Tufted).
"When the night had passed" means when the night had gone by, when one portion of it had elapsed—this is the meaning.
"Of lovely appearance" means of exceedingly desirable, charming, and pleasing appearance. For he was naturally of lovely appearance, and [now] having adorned himself...
But because he had arrived, his complexion became exceedingly beautiful. "Kevalakappaṃ" means entirely and on all sides.

Here, the word *kevala* has the sense of "without remainder," as in the expression "entirely perfect" (*kevalaparipuṇṇa*). The word *kappa* has the sense of "all around," as in "the entire Jeta Grove" (*kevalakappaṃ Jetavanaṃ*) and so forth.
"Having illuminated" (*obhāsetvā*) means having pervaded with radiance, making it a single expanse of light like the moon or the sun.
The meaning is: "having made a single light.
Regarding the description of the assembly hall of the devas (294):
"In the Sudhammā assembly hall" means [built] from the overflow of a jewel-sized pillar of a tree belonging to a woman named Sudhammā.
In the Nibbattasabhā hall, it is said, the floor was made of crystal; the pillars were made of gems;
the columns and the joints and connections between the columns were made of gold; the figures of beasts were made of coral;
the rafters, the cross-beams, and the cornices were made of the seven precious gems; the roof was covered with bricks of sapphire; and [the pinnacle] was made of gold.
The canopy and the pedestal were made of silver; the pinnacle was three hundred yojanas in length and breadth, nine hundred yojanas in circumference, and five hundred yojanas in height.
In such a Sudhamma assembly hall, Dhatarattha—the Gandhabba king among the Gandhabba deities—[arrives] with a hundred thousand koṭis of Gandhabba deities.
Surrounded by a hundred thousand koṭis, having had golden planks and golden spears taken up, Virūpakkha, the king of the Nāgas,
sat facing west in the eastern direction with the deities of two world-systems placed before him.
Virūḷhaka, the king of the Kumbhaṇḍas, surrounded by a hundred thousand koṭis of Kumbhaṇḍa deities, [carried] a hundred thousand koṭis of silver-made [planks].
Having had seats and golden spears prepared, he sat facing north in the southern direction with the deities of two celestial realms positioned before him.
The Naga King Virūpakkha, surrounded by a hundred thousand times ten million nagas, [held] a hundred thousand times ten million jewels made of mani-gems.
Having had large fruit-bearing vessels and golden spears brought, he sat facing the east in the western direction with the deities of two celestial realms before him.
Vessavaṇa, the king of the yakkhas, surrounded by a hundred thousand koṭis of yakkhas, [held] a hundred thousand koṭis of vessels made of coral.
It should be understood that he sat with large fruits and golden spears held [in his hands], facing south toward the northern direction,
with the deities of the two deva-worlds placed before him. Then,
thinking, "Our seat will be behind them," the opportunity for us to sit was reached behind them.
Beyond that, we are not permitted to enter or even look [inside]. As for the reasons for assembling here, they are exactly fourfold as previously stated.
Among those, the gathering for the commencement of the rains retreat (*vassūpanāyika*) has been explained in detail.
Just as with the commencement of the rains, so too on the full-moon day of the Great Invitation (*mahāpavāraṇā*), having assembled, [one asks]: "Today, having gone where and in whose presence..."
"We shall perform the Pavāraṇā ceremony," they deliberated. Therein, Sakka, the lord of the devas, for the most part performs the Pavāraṇā at the Mahāvihāra on Piyaṅgudīpa alone.
The other deities, having taken celestial flowers such as those from the Pāricchattaka tree and celestial sandalwood powder, each go to their own preferred place and perform the Pavāraṇā.
Thus they assemble for the purpose of performing the Pavāraṇā in unison.
In the world of the gods, however, there is a creeper named Āsāvatī. Thinking, "It will flower," the gods go to attend upon it for a thousand years.
When the Pāricchattaka tree is in bloom, they go to attend upon it for one year.
They become joyful from the moment that [tree] begins to turn yellow and its leaves fall, as it has been said:
“Bhikkhus, on whatever occasion the Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree of the Tāvatiṃsa devas has turned yellowish-white, at that time the Tāvatiṃsa devas are delighted, thinking:
‘The Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree is now yellowish-white; it will not be long before its leaves fall. Bhikkhus, on whatever occasion...”

At that time, monks, the Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree of the Tāvatiṃsa devas has its leaves fallen, it has produced buds, it has produced a network of shoots, it has produced flower-buds, and it has produced flower-clusters. At that time, monks, the Tāvatiṃsa devas are delighted, thinking:
“The Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree has now produced flower-clusters; before long, indeed...”
“It will be in full bloom, monks.

“And when that Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree is in full bloom, monks, its radiance pervades fifty yojanas all around, and its fragrance wafts a hundred yojanas with the wind. Such is the majesty of the Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree.”
When the *pāricchattaka* tree is in bloom, there is no need for climbing, nor for using a hook to bend it down, nor for using a ladder to gather the flowers.
A wind arises that strips the flowers from their stalks; a receiving wind catches them;
an entering wind brings them into the Sudhamma assembly hall of the gods; and a sweeping wind removes the withered flowers.
It is swept clean; the wind of the canopy spreads it out, dancing with the fringes and tassels of the cloth.
In the center stands the Dhamma-throne. A jeweled couch measuring one *yojana* is spread out, above which a white parasol three *yojanas* high is held aloft.
Immediately after that, the seat of Sakka, the king of the gods, is spread out. Then follows the seats for the thirty-three sons of the gods.
Then there are other highly influential deities; for some deities, however, a mere flower-calyx serves as a seat.

Having entered the assembly hall of the gods, they sit down. Then, from the flowers, a column of pollen rises up and strikes against the calyx above, settling there and making the bodies of those deities—measuring three gavutas in size—appear as if prepared with a coating of lac-dye.
It acts as if it were so. That sport of theirs reaches its conclusion after four months. Thus they assemble for the purpose of experiencing the Pāricchattaka festival.
However, on the eighth day of each month, a great proclamation for hearing the Dhamma is made in the world of the gods.
There, in the Sudhammā assembly hall of the gods, either the Great Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra, or Sakka, Lord of the Devas, or a monk who is a preacher of the Dhamma, or some other [being]...
Or a son of the gods who is a preacher of the Dhamma delivers a discourse on the Dhamma. On the eighth day of the fortnight, the ministers of the Four Great Kings;

on the fourteenth day, their sons; and on the fifteenth day, the Four Great Kings themselves go forth, taking with them golden tablets and vermilion, and travel through the villages, market towns, and royal capitals. They [look out for] such-and-such a woman—
Or suppose a man has gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and gone for refuge to the Saṅgha; he observes the five precepts;
he performs the eight Uposatha observances each month; he fulfills his service to his mother; he fulfills his service to his father;
at such-and-such a place, an offering was made with a hundred handfuls of lotuses and a vessel of flowers; and a thousand lamps were lit.
They had him hear the Dhamma at improper times; they had canopies, railings, and railings on the sides constructed, as well as a lion-throne and a lion-staircase;
he fulfilled the three types of good conduct and lived having undertaken the ten courses of wholesome action.
Having written this upon a golden plate with vermilion, they brought it and placed it in the hand of Pañcasikha. Pañcasikha [spoke] to Mātali...
He places it in his hand. Mātali, the charioteer, gives it to Sakka, the king of the gods.
When those who perform meritorious deeds are few, the book becomes small; seeing this, the devas think:
"Alas, the great multitude of people dwells heedlessly! The four states of misery will be filled, and the six celestial worlds will become empty."
They become displeased. But if the cloth is large, upon seeing it, the gods think: "Ah, how the great multitude dwells with diligence!
The four states of misery will become empty, and the six heavenly worlds will be filled.
Having performed meritorious deeds in the Buddha’s teaching, we shall have the pleasure of celebrating a festival, preceded by those who have arrived endowed with great merit."
They were delighted. Sakka, the king of the gods, took that manuscript and recited it.
As he spoke in his natural manner, his voice reached twelve *yojanas*.
When he spoke with a loud voice, it remained, covering the entire city of the gods, ten thousand *yojanas* in extent. Thus they gathered for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma.
Furthermore, it should be understood that they have assembled here for the purpose of performing the *pavāraṇā* ceremony.

"Honoring the Tathāgata" means honoring the Tathāgata by way of nine reasons. "And the well-enacted nature of the Dhamma" refers to the well-expounded nature of the Dhamma, distinguished by such qualities as being well-proclaimed;
"and the excellent practice of the Saṅgha" refers to the Saṅgha’s correct practice, distinguished by such qualities as being upright in its conduct—this is the meaning.
The Exposition of the Eight Truths (Aṭṭhayathābhuccavaṇṇanā). 296.
*Yathābhūtaṃ* means according to reality, according to its true nature (*yathāsabhāva*). *Vaṇṇaṃ* means qualities (*guṇa*). *Payirudāhāsī* means he spoke.
Regarding the phrase "practiced for the welfare of many beings" (*bahujanahitāya paṭipanno*): how did he practice? Having brought together eight qualities at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara...
Even while making the aspiration for Buddhahood, one is said to be practicing for the welfare of many beings.
These are the perfection of giving, the perfection of virtue, the perfection of renunciation, the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of energy, the perfection of patience, the perfection of truth,
the perfection of determination, the perfection of loving-kindness, and the perfection of equanimity— [practiced] for more than a hundred thousand aeons.
Even while fulfilling these ten perfections for four incalculable eons, he practiced for the welfare of the many.

Even while performing such difficult deeds as an ascetic who preached patience, as the young prince Cūḷadhammapālaka, as the elephant king Chaddanta, as the elephant kings Bhūridatta, Campeyya, and Saṅkhapāla, and as the Great Monkey, he practiced for the welfare of the many. And in his existence as Vessantara—
Having stood firm, given the great gift of seven hundred offerings, and caused the earth to quake at seven locations while reaching the pinnacle of the perfections,
he was practicing for the welfare of many beings. Furthermore, in the immediately succeeding existence, remaining in the Tusita heaven for the full span of his lifespan,
he was likewise practicing for the welfare of many beings.
Therein, having seen the five portents and being entreated by the deities of the ten thousand world-systems, he performed the five great observations; then,
having given his promise for the sake of gathering the devas, he passed away from the Tusita heaven and took rebirth in a mother’s womb—
thus practicing for the welfare of the many.
Having dwelt in his mother’s womb for ten months, even as he emerged from his mother’s womb in the Lumbinī grove;
having lived at home for twenty-nine years, even as he went forth on the Great Renunciation and took up the life of a wanderer on the banks of the Anoma River;
and having exhausted himself with striving for six years, even as he ascended the seat of enlightenment and realized omniscient knowledge.
Whether spending seven weeks at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), arriving at Isipatana and setting in motion the unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma,
performing the Twin Miracle (yamakapāṭihāriya), descending from the heaven of the gods (devorohaṇa), remaining as a Buddha for forty-five years,
relinquishing the formative forces of life (āyusaṅkhāra), or [passing away] between the twin sāla trees into the state without residue of clinging (anupādisesa)—
Even when attaining final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna, he is practicing for the welfare of many;
it should be understood that as long as even his relics the size of a mustard seed remain, he continues to practice for the welfare of many. The remaining phrases are synonyms for this very point.
In this context, each subsequent phrase explains the meaning of each preceding one.
"We do not perceive anyone else in the past, nor do we perceive anyone else now"—the meaning here is this: in the past, we perceived no one other than a Buddha; in the future, we perceive none;
and as for the present, because there is no other teacher, we perceive no one other than that Blessed One. For it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary): "The Buddhas of the past and the future..."
Having reflected, "They are indeed equal to our Teacher; why does Sakka say this? they said:
"At present, there is no other teacher who practices for the welfare of the many besides our Teacher; therefore, he says, 'I do not see [any such person]'.
And just as it is here, so too should this meaning be understood in the subsequent passages.
The terms "well-expounded" (*svākkhāta*) and so forth, as well as "wholesome" (*kusala*) and so forth, have already had their meanings explained.
Regarding the phrase "the water of the Ganges with the water of the Yamunā": at the place where the Ganges and Yamunā meet, the water blends and becomes uniform in color, fragrance, and taste;
it becomes exactly the same, like gold broken in the middle, but not like the water of the great ocean.
It is unlike [the path] at the time of social entanglement. The practice leading to the utterly pure Nibbāna is itself utterly pure.
For it is not possible to see Nibbāna in one's old age after having practiced medicine and other such arts, or by wandering in improper resorts during one's youth;
rather, only a practice leading to Nibbāna that is utterly pure is suitable, being like the simile of space. For just as even space...

Just as the moon and sun travel through the sky, moving to whatever place they desire, unattached and perfectly pure, so too the practice of a bhikkhu proceeding toward Nibbāna must be unattached and unbound to either family or group, resembling the sky.
And this very kind of practice was prescribed, spoken, and taught by the Blessed One. Therefore it is said: "It converges..."
“Nirvana and the path.
“Those who have entered upon the practice” means those established in the path. “Those who have lived [the life]” refers to those among these who have completed their residence.

“One who has found a companion”: a companion (sahāya) is so called because of traveling together with them here and there. However, this [phrase], “without a second, without a companion, peerless,” is—

It is stated in the sense of being incomparable. "Having dispelled" means that even while dwelling in the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) in their midst, he dwells having dispelled them with his mind;
the meaning is that he dwells devoted solely to delighting in solitude.
"But a gain has been accomplished for that Blessed One" means that a great gain had arisen for that Blessed One.
From what time did it arise? Having attained full enlightenment, after the passing of seven weeks, he set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma at Isipatana.

As he was gradually subduing gods and humans, having ordained the three matted-hair ascetics and gone to Rājagaha, it arose from the time of the subduing of Bimbisāra. With reference to this, it was said: "Then, indeed..."
“At that time, the Blessed One was honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated, receiving robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. Thus,
for four incalculable eons plus a hundred thousand kappas, the flood of gain and honor— arisen as the natural outflow of abundant merit—
comes surging forward like a great tide.
It is said that once, at Rājagaha, Sāvatthī, Sāketa, Kosambī, and Bārāṇasī, there arose what was called the "Bhagavā’s turn for alms-food.
There, one man wrote a note saying, "I shall give a gift after spending a hundred [pieces of money]," and tied it to the gate of the monastery.
Another wrote, "I shall spend two hundred," and another, "I shall spend five hundred."

One wrote: “I am another who will give a thousand. Another wrote: “I am another who will give two thousand. Another: “I am another who will give five, ten, twenty, or fifty. Another: “I am another who will give a hundred thousand. Another:

“I am another who will give two hundred thousand,” and having written this on a leaf, he tied it to the gate of the monastery. Even while wandering on a tour of the countryside, he sought an opportunity...
Having received [the news], the great multitude followed right behind, filling their carts with the thought, "We shall give a gift. As it is said:
"At that time, people from the countryside loaded much salt, oil, rice, and hard food onto their carts and followed closely behind the Blessed One, thinking, 'Wherever he takes his turn...'"
“We shall obtain it; we shall prepare a meal there. In this way, many other instances should be understood from the Khandhakas and the Vinaya.
However, in the case of the peerless gift (asadisadāna), this gain reached its ultimate limit. It is said that on one occasion, while the Blessed One was wandering through the countryside...
Having traveled to Jetavana, they arrived; the king invited them and gave a gift. On the second day, the citizens gave.

Again, the king’s gift was superior to theirs, and the citizens’ gift was superior to his. As many days passed in this way, the king thought: "These citizens are doing more and more each day; [they are] the lords of the earth."
"But there will be reproach, saying that the king has been defeated by the citizens in the matter of giving. Then Mallikā explained a stratagem to him.

He had a pavilion constructed in the royal courtyard using the footprints of the *sāla-kalyāṇī* tree, covered it with blue lotuses, prepared five hundred seats, and stationed five hundred elephants behind the seats, with one elephant for each seat.
For each individual monk, she had a white parasol held over him. Between every two seats, a single kṣatriya maiden adorned with all ornaments was grinding four kinds of fragrant scents.
As each batch was finished, she placed it in a fragrant mortar in the center;
another kṣatriya maiden then turned it over with her hand, which was like a blue lotus. In this manner, for each individual...
The monk had three Kṣatriya daughters as attendants; another woman, adorned with all ornaments, fanned him with a palm-leaf fan;
another took a water-vessel and strained water; another carried water from the bowl.
For the Blessed One, there were four priceless items: a foot-stool, a stand, a support-board, and [a fan].
The four items known as the "jewels of the umbrella's base" were priceless.
The gift to be offered to the youngest member of the Saṅgha was worth one hundred thousand [pieces of gold]. At that donation, the Elder Aṅgulimāla was the youngest member of the Saṅgha.
When the elephant brought near his seat was unable to approach him, they informed the king. The king asked, "Is there no other elephant?"
"But there is a rogue elephant; it cannot be brought here. "The Youngest of the Saṅgha, Great King, who is he?
"Venerable Aṅgulimāla, Blessed One. "In that case, Great King, bring that rogue elephant and station him here. They brought the elephant after adorning it.
By the power of the Elder’s majesty, [the elephant] could not even move as much as a breath from his nostrils.
He was unable to do so. In this manner, alms were given continuously for seven days.
On the seventh day, the king paid homage to the One of Ten Powers and said, "Bhagavā, please teach me the Dhamma.
In that assembly there were two ministers named Kāḷa and Juṇha. Kāḷa thought: "The royal lineage is perishing..."
“Who are these people that they should do such a thing? Having eaten, they will simply go to the monastery and fall asleep.
But what would a king’s man not do if he were to obtain this? Alas, the king’s property is being lost!
Juṇha thought: “This kingship is indeed a great thing; who else would be able to perform it? What...”
“One who, though established in kingship, is unable to give such a gift is not truly called a king.
The Blessed One, surveying the inclinations of the assembly and perceiving the dispositions of those two, thought:
“If I were to deliver a discourse on the Dhamma today according to the inclination of Juṇha, Kāḷa’s head would split into seven pieces. However, out of compassion for living beings...”
“The perfections have been fulfilled. On another day when I am preaching the Dhamma, the youth will penetrate the path and its fruit;
but for now, I shall look upon Kāḷa. Then he spoke this four-line stanza to the king:
“Indeed, the stingy do not go to the world of the gods;”
Fools do not praise giving;
but the wise person, rejoicing in the gift,
becomes happy thereby in the world beyond.
The king, being displeased, thought: "I have given a great gift, yet the Teacher has preached the Dhamma to me only briefly;
I suppose I was unable to capture the mind of the One Possessed of Ten Powers. Having finished his breakfast, he went to the monastery, paid homage to the Blessed One, and asked:
"Venerable sir, I gave a great gift, yet my expression of thanks was not great."
“It has been done. But what fault, venerable sir, is there in me? “There is no fault in you, Great King;
rather, the assembly is impure, and for that reason the Blessed One did not teach the Dhamma. But why was the assembly not pure? The Teacher revealed the deliberations of two ministers.
The king asked Kāḷa: “Is it so, dear Kāḷa? “It is so,” [he replied].
“Great King,” [he replied]. “When I am giving away what belongs to me, what part of yours is being obstructed that you cannot bear to see it?
Banish him from my kingdom,” he said. Then, having summoned Juṇha, he asked:
“Is it true, dear son, that you thought such a thing? “Yes, Great King,” he replied. “Let it be exactly according to your wish,” [the king said], and at that very moment—
Having had five hundred bhikkhus seated upon the very seats thus prepared in the pavilion, and having surrounded them with those same daughters of the khattiya clan, he said:
"Taking wealth from the royal palace, give alms for seven days exactly as I have given.
He gave accordingly. Having given, on the seventh day, he said: "May the Blessed One teach the Dhamma."
The Teacher, having performed a single expression of thanksgiving for both offerings, delivered a great discourse on the Dhamma as if he were merging two great rivers into a single flood.
At the conclusion of the teaching, Juṇha became a stream-enterer.
The King, being filled with faith, gave a "peripheral estate" (bāhiravatthu) to the One of Ten Powers. In this way, it should be understood that the Blessed One’s gain was accomplished.
"Fame has been established" means the proclamation of his praise and virtues. That too was established starting from the time the Blessed One set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion.
For from that time onwards, even Kṣatriyas spoke in praise of the Blessed One;
and Brāhmaṇas, householders, Nāgas, Supaṇṇas, Gandhabbas, deities, and even Brahmās, having uttered his renown, said: "Thus indeed is the Blessed One," and so forth.
The followers of other sects also gave a thousand [pieces of money] to Vararoja, instructing him: "Speak dispraise of the ascetic Gotama.
Having taken the thousand, he looked at the One of Ten Powers from the soles of his feet up to the tips of his hair, but seeing not even a speck the size of a writing-brush as a fault, he thought:
"Scattered with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, and adorned with the eighty minor characteristics..."

“Should anyone speak dispraise of this blameless person—who is encircled by a fathom-wide radiance, who resembles the Nandana Grove adorned with various flowers and a sky made brilliant by clusters of stars like blossoming *pāricchattaka* trees—his very mouth would turn back and his head would split into seven pieces;
there is no way to speak dispraise, for I shall speak only praise. Thus he spoke, beginning from the soles of his feet up to the tips of his hair.
He spoke in praise for more than a thousand additional verses; indeed, at the Twin Miracle, this praise reached its ultimate peak.
Thus was his fame established.
As far as the Khattiyas—meaning the Khattiyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vessas, Suddas, Nāgas, Supaṇṇas, Yakkhas, Asuras, and Devas—it was thought: "So great is he!"
"Brahmā" means that they all dwell with hearts full of affection, joyful and glad.

"But free from intoxication" means that he does not eat food out of indulgence or negligence, thinking, "So many people dwell with hearts full of affection for me," having become intoxicated by pride;
rather, the Blessed One eats food being entirely free from intoxication.
"According to his speech" means that whatever he speaks with his voice, his bodily action conforms to that; and whatever he does with his body, his verbal action conforms to that.
Either the body does not overstep the speech, or the speech does not overstep the body;
speech accords with the body, and the body accords with speech. And as follows—
“With his left side he becomes a boar,
with his right side a goat; with his cry he becomes a jackal, and with his horn an old ox.”—
This *sūkarayakkha* (boar-yakṣa), seeing boars, displays his left side which resembles a boar, seizes them, and devours them.
Seeing goats, he displays his own right flank which resembles them and, having seized them, devours them;
seeing lambs, he bleats like a lamb and, having seized them, devours them;
seeing oxen, he fashions horns resembling theirs and, when they have approached from afar thinking, "He looks like an ox," he seizes and devours them. And just as...
In the *Dhammika-vāyasa-jātaka*, when asked by the birds, the crow said: "I feed on wind;
because I feed on wind, I keep my mouth open and stand on only one leg out of fear that small creatures might die [in it].
Therefore, you too—'Practice the Dhamma, may there be blessing for you! Practice the Dhamma, O kinsmen!'"
“The practitioner of Dhamma dwells happily, both in this world and in the next.
Thus he inspired confidence among the birds, and then:
“How excellent indeed is this bird, a twice-born one who is most righteous in Dhamma!”
"Standing on one foot, he says, 'Dharma, Dharma. Thus, while the birds had come to trust him, he devoured them.

Therefore, their speech did not accord with their body, nor did their body accord with their speech; but it is not so for the Blessed One. Rather, it shows that for the Blessed One, his speech accords with his body, and his body accords with his speech.
"One who has crossed over doubt" (*tiṇṇavicikiccho*) means one whose doubts have been crossed over. Such as, "How is this? How is this?"—this kind of...
One whose doubts have departed is "one free from doubt" (*vigata-kathaṃkatho*). For instance, when the common people think: "This is a tree; what is a 'tree'?
This is a village, this is a district, this is a kingdom; what is a 'kingdom'?
Why is the trunk of this tree straight, while the trunk of that one is crooked? Why is some thorn straight, while some... [and so forth].
The Teacher is not like one who remains full of doubt, wondering: "Is the stalk crooked? Is the flower fragrant or foul-smelling? Is the fruit sweet or not sweet?
For the Teacher has entirely removed all uncertainty, knowing: "Because these elements are predominant in this way, such-and-such occurs.
And just as for those who have attained the first jhāna and so forth, [there is no doubt] regarding the second jhāna and so forth...

There is doubt. For even in the case of the Paccekabuddhas, because they lack a definitive conclusion regarding omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) as it truly is, there is indeed what is called "doubt" in a conventional sense;
but it is not so for the Buddha. This shows that the Blessed One has removed all uncertainty in every respect.
"One whose intention is fulfilled": whereas some [attain their goal] by mere virtue, some by mere insight, and some by the first jhāna... [and so on].
Some have their intentions fulfilled and their wishes perfected through the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
some merely by becoming stream-enterers... [and so on] ...some through arhatship, some through the knowledge of the disciple’s perfections, and some through the knowledge of private enlightenment.
But my Teacher is not like that; rather, he shows that my Teacher has his intentions fulfilled through the knowledge of omniscience.
The phrase *ajjhāsayaṃ ādibrahmacariyaṃ* is in the nominative case used in the sense of the instrumental; the meaning is:

"by means of the noble path—which is the primary intention (*ajjhāsaya*), the initial basis of the holy life (*ādibrahmacariya*), and the ancient holy life—one has crossed over doubt, become free from perplexity, and fulfilled one’s resolve.
[As it is said: "In regard to things unheard before, I have awakened to the truths by myself."

And because of the statement, "Therein he attained omniscience and mastery over the powers," the fulfillment of the Blessed One’s intentions was also accomplished solely by means of the Noble Path. 297.
"Just as the Blessed One" means that just as the Blessed One [is], so too [are those] in one region of Jambudīpa in the four directions.
While wandering on their alms-round, they said, expressing their longing: "O, would that the four Conquerors might teach the Dhamma!
Then others, desiring that the three [Buddhas] should wander together in the three circles, said, "There are three Perfectly Enlightened Ones.
Still others said: "Having fulfilled the ten perfections, the arising of four or three [Buddhas] is difficult to obtain; but if..."

"Even if one were to dwell in a fixed residence and teach the Dhamma, while another were to wander on tour, in this way Jambudīpa would be graced and much welfare and happiness would be attained"—having thought thus, they said, "O, dear sir! (aho vata, mārisa).
Regarding the phrase "it is impossible, there is no occasion for this" (aṭṭhānam etaṃ anavakāso), both "possibility" (ṭhāna) and "occasion" (avakāsa) are merely designations for a cause (kāraṇa).
For it is the cause that "stands" (tiṭṭhati) here, and because the fruit exists dependent upon it, it is the "basis" (ṭhāna).

And because, like space, it does not exist elsewhere without that [cause], it is the "opportunity" (avakāsa). The word *yaṃ* is in the nominative case used in the sense of the instrumental. This is what is meant:
"There is no such cause by which two Buddhas might arise simultaneously in a single world-system."
And here: “As far as the moon and sun revolve, illuminating the quarters with their radiance—
so far extends this world-system of a thousand worlds, over which your power prevails.”

In the context of the verse, a single world-system (*lokadhātu*) is just one *cakkavāḷa*. In passages where it is said, “A thousandfold world-system trembled,” a thousand *cakkavāḷas* constitute one world-system.

In passages where it is said, “If he so desired, Ānanda, the Tathāgata could make himself heard by his voice throughout a three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system, and pervade it with his radiance,” a three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system constitutes one world-system.
In the passage where it says, “And this ten-thousandfold world-system,” one thousand sets of ten thousand world-spheres (*cakkavāḷa*) constitute a single world-system.
It is with reference to that that he said, “of a single world-system. For this much is indeed called the "field of birth" (*jātikhetta*).
Furthermore, within that, Buddhas do not arise anywhere other than in the Middle Country of Jambudīpa in this particular world-sphere, because of the field of birth.
But beyond that, the very place of the Buddhas' arising is not known. "By which purpose" means by the purpose of gathering [disciples] through the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*).
Commentary on the Story of Sanaṅkumāra (300):
"Both in beauty and in glory" means both in the splendor of ornaments and retinue, and in the majesty of merit (*puñña-sirī*).
301. Regarding "Excellent, Great Brahmā," the word *sādhu* here signifies "well-pleased" (*sampasādane*). "Having understood, we rejoice" means: having known, we rejoice. 304.
Regarding the commentary on the account of the Brahmin Govinda:
"For such a long time that Blessed One has been possessed of great wisdom"—it is impossible to define it by limiting it to "only this much."
"Rather than saying that, you should consider: 'How could it be otherwise? For a very long time, indeed for an exceedingly long time, that Blessed One has been possessed of great wisdom.

Then, wishing to answer this question himself, he said: 'It is not surprising, dear sirs, that having now fulfilled the perfections and, at the seat of enlightenment, shattered the heads of the three Māras, he has realized the uncommon knowledge.'"
"If that Blessed One were to possess great wisdom [now], what would be wonderful about it?

However, I shall tell you, dear sirs, how he possessed the state of great wisdom even during the time when he was still subject to passion and while his enlightenment was not yet mature, remaining at the stage of partial knowledge.
Having thus introduced the reason for his concealment of his past life, he spoke the words beginning with "In the past, sir... and so forth.
"Purohita" means one who acts as a priest by instructing in all duties. "Govinda" means one consecrated by the Govindiya consecration;
however, his original name was something else entirely, but from the time of his consecration onward, he came to be designated as "Govinda.
"Jotipāla" means "light-protector" because of both his shining and his protecting. It is said that on the day of his birth, all weapons blazed with light.
At dawn, the king also saw his own auspicious weapon ablaze and stood there terrified.
Govinda went to attend upon the king early in the morning and asked after his rest; the king said, "How could I have a good night's sleep, Teacher?
and related the reason. "Do not fear, Great King," he replied. "A son has been born to me, and by his power—"
In the entire city, the weapons burst into flames. The King, thinking, "Could it be that my son has become my enemy?
became even more terrified. When asked, "What were you thinking, Great King? he explained the matter to him.
Then Govinda said to him, "Do not fear, Great King; this prince will not plot against you. Throughout all of Jambudīpa..."
"But there will be no one equal to him in wisdom; by my son’s word, the doubts of the great multitude shall be severed, and he will instruct you all in your duties," he said, comforting them.
The king, being pleased, gave a thousand [pieces of gold], saying, "Let this be the milk-money for the prince," and added, "Show the prince to me when he has grown up. The prince, in due course...
He had reached maturity. Because he was radiant and capable of protecting [the kingdom], they gave him the name Jotipāla.
Therefore it is said: "Because of his radiance and because of his protection, he is Jotipāla.
"Having properly entrusted" means having properly entrusted. Or rather, this is the reading itself. "One who sees the goal well" means one who is competent.
"Capable and discerning of the goal, fully discerning of the goal"—one who surpasses such a person who is fully discerning of the goal is "more fully discerning of the goal.
By the phrase "by the instruction of the young brahmin Jotipāla himself," he shows that [the teacher] instructs only after having questioned Jotipāla himself.
(305) "May there be well-being for the venerable Jotipāla": this means the welfare, growth, or attainment of distinction for the venerable Jotipāla.

The meaning is: "May it be entirely auspicious and a source of blessing. As for the "pleasing conversation": having concluded the welcoming discourse that dispels grief and is connected with death, according to the method beginning with, "Enough, Great King, do not worry;
this is the inevitable nature of all beings," [he said], "May your lordship Jotipāla not respond to my instruction"—that is, "do not give an answer"—[but rather say], "Instruct me."
When he said, "I do not instruct," the meaning is that he did not refuse the instruction itself.

"He undertook" means he established it after having made an agreement. "The people spoke thus" means that seeing him—who was wiser than his father—governing all duties and excelling in all tasks, they were joyful in heart and said: "Oh, how wise is this Brahmin Govinda!"
"Indeed, he is the Great Govinda, the brahmin," they said. This is what is meant:
"The brahmin Govinda was indeed his father; but this one, truly, is the Great Govinda, the brahmin.
This is the commentary on the sharing of the kingdom.
306. Regarding those six kṣatriyas who were called his "companions": it is said that they were Reṇu’s younger half-brothers from the same father.
Therefore, Mahāgovinda thought, "Whether this consecrated king distributes a share of the kingdom to them or not, what if I were to send them to Reṇu beforehand and have them obtain his promise?"
Reflecting thus, he approached those six khattiyas. "Rājakattāro" means ministers who carry out the king's business.
"Madanīyā kāmā" means sensual pleasures that cause intoxication and negligence. As time passes, one might not even be able to remember this; therefore, the meaning is: "Come, sirs, let us go.
"I remember, sirs"—at that time, it is said, it was a period when people were speakers of truth; therefore [he asks], "When was this said by me?"
Instead of saying what was untrue—“By whom was it seen? By whom was it heard?”—he said, “I remember it, sir. “A conversation of mutual greeting” means a welcoming discourse such as:
“Do not grieve, Great King, now that the King has passed away to the state of the gods;
this is the inevitable law for all beings; such is the nature of conditioned phenomena. “He set all the wagon-faces in order” means all...
He established six kingdoms with their capitals facing like the front of a cart. Each king’s domain was three hundred *yojanas* in extent;
however, King Reṇu’s territory for refuge was ten *gāvutas*, and in the center, Reṇu’s kingdom was like a canopy.
Why did he establish it in this way? Because those coming from time to time to see the king would [otherwise] enter another’s domain.
Without oppressing others, they will come and go only within their own respective territories.
For when one has entered another’s kingdom, people complain against him who says, "Give us food! Give us oxen!
saying, "These kings do not travel within their own conquered realms; they are causing us oppression. But for one who travels within his own conquered realm...
Thinking, “This person must surely receive this and that from us,” the people did not consider him a burden.
Having reflected on this matter, Mahāgovinda established it thus: “May the kings, being in harmony, long govern their kingdoms.
“Dantapura is for the Kaliṅgas, and Potana for the Assakas;”
“Māhissati was laid out for the Avantīs, and Roruva for the Sovīras;
Mithilā for the Videhas, and Campā among the Aṅgas was laid out;
and Bārāṇasī for the Kāsīs—these were laid out by Govinda.”
These seven cities were built by Mahāgovinda himself for the sake of those kings:
“Sattabhū, Brahmadatta, Vessabhū, Bharata together with the two Reṇus and the two Dhataraṭṭhas— these were the seven Bhāradvājas at that time.”
These are the names of those seven. Among them, one was named Sattabhū, one Brahmadatta, one Vessabhū, one Bharata (who was born together with him), one Reṇu, and two Dhataratṭhas;
these seven were the great kings who bore the burden of Jambudīpa.
The commentary on the first recitation section is finished.
Commentary on the Rise of the Renowned Sound (311):
"They approached [thinking], 'This excellence of sovereignty of ours is not through the power of another, but through the power of Mahāgovinda.'"
They thought, “Mahāgovinda has brought us seven kings into harmony and established us upon the surface of Jambudīpa;
it is not easy to repay one who has previously rendered such service. Let him alone rule over all seven of us;
let us make him our general and our chaplain; in this way, our prosperity will increase. Having reflected thus, they approached him.

Mahāgovinda also thought: "I have brought these men together in harmony; if there were another general and chaplain among them, they would take the words of their respective generals and chaplains and break with one another.
Therefore, I shall accept their positions as general and chaplain. Having reflected thus, he replied, "So be it, sir."
Regarding the phrase "and seven great brahmin householders," he appointed seven deputy chaplains with the thought:
"Whether I am present in all places or not, wherever I am not present, they shall perform the duties that ought to be done there.
It is with reference to them that this was said: "and seven great brahmin householders. Twice a day...
They are called *nahātakas* because they bathe in the evening or in the morning;
or, having bathed at the conclusion of their ascetic observances (*vatacariyā*), they thereafter neither eat nor drink together with the Brahmins—thus they are called *nahātakas*.
312. *Abbhuggacchi* means he went forth toward. At that time, it is said, people [did not act] without first addressing Brahmā.
“It would indeed be possible to rule over the entire Jambudīpa in this way. This was the very conversation that took place wherever he sat.
But as for the Great Man, it is said: “This false praise has arisen concerning me;
while the arising of praise is not a heavy matter, the guarding of praise once it has arisen is what is heavy. And yet, he did not reflect on this.”
"Even for one who acts after merely consulting [others], fame arises; but for one who acts after reflecting and consulting, it will become even more widespread.
While seeking a means to behold Brahmā, he saw him and reflected on the meaning of "I have indeed heard...
and so forth. "He approached King Reṇu"—thus, I was desirous of seeing or conversing with him in the meantime.
Thinking, "It will not be [otherwise]; since my obstacles have been severed, I shall dwell in happiness," he approached for the purpose of cutting off those obstacles;
this same method applies everywhere.
(316) "Of similar status" means having the same appearance and the same birth.

317. "Having had a new assembly hall built" means: having had a variegated dwelling constructed, complete with places for standing at night and by day, and walkways, capable of being inhabited during the four months of the rainy season, and surrounded on the outside by reeds.

"Meditating on the meditation of compassion" means: meditating on the threefold and fourfold jhānas of compassion; furthermore, by way of compassion, the remaining [meditations] are also included here.

The three divine abodes (brahmavihāra) are indeed included. "Distress and agitation" means that for one established on the plane of jhāna, there is no distress of dissatisfaction or agitation of fear;
rather, there was a longing for the arrival of Brahmā, a craving for his arrival—this is the meaning.
