Commentary on the Dialogue with Brahmā.
318. "They fear" means they have the very fear of mental terror. "Not knowing" means not understanding.

"How shall we know him? means: "In what manner should we recognize him? By what characteristics [of] 'Where does he dwell?', 'What is his name?', 'What is his clan?', and so forth, should we bear him in mind? This is the meaning.
"Knowing me as 'Kumāra'": they know me as "Kumāra" and as "the Youthful One.
"In the Brahma-world" means in the supreme world. "Sanātana" means ancient, primordial, and of old. He shows: "I am that ancient Kumāra, the Brahmā named Sanaṅkumāra.
"Thus, Govinda, know it": O wise Govinda, you should know it thus; you should hold me in this way.
“‘A seat, water, and foot-washing water, honey, and vegetables for the Brahmā;
we ask of you, sir, regarding the guest-offering (aggha); may you, sir, perform the honoring (aggha) for us.
Here, ‘aggha’ refers to that which should be presented to the guests. For this very reason, this seat has been prepared here.”
“Sit down; this water is pure; drink the water from here, wash your feet;
this is foot-ointment prepared for the benefit of the feet—rub your feet with this; this is honey and sugar.
The holy life of the Bodhisatta is not like the holy life of others; he does not say, “This tomorrow,” or “This on the third day.”

Thinking, “it will be,” one makes what is called a store. But as for honey and vegetables that are unsalted, unsmoked, and not treated with *takka*—vegetables softened with water—it was with reference to these that he said, “Please accept this,” and so forth, saying, “We ask your honor’s price.
All these are the prices of Brahmā. We ask your honor’s price regarding them. And while they were asking thus:
"May your honor do us the honor; may your honor accept this"—this is what is meant.
But does he not know that "Brahmā does not eat even one [portion] from here"? He does not not know it;
even though he knows it, he asks under the pretext of a formal duty, thinking that a guest who has come into his presence should be asked.

Then Brahmā, reflecting—“Does this wise man ask because he knows there is no possibility of my using it, or does he ask out of deceit?”—and perceiving that “he asks while standing at the head of his duty,” thought, “It is now right for me to accept;
let us accept the price you name, Govinda. Thus he said: “We accept the price which you, Govinda, declare.”
He said: "Govinda, regarding what you say—'This seat is prepared;

sit here,' and so forth—we shall indeed be considered as having sat upon that seat, we shall be considered as having drunk the water, my feet shall be considered as having been washed, they shall be considered as having been anointed with oil, and even the water-cress shall be considered as having been consumed, from the very moment it is accepted by you."
"From the moment we began, whatever you have spoken has been accepted by us. Therefore it was said: 'We accept your price, O Govinda, for that which you speak.
Having thus accepted the price, he spoke the words beginning with 'For the benefit and welfare in this very life' in order to grant an opportunity for the question."

"Having been doubtful, I have understood the questions concerning what is known by others": this means that while I was possessed of doubt, I have now become free from doubt regarding the questions known by others—those things made manifest by another because they were personally constructed by him.
"Having abandoned possessiveness": having cast off the craving for requisites, thinking "this is mine," "this is mine.
"Among men": among beings; the meaning is, "anyone who is a man among men, having abandoned possessiveness. "Become solitary": become one, standing alone.
"One who sits alone": as for the meaning of the words here, one who arises and proceeds alone is *ekodi*;

being such a one is *ekodibhūta*. "Intent upon compassion" means intent upon the jhāna of compassion; the meaning is that he has produced that jhāna. "Free from the stench of raw flesh" means devoid of the stench of excrement.
"Established herein" means established in these qualities. And herein—
"One training" means one who is training in these qualities. This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, has already been stated above by Mahāgovinda and by Brahmā. 320.
Regarding that, "ignorant of these" means "I am ignorant of these stench-like things (āmagandha); I do not know them"—this is the meaning. Speak here!
"O wise one, you who are wise and learned here—speak, tell me!

By what obstruction does this generation blow, by what defilement-obstruction is the generation obstructed that it blows putrid? 'Bound for the states of misery' means those who go to the states of misery.
'With the Brahma-world shut off' means one for whom the Brahma-world is shut off, closed. By which defilement is the generation [obstructed] from reaching the Brahma-world?"
He asks: "Is the path obstructed, covered, and concealed?
Anger, falsehood, and deceit: anger has the characteristic of being provoked; falsehood has the characteristic of deceiving others;
deceit has the characteristic of cheating by showing a semblance [of honesty]; and treachery has the characteristic of betraying a friend.

Furthermore: stinginess (*kadariyatā*), overweening pride (*atimāna*), and envy (*usūyā*)—these have the characteristics of stubbornness and miserliness, the characteristic of conceiving oneself as superior beyond [one's due], and the characteristic of being vexed by the success of others, respectively.

Desire (*icchā*), seclusion (*vivicchā*), and harming others (*paraheṭhanā*)—these have the characteristics of craving (*taṇhā*), the characteristic of miserliness, and the characteristic of cruelty (*vihiṃsā*), respectively.
And harming others. Greed, hatred, pride, and delusion: wherever greed exists, it has the characteristic of being greedy;
hatred has the characteristic of hating; pride has the characteristic of intoxication; and delusion has the characteristic of being deluded.
Those joined with these [faults] are "stinking with raw flesh": beings joined with these fourteen defilements are stinking with raw flesh.
"It does not exist; there are only the stench of raw flesh, the stench of carrion, and the stench of putrefaction," he says.
"Those bound for the states of misery have the Brahma-world concealed"—this means they are both destined for the miserable states and have the path to the Brahma-world obscured.
This sutta, when being explained, should be illustrated by the *Āmagandha-sutta*, and the *Āmagandha-sutta* should also be illustrated by this one.
"Those are not easily subdued" means that those "raw stench-fumes" (*āmagandhā*) are not easily subdued—that is, they cannot be easily suppressed or abandoned;
the meaning is that they are difficult to cast off and difficult to conquer. "Now, let the venerable Govinda consider the time" means:
"Whatever time the venerable Govinda considers appropriate for this going-forth (*pabbajjā*), let that be so; if it is thus, my coming into your presence [is also appropriate]."
Your arrival will have occurred; the discourse on the Dhamma you have delivered will have been well-spoken. Dear son, you are the foremost person in all of Jambudīpa, standing in the prime of youth;
thus, for you to renounce such great abundance of prosperity, glory, and splendor is truly extraordinary—like a scent-elephant breaking its iron fetters and departing.
“This is indeed the lineage of the Buddhas,” thus providing this strengthening encouragement to the Great Being, Brahmā Sanankumāra departed for the Brahma-world.
321. As for the Great Being, he thought: “It is not fitting for me to go forth from right here; I am of royal lineage. Thus he addressed King Reṇu.
"I shall instruct him in his welfare; therefore, I will inform the king. If he too goes forth, that would be excellent.
If he does not go forth, I will hand over the position of domestic priest and go forth myself. Having thought this, he approached the king;
thus it was said: "Then, sir, Mahāgovinda... [omitted] ...I do not delight in the office of domestic priest."

"In that regard, you should understand: 'By means of the kingdom, you alone shall know. As for the words 'I do not delight in the office of family priest,' I do not take pleasure in the position of *purohita*; I am weary of it. Know someone else as the instructor; I do not delight in the office of family priest.
Then the king, thinking, "Surely the wealth in the house of this brahmin who has been in seclusion for four months must have diminished," invited him with riches, saying:
"If there is any deficiency in your desires, I shall fulfill them for you."
Again, thinking, "Could he perhaps have been harmed by someone while living all alone? [he said]:
"I am the commander of the army on earth; whoever harms him, I shall ward off.
You are my father, I am your son; do not abandon us, Govinda!"
He said: "The meaning of this is: 'I shall ward off whoever harms you; you need only point out who it is—saying, "It is so-and-so"—and I shall know what must be done in this matter.
Or alternatively: "I am the General of the Earth (Bhūmisenāpati)," that is to say, I am the lord of the earth;
therefore, I shall hand over this kingdom to you alone. "You are the father, I am the son"—you stand in the place of a father.
"You shall remain, my son, in the place of a father. Having won over my mind, O Govinda, you yourself must exert your own will; proceed exactly as you wish.
As for me, following only your will and partaking of the alms-food provided by you, I shall serve you either with sword and shield in hand, or I shall drive your chariot."
Alternatively, the reading is: “Mā no govinda, pajahī. Its meaning is: “You remain in the position of a father;
I shall remain in the position of a son. O Master Govinda, do not abandon us; do not forsake us.
Then the Great Being, demonstrating to the king the absence of that [desire] within himself, said:
“There is no lack of sensual pleasures for me, nor is there anyone who has harmed me;
having heard the words of a non-human being, therefore I do not delight in the household life,” he said.
Regarding this, *na matthi* means “there is nothing for me”; *gaha* means “in the house. Then the king questioned him:
“What is the appearance of this non-human being? What purpose did he speak to you?
And having heard what, have you abandoned us, our home, and everything else?
In this context, the phrase “abandoned us, our home, and everything else” refers to his relinquishing of attachment toward the brahmin’s home, which was filled with all manner of prosperity.
When he was building his own house, [the builder] said: "Having heard this, you have made us, our house, and all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa without exception laugh.
Then, explaining it to him, the Great Man said: "By me who previously observed the fast," and so forth.

Therein, "by me who previously observed the fast" means by me who, having entered into solitude, lived for four months. "By me who was desirous of sacrificing" means by me who wished to perform a sacrifice.

"For me, who was like this": a fire had been kindled, "strewn with *kus*a leaves"—meaning it had been covered with *kus*a leaves and fire was begun to be ignited after adding ghee, curd, honey, and so forth;
having thus kindled the fire, the meaning here is: "for me, who stood thinking, 'I shall give alms to the great multitude.'"
“Sanaṅkumāro” means the Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra. Then the king, desiring to go forth himself as well, said, “I believe,” and so on.
In that context, “How would you speak otherwise? means: “How would you speak differently?
“We shall follow you” means: “We too shall follow you alone; we shall go forth after you,” is the sense. There is also a reading: “anuvajissāma.”
The meaning is: "We shall follow him. *Akāca* means free from thorns, that is, smooth.
"In the instruction of Govinda" means in your teaching, O Govinda. He says: "Making the venerable Govinda himself our teacher, we shall live [accordingly].
This concludes the commentary on the Invitation of the Six Khattiyas.
322. "He approached those six kṣatriyas"—having thus encouraged King Reṇu by saying, "Excellent, Great King!

It is a noble deed performed by Your Majesty that you wish to go forth into homelessness, renouncing such great royal splendor at a time when beings seize sovereignty even by killing their mother, father, brothers, sisters, and so on," he strengthened his resolve even more firmly.
Having done so, he approached him. "They reflected thus" means they reflected in the very manner the king had thought: "Perhaps the Brahmin’s wealth has diminished.
"We shall win him over with wealth" means we shall entice him, we shall win him over.
"Let as much be brought as [is required]" means let as much be brought, let it be taken—whatever you desire, that much.
"Take it," is what is meant. "By the power of you alone" means by making you the condition;
it is because of being given by you that this abundant wealth has come into being.
"If you abandon sensual pleasures" means if you relinquish both objective sensual pleasures (*vatthu-kāma*) and defilement-sensual pleasures (*kilesa-kāma*). Where...
"Attached to the world of commoners (*puthujjana-satto*)" means that the commoner is attached, clinging, and bound to those sensual pleasures. "Exert yourselves;
be firm!"—this being so, he incites the kings' enthusiasm by saying: "Begin your energy; remaining resolute in undaunted effort, be firm.
"Composed through the power of patience" means: "Be endowed with the power of patience. Thus he generates their zeal.
"This path is the straight path": this path of the meditation on compassion is called the "straight path. "This path is unsurpassed":
this very path for rebirth in the Brahma-world is called the "matchless path" and the "supreme path. "The true Dhamma is guarded by the virtuous":
and this very Dhamma is called the "Dhamma guarded by the virtuous"—namely, by the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples. Thus [is the description] of the meditation on compassion.
Even by speaking in praise of them, he merely provides reinforcement so that they do not turn back.
For who indeed, O sir, knows about life? Life, O sir, is like a bubble on the water, like a drop of dew on the tip of a blade of grass;
its nature is to perish in an instant. Who knows its course? At what moment—
"Will it break? [The answer is: "The future world must certainly be gone to;
therefore, a wise son of good family should understand by means of wisdom (*mantā*). Wisdom is called *paññā*;
the meaning is that by means of that one should deliberate, awaken, investigate, and know. Or, the locative case is used in the sense of the instrumental: 'one should awaken by means of wisdom.'"
The meaning is: it must be awakened to by means of mindfulness (*manta*) and known by means of wisdom (*ñāṇa*).
What is to be awakened to? The difficulty of knowing the nature of life and the certainty that one must go to the next world.
Having awakened to this, one must cut off all attachments, perform what is wholesome, and practice the holy life (*brahmacariya*). Why? Because for one who is born, there is no freedom from death.
The Explanation of the Invitation of the Great Brahmins, etc. (324):
"Of little power and of little gain"—O sir, this so-called "renunciation" is indeed of small value;
for from the very moment one has renounced the world after abandoning kingship, those who harass and torment the renunciant reduce him to a wretched and helpless state.
They say: "We have little gain; even after wandering through the entire village, it is difficult to find anything fit for consumption.
But this Brahminhood is of great influence due to its high renown, and of great profit because it is endowed with gains and honors.
For you, sir, are now the chief priest in all of Jambudīpa, receiving the foremost seat, the foremost water, the foremost food, and the foremost perfumes everywhere."
"He obtains the foremost position":
"Like a king among kings"—for I, sir, am now like a Wheel-turning Monarch (cakravartin) in the midst of ordinary kings;
"like Brahmā among Brahmas"—like a Great Brahmā in the midst of ordinary Brahmas; "like a deity among householders"—among the remaining householders.
In splendor, he was like Sakka, the king of the gods. 325.
Regarding the description of the addressing of his wives:
"Forty wives of equal status" means he had forty wives who were indeed of equal rank; furthermore, he had many dancing girls of the three ages.
Commentary on the Great Discourse on the Renunciation of Mahāgovinda 326.
"He wanders on tour" means he wanders on tour through the sequence of villages and market towns;
in every place he visits, there is a clamor like that surrounding a Buddha. Hearing that "the wise Mahāgovinda is coming," people beforehand prepare a pavilion.
Having had the road prepared and decorated, they went out to meet him, received him, and brought him along;
great gain and honor arose, overwhelming him like a mighty flood. "Of the seven chaplains" means of the chaplains of the seven kings.
Thus, just as nowadays in such places, when some kind of suffering arises, people say, "Homage to the Buddha!"
Thus at that time they said: "Homage to the Brahmin Mahāgovinda! Homage to the seven family priests! (327).
By the method beginning with "accompanied by loving-kindness" (*mettāsahagatena*), etc., only the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) are mentioned in the text;

however, the Great Man produced all eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) as well as the five higher knowledges (*abhiññā*). And for his disciples, he [prepared] companionship in the Brahma-world.
"He taught the path" means he explained the path for the sake of attaining coexistence with Brahmā in the Brahma-world.
"In every way" refers to those who had produced the eight attainments (*samāpatti*) and the five higher knowledges (*abhiññā*).
"Those who did not understand the teaching in its entirety" refers to those who did not know even a single attainment among the eight attainments.

They were unable to bring about rebirth. "Amogha" means possessing fruition. "Avañjhā" means not barren. "They bring forth the most inferior [rebirth]" refers to giving birth to the host of *gandhabbas*.
"Saphalā" means purposeful through rebirths in the remaining deva-worlds. "Saudrayā" means accompanied by growth (*vuḍḍhi*) through rebirth in the Brahma-world. 329.
"I remember, Pañcasikha"—by this phrase, it is said that this discourse was spoken by the Buddha.

It is not for the sake of disenchantment—that is, not for the purpose of becoming disenchanted with the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*). It is not for the sake of dispassion—that is, not for the purpose of dispassion toward the round of existence.

It is not for the sake of cessation—that is, not for the purpose of the cessation of the round of existence. It is not for the sake of peace—that is, not for the purpose of the pacification of the round of existence.

It is not for the sake of direct knowledge—that is, not for the purpose of directly knowing the round of existence. It is not for the sake of awakening—that is, not for the purpose of the departure from the sleep of the defilements (*kilesa*).
For the purpose of awakening from the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*). "Not for the sake of *nibbāna*" means not for the sake of the deathless *nibbāna*.

"For the sake of absolute disenchantment" means for the sole purpose of becoming disenchanted with the cycle of existence. Herein, "disenchantment" refers to insight (*vipassanā*); "for the sake of dispassion" refers to the Path (*magga*);
"for the sake of cessation and peace" refers to *nibbāna*; "for the sake of direct knowledge and full enlightenment" refers to the Path; and "for the sake of *nibbāna*" [refers to the goal].
It is Nibbāna alone. Thus, one should understand this discourse on the definition of terms as follows: insight is stated in one place, the Path in three places, and Nibbāna in three places.
However, according to the figurative method (*pariyāya*), all of these are indeed synonyms for the Path and synonyms for Nibbāna.
Whatever needs to be said regarding Right View and the other factors has already been stated in the *Visuddhimagga* in the commentary on the Truths (*sacca-vaṇṇanā*).
330. “Those who do not [attain] everything by means of everything” refers to those who do not know how to fulfill all four noble paths, but instead produce three, two, or even one.
“Of all these sons of good family” refers to the sons of good family who have practiced the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
“Not in vain... fruitful and abundant”—with this, he concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship.

"Having paid homage to the Blessed One and circumambulated him" means: having mentally received the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma, having rejoiced in it, and having expressed approval by praising it with speech;
then, placing his great hands in añjali upon his head as if immersing himself in the juice of clear lac, he entered into the lattice of the six-colored rays of the One Possessed of Ten Powers.
Having paid homage at four places and circumambulated [the Buddha] three times, he praised the Blessed One again and again;
then, vanishing before the Teacher, he returned to his own celestial realm.
Thus ends [the section] from the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīghanikāya*.
The commentary on the Mahāgovinda Sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Mahāsamaya Sutta:
Explanation of the Introduction.
331. *Evaṃ me sutaṃ* (Thus have I heard) is the Mahāsamaya Sutta. Herein, this is the commentary on the previously unexplained words:

*Sakkesu* means in the Sakka country. By way of etymology as set forth in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta—based on the exclamation, "Truly, these princes are Sakyas"—the name "Sakka" was given to those royal princes.
Their dwelling place, even though it is but a single district, is called "Sakka" by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhi-sadda*). In that Sakka country...
"In the country" (*janapade*). "In the Great Forest" (*Mahāvane*) means in a vast forest that was self-arisen and not planted, forming a single continuous expanse with the Himalayas.
"By all who were Arahants" means by those who attained Arahantship on the very day this Sutta was spoken.
Herein, this is the sequential account: it is said that the Sākiyas and Koliyas [lived] at the cities of Kapilavatthu and Koliya respectively.
And in the interval between [the two cities], they had the river named Rohiṇī bound with a single embankment and cultivated their crops.
Then, in the month of Jeṭṭhamūla, when the crops were beginning to wither, the laborers from both cities gathered together.
Thereupon, the inhabitants of the city of Koliya said: "This water, being carried away from both sides, belongs neither to you..."
"It will suffice for us; however, our crops will be produced by this water alone, so give this water to us.

The inhabitants of the city of Kapilavatthu said, "While you remain with your granaries filled, we shall not be able to go about with baskets, sacks, and other vessels in our hands, carrying red gold, blue gems, and black coins."
"You may wander at the doors of your own houses, but our crop too shall be produced by this very water;
give this water to us! "We will not give it. "Neither will we give it.
Having thus increased their quarrel, one stood up and struck another, and he too struck another; and so they struck one another.
Provoking the lineages of the royal families, they increased the strife.
The Koliyan laborers said: "Seize those inhabitants of Kapilavatthu and shout at them—those who lived with their own sisters like dogs, jackals, and the like!
Their elephants, horses, shields, and weapons..."
“And what will our elephants, horses, shields, and weapons do for us? The Sākiyan laborers also said:
“Now you roar, having taken up these leprous children—those who were helpless, destitute, and lived like animals in hollow trees;
what will their elephants, horses, shields, and weapons do for us? They went to him...
The ministers spoke among themselves, and the ministers spoke among the members of the royal family;
then the Sākiyas, thinking, “We shall show the strength and power of those who dwell together with our sisters,” set out prepared for battle.
The Koliyas also, thinking, “We shall show the strength and power of those who dwell in the Kola trees,” set out prepared for battle.
The Blessed One, too, at the very time of dawn, having emerged from the attainment of Great Compassion and surveying the world, saw these men setting out thus, prepared for battle.
Having seen them, he reflected: "If I go there, will this quarrel be appeased, or will it not?
While considering this, [he thought]: "I shall go there for the sake of appeasing the quarrel; [therein lie] three Jātaka stories..."
"I shall tell them, and then the quarrel will be pacified. Then, having told two Jātaka stories to illustrate the value of harmony, I will teach the Attadaṇḍa Sutta.
Upon hearing the teaching, the inhabitants of both cities will each give one hundred and fifty young men;
I will ordain them, and at that time there will be a great assembly," he resolved.
Therefore, while these preparations for battle were underway and they were setting out, he did not inform anyone;
rather, taking his own bowl and robe, he went and sat cross-legged in the air between the two armies, emitting rays of six colors.
When the inhabitants of Kapilavatthu saw the Blessed One, they exclaimed, "Our Teacher, the best of our kinsmen, has arrived! He is seen!"

Thinking, "Could it be that we are the cause of this quarrel? they reflected: "Now that the Blessed One has arrived, it is not possible for us to let a weapon fall upon the body of another; let the inhabitants of the Koliyan city kill us or cook us.
Having thus cast away their weapons and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down. The inhabitants of the Koliyan city did likewise.
Having reflected thus, they cast aside their weapons, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down.
The Blessed One, though already knowing, asked: "For what purpose have you come, Great Kings? [They replied:
"Blessed One, it was not for the sport of bathing, nor for mountain sports, nor for river sports, nor for the purpose of seeing the mountains; rather, having set up a battle at this place..."
“We have come,” they said. “On what basis, Great King, do you quarrel? “On water, Bhante. “What is water worth, Great King? “It is of little value, Bhante.
“And what, Great King, is that which is called earth worth? “It is priceless, Bhante. “And what, Great King, are khattiyas worth?
“Khattiyas, Bhante, are indeed priceless. [The Buddha continued: “Water has a small root;”
"For what purpose, O Great King, do you destroy these priceless Khattiyas? "There is no pleasure in quarreling," he replied.
"O Great King, by means of this quarrel, having created enmity in an improper place, you have been harboring a grudge against a tree deity along with a black lion for this entire eon.
Having said this, he related the Phandana Jātaka.
Then he said, "Great King, one must not be a person who relies on the word of others.
For by relying on the word of another, at the mere mention of a single hare, the herds of four-footed creatures in the Himalayas—extending for three thousand yojanas—leapt into the great ocean.
Therefore, one must not rely on the word of others. Having said this, he related the Pathavī-undriya Jātaka.
Then, saying: "Sometimes, Great King, even one who is weak sees a flaw or an opening in one who is very powerful, and sometimes the very powerful sees one in the weak.
For even the little bird Laṭukikā killed a mighty elephant," he related the Laṭukika Jātaka.
Having thus related three Jātakas for the purpose of settling the quarrel, for the purpose of illustrating concord—
He related two Jātakas. How so? Having said, "O Great King, no one is able to find an opening in those who are united," he related the Rukkhadhamma Jātaka.
Then [he said], "O Great King, no one was able to find a rift among those who were united.
But when they fell into mutual dispute, then the son of a hunter deprived them of their lives."
Having seized them and taken them away, he departed. "In contention there is no such thing as gratification," he said, and then related the Vaṭṭakajātaka.
Having thus related these five Jātakas, at the conclusion he related the Attadaṇḍasutta.
The kings were filled with faith and said: "If the Teacher had not come, we would have slain one another with our own hands, creating a river of blood."
"We shall cause [the Dhamma] to be practiced; we shall not see our sons and brothers at the door of our home, nor will there be anyone to bring us news or counter-news.
It is by relying on the Teacher that we have obtained our livelihood.
But if the Teacher had lived as a householder, sovereignty over the four great continents surrounded by two thousand islands would have come into his hands."
“If he had been born, he would have had more than a thousand sons, and thus he would have wandered about surrounded by a retinue of kshatriyas.
Having renounced that very prosperity and gone forth, he has attained full enlightenment; let him now also wander about surrounded by a retinue of kshatriyas.
Thus, the inhabitants of both cities [sent] two hundred and fifty princes each.
They gave them. The Blessed One, having ordained them, went to the Great Forest.
Because they had been ordained not out of their own inclination but out of heavy respect [for their parents], dissatisfaction arose within them.
Their former wives also sent messages to them, saying, "Noble sons, may you be weary; the household life is not stable," and so forth. Consequently, they became even more weary.
The Blessed One, perceiving their state of discontent through his supernormal knowledge, thought: "These monks, living together with a Buddha such as myself, are becoming weary.
Come now, by describing the beauty of Kuṇāla Lake and leading them there, I shall dispel their dissatisfaction.
Thus he spoke in praise of Kuṇāla Lake. They became desirous of seeing it.

“Bhikkhus, do you wish to see Kuṇāla Lake?”—“Yes, Blessed One.”—“If that is so, come, let us go.”—“Venerable sir, while the Blessed One is capable of traveling by psychic power, how shall we go?”—“You must desire to go;
I will take you along by my own power.”—“Very well, venerable sir. Then the Blessed One [took] the five hundred bhikkhus...
Having taken it, he flew up into the air, alighted upon Kuṇāla Lake, and said to those bhikkhus:
"Bhikkhus, ask for the names of those fish in this Kuṇāla Lake whose names you do not know.
They asked, and the Blessed One explained each name as it was asked. Not only of the fish, but also of [the other beings] in that...

In the forest grove, he had the names of the trees asked of him and spoke of them; likewise, at the foot of the mountain, he had the names of the bipeds, quadrupeds, and birds asked of him and spoke of them.

Then, King Kuṇāla, seated upon a staff held by two birds who were pecking at it with their beaks, approached, surrounded on the front, the back, and both sides by a multitude of birds. When the bhikkhus saw him, they said:
—“Venerable sir, we think that this one will be the king of these birds, and these others will be his retinue.
“In the same way, bhikkhus, this too is my lineage, this is my tradition. “Venerable sir, for now we see these birds;
but we wish to hear what the Blessed One has said regarding how ‘this too is my lineage, this is my tradition.’”
“Do you wish to hear it, monks? “Yes, Blessed One. “Then listen,” he said, and by reciting the Kuṇāla Jātaka adorned with three hundred stanzas, he dispelled their discontent.
At the conclusion of the teaching, they all were established in the fruit of stream-entry, and through that very path, supernatural power also came to them.
The Blessed One thought: “Let this much suffice for them.”
"O monks," he said, and leaping into the air, he went straight to the Great Forest.

Those monks, having gone at the time of departure by means of the power of the One of Ten Powers, returned at the time of arrival by their own power and descended into the Great Forest surrounding the Blessed One.
The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat, addressed those monks, and said: "Come, monks; sit down."
“I shall explain a meditation subject for the abandoning of those defilements that are to be abandoned by the three higher paths,” he said, and thus he explained the meditation subject.
The bhikkhus thought: “The Blessed One, having known our state of discontent, led us to the Kuṇāla Lake and dispelled our discontent there;
there we attained the fruit of stream-entry, but now here [he speaks] of the three paths.”
He gave them a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), saying, “It is not fitting for us to pass our time thinking, ‘We are stream-enterers’;

it is fitting for us to become like the Supreme Person. Having paid homage at the feet of the One of Ten Powers, they rose, cleared away their sitting mats, and sat down separately at the foot of trees on the mountain slopes.
The Blessed One thought: “These bhikkhus have already been diligent in their meditation subjects by nature;
moreover, for a bhikkhu who has found the right method, there is no such thing as weariness.
As they go along, they will further develop insight, attain arahantship, and come into my presence thinking, ‘We shall each report the qualities we have attained.’”
“When these have arrived, the deities from ten thousand world-systems will assemble in a single world-system;
there will be a great gathering, and it is fitting for me to sit in a secluded place. Then, having prepared a Buddha-seat in a secluded spot, he sat down.
The elder who had gone first to take up his meditation subject attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Then one after another, like lotuses blooming upon a lotus-pond, even five hundred [monks] blossomed forth.
The monk who had first attained *arahantship*, thinking, "I shall inform the Blessed One," untied his cross-legged posture, shook out his sitting mat, rose, and turned toward the One of Ten Powers.
In this way, one after another, even five hundred [monks] [approached] the dining hall.
They arrived one after another, as if entering in succession. The first to arrive, having paid homage and prepared a seat, sat down to one side;
desiring to announce the qualities he had attained, he looked back toward the path by which they had come, wondering, "Is there anyone else? and saw another, and saw yet another. Thus, all of them—
Having arrived and sat down to one side, he said, "This one did not speak to him out of embarrassment;
that one did not speak to him out of embarrassment. It is said that for those whose taints are destroyed, two thoughts arise:
"Oh, would that the world with its devas might quickly realize the qualities I have attained! and [the thought] regarding the state already attained...
Like a man who has found a treasure, he does not wish to announce it to anyone else. Thus,
when that Noble Assembly had merely begun to settle, there appeared in the world— adorned by the arising of a Buddha and bounded by the Eastern Yugandhara Mountains—
a realm entirely free from the defilements of clouds, mist, smoke, dust, and Rāhu.
For the sake of displaying its beauty, as if it were a great silver mirror-mandala raised up in the eastern direction,
he took hold of the wheel-rim and, surpassing the full moon’s orb with its splendor of a revolving silver wheel,
he set out upon the path of the wind. Thus, at such a moment, at such a time, at such an hour, the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu.
In the Great Forest, together with a great community of monks numbering about five hundred, all of whom were arhats.
Therein, the Blessed One was born in the lineage of Mahāsammata; those five hundred monks were also born into the family of Mahāsammata.
The Blessed One was born from a kṣatriya womb; they too were born from a kṣatriya womb. The Blessed One...
They too were royal renunciants. The Blessed One, having abandoned the white parasol and renounced the universal monarch’s sovereignty that was in his hands, went forth;
they too, having abandoned the white parasols and renounced the sovereignties that were in their hands, went forth.
Thus the Blessed One, in a pure place and at a pure time of night, being himself pure, was surrounded by a pure retinue.

Free from lust and surrounded by those free from lust, free from hatred and surrounded by those free from hatred, free from delusion and surrounded by those free from delusion, without craving and surrounded by those without craving,
without defilement and surrounded by those without defilement, peaceful and surrounded by the peaceful, tamed and surrounded by the tamed,
liberated and surrounded by the liberated— he shines exceedingly. This is what is called the "ground of praise," as much as one is able [to describe it].
It should be stated thus. It was said with reference to these bhikkhus: “With about five hundred bhikkhus, all of whom were arahants.

“For the most part” means that the majority had assembled; those who were sluggish did not assemble, nor did the non-percipient beings, the deities of the formless realm, or the deities absorbed in jhāna.
In this regard, the sequence of the assembly was as follows: it is said that the deities in the vicinity of the Great Forest were stirred.
—“Come, sirs! Seeing the Buddha is truly beneficial; hearing the Dhamma is beneficial; seeing the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is beneficial!

Come, come! Making such a great clamor, they arrived, paid homage to the Blessed One and to those whose taints were destroyed and who had attained Arahatship at that very moment, and stood to one side. By this same means, for each of them...
Having heard the sound, [he traveled] across the Himalayas— which extend for three thousand yojanas by way of half-gāvutas,
one gāvuta, half-yojanas, one yojana, and so forth— throughout the entire Jambudīpa: thrice through the sixty-three thousand cities,
ninety-nine hundred thousand *doṇamukha*s, ninety-six hundred thousand million ports (*paṭṭana*), and fifty-six jewel-mines.
In Pubbavideha, Aparagoyāna, Uttarakuru, and in the two thousand minor islands—that is, throughout the entire Cakkavāḷa—and likewise in the second and third Cakkavāḷas;
thus it should be understood that the deities have assembled in ten thousand Cakkavāḷas.
For here, "ten thousand Cakkavāḷas" is intended to mean "ten world-systems. Therefore it was said: "And by ten..."
"Deities from the world-systems have for the most part assembled.
When the deities have thus assembled, the entire interior of the world-sphere, up to the Brahma-world, becomes filled without any gaps—just like needles inserted closely together into a needle-case.
In this regard, the height of the Brahma-world should be understood as follows.
It is said that a stone from the Lohapāsāda, equal in size to seven upper chambers, would take four months to reach the earth when thrown down from the Brahma-world. In such a vast space,
there is no room for flowers or incense thrown from below to go upward, nor for mustard seeds thrown from above to descend downward.
In this way, the deities were present without interruption.
Just as the seated place of a wheel-turning monarch is unconfined so that high-ranking kshatriyas who arrive one after another find space, while the area beyond becomes extremely crowded,
even so the Blessed One’s seated place was unconfined for the high-ranking deities who arrived one after another.

And even the Great Brahmas obtained space. Furthermore, in the vicinity of the Blessed One—just as described in the account of the Great Parinibbāna—in a space no larger than the tip of a hair, ten, twenty, or even more than thirty deities stood, having manifested extremely subtle bodies. Sixty deities stood there.

"Of those belonging to the Pure Abodes" means of the inhabitants of the Pure Abodes. The "Pure Abodes" are the five Brahma-worlds, which are the dwellings of the pure ones—those non-returners whose taints are exhausted.

Why did this thought occur to them? It is said that those Brahmās, having entered into meditative attainment and emerged according to its duration, were looking upon the Brahma-abode as if it were a meal-house after a meal.
They saw the emptiness. Then, reflecting on where the Brahmās had gone, they realized there was a great assembly.
Thinking, "This assembly is vast; we have been left behind, and for those who are left behind, an opportunity is difficult to obtain;
therefore, as we go, let us not go empty-handed, but let us each compose a verse and go. And with that, in the great assembly..."

“We shall let him know that we have arrived, and we shall speak in praise of the One Possessed of the Ten Powers. Thus, because they had emerged from their meditative attainment and directed their attention, this thought occurred to them.
“They appeared before the Blessed One” means, in the text, that they appeared right in the presence of the Blessed One, in the very place facing him.
They were spoken as if having descended, yet the meaning should not be understood in this way.

Rather, while remaining in the Brahma-world itself, they composed the verses; one descended upon the eastern rim of the world-system, one on the southern rim, one on the western rim, and one on the northern rim of the world-system. Then...
The Brahmā who had descended upon the eastern rim of the world-system (*cakravāḷamukhavaṭṭi*) entered the blue kasiṇa meditation, emitted blue rays, and—
like one putting on a jewel-skin cloak— made his arrival known to the deities of the ten thousand world-systems.
Since the so-called "Buddha-path" cannot be obstructed by anyone, he proceeded precisely along that beaten Buddha-path.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side. Standing there, he recited a verse composed by himself.
The Brahmā who had descended upon the southern rim of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa-mukhavaṭṭi*) also entered the yellow kasiṇa attainment;
emitting golden rays and yellow light, he was as if draping a golden cloth over the deities of the ten thousand world-systems.
Having made himself known, he remained standing just as he was.

The Brahmā who had descended upon the western rim of the world-system also entered the red kasiṇa absorption, emitted red rays, and, as if enveloping the deities of the ten thousand world-systems with a fine red woolen blanket,
made himself known and remained standing just as he was on the northern rim of the world-system.

The Brahmā who had descended also entered the white-kasiṇa attainment, emitted white rays, and, as if draping a *sumana* flower-cloth over the deities of the ten thousand world-systems, made his presence known and stood right there.
However, in the text it says: "They appeared before the Blessed One. Then those deities, having paid homage to the Blessed One..."
"stood to one side"—thus both his appearance before [the Buddha] as if at a single moment and his state of standing to one side after having paid homage have been described;
this occurred in this sequence, yet they have been shown here by grouping them together.
However, in the Pāli, the speaking of the verses is stated separately for each occasion.
In this context, "great assembly" (*mahāsamaya*) means a great multitude. "Wood" (*pavana*) refers to a grove of trees. By both terms, the Blessed One stated:
"Today, in this grove, there is a great multitude, a great gathering. Then, in order to show those for whom that gathering consists, he said:
"The hosts of devas have assembled. Therein, "hosts of devas" (*devakāya*) means a collection of devas. "We have come to this Dharma-assembly" (*imaṃ dhammasamayaṃ*).
Seeing that the host of gods had thus assembled, we too have come to this assembly of Dhamma. For what reason? To behold the unconquered Saṅgha;

the meaning is: we have come for the sake of seeing this unconquered Saṅgha, which has conquered the battle today by crushing the three Māras and cannot be defeated by anyone. Having spoken this verse, that Brahmā—
Having paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood right there at the eastern rim of the Cakkavāḷa.
Then the second [monk] arrived in the same manner as described and spoke. In that context, "there, monks" (*tatra bhikkhave*) means the monks in that place of assembly.

"They composed themselves" (*samādahaṃsu*) means they applied themselves with concentration. "They made their own minds straight" (*cittamattano ujukaṃ akaṃsu*) means they made their own minds upright.
Having removed all crookedness, curvature, and wickedness, they made them straight. "Like a charioteer holding the reins" means that just as a charioteer,
when his horses are moving evenly, stands without urging or restraining them while holding all the traces with a lowered goad,
so too these five hundred [monks], possessing the sixfold equanimity and guarding their sense-faculties, [remained thus].
"The wise monks guard their faculties; we have come here to see them, Blessed One.
He too went and stood in his very place.
Then the third one came and spoke in the same manner as before. Therein, "having cut the stake" refers to the stake of lust, hatred, and delusion.

"Having cut down": the "barriers" (*paligha*) are indeed the barriers of lust, hatred, and delusion. The "city-gate posts" (*indakhīla*) are also indeed the city-gate posts of lust, hatred, and delusion.
"Having pulled up, they are unshakable" (*ūhacca maneja*): by the absence of the "thirst-plant" (*taṇhā-ejā*), these monks are "unshakable" (*aneja*).

Having pulled up and completely eradicated the city-gate posts, they wander; that is, they wander with an unhindered course in the four directions. "Pure" (*suddha*) means free from defilements. "Stainless" (*vimala*)...
"Pure. This is a synonym for that very same thing. "By the One with Eyes" means by the one possessing eyes through the five kinds of vision.
"Well-tamed" means tamed in eye, tamed in ear, tamed in nose, tamed in tongue, tamed in body, and tamed in mind.
"Excellent young elephants" means young elephants. We have come to see these young elephants being tamed by such an unsurpassed master of yoga.
"O Blessed One! He too went and stood in his very own place.

Then the fourth one came and spoke in the same manner as before. "Those who have gone there" means they have gone by way of taking refuge with full confidence. He too went and stood in his very own place.
[End of] the Commentary on the Assembly of Devas.
333. Then the Blessed One, surveying from the surface of the earth up to the limit of the Cakkavāḷa rim and as far as the Akaniṭṭha Brahma-world, saw the assembly of deities and thought:
“This is a great gathering of deities; yet these monks do not know that such a great assembly of deities has come together. Come now, I shall inform them. Having thus reflected, he—
“Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus”—all this should be expanded in full. In that context, *etaparamā* means those for whom this is the ultimate limit or measure;
thus they are called *etaparamā*. Now, because there are currently no Buddhas, the third section—“Those, bhikkhus, who at present”—was not spoken.
Why did he say, “I shall tell you, bhikkhus”? It was for the purpose of generating a state of mental readiness in the devas.
The deities thought: "The Blessed One will mention the names and clans of only those deities of great influence in such a vast assembly; what will he say about those of little influence?

Then the Blessed One, perceiving with his mind what these deities were thinking, reached his hand out of his mouth as if crushing the flesh of their hearts, and [addressed them] together with their belongings.
Like a thief seizing his prey, he perceived their mental dispositions and thought:
"I shall declare the names and clans of all the deities who have come from the ten thousand world-systems, whether they be of little power or great power.
These Buddhas are indeed great beings, distinguished among all beings, whom the world with its gods has seen, heard, and known.
There is nothing whatsoever— whether a visible object among the various objects of form distinguished by blue and so forth,
or a sound among the various objects of sound distinguished by the sound of a drum and so forth—
that does not come within the range of these [cognitions] at the gateway of knowledge. As it has been said:

“Bhikkhus, whatever in this world with its devas... [as before] ...with its devas and humans, has been seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, or investigated by the mind—that I know, that I see, that I have directly realized.
Thus, with knowledge unimpeded in every respect, the Blessed One divided all those deities into two classes according to their capacity and incapacity.
Those beings described by the method beginning with “endowed with an obstruction of kamma” are called incapable. They—

Even when dwelling in the same monastery, the Buddhas do not look after them. However, those who are "capable" (bhabba), though they may be the opposite, they go even to where they dwell at a distance and take them under their care.
Therefore, in that assembly of deities as well, having set aside those who are incapable, he took those who are capable under his care. Having taken them under his care, he discerned:
"So many here are of a lustful temperament (rāgacarita), so many are of a hateful temperament (dosacarita), and so many are of a deluded temperament (mohacarita)."
He divided them into six groups according to their temperaments. Then, considering the appropriate Dharma teaching for each, he thought:
"I shall preach the *Sammāparibbājaniya Sutta* to the deities of lustful temperament; the *Kalahavivāda Sutta* to those of hateful temperament; the *Mahāvyūha Sutta* to those of deluded temperament;
the *Cūḷavyūha Sutta* to those of discursive temperament; and the [Saddhā-sutta] to those of faithful temperament."
“I shall teach the *Tuvaṭṭaka-paṭipadā* and the *Purābheda-sutta* for those whose conduct is characterized by wisdom.

Having thus established the subject of his teaching, he again directed his mind toward that assembly, considering: “Will they understand through my own inclination, through the inclination of others, through the arising of a specific purpose, or by way of a question?
Then, knowing that they would understand “by way of a question,” he considered: “Is there perhaps anyone among the deities...”
“Having grasped his intention, is he capable of asking a question according to his own conduct? He saw that not even one among those five hundred bhikkhus was able to do so.
Then, having turned his attention to the eighty great disciples and the two chief disciples, and seeing that they too were unable, he thought:
“If he were a Paccekabuddha, would he perhaps be able?”
Realizing, “He too would not be able,” he reflected, “Perhaps someone among Sakka, Suyāma, and the others might be able.
For had anyone among them been able, he would have had that person questioned and answered for himself; yet not even among them was anyone capable.
Then this thought occurred to him: “Only a Buddha like myself could be able; but is there another Buddha anywhere?”
Spreading his infinite knowledge across infinite world-systems and surveying them, he saw no other Buddha.

This is not surprising that he would see no one equal to himself now; for even on the day of his birth, as described in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*, seeing no one equal to himself, he uttered the irreversible lion’s roar: "I am the foremost in the world. Thus...
Seeing no one else who was his equal, he thought: "If I were to ask the questions myself and provide the answers myself, these deities would not be able to penetrate the meaning.
However, if another Buddha asks the questions and I provide the answers, it will be a marvel, and the deities will be able to penetrate the meaning."

"Therefore, I shall create a manifested Buddha. Having thus entered the jhāna that serves as the basis for the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and emerged from it, he performed the preliminary work (*parikamma*) with sense-sphere consciousnesses, thinking:
"Let the grasping of the bowl and robes, the looking forward and looking around, and the contracting and extending [of the limbs] be exactly like my own.
Then, leaping over the eastern Yugandhara mountain range, he pierced the lunar disk.
He resolved with a fine-material-sphere consciousness as if he were actually emerging.
When the host of devas saw him, they said, "O sir, has another moon risen? Then, when one nearer than the moon appeared, they said, "It is not the moon;
the sun has risen. Again, when one nearer than the sun appeared, they said, "It is not the sun; it is a celestial mansion."
When he was closer still, they said, "It is not a celestial palace; it is a single son of the gods.
When he was closer still, they said, "It is not a son of the gods; it is the Great Brahmā alone. When he was closer still, they said, "It is not the Great Brahmā;
another Buddha has arrived, sir! Thereupon, the ordinary deities thought: "First, of a single Buddha..."
“This assembly of deities—how great will it be for the two of them? The noble deities thought:
“There are no two Buddhas in a single world-system; surely another Buddha, identical to the Blessed One himself, has been created by him.”
Then, while that assembly of devas was looking on, the created Buddha arrived;

without even bowing to the One Possessed of Ten Powers, he took a seat prepared at a level equal to his own in the place directly facing him. The Blessed One possessed the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, and the created one likewise possessed the thirty-two;
from the body of the Blessed One rays of six colors issued forth, and from the body of the created one as well.
The rays from the Blessed One’s body struck the body of the created form, and the rays from the created form’s body struck the body of the Blessed One.
Emerging from the bodies of both Buddhas, they ascended as far as the Akaniṭṭha realm,
then turned back, descended over the heads of the deities, and [re-entered] at the rim of the world-system’s mouth.
They were established [there]. The entire interior of the Cakkavāḷa shone like a shrine-hall covered with golden curved rafters.
The deities of ten thousand Cakkavāḷas gathered together in a single Cakkavāḷa and, having entered within the radiance of the two Buddhas, stood there.
Even as he sat down, the created Buddha praised the abandonment of the defilements at the Bodhi-seat of the One Possessed of Ten Powers:
“I ask the Sage of abundant wisdom,
who has gone to the further shore, who is fully extinguished, whose mind is steadfast; who,
having departed from the home life, has cast off sensual desires.”
“How should a bhikkhu wander rightly in the world?”—thus he spoke this verse.
The Teacher, thinking, “I shall announce the names and clans of the deities who have come one after another in order to generate mental clarity,” said, “I will explain, O bhikkhus,” and so forth.
In that context, “I shall proclaim a *silaoka* (verse)” means I shall set forth a collection of words regulated by syllables and phrases.

"Wherever the earth-dwelling deities were dependent" means that in whatever places the earth-dwelling deities resided, he praised those monks with the words "those who dwell in mountain clefts," and so forth;
the meaning is that those monks were dependent upon the interior of the mountains.
"Resolute" means having directed their minds [toward the goal]. "Concentrated" means undistracted.
"Puthu" means many people. "Sīhāva sallīnā" means they are hidden like lions, having attained a state of solitude.
"Lomahaṃsābhisambhunoti" means they stand having overcome the bristling of the hair; that is to say, they are fearless.
"Odātamanasā suddhā" means being pure by having a bright mind. "Vippasannāmanāvilā" means serene and undisturbed.
"Knowing more than five hundred" means knowing that there were more than five hundred bhikkhus together with the Perfectly Enlightened One.
"In the forest near Kapilavatthu" refers to the grove grown in the vicinity of Kapilavatthu. "Then the Teacher addressed" means he addressed them at that time.
"Disciples who delight in the teaching" refers to those disciples because they had become [his followers] at the conclusion of hearing his own Dhamma discourse.
“Delighting in the teaching of the three trainings” means delighting in the dispensation (*sāsana*).
All of this is stated as if it were spoken by another, following the words, “I shall proclaim his fame.
“The hosts of devas have arrived; know them, O bhikkhus”—this means, “know them by means of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).”
He spoke for the purpose of inciting the bhikkhus toward the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhuñāṇa*). And they applied themselves with ardor, having heard the Buddha’s teaching;
those bhikkhus, having heard that teaching of the Buddha, immediately exerted energy for that purpose.
As soon as they had applied such ardor, knowledge appeared to them. Of what kind? It was the knowledge of the divine eye, which is the vision of non-human beings (*amanussa*).
It arose. It was not produced by them at that moment through preparatory effort; rather, it was accomplished solely by means of the Noble Path.
However, they merely made a formal resolve for the purpose of seeing non-human beings.
The Teacher also said, "Bhikkhus, you have knowledge; bring it forth and understand with it," referring precisely to this when he said, "Understand, bhikkhus."
"Appeke satam addakkhun" means that among those bhikkhus, some bhikkhus saw a hundred non-human beings (*amanussa*). "Sahassam atha sattari" means some saw a thousand; some saw seventy thousand.

"Satam eke sahassānam" means some saw a hundred thousand. "Appekenantam addakkhun" means they saw a vast number; the meaning is that they saw an indefinite amount by way of hundreds and thousands. Why? Because...
"All directions were pervaded; they were filled and completely full.
And "having understood all that" means having known everything seen by each one of them individually.
"Having discerned with the eye" means having established it through direct perception, like a line on the palm of the hand, the possessor of the eye (cakkhumā) by means of the five eyes.
The Teacher. Then he addressed them: he spoke this very verse previously mentioned for the purpose of proclaiming their names and clans.
"Know these ones," "see," "look upon"—those whom I shall proclaim; such is the connection here.
"With words" means with speech. "In successive order" means according to sequence.
335. “Seven thousand yakkhas, earth-dwellers of Kapilavatthu”:

he says that there were seven thousand earth-dwelling yakkhas who had been reborn right here in dependence on Kapilavatthu. “Possessing psychic power” means endowed with divine psychic power (*iddhi*).
“Possessing radiance” means possessed of majesty. “Possessing beauty” means possessed of physical beauty. “Possessed of fame” means possessed of a retinue.
"Rejoicing, they have come forth" means they have arrived with joyful hearts.

"To the assembly of bhikkhus in this great forest" means they have come into the presence of the bhikkhus for the purpose of seeing the bhikkhus. Alternatively, *samitiṃ* means a gathering; thus the meaning is also that they have come to see the assembly of bhikkhus.
"Six thousand from the Himavanta" refers to the six thousand yakkhas born on the Hemavata mountain; they are all of various colors, such as blue and so forth.
"Three thousand from Sātāgira" refers to the three thousand yakkhas born on the Sātāgiri mountain.
Thus, these together total sixteen thousand.
"Five hundred Vessāmittas" means five hundred [yakkhas] born on Mount Vessāmitta.
"Kumbhīra of Rājagaha" refers to the yakkha named Kumbhīra, who was born in the city of Rājagaha. "The abode of Vepulla" means that Mount Vepulla is his abode;
the meaning is that it is his place of residence. "Furthermore, a hundred thousand..."
"He pays homage to the yakkhas" means he pays homage to more than a hundred thousand yakkhas.
Kumbhīra, the king of Rājagaha— having come to this assembly in the forest— he too, along with his retinue,
has come to this forest to see the assembly of bhikkhus.
336. "The king Dhataraṭṭha rules over the eastern direction" means he governs the eastern quarter.
"Lord of the Gandhabbas" means he is the eldest among the Gandhabbas in all four directions; they all abide under his authority.
"The Great King of great renown" means this Great King possesses a vast retinue.
"He has many sons, named Indra, who are very powerful" means that Dhatarattha has many very powerful sons, all of whom bear the name of Sakka, the king of the gods.
"Virulha rules over it" means that Virulha governs that quarter.

"He too has sons" means that he likewise has sons of the same kind. In the Pali text, however, they write "mahabbalā" (very powerful), whereas in the Commentary, the reading "mahābalā" (of great strength) appears in all instances.
“Dhataraṭṭha in the eastern quarter, Virūḷhaka to the south;
Virūpakkha to the west, and Kuvera in the northern quarter.
These four great kings [reign] all around the four quarters.”
“Displaying their splendor, they stood in the forest of Kapilavatthu.
These verses, however, are spoken by way of a comprehensive summary.
And this is the meaning here: in the ten-thousandfold world-system, there are great kings named Dhatarattha; all of them—

Accompanied by a retinue of hundreds of thousands of millions of gandhabbas, they arrived from the Great Forest of Kapilavatthu in the eastern direction and stood filling the interior of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).
Likewise, Virūḷhaka and the others [arrived] from the southern direction and so forth. For this reason it was said:
"Shining brightly, they stood in the four directions all around. This, indeed, is what is meant: "All around the world-systems..."
"Having come from the four quarters, they stand upon the mountain peaks blazing intensely like masses of fire.
However, because they came specifically with reference to the Kapilavatthu forest, even though they stood filling the entire world-system and were equal in extent to that world-system,
they are described as being "in the forest of Kapilavatthu."
337. "The deceitful servants of those [kings] have come": there are servants of those great kings who are possessed of the deceit characterized by concealing the evil they have committed;
they are crooked in conduct, and because they deceive the world through face-to-face and behind-the-back trickery, they are called "deceitful" (*vañcanika*);
and because they are endowed with fraudulent craftiness (*kerāṭiya-sāṭheyya*), they are called "crafty" (*saṭha*). They too have arrived.
The meaning is as follows: Māyā, Kuṭeṇḍu, Viṭeṇḍu, Viṭucca, and Viṭuṭa—these companions were all indeed illusionists (*māyākāraka*).
Among them, however, one was named Kuṭeṇḍu and another was named Viṭeṇḍu; in the Pāḷi, however, they are written as "Veṭeṇḍu.
One was named Viṭucca and another was named Viṭuṭa. As for "Saha," that Viṭuṭa had also come along with them.

Candana, Kāmaseṭṭha, Kinnighaṇḍu, and Nighaṇḍu—there is another named Kinnighaṇḍu (though in the Pāḷi it is written as “Kinnughaṇḍu”). And Nighaṇḍu refers to another named Nighaṇḍu; these are the number of slaves.
Following this, however: “Panāda and Opamañña, Devasuta and Mātali;
Cittasena the Gandhabba, King Naḷa, and Janesabha.”
“Āguṃ Pañcasikha and Timbarū, and Sūriyavaccasā”—these are the kings of the gods.
Therein, “Devasuta” means the charioteer of the gods. “Cittasena” refers to Citta, Sena, and Cittasena. “Gandhabba”:
this Cittasena is a son of the gods belonging to the Gandhabba host; it is not he alone, but all [of them].
Peta, Panāda, and the others are indeed Gandhabbas. Naḷorāja is the name of a certain son of the gods, a maker of reeds.
Janesabha is the son of the gods Janavasabha. “And Pañcasikha came” means that the son of the gods Pañcasikha arrived.
Timbarū is the king of the Gandhabba deities named Timbarū. Sūriyavacchasā is his daughter.
"These and other kings, Gandhabbas together with their kings"— this means that these Gandhabba kings mentioned by name,
along with other many Gandhabbas together with these kings, approached joyfully;
the sense is that they came to this forest, the assembly of the monks, with hearts glad and elated.
338. "Then the Nāgas came" means that the Nāgas from Vesālī—namely, the Tacchaka Nāgas and the Nāgas dwelling in the Nāgasada Lake—along with the assembly of Tacchaka Nāgas, arrived;
this is the meaning. "Kambala and Assatara" refers to Kambala and Assatara.
It is said that these two dwell at the foot of Sineru; they are powerful Nāgas and Pāyāgas who cannot be carried off even by Supaṇṇas.
"Along with their kinsmen" means they came together with the community of their relatives who dwell at Payāga-tīrtha.
"The Yamunā and Dhatarattha [nāgas]" refers to the nāgas dwelling by the Yamunā river and those born into the Dhatarattha clan.
"The great nāga Erāvaṇa" refers to the divine son Erāvaṇa; he is not a nāga by birth, but is designated as such by way of conventional usage.
"Sopāgāti" means he too has come.
"Those who seize the nāga kings by force" refers to those of the aforementioned kind who, overcome by greed, act with violence to seize and take them away.
"Divine birds, winged ones with purified vision" means they are divine due to their divine power, [born] from the mother's womb...
And because they are born twice—from the egg and [again] from the shell—they are called *dija* (twice-born). Because they possess wings, they are *pakkhī* (winged).
Because their eyes are capable of seeing *nāgas* even at a distance of a hundred *yojanas* or a thousand *yojanas*, they have purified vision (*visuddhacakkhu*).

"They reached the middle of the forest through the air" means that they arrived at this great forest solely by way of the sky. "The variegated *supaṇṇas*"—this is their name; thus, their name is "the variegated *supaṇṇas*."
At that time, the Nāga king was free from fear; the Buddha had made him safe from the Supaṇṇas.

Therefore, they all called out to one another with gentle words, conversing like friends and like kinsmen, greeting each other with joy, embracing, taking hands, and placing their hands upon the shoulders, their hearts filled with delight and gladness. The Nāgas and Supaṇṇas took refuge [in the Buddha].
They have gone for refuge to the Buddha alone, to the Awakened One himself.

(339) "Conquered by the wielder of the thunderbolt" means they were conquered by Indra, the king of the gods. "The asuras who dwell in the ocean" refers to all those brothers of Vāsava—Sujātā the asura maiden being among them—who possess supernatural powers and great renown.
Among them, Kālakañja and Mahābhisas came having manifested themselves in massive and terrifying forms.
"Asurā dānaveghasā" refers to other archer-asuras named Dānaveghasā.
"Vepacitti, Sucitti, and Pahārāda, together with Namuci"—these are the asura Vepacitti, the asura Sucitti, and Namuci the son of Māra;
he arrived together with these asuras. These asuras dwell in the great ocean, while this one dwells in the Paranimmita-vasavatti heaven.
"Why has he come together with these? [The answer is: "Because of his lack of desire (*acchandikatā*). For they too were without desire and incapable; this one was just like them.
Therefore, he came having harmonized according to their elements (*dhātu*).
And "the hundred sons of Bali" means the hundred sons of the great asura Bali. "All named Verochana" means all [were named] Verochana.

They bore the same name as their own maternal uncle, Rāhu. Having girded themselves with their own snares—meaning, having girded themselves with their own snares and all having put on their armor—they approached Rāhu Bhadda;

that is, they drew near to Rāhu, the lord of the asuras. "Now is the time, O Blessed One," [they said]; "may it be well with you; the time has come for you to approach the forest where the assembly of monks is gathered."
The meaning is: "to see the community of bhikkhus. 340.

*Āpo ca devā pathavī, tejo vāyo tadāgamun*ti: the deities named "Water" (*āpa*) and so forth, who were produced by performing preparatory work (*parikamma*) upon the water-kasiṇa and the others, arrived.
*Varuṇā vāraṇā devā, somo ca yasasā sahā*ti: the Varuṇa deities, the Vāraṇa deities, and Soma together with Yasa.
The meaning is that the gods named Vāraṇadevatā and Somadevatā arrived together with the god named Yasas.

"Belonging to the body of loving-kindness and compassion" means gods reborn after having performed the preliminary practice (*parikamma*) for the jhāna of loving-kindness (*mettā*) and the jhāna of compassion (*karuṇā*).
"The glorious gods have come"—these gods of great renown have also arrived.
"Ten bodies in ten ways": the meaning is that all those ten classes of deities (*devakāya*), standing in ten groups, have come with various colors such as blue and so forth.
"And the Veṇḍu gods" means the Veṇḍu deities. "And Sahali" means the Sahali deities. "And two Asamas, the Yamakas" means the two Asama deities and the twin (*yamaka*) deities.
"The deities who are followers of the Moon" means they have come placing the Moon in front of them.
The deities who depend on the moon came placing the moon in front; likewise, the deities who depend on the sun came placing the sun in front.
"Placing the constellations in front" means that the deities who depend on the constellations also came placing the constellations in front.
"The slow-moving clouds have come" refers to all these: the wind-clouds, the rain-clouds, and the heat-clouds.
The inhabitants of the Valāhaka realm are called “Mandavalāhakas”; the meaning is that they too have arrived. Among the Vasus, Vāsava is the best;
Sakka, who is called Purindada, has also arrived—he who is the chief of the Vasu deities, known as Vāsava, and who is capable (sakkoti) and is called Purindada. He too has come.
"Ten times tenfold are their bodies": these ten classes of gods have also arrived in ten divisions. "All of various colors": they possess various colors by way of blue and so forth.
"Then came the Sahabhū gods": then the gods named Sahabhū arrived.
"Like flaming crests of fire": blazing like crests of fire. It is also said that "Jala," "Aggi," and "Sikhāri" are their names. And the Ariṭṭhakas...
The Rojas and the Ariṭṭhakadevas are the Rojas-devas. Those who shine like the umā flower are the Umāpuppha-devas;
for the radiance of their bodies resembles the umā flower, and therefore they are called "those who shine like the umā flower.
The Varuṇas and the Sahadhammas—these two groups—and the Accutas and the Anejakas—the Accuta-devas and the Anejaka-devas.
*Ca*: "Suleyyarucirā" means both the Suleyyas and the Ruciras have arrived. "Āguṃ vāsavanesino" means the gods named Vāsavanesīs have arrived.
"Dasete dasadhā kāyā" means these ten classes of deities have also arrived in ten groups.

"Samānā mahāsamānā" means both the Samānas and the Mahāsamānas. "Mānusā mānusuttamā" means both the Mānusas and the Mānusuttamas. "Khiḍḍāpadosikā āguṃ, āguṃ manopadosikā" means the Khiḍḍāpadosika and Manopadosika deities have arrived.
Then the *harayo devā* came; these are known as the *haridevā*, who have arrived. And those called the *lohitavāsino*—the "red-robed ones"—have also arrived.
The *pāragā* and *mahāpāragā*—these two types have also arrived. These ten bodies in ten groups—these ten divine hosts have likewise arrived in tenfold fashion.
The *sukkā*, *karambhā*, and *aruṇā*—these three, beginning with the *sukkā*, have arrived together with the *veghanasā*.
And they have arrived. "Led by the Odātagayhas" means the gods named Odātagayhas, the leaders, have arrived.
"The wise gods have come" means the gods named Vicakkhaṇas have arrived.
"The Sadāmattas and the Hāragajas" refers to both the Sadāmattas and the Hāragajas. "And the illustrious ones" refers to those endowed with glory.
And the Missaka devas. Pajjunna came raining; thus Pajjunna, the king of the gods, arrived while raining.
"He who rains upon the quarters" means that whichever direction he goes to, there the rain falls.
"These ten are the ten-fold hosts" means that these ten classes of devas also arrived in ten groups.
“Khemiyā, Tusitā, Yāmā” means the Khemiyā devas, the inhabitants of the Tusita city, and the inhabitants of the Yāma deva-world.
“And the illustrious Kathakā” means the Kathaka devas endowed with glory; however, in the Pāḷi it is written as “Kaṭṭhakā.
“Lambītakā and Lāmaseṭṭhā” means the Lambitaka devas and the Lāmaseṭṭha devas. “And those named Joti, the Āsavas” [reside] on the summit of the mountain.
There are those called the *joti-devas*, shining like a mass of fire from a whetted blade; the meaning is that these and the *āsā-devas* have arrived.
In the Pāḷi, however, they are written as "those named *jāti*. The *āsā-devatās* are called *āsava* by way of their desire (*chanda*).
The *Nimmānarati* gods have come, and then the *Paranimmita* gods. "These ten bodies in ten ways"—these ten classes of gods also arrived in ten groups.
"Sixty classes of devas": these and the ten groups beginning with the Āpa-devas constitute the sixty classes of devas;
all of them possess various colors by way of blue and so forth. "They come according to their names": they have arrived by way of their respective names or name-portions.
"And others who are similar to them": and there are others as well who are similar to them—in both color and name—being exactly like this in other world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).
"O gods, they too have indeed come"—with this single phrase, he points out all the deities, grouping them together like a bundle or a packet.
Having thus pointed out the hosts of gods within ten thousand world-systems, he now speaks the verse beginning with "pavuṭṭhajāti" to show the purpose for which they have come.
Its meaning is as follows: "He whose birth has been cast off (pavuṭṭhā) and gone away (vigatā) is the Noble Saṅgha."
"Those of noble birth" (*pavuṭṭhajāti*): we shall see that noble-born one who is "without a stake" (*akhīla*) due to the absence of the stakes of lust, hatred, and delusion;

who is "one who has crossed the flood" (*oghatinna*) because he stands having crossed over the four floods; who is "without taints" (*anāsava*) due to the absence of the four taints; who is a "Noble Saṅgha";
who is a "Nāga" because he has crossed those very floods and does not commit evil; and who is "one who has gone beyond the unconditioned" (*asitātika*).

"They all came under their respective names for this purpose: 'May we behold the One of Ten Powers, who has transcended the state of darkness and shines with glory like the moon,' as well as others who were like them.
Now, showing the Brahmās, he said: "Subrahmā, Paramatta, and so forth. Therein, "Subrahmā" refers to one.

Brahmā. Furthermore, even from the highest realm, it was Brahmā himself. "The sons of the powerful one together"—these noble Brahmas, the sons of the Blessed Buddha who possesses supernormal power, arrived together.
"Sanaṅkumāra and Tissa"—both Sanaṅkumāra and the Great Brahmā Tissa.
"He too came"—he also arrived.
“He stands as Mahābrahmā over a thousand Brahma-worlds;
reborn there, he is radiant, of terrifying form, and glorious.”— In this context,
“a thousand Brahma-worlds” refers to a thousand world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*) with one finger, and ten thousand world-systems with ten fingers.
A thousand Great Brahmas, capable of pervading with light, arrived.
"A Great Brahma stands supreme" means that each individual Great Brahma stands having overcome other Brahmas. "Reborn" means born in the Brahma-world.
"Radiant" means endowed with majestic power. "Of terrifying form" means of massive body, [measuring] two or three Magadhan village-tracts.
"Of equal measure in personal form. "Possessing glory" means endowed with glory known as the splendor of his personal form.

"Ten lords have come here, independent wielders of power": among these thousand Brahmās, ten such lords—Great Brahmās who each individually exercise independent authority—have arrived. And from their midst...
"Come, Hārita is surrounded!"—thus the Great Brahmā named Hārita, accompanied by a retinue of one hundred thousand Brahmās, arrived in their midst. 342.
"And all those who have come, including the gods with Indra and Brahmā"—this refers to the entire host of gods who have come with Sakka, the king of the gods, as their leader;
and the entire host of Brahmās who have come with the Great Brahmā Hārita as their leader.
"Moreover, 'Māra’s army has advanced' means that Māra’s army has approached. 'Behold the folly of Kaṇha' means:
behold the childish nature of the black Māra.
'Come, seize them, bind them!'—thus he commanded his own retinue. 'Let them be bound by passion'—all this [is said]."
"Let this circle of gods be bound by passion for you. Surround them on all sides;
let no one release you, and let not even one among you release even one of these. There is also a reading, "mā vo muñceyyā," which has the same meaning.
Thus, in that great assembly, Mahāsena—Kāla—dispatched his army. In this way, at that great gathering, Māra Mahāsena [sent forth] the Māra-army.
*Apesayi*: having struck the surface with his hand—that is, having struck the surface of the earth with his hand. *Saraṃ katvāna bheravaṃ*:
having produced a terrifying sound—that is, having produced a fearsome roar for the purpose of making Māra appear like a physician [to diagnose him].
Like a rain-cloud in the monsoon season, "thundering with lightning"—that is, like a rain-cloud in the monsoon season accompanied by lightning, he let out a great roar.
Roaring. At that time he turned back; at that moment, having displayed that terrifying form, Māra retreated. "Agitated, he could not abide by his own will":
being thoroughly enraged and provoked, unable to bring anyone under his control, he could not abide by his own will (*asayaṃvaso*);
lacking self-mastery, he turned back against his own wish. It is said that the Blessed One thought, "This Māra..."
Seeing this great assembly, he realized: “Thinking, ‘I will create an obstacle to the clear realization,’ Māra is dispatching his army here and there and displaying himself as the terrifying Māra.

This is the nature of the Blessed One: wherever a clear realization is not to take place, he does not prevent Māra from displaying himself as the terrifying one; however, where a clear realization is to occur...
In that assembly, he resolved that just as the assembly would neither see Māra’s form nor hear his voice, so it should be.

And since there would be a great realization (*abhisamaya*) in this gathering, he resolved that just as the deities would neither see his form nor hear his voice, so it should be. Therefore it was said: “Then he turned back.”
"Agitated, he is not in his own power.
Having directly known all that and having discerned it, the Visionary One—the Blessed One—having understood and determined all that, said:
"The army of Māra has advanced; know them, O monks! Monks, the army of Māra has advanced; you [should] know them.
"Know what is appropriate for yourselves; enter the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti)," he said.
