They applied themselves with ardor; they exerted energy for the purpose of entering the attainment of fruition.
Māra and his army departed from afar by those noble ones who were free from lust. Not even a single hair of theirs quivered. Of those who were free from lust...
They did not even stir a single hair. Then Māra, addressing the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, spoke this verse:
“All have conquered the battle, transcended fear, and are renowned;
Your disciples, O Knower of Men, rejoice together with all beings.”

In this context, "they rejoice together with the beings" means that they rejoice and exult together with the noble ones (ariyas) who have been born as beings within the teaching of the One Possessed of Ten Powers. "Among people" means well-known, famous, and renowned among people.

Furthermore, this discourse known as the *Mahāsamaya Sutta* is dear and pleasing to the deities; therefore, when one pronounces a blessing in new places, this very sutta should be recited. It is said that the deities think, "We shall hear this sutta."

They wander about with their ears attentive. At the conclusion of his teaching, one hundred thousand times ten million deities attained Arahantship, while the number of those who attained the stage of Stream-enterer and beyond was beyond counting.
Regarding the affection and esteem he held for the deities, there is this account: it is said that at the entrance to the Nāga Cave in the Koṭapabbata Monastery...
A certain daughter of the gods dwelt in a tree by the river. A young man was reciting this discourse within a cave.
Having heard it, at the conclusion of the discourse, the daughter of the gods gave a cry of approval with a loud voice, saying, "Who is this? "I am a daughter of the gods, venerable sir," he replied.
"Why did you give a cry of approval? "Venerable sir, on the day when the One Possessed of the Ten Powers sat in the Great Forest and spoke this..."
"Having heard the discourse today, I have heard it; this Dhamma has been well grasped by you, not omitting even a single syllable of what was spoken by the Blessed One.
"Did you hear it as the One of Ten Powers was speaking? "Yes, venerable sir. "It is said there was a great assembly of deities;
standing where did you hear it?"
"Venerable sir, I am a deity dwelling in the Great Forest. When deities of great power were arriving, I could find no space in Jambudīpa;
therefore, having come to this island of Tambapaṇṇi and standing at Jambukolapaṭṭana, I began to listen.
There too, when deities of great power were arriving, I gradually retreated until I reached the Rohaṇa province."
"Having entered into the ocean from behind the great village with water reaching up to their necks, they stood there and heard it.
"Deity, do you see the Teacher from a distance away from where you are standing? "What are you saying, venerable sir?
Thinking, 'The Teacher, while teaching the Dhamma in the Great Forest, is looking at me alone without interruption,' I was feeling shy and hid among the waves."
"On that day, it is said, one hundred thousand times ten million deities attained arahantship; did you also attain arahantship then? "No, venerable sir.
"Did you perhaps attain the fruit of non-returning? "No, venerable sir. "Did you perhaps attain the fruit of once-returning?
"No, venerable sir. "It is said that the deities who attained the three paths were beyond counting."

"Do you think, 'I have become a stream-enterer'? Because she had attained the fruit of stream-entry on that very day, the deity was filled with joy and said, "The noble one asks what ought not to be asked.
Then that bhikkhu said to her, "But is it possible, O deity, for you to show us your own form?
"It is not possible, venerable sir, to show the entire body; [only] as much as a finger-joint," she replied.
Thinking, "I shall show it to the noble sir," he inserted his finger through the keyhole toward the interior of the cave; it was as if a thousand moons and a thousand suns had risen at once.
The goddess said, "Be heedful, venerable sir," and after bowing to the young bhikkhu, she departed.
Thus this sutta is dear and pleasing to the deities; the deities cherish it.
Thus ends the commentary on the Mahāsamaya Sutta in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya. 8.
Commentary on the Sakkapañha Sutta.
Nidānavanṇanā 344.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Sakkapañha Sutta. Herein, this is the commentary on the words not [already] explained:
"The brahmin village named Ambasaṇḍā. It is said that this village was situated not far from the Ambasaṇḍā [forest], and therefore it was called simply "Ambasaṇḍā."
It is called Vebhāra. Regarding "on Mount Vediyaka," it is said that this mountain was surrounded on all sides by a grove of blue forest resembling a jeweled railing (maṇivedikā) growing at its base;
therefore, it came to be known specifically as "Mount Vediyaka.
Regarding "in the Indasāla Cave," formerly there was a cave between two mountains, and an Indasāla tree stood before it.

Because of the door, it came to be known as the "Indasāla Cave. Then, having surrounded it with walls and fitted it with doors and windows, they constructed a grotto beautifully finished with plaster work and adorned with various floral and creeper designs, and presented it to the Blessed One.
However, due to its former designation, people continue to recognize it simply as the "Indasāla Cave. With reference to that—
It was said, "In the Indasāla Cave.
"Zeal arose" means a righteous effort emerged. But is he not one who has seen the Blessed One frequently?
There is no such gathering of deities where he has not previously come; he dwells in heedfulness equal to Sakka himself.
There is no such thing as a "son of the gods" (devaputta). Then why did such an enthusiasm arise in him, as if he had never before seen a Buddha?
It was because he was terrified by the fear of death. At that time, it is said, his lifespan had come to an end;
having seen the five omens, he realized, "My life is now exhausted. And as for those sons of the gods...

The signs of death become manifest; among them, those who have been reborn in the deva world by means of a limited meritorious deed fall into fear and terror, thinking, "Where indeed shall we now be reborn?

However, those who have been reborn having performed many merits and established a refuge from fear—having practiced giving, guarded their virtue, and developed meditation—they [reflect upon] the gifts they themselves gave, the virtue they protected, and the meditation they cultivated.
Having come [to this world], they do not fear, thinking, "We shall experience prosperity in the higher celestial worlds.
But Sakka, the king of the gods, having seen the portents, [prepared] the divine city of ten thousand yojanas, the Vejayanta palace one thousand yojanas in height,
the Sudhamma assembly hall of the gods three hundred yojanas in extent, and the Pāricchattaka tree one hundred yojanas in height.
Having surveyed all these perfections— the sixty-yojana Pāṇḍukambala stone, two and a half koṭis of celestial nymphs in the two deva-worlds,
the Nandana Grove, the Cittalatā Grove, the Missaka Grove, and the Phārusaka Grove—
he was overcome by fear, thinking: "Alas, this perfection of mine is surely perishing!"

Then, looking about with the thought, "Is there perhaps some ascetic or brahmin, the Grandfather of the World, or Mahābrahmā, who might extract the dart of grief from my heart and make this prosperity stable? he saw no one;
yet he further perceived that even for a hundred thousand beings like himself, the Perfectly Enlightened One is able to extract the arisen dart of grief.
“...is capable. Now, while he was reflecting in this way, at that time an eagerness arose in Sakka, the lord of the devas, to see the Blessed One.
He wondered: “Where does the Blessed One dwell now? In which country, and depending upon which city?”
"Whose requisites does he enjoy while dwelling teaching the Deathless Dhamma to whom? "He saw"—that is, he perceived and penetrated.
"Mārisa" is a term of endearment, a specific mode of address used by the deities;
it is also said to mean "free from suffering. Why did he address the deities? For the sake of companionship. It is said that previously, in the Saḷalaghara, he [had been] with the Blessed One...
While the Teacher was dwelling there, he went alone to see him. The Teacher thought, "His knowledge is not yet mature;
however, after a few days have passed, while I am dwelling in the Indasāla Cave, he will see five portents.
Terrified by the fear of death, he will approach the deities in two celestial realms, ask fourteen questions, and at the conclusion of the answer to the question on equanimity—"
Thinking, "He will establish eighty thousand deities in the fruit of stream-entry," he did not grant him permission.
[The deity] thought, "In the past as well, because I went alone, the Teacher did not grant me permission;

surely there is no underlying support for my attainment of the path and its fruits. But if there is such support for even one person, then even for an assembly as vast as the limits of the world-system—"
"The Blessed One is indeed teaching the Dhamma. Surely there must be some god in one of the two heavenly worlds who possesses the necessary spiritual potential (*upanissaya*);
it is with reference to him that the Teacher will teach the Dhamma. Having heard it, I too shall pacify my own distress.
Having thought thus, he addressed his companion for the sake of going together.
"Thus may it be well with you, O Blessed One," said the Tāvatiṃsa devas. "So be it, Great King! Let us go to see the Blessed One;

the arising of a Buddha is rare to encounter. It is well with you, since instead of saying, 'Let us go for a mountain game or a river game,' you have directed us to such places as these. They assented, accepting his words with their heads.
345. He addressed Pañcasikha, the son of the Gandhabba gods. [Question: Why did he address him separately when he was already addressing the gods?

[Answer: It was for the purpose of creating an opportunity. For it occurred to him: "It is not fitting to approach the Teacher while taking along deities from two different heavenly realms, as if striking them with a yoke-pole;
however, this Pañcasikha is [a follower] of the One of Ten Powers."
"The attendant Vallabha goes at whatever moment he desires, asks questions, and listens to the Dhamma.
Having sent him forward and secured an opportunity, I shall approach him when he has created that opening and ask my question.
Thus he addressed him for the purpose of securing an opportunity.
"So be it, may it be well with you," he replied, further strengthening Devānaminda’s resolve by saying, "So be it, Great King;
may it be well with you, since instead of saying, 'Come, dear sir, let us go to see garden sports or theatrical performances,' you say, 'We shall see the Buddha, we shall hear the Dhamma.
Having thus assented to the words of the Lord of the Devas, he—
He came to attend upon him, accompanying him, walking together with him.
Therein, "beluvapaṇḍu" means pale-colored like a ripe *beluva* fruit.

It is said that it had a frame made of gold, a neck-staff (*daṇḍa*) made of sapphire (*indanīla*), strings made of silver, and coverings made of coral; the sounding board (*vīṇāpattaka*) was a *gāvuta* in length.
The place where the strings are fastened is one *gāvuta*, and the upper staff is one *gāvuta*; thus, the lute (*vīṇā*) is three *gāvutas* in measure.

So, taking that lute, he tuned it with fifty strings, struck it with his fingertips, and emitting a sweet sound of song, stood to one side, making the other devas know the time for Sakka’s departure. Thus, of him—
When the hosts of devas had assembled at the sound of singing and instrumental music, Sakka, lord of the devas, … [as before] … appeared on Mount Vediyaka. 346.
“An exceeding radiance has arisen”: on other days, there is an arising of radiance through the radiance of only one deva, or Māra, or a Brahmā;
but on that day, it was through the radiance of the devas in two celestial worlds.
He became exceedingly radiant, a single mass of light, resembling the time when a thousand moons and suns have risen.

"People in the surrounding villages" means people in the villages all around. It is said that Sakka arrived there while it was still the natural time for the evening meal and the village children were playing in the center of the village;
therefore, having seen him, the people spoke thus. And yet, during the middle watch...
"The deities approach the Blessed One; why has this one come even during the first watch of the night?
[The answer is: "Because he was terrified by the fear of death. "What indeed is this? [means: "O sir, what indeed is this?
Which deity or Brahmā of great power is approaching today to ask the Blessed One a question and to hear the Dhamma? How indeed..."
"Ah, Blessed One! He will answer our questions and teach us the Dhamma.
It is a gain for us, that our Teacher—who dispels the doubts of the deities in this way—dwells in a monastery not far from here; we shall be able to give him even a portion from a bowl or a ladle.
Thus, moved with a sense of urgency, their hair standing on end and bristling, they joined their ten fingers together in a radiant salutation.
Placing their joined palms to their heads, they stood paying homage.
347. "Difficult to approach" means difficult to attend upon. I am possessed of lust, hatred, and delusion; the Teacher is free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion.
Therefore, Tathāgatas are difficult for one such as I to attend upon. "Meditators" refers to those who meditate by means of contemplation on the characteristics [of phenomena].
He meditates by means of reflection upon the object (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*), and because he delights in that very meditation, he is "one who delights in meditation" (*jhānaratā*).
"Secluded at that time" (*tadantaraṃ paṭisallīnā*) means either secluded at that particular interval or secluded at this present moment.

Therefore, not only is he difficult to approach because he is a meditator and one who delights in meditation, but he is also difficult to approach because he is currently secluded. "You should inspire confidence" (*pasādeyyāsi*) means you should win his favor.
He says, "Please grant me the opportunity and give it to me. Regarding the phrase "taking the beluva-wood lute," one might ask:
"Was it not already taken previously? Yes, it was taken. However, it had been resting on the shoulder during the journey;
now, having placed it in his left hand and prepared it for playing, he took it up. Therefore it is said, "taking."
Commentary on the Verses Sung by Pañcasikha 348.
*Assāvesī* means she announced. *Buddhūpasañhitā* means having the Buddha as its object, or having the Buddha as its basis; this is the meaning. The same applies to the remaining phrases.
Regarding the line *Vande te pitaraṃ bhadde, timbaruṃ sūriyavacchase*: here, *sūriyavacchasā* means one whose body is like the sun.
It is said that from the tip of this goddess’s foot a ray of light rises up to her hairline;
therefore, she appears like the orb of the young sun, and thus they know her as “Sūriyavacchasā” (She Whose Foot is Like the Sun). Referring to her, he said:
“Bhadde Sūriyavacchase, I pay homage to your father, Timbaru, the king of the Gandhabba deities,” [and] “by whom you were born, O beautiful one. By whom...
"O auspicious one, beautiful in every limb, you who were born depending upon King Timbaru as your cause—
you who produce joy for me and increase my gladness and happiness—
just as the wind is desired and beloved by those overcome with sweat for the purpose of removing that sweat."
"Manāpo" means "pleasing," such is the sense. "Like water for one who thirsts" refers to one who desires to drink, who is thirsty, and who is overcome by thirst.
"Aṅgīrasī" means she whose limbs (aṅga) possess rays (rasmi); addressing her with reference to that very quality, he says it.
"Like the Dhamma of the Arahants" means like the nine supramundane states (navalokuttara-dhamma) of the Arahants.
"Jighacchato" means one who desires to eat, being overcome by hunger. "As if with water on a blazing fire":
just as someone might extinguish a blazing fire with a jar of water, so he says, "Extinguish this fever of sensual lust that has arisen in me because of you.
"Endowed with the pollen of filaments" means endowed with the pollen of lotus stamens. "Like an elephant tormented by heat" refers to an elephant distressed by the summer heat.

"Like that. He says: "When shall I descend into those breasts, the space between them, and the belly, and find happiness and pleasure? Just as that elephant, having plunged into a lotus pond and drunk, finds happiness and satisfaction while submerged after making its head and trunk visible, so too he speaks thus:
"When indeed shall I descend into your breasts, the space between them, and the belly, and obtain happiness and satisfaction?"
“Like an elephant with its goad removed, I have conquered the prodding stick and the javelin;

I do not perceive a cause [for my downfall], for I am well-matched with her whose thighs are like the trunks of *lakṣaṇa* trees.”—In this context, the *tutta* is said to be the goad-stick used for piercing near the base of the ears. The *tomara* is the javelin-stick used for piercing the feet and other such parts.
The *aṅkuśa* is a curved hook used for piercing the head [of an elephant].
Now, when an elephant is in rut and unrestrained—having transcended the hook—even when being prodded with the hook, it does not come under control.
Out of pride and arrogance, thinking, "I have conquered the goad and the lance, since I do not even submit to the hook," it fails to perceive the truth of its situation. Just as...

Just as that elephant with its bit removed does not perceive any reason [for fear], thinking, "The goad and the tomara have been conquered by me," even so, I too—being intoxicated, maddened, heedless, and like one demented by the thighs of this woman endowed with auspicious marks—do not perceive any reason at all; thus he speaks.
Or alternatively: just as the elephant with its bit removed, so too am I, being intoxicated by the thighs of this woman endowed with auspicious marks.
Therefore, I do not understand the cause of my dispassion. Why? Because, as if by that Naga, my goad and spear have been won;
I do not accept the words of anyone who speaks.
"I am greedy-minded for you, O Bhaddā, O Lakkhaṇūru"—that is, my mind is bound to you. Or, "greedy-minded" means greed.
*Ajjhupetacitto*: the mind has been transformed; that is, it remains having abandoned its natural state.
*Paṭigantuṃ na sakkomīti*: I am unable to turn back. *Vaṅkaghastova ambujo*: like a fish that has swallowed a hook. There is also a reading *ghaso*, which has the same meaning. *Vāmūrū*:
thighs shaped in a beautiful manner, or rather, thighs resembling the trunk of a plantain tree. *Sajāti āliṅga*: she embraced him.
“Mandalocanā” means that women do not look with sharp [vision], but rather perceive and gaze gently; therefore they are called “Mandalocanā.
“Palissaja” means to embrace on all sides. “Etaṃ me abhipatthitaṃ” means this has been frequently desired by me.
“Appako vata me santo” means being naturally dull-witted. “Vellitakesiyā” means having released the hair [so that it hangs] down the back.
"Vellitakesī" means one whose hair moves and flows like a snake when let loose; [the phrase] "of that Vellitakesī.
"Anekabhāvo samuppādī" means it arose in many ways; or, the reading is "anekabhāgo," meaning it was divided into many parts.
It is "pabhinna" in various modes, just like a gift given to an *arahant*—that is, a gift bestowed upon an *arahant*.

"Whatever merit I have performed" means whatever merit has been performed by me. "Among such Arhats" means among those Arhats who have attained the characteristics of a *tādi* (such-like one). "May it ripen together with you" means may all of it grant its fruition together with you alone.
"Solitary" means having entered into a state of oneness. "The wise one mindful": "wisdom" (*nepakka*) is what is meant;
one endowed with that is "wise. Because of being endowed with mindfulness, he is "mindful. "The sage seeking the Deathless": just as that Buddha-sage [seeks] the Deathless...
"He seeks and searches for Nibbāna"—thus, O Suriyavaccasā, I seek and search for it.
Or alternatively, the meaning is: "Just as he wanders seeking, searching, and striving for the Deathless, so do I wander seeking, searching, and striving for it.
And: "Just as the Sage would rejoice having attained supreme enlightenment"—just as the Buddha-Sage, seated upon the seat of enlightenment (bodhipallaṅka), rejoiced.
"Having attained omniscient knowledge, he would rejoice and be satisfied. "In this way he would rejoice" means: "In this very same way, having entered into union with you, I too would rejoice;
I would become filled with rapture and gladness," she says.
"I would choose you as my bride, O Bhaddā"—here *āha* is a vocative particle—addressing her as "O Bhaddā, Suriyavaccasā, by Sakka, the lord of the gods."
“Why do you not take the sovereignty of the gods in the two divine worlds, O Suriyavaccasā?
When these boons were thus offered, having renounced the sovereignty of the gods, [I thought], “I shall choose Suriyavaccasā. This means that I would desire her as my choice; I would take her.
“Like a sal tree, she does not bloom for long”—at the city gate of your father there was a sal tree that had blossomed, but it did not remain in bloom for long. That...
Exceedingly captivating, like a *sāla* tree in full bloom not long ago.
"I pay homage, I offer salutations, to your father, O wise one"—thus I worship your most glorious father. "He whose daughter was such as this"—referring to him who had a daughter like her.
349. Regarding the phrase "they blend together": why do you describe the qualities of both the sound of the song and the sound of the lute? What is there [in that]?
Does the Blessed One have lust? No. In such situations, the Blessed One remains equanimous through the sixfold equanimity;
he merely knows what is desirable and undesirable, but he does not become attached to it. And this has been said:
"Friends, the eye exists in the Blessed One, the Blessed One sees forms with the eye, yet there is no desire-lust in the Blessed One; his mind is perfectly liberated."
“The Blessed One has ears, friend,” and so forth. However, if he had not spoken in praise, Pañcasikha would not have known that “an opportunity has been granted to me.

Then Sakka, thinking, “An opportunity has not been granted to Pañcasikha by the Blessed One,” would have taken the deities and turned back from that very spot; consequently, there would have been a great loss. [Regarding] the praise...
However, when it was said, "The Blessed One has granted Pañcasikha an opportunity," he approached him together with the deities;

having asked his question and received the answer, and knowing that at the conclusion of that exposition Pañcasikha would, along with eighty thousand deities, be established in the fruit of stream-entry, he spoke in praise of him.
In that context, "when was it knotted? means when was it tied together and compacted.
"At that time, venerable sir," refers to that eighth week starting from the moment of your attainment of enlightenment.
"Bhaddā by name, Suriyavacchasā"—by name she was Bhaddā, and by virtue of her physical excellence she was Suriyavacchasā. "Sister" is a term of conventional address.
The meaning is "the daughter of a god. "Lusting after another" means she desires or longs for another. "While dancing" means while she was performing a dance.
It is said that on one occasion she went with the gods of the Realm of the Four Great Kings to see a dance for Sakka, the king of the gods; and at that moment, Sakka [heard] the Tathāgata...
She recited eight qualities as they truly were. Thus, having gone that day, Naccantī heard [the conversation].
350. Regarding the description of Sakka’s approach:
the Blessed One greets him by saying, "Does it harmonize with you? and so forth; Pañcasikha...
He exchanged greetings. While reciting verses, Pañcasikha offered his salutations, and the Blessed One returned the greeting. "Addressed" means he made himself known.
It is said that this thought occurred to him: "This Pañcasikha was sent by me on my business and is now performing his own task;
yet, standing in the presence of such a Teacher, he speaks words connected with the strands of sensual pleasure, which are unbecoming."
"Actors are indeed shameless; while speaking, they might even display a change of expression. Come now, let me make him aware of my work," he thought, and then addressed him.
"And so, 'the Tathāgata'—this is a phrase established by the Elders who compiled the Dhamma. 'Abhivadanti' means they speak with words of increase by way of accepting a salutation.
'Abhivadito' means addressed with words of increase. 'Urundā samapādī' means it became vast and open; the darkness within the cave vanished. 'Āloko udapādi' means light arose."
The darkness that was naturally in the cave has vanished, and light has arisen. All of this is the statement of the compilers of the Dhamma.
"For a long time, O Bhante," means for a long period; the meaning is that from long ago I have been desirous of seeing [you].
"Because of various duties and obligations" refers to the fact that the daughters and sons of the gods are born upon one's lap, while the foot-attendants [are born] at the feet.
Women are reborn upon the couches; deities who provide ornaments and adornments are reborn surrounding those couches;
and attendants are reborn within the celestial mansion (vimāna). For these beings, there is no such thing as the performance of labor.
However, those who are reborn in the borderlands cannot be determined [as belonging to anyone], such that one could say, "These belong to you" or "These belong to me."
Being unable to decide, they make a wager and ask Sakka, the king of the gods. He says, "They belong to whichever one’s mansion is closer.
If both are at an equal distance, he says, "They belong to whichever one she stood looking toward while gazing at the mansion.
If she does not look toward even one of them, [he assigns them] for the purpose of ending the dispute between the two.
He makes it his own possession. Even activities such as playing are indeed things that ought to be done.
Referring to such duties as these, he said, "by this or that business or duty.
"In the salaḷa-hut" means in the fragrant chamber made of salaḷa wood. "By a certain concentration"—at that time, it is said, the Blessed One...
Having perceived that Sakka’s knowledge was still immature, [the Buddha], desiring not to grant him leave, sat in the meditative attainment of the fruition (phalasamāpatti).
Not knowing this, he said, "By means of some other concentration. As for the name *bhūjati*: it is called *bhūjati* because she enjoys herself;
she is a celestial maiden (*devadhītā*) who serves as his foot-maid. It is said that she had attained two fruits; therefore, her...

There was indeed no delight for her in the world of the gods. Having come constantly to attend upon the Blessed One, she stood paying homage to the Blessed One with her hands placed in añjali at her head.

Because he emerged from that concentration due to the sound of the wheel-rims, one should certainly not say, "One who has attained meditative absorption hears a sound. For did not the Blessed One [hear the sound] of Sakka, the lord of the devas?
“Moreover, he says: ‘I have emerged from that concentration by means of the sound of the venerable one’s wheel-rims. Let alone the sound of the rims;
one who has attained meditative absorption does not hear even the sound of a pair of conchs being blown at the root of his ear, nor even the crash of a thunderbolt.
But the Blessed One [remained] for so long a time, granting Sakka an opportunity...”
Having resolved, "I shall not do so," he entered the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) according to the time.
Sakka, thinking, "The Teacher no longer makes room for me," circumambulated the fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭī), turned his chariot back, and sent it toward the world of the gods.
The courtyard of the fragrant chamber resounded with the sound of the chariot as if it were the music of the fivefold orchestra.
Because the Blessed One had emerged from attainment according to the time limit he had determined, the first adverting of the mind arose at the very sound of the chariot;
therefore, he spoke thus.
(Commentary on the Gopaka-vatthu)
353. “One who fulfills the precepts” means one who fulfills the five precepts. “Having discarded womanhood”:

womanhood is indeed a hindrance; for while remaining in womanhood, it is not possible to experience the glory of a Wheel-turning Monarch, nor the glories of Sakka, Māra, or Brahmā, nor is it possible to attain the enlightenment of a Pacceka Buddha or Perfect Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi). Thus, regarding womanhood...
"Virājeti" means to cause to fade away. "Purisattaṃ" (manhood) is this great, best, and supreme state;
thinking, "By standing upon this, it is possible to attain these successes," one thus develops manhood. She too did so. Therefore it is said:
"Having caused womanhood to fade away and having developed manhood. "Hīnaṃ gandhabbakāyaṃ" means the inferior, wretched realm of the Gandhabbas.
The Gandhabba host. But why were they born there with such purified virtue? Because of their previous attachment.
It is said that even in the past this was their dwelling place; therefore, they were born there by way of that attachment.
"Attendance" means the attendance hall. "Service" means the state of attending upon. They come thinking, "We shall serve them with songs and instrumental music."
"Paṭicodesī" means he reminded [them]. It is said that upon seeing them, he thought, "These sons of gods are exceedingly radiant and possess great beauty;
what deed must they have performed to come here? As he reflected, he saw that they had been monks.
Then, considering, "May they be monks who have fulfilled their moral discipline," he perceived that they were indeed "fulfillers. "Fulfillers..."
Investigating whether they possessed other qualities or not, he saw that they were "attainers of jhāna.
Investigating where they resided, he saw that they were "my own personal attendants" (*kulūpaka*).
Those of pure virtue are reborn wherever they wish among the six deva-worlds; however, these ones were not even in the higher deva-worlds.
They have been reborn. Those who have attained the jhānas are reborn in the Brahma-world, yet these have not been reborn in the Brahma-world.
However, by abiding by their instruction, I was reborn as a son on the lap of Sakka, the Lord of Devas and ruler of the deva-world;
whereas these have been reborn in the inferior body of a gandhabba. These individuals are those who pierce with eight arrows. Having rolled [the matter over]...
Thinking, "I shall pierce them deeply after twisting their words," he rebuked them with the words beginning with "Whence your faces?
and so forth. Therein, "Whence your faces? means: while the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma facing you, whence were your faces?
Were you distracted by something else, looking here and there, or were you perhaps asleep? "Duddiṭṭharūpaṃ" means having seen that which is of a difficult-to-see nature.

It was improper. Regarding the phrase "one who lives according to the Dhamma": it refers to one who follows the practice established in the teaching of a single Teacher and has performed meritorious deeds.

When those two gods were thus addressed by the divine son Gopaka, and further rebuked with words such as, "Oh, you are shameless and devoid of moral dread," they regained their mindfulness even in this very life.
They thought, "The Brahmā-purohita heaven—surely one can obtain what is called a 'gift' by coming with actors who dance, sing, and play instruments;
yet this man has been crackling like a hearth into which salt has been thrown ever since we first saw him.
What could this be? As they reflected, [they realized] his state as a recluse and the purity of his virtue.
Seeing that she had attained *jhāna* and was his own family priestess (*kulūpikā*), he thought: "Those of pure virtue are reborn in whichever of the six deva-worlds they desire;
those who have attained *jhāna* are reborn in the Brahma-world. We were unable to be reborn even in the higher deva-worlds or the Brahma-world.
Yet, by abiding by our instruction, this woman has been reborn above us. We..."
"Having been monks, we practiced the holy life under the Blessed One, yet we were reborn in the inferior body of a gandhabba.
It is for this reason that he reproaches us so. Realizing this, as they listened to his words, two among them attained the mindfulness of the first jhāna;
taking that jhāna as their basis and contemplating conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra), they established themselves in the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala).

Then that limited body of theirs belonging to the sense-sphere realm was unable to sustain them. Therefore, they passed away from there at once and were reborn among the Ministers of Brahmā (Brahmapurohita).
And that body of theirs was produced only while they remained there. Hence it is said:
"Venerable sir, when those two deities were rebuked by the young god Gopaka, mindfulness arose in them even in this very life..."
"They obtained a body among the Brahmapurohitas.
In this context, "in this very life" (diṭṭheva dhamme) means they obtained mindfulness of jhāna within that very same personal existence.
Having passed away while remaining right there, they obtained a body among the Brahmapurohitas—that is, a body belonging to the Brahmapurohita realm. This is how the meaning should be understood.
"But one god," however, was a certain son of the gods who, unable to sever his attachment, indulged in sensual pleasures and remained a resident right there.
"And I served the Sangha" means that I attended upon the Sangha.
"Because of its excellence" means because of the beauty of the Dhamma. "Reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three" means reborn in the city of the Thirty-Three, among the thirty-three [gods].
"Having entered the company of the gandhabbas, he dwells there as a resident" means having entered [that state] by becoming a resident in the company of the gandhabbas.
"And we who were formerly human beings" should be understood in connection with this: "we who were formerly human beings served [him] with food and drink."

*Pādūpasaṅgayha*: having clasped his feet—that is, having honored them by providing water for washing the feet and ointment for the feet, and having also paid homage. *Sake nivesane*: in one's own house. This word is also connected with the phrase "we have waited upon him.

*Paccattaṃ veditabbo*: it is to be known by oneself. *Ariyānaṃ subhāsitāni*: the well-spoken words of the Noble Ones—the well-spoken words of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, as they are being spoken by you.

"But you, approaching the Best"—that is, approaching the Buddha, the Blessed One, who is supreme, or [approaching] the unsurpassed teaching of the Buddha. "The holy life" (*brahmacariya*) means the best way of conduct. "Rebirth among the beings" (*bhavatūpapatti*) means birth among those beings.
"While I am living at home" means while I am dwelling in the midst of the household.
"This very day" (*svajja*) means that today. "A disciple of Gotama" (*gotamasāvaka*): here, Gopaka is called a disciple of Gotama. "Having approached" (*samecca*) means having come together.
"Come, let us exert ourselves, let us strive!"—let us indeed exert and strive.
"Mā no mayaṃ parapessā ahumhā"—here *no* is merely a particle; the meaning is: "May we not become merely those who carry out another's bidding.
"The teachings of Gotama"—here, it is the first jhāna, which has been naturally penetrated, that is called "the teachings of Gotama"; recollecting that...
"Having recollected" is the meaning.
"Having purified their minds" means having purified the minds [previously] attached to the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).

"The danger in sensual pleasures": they saw the danger in sensual pleasures by way of suppression through the first *jhāna*, and by way of eradication through the third path (*tatiya-magga*). "The fetters and bonds of sensual pleasure."
The fetters of sensual desire and the bonds of sensual desire. "The yokes of the Evil One" means they have become the yokes of Māra the Evil One;
the meaning is that they have become his bonds. "Difficult to transcend" means difficult to overcome.
"The gods together with Indra and together with Pajāpati" refers to those assembled with Indra as their chief, and those assembled with Pajāpati, the king of the gods, as their chief.
"Together with their wives. "Seated in the assembly hall" means seated in the assembly hall; the sense is that they were sitting there. "Heroes" means the brave.
"Free from passion" means those who have transcended passion (*vītarāga*). "Making it stainless" means making and producing the stainless path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*).
Like an elephant, having severed their own bonds—the fetters of sensual craving—they surpassed the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
"Of one who has become filled with spiritual urgency" means of Sakka, who had developed a sense of urgency.
"Overcome by sensual desires" means overcome by both kinds of sensual desires. "Deprived of mindfulness" means devoid of the mindfulness associated with meditative absorption (*jhāna*).
"Among those three" refers to among those three persons. "One dwells here in the household" means that among them, only one dwells in the inferior body (the human realm).
"Born. "Following the path to full enlightenment" means following the path of the non-returner (anāgāmimagga). "Even despising the gods" means despising and humbling the two worlds of the gods;

because they are concentrated through access and absorption concentration (upacārappanāsamādhīhi), they have risen into the air and gone along, scattering the dust from their own feet upon the heads of the deities.
"In this way, there is the manifestation of the Dhamma here" means that in this Dispensation (sāsana),
there is such a manifestation of the Dhamma by which disciples come to be endowed with these qualities. "No disciple there has any doubt" means that among those disciples,
not even a single disciple has any doubt regarding the Buddha and the others, or regarding their state of being oriented toward the four quarters— that is, moving unimpeded in all directions.
“He dwells ungraspable. Now, speaking in praise of the Blessed One, he said:
“We pay homage to the Buddha, the Conqueror, the Lord of Men, who has crossed the flood and severed doubt. In this context, “severed doubt” means one whose doubt is cut away.
“Lord of Men” means the supreme among all the world.
"Whatever Dhamma of yours": whatever Dhamma belongs to you. "They have attained it": those sons of the gods have realized it. "The body of the Brahmapurohitas":
while we were still looking on, the body of the Brahmapurohitas [appeared]. This is what is meant:
having understood that Dhamma of yours, those two among those three persons, while we were still looking on, attained the state of the Brahmapurohitas.
"Having realized the distinction of the paths and fruits, they attained them; we too have come, O Venerable Sir, out of faith in that Dhamma.
"We have come" means we have arrived. "If the Blessed One grants us the opportunity, we would ask a question, O Venerable Sir"—the meaning is:
if the Blessed One gives us leave, then, having been granted leave by the Blessed One, we would ask a question, O Venerable Sir.
The Story of the Young Brahmin Magha (355).
"This yakkha has been pure for a long time" means he has been pure since a long period ago. How long ago?
Since the time he was the young brahmin Magha in the village of Macala in the kingdom of Magadha, before the Buddha had appeared. At that time, it is said, he...
One day, rising early, he went to the center of the village where the people were performing their communal work.
Having cleared away the heap of dust and debris from his own standing place with the very edge of his foot, he made it beautiful. Another person came and stood there.
Regaining his mindfulness at that very moment, [he saw] a space about the size of a threshing floor in the middle of the village.
Having cleared the ground, scattered sand over it, and brought firewood, he would kindle a fire during the cold season;
then both young and old people would come and sit there.
Then, one day, this thought occurred to him: "We go to the city and see the king, the royal ministers, and others."
Regarding these very moon and sun, people say, "The son of a deity named Canda, and the son of a deity named Suriya.
"What indeed did they do to attain such splendors?
Then, thinking, "It was nothing other than the performance of meritorious deeds," he reflected, "I too must perform meritorious deeds that bestow such splendors as these."
Thus, rising early and drinking rice-gruel, he took a hatchet, a bill-hook, a pickaxe, and a pestle in his hands and went to the crossroads.
With the pestle, he lifted up stones and rolled them away;
he removed trees that obstructed the axles of vehicles, leveled the uneven ground, built a hall at the crossroads, dug a lotus pond, and constructed a bridge.
Having performed his work thus during the day, he returned home when the sun had set. Another asked him:
"Sir Magha, you have gone out early in the morning and now return from the forest in the evening; what work do you perform? "I perform meritorious deeds," he replied.
"I am clearing the path leading to the heavenly realm. "What is this so-called 'merit,' sir? "Do you not know it? "Yes, I do not."
“I know them. “When you went to the city, did you see those kings, royal ministers, and others before?
“Yes, I saw them before. “Did they obtain that position by performing meritorious deeds? I too am performing such deeds that grant a fortune like this.
“Have you heard before of the deva-son named Canda and the deva-son named Suriya? “Yes, I have heard it before.”
"I shall clear the path leading to that heaven. But he asked: "Is this meritorious deed suitable for you alone, and not for others?
He replied: "It has not been forbidden to anyone. [The other said: "If that is so, then tomorrow, when it is time to go to the forest, give me some of it as well.
On the following day, he took him and went; thus, thirty-three men of youthful age in that village [prepared to go].
All of them became his followers. Having become of one mind, they wandered about performing meritorious deeds.
Whatever direction they went, they leveled the road in a single day;
they completed the digging of lotus ponds, the building of halls, and the construction of bridges in a single day.

Then the village headman thought to himself: "In the past, when these men were drinking liquor and committing acts such as killing living beings, I received wealth from them both by way of fines and by way of taxes.
Now, since the time they have begun performing meritorious deeds, this income is no longer available; well then, let me cause a rift between them and the royal court. And so he [approached] the king.
“Having approached them, O Great King, I saw the thieves. “Where, dear sir? “In my village, Your Majesty. “What are these so-called ‘thieves,’ dear sir?
“They are offenders against the king, Your Majesty. “What is their caste, dear sir? “They are of the householder caste, Your Majesty.
“What will householders do? Why did you not tell me, knowing as you did? “Out of fear, Great King, I did not speak.”

"Now, do not hold me in fault. Then the king, believing that "this one is crying out at me with a great cry," gave him leave and sent him forth, saying, "In that case, go; you yourself bring them back.
Having gone there, he worked in the forest for the day, ate his evening meal, and sat down in the middle of the village, thinking, "What work shall we do tomorrow?"
While they were deliberating, "Shall we level the road? Shall we dig a lotus pond? Shall we build a bridge?", they surrounded him and, saying, "Do not struggle!
This is by the king's command," they bound him and departed.
Then their wives, hearing that "your husbands have been bound and led away for being thieves who offended the king," cried out, "It has taken far too long! and [the huts] collapsed.
"These people stay in the forest day after day, saying, 'We are performing meritorious deeds. All their work has fallen into ruin;
nothing at all increases in their homes; they are well-bound and well-seized," they said.
The village headman then took them and presented them to the king. Without even investigating, the king said, "Have them trampled by an elephant."
He said: "While they were being led away, Magha said to the others, 'Sirs, will you be able to do my bidding?
They replied, 'It was precisely by doing your bidding that we have fallen into this danger; nevertheless, we shall do your bidding. Speak, sir, what shall we do?
He said, 'In this world, sir, for those who wander in the cycle of existence, this is indeed a constant state; but what [is there to say]?"
"Are you thieves? "We are not thieves. "The performance of a declaration of truth (*saccakiriya*) is a support for this world;
therefore, all of you perform a declaration of truth, saying: 'If we are thieves, let the elephant trample us; if we are not thieves, let him not trample us.
They did so. The elephant was unable even to approach; crying out, he fled. [They struck] the elephant with goads, spears, and hooks...
Even while they were threshing him, they were unable to lead him away. They reported to the king, "We are not able to lead the elephant away.
[The king said,] "In that case, cover him with a mat on top and have him trampled. When the mat was placed on top, he fled, crying out with a double roar.
Having heard this, the king summoned the slanderer and asked, "My son, does the elephant not wish to be trampled?"
“Yes, Your Majesty, the eldest brahmin knows the spell; this is indeed the power of the spell. The king had him summoned and asked, “Is it said that you possess a spell?
“No, Your Majesty, I have no spell. However, we performed an act of truth (saccakiriya), saying:
‘If we are thieves to the king, let him crush us; if we are not thieves, let him not crush us. By means of that act of truth—”
"This is not his power. "But what then, father, do you do for work?
"Your Majesty, we level the roads, we build rest-houses at the crossroads, we dig lotus ponds, and we construct bridges;
thus we have lived performing such meritorious deeds."
"For what purpose do you slander us? [They replied: "When we were negligent, he obtained this and that;
when we were diligent, it was not there. For this reason. "Dear ones, this elephant is indeed an animal, yet even he knows your virtues.
Though I am a human being, I do not know them. Your village of residence must be brought back to you alone."
"Having made this offering, let this elephant also be yours alone, and let even the slanderer become your slave.
From now on, perform meritorious deeds for me as well," he said, and having given them the wealth, he dismissed them.
Having taken the wealth, they mounted the elephant in turn and went along, deliberating: "Friends, so-called 'meritorious deeds' are for the sake of future existence..."
"It is performed [in future lives], but for us, like a blue lotus blooming within the water, it yields its fruit in this very existence.
Now we shall perform even more merit. "What shall we do?
"Having established a permanent site at the crossroads of the four great highways, let us build a rest-house for the multitude; however, we shall build it so that women have no access to it."
"For while we were being taken away after being seized as 'thieves,' not even a single woman among them gave so much as a thought [to our safety], but rose up saying, 'They are well bound!
They are well caught! Therefore, I shall give them no share.
Having gone to their own homes, they gave thirty-three mouthfuls of food to the elephant and brought thirty-three handfuls of grass; all of that was for the elephant.
It was born filling his belly. They entered the forest and felled trees; as each tree was cut down, an elephant dragged it away and placed it on the cart-track.
Having stripped the bark from the trees, they began the work of building a hall.
In Magha’s house there were four wives: Sujātā, Sudhammā, Cittā, and Nandā. Sudhammā...
She asked the carpenter, "Father, these companions go out early and return in the evening; what work are they doing?
"They are building a hall, mother," he replied. "Father, build me a share of the hall as well and give it to me.
"We will not make one with shares for women," they said. She gave the carpenter eight kahāpaṇas and said, "Father, by whatever means possible..."

“Prepare my alms-bowl,” he said. He replied, “Very well, mother,” and taking his axe and hatchet earlier than usual, stood in the middle of the village and cried out in a loud voice, “Why, sirs, do you not set out even now?
Knowing that everyone had already ascended the road, he said, “You may go on ahead; I have some business to attend to,” and left them behind.
Having made another path and climbed it, he cut down a tree growing near a water-pool, trimmed it, polished it smooth, and brought it back, placing it in the Sudhamma Hall, saying:
"On the day I tell you to give it, you should bring it out and give it.

Then, when the work of gathering materials was finished, beginning from the preparation of the ground, he proceeded with the piling up [of the foundation], the binding together [of the structure], and the raising of the pillars.

When the assembly of rafters, the central ridge-pole, and the binding of the bedstead had been completed, that carpenter sat upon the bedstead with its central ridge-pole and, lifting up the rafters from the four directions, said:
"Sir, there is one thing forgotten. "What is it, sir, that you have forgotten?
You forget everything! "Sir, where will these rafters be established? "Upon the central ridge-pole."
"It is necessary to obtain a name. "Sir, where can one obtain it now? "It can be obtained in the houses of noble families.
"Go about and ask for it. They entered the village and, having asked, said at the door of Sudhammā's house, "Is there a *kaṇṇikā* (ornamental medallion) in this house?
She replied, "There is. "Then take the price. "I have no price."
“I will take it, provided you give me my share; I shall give it to you,” he said. “Come now, let us not give a share to this woman;
let us go to the forest and cut down a tree,” they said, and so they departed.
Then the carpenter asked, “Father, why was the keystone not obtained? They explained the matter to him. The carpenter—
Sitting on the central couch, he looked up at the sky and said, "O friends, today’s constellation is auspicious;
it will not be possible to obtain such an alignment again for another year.
Furthermore, the building materials you have brought with such great hardship will rot in this very spot for an entire year. When the time comes for you to be reborn in the world of the gods—"
He said, "Let there be a hall in one corner of that as well; bring it here.
Until they returned again, she had the letters "This hall is named Sudhammā" inscribed on the lower surface of the capital, wrapped them in new cloth, and set them aside.
When the workmen arrived, they said, "Bring the capital, you fellows! Let it be what it may!"
“We shall give you your share as well,” they said. She brought it out and gave it to them, saying, “Dear ones, do not unfasten this cloth until eight or sixteen rafters have been laid.
They accepted it, saying, “Very well,” and having taken it, they unfastened the cloth only after the rafters had been laid.
A certain villager, looking up, saw the letters and asked, "What is this, sir?
He summoned a man who was an expert in scripts and showed it to him. The man said, "This hall is named Sudhammā. "Bring it down, sir!
We have built this hall from the very beginning and have not even received its name; yet here it is, because of a mere *kaṇṇikā* tree worth only a jewel!"
"Let us have a hall built in our own names," they cried out. Even as they were crying out, the carpenter set in the rafters, fixed the pins, and completed the work on the hall.
They divided the hall into three parts: in one section they made a dwelling place for the lords, and in another...
[He saw] those who were miserable, and among them, those who were sick. Thirty-three people, having prepared thirty-three mats, gave a signal to the elephant:
"When a traveler arrives and sits upon whichever mat has been spread out, take him and establish him in the very house of the owner of that mat.
All his services for the feet, services for the back, food, meals, and bedding—"

"The burden will fall upon the owner of the plank itself. Thus, the elephant took each person as they arrived and led them to the owner's house, where the owner performed for him whatever task was required that day.
Meanwhile, the young brahmin Magha had a *koviḷāra* tree planted in a spot not far from the hall, and he placed a stone slab at its base.
They were spread out. His wife, named Nandā, had a lotus pond dug not far away; Cittā had flowering trees planted;
but the eldest of all, Sudhammā, wandered about taking a mirror and adorning her own person.
Magha said to her: "Bhadde Sudhammā, the hall has become full of footprints; Nandā has had a lotus pond dug; Cittā has [planted] flowering trees..."
He caused [trees] to be planted. But she said, "You have no merit of your own;
perform a single meritorious deed, my dear," and having said this, she devoted herself solely to adorning her own person.
Magha remained for the full span of his lifespan, and after passing away from there, he was reborn as Sakka in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven; they too...
Thirty-three village people, having passed away, were reborn as thirty-three sons of gods in his very presence.
Sakka’s palace named Vejayanta rose seven hundred yojanas high; its banner rose three hundred yojanas high;
and by the power of the koviḷāra tree, its trunk was fifteen yojanas in circumference with a perimeter of three hundred yojanas all around.
The Pāricchattaka tree arose; as a result of the stone slab, a sixty-yojana Paṇḍukambala rock arose at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree.
As a result of the Kaṇṇikarukkha tree of Sudhammā, the Sudhammā divine assembly hall arose, measuring three hundred yojanas.
As a result of the Nandā lotus pond, the Nandā [lotus pond] arose, measuring fifty yojanas.
A lotus pond named Nāma arose. As a result of Citta’s gift of flowering creepers and cloth, a sixty-league park named the Cittalatāvana Grove arose.
Sakka, the king of the gods, sat upon a golden couch one league high in the Sudhamma assembly hall of the gods, [which was] three leagues [in extent].

While a white parasol was being held over him by those sons of gods and daughters of gods, and surrounded by two and a half billion celestial musicians as well as the deities of the two heavenly realms, he surveyed his great prosperity; seeing those three women, he thought, "These at least are visible;
where is Sujātā? and looking about, [he saw her] in a mountain cave, having disregarded his words.
Having seen that she had been reborn as a crane-bird, he descended from the world of the gods and went into her presence.
As soon as she saw him, she recognized him and hung her head. "Foolish woman, why do you not now lift up your head?
You spent your time adorning only your own person, disregarding my words. [I told you of] Sudhammā, Nandā, and Cittā..."
And when great prosperity had been produced, he said, "Come, see our prosperity," and having led her to the world of the gods and placed her in the Nandā lotus pond, he sat down upon a couch.
The female dancers asked, "Where have you gone, Great King? Although he did not wish to tell them, he was pressed by them.
“Near Sujātā,” he said. “Where was she reborn, Great King? “At the foot of a ravine. “Where is she now?
“She has been left behind at the Nandā lotus pond. “Come, sirs, let us go see our lady! they all went there.
Previously, having been the eldest of them all, she had treated them with contempt; but now, when they saw her, they said: “Look!...”
Saying things such as, "O, our noble lady’s face is like a crab-pricking needle," they played in jest.
Being greatly distressed, she said to Sakka, the king of the gods: "Great King, what will these golden, silver, and gem-studded palaces, or even the Nandana lotus pond, do for me?
O Great King, for living beings, their own birthplace alone is a source of happiness."
“Release me right there at the foot of the cave. Sakka released her there and said, “Will you do as I say?
“I will, Great King,” she replied. “Take the five precepts and guard them without breach;
within a few days, I shall make you their leader. She did exactly so.
After a few days had passed, Sakka, wondering, "Is it possible to protect one's virtue?
went there in the form of a fish, lying on its back, and approached her on the surface of the water. Thinking, "This must be a dead fish," she went up and seized it by the head.
The fish flicked its tail. She thought, "I suppose it is still alive," and released it back into the water. Sakka then appeared in the sky.
Standing there, he said, "Excellent, excellent, Rakkhasī! If you guard this training rule (*sikkhāpada*) in this manner, in just a few days I shall make you the chief of the dancers.
Her lifespan was also five hundred years; yet she did not obtain even a single day's full meal.
Though she became parched, utterly withered, and emaciated, she passed away without breaking her virtue (*sīla*), and was reborn in Bārāṇasī.
She was reborn in the house of a potter.
Sakka, looking to see where she had been reborn, saw her and thought, "It is not possible to bring her here from there;
I shall provide her with a means of livelihood. He filled a cart with golden plantains and sat down in the middle of the village in the guise of an old man.
“Take the cardamom roots! he cried out. The villagers from all around came and said, “Give them to us, dear sir.
He replied, “I give them to those who guard their virtue; you must guard your virtue. They said, “Dear sir, we do not even know what virtue is like;
give them for a price. He said, “I give them only to those who guard their virtue. “Come now, you—”
“Who is this Elder Eḷālu?! they cried, and everyone turned back.
The girl asked, “Mother, you went for the sake of Elder Eḷālu; why have you returned with empty hands? “Who is this Elder Eḷālu, mother? she asked.
“I am giving him to those who guard their virtue,” he replied. “Surely his daughter possesses virtue! she thought.
They continued eating and said, "We do not even know what the precepts are.
Thinking, "I shall bring some for her," she went and said, "Dear father, give me some eḷāluka fruit. "Are you observing the precepts, mother? "Yes, dear father, I am observing them.
"Then this has been brought specifically for you by me," he said, and having placed it at the door of the house along with the carriage, he departed. She too [observed them] for as long as she lived.
Having guarded her virtue and passed away, she was reborn as the daughter of the asura Vepacitti. By the radiance of her virtue, she became beautiful.
Sakka, looking to see where she had been reborn, saw that she had been reborn in the abode of the asuras and that today was the auspicious occasion for her marriage. He then assembled the asuras.
Seeing this, she thought, "Now, by whatever means necessary, I must bring her here.
She assumed the form of an asura, went there, and stood among the asuras. Her father placed a garland of flowers in her hand, saying, "Tell your husband:
'Throw this upon whomever you desire. As she looked about, she saw Sakka due to their past association.
Having conceived affection for him, thinking, "This is my husband," she threw a garland over him. He took her by the arm and flew up into the air.
At that moment, the Asuras became aware of it; they pursued them, crying out, "Seize him!
Seize him! This is old Sakka, our enemy; we will not give our daughter to him! Vepacitti asked, "By whom was she brought?"
“Great King, Jarasakka [is the best],” he said. “Among the rest, this one alone is the most excellent; go away!
Sakka led him away and established him in the position of chief among the two hundred and fifty million celestial dancers. She requested a boon from Sakka:
“Great King, in this world of the gods I have no mother, father, brother, or sister. Wherever—”
“Go, Great King; wherever you go, go taking me with you. Sakka gave his promise, saying, “Very well.

Thus, having perceived his state of purity since the time he was the young brahmin Magha in the village of Macala, the Blessed One said, “For a long time this yakkha has been pure. “Beneficial” (*atthasañhita*) means connected with the goal, connected with the purpose.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Questions.
357. What are the fetters? What are the bonds? Being bound by what bond? "Many folk" means many people. "Free from enmity" means free from resentment.
"Free from weapons" means liberated from the weapons of arms and the punishment of fines. "Free from adversaries" means without enemies.
"Free from ill will" means devoid of dejection. "May we dwell free from enmity" means: "Oh, may we indeed dwell without enmity toward anyone."

"Having given a gift and performed an act of worship, they make this aspiration: 'May we, without giving rise to anger toward anyone, enjoy [this] together with a thousand attendants, each holding a celestial nymph in their hand.
Thus it is for them; that is, such is their aspiration. And yet—despite such an aspiration."
The fetters of envy and avarice (*issā-macchariya-saṃyojana*): envy has the characteristic of envying the success of others;
avarice has the characteristic of being unable to endure others sharing in one’s own success. Those for whom envy and avarice are fetters are "those with the fetters of envy and avarice.
This is the summary here. For a detailed account, however, [the definitions of] envy and avarice are as follows:
These are exactly as described in the Abhidhamma.
However, here, due to stinginess regarding one's dwelling (*āvāsamacchariya*), one becomes a *yakkha* or a *peta* and wanders about with the refuse of that very dwelling on one's head.
Due to stinginess regarding one's family (*kulamacchariya*), upon seeing others performing acts of giving and so forth within that family, [one becomes resentful].
As he thinks, "Alas, this family of mine is divided," blood gushes from his mouth, there is purging from his bowels,

and even his intestines come out in pieces. Having been stingy with gains belonging to the Saṅgha or a group by being miserly over them and then consuming them as if they were his own private property, he becomes a *yakkha* or a *peta*.

Or he is reborn as a great python. However, due to his envy regarding the excellence of his own physical appearance and his envy regarding the Dhamma of the scriptures, he praises only his own appearance and not that of others.
By speaking of various faults such as "What kind of appearance is this?
and by not giving any portion of the scriptures to anyone, he becomes both ugly and deaf-mute.
Furthermore, through stinginess regarding one’s dwelling, one is cooked in the Iron House (Lohageha). Through stinginess regarding one’s family, one becomes one who gains little.
Through stinginess regarding gain, one is reborn in the Excrement Hell (Gūthaniraya). Through stinginess regarding physical beauty, even when reborn in a state of existence, one lacks beauty.
Through stinginess regarding the Dhamma, one is reborn in the Kukkuḷa Hell. This fetter of envy and stinginess, however, is abandoned by the path of stream-entry.
As long as that [defilement] is not abandoned, even though gods and humans aspire for freedom from enmity and so forth, they are still not liberated from enmity and the rest.
Regarding the phrase "I have crossed over doubt" in this question, he says that his doubt has been crossed over after hearing your words;
he does not indicate having crossed over doubt by means of the Path. "Doubt has vanished" means: "What is this? What is that?"—such is the nature of doubt.
This doubt, too, has been dispelled. 358.

The introductory sections (*nidāna*) and so forth have already had their meaning explained. "The source of the pleasant and the unpleasant" means that stinginess (*macchariya*) has its source in pleasant beings and formations, while envy (*issā*) has its source in unpleasant beings and formations;
or else, both have both as their source. For one who has gone forth, there are indeed co-residents (*saddhivihārika*) and others [who are pleasant].
To a householder, children and others, or even creatures such as elephants and horses, are dear, cherished, and beloved;
he cannot endure not seeing them for even a moment. Seeing another obtain such a beloved being, he becomes envious, thinking: "This person has some business with us;
give him [the creature] back for just a moment. Thus he speaks to that very person.
When asked by others, one practices stinginess by saying things such as, "It cannot be given," or "It will cause weariness," or "It will cause distress.

In this way, both [types of stinginess] have as their source beloved beings. Furthermore, when a monk has his bowl, robes, and requisites, or a householder has ornaments and other articles that are dear and pleasing to him, and another person develops a similar desire for them—
Having seen [this], he feels envy, thinking, "O, may such a thing not happen to him!
Or, even when asked, he acts with stinginess, saying, "We too would claim this as our own; it cannot be given. Thus, both [envy and stinginess] have the formation of the pleasant as their cause.
Furthermore, having obtained those aforementioned unpleasant beings and formations, even if they are disagreeable to him—
Nevertheless, because the defilements function in a perverted manner, one either feels envy, thinking, "Who else besides me is a recipient of such gains?",
or one feels stinginess, refusing to give even for a short time when asked. Thus,
both of these are rooted in the formations of unloved beings.
"Desire as a cause" (*chandanimitta*): herein, desire is fivefold—desire for seeking, desire for acquisition, desire for enjoyment, desire for hoarding, and desire for giving away.
What is desire for seeking? Here, someone who is unsatisfied and filled with longing seeks forms; he seeks sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and wealth. This is desire for seeking.

What is the desire for acquisition (*paṭilābhachanda*)? Here, someone, being unsatisfied and having given rise to desire, acquires a form, a sound, a smell, a taste, a tangible object, or acquires wealth.

This is the desire for acquisition. What is the desire for enjoyment (*paribhogachanda*)? Here, someone, being unsatisfied and having given rise to desire, enjoys a form, a sound, a smell, a taste, a tangible object, or enjoys wealth. This is the desire for enjoyment.
What is the desire for hoarding? Here, someone who is unsatisfied and full of longing accumulates wealth, thinking, "It will be useful in times of misfortune. This is the desire for hoarding.

What is the desire for distribution? Here, someone who is unsatisfied and full of longing distributes wealth to elephant-riders, horse-riders, charioteers, and archers, thinking, "These will protect me, guard me, and look after my interests. This is the desire for distribution.
“They will surround [him]”—this is the desire for response (*vissajjanachanda*). These are the five types of desire. Here, it is merely craving (*taṇhāmatta*) that is intended;
it is with reference to this that this was said.

Regarding the phrase “the source of applied thought” (*vitakkanidāna*), it refers to the applied thought of deliberation (*vinicchayavitakka*) as stated thus: “In dependence on gain, there is deliberation.”

As for "applied thought" (*vitakka*): "discernment" (*vinicchaya*) refers to two kinds of discernment—the discernment of craving (*taṇhā-vinicchaya*) and the discernment of views (*diṭṭhi-vinicchaya*).
The eight hundred modes of craving’s wandering are called the discernment of craving; the sixty-two views are called the discernment of views.
Indeed, it is on account of this aforementioned discernment of craving that there is no defining of what is desirable and undesirable, or what is pleasant and unpleasant.
For that very same thing is desirable to one person and undesirable to another, as in the case of the foot-rotting flesh of wild animals for borderland kings and those from the Middle Country.
When craving has been determined by way of its objects—having been analyzed—that acquired basis is [evaluated] thus:
"There will be this much of form, this much of sound, this much of odor, this much of taste..."
“‘This much will be for touch; this much will be mine; this much will be for another; this much I shall store away;
this much I shall give to another’—such determination arises through the discernment of thought.
Therefore it was said: ‘Desire, O Lord of Devas, has its source in thought.’”

"Having proliferation, perception, and conceptualization as its source": there are three kinds of proliferation (*papañca*): the proliferation of craving (*taṇhā-papañca*), the proliferation of conceit (*māna-papañca*), and the proliferation of views (*diṭṭhi-papañca*).
Among these, the eighty-nine modes of the wandering of craving are called the proliferation of craving;

the ninefold conceit is called the proliferation of conceit; and the sixty-two views are called the proliferation of views. Of these, it is the proliferation of craving that is intended here. In what sense?
Papañca? It is papañca in the sense of leading to a state of being intoxicated and heedless. The perception associated with that is "papañca-perception.

"Sañkhā" refers to a constituent part, as in such passages as, "For the proliferation of conceptualization (papañca-saṅkhā) has its source in perception. Thus, "having its source in the constituent part of papañca-perception" means that thought (vitakka) has its source in the constituent part of papañca-perception.

"Leading to the cessation of the formations of conceptual proliferation": this asks for the path together with insight—that which leads to, and is appropriate for, the destruction, cessation, and subsiding of these formations of conceptual proliferation. 359.
Then the Blessed One began [his teaching] on the three feelings, starting with "He abandons joy. But what was it that the Blessed One asked?
Was it spoken unasked, or asked; with a sequence, or without a sequence? It was spoken only when asked, not unasked;
only with a sequence, not without a sequence. For to devas, the formless is more manifest than the formed;
even within the formless, feeling is more manifest. Why? Because for devas, the body born of karma is powerful, while the body born of physical nutriment is subtle.
Because the body born of kamma is so subtle and because the kamma-born [elements] are so powerful, they do not persist even after one meal has passed;
they dissolve like a lump of ghee placed on a hot stone—all this should be understood according to the method already stated in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*.
Therefore, the Blessed One began with the three feelings for Sakka. For there are two kinds of meditation subjects: the meditation subject consisting of form (*rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna*) and...

And there is the immaterial meditation subject (*arūpakammaṭṭhāna*). This very same thing is also called "the discernment of the material" (*rūpapariggaha*) and "the discernment of the immaterial" (*arūpapariggaha*).

In this regard, the Blessed One teaches the meditation subject of the material to one for whom the material is manifest, by way of either concise attention or detailed attention, while expanding upon the analysis of the four elements. To one for whom the immaterial is manifest, [he teaches the immaterial meditation subject].

He taught him the immaterial meditation subject (*arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna*). In teaching it, he did so only after first showing him the material meditation subject (*rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna*) which serves as its basis;
however, since the immaterial meditation subject is well-known to the gods, he began with feeling (*vedanā*) by way of that immaterial meditation subject.
For there are three ways of application (*abhinivesa*) to the immaterial meditation subject: by way of contact (*phassa*), by way of feeling (*vedanā*), and by way of consciousness (*citta*).

How so? For in the case of some person, when the meditation subject of material form has been grasped either in brief or in detail, the first impact of the mind and mental factors upon that object is manifest as contact arising while touching that object.
In the case of another, feeling arising while experiencing that object is manifest.
For some, when they have grasped that object, the consciousness arising as it cognizes it becomes evident.
In that case, for one to whom contact is evident, it is not contact alone that arises;
along with it, feeling also arises experiencing that very same object, perception also arises perceiving it, and volition also arises intending it.
Since volition (*cetanā*) and consciousness (*viññāṇa*), which cognizes, also arise, he grasps [the process] as consisting of exactly five factors, beginning with contact (*phassa*).
For one to whom feeling (*vedanā*) is clear, it is not merely feeling that arises;

along with that, contact (*phassa*) also arises as it touches that very same object, perception (*saññā*) arises as it perceives, volition (*cetanā*) arises as it wills, and consciousness (*viññāṇa*)... [arises as it cognizes].
He discerns that consciousness also arises only within the pentad beginning with contact. For one to whom consciousness is clear, he understands:
"It is not only consciousness that arises; along with it, contact also arises as it touches that very same object;
feeling also arises as it experiences it; perception also arises as it perceives it; and volition also arises as it intends."
He examines only those phenomena consisting of contact as the fifth.
Investigating, "Upon what are these phenomena consisting of contact as the fifth supported? he understands:

"They are supported by the physical basis. The "physical basis" refers to the body composed of the four great elements, with reference to which it was said: "And this consciousness of mine is here attached."
"Bound herein"—this, in terms of meaning, consists of both the primary elements (*bhūta*) and the derived forms (*upādārūpa*).

Thus, here he sees only name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*): "matter" is the aggregate of form, and "name" refers to the four immaterial aggregates; it is merely the five aggregates. For the five aggregates are not separate from name-and-form.
Or, there is no name-and-form (nāmarūpa) apart from the five aggregates. Examining thus, "What is the cause of these five aggregates?", he sees that they have ignorance and so forth as their cause.
Then, by way of name-and-form together with its conditions, he understands: "This is both the condition and the conditioned;
there is no other being or person here, but only a mere heap of pure formations."
Having applied the three characteristics and contemplating according to the sequence of insight meditation— “impermanent, suffering, non-self”— he wanders about.
Desiring penetration day after day, on such a day as that, having obtained a favorable climate, a favorable person, favorable food,
or a favorable opportunity for hearing the Dhamma, he sits cross-legged and applies insight meditation.
Having reached the summit, one is established in Arahantship. Thus, for these three persons, the meditation subject has been explained up to the stage of Arahantship.
But here, the Blessed One, while explaining the formless meditation subject, spoke by way of feeling (*vedanā*). For it is by way of contact (*phassa*) that...
When described by way of consciousness, this [feeling] is not evident; it appears as if it were darkness.
However, it becomes evident by way of feeling. Why? Because the arising of feelings is evident. For the arising of pleasant and painful feelings is evident.
When a pleasant feeling arises, it then agitates and massages the entire body.

It arises as if pouring out, as if overflowing with clarified butter purified a hundred times, as if anointing with oil refined a hundred times, as if extinguishing a feverish heat with a thousand jars of water, uttering the words, "Oh, what bliss! Oh, what bliss!
And when suffering arises, it arises shaking the entire body.

It arises while uttering cries of "Alas, what suffering! Alas, what suffering! as if being crushed, as if being spread out, as if being drenched with molten copper, or as if a cluster of firebrands were being thrown onto dry grass and forest undergrowth in the wilderness.
Thus, the arising of pleasant and painful feelings becomes manifest.
But the neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling] is difficult to illustrate, as if overwhelmed by darkness.

It becomes clear to one who grasps it through its underlying principle as the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling that consists in a neutral state, occurring when pleasure and pain have departed by way of the negation of what is agreeable and disagreeable.
How so? Just as, for example, the tracks of a deer that has fled after climbing onto a rock in the middle of its path.
Just as a deer-hunter, while walking, sees the footprints on both the near and far sides of a flat rock but does not see them in the middle, yet knows by inference:
"He ascended from here, he descended from there, and he must have gone through this spot in the middle of the rock";
so too, the arising of pleasant feeling is manifest like the footprint at the place of ascent, whereas [the footprint] at the place of descent—

Just as the arising of painful feeling becomes evident like a footprint— whereby one grasps it by way of its method, thinking "having ascended from here, having descended from there, it has gone thus in the middle"— so too,

for one who grasps it by way of its method as the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling that consists in the neutral state through the negation of the pleasant and the unpleasant when pleasure and pain have departed,
that feeling becomes evident. In this way, the Blessed One [taught] first the meditation subject of material form.
Having spoken thus, he subsequently demonstrated the immaterial meditation subject by way of feeling.

And it was not only here that he demonstrated it in this manner; [he did so] in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna, in the Satipaṭṭhāna of the Majjhima Nikāya, in the Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhaya, in the Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya, in the Cūḷavedalla Sutta, in the Mahāvedalla Sutta, and in the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta.
In the *Māgaṇḍiya Sutta*, the *Dhātuvibhaṅga*, the *Āneñjasappāya*, and the entire *Vedanāsaṃyutta*— in these and many other discourses—
he first taught the meditation subject of form (*rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna*) and subsequently presented the meditation subject of the formless (*arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna*) by way of feeling (*vedanā*).
