And just as in those various instances, so too here in this *Sakkapañha*, he first [taught] the meditation subject of form.
Having spoken thus, he subsequently demonstrated the immaterial meditation subject by way of feeling.
Herein, the material meditation subject is merely the object of that feeling and is therefore condensed; consequently, it will not have appeared in the text.
To show specifically that gateway of application by way of feeling which is evident in the immaterial meditation subject, [he said:]
“Somanassa, O Lord of Devas,” he said, and so forth. Therein, “of two kinds” means of two types, that is, by way of two portions.
“Such happiness as this should not be cultivated” means that such household-based happiness should not be cultivated.
As for what is called household-based happiness: “In this regard, what are the six kinds of household-based happiness? [They are those] cognizable by the eye... [and so on].
When joy arises from regarding the acquisition of forms that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, and delightful, associated with worldly bait;
or when it arises from recollecting what was previously acquired, past, ceased, and changed—
such joy as this is called "based on the household life."
“Joy”: this refers to the joy based on the strands of sensual pleasure mentioned in regard to the six sense-doors.
“Such joy as this should be cultivated” means that such joy based on renunciation should be cultivated.
As for what is called “joy based on renunciation”: “In this context, what are the six kinds of joy based on renunciation? It is simply regarding forms... [and so forth].

"Having understood impermanence, and having understood change, fading away, and cessation—both formerly and now all those forms are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—for one who sees this thus as it really is with right wisdom, joy arises.
That kind of joy is called joy based on renunciation. Thus [he said].

When a desirable object enters the range of the six sense doors, one who is able to arouse and intensify insight by way of impermanence and so forth, and who experiences joy born from the thought, "My insight has been intensified," that is the joy that has arisen. As for the phrase "to be cultivated":
this refers to the joy that arises through renunciation, through insight, through recollection, and through the first jhāna and so forth; such joy is what is called "to be cultivated."
In that regard, as for "with applied thought and sustained thought," one should understand that among the mental joys based on renunciation (*nekkhamma*),

there is that joy which arises by way of renunciation, by way of insight (*vipassanā*), by way of recollection (*anussati*), and by way of the first jhāna— namely, the joy with applied and sustained thought.
As for "without applied thought and without sustained thought," however, this refers to [the joy] by way of the second and third jhānas.
One would know: "Arisen is joy that is without applied thought and without sustained thought.

Of those two which are without applied thought and without sustained thought, that which is without applied thought and without sustained thought is more excellent; this is the meaning. What is expressed by this?
The two types of Arahantship are expressed. How so? It is said that one bhikkhu [attains it] with applied thought and sustained thought...
Having established insight into mental joy (*somanassa*), while investigating, "What is this mental joy dependent upon? he understands, "It is dependent upon the physical basis (*vatthu*).

Thus, following the same method explained in the section on the five factors beginning with contact, he gradually establishes himself in Arahantship. Another, having established insight into mental joy that is without applied thought and sustained thought (*avitakka-avicāra*), establishes himself in Arahantship by the same method already described. In this regard, even for those who are attached to mental joy...

That which is without applied thought and without sustained thought is more sublime than that which is with applied thought and with sustained thought. Insight with sustained thought is more sublime even than insight accompanied by joy and with applied thought and sustained thought.

The attainment of fruition accompanied by joy and without applied thought and sustained thought is indeed more sublime even than the attainment of fruition accompanied by joy and with applied thought and sustained thought. Therefore the Blessed One said: "Those who are without applied thought..."
"Without investigation, those [states] are more refined. 361.
"Such grief as this should not be indulged in" means that such grief based on the household life should not be indulged in.
As for what is called grief based on the household life: "In this regard, what are the six kinds of grief based on the household life? [They are the griefs] regarding things cognizable by the eye..."
"Regarding forms that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, charming, and connected with worldly gain:
when one regards their non-attainment as non-attained, or when one recollects what was previously unobtained, past, ceased, and changed, sorrow arises.
Such sorrow as this is called 'sorrow based on the household life.'"

Thus, for one who reflects: "I have not experienced, I shall not experience, nor do I experience a desirable object at the six sense doors," there arises mental distress based on the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*).
Such mental distress is to be cultivated; that is, such mental distress based on renunciation (*nekkhamma*) is to be cultivated. [This refers to] mental distress based on renunciation.
[The section] named: "In this regard, what are the six kinds of grief based on renunciation?
Having understood the impermanence of forms, their change, fading away, and cessation;
and having seen with wisdom, as it truly is, that both past forms and present ones—all those forms—are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—one dwells in the unsurpassed liberations."
He arouses a longing, thinking: "When indeed shall I enter and dwell in that sphere which the Noble Ones now enter and dwell in?

Thus, for one who arouses a longing for the unsurpassed liberations, there arises mental distress conditioned by that longing; such mental distress as this is called "mental distress based on renunciation."
Thus, when desirable objects have entered the range of the six sense-doors,

one should establish a longing for the noble fruit-dhammas known as the supreme liberation; then, failing to be able to exert oneself by establishing insight (*vipassanā*) through the aspects of impermanence and so forth for the sake of attaining them—
even after exerting insight for this fortnight, this month, or this year— one [reaches] the noble plane.
One who grieves cannot overcome the sorrow that has arisen. Regarding the phrase "to be cultivated":

the sorrow that arises by way of renunciation (*nekkhamma*), by way of insight (*vipassanā*), by way of recollection (*anussati*), and by way of the first jhāna and so forth, is what is called "to be cultivated.

In that regard, even among the two kinds of sorrow—namely, that which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought (*savitakka-savicāra*)—it is only the household-based sorrow (*gehasita-domanassa*) [that is not to be cultivated].

That which is called "mental grief accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought" (*savitakkasavicāra-domanassa*) refers to the mental grief that has arisen through renunciation, through insight (*vipassanā*), through recollection (*anussati*), or through the first and second jhānas;
this should be understood as "mental grief without applied thought and sustained thought" (*avitakka-avicāra-domanassa*).

However, in an absolute sense (*nippariyāya*), there is no such thing as "mental grief without applied thought and sustained thought. For the faculty of mental grief (*domanassindriya*) is, in one respect, [always accompanied by applied and sustained thought].

It is both unwholesome and accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought; however, it is described as "with applied thought and sustained thought" and "without applied thought and sustained thought" by way of the monk’s conceptualizing.

In this regard, the method is as follows: here, a monk [perceives] states with applied thought and sustained thought, as well as states without applied thought and sustained thought, which serve as conditions for mental displeasure.

Furthermore, taking "dejection" (*domanassa*) to refer to the states of the Path and Fruition that have arisen precisely conditioned by dejection, and by way of demonstrating the practice of others, [one reflects]:
"When indeed will insight be established in me regarding dejection accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought (*savitakkasavicāra*)?

When regarding dejection without applied thought and sustained thought (*avitakkaavicāra*)? And: "When indeed will the attainment of the fruit (*phalasamāpatti*) regarding dejection accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought [occur] in me?"

Thinking, "When will the attainment of the fruit that is without applied thought, without sustained thought, and free from mental distress arise?", he undertakes a practice lasting three months, six months, or nine months.
Having undertaken the three-month practice, he keeps watch for one watch during the first month, allowing himself two watches of sleep; in the middle month, he keeps watch for two watches.
He makes an opportunity for sleep during one watch of the night; and during the last month, he sustains himself by walking meditation and sitting alone.
If he thus attains *arahantship*, that is well. If he does not attain it, he further restricts himself to six months.
There too, having practiced according to the method described for two months at a time, if he is unable to attain *arahantship*, he further restricts himself to nine months.
He takes it up. There too, having practiced in that same manner for three months each time, if he is unable to reach Arahantship, dejection arises in him as he reflects:
"Alas, I have not obtained the opportunity to perform the invitation of purification together with my fellow celibates.
Tears flow like streams, as happened to the Elder Mahāsīva, who dwelt in a mountain cave near a village.
The Story of the Elder Mahāsīva:
It is said that the Elder taught eighteen great assemblies. By abiding by his instruction, thirty thousand bhikkhus attained arahantship.
Then, one bhikkhu thought: "My own internal qualities are indeed immeasurable; but what kind [of qualities] do my [teachers possess]?"
Reflecting on "the virtues of the teacher," he saw that the teacher was still an ordinary person (*puthujjana*).
Thinking, "Our teacher is a refuge for others, yet he is unable to become one himself;

I shall give him instruction," he traveled through the air, descended near the monastery, approached the teacher as he sat in his daytime resting place, performed the proper duties, and sat down to one side.
The Elder asked, “For what reason have you come, alms-collector? “I have come, venerable sir, to receive a single expression of thanks.
“There will be no opportunity for that, friend. “I shall ask when you are standing at the Vitakkamāḷaka pavilion, venerable sir. “Others are asking there as well.
“Then on the path while walking for alms, venerable sir. “Others are asking there too.”

"At the place where the double-layered lower robe (*dupaṭṭanivāsana*) is worn, at the place where the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) is put on, at the place where the bowl (*patta*) is taken out, after wandering through the village, at the time of drinking rice-gruel in the assembly hall—'Venerable Sir' (*bhante*). Therein, the elders of the commentaries dispel their own doubts, saying 'Friend' (*āvuso*).
At the time of departing from within the village, one thinks, 'I will ask, Venerable Sir. Even there, others ask."
"Friend. "Venerable sir, on the way; venerable sir, at the dining hall after the meal is finished;
venerable sir, at the daytime resting place; venerable sir, at the time for washing the feet; venerable sir, at the time for washing the face? "At that time, others were asking.
From then on, until dawn, others asked, "Friend. [He said this] when he had taken a tooth-stick and was going for the purpose of washing his face.
"Venerable sir? "At that time, others were asking. "When you had washed your face and were on your way back, 'Venerable sir?
At that time too, others were asking. "When you had entered your lodging and were seated, 'Venerable sir? At that time too, others were asking.
"Venerable sir, surely after washing your face, entering your lodging, and having warmed yourself by sitting cross-legged three or four times—"
"For those performing their work with wise attention, there must be time for an opportunity;
you will not even obtain the moment of death, venerable sir. Venerable sir, like a wooden plank, you are a support for others but are unable to support yourself.
I have no need for your expression of appreciation," he said, and having leaped into the air, he departed.
The Elder, realizing, “This bhikkhu has no business with the scriptures;
rather, he has come thinking, ‘I shall be a goad for me,’” thought, “Now there will be no opportunity; I shall depart at dawn.
Having placed his bowl and robes nearby, he spent the entire day, as well as the first and middle watches of the night, teaching the Dhamma, and then during the last watch—
When one elder had gone out after receiving his daily recitation, [the other] took up his bowl and robes and went out together with him.
The resident pupils thought, "The teacher has gone out due to some distraction. When the elder had gone out, someone perceived him as being a fellow monk from the same school.
The Elder, thinking, "What is this so-called 'Arahatship' for one like me?
I shall attain it within two or three days and then return," departed without informing his pupils.

On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āsāḷhī, he went to a mountain retreat near a village, ascended a walking path, and while attending to his meditation subject, he was unable to realize Arahatship that day.
When the Uposatha day arrived, he thought: "I came thinking, 'In two or three days I shall attain Arahatship,' but I was unable to attain it.

For three months, however, I shall know it to be as if it were only three days, until the Great Invitation (Mahāpavāraṇā). Although he entered the rains retreat with this intention, he was still unable to attain it.
On the day of the Invitation, he reflected: "I came thinking, 'In two or three days I shall attain Arahatship.'"
“I have been here for three months, yet I have not succeeded; however, my fellow celibates are performing the invitation ceremony for purification.
As he was reflecting thus, streams of tears flowed from his eyes. Then he thought:
“The fruit of the Path will not arise for me on this couch through the four postures; until I have attained Arahatship, I shall never stretch out my back upon this couch, nor my feet.”
Thinking, "I shall wash it," he raised the bed and set it aside. Again during the following rainy season, he was unable to attain Arahantship.
During twenty-nine *pavāraṇā* ceremonies, streams of tears flowed forth. Village children sewed the cracked spots on the Elder’s feet with thorns;
even while playing, they would say, "It is like that of the noble Elder Mahāsīva."
"May my feet be restored," they cried out, performing a *dava* ceremony.
On the day of the Great Invitation (*mahāpavāraṇā*) after thirty years, the Elder was standing leaning against a support-board when he thought:
"Now that I have practiced the duties of a recluse for thirty years, I have not been able to attain Arahantship; surely, in this..."
He thought, "There is neither the Path nor the Fruit within this body; I have not obtained the opportunity to perform the invitation for purity (*visuddhipavāraṇā*) together with my fellow celibates.
As he was thinking thus, dejection arose within him and streams of tears flowed forth.
Then, a certain daughter of the gods stood nearby weeping. "Who is it here that weeps? "It is I, venerable sir."

“...the daughter of a deva. “Why are you weeping? “Venerable sir, by weeping, the fruit of the path was realized; thinking, ‘Because of that, I too shall realize one or two fruits of the path,’ I am weeping.
Then the elder said, “O Great Sīva, even the devas play with you; it is fitting—”
Thinking, "Is this indeed so for you? he increased his insight and attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).

He thought, "Now I shall lie down," and after attending to his lodging, arranging his bed, and providing water at the washing place, he sat on the step of the staircase thinking, "I will wash my feet."
His disciples, reflecting, "Our teacher has gone for thirty years to practice the ascetic life;

was he able to produce some distinction or not? saw that he had attained arahantship and was sitting down to wash his feet, and they thought, "While disciples like us were remaining, our teacher washed his own feet..."
"It is impossible that he will wash them; I shall wash them, I shall wash them!
Having said this, even thirty thousand [devas] traveled through the air, paid homage, and said, "Venerable sir, we shall wash your feet. [The Buddha replied:
"Friends, it has now been thirty years since my feet have been washed. Stay back; I alone shall wash them."
Sakka, too, reflecting thus: “My noble master, the Elder Mahāsīva, has attained Arahantship;
yet when thirty thousand pupils come to him saying, ‘We will wash his feet,’ he does not allow them to wash his feet.
But while a attendant such as I am stands by, it is impossible that he would think, ‘My noble master will wash his own feet’; therefore, I shall wash them,” he reached this conclusion.
Having done so, he appeared in the presence of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus together with Queen Sujātā.

Placing the asura maiden Suja in front of him, he requested space, saying, "Go away, venerable sirs, it is a woman," and then approached the Elder, paid homage, and sat down before him in the *ukkuṭika* posture, saying, "Venerable sir, I shall wash your feet. [The Elder replied: "Kosiya, now for me... [thirty...]

"For years my feet have been unwashed; moreover, the natural odor of a human body is loathsome even to the devas, appearing like a corpse hanging from one's neck even to those standing a hundred yojanas away. I myself shall wash them.
"Venerable sir, this odor is not perceived; however, the fragrance of your virtue transcends the six heavenly worlds."
Having reached the peak of existence, he stood there. "Venerable sir, there is no fragrance superior to the fragrance of virtue;
it is by the fragrance of your virtue that I have come," he said, and grasping the monk’s ankle with his left hand, he massaged the sole of his foot with his right hand.
The feet were like those of a young child. Having washed the feet and paid homage, Sakka departed for the world of the gods.

Thus, it should be understood that for a bhikkhu who reflects, "I do not obtain the invitation of purification together with my fellow celibates," the grief that has arisen— by way of his conceptualizing—

is stated as both "grief accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought" and "grief without applied thought and without sustained thought" with respect to the object of insight, the insight itself, the path, and the fruit.
Therein, one bhikkhu, having established insight into sorrow accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, investigates: "Upon what is this sorrow dependent?

Investigating thus, he understands: "It is dependent upon the physical basis. Then, by the very method described in the section on the pentad of contact, he gradually establishes himself in Arahantship.
Another, having established insight into sorrow that is without applied thought and without sustained thought...
In the same manner as previously described, one becomes established in Arahantship.

In this regard, even among the states of mental distress (*domanassa*) that have been clung to, the state without applied thought and sustained thought (*avitakka-avicāra*) is more sublime than that with applied and sustained thought (*savitakka-savicāra*). Insight into mental distress without applied and sustained thought is more sublime than insight into mental distress with applied and sustained thought. And the attainment of the fruit (*phalasamāpatti*) of mental distress without applied and sustained thought is indeed more sublime than the attainment of the fruit of mental distress with applied and sustained thought.
They are more sublime. Therefore the Blessed One said: “Those states that are without applied thought and sustained thought are more sublime.
(362) “Such equanimity as this should not be cultivated” means that such household-based equanimity should not be cultivated.
Regarding household-based equanimity, it is said: “In this regard, what is household-based equanimity? Upon seeing a form with the eye, equanimity arises in the fool...”

“Such equanimity as belongs to the deluded worldling—who has not conquered the flood, who has not conquered the result [of karma], who does not see the danger, and who is an unlearned worldling—does not transcend form; therefore, that equanimity is said to be ‘based on the household life.
Thus, when a desirable object enters the range of the six sense doors, it is like flies clinging to a lump of sugar.
Equanimity based on the strands of sensual pleasure—which arises attached and clinging right there, without transcending forms and so forth—should not be cultivated.
Such equanimity as this should be cultivated means that equanimity based on renunciation should be cultivated. [That is] based on renunciation.
Regarding equanimity (*upekkhā*): "In this context, what are the six kinds of equanimity based on renunciation?

Having understood the impermanence of forms, their change, fading away, and cessation, one sees them as they truly are with right wisdom, thinking: 'Both past forms and those of the present—all forms are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change. Thus it arises."
“Equanimity: such equanimity as this transcends form; therefore, that equanimity is said to be ‘based on renunciation.

Thus, when desirable or undesirable objects have entered the range of the six sense doors, the insight that arises in one who is not attached to the desirable, not repelled by the undesirable, and who does not become deluded through lack of equanimity, is associated with knowledge.
Equanimity (upekkhā). Furthermore, the neutral equanimity that is similar in nature to feeling is also called "equanimity" here. Therefore, regarding the phrase "should be cultivated":

this refers to the equanimity that arises by way of renunciation, by way of insight, by way of the bases of mindfulness, and by way of the first, second, third, and fourth jhānas; such equanimity is what is meant by "should be cultivated."

In this context, regarding that which is "with applied thought and sustained thought," one should understand it as the equanimity based on renunciation that has arisen by way of renunciation, insight, the bases of mindfulness, and the first jhāna.
Regarding that which is "without applied thought and without sustained thought," however, it is that which has arisen by way of the second jhāna and so forth.
One should know that which is without applied thought and without sustained thought as equanimity (*upekkhā*).

Regarding those two states that are without applied thought and without sustained thought, "the more excellent" means that among these two, that which is without applied thought and without sustained thought is the more excellent. What is expressed by this? The Arahantship of two [types of persons] is expressed.
For one bhikkhu, having established insight (*vipassanā*) upon equanimity accompanied by applied and sustained thought, [perceives]: "This equanimity..."

Investigating, "What is it dependent upon?", he understands, "It is dependent on the physical bases. In this way, following the sequence described in the section on the fivefold contact, he gradually establishes himself in Arahantship.
Another, having established insight into equanimity that is without applied thought and without sustained thought, establishes himself in Arahantship in the same manner as described.
Even regarding the equanimity adhered to therein, [he proceeds] from that which is with applied thought and sustained thought...

Those without applied thought and without sustained thought are more excellent. Insight with equanimity that is without applied thought and without sustained thought is more excellent than insight with equanimity accompanied by applied and sustained thought.

The attainment of the fruit with equanimity that is without applied thought and without sustained thought is indeed more excellent than the attainment of the fruit with equanimity accompanied by applied and sustained thought.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "Those which are without applied thought and without sustained thought are more excellent."

"O Lord of Devas, a bhikkhu who practices in this way has practiced the path leading to the cessation of the conceptual proliferations of perception," thus the Blessed One concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship.
But Sakka attained the fruit of stream-entry. For the intention of the Buddhas is never inferior; it is always sublime. Even for a single person...
Even when teaching many doctrines, the Blessed One takes his stand upon Arahantship alone as the pinnacle.

However, depending on their own corresponding *upanissaya* (adequate causes), some beings become stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), some once-returners (*sakadāgāmī*), some non-returners (*anāgāmī*), and some Arahants.
For the Blessed One is like a king, and those to be trained are like the princes. Just as a king, at the time of a meal, [eats] according to his own measure...
Having scooped up a morsel of food, he brings it to the princes; they then make a mouthful from it according to the size of their own mouths.
In the same way, the Blessed One reaches the peak of attainment through the fruit of Arahantship itself by means of a teaching suited to his own inclination.

Those to be trained [receive] at least the fruit of stream-entry, or else the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, or Arahantship, according to the measure of their own underlying potential (*upanissaya*).

...or they took [the offerings]. But Sakka became a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*). Having become a stream-enterer, he passed away right there in the presence of the Blessed One and was reborn as a young Sakka.
For when deities pass away, no trace of the movement of their bodies is perceived;
it is like the flickering of a lamp’s flame. Therefore, the other deities did not know [what had happened]. Sakka—
However, because he himself had passed away and the Blessed One possessed unimpeded knowledge, only these two individuals knew [the truth]. Then Sakka thought:
"The Blessed One has indeed described for me only the fruits produced in the three states;
yet this path or fruit cannot be grasped by leaping up like a bird. [I must seek] the preliminary practice of the way leading thereto..."
"He must have been developed. Well then, I shall ask him about the preliminary practice leading up to one whose taints are destroyed.
Thus he spoke, beginning with "But how, dear sir, did you practice," while inquiring after that. Therein, "for the restraint of the Pātimokkha" means:

"For the sake of the restraint of the supreme, foremost virtue. The passage beginning with "bodily conduct as well" is stated for the purpose of showing the Pātimokkha restraint by way of the bodily conduct that is to be cultivated and so forth.
Furthermore, this discourse on virtue should be explained either by way of the courses of action (kamma-patha) or by way of the formal designations (paññatti).
In that regard, when explaining by way of the courses of action, first, unwholesome bodily conduct consists of killing, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct.
It should be explained. When explaining by way of designation (*paṇṇatti*), it should be explained by way of the transgression of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) designated for the door of body.

Right bodily conduct to be practiced should be explained by way of the abstinence from killing living beings and so forth, as well as by the non-transgression of the training rules designated for the door of body.

Wrong verbal conduct not to be practiced should be explained by way of verbal misconduct such as false speech and so forth, as well as by the transgression of the training rules designated for the door of speech.

And it should be explained as follows. Right conduct of speech (*vacī-samācāra*) should be explained by means of abstaining from false speech and so forth, as well as by non-transgression of the training rules prescribed for the door of speech.
As for seeking (*pariyeṣaṇā*), it refers exclusively to seeking by means of body and speech.

Although this is already included by the inclusion of right conduct of body and speech, since that which is called the "virtue consisting of the eight factors of livelihood" arises only in these two doors and not in the air, [the term "seeking"] is used here for the purpose of showing the virtue of the eightfold livelihood.
They are spoken of separately. Therein, the search for what is not to be cultivated should be explained by means of the ignoble search;
the search for what is to be cultivated, by means of the noble search. For this has been said: "Monks, there are these two searches: the ignoble search and the noble search. Which..."
And what, monks, is the ignoble search? Here, monks, someone who is himself subject to birth seeks what is likewise subject to birth;
being himself subject to aging, subject to sickness, subject to death, subject to sorrow, and subject to defilement, he seeks what is likewise subject to defilement.
And what, monks, do you say is subject to birth? Wife and children, monks, are subject to birth; male and female slaves are subject to birth;
goats and sheep are subject to birth; chickens and pigs are subject to birth; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to birth;
gold and silver are subject to birth. These acquisitions, monks, are subject to birth; herein this—
Attached, infatuated, and clinging, being himself subject to birth, he seeks out what is subject to birth.
And what, monks, do you call subject to aging? Wife and children, monks, are subject to aging... [as before] ...he seeks out what is subject to aging.
And what, monks, do you call subject to sickness? Wife and children, monks, are subject to sickness.
Male and female slaves subject to illness; goats and sheep; chickens and pigs; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares subject to illness.
These acquisitions, monks, are subject to illness; being himself subject to illness, one becomes attached, infatuated, and obsessed with them, and seeks only what is subject to illness.
"And what, monks, do you say is subject to death? Wife and children, monks, are subject to death... [and so on] ...he seeks only that which is subject to death.
And what, monks, do you say is subject to sorrow? Wife and children... [and so on] ...he seeks only that which is subject to sorrow.
And what, monks, do you say is subject to defilement?... [and so on] ...gold and silver are subject to defilement."
“Monks, these acquisitions (upadhī) are subject to defilement; herein this person is bound, infatuated, and obsessed.
Being himself subject to defilement, he seeks only that which is subject to defilement. This, monks, is the ignoble search.

Furthermore, it should be understood that all improper seeking (anesanā)—whether it occurs in five ways by means of hypocrisy and so forth, in six ways by means of improper resort, or in twenty-one ways by means of medical practice and so forth—is indeed the ignoble search.

“And what, bhikkhus, is the noble search? Here, bhikkhus, someone being himself subject to birth, having understood the danger in what is subject to birth, seeks the unborn, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna;

being himself subject to aging, to illness, to death, to sorrow, and to defilement, having understood the danger in what is subject to defilement, [he seeks the undefiled, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna].”
Having understood this, one seeks the unsurpassed security from bondage, Nibbāna, which is undefiled. This is called the noble search (*ariyā pariyesanā*).

Furthermore, it should be understood that the noble search also includes seeking by means of right livelihood through alms-gathering, having abandoned the five kinds of hypocrisy and the like, the six improper resorts, and the twenty-one modes of wrong search.

And herein, whatever has been stated as "not to be cultivated" refers to the time prior [to the path], starting from the time when one gathers the requisites, makes the preparations, and goes forth for the commission of killing living beings and so forth.

From that point on, it must certainly not be cultivated. The other [type of conduct] should be cultivated from the very beginning; even if one is unable to do so physically, one should at least arouse the intention to do so.
Furthermore, the bodily conduct of those such as Devadatta who strive for the sake of causing a schism in the Saṅgha and so forth must not be cultivated;
rather, that which proceeds by going to pay homage to the Three Jewels two or three times a day and so forth [should be cultivated].
One should cultivate bodily conduct such as that of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, the General of the Dhamma, and others.
One should not cultivate verbal conduct like that of Devadatta and others, who broke their word by means of sending archers and the like;

rather, one should cultivate verbal conduct such as that of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, the General of the Dhamma, and others, which proceeds through the praising of the virtues of the Three Jewels and similar acts.
It should be cultivated. The pursuit of those such as Devadatta and others, who pursue the ignoble search, should not be cultivated;
rather, the pursuit of those such as the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, and the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, who pursue only the noble search, should be cultivated.
"Practicing thus" means having abandoned the bodily and verbal conduct and the pursuit that should not be cultivated, [one practices] those [conducts and pursuits] that should be cultivated.
"O Lord of Devas, a bhikkhu who is practicing for the sake of fulfillment is said to be practicing for the sake of restraint by the Pātimokkha, which is the supreme and foremost restraint of virtue.
Thus the Blessed One spoke of the preliminary practice leading up to the attainment of one whose taints are destroyed.
The Exposition of Restraint of the Faculties.
365. In the second question, "for the restraint of the faculties" (*indriyasaṃvarāya*) means for the closing of the faculties, that is, for guardedness of the doors and restrainedness of the doors.

In its answer, however, the passage beginning with "even a form cognizable by the eye" is stated for the purpose of demonstrating the restraint of the faculties by way of forms and so forth that are to be cultivated.
Therein, "it has been said thus" refers to what was heard in the preceding answers to the questions on mental joy (*somanassa*) and so forth; by this [statement] as well—

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, Sakka, Lord of the Devas, having gained eloquence with the thought, "I must become such as this," addressed the Blessed One with these words beginning, "Indeed, venerable sir, for this...
The Blessed One gave him the opportunity and remained silent; for even one who desires to speak may be unable to accomplish the purpose. To accomplish the purpose...
If one were capable but did not wish to speak, the Blessed One would not grant him the opportunity;
however, because this person both wished to speak and was capable of accomplishing the purpose, the Blessed One granted him the opportunity.
In that regard, regarding the passage beginning with "such as this should not be cultivated," the summary is as follows: whatever form, when seen, gives rise to lust and so forth—
The meaning is that whatever, when seen, gives rise to lust and so forth, should not be cultivated, should not be looked at, and should not be gazed upon.

However, that which, when seen, causes the perception of foulness (*asubhasaññā*) to become established, or inspires confidence (*pasāda*), or results in the attainment of the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*), should be cultivated.

Furthermore, regarding a sound that one hears—whether it be a syllable of the mind or a mental expression—if lust and other defilements arise from hearing such a sound, [that sound] is likewise [to be avoided].
It should not be cultivated. However, even the singing of a slave-girl carrying a water-jar—if by hearing it, confidence arises or revulsion is established—such a sound should be cultivated.

As for a scent, if by smelling it, lust and other defilements arise, such a scent should not be cultivated. But if by smelling a scent, there is the attainment of the perception of foulness and so forth, such a scent should be cultivated.

Any taste from which lust and other defilements arise upon tasting it should not be indulged in. However, that taste from which the perception of repulsiveness toward food arises upon tasting it, and by virtue of which one is able—relying on physical strength—to enter the plane of the Noble Ones (ariyabhūmi) as a result of having tasted it, may be consumed;
just as in the case of the novice Sīva, the nephew of the Elder Mahāsīva, while he was actually eating.
Either the destruction of the defilements occurs, or such a flavor should be cultivated.
Whatever tangible object, when touched, gives rise to lust and other such states, such a tangible object should not be cultivated.

However, whatever tangible object, when touched, results—as in the case of the Elder Sāriputta and others—in both the destruction of the taints and the firm exertion of energy, [that should be cultivated].
And future generations are assisted by following one's example; such is the tangible object (phoṭṭhabba) that should be cultivated.
It is said that the Elder Sāriputta did not stretch out his back upon a bed for thirty years. Likewise the Elder Mahāmoggallāna.
The Elder Mahākassapa did not stretch out his back upon a bed for one hundred and twenty years. The Elder Anuruddha [did so] for fifty...
As for the years: the Elder Bhaddiya [lived] thirty years; the Elder Soṇa, eighteen years;
the Elder Raṭṭhapāla, twelve; the Elder Ānanda, fifteen; the Elder Rāhula, twelve; the Elder Bākula, eighty years;
and the Elder Nāḷaka did not stretch out his back upon a bed until his final nibbāna.
Those mental phenomena which, when one attends to them, give rise to lust and so forth;
or by way of covetousness and the like, such as the thought, "O, may what belongs to others—their wealth and requisites—be mine," and so on;

such phenomena are not to be cultivated. However, those [phenomena] that arise through the mode of loving-kindness and so forth, such as "May all beings be free from enmity," or those belonging to the three [types of persons]...
Such things are the qualities of the elders that should be cultivated. It is said that on the day of entering the rains retreat, three elders made an agreement:
"Unwholesome thoughts, such as thoughts of sensual desire, must not be entertained.
Then, on the day of the Pavāraṇā ceremony, the senior of the Saṅgha asked the junior of the Saṅgha: "Friend, during these three months, how much scope was given for the mind to run about?"
“No, venerable sir, I did not allow him to run outside the boundary of my cell. He asked a second time: “What about you, friend?
“I did not allow him, venerable sir, to run outside the dwelling-house. Then they both asked the elder:
“But what about you, venerable sir? “I did not allow him, friends, to run outside the five aggregates that constitute my own internal self.”
“Venerable sir, you have done what is difficult. Such a state cognizable by the mind should be cultivated.

366. “Those of one-sided doctrine” (*ekantavādā*): their doctrine has only one end, not a doctrine that has gone in two directions; thus they are "those of one-sided doctrine," for they speak of only one thing—this is what he asks.

“Of one-sided virtue” (*ekantasīlā*): those of uniform conduct. “Of one-sided desire” (*ekantachandā*): those of a single conviction. “Of one-sided attachment” (*ekantaajjhosānā*): those of a single final conclusion.
"O Lord of Devas, this world indeed consists of many elements and various elements; O Lord of Devas, this world has many inclinations and various inclinations.
When one wishes to go, another wishes to stay. When one wishes to stay, another wishes to lie down.
Two beings with the same inclination are rare to find. In this world of many elements and various elements, that which..."
Whatever element (*dhātu*) and whatever inclination (*ajjhāsaya*) beings adhere to and grasp, that alone it is.
"With persistence and misapprehension" means with both force and misapprehension. "Adhering, they express" means having firmly grasped, they express, speak, illuminate, and praise.
"This alone is truth, all else is false" means: "Only our own word is the truth."
"The speech of others is vain, empty, and purposeless.
"The ultimate goal" (*accantaniṭṭhā*): "End" (*anto*) is said to mean destruction; those whose goal has transcended the end are "those for whom the goal is ultimate.
That which is their goal—that supreme consolation, Nibbāna—is called "permanent" because it transcends the destruction of all things.
*Yogakkhema* is a name for Nibbāna itself; those for whom security from the bonds (*yogakkhema*) is ultimate are *accantayogakkhemī*.
They practice the noble path, which is *brahma* in the sense of being supreme, thus they are *brahmacārī*. Those who practice the holy life for the sake of the ultimate goal are *accantabrahmacārī*.
*Pariyosāna* is also a name for Nibbāna; those for whom the ultimate end (*pariyosāna*) is absolute are *accantapariyosānā*.
"Released by the destruction of craving" (*taṇhāsaṅkhayavimuttā*): "the destruction of craving" (*taṇhāsaṅkhaya*) refers to both the Path and Nibbāna.

The Path is called the "destruction of craving" because it destroys—that is, eliminates—craving. Nibbāna is called the "destruction of craving" because, by resorting to it, craving is destroyed and eliminated.
Thus, they are "released by the Path which is the destruction of craving," meaning they are released and fully intent upon Nibbāna, the destruction of craving.
They are liberated through the destruction of craving.
At this point, fourteen great questions have been answered by the Blessed One. As for what are called the "fourteen great questions": envy and stinginess constitute one question;
the pleasant and the unpleasant, one; desire, one; thought, one; conceptual proliferation, one; and joy, one.
Mental distress is one; equanimity is one; bodily conduct is one; verbal conduct is one; pursuit is one;
restraint of the faculties is one; the manifold elements are one; and the ultimate goal is one.
(367) "Agitation" (*ejā*) is said to be craving in the sense of shaking. It is a disease in the sense of oppression, and it is a corruption in the sense of internal defilement.
A tumor (*gaṇḍa*); an arrow (*salla*) in the sense of having entered [into the body].

Therefore, "this person": because *ejā* (the impulse) drags a person here and there for the sake of rebirth in accordance with the karma performed by itself, therefore this person encounters high and low states according to those various existences (*bhava*). He is high in the Brahma-world; he is low in the deva-world. In the deva-world...
High in the world of humans, low in the world of humans; high in the world of humans, low in the states of misery (apāya).
"Of whom, venerable sir" (*yesāhaṃ, bhante*) means "of whom, venerable sir. Here, however, by way of euphonic combination (*sandhi*), it becomes "yesāhaṃ.

"As I have heard and as I have mastered" (*yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ*) means just as I have both heard and learned it, so [I speak]. "I teach the Dhamma" means I teach the Dhamma consisting of the seven bases of conduct (*sattavatapada*).
"And I am not one of them" means that I do not become a disciple of theirs. By saying "But I, venerable sir," and so forth, he makes known his own status as a stream-enterer.
This concludes the commentary on the discourse regarding the attainment of joy.
"Attainment of the Vedas" means the attainment of satisfaction. "The battle of the devas and asuras" is the conflict between the devas and the asuras.
"Arrayed for combat" means they have come together, as if reaching the state of striking forehead against forehead.
It is said that at times there is a battle between them on the surface of the great ocean; however, in that case, there is no mutual slaughter by means of cutting, piercing, and so forth.
There is no [real] victory or defeat there, like a fight between wooden rams; sometimes the devas win, sometimes the asuras.
Regarding that battle in which the devas defeated the asuras so that they would not return again, he said, "But in that, venerable sir," and so forth.
"Both of these" means both of these. Both kinds of nutritive essence (*ojā*) are here.
Thinking, "In the world of the gods, the gods themselves will enjoy [these things]," as he reflected thus, a powerful rapture and joy arose within him.

"With the scope of the rod" (*sadaṇḍāvacara*) means *sadaṇḍāvacaraka*; by the inclusion of the "rod," it is shown that it was accompanied by the taking up of weapons—that is, it was not one in whom the rod and weapons had been laid down.
"For the sake of absolute disenchantment" means for the purpose of becoming utterly disenchanted with the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
All of this has already been stated in the Mahāgovinda Sutta.
369. *Pavedesi* means he spoke and explained. *Idheva* means in this very place.
*Devabhūtassa me sato* means while I was existing as a deva. *Punarāyu ca me laddho* means that by the ripening of another kamma, life was obtained by me once again.
By this, he reveals both his state of passing away and his state of rebirth.
"Celestial bodies" means celestial self-identities. "Having abandoned a non-human lifespan" means having relinquished a divine lifespan.
"Unconfused, I shall enter the womb"—this is because his destination is certain; thus, being unconfused. "Where my mind delights"—wherever my mind [finds pleasure].
"‘I shall delight; I shall enter the womb right there in a kṣatriya family or the like’—this indicates that seven times he will [be reborn] among gods and humans.
‘I shall dwell according to the rule’:
even though reborn among humans, because he is incapable of taking the life of his mother and so forth, the meaning is that he will dwell by way of the rule, the cause, and the even."
"If there will be full enlightenment" refers to the path of the once-returner; it indicates: "If I shall become a once-returner.
"I will dwell as one who has known" means: "I will dwell having the desire to know what is not yet known. "That itself will be my end" means:
"That very [state] will be my end in the world of humans."
"I shall become a god again, supreme in the world of the gods"—this means he says, "I shall become Sakka, the lord of the gods, supreme once more in the world of the gods.
"While the final [existence] is occurring" means while the final birth is taking place.
"That will be my dwelling"—referring to those Akaniṭṭha gods who are foremost in both lifespan and wisdom, and who are more excellent than all other gods; that will be my dwelling at the end.

It will come to pass. It is said that he, having passed away from that state of Sakka, because he had attained the path of the non-returner (*anāgāmimagga*) in that existence, will become one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha heaven;
being reborn in the Aviha and other realms, he will finally be reborn in Akaniṭṭha.
It was with reference to him that this was said. It is said that he will dwell in the Aviha heaven for a thousand eons, and in the Atappa heaven...

For two thousand eons [in the Ābhassara realm], four thousand eons in the Sudassa realms, eight in the Sudassī realms, and sixteen in the Akaniṭṭha realm—thus he will experience a lifespan of thirty-one thousand eons as a Brahmā.

Indeed, these three—the Sakka king of gods, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, and the great female lay follower Visākhā—possess an identical measure of life; they are beings who delight in the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa).
Indeed, there are none who share in such happiness equal to these.
(370) "One whose intention is unfulfilled" means one whose desires are not yet completed. "Whom I consider to be ascetics" refers to those whom I consider to be ascetics living in seclusion.
"Accomplishment" means the bringing about [of a goal]. "Failure" means the non-accomplishing. "They do not accomplish" means they are unable to speak after having accomplished [the goal].
"Ādiccabandhu" (Kinsman of the Sun): The sun is of the Gotama clan, and the Blessed One is also of the Gotama clan;
therefore he spoke thus. "What we were doing": what we previously did as an act of homage to Brahmā. "Equal with the devas": together with the devas;
this shows that from now on, henceforth, there is no longer for us the performance of homage to Brahmā. "We shall do it ourselves": we shall perform the homage ourselves.
371. "Having struck" (*parāmasitvā*): with a joyful heart, as if striking his companion's hand with his own hand, he struck the earth;
or, having struck it for the sake of making it a witness, [he thought], "Just as you are immovable, so am I, O Blessed One.
"Questions asked" (*ajjhiṭṭha-pañhā*): questions requested, questions desired. The rest is everywhere self-evident.
Thus ends the commentary on the Sakkapañha Sutta in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya. 9.
The commentary on the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta.
Commentary on the Section on the Summary (Uddesavāra-kathāvaṇṇanā) 373.
“Thus have I heard” refers to the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta. Herein, this is the commentary on the words not previously explained:

For what reason did the Blessed One speak this discourse, beginning with “This, monks, is the one-way path”? It was because the inhabitants of the kingdom of Kuru possessed the capacity to receive a profound teaching.
It is said that the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen dwelling in the kingdom of Kuru,
because that country was endowed with favorable conditions such as the climate, were always healthy in body and clear in mind through the enjoyment of those suitable climatic conditions.
Being thus supported by the health of their minds and bodies, they possessed the strength of wisdom capable of receiving profound discourse.

Thus it was. Therefore, perceiving their capacity to receive this profound teaching, the Blessed One assigned a meditation subject leading to Arahantship in twenty-one instances and spoke this *Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta* of profound meaning.
For just as a man, having obtained a golden casket, might place various flowers within it, [so did he bestow this teaching upon them].
Or, just as one might obtain a golden casket and place the seven precious gems within it, so too did the Blessed One, having obtained the assembly of those dwelling in the kingdom of Kuru,
teach the profound instruction. For this very reason, there are other profound meanings here in the Dīgha Nikāya,
such as the Mahānidāna Sutta, and in the Majjhima Nikāya, the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta, the Sāropama Sutta, the Rukkhopama Sutta, the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta, and the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta.
He also taught other discourses concerning the "conducive to the imperturbable.
Furthermore, in that region, the four assemblies naturally dwelt devoted to the practice of the development of the foundations of mindfulness;
even the slaves, laborers, and attendants spoke only of topics connected with the foundations of mindfulness.
Even at places such as water-crossings, bathing-ghats, or spinning-places, useless talk does not arise.
If some woman, when asked, "Mother, which meditation on the foundations of mindfulness do you attend to?
should reply, "None at all," they reproach her, saying, "Shame on your life! Though you live, you are like one who is dead. Then...
Having admonished him, saying, "Do not do this again," they cause him to learn one of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).

But to her who says, "I am attending to such-and-such a foundation of mindfulness," they give their approval, saying, "Excellent, excellent! and [say]: "Your life is well-lived; you have indeed attained human birth; for your sake..."

They praise [the Buddha] with such words as, “The Perfectly Enlightened One has appeared. Not only those of human birth, but even animals dwelling in dependence upon them, are possessed of attention directed toward the foundations of mindfulness.
In this regard, there is this story: it is said that a certain actor was wandering about teaching a young parrot. He [entered] the nunnery...
Having lived there in dependence [upon the community], he departed at the time of leaving, forgetting his young parrot chick. The female novices took him and cared for him;
they gave him the name Buddharakkhita. One day, seeing him sitting before her, the Great Elder said, "Buddharakkhita.
"What is it, Noble Lady? he asked. "Do you have any mental application toward meditation? she asked.
“There is not, venerable sir. “Friend, it is not fitting for one living in the presence of those who have gone forth to be negligent of one’s own person;
some degree of mental attention must be maintained. As for you, you will not be able to attend to anything else, so repeat the recitation:
‘Bone, bone. Abiding by the elder nun’s instruction, he went about repeating the recitation: “Bone, bone.”
One day, early in the morning, as he was sitting on the top of an archway basking in the morning sun, a bird seized him with its talons.
He cried out, "Kiri kiri! Hearing this, the novice nuns exclaimed, "Venerable Sir, Buddharakkhita has been caught by a bird!
Let us release him! Taking up clods of earth and other objects, they pursued him and freed him. Having brought him back, they stood before him.
The Elder Nun asked, "Buddharakkhita, when you were seized by the bird, what were you thinking? "Venerable Lady, I was not thinking of anything else. I was only thinking:
'A heap of bones is taking up another heap of bones and going; at which spot will it scatter?
Thus, Venerable Lady, I was thinking only of the heap of bones. "Excellent, excellent, Buddharakkhita!"
"In the future, it will be a condition for the destruction of existence for you. Thus, even those animals there were possessed of mindfulness and mental attention.
Therefore, the Blessed One, generating in them precisely the wisdom of the foundations of mindfulness, spoke this sutta.
In that context, "the single way" means the one path. For regarding the path—
“Path, road, way, track, straight course, journey, vehicle;
boat, ford, bridge, raft, and ferry-crossing”—these are its many names.
Here, however, it is spoken of by the name of "going" (*ayana*); therefore, "this, monks, is the one-way path."
In this context, the meaning should be understood as follows: "Monks, this is a single path; this path does not branch into two ways.
Alternatively, it is called *ekāyana* because it is to be traveled by one (*ekena ayitabbo*). "By one" means by one who has abandoned the company of crowds and whose mind is secluded and withdrawn.
It is "to be traveled" (*ayitabbo*), meaning it is to be practiced; or, it is a "path" (*ayano*) because one goes by means of it—namely, those going from saṃsāra to Nibbāna.
The meaning is as follows: *ekāyana* means the way (*ayana*) of one (*eka*). "Of one" means of the best (*seṭṭha*). And the Blessed One is the best of all beings;
therefore, it is said "of the Blessed One. For although others also travel by that way, even so, it is the way of the Blessed One alone, because it was brought forth by him.
As it is said: "For that Blessed One, brahmin, [is the one who] of the unarisen path..."
“...the arouser,” and so forth. Or, it is called *ayana* because it goes; the meaning is that it proceeds or continues. It is “the single way” (*ekāyana*) because it is a way in one [place];
what is meant is that it proceeds only within this very Dhamma and Vinaya, and not elsewhere.
As it was said: “In this Dhamma and Vinaya, Subhadda, the Noble Eightfold Path is found. This refers specifically to the distinction in the teaching.
In meaning, however, it is one and the same. Furthermore, it is called "the single path" (*ekāyana*) because it goes to one thing.
Although it proceeds by way of various methods of cultivation during its earlier stages, it is said that in its later stage it goes to only one thing: Nibbāna. As Brahmā Sahampati said:
"The single path for seeing the end of birth."
One who is compassionate for their welfare understands the path;
by this path, those of old have crossed over,
and those who will cross and those who are crossing the flood do so.
However, some, following the method of the verse "They do not go to the further shore twice," claim that it is called "the single path" because one goes to Nibbāna only once;
this is not tenable. For regarding this meaning, the phrasing ought to have been "going once" (*sakiṃ ayana*).
But if the meaning were "its going is one" or "its course and proceeding are one," then...
If one were to apply [the term] in this way, the phrasing would be consistent, but the meaning does not fit in either case. Why?

Because here it is the preliminary path (*pubbabhāgamagga*) that is intended. For it is the preliminary path of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), which proceeds with the body and so forth as its four objects, that is intended here, and not the supramundane (*lokuttara*) path.
Moreover, that [preliminary path] comes many times, and its coming occurs repeatedly.

Furthermore, in the past, there was indeed a discussion among the great elders regarding this point. The Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷanāga said, "It is the path of the preliminary stage of the foundations of mindfulness.
But his teacher, the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷasumana, said, "It is the mixed path. "Venerable sir, is it the preliminary stage? "It is mixed, friend.
When the teacher spoke thus again and again, [the other] did not oppose him and remained silent. [Thus ends] the question.
They rose up without having reached a decision. Then, as the teacher-thera was going to the bathing place, he thought:
"I have taught the mixed path, yet Cūḷanāga speaks of it as the 'pubbabhāga-magga' (the preliminary path).
What, indeed, is the certainty here? While turning over the Sutta from the beginning, he [recalled]: "Bhikkhus, whoever, in this way..."
He observed at this point: "One should develop [this] for seven years. There is no such thing as a supramundane path that, having arisen, persists for seven years;

the mixed path spoken of by me is not being obtained. Realizing that only the preliminary path seen by Cūḷanāga is being obtained, he went when the Dhamma was being proclaimed on the eighth day, when the Saṅgha had gathered.
It is said that the ancient elders were fond of hearing the Dhamma; as soon as they heard the sound, they would rush forward all at once, each crying out, "I first! I first!
On that particular day, it was the turn of the elder Cūḷanāga.
Having sat upon the Dhamma-seat and taken up the fan, when the preliminary verses had been recited, this thought occurred to the elder as he stood behind the seat:
—“I will not speak after sitting down in private. For the ancient elders were free from envy.
They did not wander about merely carrying their own likes like a load of sugarcane; rather, they took up what was reasoned and rejected what was unreasoned.
Therefore, the elder said, “Friend Cūḷanāga. He, like the voice of a teacher, established the Dhamma.
“What is it, venerable sir? he asked. “Friend Cūḷanāga, the mixed path spoken of by me is not found;
only the preliminary stage of the foundation of mindfulness spoken of by you is found. The Elder thought:
“Our teacher is one who has mastered all the scriptures, a master of the Three Piṭakas, and a Buddha in learning; yet even such a bhikkhu as this is confused by this question. In the future, my...”
Thinking, "My brothers will stir up this question; therefore, having grasped the Sutta, I shall make this question immovable," [he quotes] from the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*:
"The path of the single way is said to be the preliminary path of the foundations of mindfulness.
Of paths, the Eightfold is best; of truths, the Four Noble Truths are supreme.
Dispassion is the best of all things, and the Visionary is the best among bipeds.
This alone is the path, and no other, for the purification of vision;
therefore, you should practice this, which crushes the army of Māra.
"By practicing this, you will make an end of suffering"—having cited this sutta, he established [the definition].
In what sense is it called the "path"? It is the path in the sense of leading to Nibbāna and in the sense of being sought by those who desire Nibbāna.

"For the purification of beings" means for the sake of purifying those beings whose minds are defiled by stains such as lust and so forth, and by secondary corruptions such as covetousness and improper greed.
For indeed, by this very path, after four incalculable eons plus one hundred thousand aeons from now,
in the very next aeon, there arose [Buddhas] named Taṇhaṅkara, Medhaṅkara, Saraṇaṅkara, and Dīpaṅkara.

Beginning with the Buddha and ending with the Sage of the Śākyas, there have been many perfectly enlightened Buddhas (*sammāsambuddha*), hundreds of individual Buddhas (*paccekabuddha*), and countless noble disciples (*ariyasāvaka*).

All these beings, having washed away the impurities of the mind, attained supreme purity. However, by way of the impurities of form (*rūpa*), there is no such designation of defilement or purification. For it is thus:
“By a defiled form, young men are defiled;
when form is pure, they are purified—this was not declared by the Great Seer.
By a defiled mind, young men are defiled;”
“When the mind is pure, they are purified,” so it was said by the Great Seer.

As he said: “Bhikkhus, through the defilement of the mind beings are defiled; through the purification of the mind they are purified. And that purification of the mind occurs by means of this path of the foundations of mindfulness. Therefore he said, “for the purification of beings.
“For the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation” means for the surmounting—that is, for the abandoning—of sorrow and lamentation.

This is the purpose; for this path, when developed, leads to the transcendence of sorrow, as in the case of the Great Minister Santati and others, and to the transcendence of lamentation, as in the case of Paṭācārā and others. Therefore he said: "for the transcendence of sorrow and lamentation.
For although the Great Minister Santati—
“Purify that which was in the past; let there be nothing for you in the future;
if you do not grasp at anything in the middle, you will wander in peace.
Upon hearing this verse, she attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Paṭācārā—
“Sons are no refuge, nor father, nor kinsmen;
for one seized by the End-maker, there is no refuge among relatives.

Having heard this verse, she was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*). However, because [she had not yet attained realization] regarding any of the body, feelings, mind, or phenomena...
There is no such thing as meditation without taking hold of the Dhamma; therefore, it should be understood that they too have transcended sorrow and lamentation by this very path.
"For the subsiding of pain and dejection" means for the subsiding—meaning the cessation—of these two: bodily pain and mental dejection.
For this path, when developed, [leads to the goal] just as it did for the Elder Tiṣya and others.
It leads to the subsiding of suffering and, like that of Sakkā and others, to the subsiding of mental distress.

Herein, this is the clarification of the meaning: It is said that in Sāvatthī, a son of a householder named Tissa, having renounced forty crores of gold, went forth and dwelt in a forest remote from villages. His younger brother’s wife said, "Go,..."
"Do not deprive him of life," he said, and dispatched five hundred bandits. They went, surrounded the Elder, and sat down.
The Elder asked, "Why have you come, lay followers? "To deprive him of life. "Lay followers, take me as your surety;
grant him his life for this one night. "Who is your surety, ascetic, in this matter?"
"Will it happen? The Elder took a large stone, broke both his thigh bones, and said, "It is sufficient, lay follower;
I am your guarantor. They departed and, having made a fire at the head of the walking path, lay down.
As the Elder suppressed the pain and reflected upon his virtue, rapture and gladness arose in him, supported by his perfectly pure virtue.
Then, gradually increasing his insight and practicing the duties of a recluse throughout the three watches of the night,
he attained Arahantship at the rising of the dawn and uttered this inspired utterance:
“Having split both my feet, I shall make you recognize me.”
“I am ashamed, I am humiliated by death with its lustful attachment.
Having reflected thus, I saw things as they truly are;
when the dawn had arrived, I attained arahantship.”

Furthermore, thirty other bhikkhus, having received a meditation subject from the Blessed One and entered the rains retreat in a forest dwelling, lived there after saying, "Friends, the duty of a recluse must be performed throughout the three watches of the night; one must not come into the presence of another.
While they were performing their duty as recluses and were nodding off at dawn, a tiger—
Having arrived, he went along seizing one bhikkhu at a time. Not a single one uttered even the words, "A tiger has seized me!
Thus, when five or ten bhikkhus had been devoured, on the Uposatha day they asked, "Friends, where are the others?
Having learned the truth, they thought, "Now we too shall be called 'seized' by what has already been seized," and so they lived on. Then, [he seized] another...
A tiger seized the young bhikkhu in the same manner as before. He cried out, "A tiger, Bhante!
The bhikkhus, taking up walking sticks and torches, pursued it, thinking, "We shall release him.
The tiger climbed onto a place where the bhikkhus could not go—a precipitous cliff—and began to devour the bhikkhu, starting from his big toe. The others also said, "Now, good man..."
"There is nothing for us to do; it is in such circumstances that the distinction among monks becomes manifest," they said.

While lying within the tiger's mouth, he suppressed that painful sensation and developed insight (*vipassanā*); at the moment the tiger had eaten him down to his ankles, he became a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*);
at the moment it had eaten him down to his knees, he became a once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*); and at the moment it had reached his navel...
Having become a non-returner at the time of eating, and having attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) even before the heart-flesh was consumed,
he uttered this inspired utterance:
“Virtuous, perfected in vows, wise and well-concentrated;”
Having succumbed to negligence for a moment, my mind was seized by a tiger.
Having been caught in a cage and placed upon a stone, [I thought:
"Let the tiger eat me as it pleases, for the sake of my bones and my sinews."
"I shall exhaust the defilements; I shall attain liberation.
Furthermore, there was another elder named Pītamalla, who, in his time as a householder, had traveled to Tambapaṇṇidīpa carrying a banner across the three kingdoms.
Having seen the king and received the king's favor, one day, while passing through the door of a straw-mat shop, he—
“Bhikkhus, form is not yours; abandon it. When it is abandoned by you, it will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.
Upon hearing these words of “not yours,” he thought, “So, indeed, form is not mine, nor is feeling.
Taking that very [teaching] as his goad, he went out, proceeded to the Mahāvihāra, and requested the going-forth.
Having gone forth and received full ordination, and having mastered the two Matikas, he took thirty bhikkhus and went to the courtyard of Gabalavāliya, where he practiced the duties of a recluse.
As his feet were failing him, he walked by means of his knees.
During the night, a deer-hunter, thinking him to be a deer, struck him. The spear passed right through him; he [took] that spear...
Having had the openings of his wounds closed up with rolls of grass, he had himself seated upon a stone slab;
and having requested a secluded place and developed insight, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Then, making a coughing sound to inform the monks who had come, he explained it to them and uttered this inspired utterance (udāna):
“This was spoken by the Best of Buddhas, the Teacher supreme over all the world:
‘This form is not yours; you should abandon it, O monks.
Truly, conditioned phenomena are impermanent, subject to arising and passing away.’”
“Having arisen, they cease; their subsiding is blissful.
Thus, first of all, this path leads to the cessation of suffering, as in the case of the Elder Tissa and others.
But Sakka, the Lord of the Devas, having seen five kinds of portents for himself and being terrified by the fear of death, [approached the Buddha].
Filled with dejection, he approached the Blessed One and asked a question.

At the conclusion of the answer to his question on equanimity, he, together with eighty thousand deities, was established in the fruit of stream-entry. His rebirth there returned once more to its natural state.
The young deity Subrahmā also enjoyed the splendors of heaven, surrounded by a retinue of a thousand nymphs. Therein, five hundred...
The nymphs, while plucking flowers from the tree, fell down and were reborn in hell.
Observing, "Why are these taking so long?", he perceived that they had been reborn in hell. Then, examining, "How long is my own lifespan?", he understood that his life was exhausted;
seeing that he too would fall and be reborn in that very same hell, he became terrified.
Being overcome with extreme dejection, [he thought], "Only the Teacher will dispel this dejection of mine, and no one else.
Taking the remaining five hundred celestial nymphs with him, he approached the Blessed One and asked this question:
"This mind is constantly terrified; the intellect is constantly agitated."
"When difficulties have not yet arisen, and when they have already appeared—
if there is anyone who is undaunted, tell me of him when you are asked.
Then the Blessed One said to him:
“I see no safety for living beings except through awakening, except through restraint of the sense faculties, and except through the relinquishing of everything.
At the conclusion of this teaching, together with five hundred celestial nymphs, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry, and [he attained] that excellence.

"Having made it stable, he went indeed to the world of the gods. Thus, it should be understood that when this path is developed, it leads to the subsiding of mental distress, just as it did for Sakka and others.
"For the attainment of the method" (*ñāyassa adhigamāya*): "method" (*ñāya*) refers to the Noble Eightfold Path; it is for the sake of its attainment, for its reaching.
This has been said. For this mundane path of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), cultivated in the prior stage, leads to the attainment of the supramundane path.
Therefore he said, "for the attainment of the method" (ñāyassa adhigamāya).

"For the realization of Nibbāna" means for the realization of the Deathless, which has received the name "Nibbāna" because it is devoid of the craving-furnace, [that is,] for its direct personal experience.
This has been stated. For this path, when cultivated, accomplishes the realization of Nibbāna in due course. Therefore he said, "for the realization of Nibbāna.
In that context, although the overcoming of sorrow and so forth are established by implication when it is said "for the purification of beings," [they are nonetheless mentioned].
However, with the exception of those skilled in the application of the Dispensation (*sāsana-yutti*), these are not evident to others;
nor does the Blessed One first make people skilled in the application of the Dispensation and only afterwards teach the Dhamma.
Rather, he makes known each respective meaning by means of this or that very Sutta. Therefore, whatever meaning the "one-way path" (*ekāyana-magga*) establishes here, that is made manifest.
Having done so, he spoke the passage beginning with “for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation,” showing this.
Or rather, because that purification of beings which leads to the one-way path occurs through the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation;
the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation occurs through the subsiding of pain and dejection; and the subsiding of pain and dejection occurs through the attainment of the True Way (ñāya).

The attainment of the method is for the realization of Nibbāna. Therefore, showing this purpose as well, he said "for the purification of beings," and then spoke "for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation," and so forth.
Moreover, this is a praise of the one-way path. For just as the Blessed One [said]: "Bhikkhus, the Dhamma..."
“I shall teach the holy life that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with its meaning and its phrasing, entirely complete and pure;
that is to say, the six sets of six. Thus he praised the teaching of the six sets by means of eight phrases.
And just as in the teaching on the noble lineages, [he said]: “Bhikkhus, there are these four noble lineages...”

He praised it with nine terms: "It is the foremost, ancient, traditional, primal, unmixed, never before mixed, not being mixed now, not to be mixed in the future, and unrebuked by wise recluses and brahmins.
Likewise, he praised this single path leading to the purification of beings with seven terms beginning with "for the purification of beings. Why?
This was for the purpose of generating enthusiasm in those bhikkhus; for having heard this praise, those bhikkhus [would think]:
"It is said that this path destroys the four calamities—sorrow, which consists of heart-wrenching anguish; lamentation, which consists of verbal outpouring;
pain, which consists of physical unpleasantness; and grief, which consists of mental unpleasantness—and it leads to purification and the method."
Thinking, “‘Nibbāna’ brings about three distinctions,” they will become inspired and consider that this teaching on the Dhamma should be learned,
mastered, memorized, and recited, and that this path should be developed. Thus, for the sake of generating enthusiasm in those bhikkhus,
he spoke in praise of it, just as a wool merchant and others speak in praise of wool and other such goods.

For just as when a merchant of yellow blankets worth a hundred thousand pieces proclaims, “Take a blanket!”, people do not yet know which blanket it is; for even hair-blankets, wool-blankets, and the like—which are foul-smelling and rough to the touch—are still called “blankets.
But when that Gandhāraka merchant [offers] a fine, red blanket...
It is proclaimed, "It is bright, it is pleasant to touch," and then those who are capable take hold of it;
even those who are not capable desire to see it. In the same way, when it is said, "Bhikkhus, this is the one-way path," it is not yet evident which specific path is meant.
For various kinds of paths that do not lead to liberation are also called "paths. [Of beings...]

But when the passage beginning with "for the purification of beings" was spoken, [the Blessed One] spoke "for the purification of beings" and so forth while praising [this path], thinking: "When it is said that 'this path indeed destroys the four calamities and brings about the three distinctions,' those who have conceived such zeal will think:
'This teaching of the Dhamma should be learned, mastered, memorized, and recited; and this path should be developed. Thus he spoke.

And just as there is the simile of the merchant of the pale woolen blanket worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], so too should the similes of the merchant of the red Jambūnada gold water-clearing jewel, the extremely pure pearl-jewel, coral, and so forth, be brought here.
*Yadidaṃ* is a particle; its meaning is "those which are these. *Cattāro* is a delimitation by number.

By this, it indicates that there are neither fewer nor more than that, thus showing the delimitation of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*). *Satipaṭṭhānā* refers to the three foundations of mindfulness.
The object of mindfulness (*satigocara*) is also threefold: the Teacher’s transcendence of aversion and attachment toward disciples who have entered the path, as well as mindfulness itself.
For in such passages as, "Bhikkhus, I will teach you the arising and the passing away of the four foundations of mindfulness; listen to that...
And what, bhikkhus, is the arising of the body? The arising of nutriment is the arising of the body," the object of mindfulness is indeed present.
It is called "foundation of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhāna*). Likewise in such passages as: "The body is the foundation, not the mindfulness;
but mindfulness is both the foundation and the mindfulness," and so forth. Its meaning is as follows: it is a *paṭṭhāna* (foundation) because mindfulness is established (*patiṭṭhāti*) in it.

What is it that is established? Mindfulness. The foundation of mindfulness is *satipaṭṭhāna*. Alternatively, *paṭṭhāna* means a primary station (*padhānaṃ ṭhānaṃ*). It is the foundation of mindfulness.
*Satipaṭṭhāna* is like the elephant’s post or the horse’s hitching post.

In the passage, “The three foundations of mindfulness which the Noble One cultivates; by cultivating which the Noble One is worthy to instruct a community,” the Teacher’s state of having transcended aversion and attachment toward disciples who have practiced in three ways is called “foundation of mindfulness.”

It has been stated. Its meaning is as follows: it is a "foundation" (*paṭṭhāna*) because it is to be established; the meaning is that it is to be set forth. By what is it to be established? By mindfulness.

A foundation by means of mindfulness is "foundational mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhāna*). However, in such passages as, "The four foundations of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment," it is mindfulness itself that is called "foundational mindfulness. Its meaning is as follows:
It is called *paṭṭhāna* because it "stands forth" (*paṭṭhāti*). The meaning is that it stands near, plunges in, leaps forward, and spreads out as it proceeds.
