Mindfulness itself is the foundation of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*). Alternatively, it is mindfulness in the sense of remembering, and a foundation in the sense of standing forth.
Thus, it is both mindfulness and a foundation, which is why it is called the foundation of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*). This is what is intended here.

If this is so, why is the plural form used for "foundations of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhānā*)? Because of the multiplicity of mindfulness. For these mindfullnesses are many due to the diversity of their objects.
Then why is the singular form used for "the path" (*maggo*)? Because of its unity in the sense of being a path.
For all four of these mindfullnesses attain unity in the sense of being a path. For it has been said: "In what sense is it a 'path'? In the sense of going to Nibbāna."

"And because they are to be sought by those seeking Nibbāna in the sense of a path. Furthermore, these four, in the course of fulfilling their functions regarding objects such as the body and so forth, lead to Nibbāna; and from the very beginning, they are sought by those seeking Nibbāna.
Therefore, all four are called "one path. This being the case, through the sequence of the words, it remains coherent with the context.
There is an exposition such as: “Monks, I shall teach you the path that crushes the army of Māra; listen to that...
What, monks, is the path that crushes the army of Māra? It is this: the seven factors of enlightenment,” and so forth.
Just as “the crusher of Māra’s army” and “the seven factors of enlightenment” are one in meaning, here it is only the phrasing [that differs].
There is only a difference in name. Thus, "the path of the single way" and "the four foundations of mindfulness" are one in meaning;

here there is only a difference in phrasing. Therefore, because they are one in terms of being the path, the singular number is used. Because mindfulness is manifold due to the diversity of its objects, the plural number should be understood.
But why did the Blessed One teach exactly four foundations of mindfulness, neither fewer nor more? It is for the benefit of those to be trained.

For among those to be trained—who fall into two groups each according to whether they are dull or sharp, consisting of those of craving-temperament, view-temperament, those who rely on serenity, and those who rely on insight—the path of purification for one of dull craving-temperament is the gross foundation of mindfulness consisting of contemplation of the body;
for one of sharp craving-temperament, it is the subtle foundation of mindfulness consisting of contemplation of feelings. It is the same for one of view-temperament.

For one of dull faculty, the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of mind that has not reached an excessive degree of analysis is the path to purification; for one of sharp faculty, the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of mental objects that has reached an excessive degree of analysis is the path to purification.
Furthermore, for one of dull faculty who is a practitioner of serenity, the first foundation of mindfulness—whose sign is to be attained without difficulty—is the path to purification;
for one of sharp faculty, it is [the first foundation of mindfulness] with a gross object.

The second is [taught] because of its non-contradiction. For one who follows the vehicle of insight (vipassanāyānika), the third has an object that is not overly analyzed, while for one of sharp faculties, the fourth has an object that is overly analyzed. Thus, exactly four are taught, neither fewer nor more.

Alternatively, they are taught for the purpose of abandoning the perversions (vipallāsa) of beauty, pleasure, permanence, and self. For the body is indeed impure, yet it is perverted by the perversion of beauty therein.
Beings. For the purpose of abandoning that perversion by means of seeing the nature of foulness therein, the first foundation of mindfulness was taught for them.

Furthermore, although feeling and the other aggregates are grasped as pleasant, permanent, and self, feeling is actually suffering, the mind is impermanent, and mental phenomena are non-self; and it is toward these that beings are perverted by the perversions of pleasure, permanence, and self.

It should be understood that the remaining three [foundations of mindfulness] are taught for the purpose of abandoning those perversions by means of seeing the state of suffering and so forth therein;
thus, they are taught as exactly four—neither fewer nor more—for the purpose of abandoning the perversions of beauty, pleasure, permanence, and selfhood.

Furthermore, it is not only for the purpose of abandoning the perversions, but also for the purpose of abandoning the four floods (*ogha*), yokes (*yoga*), taints (*āsava*), ties (*gantha*), clingings (*upādāna*), and destinations (*gati*).

It should be understood that exactly four [foundations of mindfulness] are taught for the purpose of fully understanding the fourfold nutriment. This, first of all, is the method according to the treatise (*pakaraṇa*).

In the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), however, it is stated that there is only one foundation of mindfulness by way of its refuge and its convergence into unity, but it is fourfold by way of its objects. For just as in a city with four gates, those coming from the east...
Taking merchandise acquired in the eastern direction, those coming from the east enter the city itself through the eastern gate; likewise from the south and from the west.
Those coming from the north take merchandise acquired in the northern direction and enter the city itself through the northern gate;
it should be understood that this is exactly so. For the great city of Nibbāna is like that city.
The supramundane Eightfold Path is like a gate, and the body and so forth are like the eastern direction and so on.
Just as those coming from the east, having taken merchandise from the eastern quarter, enter the city itself through the eastern gate,
so too those coming by way of the gateway of contemplation of the body develop the fourteen-fold contemplation of the body.
By means of the Noble Path produced through the power of the development of the contemplation of the body, they all converge upon a single Nibbāna.
Just as those coming from the south, taking merchandise originating in the southern region,
enter the city itself by way of the southern gate, so too do those coming by way of the contemplation of feelings enter by means of the ninefold contemplation of feelings.
Having developed the Noble Path produced by the power of the development of the contemplation of feelings, they converge upon Nibbāna alone.
Just as those coming from the west take goods originating in the western region and enter the city through the western gate,
so too do those coming by way of the contemplation of mind enter [Nibbāna] by means of the sixteenfold contemplation of mind.
Having developed the noble path produced by the power of the development of the contemplation of mind, they all converge upon the single Nibbāna.
Just as those coming from the north take merchandise originating in the northern region and enter the city through the northern gate,
so too those coming by way of the contemplation of phenomena develop the fivefold contemplation of phenomena.
Through the Noble Path produced by the power of the development of the contemplation of phenomena (*dhammānupassanābhāvanā*), they converge upon one and the same Nibbāna. Thus,

it should be understood that although there is only one single foundation of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) by way of its refuge and its convergence into unity, it is spoken of as fourfold by way of its objects (*ārammaṇa*).
“What are the four?”—this is a question expressing a desire to speak. “Here” means in this teaching. “Bhikkhus” is an address to the persons who receive the Dhamma.

“Monks” (bhikkhū) is a designation for those persons who accomplish the practice; although others, both gods and humans, also accomplish the practice, he says “monks” because of the excellence of that practice and because it demonstrates the state of being a monk through such practice.
For among those who receive the Blessed One’s instruction, the bhikkhu is the best, because he is the fit vessel for every kind of instruction.

Therefore, because of his excellence, he is called "the bhikkhus. When he is included, the rest are indeed included, just as when a king is mentioned in reference to his processions and so forth, the rest of the retinue is implied. And whoever practices this path—
He says "a bhikkhu" both to show that one becomes a bhikkhu through practice and because one who is practicing—
whether a deva or a human— is indeed reckoned as a bhikkhu, as it is said:
"Even if adorned, if he should live in accordance with the Dhamma..."
“Peaceful, self-controlled, disciplined, and living the holy life;
having laid aside the rod toward all beings—
he is a brahmin, he is an ascetic, he is a bhikkhu.”

"Kāya" means the physical body (*rūpakāya*). For here, the physical body is intended as "body" (*kāya*) in the sense of a collection of parts and limbs, such as hair and so forth, just like a "body of elephants" or a "body of chariots. And just as it is in the sense of a collection, so too it is in the sense of the origin (*āya*) of things that are loathsome (*kucchita*).
For it is the source (*āya*) of those things that are most repulsive; thus it is a "body" (*kāya*). "Origin" (*āya*) means the place of arising. In this regard:
The meaning of the words: it comes from there, thus it is "āya" (source/origin). What comes? Defiled things such as hair and so forth. Thus, the source of defiled things is the "kāya" (body).

"Contemplating the body" (*kāyānupassī*) means one whose nature is to contemplate the body, or one who is contemplating the body. Although "in the body" (*kāye*) has already been stated, the second mention of "body" in "contemplating the body" (*kāyānupassī*) should be understood as being made for the purpose of demonstrating the defining of the object, its resolution of the mass, and its analysis as distinct from other factors.
Therefore, it is shown that there is no contemplation of feelings or of mind-objects in the body; rather, there is only contemplation of the body itself.
Thus, by demonstrating the mode of contemplating the body specifically upon the basis known as the "body," its distinctness from other modes is established.

Likewise, one does not contemplate a single phenomenon in the body apart from its various limbs and members, nor does one contemplate a woman or a man apart from the hair of the head, body hair, and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding the body here— which is comprised of a collection of primary elements (*bhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāya*)— one does not contemplate it as a single phenomenon distinct from those elements and derived matter;
rather, one contemplates it as a collection of limbs and members, like one who contemplates the parts of a chariot, or as a collection of head-hairs, body-hairs, and so forth,
like one who contemplates the components of a city, or like one who separates the layers of leaves from a plantain trunk, or like one who unbinds an empty fist.

And because one contemplates only the collection of primary and derived elements, the dismantling of the compact mass is demonstrated by seeing the physical basis designated as "body" merely as a collection of various kinds.
For here, no body, woman, man, or any other phenomenon is perceived apart from the aforementioned collection; there is only the mere collection of the phenomena already mentioned.
Nevertheless, beings form various kinds of wrong attachments. Therefore the ancients said:
"What one sees is not seen; what is seen, one does not see.
Not seeing, the deluded one is bound; being bound, he is not released."
It was stated, "for the purpose of demonstrating the resolution of the compact mass," and by the word "etcetera" (ādi), this further meaning should also be understood here.
For it is said that one is a "contemplator of the body" (kāyānupassī) with respect to this very body, and not a contemplator of other phenomena.

Just as people might contemplate water in a mirage even though no water exists there, so too [one contemplates] this very body—which is actually impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul—as being such.

The meaning is that one does not contemplate the body as being permanent, pleasant, self, or beautiful; rather, one contemplates the body precisely through the modes of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and foulness.
Alternatively, this refers to the body described later in the following manner: "Here, monks, a monk, having gone to the forest...
[and so on]... he breathes in mindful and breathes out mindful," beginning with inhalation and exhalation and ending with the collection of atoms and the bones.
And as for that which is called "body" in the *Paṭisambhidā*— namely, "here someone contemplates the earth-body as impermanent,

the water-body, the fire-body, the air-body, the hair-of-the-head-body, the hair-of-the-body-body, the skin-body, the flesh-body, the blood-body, the sinew-body, the bone-body, and the bone-marrow-body"—
because one contemplates all of that within this very body, one is "a contemplator of the body in the body."
The meaning should be understood in this way as well.

Alternatively, it means "contemplating the body" (*kāyānupassī*) because one does not contemplate anything whatsoever within the body that could be grasped as "I" or "mine," but rather contemplates each respective collection of various phenomena, such as head-hairs, body-hairs, and so forth;
thus, one is "contemplating the body" in the sense of contemplating the body defined as the collection of phenomena beginning with head-hairs.
The meaning should be understood in this way. Furthermore,

it is because of contemplating the entire body— defined as the collection of modes such as the characteristic of impermanence and so forth— in the manner taught in the *Paṭisambhidā* by the gradual sequence beginning with, “He contemplates this body as impermanent, not as permanent.”
"Contemplating the body in the body"—this meaning should also be understood in this way.

For thus, this bhikkhu who has entered upon the practice of contemplating the body in the body contemplates this body as impermanent by means of the seven contemplations beginning with the contemplation of impermanence, and not as permanent;
he contemplates it as suffering, and not as pleasure; he contemplates it as non-self...
[He views it] as not-self. He becomes disenchanted with it, does not delight in it; he becomes dispassionate toward it, does not become impassioned;
he causes its cessation. He does not cause its origination; he relinquishes it, does not grasp at it. Contemplating that [body] as impermanent, he abandons the perception of permanence;
contemplating it as suffering, he abandons the perception of pleasure; contemplating it as not-self, he abandons the perception of self; becoming disenchanted...
It should be understood that he abandons delight; becoming dispassionate, he abandons lust; causing cessation, he abandons origination; relinquishing, he abandons grasping.
"Dwells" means he conducts himself. "Ardent": one who scorches (ātāpeti) the defilements within the three realms of existence is "ardent" (ātāpī); this is a name for energy.
One who has ardor is "ardent" (*ātāpī*). "Possessed of clear comprehension" means endowed with the knowledge termed clear comprehension (*sampajañña*).

"Possessed of mindfulness" means endowed with the mindfulness that encompasses the body. Now, because one contemplates after having encompassed the object by means of mindfulness—since there is no such thing as contemplation for one devoid of mindfulness—it was said: "And mindfulness..."

“Monks, I declare this to be beneficial in all respects. Therefore, by the words “he dwells contemplating the body in the body,” the foundation of mindfulness consisting in body-contemplation has been stated.
Alternatively, because for one who lacks ardor, internal contraction acts as an obstacle;
because one who lacks clear comprehension is confused regarding the adoption of skillful means and the avoidance of unskillful means; and because one who lacks mindfulness—
He is incapable of not abandoning skillful means and of not grasping at what is not skillful means; therefore, that meditation subject does not succeed for him.
Consequently, it should be understood that the words "ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful" were spoken in order to show those qualities by whose power it succeeds.

Thus, having shown the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body and its factor of association, it is now said, "having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world," in order to show its factor of abandonment.
Therein, "having removed" means having removed by way of abandonment through substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgavinaya*) or by way of suppression (*vikkhambhanavinaya*).
"Regarding the world" means regarding that very body; for here, the body is called "the world" (*loka*) in the sense of breaking up and falling apart.

This is what is intended. However, since covetousness and dejection are not abandoned in the body alone, but are indeed abandoned in feeling and the other aggregates as well, it is therefore stated in the *Vibhaṅga*: "The five aggregates of clinging are the world.
Alternatively, this was said by way of extracting the meaning because those phenomena are reckoned as the world. As for what was said: "In this context, what is the world?"
"This very body is the world"—this is precisely the meaning here. "Having removed covetousness and dejection regarding that world"—the connection should be understood in this way.

Since, however, covetousness is included under the term "covetousness" (abhijjhā) and ill-will is included under the term "dejection" (domanassa), the abandoning of the hindrances is shown by means of demonstrating these two powerful factors comprised within the hindrances.
It should be understood that this is what is meant.
Furthermore, it should be understood specifically that by the removal of covetousness (*abhijjhā*), there is the removal of attachment rooted in bodily success;

by the removal of ill-will (*domanassa*), there is the removal of aversion rooted in bodily failure; and by the removal of covetousness, there is the removal of delight in the body, while by the removal of ill-will...

Through the cultivation of the body, the abandoning of non-delight is stated; through the removal of covetousness, the setting aside of the unreal qualities of beauty, pleasure, and so forth, regarding the body;
and through the removal of displeasure, the elimination of the real qualities of ugliness, pain, and so forth, regarding the body.
By this, the power of yoga and the capability for yoga of the practitioner are illuminated. This is the power of yoga.
For this is so: namely, that he is free from attraction and repulsion, enduring both the unpleasant and the pleasant, and is devoid of the addition of what is unreal and the removal of what is real.
Being thus free from attraction and repulsion, enduring the unpleasant and the pleasant, and neither adding the unreal nor removing the real, he is capable of yoga.

Another method: In the phrase "contemplating the body in the body," the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) is stated by way of contemplation (*anupassanā*). In the phrase "he dwells" (*viharati*), the maintenance of the body for one who possesses the meditation subject is stated by way of the dwelling mentioned there.
Furthermore, in the phrases beginning with "ardent" (*ātāpī*), right effort is indicated by ardency;
the universal meditation subject is indicated by mindfulness and clear comprehension; and the means for maintaining the meditation subject is indicated [by these qualities].

Or alternatively, it should be understood that "serenity" is obtained by way of mindfulness through the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*), while "insight" is through clear comprehension (*sampajañña*), and "the power of development" is through the removal of covetousness and dejection.
In the *Vibhaṅga*, however, regarding the term "contemplating" (*anupassī*): "What is contemplation? It is wisdom, understanding, investigation, thorough investigation..."
Investigation of phenomena is discernment, close observation, thorough examination, wisdom, skill, sagacity, discrimination, reflection, scrutiny,
vast intelligence, guidance, insight, clear comprehension, a goad, wisdom, the faculty of wisdom,
the power of wisdom, the sword of wisdom, the palace of wisdom, the light of wisdom, the radiance of wisdom, and the lamp of wisdom.
The jewel of wisdom (*paññā-ratana*)—namely, non-delusion (*amoha*), investigation of phenomena (*dhammavicaya*), and right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*)—this is called "contemplation" (*anupassanā*).
One who is endowed with this contemplation, fully endowed, approached, fully approached, attained, and possessed of it, is therefore called "one who contemplates" (*anupassī*).
"Dwells" (*viharati*) means he conducts himself, proceeds, protects, maintains, sustains, moves about, and abides; therefore, it is said "he dwells."

"Exerting himself": therein, what is exertion? That which is the arousal of mental energy, endeavor, striving, effort, diligence, perseverance, firmness, steadfastness, unrelaxed exertion, not laying down the burden, not casting off the yoke, the grasping of the burden, energy, the faculty of energy, the power of energy, and right effort—this is called exertion.
He is endowed with this ardor... [as before] ...possessed of it; therefore he is called "ardent. As for "clearly comprehending" (*sampajāna*):

therein, what is clear comprehension? It is that which is wisdom (*paññā*), understanding, investigation, thorough investigation, investigation of phenomena, discernment, close examination, comparative examination, sagacity, skill, subtlety, discrimination, reflection, scrutiny, breadth, and intelligence.

Insight is the guide, clear comprehension is the goad; it is wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the sword of wisdom, the palace of wisdom, the light of wisdom, the radiance of wisdom, the lamp of wisdom, the jewel of wisdom, non-delusion, the investigation of phenomena, and right view—this is called clear comprehension.
One who is possessed of this clear comprehension ... [as above] ... is endowed with it; therefore, it is so called.
"Clearly comprehending" (*sampajāna*): "Possessing mindfulness" (*satimā*). In this context, what is mindfulness (*sati*)?

That which is mindfulness, constant mindfulness, specific mindfulness, mindfulness, the state of remembering, the state of bearing in mind, the state of not losing, the state of not forgetting; mindfulness, the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, right mindfulness—this is called mindfulness.
One who is endowed with this mindfulness... [as before] ...is possessed of it; therefore, one is called "possessing mindfulness."

"Having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world. Herein, what is the world? This very body is the world; moreover, the five aggregates of clinging are the world—this is called the world.
Herein, what is covetousness? Whatever lust, infatuation, inclination, compliance, delight, lustful delight, and infatuation of mind there is—this is called covetousness. Herein, what is dejection?
That mental state which is unpleasant, that mental state which is painful, the unpleasant and painful feeling born of mental contact—
this is called grief (*domanassa*). Thus, both this covetousness and this grief are, in this world, disciplined,
thoroughly disciplined, calmed, stilled, subsided, come to an end, passed away, dissolved, dispelled, withered away.
“Wasted away and brought to an end; therefore it is said: ‘having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. Thus the meaning of these words has been stated.

This should be understood according to how this method of the Commentary accords with that [explanation]. This, then, is the commentary on the meaning of the summary of the Foundation of Mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body.
Now, regarding feelings, mind, and mental objects: “He dwells contemplating mental objects in mental objects... pe... having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.”

In this context, regarding such passages as "contemplating feelings in feelings," the purpose for restating feelings and the other aggregates should be understood in the same manner as was explained under the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*).
"Contemplating feelings in feelings," "contemplating the mind in the mind," and "contemplating phenomena in phenomena":
here, "feelings" refers to the three types of feeling, and these are exclusively mundane (*lokiya*). The mind is also mundane, as are the phenomena.
Their detailed classification will become clear in the section on exposition (*niddesa*).

However, here it should be understood that one who contemplates those [feelings] in the manner that feelings are to be contemplated is "one who contemplates feelings in feelings. This same method applies to the mind and mental objects as well.

And how are feelings to be contemplated? First, pleasant feeling is to be contemplated as suffering, painful feeling as a dart, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as impermanent. As it has been said:
“He who has seen pleasure as suffering, and has seen suffering as a dart,
and has seen the peaceful state that is neither-suffering-nor-pleasure as impermanent—
he indeed is a bhikkhu with right vision, who shall wander in peace.”
All these indeed should be contemplated as "suffering. For this has been said: "Whatever is felt, that I declare to be suffering.

Furthermore, they should be contemplated according to pleasure and pain. As it was said: "Pleasurable feeling is pleasant in its persistence and painful in its change"—all of this should be expanded upon.
Moreover, they should be contemplated by way of the seven contemplations beginning with impermanence.
They are to be contemplated. The rest will become clear in the section of the detailed exposition (*niddesavāra*) itself.

Regarding mental states (*cittadhamma*), first, consciousness (*citta*) is to be contemplated by way of its various distinctions—such as object, predominance, conascence, plane, kamma, result, and functional—as well as by way of the contemplations of impermanence and so forth, and by way of the distinctions such as "with lust" (*sarāga*) and so on, which appear in the section of the detailed exposition.

Phenomena (dhammā) are to be contemplated by way of their specific characteristics (salakkhaṇa), general characteristics (sāmaññalakkhaṇa), the phenomenon of emptiness (suññatadhamma), the contemplations on impermanence and so forth, and the various classifications such as "the aggregate" (khandha) mentioned in the section on exposition. The rest is exactly as previously stated.

Furthermore, although it is true that for one who has abandoned covetousness and dejection regarding the world known as the body, those same states have likewise been abandoned regarding feeling and the other aggregates.
However, it is stated in all instances both with reference to various individuals and by way of the development of the foundations of mindfulness at each moment of consciousness. Or rather,
it should be understood that since what is abandoned in one place is abandoned in the others as well, this was stated for the purpose of showing its abandonment there too.
The Exposition of the Summary is finished.
374. Commentary on the Section on Mindfulness of Breathing in the Contemplation of the Body:
Now, just as a skilled basket-maker [produces] coarse mats, fine mats, baskets, boxes, bags, and so forth,
Just as one desiring to make various utensils might obtain a single large bamboo, split it into four parts, and then,
taking each individual section of bamboo and splitting it further, fashion those various utensils; even so, the Blessed One,

desiring to bring about manifold kinds of distinguished attainment for sentient beings through the teaching on the foundations of mindfulness, [takes] this single right mindfulness and [expounds it as] "the four foundations of mindfulness."
"Which four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body," and so on;

having thus divided [the subject] into four ways according to its objects, and then taking each individual foundation of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), he began the section of the exposition by analyzing the body with the words, "And how, monks," and so forth.
In this context, the phrase beginning with “And how” (*kathañca*) is a question intended to provide a detailed exposition. Here, however, is the summary of the meaning:
“In what manner, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating the body as a body?

This same method applies to all the sections of questions. “Here, monks, a monk” (*idha bhikkhave bhikkhu*): “here” (*idha*) refers to a monk within this Dispensation (*sāsana*). Now, the word “here” (*idha*) in this instance [refers] to that which produces every mode of contemplation of the body.
It is an exposition of the Teaching that serves as the support for the person, and it negates the existence of such [a state] in other teachings.
For this has been said: “In this very place, monks, is the ascetic... [and so on] ...empty are the doctrines of others of ascetics other than these.
Therefore it was said: “Monks in this Teaching.”
“Having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut”—this illustrates his selection of a dwelling suitable for the development of the foundations of mindfulness.
For this bhikkhu’s mind, having long been dissipated among objects such as forms, does not wish to enter the path of the meditation subject;
it runs only along the wrong road, like a chariot yoked to wild oxen. Therefore, just as...
Suppose a cowherd, wishing to tame a fraudulent calf that had grown fat by drinking all the milk from a fraudulent cow,
were to remove it from the cow, drive a large post into the ground in a secluded spot, and bind it there with a rope. Then, that calf,
after struggling here and there, being unable to escape, would sit down right beside that very post.

Or it might fall upon him; even so, this bhikkhu, desiring to tame his corrupted mind—which has long been nourished by drinking the flavors of objects such as visible forms—should withdraw from such objects as forms and enter the forest, the foot of a tree, or an empty hut.
There, he must bind it to the pillar of the object of mindfulness with the rope of mindfulness. In this way, for him—
Although that mind has flitted hither and thither, being unable to escape by severing the tether of mindfulness because it cannot find its former habitual object,
it settles down and lies down upon that very same object by way of access and absorption.
Thus said the ancients:
"Just as a man here would tie up a young ox to a post, so too should he firmly bind his own mind to the object of mindfulness.

In this way, that lodging becomes suitable for the development [of meditation]. Therefore it was said: "This is the exposition of his selection of a lodging suitable for the development of the foundations of mindfulness."

Furthermore, since this meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*)— which is the pinnacle of body-contemplation and the proximate cause for the distinguished attainments and the pleasant dwellings in the present life of all Buddhas,
Paccekabuddhas, and disciples— is not easy to accomplish without abandoning a village settlement crowded with the sounds of men,
women, elephants, horses, and so forth, because sound is a thorn to jhāna; however, it is easy for a practitioner of yoga in a forest devoid of villages.

Having taken up this meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) and attained the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānacatutthajjhāna), and having made that very jhāna the foundation, one contemplates mental formations (saṅkhāra) and attains the highest fruit, which is Arahantship.
Therefore, showing him a suitable dwelling place, the Blessed One said: “Having gone to the forest,” and so forth.
For the Blessed One is like a master of site-selection (*vatthuvijjācariya*).

Just as a master of site-selection, having seen a piece of land for a city and having thoroughly examined it, points out, "Build the city here," and when the city is successfully completed, receives great honor from the royal court; even so, [the Blessed One] has thoroughly examined a suitable dwelling place for the practitioner (*yogāvacara*).
“He instructs, ‘Here the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) should be practiced.

Then, when the yogi practicing that meditation subject there has gradually attained Arahatship, he receives great honor, thinking, ‘Truly, that Blessed One is a Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha).
This bhikkhu, however, is said to be like a leopard. For just as a great king of leopards [enters] the thicket of grass in the forest...”
Just as a hunter, having hidden himself by relying on a forest thicket, a jungle thicket, or a mountain thicket, captures wild animals such as deer, buffalo, oxen, and boars;
even so, this bhikkhu who devotes himself to the meditation subject in the forest and other such places captures, in due order, both the four paths and the four noble fruits. Thus said the ancients:
“Just as one called a leopard, having hidden, seizes a deer;
even so this son of the Buddha, devoted to practice and possessing insight,
having entered the forest, seizes the supreme fruit.”
Showing him a forest lodging as a place suitable for the speed of his exertion, the Blessed One said, “Having gone to the forest,” and so forth.
Hereafter, whatever remains to be said regarding this section on mindfulness of breathing has already been stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.
“Just as, monks, a skilled turner,” etc.—this is merely a simile; and as for “internally, with regard to the body,” this...
Only that which has not yet arrived there reaches the state of absorption (appanā); the rest has already arrived.
As for that which has not yet arrived, one who "sees" it therein is skillful and clever.
"Stretching out long" means stretching out the hands and feet while drawing long lines when painting large objects such as drums or lotuses. "Stretching out short" refers to [painting] small objects.

Just as one who draws out a toothpick or a needle-piercer drags it very slowly and gently while writing, so too, this bhikkhu—by way of the long or short in-breaths and out-breaths occurring through the course of the journey and the limited duration—knows:
"Breathing in long, I breathe in long," and so on, up to: "He trains thus: 'I shall breathe out. As he trains in this way...
The four jhānas arise with the sign of inhalation and exhalation as their object. Having emerged from jhāna, he either examines the inhalations and exhalations or the factors of the jhāna.

In that regard, one who works with the inhalations and exhalations asks: "Upon what are these inhalations and exhalations supported? They are supported by the physical base (vatthu). The physical base..."
“Name is the body born of karma; the body born of karma consists of the four great elements and derived form”—thus he discerns form.

Then, he discerns name as the pentad beginning with contact that has that [form] as its object. Having thus discerned name-and-form, while seeking its condition, he sees dependent origination beginning with ignorance, and realizes:
“This is merely a collection of phenomena consisting of conditions and the things arisen from conditions.”

“there is no other being or person,” he crosses over his doubts. Applying the three characteristics to name-and-form together with its conditions and developing insight, he gradually attains Arahantship.
This is the gateway to liberation for a single bhikkhu leading up to Arahantship.

One who practices through jhāna also reflects: “Upon what are these jhāna factors dependent? They are dependent on a physical basis (*vatthu*). Now, the physical basis is the body composed of the four great elements.”
Having defined name-and-form—namely, "the factors of jhāna are name, and the body born of kamma is form"—and seeking its condition, he sees the mode of conditions beginning with ignorance.
Seeing that "this is merely a collection of conditioned phenomena and their conditionally arisen states;
there is no other being or person," his doubts are dispelled. Having applied the three characteristics to name-and-form together with its conditions, he practices insight.
Increasing it step by step, he eventually attains Arahatship. This is the gateway to liberation for a single bhikkhu leading up to Arahatship.
Thus, "internally" means he dwells contemplating the body in the body with respect to his own body of inhalation and exhalation;

"externally" means with respect to another’s body of inhalation and exhalation; and "both internally and externally" means at one time with respect to his own body and at another time with respect to another’s.
"In the body of in-breaths and out-breaths": by this, the time when he moves back and forth, having set aside the meditation subject he has mastered, is described.
However, at one time both of these are not obtained.
"Contemplating the nature of arising" means, for example, as a blacksmith [contemplates] his bellows and the bellows-tube and the relevant [work].

Just as wind moves back and forth in dependence upon effort, so too, in dependence upon the body composed of the four great elements, the nostrils, and the mind, the body of inhalation and exhalation moves back and forth for the bhikkhu.

Since phenomena such as the body are subject to arising, one who contemplates them is said to "dwell contemplating the nature of arising in the body. [Likewise,] one who contemplates the nature of passing away...
Just as when a bellows is removed, its pipe broken, and the corresponding effort is absent, that wind does not circulate;
even so, when the body is broken, the nostrils are destroyed, and the mind has ceased, that which is called the "body of inhalation and exhalation" no longer functions.
Thus, seeing that the cessation of the body and so forth leads to the cessation of inhalation and exhalation, he is "one who contemplates the nature of vanishing."

Or he dwells in regard to the body; thus it is said. "Contemplating the nature of arising and passing away" means contemplating, at times, its arising and at times, its passing away. "Or else, 'there is the body'":
there is only the body, not a being, not a person, not a woman, not a man, not a self, not what belongs to a self, not "I," not "mine," not anyone, and not anything belonging to anyone.
Thus his mindfulness is established.
The phrase "just enough" (*yāvadeva*) is a definition that delimits the purpose. This is what is meant: that mindfulness which is established is not for any other purpose;
rather, it is just enough for the sake of mere knowledge—for the purpose of the measure of knowledge that progresses further and further.

The meaning is: for the sake of the measure of mindfulness and for the sake of the increase of mindfulness and clear comprehension. "He dwells independent" means that he dwells indeed independent by way of the dependence on craving and the dependence on views.
"And he does not cling to anything in the world" means that he does not grasp at anything in the world—whether form... or consciousness—as "this is my self" or "this belongs to my self."

"Even so" (*evampi*) is the particle *pi* used in the sense of a summary with reference to what follows. By this phrase, the Blessed One shows that he has concluded the instruction on the section concerning mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānapabba*).
In this context, the mindfulness that grasps the in-breath and out-breath is the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*); the prior craving that originates it is the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*);
the non-occurrence of both is the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*); and the full understanding of suffering and the abandoning of the origin [are the truths of the path].
The Noble Path, which has cessation as its object, is the Truth of the Path. Thus, by striving through the Four Truths, one attains Nibbāna.
This is the door to deliverance for a bhikkhu intent upon inhalation and exhalation, leading up to Arahantship.
The section on mindfulness of breathing is concluded.
Commentary on the Chapter on the Postures (Iriyāpathapabba): 375.
Having thus analyzed body-contemplation by way of inhalation and exhalation, he now says, "And furthermore," etc., in order to analyze it by way of the postures.
In this regard, although even dogs, jackals, and the like know "we are going" when they are walking, [the text proceeds as follows].
But this was not said with reference to such a kind of knowing.

For such a kind of knowing does not abandon the perception of a being, does not eradicate the notion of self, and there is neither a meditation subject nor the development of the foundations of mindfulness.
However, the knowing of this bhikkhu abandons the perception of a being, eradicates the notion of self, and constitutes both a meditation subject and—
And there is the development of the foundations of mindfulness. For this was said with reference to such clear comprehension as: "Who goes? Whose is the going? For what reason does one go?
The same method applies to standing and so forth.
In that regard, who goes? No being whatsoever or person goes. Whose is the going? It belongs to no one.
It is the going of a being or a person. For what reason does one go? One goes by means of the expansion of the air-element produced by mental activity.

Therefore, one understands thus: "I am going"—a thought arises, that [thought] generates the air, the air generates the intimation, and by the expansion of the air-element produced by mental activity, there is the projection of the entire body forward.
"Going" is what is said. The same method applies to standing and the other postures as well.
For there too, the thought "I am standing" arises; that [thought] generates wind; the wind generates intimation (*viññatti*);
and the state of the entire body being raised from its base through the expansion of the wind element produced by the mental activity is "standing."
It is said thus: “I am sitting”—this thought arises; it generates wind; the wind generates intimation (*viññatti*).
Through the expansion of the wind-element produced by mental activity (*cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāra*), the contraction of the lower body and the raising of the upper body is called "sitting.
“I am lying down”—this thought arises; it generates wind; the wind [generates intimation]...

It generates what is called "stretching" or "lying down," which is the spreading out of the entire body across [the surface] through the expansion of the air-element of mental activity (*cittakiriyavāyodhātu*).
For one who understands in this way, it occurs thus: "A being goes; a being stands.
Yet, in actual fact, there is no being whatsoever that is going or standing. Just as one says, "The cart goes; the cart..."
It is said, "the cart stands," yet there is no such thing as a cart that either moves or stands;
rather, when four oxen have been yoked and are being driven by a skillful charioteer, it is merely a conventional expression to say, "the cart moves" or "the cart stands.
In the same way, in the sense of not knowing, the body is like the cart, and the winds of mental consciousness are like the oxen.
The mind is like a charioteer. When the thought “I go” or “I stand” arises, the air element arises producing an intimation;
through the diffusion of the air element of mental activity, going and so forth proceed.
Thereafter, there occurs the mere conventional expression: “the being goes,” “the being stands,” “I go,” or “I stand. Therefore he said:
Just as a boat goes by the force of the wind, or an arrow by the force of the bowstring,
so does this body go, driven by the winds. Just as [a puppet] moves by means of strings, so too does this [body] move by means of the string of the mind.
“Even when the body and the sense-faculties are engaged, they go, stand, and sit.
What being indeed is there here who, without causes and conditions,
could stand or move by his own power?”

Therefore, one who observes walking and so forth as they occur solely by way of the cause-condition (hetupaccaya) should be understood thus: "When going, he knows 'I am going'; when standing, sitting, or lying down, he knows 'I am lying down.

Alternatively, the statement "in whatever way his body is disposed, in that way he knows it" is a comprehensive expression. This means: in whatever manner his body is situated, in that very manner he knows it.
He understands: "That which exists in the mode of going, he goes. He understands: "That which exists in the modes of standing, sitting, and lying down, he lies down.
Thus, "internally" means that he dwells contemplating the body as a body by way of observing his own four postures.
"Externally" means by way of observing another's four postures. "Internally and externally" means at times...
One dwells contemplating the body in the body by grasping one’s own four postures at the proper time, and likewise those of another.

Regarding the phrases "contemplating the nature of arising" and so forth, the arising and passing away of the aggregate of form should be drawn out in five ways according to the method beginning with "the arising of form from the arising of ignorance," and so on.
It is with reference to this that it is said here: "contemplating the nature of arising," and so forth.
It has been said. The passage beginning with "Or else, for him there is a body" is exactly like what was stated before.
Here too, the mindfulness that encompasses the four postures is the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*); the prior craving that originates it is the truth of origin (*samudayasacca*);
the non-occurrence of both is the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*); and the full understanding of suffering and the abandoning of its origin [are the truths of the path].
The Noble Path, which has cessation as its object, is the Truth of the Path. Thus, by striving through the four truths, one attains Nibbāna.
This is the door to deliverance for a single bhikkhu who maintains the four postures, leading up to Arahantship.
The section on the postures is finished.
Commentary on the Section on the Fourfold Clear Comprehension (Catusampajañña-pabbavaṇṇanā) 376.

Having thus analyzed body-contemplation by way of the postures, he now speaks the passage beginning with “Furthermore” (*puna caparaṃ*) in order to analyze it by way of the fourfold clear comprehension (*catusampajañña*).
Therein, terms such as “in going forward” (*abhikkante*) and so forth have been explained in the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta*. Thus internally...

Thus, by means of embracing the fourfold clear comprehension (*catusampajañña*), he dwells contemplating the body in the body, either in his own body or in another’s body, sometimes in his own body and sometimes in another’s body.

Here too, in the phrases "contemplating the nature of arising and passing away" and so forth, it is the arising and passing away of the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) alone that should be extracted. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
Herein, mindfulness that encompasses the four kinds of clear comprehension is the truth of suffering; the prior craving that originates it is the truth of the origin;
the non-occurrence of both is the truth of cessation; and the Noble Path of the kind described is the truth of the path.
Thus, by striving through the four truths, one attains Nibbāna. This refers to one person who possesses mindfulness encompassing the four kinds of clear comprehension.
By means of the bhikkhu, [this practice] is a gateway to deliverance leading up to Arahatship.
The section on the four kinds of clear comprehension is finished.
The commentary on the section on attention to repulsiveness.

377. Having thus analyzed the contemplation of the body by way of the four kinds of clear comprehension (*catusampajañña*), he now speaks the passage beginning with "And furthermore" in order to analyze it by way of attention to the repulsive (*paṭikūla-manasikāra*).

Regarding that, whatever needs to be said concerning the phrases "this very body," and so forth, has all been stated in full detail in the *Visuddhimagga* within the section on the meditation subject of mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati-kammaṭṭhāna*). [The word] "both-mouthed" (*ubhatomukhā*)...
"Below and above" means it is joined with two openings. "Of various kinds" means of diverse sorts.
Herein, this is the correlation of the simile: the body composed of the four great elements is like the bag open at both ends;
the thirty-two aspects beginning with head-hairs are like the various kinds of grain mixed and poured into it; and the man with good eyesight is...
Just as for a farmer when he has released that sheaf and is reviewing it, at which time the various kinds of grain become manifest;
so too should the time when the thirty-two aspects (dvattiṃsākāra) become clear to the practitioner be understood. Thus, "internally" means:

by thus counting the head-hairs and so forth, one is a contemplator of the body (kāyānupassī) either in one's own body, or in another's body, or sometimes in one's own body and sometimes in another's body.
He dwells. From this point onward, it is exactly according to the method already stated.
For here, however, the application should be understood by making the connection thus: mindfulness that grasps the thirty-two aspects is the truth of suffering. The rest is just as before.
The section on attention to repulsiveness is finished.
Commentary on the Section on Attention to Elements (Dhātumanasikārapabba) 378.
Having thus analyzed the contemplation of the body by way of attention to repulsiveness, he now says "And furthermore," etc., in order to analyze it by way of attention to elements.
Herein, this is the commentary on the meaning together with a correlation through similes.
Just as some butcher, or a pupil supported by that very butcher’s food and wages, having slaughtered a cow and carved it up,
might sit at the crossroads— which is to say, the middle point where four great highways leading to the four directions meet—
dividing it into portions; even so, a bhikkhu, with respect to whichever of the four postures...
Because it remains in its own state, it is "as it is" (*yathāṭhita*);
and because it is as it is, he reviews the body as it has been placed thus: "In this body there is the earth element... [and so on] ...the air element.
What is meant? Just as when a butcher is feeding a cow, or bringing it to the slaughterhouse, or having brought it there—

In that case, even for one who has bound it and set it down, or is killing it, or is watching it being killed, the perception "cow" does not disappear so long as he has not split it open and divided it into its constituent parts.
But once he has divided it and is sitting there, the perception "cow" disappears and the perception "meat" arises. It does not occur to him: [that it was a cow].
—"I am selling the cow, these people are taking the cow"—so it occurs to him.

But then it becomes: "I am selling the meat, these people are taking the meat. In the very same way, for this bhikkhu, even when he was formerly a foolish worldling—both as a householder and after having gone forth—the perception of "a being" or "a person" does not disappear at all.

As long as one does not analyze this very body, however it is placed or disposed, by breaking it down into its compact components and reviewing it according to its elements, so long will the perception of a living being not disappear for him.
However, when he reviews it according to the elements, the perception of a living being vanishes and his mind becomes established through the mode of the elements.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “He reviews this very body, however it is placed or disposed, according to the elements.”
“There are in this body the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.

Just as, monks, a skilled butcher—or his apprentice—[examines a cow]... up to ... “the air element,” so too, monks, the meditator is like the butcher; the perception of a living being is like the perception of a cow;
the four crossroads are like the four postures; and the act of sitting after having analyzed [the body] into its parts is like the contemplation according to elements.
This concludes the commentary on the textual passage here. The discussion of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), however, has been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.

Thus, "internally" means that by means of this comprehension of the four elements, one dwells contemplating the body in one's own body, or in another's body, or at times in one's own body and at times in another's body. From this point onward, the method is exactly as previously stated.
For here, the way of escape should be understood by making this application: "The mindfulness that discerns the four elements is itself the truth of suffering.
The rest is exactly as before.
The section on the contemplation of elements is finished.
Commentary on the Nine Cemetery Meditations (Navasivathikapabbavaṇṇanā) 379.

Having thus analyzed the contemplation of the body by way of attention to the elements, he now says, "And furthermore," etc., in order to analyze it by way of the nine cemetery meditations (*sivathikapabbā*).
Therein, "seyyathāpi passeyya" means "just as one might see. "Sarīraṃ" means the body.

"A dead body" (*matasarīraṃ*). "Cast away in a charnel ground" (*sivathikāya chaḍḍitaṃ*) means discarded in a cemetery. "One day dead" (*ekāhamataṃ*) means belonging to one who has been dead for one day.
"Two days dead" (*dvīhamataṃ*) means belonging to one who has been dead for two days. "Three days dead" (*tīhamataṃ*) means belonging to one who has been dead for three days.
Because of its bloatedness—having risen up in succession due to the exhaustion of life-force by the wind, like a blacksmith’s bellows—it is swollen.
"Swollen" (*uddhumāta*) means that which is indeed swollen, thus "the swollen" (*uddhumātaka*). Or, because it is loathsome, the loathsome swelling is "the swollen" (*uddhumātaka*).
"Blue-black" (*vinīla*) refers to a discolored state; that which is indeed blue-black is "the blue-black" (*vinīlaka*).
Or, because it is loathsome, the loathsome blue-black is "the blue-black" (*vinīlaka*). [It appears] red in places where flesh has protruded, and white in places where pus has accumulated.
This is generally a designation for a corpse that is blue-black in color in its dark places, as if covered by a blue cloth.
It is "festering" (*vipubbaka*) because pus is oozing out from nine broken areas or openings of wounds;
it is "festering" simply because it has become putrid. Alternatively, it is "festering" because it is loathsome and foul-smelling. It has "become festering" (*vipubbaka-jāta*) in that state.
"Gone" means it has become putrid.
"He applies this very body" means that the bhikkhu brings this body of his together with that [other] body by means of knowledge; he draws them together.
How? "This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a character, and not exempt from this. This is what was said.
"It exists"— because of the presence of these three factors, namely vitality (*āyu*), heat (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), this body is capable of standing,
walking, and so forth; but with their departure, this body too is of such a nature, of such a putrid essence, destined for such a state,
and will become subject to such transformations as bloating and the like— it has not transcended this, it has not gone beyond the state of bloating and so forth.
"Thus internally" means that by thus apprehending the bloated corpse and so forth, one dwells contemplating the body in one's own body, or in another's body,
or at times in one's own body and at times in another's body.
"Being devoured" means sitting upon the belly and so forth, and repeatedly tearing away the flesh of the belly, the flesh of the lips, the flesh of the eyeballs, and so on.
"Being devoured": "With flesh and blood remaining" means it is still joined with some residual flesh and blood.
"Smeared with flesh and blood" is said with reference to the fact that even when the flesh has been exhausted, the blood does not dry up.
"By another" means by another direction or part. "The bone of the hand" refers to the sixty-four types of bones in the hand as a distinct category.
Scattered separately. The same method applies to foot-bones and so forth.
"More than a year old" means having passed a full year. "Putrid" means that those kept in the open air become putrid after just more than a year due to contact with wind, heat, and rain;
however, those buried underground remain for a much longer time. "Reduced to powder" means...
Having become powder, they are scattered about. In every instance, the application should be made according to the method stated as "he [sees] this very [body]" by way of being devoured and so forth.

Thus, "internally" means that by thus comprehending [the body] through being devoured and so on, until it reaches the state of powder, he dwells contemplating the body in his own body, or in another's body, or at one time in his own body and at another time in another's body.
But standing here, the nine charnel-ground contemplations (*śivathikā*) should be combined. For all those described by way of the formula beginning with "one dead for one day" constitute one;
that described as "being eaten by crows," etc., is another; the skeleton with flesh and blood still attached by sinews is another;
the one smeared with flesh and blood but devoid of sinews is another; and the one from which the flesh and blood have departed is another.

"One [contemplation] is on the connectedness of the sinews; one is on the bones being separated from their connections, and so forth; one is on the bones being whitened, resembling the color of a conch shell;
one is on the bones being heaped up, three years old; and one is on the bones being rotten and reduced to powder.
'In this way, monks,' he said, concluding the meditation on the body after showing these nine cemetery contemplations."
In this context, mindfulness that takes up the nine cemetery contemplations is the truth of suffering; the prior craving that gives rise to it is the truth of the origin;

the non-occurrence of both is the truth of cessation; and the Noble Path—which fully understands suffering, abandons the origin, and has cessation as its object—is the truth of the path. Thus, by striving through the four truths, one attains Nibbāna.
This is the gateway to liberation leading as far as Arahantship for those bhikkhus who take up the nine cemetery contemplations.
The section on the nine cemetery contemplations is finished.
And at this point, the sections on mindfulness of breathing, the postures, the four kinds of clear comprehension, and the reflection on repulsiveness [are concluded].
The section on the contemplation of elements and the nine cemetery contemplations—thus the fourteen sections of the contemplation of the body are completed.
Among these, only the two sections on mindfulness of breathing and the contemplation of repulsiveness are subjects for meditation leading to absorption (*appanā*);

however, because the cemetery contemplations are taught by way of contemplating the danger (*ādīnava*), the remaining twelve are only subjects for meditation leading to access concentration (*upacāra*).
The contemplation of the body is finished.
380. Having thus explained the foundation of mindfulness of the contemplation of the body in fourteen ways, the Blessed One now [explains it] in nine ways.
In order to explain the contemplation of feelings (*vedanānupassanā*), he said, "And how, monks... and so forth. Therein, regarding "pleasant feeling":
the meaning is that when experiencing a pleasant feeling, whether physical or mental, one understands, "I am experiencing a pleasant feeling.
In this regard, it may be granted that even infants lying on their backs, while experiencing pleasure at the time of drinking milk and so forth, [understand] "pleasure..."
“They understand: ‘I am feeling a feeling. However, this statement was not made with reference to such a kind of knowing.

For such a kind of knowing does not abandon the perception of a being, does not eradicate the notion of self, and is neither a meditation subject nor the development of the foundations of mindfulness.
But the knowing of this bhikkhu abandons the perception of a being and eradicates the notion of self.
This is both a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) and the development of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna-bhāvanā*).
For this was said with reference to experiencing with full awareness in this way: "Who feels? Whose is the feeling? By what cause is there feeling?
In that context, as for "who feels," no being or person whatsoever feels. As for "whose is the feeling," it belongs to no one at all.
It is the feeling of a being or a person. For what reason?

Because feeling has the physical basis (*vatthu*) as its object (*ārammaṇa*); therefore, he understands thus: "Feeling itself feels by taking this or that basis of pleasure and so forth as its object;
however, based on the occurrence of that feeling, the mere conventional expression 'I feel' arises. Thus, the basis...

One should understand that "he knows, 'I feel a pleasant feeling'" by observing that it is feeling itself which feels, having made [the object] its objective support, just like a certain elder at Cittala Pabbata.
It is said that when the elder was unwell, he groaned with intense pain and rolled back and forth; then one [person]...
The young man asked, "Venerable sir, which part of your body is pained? "Friend, there is no such thing as a separate place that is pained;
it is simply feeling that feels by taking the physical basis as its object.
"From the moment one knows this, is it appropriate, Venerable sir, to endure [the pain]? "I endure it, friend. "Endurance, Venerable sir, is better."
The Elder consented. The wind tore at him down to his heart, and his intestines became heaped together upon the bed.
The Elder showed them to the young monk, saying, "Friend, can you endure this much? The young monk remained silent.
The Elder, having balanced his energy and attained Arahatship along with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), passed away into Parinibbāna as one who has reached the summit.

And as with pleasant feeling, so too with painful feeling... [and so on] ...when feeling a non-sensual neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one understands: "I feel a non-sensual neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

Thus, after the Blessed One had taught the meditation subject of the material form, while teaching the meditation subject of the immaterial, he did so because it is more evident when explained by way of contact or by way of consciousness.
It does not exist; it appears like darkness. However, because the arising of feelings is manifest, it becomes manifest by way of feeling.
Therefore, as in the *Sakkapañha*, here too he taught the formless meditation subject (*arūpakammaṭṭhāna*) by way of feeling.

In that regard, the method of exposition beginning with, "For the meditation subject is twofold: the form meditation subject (*rūpakammaṭṭhāna*) and the formless meditation subject," is found in the *Sakkapañha*.
It should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.
In that context, regarding the passage beginning with "pleasant feeling," there is this further way of understanding: "He understands, 'I feel a pleasant feeling.
This is because at the moment of a pleasant feeling, there is an absence of painful feeling; thus, while feeling a pleasant feeling, [he understands]: "Pleasant..."
He understands: “I experience feeling itself. Because of the absence now of those painful feelings that previously occurred, and because of the prior absence of this pleasant feeling, he understands:
“Feeling is indeed impermanent, unstable, and subject to change.
Thus he is fully aware therein. And this was said by the Blessed One:

“Aggivessana, at the time when one experiences a pleasant feeling, at that time one does not experience a painful feeling, nor does one experience a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; at that time, one experiences only a pleasant feeling.
Aggivessana, at the time when one experiences a painful feeling... [or] a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, at that time...”
At that time, one experiences a pleasant feeling; one does not experience a painful feeling, nor does one experience a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling at that time.

Yet, Aggivessana, even a pleasant feeling is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation. Even a painful feeling... [and] even a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is likewise.

“Feeling, Aggivessana, is impermanent... [and so on] ...it is subject to cessation. Seeing thus, Aggivessana, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with pleasant feeling, disenchanted with painful feeling, and disenchanted with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, there arises the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’”
“Knowledge arises; one understands: ‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
Regarding the phrases “sensual pleasure” and so forth: sensual pleasure refers to the six types of worldly joy-feelings based on the bait of the five strands of sensual desire.
Spiritually unworldly pleasure refers to the six types of joy-feelings based on renunciation. Worldly pain refers to the six types of grief-feelings based on the household life.
The "unworldly painful" refers to the six feelings of mental grief based on renunciation (*nekkhamma*).

The "worldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant" refers to the six feelings of equanimity based on the household life (*geha*). The "unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant" refers to the six feelings of equanimity based on renunciation.
Their detailed classification has already been stated in the *Sakkapañha* [Sutta].

"Thus internally" means that by thus grasping pleasant feeling and so forth, he dwells contemplating feelings in his own feelings, or in the feelings of another, or at one time in his own feelings and at another time in the feelings of another. Regarding the phrase "contemplating the nature of their arising and passing away":
here, by means of five ways for each—such as "with the arising of ignorance there is the arising of feeling," and so on—he [contemplates] the feelings.

Seeing both arising and passing away, it should be understood that "he dwells contemplating the nature of arising in feelings, or he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in feelings, or at times he dwells contemplating the nature of arising in feelings, and at times he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in feelings.
From here on, the method is exactly as stated in the section on contemplation of the body; for only—

Here, mindfulness that comprehends feeling is the truth of suffering; having made this connection, the door to deliverance for the bhikkhu who comprehends feeling should be understood. The rest is exactly the same.
Thus ends the contemplation of feelings.
Commentary on the Contemplation of Mind (Cittānupassanā) 381.

Having thus explained the foundation of mindfulness through the contemplation of feelings in nine ways, he now spoke the passage beginning with "And how, bhikkhus," in order to explain the contemplation of mind in sixteen ways.
Therein, "with lust" (*sarāga*) means accompanied by the eight types of greed.

"Free from lust" (*vītarāga*) refers to the mundane wholesome and indeterminate [states]. However, because this is an investigation (*sammasana*) and not a combination of phenomena (*dhammasamodhāna*), no supramundane state is found here even in a single word.
The remaining four unwholesome consciousnesses partake neither of the former category nor of the latter.
"With hatred" (*sadosa*) refers to those accompanied by the two kinds of mental grief (*domanassa*). "Free from hatred" (*vītadosa*) refers to the mundane wholesome and indeterminate [states].
The remaining ten unwholesome consciousnesses belong neither to the first category nor to the second.
"With delusion" (*samoha*) is twofold: that accompanied by doubt (*vicikicchā-sahagata*) and that accompanied by restlessness (*uddhacca-sahagata*).
However, since delusion arises in all unwholesome states, the remaining ones are also included here. Indeed, within this very dyad, there are twelve unwholesome consciousnesses.
"Exhausted" means [states] associated with delusion. "Free from delusion" refers to mundane wholesome and indeterminate states. "Contracted" refers to that which is overcome by sloth and torpor;
for this is called a constricted mind. "Distracted" refers to that which is accompanied by restlessness;
for this is called a scattered mind. "Lofty" refers to the fine-material and immaterial spheres. "Not lofty" refers to the sense-sphere. "Surpassable" refers to the sense-sphere.

"Anuttara" (supreme) refers to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) and the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*). Even there, the fine-material sphere is "with a superior" (*sauttara*), while the immaterial sphere alone is "supreme" (*anuttara*).
"Concentrated" (*samāhita*) means that which possesses either absorption concentration (*appanāsamādhi*) or access concentration (*upacārasamādhi*).

"Unconcentrated" (*asamāhita*) means devoid of both types of concentration. "Liberated" (*vimutta*) means liberated by way of liberation through substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgavimutti*) and suppression-liberation (*vikkhambhanavimutti*). "Unliberated" (*avimutta*)...
It is devoid of both types of liberation. Furthermore, there is no occasion here for the liberations consisting in eradication, subsiding, and renunciation.

Thus, by means of grasping [the mind] as "with lust" and so forth, one observes whichever mind occurs at whichever moment—whether in one's own mind or in another's mind, or sometimes in one's own [mind]. "Internally" (ajjhattaṃ) refers to this.
Or at times he dwells contemplating the mind in another’s mind.

Regarding the phrase “contemplating the phenomena of arising and passing away,” here the arising and passing away of consciousness should be drawn out by means of five modes each: namely, with the arising of ignorance there is the arising of consciousness, and so forth.
From this point on, it is exactly according to the method already stated; for here, however, it is the grasping of the mind [that is emphasized].
Having thus applied the words as "there is the truth of suffering," the gateway to deliverance for the bhikkhu who is discerning the mind should be understood.
The rest is exactly the same.
The contemplation of the mind is finished.
Commentary on the Section on the Hindrances in the Contemplation of Mental Objects (Dhammānupassanā) 382.

Having thus explained the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of the mind in its sixteen aspects, the Blessed One now spoke the passage beginning with “And how, bhikkhus,” in order to explain the fivefold contemplation of mental objects.
Furthermore, by means of the contemplation of the body, the Blessed One [taught] the discernment of pure form.

The pure comprehension of the formless has been explained through the contemplations of feeling and mind. Now, in order to explain the comprehension of the mixed (form-and-formless), he said, "And how, bhikkhus," and so forth.
Or rather, through the contemplation of the body, only the comprehension of the aggregate of form was explained;
through the contemplation of feeling, only the comprehension of the aggregate of feeling; and through the contemplation of mind, only the comprehension of the aggregate of consciousness.
Now, in order to explain the discernment of the aggregates of perception and mental formations as well, he said, "And how, bhikkhus," and so forth.
Therein, "existent" means existing by way of frequent occurrence;
"non-existent" means not existing either by way of non-occurrence or because it has been abandoned. "And how" means by whatever cause the arising of sensual desire occurs.
"And he understands that" means he understands that cause. In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all instances.
In that regard, through improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) toward a beautiful sign (*subha-nimitta*), sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) arises.
A "beautiful sign" refers both to what is beautiful as a sign and to a beautiful object as a sign. "Improper attention" means...

Improper attention is attention that follows a wrong path; it is the attention that regards what is impermanent as permanent, what is suffering as happiness, what is non-self as self, or what is foul as beautiful.

For one who frequently engages in such [attention] toward those [objects], sensual desire arises. Therefore the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, there is the sign of the beautiful; therein, there is frequent improper attention."
“This nutriment leads to the arising of unarisen sensual desire, or to the increase and expansion of sensual desire that has already arisen.

However, its abandonment occurs through wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) toward the sign of the foul (*asubhanimitta*). Now, the “sign of the foul” refers both to the foul itself and to the foul as an object.
“Wise attention” means attention by way of skillful means, attention by way of the path, [and the contemplation] of the impermanent as “impermanent.”
or the attention directed toward suffering as suffering, toward non-self as non-self, or toward the unattractive as unattractive.
For one who frequently practices that therein, sensual desire is abandoned. Therefore the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, there is the sign of the unattractive;
frequent and thorough attention directed toward it is the nutriment for unarisen sensual desire."
“...for the non-arising of unarisen sensual desire, or for the abandoning of arisen sensual desire.
Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of sensual desire:

apprehending the sign of foulness, devotion to the development of foulness, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, having virtuous friends, and appropriate talk. For there are ten kinds of...

Sensual desire is abandoned by one who grasps the sign of foulness, by one who develops it, by one who keeps the doors of the sense faculties guarded, and also by one who knows the proper measure in eating—one whose habit is to drink water and sustain himself when there is space for only four or five morsels. For this very reason it is said:
"Without having eaten four or five morsels, one should drink water; ... [the rest of the verse follows] ..."
“It is sufficient for the comfortable dwelling of a bhikkhu who is resolute.
Even for one who serves virtuous friends like the Elder Tissa the Asubha-practitioner, who delights in the cultivation of foulness, sensual desire is abandoned;
it is also abandoned through appropriate talk based on the ten kinds of foulness while standing, sitting, and so forth. Therefore, it is said:

—“Six things lead to the abandoning of sensual desire. Furthermore, he understands that for one who has abandoned sensual desire by means of these six things, there is no further arising of it in the future through the path of arahantship.
However, ill will arises through improper attention toward the sign of repulsion; therein, repulsion also...
The sign of resistance (*paṭighanimitta*)—that which has resistance as its object—is also the sign of resistance. Unwise attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) has the same characteristic everywhere.
For one who frequently directs the mind toward that sign, ill will (*byāpāda*) arises. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Bhikkhus, there is the sign of resistance; the frequent application of unwise attention thereto is the nutriment for the arising of [unarisen ill will]..."
“Or for the arising of ill will, or for the increase and expansion of ill will that has already arisen.
However, through appropriate attention (*yonisomanasikāra*), there is the abandoning of it by means of the liberation of mind through loving-kindness (*mettā cetovimutti*).

In this context, when “loving-kindness” is mentioned, both absorption (*appanā*) and access concentration (*upacāra*) are included. “Liberation of mind” refers specifically to absorption. Appropriate attention has the characteristics already described.
For one who frequently practices that [loving-kindness] therein, ill will is abandoned. Therefore the Blessed One said:

“Bhikkhus, there is the liberation of mind through loving-kindness; the frequent application of wise attention thereto is the nutriment for the non-arising of unarisen ill will and for the abandoning of arisen ill will.”
Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of ill-will:

the apprehension of the sign of loving-kindness, devotion to the development of loving-kindness, reflection on one’s own karma as one’s own property, frequent analytical reflection, having virtuous friends, and appropriate conversation.

For ill-will is abandoned even by one who apprehends loving-kindness by means of any one of these: specifically directed, non-specifically directed, or by the suffusion of the quarters; and by way of the specific or non-specific suffusion.
Even for one cultivating loving-kindness (*mettā*), [it is said]: "What will you do by being angry with this person? Will you be able to destroy his virtue (*sīla*) and so forth?
Are you not one who has come by your own karma and will go away by your own karma alone?
Indeed, being angry with another is like desiring to strike someone while holding glowing embers, red-hot iron needles, or excrement."
"He exists. Even if he is angry with you, what will he do? Will he be able to destroy your virtue and other qualities?

Having come by his own karma, he will depart by his own karma alone; like an unaccepted gift or a handful of dust thrown against the wind, this anger of his will fall back upon his own head. Thus, [one should reflect] regarding both oneself and another.
Ill will is abandoned by one who reflects on the fact that one is the owner of one’s own kamma; by one who, having reflected on both types of ownership of kamma, stands firm in discernment;
and by one who serves a virtuous friend like the Elder Assagutta, who delights in the cultivation of loving-kindness.
It is also abandoned through talk based on loving-kindness that is suitable for the occasion, whether standing, sitting, or otherwise. Therefore it was said: "Six..."

“...these qualities lead to the abandoning of ill will. Furthermore, he understands that through these six qualities, there is the non-arising in the future of the ill will already abandoned by means of the path of the non-returner.
