Regarding discontent and the rest, sloth and torpor arise through unwise attention. *Tandī* is indeed bodily laziness.
“Yawning” (vijambhitā) means the bending of the body. “Drowsiness after a meal” (bhattasammada) means intoxication from food or a feverish state caused by food.

“Lethargy of the mind” (cetaso līnattaṃ) means a state of sluggishness in consciousness. Sloth and torpor arise in one who frequently practices unwise attention (ayonisomanasikāra) toward these states, such as discontent and the rest.
Therefore he said: “There is, bhikkhus, discontent, lethargy, yawning, drowsiness after a meal...”

“Mental sluggishness, and frequent improper attention directed toward it—this is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen sloth and torpor, or for the increase and expansion of sloth and torpor that have already arisen.
However, their abandonment occurs through proper attention directed toward the element of initiative and so forth. The “element of initiative” (ārambhadhātu) refers to the initial exertion of energy.
The element of exertion (*nikkamadhātu*) is called such because it has emerged from indolence; it is stronger than that.
The element of striving (*parakkamadhātu*) is called such because it advances to ever higher states; it is even stronger than that.
When one frequently applies wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) to this threefold energy, sloth and torpor are abandoned. Therefore he said: "There is, bhikkhus, the element of instigation..."

“The element of exertion, the element of striving, and frequent application of wise attention to them—this is the nutriment for the non-arising of unarisen sloth and torpor, and for the abandoning of arisen sloth and torpor.
Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of sloth and torpor: taking note of the sign of overeating, changing one’s posture, and so forth.
Perception of light, attention, dwelling in the open air, having virtuous friends, and appropriate conversation.
For when one who has eaten food that is like a hand-brought meal, a meal from a bowl, a meal with a cloth, a meal from a crow’s beak, or a meal that fills one’s belly,
sits in a night-station or a day-station practicing the duty of a recluse, sloth and torpor come upon him like a great elephant spreading out its trunk.
Furthermore, for a bhikkhu who has drunk water after setting aside space for four or five morsels of food and whose nature is to subsist on that much, [excessive eating] does not occur;
thus, even for one who takes the sign in this way regarding over-eating, sloth and torpor are abandoned.

Even for one who changes from whichever posture sloth and torpor have overcome him to another, [they are abandoned]; and at night, by means of the light of the moon, the light of a lamp, or the light of a fire.

Thinness and torpor are abandoned by one who attends to the light of the sun during the day, by one who dwells in the open air, and by one who serves spiritual friends like the Elder Mahākassapa who have abandoned thinness and torpor. They are also abandoned through talk concerning the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) that are appropriate for standing, sitting, and so forth.
Therefore it was said: "Six things [lead] to the abandoning of thinness and torpor..."

“...they lead to abandoning. Furthermore, he understands that through these six qualities, there is the non-arising in the future of the sloth and torpor already abandoned by means of the path of Arahantship.
Through unwise attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*), restlessness and remorse arise when there is no tranquility of mind. “No tranquility” means:
The state of non-quiescence is, in meaning, simply restlessness and remorse.
In this regard, restlessness and remorse arise in one who frequently engages in improper attention (*ayonisomanasikāra*). Therefore it was said: "Bhikkhus, there is non-quiescence of the mind;
therein, frequent engagement in improper attention is the nutriment for unarisen restlessness and remorse..."
“...for the arising of restlessness and remorse, or for the increase and expansion of restlessness and remorse that have already arisen.
However, through wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*), there is the abandoning of this [restlessness] within the tranquility of the mind known as concentration (*samādhi*). Therefore he said:
“Bhikkhus, there is tranquility of the mind; frequent application of wise attention to it is its nutriment.”
“for the non-arising of unarisen restlessness and remorse, and for the abandoning of arisen restlessness and remorse.
Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of restlessness and remorse:

being well-versed in the teachings, asking questions, knowing what has been established in the Vinaya, associating with the elders, having virtuous friends, and engaging in appropriate conversation. For indeed, by means of great learning...

Restlessness and remorse are abandoned even by one who learns one, two, three, four, or five Nikāyas according to the text and according to the meaning; by one who frequently inquires about what is allowable and what is not;
by one who is already knowledgeable through mastery in the formulations of the Vinaya; by one who approaches elder and senior Theras; and by one similar to the Elder Upāli.

For one who serves a virtuous friend who is a master of the Vinaya, restlessness and remorse are abandoned; they are also abandoned through appropriate talk concerning what is allowable and what is unallowable while standing, sitting, and so forth.
Therefore it is said: "Six things lead to the abandoning of restlessness and remorse. When restlessness and remorse have been abandoned by means of these six things, as for restlessness...
He understands: "By means of the path of Arahatship, there is the non-arising of remorse in the future; by means of the path of Non-returning, there is the non-arising of doubt in the future.
Doubt arises through improper attention toward things that are grounds for doubt.
Things that are grounds for doubt are indeed doubt itself, because they are the cause for the repeated arising of doubt. In that regard, improper attention...
In one who frequently engages [with such things], doubt arises. Therefore it was said: "Bhikkhus, there are states that are a basis for doubt;
frequent improper attention toward them is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen doubt, or for the increase, expansion, and abundance of doubt once it has arisen."
Its abandonment, however, occurs through wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) toward wholesome and other such phenomena; therefore he said:

"Bhikkhus, there are wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, blameworthy and blameless phenomena, phenomena to be cultivated and not to be cultivated, inferior and superior phenomena, and dark and bright phenomena with their counterparts.
In this regard, frequent application of wise attention is the nutriment for the non-arising [of unarisen unwholesome states]..."
“...or for the non-arising of doubt that has not yet arisen; or for the abandoning of doubt that has already arisen.
Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of doubt:
being learned, asking many questions, knowing the Vinaya thoroughly, abundance of resolute conviction, having virtuous friends, and appropriate talk. For by means of great learning as well—
Doubt is abandoned by one who learns even one or—peyyāla—up to five Nikāyas according to both the text and the meaning;
by one who frequently engages in inquiry concerning the Three Jewels; by one who has attained mastery over the Vinaya;
by one who possesses frequent resolve known as confident faith (okappaniya-saddhā) in the Three Jewels; and by those such as the Elder Vakkali, who are resolved through faith (saddhā-adhimutta).

Doubt is abandoned by serving a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitta), and it is also abandoned through talk concerning the qualities of the Three Jewels that is appropriate for one’s welfare while standing, sitting, and so forth.
Therefore it is said: “Six things lead to the abandoning of doubt.
When doubt has been abandoned by these six things, [it is further abandoned] by the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga).
"He understands: 'In the future there is non-arising.

Thus, with respect to internal phenomena—by means of this grasping of the five hindrances—one dwells contemplating phenomena in one's own phenomena, or in another's phenomena, or at times in one's own phenomena and at times in another's phenomena. [This concerns] their arising and passing away.

In this context, regarding the signs of beauty, the signs of ugliness, and so forth, the [factors] mentioned in relation to the five hindrances by way of improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) and proper attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*) are to be extracted [and applied]. From here on, it is exactly according to the method already stated.
For here, having made the application thus—"the mindfulness that discerns the hindrances is the truth of suffering"—this is the door to deliverance for the bhikkhu who discerns the hindrances.
This is to be understood. The rest is exactly the same.
The section on the hindrances is finished.
Commentary on the section on the aggregates.
383. Having thus analyzed the contemplation of phenomena by way of the five hindrances, he now says "And furthermore," etc., in order to analyze it by way of the five aggregates.
Therein, "in the five aggregates of clinging" (*pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu*): the aggregates of clinging are the aggregates that are the basis for clinging;
the meaning is that they are clusters or heaps of phenomena that have become conditions for clinging. This is the sense here.
This is the summary. For a detailed exposition, however, the discussion of the aggregates (*khandha*) is set forth in the *Visuddhimagga*.

Thus, regarding "this is material form" (*rūpa*): one understands material form by way of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), knowing that this is material form, that this is the extent of material form, and that there is no material form beyond this.
The same method applies to feeling (*vedanā*) and the other aggregates. This is the summary here; for a detailed treatment of material form and the rest, see the *Visuddhimagga*.
These have been explained in the Khandha-kathā itself. Thus, "the arising of form" refers to the arising of form in five ways, by way of the arising of ignorance and so forth.
Thus, "the passing away of form" refers to the passing away of form in five ways, by way of the cessation of ignorance and so forth.
This same method applies to feeling and the other aggregates as well. This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, is in the Visuddhimagga.
This was stated in the discourse on the knowledge of arising and passing away (*udayabbayañāṇa*).

Thus, "internally" means that by way of grasping the five aggregates, he dwells contemplating phenomena among his own phenomena, or among another's phenomena, or at one time among his own phenomena and at another time among another's phenomena. [He dwells] with regard to their arising and passing away.

In this context, it should be drawn out by way of the fifty characteristics stated regarding the five aggregates in such passages as, “With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of form,” and so forth. From here on, the method is exactly the same.

For here, the application is made thus: mindfulness that discerns the aggregates is itself the truth of suffering; and this constitutes the door to deliverance for the bhikkhu who discerns the aggregates.
This is how it should be understood. The remainder is exactly the same.
The section on the aggregates is finished.
Explanation of the section on the sense bases.

384. Having thus analyzed the contemplation of phenomena by way of the five aggregates, he now speaks the words beginning with "And furthermore" in order to analyze it by way of the sense bases (*āyatana*).

Therein, "in the six internal and external sense bases" refers to the six internal ones—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—and the [six external ones]—visible form, sound, odor, flavor, tangible object, and mental objects.
Regarding these six external [bases]: "He understands the eye" means he understands the sensitivity of the eye (*cakkhupasāda*) by way of its specific characteristic and individual essence.
"He understands forms" means he understands external form produced by the four [elements] by way of their specific characteristics and individual essences.
"And the fetter that arises dependent on both of those" refers to that which arises dependent on both that eye and...
And regarding form, both [the internal and external] are dependent upon one another.
Ten kinds of fetters arise: the fetter of sensual lust, ill will, conceit, views, doubt, adherence to rules and observances, lust for existence, envy, avarice, and the fetter of ignorance;
and he understands them according to their actual nature and characteristics.
But how does this arise? First, in the case of the eye-door:

when one relishes and delights in a desirable object that has come into range by way of sensual gratification, the fetter of sensual lust arises. When one becomes angry at an undesirable object, the fetter of aversion arises.
And when one thinks, "Who else besides me is capable of discerning this object?"—[the fetter of pride arises].
The fetter of conceit arises. For one who grasps at this form-object as permanent and stable, the fetter of views arises.
For one who doubts, thinking, "Is this form-object a being, or is it not a being?", the fetter of doubt arises.
For one who yearns for existence, thinking, "Ah, this has become easily obtainable for us in a state of prosperity," the fetter of lust for existence arises.

The fetter of adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa-saṃyojana*) arises for one who adopts such rules and observances, thinking, "In the future as well, it will be possible to obtain such [results] by undertaking these rules and observances.

The fetter of envy (*issā-saṃyojana*) arises in one who is envious, thinking, "Oh, may others not obtain that same objective support of form (*rūpārammaṇa*)! [This occurs regarding] the objective support of form obtained by oneself.
The fetter of stinginess arises for one who is stingy toward another. The fetter of ignorance arises through the ignorance that is co-nascent with all [the other fetters].
And as for the phrase "of that which has not arisen": by whatever cause, through its non-manifestation, that tenfold [set of fetters] remains unarisen...

There is the arising of a fetter, and he understands that cause. And as to how it arises for one who has arisen: by way of its manifestation, in the sense of not having been abandoned, he understands the cause by which there is the abandoning of each of those ten kinds of fetters when they have arisen.
And as to how it is abandoned: by way of abandonment through substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga*) and suppression (*vikkhambhana*).
He also understands the reason why that tenfold fetter, once abandoned, does not arise again in the future. By what cause, then, does it not arise again in the future?

First, the fivefold fetter consisting of views, doubt, adherence to rules and observances, envy, and avarice does not arise again in the future by means of the stream-entry path (*sotāpatti-magga*). As for the two fetters of sensual lust and ill will...

The non-arising of the gross [defilements] occurs through the path of once-returning; that of the subtle [defilements] through the path of non-returning; and that of the three fetters—conceit, lust for existence, and ignorance—through the path of Arahantship.
This same method applies to such passages as "he understands the ear and sounds," and so forth.
Furthermore, the detailed discussion on the sense bases (āyatana) here should be understood according to the method already explained in the *Visuddhimagga* in the exposition of the sense bases.

"Thus internally" means: he dwells contemplating phenomena in himself by way of grasping the internal sense bases; or he dwells contemplating phenomena in another by way of grasping the external sense bases;
or at one time he dwells contemplating phenomena in himself, and at another time in another.
Furthermore, regarding their arising and passing away, the arising of the eye-sense base from the arising of ignorance refers to the sense base of form within the aggregate of form.

In the formless bases (*ārūpāyatana*), the mind base (*manāyatana*) should be extracted according to the method already stated for the consciousness aggregate (*viññāṇakkhandha*), and the mental-object base (*dhammāyatana*) for the remaining aggregates;
supramundane states (*lokuttaradhamma*) are not to be included. From this point on, it follows the same method as previously stated.
For here, one should apply the connection thus: "The mindfulness that discerns the bases is itself the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*)," and so forth for the monk who discerns the bases.
The gateway to liberation should be understood. The rest is exactly the same.
The section on the sense bases is finished.
Commentary on the section on the factors of enlightenment.

385. Having thus analyzed the contemplation of phenomena (*dhammānupassanā*) by way of the six internal and external sense bases, he now speaks the words beginning with "And furthermore" in order to analyze it by way of the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*).
Therein, "among the factors of enlightenment" means among the factors of a being who is awakening.
"Present" means existing by way of having been acquired. "Mindfulness-enlightenment-factor" means the factor of full enlightenment known as mindfulness.
For here, "enlightenment" (sambodhi) refers to the practitioner (yogāvacara) who awakens starting from the moment he has begun insight (vipassanā).

Alternatively, that collection of seven factors beginning with mindfulness, by means of which he awakens—rising from the sleep of the defilements or penetrating the Truths—is itself the "enlightenment" as a collection of factors (dhammasāmaggi).
A "factor of enlightenment" (sambojjhaṅga) is a limb (aṅga) of that enlightenment, or of that collection of enlightenment-factors.
Therefore it was said: "the enlightenment factor known as mindfulness. The meaning of the words for the remaining enlightenment factors should also be understood in this same manner.
"Non-existent" means not present by way of non-attainment. And as in the cases of "for one in whom it has not arisen," etc., [it refers] to the mindfulness enlightenment factor.
To that extent, the arising occurs as follows: "Bhikkhus, there are states conducive to the mindfulness enlightenment factor;

the frequent application of wise attention to them is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen mindfulness enlightenment factor, or for the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen mindfulness enlightenment factor. In this regard:
Mindfulness itself is the state conducive to the mindfulness enlightenment factor. Proper attention has the characteristic already described.
When one frequently engages in that [attention] therein, the mindfulness enlightenment factor arises.
Furthermore, four things lead to the arising of the mindfulness enlightenment factor: mindfulness and clear comprehension, and the avoidance of persons who are forgetful.
"Attending to mindfulness, associating with persons who possess it, and being intent upon that.

For, in the seven instances beginning with "excellent," one should practice through mindfulness and clear comprehension; by avoiding persons of muddled mindfulness who are like crows dropped food; by associating with persons established in mindfulness such as the Elder Tissadatta and the Elder Abhaya;
and by having a mind inclined, leaning, and bent toward the arousal of mindfulness during standing, sitting, and other activities.

And the mindfulness enlightenment factor arises. Furthermore, he understands that for one in whom it has arisen through these four causes, its cultivation reaches completion by means of the path of Arahantship.
As for the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor: "Bhikkhus, there are wholesome and unwholesome phenomena... [and so on] ... dark and bright with their counterparts."

“...frequenting wise attention toward phenomena; this is the nutriment for the arising of the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor that has not yet arisen, or for the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor that has already arisen.
Thus there is its arising.
Furthermore, seven things lead to the arising of the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment (*dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga*):
being a questioner; making the basis pure; balancing the faculties; avoiding persons of weak wisdom; associating with persons of wisdom;

reflecting on the course of profound knowledge; and devotion thereto. Therein, "being a questioner" refers to [inquiring about] the aggregates, elements, bases, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, factors of the path, jhāna-factors, serenity, and insight.
Abundance of inquiry based on the purpose. "Making the basis clean" means making the internal and external bases pure.
For when one's hair of the head, nails, and body hair are long, or when the body is swollen with humors and smeared with sweat and dirt, then the internal basis is unclean and impure. But when...
When the robe is worn out, soiled, and foul-smelling, or when the lodging is dirty, then the external basis is unclean and impure.
Therefore, by having the hair and so forth cut, by making the body light through emetics and purgatives,
and by means of anointing and bathing, the internal basis must be made clean.
The external objects must be made clear by means of sewing, washing, dyeing, ironing, and so forth.
For when these internal and external objects are not clear, the knowledge regarding the arisen states of consciousness and mental factors is also unclear and impure;
it is like the radiance of a lamp flame arising from an oil-soaked wick that depends upon an impure oil lamp and wick.

Likewise, when the internal and external bases are purified, the knowledge regarding the consciousness and mental factors that arise therein also becomes clear and pure, like the radiance of a lamp flame arising in dependence upon a lamp-wick and refined oil.
Therefore it is said: "The act of purifying the basis conduces to the arising of the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment."
The "balancing of the faculties" means making the faculties, beginning with faith, equal in strength.
For if his faculty of faith is strong while the others are weak, then the faculty of energy will be unable to perform its function of exertion,
the faculty of mindfulness its function of establishing, the faculty of concentration its function of non-distraction, and the faculty of wisdom its function of seeing.

He is unable [to do so]. Therefore, it should be diminished either by reflecting on the specific nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*), or by non-attention (*amanasikāra*) in such a way that the mind becomes strong when attending to it. The story of the Elder Vakkali is an illustration in this regard.
However, if the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*) is too strong, then the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) is unable to perform its function of resolution (*adhimokkha*).

The others do not [function] by way of the differentiation of their respective functions. Therefore, that [hindrance] must be abandoned through the cultivation of serenity and the other [factors]. In this regard, the story of the Elder Soṇa should be cited.
Likewise, in the case of the remaining factors, when one among them is predominant, it should be understood that the others are incapable of performing their own respective functions.
In particular, however, they praise here the balance of faith and wisdom, as well as concentration and energy.

For one who has strong faith but weak wisdom is blindly devoted; he places his confidence in what is not a proper ground. One who has strong wisdom but weak faith sides with the "quarrelsome faction" (kerāṭika-pakkha);
like a disease arising from medicine, he becomes incurable. Merely by the arising of the thought [of generosity], it is wholesome.
"He falls" means that by overreaching and failing to practice giving and the other perfections, one is reborn in hell. Through the balancing of both, one gains confidence in the object itself.
However, when concentration is strong but energy is weak, because concentration belongs to the side of indolence, it is overcome by indolence.
When energy is strong but concentration is weak, because energy belongs to the side of agitation, it is overcome by agitation. Concentration...
However, when conjoined with energy, one cannot fall into indolence; when energy is conjoined with concentration, one cannot fall into agitation.
Therefore, both should be made equal. For it is through the balancing of these two that absorption (*appanā*) occurs.
Furthermore, for one whose work is concentration, even strong faith is appropriate. One who thus has faith and resolves [upon the object] attains absorption.
He will attain it. Regarding concentration and wisdom, however, for one whose practice is centered on concentration, strong one-pointedness is required;

for in this way he attains absorption (*appanā*). For one whose practice is centered on insight (*vipassanā*), strong wisdom is required; for in this way he attains penetration of the characteristics.
Yet, absorption certainly occurs even when there is an equilibrium between the two. Mindfulness, moreover, is powerful in all cases.

It is appropriate. For mindfulness protects the mind from falling into agitation through faith, energy, and wisdom—which belong to the side of agitation—and from falling into indolence through concentration—which belongs to the side of indolence.
Therefore, it should be sought everywhere, just as salt seasoning is required for all curries, or as a minister with general jurisdiction is required for all royal affairs.
Therefore he said: "And mindfulness has been called 'all-beneficial' by the Blessed One; for what reason?
Because the mind has mindfulness as its refuge, and mindfulness is manifested as protection; without mindfulness, there is no uplifting or restraining of the mind.
Avoiding persons of poor wisdom means keeping far away from dull-witted individuals who have not penetrated the analysis of the aggregates and so forth. Associating with persons possessing wisdom...
"Associating with persons endowed with the wisdom of rise and fall" means associating with individuals who possess the wisdom that discerns the fifty characteristics.
"Reflecting on the conduct of profound knowledge" means reflecting on the various manifestations of profound wisdom as it operates regarding the profound aggregates and so forth.
"Devotion thereto" means, while standing, sitting, and so on, for the purpose of arousing the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena.

He understands: "The mind has a downward slope, a downward tendency, and a downward inclination. He understands: "In this way, for wisdom that has arisen, there is the fulfillment of its development through the path of arahantship.
Regarding the energy enlightenment factor: "Bhikkhus, there is the element of initiative, the element of exertion, and the element of perseverance;
frequent and thorough attention directed toward these is the nutriment for the unarisen energy enlightenment factor [to arise]."

“...it leads to the arising of the energy enlightenment factor, or to the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the energy enlightenment factor that has already arisen”—thus there is its arising.
Furthermore, eleven things lead to the arising of the energy enlightenment factor: reflecting on the fear of the states of misery (apāya);...
Seeing the benefits; reviewing the path of travel; honoring the almsfood; reviewing the greatness of the inheritance;
reviewing the greatness of the Teacher; reviewing the greatness of the lineage; reviewing the greatness of one’s fellow practitioners of the holy life;
avoiding persons who are indolent; associating with persons who have aroused energy; and being intent upon that.
Therein, even during the experience of great suffering in the hells starting from the time of being subjected to the fivefold torture and bondage;
even when caught by nets, fish-traps, and the like in the animal realm; even when pierced by lashes of whips, thorns, and so forth, while carrying carts and the like;
and even for many thousands of years, or even for the duration of an interval between Buddhas (*buddhantara*), in the realm of hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*) due to hunger and thirst—
Even at a time of illness, or when experiencing the sufferings of wind, heat, and so forth with a physical frame consisting of nothing but skin and bone,
measuring sixty or eighty cubits in size among the Kālakañcika Asuras, it is impossible to arouse the energy factor of enlightenment;
"This very moment is the time for you, monk, to exert energy"— thus, even for one reflecting on the fear of the states of misery, the energy factor of enlightenment arises.
"It is not possible for one who is lazy to attain the nine supramundane states; it is only possible for one who has aroused energy—this is the benefit of energy.

Thus it arises for one who sees the benefits. Also, for one who reflects on the path of travel: "The path traveled by all the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Great Disciples must be traversed, and that cannot be traversed by one who is lazy. Thus it arises for one who reviews the route of progress.
It arises. Those people who attend upon him with almsfood and so forth are neither his relatives, nor his slaves or laborers;
nor do they give excellent robes and other requisites thinking, "We shall live depending on him. Rather, they give them while expecting that their own acts will bear great fruit.
Even the Teacher [says], "Having used these requisites, this person will be full of physical strength..."
The requisites were not permitted for you with the thought, "He will dwell in comfort.
Rather, those requisites were permitted with the thought, "While making use of these, he will perform the duty of a recluse (samaṇadhamma) and be liberated from the suffering of saṃsāra.
Now, as you dwell indolent, you will not honor that alms-food; for it is only for one who has aroused energy that there is the honoring of alms-food.
"It is called [a 'name']"—thus it arises even for one reflecting on the honoring of alms-food, as in the case of the Elder Ayya Mitta.
It seems that the elder resided at a place called Kassaka Lēna. In his village of alms-round, a certain great female lay devotee (mahā-upāsikā) looked after him, treating him as her own son.
One day, while she was going to the forest, she said to her daughter: "Daughter, at such-and-such a place..."
“In this place there are old rice grains; in that place is ghee, in that place is milk, and in that place is molasses.
When your brother, the noble Mitta, arrives, cook a meal and give it to him along with the milk, ghee, and molasses, and you may eat as well.
As for me, however, yesterday I ate stale food kept over from the previous day with sour gruel.”
“Mother, what will you eat during the day? “Put some leaf-greens in it, mother, and having cooked sour gruel with broken rice, set it aside.
The Elder, having put on his robe and while taking out his bowl, heard that sound and admonished himself:
“It seems the Great Laywoman eats discarded food with sour gruel; she will even eat broken-leaf sour gruel during the day.”

However, she mentions old rice and other provisions for your sake; yet, depending on you, she does not expect a field, a dwelling, food, or clothing in return. Rather, she gives while aspiring after the three kinds of success.
Will you be able to grant her those successes, or will you not? This, moreover—

“Alms-food cannot be taken by you while you are possessed of lust, hatred, and delusion. Having thus spoken, he placed the bowl in its bag, untied the neck-string, turned back, and went to Kassapa’s cave.
There, having set the bowl on the lower part of his bed and the robe on the robe-stand, he sat down, resolving upon energy with the thought: “I will not leave until I have attained arahantship.”
The bhikkhu who had lived diligently for a long time, having increased his insight, attained Arahantship even before the morning meal.
Like a blooming lotus, he sat with a smile, his great taints exhausted. The deity dwelling in the tree at the entrance of the cave said:
“Homage to you, O noble steed among men! Homage to you, O supreme among men!”
“Since your taints are exhausted, you are worthy of offerings, O venerable one!
Having uttered this inspired utterance (udāna), she said, “Venerable sir, by giving almsfood to Arahants such as yourself who have entered for alms, elderly women will be freed from suffering.
The Elder rose, opened the door, and [waited] for the time.
Looking out, he realized it was already dawn; taking his bowl and robe, he entered the village.
The girl, having prepared the meal, sat watching at the door, thinking, "Now my brother will arrive; now he will arrive.
When the Elder arrived at the door of her house, she took his bowl and [filled it] with food mixed with ghee and molasses.
Having filled a bowl of milk-rice, she placed it in his hands. The Elder, having offered the blessing, "May there be happiness," departed.

She remained standing, gazing after him; for at that time the Elder’s complexion was exceedingly pure, his faculties were serene, and his face shone with great brilliance like a ripe palm fruit released from its bond.
The Great Laywoman, having returned from the forest, asked, "What is it, mother? Has your brother come? She related the entire account of what had occurred.
The laywoman, realizing that today her son’s task of going forth had reached its conclusion, said, "Mother, is your brother finding delight in the Buddha’s teaching? Is he not weary of it?"
Now, this inheritance of the Teacher is indeed great— namely, the seven treasures of the noble ones—
and it is not possible for one who is indolent to take hold of it. For just as parents cast out a son who has gone astray, saying,
"He is no son of ours," and he does not receive their inheritance after their passing, even so the indolent person [is excluded from] this inheritance of the noble treasures.
"It is not one who is indolent who attains it; rather, it is one who has aroused energy who attains it"—this reflection arises even for one contemplating the greatness of the inheritance.

Furthermore, your Teacher was great: for at the time of your Teacher’s conception in the mother’s womb, at his Great Departure, at his full enlightenment, at the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, at the Twin Miracle, at the descent from the deva-world, and even at the relinquishing of the life-force—[in all these he was great].
Even at the time of his final *parinibbāna*, the ten-thousandfold world system trembled;
is it fitting for you, having gone forth in the dispensation of such a Teacher, to be indolent? Thus, by reflecting on the greatness of the Teacher, [indolence] arises.
Furthermore, by birth, you are not of lowly origin now, but belong to the royal lineage of King Okkāka, descended from the unbroken succession of the Great Elect (*Mahāsammata*).
"You are born as the grandson of the Great King Suddhodana and Queen Mahāmāyā, and the younger brother of the auspicious Rāhula;
it is not fitting for one such as you, a son of the Conqueror, to dwell in idleness"— thus it arises even for one who reflects upon the greatness of their birth.
"Sāriputta and Mahāmoggallāna, as well as the eighty great disciples, penetrated the supramundane Dhamma through energy alone;

you are following the path of these fellow practitioners of the holy life—do you follow it or not? Thus, it arises even for one who reflects upon the greatness of their fellow practitioners of the holy life.
He understands that this [energy] arises even for one who avoids lazy persons— those resembling pythons lying with their bellies full, having abandoned both physical and mental effort—
and even for one who associates with persons who have initiated energy and are resolute, and even for one whose mind is inclined, directed, and bent toward the generation of energy while standing,
sitting, and so forth. Furthermore, he understands that once it has thus arisen, its fulfillment through cultivation occurs by means of the path of Arahantship.
The arising of the joy enlightenment factor occurs as follows: "Monks, there are states conducive to the joy enlightenment factor;

frequent, thorough attention directed toward them is the nutriment that leads to the arising of the unarisen joy enlightenment factor, and to the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen joy enlightenment factor. In this regard:
Rapture itself is what is called the states conducive to the rapture enlightenment factor. The attention that arouses it is called wise attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*).
Furthermore, eleven things lead to the arising of the rapture enlightenment factor:

recollection of the Buddha, of the Dhamma, of the Saṅgha, of virtue, of generosity, and of the deities; recollection of peace; avoidance of persons who are harsh; and cultivation of persons who are gentle.

"Reflecting on the suttas that inspire confidence and being intent upon them. For when one recollects the qualities of the Buddha, the enlightenment factor of rapture arises, pervading the entire body up to the stage of access concentration;

and likewise for one who recollects the qualities of the Dhamma and the Saṅgha, or even for one reflecting on the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla) that has been guarded unbroken for a long time.
Even for a householder, when reflecting on the ten precepts or the five precepts;

or when, during times of famine, fear, and so forth, having given choice food to fellow practitioners of the holy life, reflecting on that act of generosity, thinking, "In this way indeed we have given";
or even for a householder at such a time, reflecting on the gift given to those possessed of virtue—by whatever qualities such deities are endowed, [they are reborn there].
Even for one who has attained the state of a deva, and even for one reflecting upon the presence of such qualities within oneself,
the defilements suppressed by meditative attainment do not manifest for sixty or seventy years; likewise,
even for one reflecting upon the harshness indicated by a lack of reverence toward the Buddha and others during visits to shrines, the seeing of the Bodhi tree, or the seeing of elder monks.

Even for one who avoids coarse persons—who are like dust on the back of a donkey due to a lack of confidence and affection—and even for one who serves gentle persons whose minds abound in confidence toward the Buddha and others;
even for one who reflects upon the inspiring discourses that illuminate the virtues of the Triple Gem;
and even for one whose mind is inclined, directed, and bent toward generating joy during standing, sitting, and other postures.
It arises. He understands: "When it has thus arisen, its fulfillment through development occurs by means of the path of arahantship.
Regarding the tranquility enlightenment factor: "Monks, there is bodily tranquility and mental tranquility;
frequent, thorough attention directed toward them is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen tranquility enlightenment factor, or for the further development of that which has already arisen."
“Or it leads to the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen factor of tranquility (passaddhisambojjhaṅga)”—thus there is its arising.
Furthermore, seven things lead to the arising of the factor of tranquility: the practice of consuming refined food;... [and so forth].

These are: the practice of pleasant seasons, the practice of pleasant postures, the application of equanimity, the avoidance of persons with agitated bodies, the cultivation of persons with tranquil bodies, and devotion to that [tranquility].

For even when one eats choice, succulent, and suitable food, and [encounters] a suitable season and posture among the cold and hot seasons and the various postures such as standing, etc., [tranquility arises].
Tranquility arises even for one who cultivates [the postures]. However, this was not said with reference to one who is of the nature of a Great Man (mahāpurisa) and capable of enduring all postures.

It arises only for one who possesses both similar and dissimilar [postures], and who, having avoided the dissimilar postures, cultivates those that are similar. "The practice of equanimity" refers to oneself.
And there is the reflection on one's own and another’s ownership of kamma. This arises through this practice of equanimity.
It arises for one who avoids a person whose body is agitated as they wander about harassing others with clods, sticks, and so forth;
and for one who attends upon a person whose hands and feet are restrained and whose body is tranquil; and for the purpose of producing tranquility while standing, sitting, and so on.

It arises even for one whose mind is inclined, bent, and leaning toward it. He understands that when it has thus arisen, its fulfillment through development occurs by means of the path of arahantship.
Regarding the concentration enlightenment factor: "Bhikkhus, there is the sign of serenity, the sign of non-distraction;
frequent, thorough attention directed thereto is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen concentration enlightenment factor, or for the further development of the arisen one."
“Or it leads to the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of concentration”—
thus there is arising. In this context, serenity itself is the sign of serenity, and in the sense of non-distraction,
it is the sign of non-confusion.
Furthermore, eleven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of concentration:
making the basis pure, balancing the faculties, skill in the sign, uplifting the mind at the proper time, restraining the mind at the proper time,
gladdening the mind at the proper time, looking on with equanimity at the proper time, and avoiding persons who are unconcentrated.
[It consists of] associating with persons who are concentrated, reviewing the jhānas and liberations, and being intent upon them.
Therein, the purification of the basis and the balancing of the faculties should be understood in the manner already stated.
Skill in the sign means skill in grasping the sign of the kasiṇa. "Upholding the mind at the proper time" means:

At whatever time the mind is sluggish due to excessive laxity of energy and so forth, at that time its uplifting occurs through the arousing of the enlightenment factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, and rapture.

"Uplifting the mind at the proper time" means: at whatever time the mind is agitated due to the exertion of energy and so forth, at that time [its settling occurs] through the arousing of the enlightenment factors of tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.

Its restraint. "Encouragement at the proper time" means that when the mind becomes disenchanted due to a deficiency in the application of wisdom or because it has not attained the bliss of tranquility, one should then stir it up by reflecting upon the eight grounds for spiritual urgency (*saṃvegavatthu*).
The eight grounds for spiritual urgency are: birth, aging, sickness, death—these four—and the suffering of the states of deprivation (*apāya*).
Fifth: suffering rooted in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) in the past, suffering rooted in the cycle of existence in the future, and suffering rooted in the search for nutriment in the present.
Furthermore, one generates confidence by recollecting the qualities of the Triple Gem; this is called "encouragement at the proper time" (*samaye sampahaṃsanatā*).
"Equanimity at the proper time" (*samaye ajjhupekkhanatā*) refers to that time when, having relied upon right practice, [the mind] is neither sluggish nor agitated.

When the mind proceeds evenly upon its object, without relish, having entered the path of serenity (samatha), it then no longer requires the application of exertion, restraint, or encouragement, just as a charioteer does not need to do so when his horses are proceeding evenly.
This is called "equanimity at the proper time" (samaye ajjhupekkhanatā).
Avoidance of persons who are not concentrated refers to those who have not yet attained access concentration (upacāra) or absorption (appanā).

Avoiding from afar those persons whose minds are distracted; "cultivating persons with concentrated minds" means attending upon, associating with, and revering those whose minds are concentrated by means of access (upacāra) or absorption (appanā).
"Devotion to that" means having a mind that is inclined, directed, and bent toward the production of concentration itself during standing, sitting, and so forth. For one who practices in this way:
This arises. And he understands: "When it has thus arisen, its fulfillment through development occurs by means of the path of Arahatship.
Regarding the enlightenment factor of equanimity: "Bhikkhus, there are states conducive to the enlightenment factor of equanimity;

frequent and thorough attention directed toward them is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of equanimity, or for the further development of that which has already arisen."
“Or it leads to the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of equanimity”—thus there is its arising.
In this context, equanimity itself is what is meant by “states conducive to the enlightenment factor of equanimity.
Furthermore, five things conduce to the arising of the enlightenment factor of equanimity: equanimity toward beings and equanimity toward formations.
Avoiding persons who dally with the formations of beings, associating with persons who are neutral toward the formations of beings, and being intent upon that [neutral state].
Therein, one arouses neutrality toward beings in two ways: "You have come by your own kamma and you will go by your own kamma;
this person too has come by his own kamma and he will go by his own kamma; you..."
"Whom do you cherish?"—thus by reflecting on the ownership of one's own actions (*kammassakatā*); and "In the ultimate sense, there is no self at all;
who are you that cherishes whom?"—thus by reflecting on the absence of a sentient being (*nissatta*). In these two ways, he arouses equanimity toward conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra-majjhattatā*):
"This robe, in due course, will undergo changes in its color and reach a state of decay..."
“Having become a foot-wiping cloth, it will be discarded at the end of a staff; moreover, if it had an owner, he would not allow it to be destroyed like this.
Thus, by reflecting on its ownerless state, and by reflecting on its temporary nature as follows: “This is not for long; it is only for a short time. Just so...
And as it is with robes, so should the application be made regarding bowls and other requisites.
Regarding the phrase "avoiding persons who cherish the seven conditioned things":

here, a person—whether a householder who cherishes his own sons, daughters, and so forth, or one gone forth who cherishes his own pupils, co-residents, preceptors, and so forth—who performs for them with his own hands such tasks as cutting hair, sewing with a needle, washing robes, dyeing them, boiling bowls, and so on.
Not seeing him for even a moment, he looks here and there like a startled deer, wondering, "Where is that novice? Where is that young man?

Even when requested by another for the sake of shaving hair or similar tasks, saying, "Please send such-and-such a one for a moment," he replies, "We ourselves do not perform that work; you will only weary yourselves by taking him along."
He does not give; this is what is called being "clutching like a seven-year-old.
But he who treats robes, alms-bowls, water-pots, walking-sticks, and so forth as his own property, and does not even allow another’s hand to touch them, when asked for them temporarily, says:
"We ourselves do not use these because we regard them as our own; what [use have you for them]?"

"I shall give," he says; this is called a person who is partial toward formations (*saṅkhārakelāyana*). But he who is neutral and indifferent toward both of these two grounds is called a person who is neutral toward beings and formations (*sattasaṅkhāramajjhatta*).

Thus, this factor of enlightenment of equanimity (*upekkhāsambojjhaṅga*) belongs to one who avoids from afar such a person who is partial toward beings and formations, as well as to a person who is neutral toward beings and formations.
It arises even for one who is practicing, and even for one whose mind is inclined, directed, and leaning toward its production while standing, sitting, or otherwise engaged.
Furthermore, he understands that for that which has thus arisen, there is the fulfillment of development through the path of Arahantship.
Thus, "internally" means: having thus grasped the seven factors of enlightenment within himself, or [having grasped them] in another at the proper time...
Or, having comprehended the factors of enlightenment (sambojjhaṅga) either in oneself or in another at the proper time, one dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena.
Herein, the arising and passing away of the factors of enlightenment should be understood by way of their production and cessation.

From this point on, it is exactly according to the method already stated; for the only difference here is that the mindfulness which comprehends the factors of enlightenment is to be applied as the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca).
Having done so, the gateway to liberation for the bhikkhu who masters the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) should be understood. The remainder is exactly the same.
The section on the factors of enlightenment is finished.
Now follows the commentary on the section on the four noble truths (catusacca).

386. Having thus analyzed the contemplation of phenomena (*dhammānupassanā*) by way of the seven factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*), he now speaks the passage beginning with "And furthermore" in order to analyze it by way of the Four Noble Truths.

Therein, regarding the phrase "he understands as it really is: 'This is suffering,'" setting aside craving, he understands the phenomena belonging to the three planes of existence according to their true nature as "this is suffering. And of that very [suffering]...

The meaning is that one understands, according to their true nature, the prior craving that generates and originates suffering as "this is the origin of suffering"; the non-occurrence of both [suffering and its origin], which is nibbāna, as "this is the cessation of suffering";

and the Noble Path—which consists of the full understanding of suffering, the abandoning of its origin, and the realization of its cessation—as "this is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."
The remaining discussion on the Noble Truths—excluding the word-by-word commentary on birth and the other factors—is already explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*. 388.
In the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), however, regarding the question "And what, monks, is birth?", it says: "Monks, that which is birth is also suffering."
When it is asked, "Birth has been thus described; what is that?", the meaning should be understood in this way for all such questions.

"Of those various beings" is a term inclusive of all beings, as there is no restriction [to specific ones] such as "of these. "In this or that order of beings" is likewise a term inclusive of all orders of beings.
Birth (*jāti*) is the act of being born; it refers to the first manifestation of the aggregates together with their variations.
It is a designation (*adhivacana*). "It has arisen" (*sañjāta*) is a synonym for that very same thing, adorned with a prefix.

That same [arising] is "descent" (*okkanti*) in the sense of descending in the manner of having entered. It is "manifestation" (*abhinibbatti*) in the sense of manifesting as what is termed "origination.
Thus, this fourfold [explanation] is called conventional discourse (*sammutikathā*). However, "the manifestation of the aggregates" (*khandhānaṃ pātubhāvo*) is ultimate discourse (*paramatthakathā*).
In the cases of existence with one aggregate and so forth, there is only the manifestation of aggregates—whether one, four, or five in number—and not of a person (*puggala*);
yet, when those [aggregates] exist, it is merely a conventional expression to say that "the person has manifested. Regarding "the acquisition of the sense-bases" (*āyatanānaṃ paṭilābho*):
the sense-bases are said to be "acquired" precisely as they are manifesting; the meaning is that this is their acquisition, which is to say, their manifestation.

389. The Exposition of Aging (*jarā*). "The state of decaying" (*jīraṇatā*) is the exposition of its mode of manifestation. "Brokenness" (*khaṇḍicca*) and so forth are the exposition of its transformation.
For in childhood, the teeth are even and white; as they gradually ripen, they undergo a change of color and fall out here and there.
Then, taking both what has fallen and what remains, they are called "broken teeth" (*khaṇḍitadantā*). "Broken" (*khaṇḍitā*) [is the term used].
The state of being broken is called "brokenness" (*khaṇḍicca*).

Hair and body hair that have gradually become white are called "gray hairs" (*palita*). One who has gray hairs is "gray-haired" (*palita*); the state of being gray-haired is "gray-hair-ness" (*pālicca*).

Due to the depletion of flesh and blood by the assault of the wind of old age, there are wrinkles upon the skin; one who has such a wrinkled skin is "wrinkle-skinned" (*valittaca*); the state of being so is "wrinkle-skin-ness" (*valittacatā*).
To this extent, manifest aging has been shown by way of observing changes in the teeth, hair, and body-hair.

For just as the path traversed by water, wind, or fire—by means of the breaking, crushing, or burning of grasses, trees, and so forth—becomes manifest, yet that traversed path is not those very waters and so on; even so, [aging is manifest through its effects].
The path traversed by aging through the breaking and crumbling of teeth and so forth is evident; it is apprehended even with the eyes open.
Yet, aging is not merely the state of being broken and so forth. For aging itself is not cognizable by the eye-consciousness.

However, because the life-span of one who has reached aging diminishes, aging is described as "the destroyer of life" (*āyuno saṃhānī*) by way of a metaphorical designation based on its result. Because [the faculties] were very clear during childhood...

The faculties such as the eye, which are capable of grasping even their own subtle objects with ease, become fully ripened, disordered, and dull when one has reached old age; they then become incapable of grasping even their own gross objects.
Therefore, "the ripening of the faculties" is also spoken of by way of a metaphorical designation for the result.

390. In the explanation of death (*maraṇaniddesa*), the term *yaṃ* is a neuter designation referring to death; the construction here is: "that which is called death is called passing away (*cuti*), it is called vanishing (*cavanatā*).
In this context, "passing away" (*cuti*) is a designation for its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). "Vanishing" (*cavanatā*) is a designation for its mode of manifestation (*ākāra*).
When one has reached death, the aggregates (*khandhā*) break up, disappear, and go beyond the range of sight; therefore [it is so called].

That dissolution is called "disappearance. "Death by death" (*maccumaraṇa*) refers to death as death, not momentary death. "The performance of time" (*kālakiriyā*) means the performance of the time of death.

All of this is merely conventional discourse (*sammuti*). However, "the dissolution of the aggregates" (*khandhānaṃ bheda*) is ultimate discourse (*paramattha*). In the case of the one-aggregate existence (*ekavokāra-bhava*) and so forth, it is precisely the dissolution of the aggregates—whether one, four, or five—that constitutes [death].
It does not belong to a person; rather, when that [body] exists, the conventional expression "the person has died" occurs as a mere designation.
"The casting off of the carcass" means the casting off of the personal existence (*attabhāva*). For when one has reached death, the personal existence falls away like a useless log;
therefore, it is called "the casting off of the carcass. It is the cutting off of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).
But death in its ultimate sense (*paramattha*) consists of all its modes. This very thing is also called "conventional death" (*sammuti-maraṇa*).
For it is only by grasping the cutting off of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) that worldly people say, "Tissa has died," or "Phussa has died.
(391) "By misfortune" means by any kind of misfortune among those such as the loss of relatives. "By a state of suffering" means by execution, imprisonment, and so forth.

By way of the cause of suffering. "Touched" means overwhelmed or overcome. "Sorrow" (*soka*) is that which arises in one who is overcome by any of the calamities concerning relatives, or by execution, imprisonment, and so forth; it is sorrow characterized by grieving.
"State of grieving" (*socitatta*) is the condition of having grieved. Furthermore, because this arises drying up and completely parching within, [it is called grief].
Therefore, it is called "inner grief" (*antoso-ka*) and "inner lamentation" (*antopariso-ka*).

(392) It is *ādeva* because by means of this they cry out and wail, repeatedly addressing [others], saying, "My daughter! My son! It is *parideva* because by means of this they wail while praising various qualities [of their loved ones]. The following two terms are further descriptions of that same state. (393) *Kāyikaṃ* means having the sensitive body (*kāyapasāda*) as its basis.
It is *dukkha* in the sense of being painful. *Asātaṃ* means not sweet. *Kāyasamphassajaṃ dukkhaṃ* means suffering born from bodily contact. *Asātaṃ vedayitaṃ* means an unpleasant experience.
394. *Cetasika* means associated with consciousness (*cittasampayutta*). The rest is exactly as explained under [the section on] suffering (*dukkha*). 395.

*Āyāsa* is mental fatigue that has reached the state of sinking and despondency. *Upāyāsa* is a more intense form of *āyāsa*. Following those, there are two descriptions of states (*bhāva*) illustrating the absence of self and what belongs to a self.
398. *Jātidhammānaṃ* means having the nature of birth. *Icchā uppajjati* means craving (*taṇhā*) arises. *Aho vata*... [means "O, may it be so!"]
Aspiration (*patthanā*). "But this is not [attained] by mere wishing": thus, the non-returning of birth cannot be attained through wishing alone without the cultivation of the path.
"This too" (*idampi*): the particle *pi* is used here in reference to the remaining factors mentioned below.
"Whatever they wish for": whatever unobtainable object one wishes for, the very wishing for that unobtainable object is suffering (*dukkha*). This same method applies everywhere.

399. In the exposition of the aggregates (*khandha-niddesa*), "that which is matter and is an aggregate of clinging" is the "aggregate of clinging to matter" (*rūpupādānakkhandha*); this applies in all cases.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Truth of Origin (*samudaya-sacca-niddesa-vaṇṇanā*):

400. "That which is this craving": that which is this craving. "Leading to renewed existence" (*ponobbhavika*): the making of renewed existence is "renewed existence" (*punobbhava*); [it is] renewed existence...
It has virtue as its nature, thus it is "leading to renewed existence. It has gone together with the passion of delight, thus it is "accompanied by the passion of delight" (*nandīrāgasahagatā*).
What is meant is that it has reached a state of essential identity with the passion of delight. "Rejoicing here and there" means rejoicing wherever there is a personal existence (*attabhāva*);
or else, it means rejoicing here and there among objects such as forms and so forth.
"Delighting in forms" means delighting in sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects. "Seyyathidaṃ" is a particle;
its meaning is "and what is that? "Craving for sensual pleasures" (*kāmataṇhā*) is a name for attachment to the five strands of sensual pleasure.
"Craving for existence" (*bhavataṇhā*) is craving for becoming; it refers to that which arises by way of longing for existence and is accompanied by the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*).

This is a designation for passion for existence in the fine-material and immaterial realms, as well as for attachment to meditative absorption (*jhāna*). Craving for non-existence (*vibhavataṇhā*) is craving for non-existence;
it is a designation for passion accompanied by the annihilationist view (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*).
Now, in order to show the objective basis (*vatthu*) of that craving in detail, he said: "But that... and so forth. Therein, "arises" means:

"It is born. "It settles" means it establishes itself through repeated occurrence. "That which in the world is a lovely form, a pleasant form" refers to that which in the world has a nature of endearment and a nature of sweetness.

In the passages beginning with "In the world, the eye," beings who are settled in prosperity through their attachment to the eye and so forth in the world [regard] their own eye as being like the surface of a mirror and so on...
Following the perception of the signs, they imagine the fivefold translucent matter to be like a jeweled lion-window opened in a golden palace;
they imagine the ear to be like a silver tube or like a string of pearls;
they imagine the nose—which receives the designation "high-bridged"—to be like a rolled-up green palm-leaf cylinder; and the tongue to be like a piece of red woolen cloth.
They imagine their own voice to have a soft, smooth, and sweet tone, like that of a sāla tree trunk; they imagine their body to be like a golden archway;
and they imagine their own mind to be unsurpassed and sublime compared to the minds of others. They imagine their own form to be like the color of a golden *kaṇikāra* flower and the like;
their sound to be like the gentle cooing of a intoxicated female karavīka bird or the resonance of a jeweled flute; and [the various qualities] obtained by themselves...
They imagine, "Who else possesses such objects as these scents, which arise from the fourfold origination?
As they imagine thus, those forms of the eye and so forth become both dear and pleasant to them.
Then, craving that has not yet arisen arises in them toward those objects, and craving that has already arisen increases further and further through its repeated occurrence.
It settles there. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "The eye is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world;
it is here that this craving, when arising, arises," and so forth. In this context, "when arising" means that whenever it is arising, it arises right here.
This same method applies everywhere.

Commentary on the Exposition of the Truth of Cessation (Nirodhasaccaniddesavaṇṇanā): 401. All such terms as "the remainderless fading away and cessation" (*asesavirāganirodha*) are synonyms for Nibbāna.
For it is by coming to Nibbāna that craving fades away and ceases without remainder; therefore, it is called "the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving."
By resorting to Nibbāna, craving is abandoned, relinquished, released, and no longer clung to;
therefore, Nibbāna is called "renunciation, relinquishment, liberation, and non-attachment.

For Nibbāna is indeed one alone, yet its names are many, corresponding to the opposites of all conditioned phenomena. They are as follows: the fading away without remainder, the cessation without remainder... [and so forth].
Relinquishment, renunciation, liberation, non-attachment, the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion, the destruction of craving, non-arising, non-occurrence,
the signless, the wishless, non-acquisition, non-relinking, non-rebirth, non-going, the unborn, the unaging, the disease-free,
the deathless, the sorrowless, the lamentation-free, the despair-free, and the undefiled.
Now, although craving has been cut off by the Path and has reached non-arising by resorting to Nibbāna, the Blessed One said "But as for that...
and so forth, in order to show its absence in those very objects where its arising was previously demonstrated.
In this regard, it is just as if a man, seeing a bitter gourd creeper growing in a field, were to search for its root starting from the tip and then cut it out.
Having withered away step by step, it would reach a state beyond designation. Then, one might say that the bitter gourd had ceased and was abandoned in that field;
even so, craving for the eye and the other sense bases is like the bitter gourd in the field.
Cut off at the root by the Noble Path, it reaches non-arising upon reaching Nibbāna. Having thus gone, it no longer exists within those bases, as in the case of the field.
It is no longer perceived, like a bitter gourd.
And just as if they were to bring thieves from the forest and execute them at the southern gate of a city, whereupon it would be said,
"The thieves are in the forest" or "The thieves have been killed," so too is craving [located] among the eye and other faculties, while it is actually at the southern gate.

Because they have ceased by arriving at Nibbāna—just as thieves do upon reaching a safe place—they are said to be "ceased in Nibbāna. Yet, though thus ceased, these [defilements] are not perceived within those bases (vatthu), like thieves in a forest.
Therefore, showing that their cessation occurs right there [in Nibbāna], he said:
"The eye is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world; herein this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned; herein, when ceasing, it ceases," and so forth.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Truth of the Path (Maggasaccaniddesavaṇṇanā) 402. "This very [path]" is a restriction intended to exclude other paths. "Noble" (ariya):

it is noble because it is remote from the defilements to be abandoned by each respective path, and because it brings about the state of a noble one (ariya). By the passage beginning with "knowledge regarding suffering," the meditation subject of the four truths is presented.
...has been shown. Therein, the first two truths are the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), and the latter two are the cessation of the round (*vivaṭṭa*).
Among these, a monk has a focused application of his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna-abhinivesa*) toward the round, but there is no such focused application toward the cessation of the round.
For the first two truths are taught both in brief as "the five aggregates are suffering, craving is its origin," and [in detail] as "which are the five aggregates?"...
Having learned in detail from the teacher in the manner beginning with “the aggregate of form,” the practitioner performs the work by repeatedly turning it over in speech.
Regarding the other two truths, however, he performs the work by hearing that the truth of cessation is desirable,
lovely, and agreeable, and that the truth of the path is desirable, lovely, and agreeable.
Acting in this way, he penetrates the four truths by a single penetration and realizes them through a single clear comprehension (*abhisamaya*).
He penetrates suffering through the penetration of full understanding; the origin, through the penetration of abandoning; cessation, through the penetration of realization;

and the path, through the penetration of cultivation. [He realizes] suffering through the clear comprehension of full understanding... [and so on] ...the path through the clear comprehension of cultivation.
He realizes [the truths]. Thus, in the prior stage, he has mastery, inquiry, hearing, retention, reflection, and penetration regarding two truths;

however, regarding the other two, there is only hearing and penetration. At a later stage, there is penetration by way of function regarding three truths, and penetration as an object regarding cessation.
But reflective contemplation occurs for one who has already attained the truths. And since this person is a beginner, that [contemplation] is not mentioned here.

And prior to this monk’s discernment, there was no application of attention, mental advertence, or reviewing such as: “I fully understand suffering, I abandon its origin, I realize its cessation, I develop the path.
These arise only from the time of discernment onward. Later on, however, suffering is indeed fully understood... [and so on] ...the path is indeed developed.
It is so. Among those, two truths are profound because they are difficult to see; two are difficult to see because they are profound.
For the truth of suffering is manifest in its arising, since even when encountering stumps, thorns, blows, and the like, one exclaims, "Oh, what suffering!
The origin [of suffering] is also manifest in its arising, by way of the desire to eat, the desire to consume, and so forth. From the penetration of its characteristic...
But both [of these] are profound. Thus, they are profound because they are difficult to see.

However, the effort required to perceive the other two is like stretching out one’s hand to grasp the peak of existence, like stretching out one’s foot to touch the Avīci hell, or like placing the tip of a hair split a hundredfold against another tip. Thus, because of their profundity...

They are difficult to see. Thus, with reference to the arising of preliminary-stage knowledge by way of apprehension and so forth regarding the four truths—which are profound because they are difficult to see and difficult to master—it was said:
"This is knowledge regarding suffering," and so on. However, at the moment of penetration (*paṭivedha*), that knowledge is indeed one and the same.
The intentions of renunciation (*nekkhamma-saṅkappa*) and so forth are diverse in the preliminary stage due to the diversity of the perceptions of abstaining from sensuality, ill-will, and cruelty;

however, at the moment of the Path, a single wholesome intention arises, fulfilling the factor of the Path by means of ensuring the non-arising of unwholesome intentions that have arisen in these three instances through their respective cessation. This is called right intention (*sammā-saṅkappa*).
The abstinences from false speech and so forth are diverse in the preliminary stage due to the diversity of the perceptions of abstaining from false speech and the rest;

however, at the moment of the Path, there arises only a single wholesome abstinence that fulfills the path-factor by means of preventing, through the severance of its basis, the unwholesome and immoral volition that had arisen in these four instances. This is called Right Speech.

Although the abstinences from killing living beings and so forth are diverse in the preliminary stage due to the diversity of the perceptions of abstaining from killing and so on, at the moment of the Path, however, there arises only a single wholesome abstinence.
This arises by way of non-doing, by way of cutting off, and by way of establishing the non-arising of the unwholesome and immoral volition that had arisen in these three instances;
thus fulfilling the factor of the Path, it is called Right Action (sammākammanta).
"Wrong livelihood" (*micchā-ājīva*) refers to misconduct of body and speech undertaken for the sake of food, drink, and so forth. "Having abandoned" (*pahāya*) means having avoided it.
"By right livelihood" (*sammā-ājīvena*) means by a livelihood praised by the Buddha. "He makes his living" (*jīvitaṃ kappeti*) means he maintains the continuity of life.

Furthermore, although right livelihood is manifold in the preliminary stage due to the diversity of perceptions regarding the refraining from hypocrisy (*kuhana*) and other such faults, at the moment of the Path (*magga-khaṇe*)—

However, in these very seven instances, there arises a single wholesome abstention (*kusalaveramaṇī*) which fulfills the factor of the path (*maggaṅga*) by means of establishing the non-arising [of misconduct] through the analysis of word-divisions (*padapaccheda*) regarding the unwholesome volition of wrong livelihood that has arisen; this is called right livelihood (*sammā-ājīva*).
Regarding the phrase "of those not yet arisen": it refers to those that have not arisen within one’s own existence (*bhava*) or toward such an object (*ārammaṇa*), or [those of] another.
But having seen [unwholesome states] arising, one thinks, "O, may such evil, unwholesome states not arise in me!
Thus, for the sake of the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states, one generates desire.
"Generates desire" means one generates the desire for energy that accomplishes the practice for their non-arising. "Exerts effort" means one makes an exertion. Energy...
"He exerts" means he sets forth energy. "He uplifts the mind" means he makes the mind uplifted by means of energy.
"He strives" means he sets forth the striving [with the thought]: "Let there remain only skin, sinews, and bone.
"Of those arisen" refers to those that have previously arisen in oneself by way of active manifestation. "Now I shall not allow such [states] to arise" [is the intent].
He generates desire for their abandoning. "Of wholesome states not yet arisen" refers to the first jhāna and so forth that have not yet been attained.

"Of those already arisen" refers to those very same states that have been attained. "For their stability" means for the purpose of their persistence by way of a continuous succession of repeated occurrences.
"For their non-confusion" means for the purpose of their non-destruction. "For their increase" means for their further development. "For their abundance" means...
"For the sake of expansion" means for the sake of fulfilling development. This right effort is diverse in its preliminary stage due to the diversity of the mental states involved—
such as the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states and so forth— but at the moment of the Path,
it is a single wholesome energy that fulfills the path-factor by accomplishing its function within these very four bases.
It arises. This is called right effort (*sammāvāyāma*).

Right mindfulness (*sammāsati*) is diverse in the preliminary stage due to the diversity of the minds that grasp the body and so forth; however, at the moment of the Path, it arises as a single mindfulness, fulfilling the factor of the Path by accomplishing its function in four ways. This is called right mindfulness.

The jhānas are diverse both in the preliminary stage and at the moment of the Path; in the preliminary stage they are diverse by way of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), whereas at the moment of the Path...
By way of various paths. For one person, the first path belongs to the first jhāna, while the second path and so forth may belong to the first jhāna or to any one of the second jhāna and beyond.

For another person, the first path may belong to any one of the second jhāna and beyond, while the second path and so forth may belong to any one of the second jhāna and beyond or to the first jhāna. Thus, all four [paths] are likewise.
The paths are similar, dissimilar, or partially similar by way of the jhānas. However, this distinction arises through the restriction of the foundational jhāna (pādakajjhāna).
First, regarding the restriction of the foundational jhāna: for one who has attained the first jhāna and, having emerged from that first jhāna, practices insight (vipassanā), [the path is similar].
The path that arises is associated with the first jhāna; however, the path-factors and enlightenment factors are complete therein.
For one who emerges from the second jhāna and practices insight, the path that arises is associated with the second jhāna;
here, there are seven path-factors. For one who emerges from the third jhāna and practices insight, the path that arises is associated with the third jhāna. As for the path-factors...

In this case, there are seven factors; the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅgas) are six. This same method applies from emerging from the fourth jhāna up to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana).
It has been stated that in the formless realm (ārūpa), the fourfold and fivefold jhānas arise, and that these are supramundane (lokuttara), not mundane (lokiya);
how is it so here? Here too, having emerged from the first jhāna and so forth, and having attained the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga), one enters the formless attainment (arūpasamāpatti).

Having developed that [path], he is reborn in the formless realm; there, three paths belonging to that jhāna arise for him. Thus, it is the foundational jhāna itself that determines [the rebirth]. Some elders, however, say: "The aggregates that serve as the object of insight determine it. Others say: "The inclination of the individual determines it. Still others say: "Insight leading to emergence determines it. The adjudication of these views is as follows: [The commentary continues: It is the path that determines the rebirth. For it is said: "When a noble disciple has abandoned the five lower fetters, he is of two kinds: one who attains nibbāna in the interval, and one who attains nibbāna upon landing... And so forth. Therefore, it is the path that determines the rebirth. But how does it determine it? By way of its own specific qualities. For the path possesses the specific qualities of the particular plane [of existence] where one is reborn. Thus, by means of its own specific qualities, the path determines the rebirth. Furthermore, the path determines the rebirth by way of its own function. For the function of the path is to abandon defilements and to lead to the attainment of nibbāna. Thus, by way of its own function, the path determines the rebirth. Moreover, the path determines the rebirth by way of its own fruit.

For the fruit of the path is the attainment of nibbāna. Thus, by way of its own fruit, the path determines the rebirth. Consequently, it is the path that determines the rebirth. As for the other views, they are merely speculative opinions. Therefore, one should not rely on them. One should rely only on the path. For the path is the true refuge, the true protection, and the true island. Thus, it is the path alone that determines the rebirth. This is the definitive conclusion.
This is to be understood according to the method explained in the *Visuddhimagga* in the section on insight leading to emergence.
"This, monks, is called right concentration": this is called mundane right concentration in its prior stage and supramundane right concentration in its subsequent stage.
"Thus internally" means: having thus comprehended the four truths for oneself, or for another, at the proper time...
Or, having comprehended the four truths for oneself or for another at the appropriate time, one dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena.
Here, however, the arising and passing away should be understood by way of the occurrence and cessation of the four truths as they apply.
