From this point on, it is exactly according to the method already stated; for here, mindfulness that comprehends the four truths is the truth of suffering.
Having applied it in this way, the gateway to liberation for the bhikkhu who comprehends the truths should be understood; the rest is exactly the same.
The section on the Four Truths is finished. 404.
Up to this point, there have been the sections on mindfulness of breathing, the four postures, the four kinds of clear comprehension, and the thirty-two aspects.

The twenty-one meditation subjects are: the analysis of the four elements, the nine cemetery contemplations, the contemplation of feelings, the contemplation of the mind, the discernment of the hindrances, the discernment of the aggregates, the discernment of the sense bases, the discernment of the factors of enlightenment, and the discernment of the truths.

Among these, mindfulness of breathing, the thirty-two aspects [of the foul], and the nine cemetery contemplations constitute the eleven meditation subjects for absorption (*appanā*). Thus says the Elder Mahāsīva, the reciter of the *Dīgha Nikāya*.

However, he said, "The nine cemetery contemplations are taught by way of the contemplation of danger. Therefore, according to his opinion, there are only two subjects of meditation for absorption (*appanā-kammaṭṭhāna*);
the rest are subjects of meditation for access concentration (*upacāra-kammaṭṭhāna*). But does fixed attention (*abhinivesa*) arise in all of these?
It does not arise. For fixed attention does not arise in the case of the clear comprehension of postures (*iriyāpatha-sampajañña*) or the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*).
“...it arises in regard to the knowledges. However, the Elder Mahāsīva said: “Adherence also arises in regard to these:
‘Do I have the four postures or not? Do I have the four kinds of clear comprehension or not?
Do I have the five hindrances or not? Do I have the seven factors of enlightenment...’”
"Or does it not exist?"—thus one grasps at it. Therefore, clinging arises everywhere.
"Whoever, monks"—that is, whoever, monks, be they a monk, a nun, a male lay follower, or a female lay follower—"should develop thus":
they should develop according to the sequence of development as explained from the beginning. "Is to be expected."

"Desirable" means it is to be expected; "certainly to occur" is the meaning. "The other" refers to *arahatta* (Arahatship). "If there remains a substrate of clinging" (*upādisesa*) means if a residue of clinging (*upādānasesa*) has not been fully exhausted.
"Non-returning" (*anāgāmitā*) is the state of being a non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
Having thus shown the quality of leading to liberation (*niyyānikabhāva*) of the Dispensation by way of seven years, [the text] further shows it even in a shorter time than that.
"Teaching at the proper time," he said, "let them stay, O bhikkhus," and so forth. All of this was spoken with reference to a person of middling faculties among those to be trained;
however, with respect to one of sharp wisdom, it is said: "If instructed in the morning, he will attain distinction by evening;
if instructed in the evening, he will attain distinction by morning. Thus the Blessed One [taught] that which leads to liberation.
"Monks, this is my teaching," having thus shown, he delivered the discourse taught with the peak of Arahantship across twenty-one points, concluding:
"Monks, this is the one-way path... pe ...it was said, and it was said with reference to this.
The remainder is of plain meaning. At the conclusion of the teaching, however, thirty thousand monks—
"They were established in Arahatship.
Thus ends the commentary on the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta in the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīghanikāya*.
10. Commentary on the Pāyāsi-rājañña Sutta 406.
"Thus have I heard" introduces the Pāyāsi-rājañña Sutta. Herein, this is the commentary on the words not previously explained: *Āyasmā* is a term of endearment.
*Kumārakassapo* is his name. However, because he went forth while still a youth, the Blessed One said, "Call Kassapa."
When it was said, "Give this fruit or hard food to Kassapa," [the king asked], "To which Kassapa? [The reply was], "To Kumārakassapa.
Because he had thus received that name, from then on, even in his old age, he was called only "Kumārakassapa.
Furthermore, because he was the king's foster son, they also knew him as Kumārakassapa.

This, however, is the account of how he manifested his past practice, beginning from his previous efforts: It is said that during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, the Elder was the son of a merchant.

Then one day, seeing the Blessed One appointing a certain disciple as foremost among those who speak with eloquence, he gave alms to the Blessed One for seven days and made this aspiration: "May I too, Blessed One, in the future..."
Having made the aspiration, "May I become a disciple of the Buddha like this elder, one who is skilled in varied discourse," he performed meritorious deeds;
however, having gone forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, he was unable to achieve any distinction.
At that time, it is said, when the dispensation of the Blessed One [Gotama] had passed away and was declining, five bhikkhus bound a ladder, ascended a mountain, and practiced the duty of a recluse.
They performed [the rites]. On the third day, the senior elder of the Saṅgha attained Arahatship; on the fourth day, the junior elder became a Non-returner (Anāgāmī);
the other three, being unable to produce any further distinction, were reborn in the world of the gods.
While they were enjoying prosperity among gods and humans for the duration of an interval between Buddhas, one of them was born in Takṣaśilā.
Having been reborn in a royal family, he became a king named Pakkusāti.

Having gone forth for the sake of the Blessed One and while traveling toward Rājagaha, he heard the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma at a potter’s workshop and attained the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala).
Another was reborn in a noble family at a certain seaport; having boarded a ship, his vessel was wrecked, and he [clad himself] in garments of bark.
Having put on his robes and attained success in gain, he gave rise to the thought, "I am an arahant.
Then, being exhorted by a deity who desired his welfare—who said, "You are not an arahant; go, approach the Teacher, and ask him a question"—he did so and attained the fruit of arahantship.
He was born in Rājagaha from the womb of a certain noble maiden.
She, having first requested her parents for the going forth but not obtaining it, went to her family home and conceived a child.
Not even knowing she was pregnant, she gratified her husband; with his permission, she went forth among the bhikkhunīs. When they saw the signs of pregnancy in her...
The bhikkhunīs questioned Devadatta; he said, "She is no longer a samaṇī. They questioned the One of Ten Powers (the Buddha).

The Teacher directed the Elder Upāli to take charge of the matter. The Elder summoned the families residing in the city of Sāvatthī and the female lay disciple Visākhā, and while investigating the case, he declared, "The pregnancy was conceived before [her ordination];
her admission into the Order is valid. The Teacher said, "It has been well-judged."
“An adjudication! he said, giving his approval to the Elder. That bhikkhunī gave birth to a son who resembled a golden image.

Taking him, King Pasenadi of Kosala raised him. Having given him the name Kassapa, and having adorned him later on, the king brought him into the presence of the Teacher and had him ordained. Thus, because he was the king’s foster-son...

“They recognized him as ‘Kumārakassapa. One day, while he was performing the duties of a recluse in the Andhavana forest, benevolent deities had him learn certain questions and said to him, ‘Ask the Blessed One about these questions.

The Elder asked the questions, and at the conclusion of the answers to those questions, he attained Arahatship. The Blessed One also placed him in the foremost position among the monks who were eloquent speakers.”
Setavyā is the name of that city. "To the north of Setavyā" means in the northern direction from Setavyā.
"A khattiya" refers to an unanointed king. "A resort of views" (diṭṭhigata) is simply a view;

just as when one says "a resort of feces" or "a resort of urine," there is nothing other than feces and so forth, so too a resort of views is simply a view. "In this way it does not exist" refers to each respective reason.
Having made this pretext, he says, "It is not even like this. "Before... [and so on] "...he persuades" means as long as he has not yet persuaded him.
411. Commentary on the Simile of the Moon and Sun:
"These, Master Kassapa, are the moon and sun. It is said that when questioned by the Elder, he thought: "This ascetic..."
First, he brought forward the simile of the moon and the sun: "He will be like the moon and the sun in wisdom; he cannot be overcome by another.
However, if I were to say, "The moon and the sun are in this world," he would entangle me with questions such as, "What do these two rest upon?
What is their size? How high are they? But I am able to disentangle this.
“I will not be able to say, ‘In the other world,’ for him. That is why he spoke thus.
However, not long before that, the Blessed One had related the Sudhābhojanīya Jātaka.
In that [Jātaka], it is stated: “Canda was the son of the gods Canda; Suriya was the son of the gods Suriya. And this was the Jātaka related by the Blessed One.
Or, if a Sutta were spread throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, one could not say, "There are no sons of the gods dwelling here," because he thought thus;
therefore, he said that those gods are not humans. 412.
"But is there, Prince, a way (pariyāya)?"—he asks this meaning: "Is there a reason (kāraṇa)?"—"They are afflicted" means by what is termed discordant feeling (visabhāga-vedanā).
"Afflicted by illness" means possessed of disease. "Suffering" means having fallen into pain. "Grievously ill" means severely ill. "Trustworthy" means: "I trust you;
you are trustworthy to me," the meaning being that your words are to be believed.
"Reliable" means: "I have confidence in you; you are reliable to me," the meaning being that you are to be trusted.
413. Explanation of the Simile of the Thief, etc.: "Having pointed out" means having shown them their own person and the goods to be recovered;
"having caused them to accept," is the meaning. "While he is prattling" means while he is prattling variously, saying, "My son! My daughter! My wealth!"
“Among the wardens of hell” means among those beings who act as the executioners of karma in hell. As for those who say, “Karma itself performs the function of the executioner;
there are no wardens of hell,” they contradict the *Devadūta Sutta*, which states: “Then, monks, the wardens of hell [seize him].
For just as there are men acting as executioners in royal courts in the human world, so too are there wardens of hell in hell.
415. “With bamboo scrapers” means with bamboo shavings. “Wipe well” means wipe so that it is thoroughly cleaned; the meaning is, “remove [the impurity]. “Impure” means unpleasant.
“Considered impure” means either being a portion consisting of impurity, or being known as impure.
“Foul-smelling” means having the odor of a corpse. “Repulsive” means connected with what should be loathed. “Disgusting” means bringing about aversion even by the mere sight of it.

"Afflicts" (*ubbādhati*) means that after bathing twice a day and changing clothes three times, the scent of even humans such as universal monarchs (*cakkavatti*), though they be adorned and decorated, afflicts deities standing a hundred leagues away like a corpse hung around their necks.

(416) Furthermore, he speaks by way of those who undertake and observe the five precepts, beginning with the abstention from taking life. Regarding the phrase "of the Thirty-three," he says this to indicate: "Let alone those born in distant realms—do not come here; why do these [deities] not come?"

418. "I think you speak like one born blind" means he appeared like one who was blind from birth. "Forest and woodland tracts": they are called *arañña* because they possess the characteristics of the forest, and *vanapattha* because they consist of great forest thickets.

"Remote" means far away. 419. "One of beautiful character" means one whose nature is lovely due to that very virtue. "Averse to suffering" means not desiring suffering. "It will be better" means the intention is that there will be the happiness of a fortunate rebirth in the next world.
420. "In the throes of labor" means having reached the time of delivery; her womb is fully matured and she will give birth before long.
"Useful" (*attha*) means she will become one who provides enjoyment; "a servant for the feet. "Calamity and ruin" (*anayabyasana*) means great suffering.

"Prosperity" (*aya*) is happiness; "non-prosperity" (*anaya*) is the opposite of prosperity, which is suffering. That which completely destroys (*byasati*) and scatters (*vikkhipati*) all happiness is "ruin" (*byasana*).
Thus, non-prosperity itself is ruin—this is the meaning of "calamity and ruin"—which is to say, great suffering. "Improperly" (*ayoniso*) means by an incorrect method.
“They do not ripen what is unripe” means they do not cut short the life-span prematurely while it is still unripened and not exhausted.
“They await its full ripening” means they wait for the time when the life-span has reached its full maturity. This was also said by the General of the Dhamma:
“I do not rejoice in death, nor do I rejoice in life;”
"And I await my time, like a servant waiting for his wages.
(421) "Having broken through" means having broken through the coating of clay.
(422) "Delightfulness" means the state of being delightful. "Velāsikā" means those devoted to play. "Komārikā" means young girls.
"When they are living, do they see you entering or exiting during the time of seeing a dream?
He said this taking the movement of the mind here as "the living soul" (*jīva*), for he perceives that as the living soul there.
423. *Jiyāyā* means by the bowstring; the meaning is "having wrapped it around the neck. *Patthinnatara* means more rigid. By this...
What does this show? You say that during the lifetime of a being there are five aggregates;
however, at the time of death, only the aggregate of form remains, while the other three aggregates cease to function and the aggregate of consciousness departs.
The remaining aggregate of form ought to become lighter, yet it becomes even heavier. Therefore, this shows that no one goes anywhere.
424. They are extinguished, their heat having been stilled.
425. "Without harming" means without destroying. "He becomes half-dead" means he has begun to die; he is half-dead.
"Shake it away" means move it toward the near side. "Shake it out" means move it toward the far side. "Shake it off" means move it back and forth. And that sphere...
“He does not experience” means that he does not discern that visible-object base with that eye. This method applies everywhere. 426. “Conch-blower” means a conch-blower.
“Having blown” means having sounded it. 428. “Fire-worshipper” means one who tends the sacrificial fire.

“I would produce” means I would bring about; or, I would cause [him] to reach a long life. “I would nourish” means I would support him with food and so forth. “I would increase” means I would cause him to attain growth. “Together with the fire-drills” means the pair of fire-sticks.
429. “Even kings beyond [my realm” means that kings in other kingdoms and other countries also know [this]. “Incapable” means unskilled and unwise.
“Even by anger” means: thinking, “I shall uphold and maintain this speculative view even by means of the anger arising toward those who speak thus to me,” one takes it up and wanders about.
“By hypocrisy” means by the characteristic of hypocrisy regarding the reasons stated by you.
“Even with mud. “With moss” means even with moss characterized by being held together in a pair with her.
430. “A leaf of *harītaka*” means any kind of *harītaka* fruit; the meaning is that it is not even a leaf from a fresh grass.
“A quiver fastened” means a quiver for a fastened bow. “Vessels filled with water” means those completely full of water.
"Paths and ravines. "Yokes" means oxen. "One who has gone out much" means one who has gone out many times or has been gone out for a long time.
"With the goods as they were brought" means with whatever goods—grass, wood, or water—you have loaded; that is, with what was brought, what was loaded, and what was taken up.
"Of little value" means of low price. "Merchandise" means goods.
Commentary on the Simile of the Dung-Carrying Woman, etc.
432. *Mama ca sūkarabhattan’ti*: “And this is my food, as it is for pigs. *Uggharantan’ti*: “Trickling out” means trickling upward.
*Paggharantan’ti*: “Dripping” means flowing downward. *Tumhe khvettha bhaṇetha’ti*: “Indeed, you yourselves should say here... [End of excerpt]
"Here, they say. Or rather, this is the reading itself. For it is said: "Indeed, this is my pig-food"—meaning, indeed, this excrement is food for pigs.
"He swallows every loss as it comes" means he swallows every pill of defeat as it arrives. "I shall overcome" means [the act of] overcoming.
“I will perform,” meaning “I will perform an offering. “We will play with dice” means we will play with sweets.
“Smeared with the highest potency” means smeared with poison of supreme power. 436.
“Village site” (gāmapaṭṭa) refers to a portion of land from which a village has been established. There is also a reading “village plot” (gāmapada); the meaning is the same.
*Saṇabhāraṃ*: a load of *saṇa* grass. *Susannaddho*: well-bound. *Tvaṃ pajānāhi*: you should know;
it means "if you wish to take it, then take it.
*Khomaṃ*: linen cloth. *Ayaṃ*: black iron. *Lohaṃ*: copper. *Sajjhaṃ*: silver. *Suvaṇṇaṃ*: a gold *māsaka* coin. *Abhinandiṃsu*: they rejoiced; they were satisfied.
437. *Attamano* means with one’s own mind pleased, with a contented heart. *Abhiraddho* means deeply confident.
*Pañhāpaṭibhānāni* means the arising of questions. *Paccanīkaṃ kattabbaṃ* means I thought it should be treated as something contrary or opposed;
the meaning is that he stood having taken a contrary position.
438. "They undergo destruction" means they undergo destruction, ruin, and death.

"Not of great fruit" means it does not become of great fruit by way of its resultant fruit (*vipākaphala*). "Not of great benefit" means it does not become of great benefit by way of the benefit of its qualities (*guṇānisaṃsa*).

"Not of great radiance" means it does not become of great radiance by way of the radiance of its power (*ānubhāvajuti*). "Not of great expansion" means it is not of great expansion by way of the expansion of its result (*vipākavipphāratā*).
It does not exist. "Seed and plough" means both seed and plough. "In a bad field" means in a field that is poor and devoid of essence.
"On bad ground" means on uneven terrain. "One would plant" means one would set it down.
"Rotten" means cut and broken. "Putrid" means devoid of essence. "Struck by wind and sun" means struck by wind and sun, their vitality exhausted.

"Taking what is without essence" means taking straw that is devoid of the essence of rice. "Not lying comfortably" refers to those [sheaves] which, having been dried and piled in a granary, are said to be "lying comfortably";
however, these are not like that. "One would pour down upon" means one would cause to enter;
it does not mean it would rain properly, but rather that it would not rain every half-month, every ten days, or every five days.

The meaning is this: "Api nu tāni" means: given that there are such defects in the field, the seed, and the rain, would those seeds attain upward growth by means of sprouts, roots, leaves, and so forth, downward development, and all-around abundance? "Evarūpo kho, rājañña, yañño" means:
O Prince, such a sacrifice—namely, such a gift—is [defective] because it is produced through the harming of others, and because of the donor and the recipient.
Because it is impure, it does not yield great fruit. "Such, O Rājanya,
is the sacrifice" means that such a gift by a Rājanya— due to the absence of injury to living beings on the part of the one who provides the requisites,

due to the absence of injury to living beings on the part of the donor himself, due to the donor being virtuous, and due to the recipient being endowed with qualities such as right view— is of great fruit.
...it occurs. However, if one receives a recipient who has emerged from cessation and possesses an abundance of virtues, and if the volition is vast, it yields its fruit in this very life.
439. Having heard this Dhamma talk of the Elder, King Pāyāsi invited the Elder for seven days.
Having given a great almsgiving to the Elder, he then established a practice of giving for the multitude from that time forward. With reference to this, it was said:
"Then Pāyāsi the prince," and so forth. In that context, *kaṇājaka* means rice mixed with broken grains, rice from which the husks have been removed.
*Bilaṅgadutiya* means accompanied by sour gruel (*kañjika*). *Dhorakāni ca vatthāni* means coarse garments. *Guḷavālakāni* means...
"Clumps of sugar" means large clumps of sugar situated in heaps. "In this way he points out" means he instructs in this manner. "Even with his foot" means even by means of his foot.
(440) "Without respect" refers to a gift given devoid of faith, a gift from one lacking confidence. "Not with his own hand" means not by means of his own hand. "Without honor" means devoid of honor;
it means he did not give after having manifested honor, nor having made his mind refined.
*Apaviddhaṃ* means discarded or fallen away. *Suññaṃ serīsakaṃ* means he approached a certain empty silver mansion called Serīsaka.
It is said that because there was a great sirīsa tree at its gate, it is called "Serīsaka. 441.
Regarding the venerable Gavaṃpati: it is said that in his previous human life, the elder was the eldest of a group of cowherd boys.

Having cleared the root of a great sirīsa tree and strewn it with sand, he seated a forest-dwelling elder (piṇḍapātika-thera) at the foot of the tree, gave him the food he had obtained himself, and passed away. By the power of that deed, he was reborn in that silver mansion.
A sirīsa tree stood at the door of the mansion; it bears fruit once every fifty years, and after that, [another] fifty...
"Many years have passed," [thinking thus], the young god (devaputta) was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega).
At a later time, having been reborn among humans during the era of our Blessed One, he heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma and attained Arahantship.
However, due to his former habit, he frequently went to that very same celestial mansion for his midday rest; it is said that it was pleasant for him in all seasons.
With reference to this, it was said: "At that time, the Venerable Gavampati," and so forth.
"Having given a gift with due care" means that he gave even another's property as a gift with due care.
"He announced thus" means he announced in the manner beginning with, "Give a gift with due care. And having heard that announcement from the Elder...
The great multitude, having given gifts with due respect, was reborn in the world of the devas.

However, the attendants of the nobleman Pāyāsi, although they gave gifts with due respect, went there out of attachment and were reborn in his very presence. It is said that this *disācārika-vimāna* (the wandering celestial mansion) was located in the Vaṭṭanī forest.
And one day, the deva-son Pāyāsi, having shown [himself] to the merchants... [his own...]
He related the account of the deed.
Thus ends the commentary on the Pāyāsi-rājañña-sutta in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya.
The commentary on the meaning of the Mahāvagga is completed.
The commentary on the Mahāvagga is finished.
